title: The Paper season two review – one of the best comedies on TV right now | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: This spin-off from the US Office is so brilliant that it might even eclipse its mother show. And as for the hilarious Sabrina Impacciatore – just hand her all the awards!
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: This spin-off from the US Office is so brilliant that it might even eclipse its mother show. And as for the hilarious Sabrina Impacciatore – just hand her all the awards!
Content: Wildly funny … Sabrina Impacciatore as Esmeralda in The Paper.Photograph: Peacock/SkyView image in fullscreenWildly funny … Sabrina Impacciatore as Esmeralda in The Paper.Photograph: Peacock/SkyTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewThe Paper season two review – one of the best comedies on TV right nowThis spin-off from the US Office is so brilliant that it might even eclipse its mother show.  And as for the hilarious Sabrina Impacciatore – just hand her all the awards!Stuart HeritageThu 10 Sep 2026 17.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePity the poor TV writer foolish enough to make a show about journalism. The world is full of inaccurate and illogical medical dramas, but they survive because real life doctors and nurses only tend to grumble about them to themselves. But when you make an inaccurate and illogical show about journalists, real life journalists get to yell about it from the streets. This is probablywhy Aaron Sorkin’s The Newsroom ended so early, because we all got to bleat about it through our little megaphones.The makers of The Paper must have been anticipating a similarly rough ride. It is, after all, explicitly a sitcom about the death of print media, and, Lord knows, nothing wounds us like staring the truth in the face. And yet last year’s first season emerged as one of the best new comedies on television.Technically, a spin-off from the American version of The Office, it centred around the reporters of the dwindling Toledo Truth Teller newspaper. Forced to share an office with a (much more successful) toilet paper company, its skeleton staff were made to either copy and paste wire stories on to its content management system, or write clickbait drivel. It was bleak but, you had to admit, at least it knew the state of things.Things turned around with the appointment of crusading new editor Ned Sampson ( Domhnall Gleeson), who strived to return the paper to its former glories. Last season ended on a moment of glory, with the paper winning a prestigious local award for journalism. As season two begins, it becomes clear that this did not change much.This is still very much a show about a struggling operation. A billboard bought to trumpet its success ends up reminding locals to cancel their subscriptions. An obituary of a beloved colleague goes off the rails when it becomes apparent that he had a comically dark secret life. Everyone gets annoyed by overzealous push notifications.The year of Domhnall Gleeson: ‘No one talks about actors’ dedication. But I had a perm for five months!’Read moreA show with such devotion to an issue – make no mistake, this is a love letter to journalism – always has the potential to come off as unpalatably worthy, but The Paper avoids this thanks to its absolutely stacked cast. Gleeson, in the lead role, has aLeslie Knope-ish can-do spiritthat sometimes overtakes him. Tim Key returns as a slightly villainous corporate strategist, although for some reason he only appears fitfully this time around. Lisa Gilroy makes a very strong first impression as an oversharing HR officer.But, really, the show belongs to Esmeralda Grand, played impeccably by Sabrina Impacciatore. Esmeralda feels like she’s been beamed in from another show entirely. While everything else about The Paper feels like a naturalistic workplace comedy, Impacciatore’s Esmerelda is big and broad and loud. She’s a whirlwind of pratfalls and gesticulations and wildly overcooked reaction shots. At one point this season she gets nailed into a crate. At another she dresses up as a teenage boy and beats up her own son. None of it should work, but somehow all of it does. There are, quite honestly, not enough awards in the world to give her.The Paper is also becoming a masterclass in the sort of will they/won’t they romantic storylines that tend to propel US sitcoms to the big leagues. The main one exists between Gleeson’s Ned and Chelsea Frei’s Mare, who shared a kiss in last year’s finale and now have to navigate a secret on-off relationship, but this time almost everyone in the cast finds themselves in the same situation. There are definitely two more will they/won’t theys, one of which comes about during an exceptional piece of physical comedy in a tornado, but there might even be more than that. It’s a lot to keep up with.But, if that’s overload, then so be it. You get the sense that this could be The Paper’s chance to become as big as its mother show, and the producers are throwing everything at the wall to get it there. By no means does the show have a guaranteed future – a recent interview with Gleeson hinted at the uncertainty of a third season – but a show like this deserves to come back year after year. A warm, funny workplace sitcom that actually has something to say is a rare thing indeed. It would be a terrible thing to see it go the way of local newspapers.The Paper was on Sky One and is on Now. In the US, it airs on Peacock. In Australia it airs on Binge and Foxtel.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionTV comedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Francophiles, Norman outfits and broken threads: visitors see Bayeux tapestry in UK for first time | Bayeux tapestry | The Guardian
description: Visitors got a first glimpse of the medieval artefact after it went on display at the British Museum in London
Author: Rachel Hall
Headline: Visitors got a first glimpse of the medieval artefact after it went on display at the British Museum in London
Content: 1:54Visitors delighted to see Bayeux tapestry on display in the UK for the first time – videoBayeux tapestryFrancophiles, Norman outfits and broken threads: visitors see Bayeux tapestry in UK for first timeVisitors got a first glimpse of the medieval artefact after it went on display at the British Museum in LondonRachel HallThu 10 Sep 2026 12.42 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 17.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the dayBayeux tapestrytickets were released, Megan Stockwell was at the beach. She was so determined to lock down her spot, that she sat with her toes in the sand for an hour, waiting in the online queue.“The whole ticket buying experience felt like what other people would do to get Taylor Swift tickets. I was like, ‘oh God, am I, like, the geek version of this?’” she recalled.View image in fullscreenMegan Stockwell outside the British Museum.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianLike any committed Swiftie, Stockwell felt confident the experience would be worth the hassle and cost. As a self-professed Francophile, she was fascinated by how the tapestry, which is temporarily housed at the British Museum until next July, tells the story of the Franco-British relationship through the Norman conquest, culminating in the battle of Hastings.“You just grow up learning so much about it – at primary school, in history studies. You’ve always got some mention of the Bayeux tapestry, the Normans, the fact there’s even three lions on the back of our pound coins comes from Normandy.“We’ve got such a close connection between French and British culture, our language and everything. This sort of feels like a visual representation of that,” she said.Stockwell’s dogged pursuit of tickets, fascination with the Franco-British relationship, and childhood memories of learning about the battle of Hastings, were experiences shared by many of the visitors on the exhibition’s opening day.Cydney, who lives in Texas, also drew inspiration from her experience queueing for concert tickets to secure a coveted opening day spot. She had woken up at 3am local time to join an online queue for an hour and half to secure them when they were released.Why the Bayeux tapestry and Franco-British relations are natural bedfellowsRead moreShe anticipated it would be worth it: “It’s going to be life-changing, we’re so excited.”View image in fullscreenCydney, who lives in Texas, said seeing the tapestry would be ‘life-changing’.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianCydney had studied history for her undergraduate degree. “So I just really am interested to see what a significant artefact would be and to see how this is basically where the history of England and the UK as we know it really all began. Seeing something so old is just incredible and honestly such an honour.”Her feelings were echoed by Adrian Harris, who was so moved to catch the exhibition that he signed up for British Museum membership purposely to gain early access to tickets. He ended up the second person through the doors on Thursday morning, after joining a “really jolly” queue at 9.30am.View image in fullscreenAdrian Harris.Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian“It was incredible. It was very, very moving to walk down the steps and to see the length and breadth of it. And I think they’ve done it so well, the British Museum. It was very profound to see it,” he said, adding he had been especially thrilled to spy Westminster Abbey, where he works, on the cloth.He noted that although he was one of the first through the doors, he felt that 40 minutes was a restricted timeframe to see the 68-metre tapestry, though he observed that attendants were diligent in ushering people along.A number of ticket holders for the Bayeux tapestry at a special first viewing last weekend were reportedly turned away after other visitors took too long to view it. The French owners of the tapestry have issued strict orders on when lights must be turned off in order to preserve the work.Richard and Madeleine Abramson, who were in the first group alongside visitors dressed in Norman costumes, agreed that 40 minutes was a short time, but that it was being well policed. “They’re very clear at the beginning there’s a maximum time … they’re very carefully moving you on,” said Madeleine.However, the oversight did not dampen the pair’s enthusiasm. “It was pretty awe-inspiring,” said Richard. “It’s very well presented, it develops like a film. It’s got a story to tell: it starts quietly, then it gets more intrigue and then you get to the action and it builds up to the battle, which is quite violent.”Madeleine felt the tapestry loomed large for many former English schoolchildren. “Of all the history lessons you have, every child remembers 1066,” she said, adding that the fact the tapestry was woven by female embroiderers also resonated. “[That they] told this whole story is still phenomenal,” she said.View image in fullscreenRichard and Madeleine Abramson said the exhibition was ‘pretty awe-inspiring’.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianVivien and Karen had travelled from Hampshire to see the tapestry, also buoyed up by memories of their school days. “We learned about it at school. It’s something that’s always been in the back of your mind, then all of a sudden it’s here, so why not?” said Karen.Vivien practises needlework, and was especially excited to witness the craftsmanship up close. “I’ll be looking for the two broken threads,” she said.Denise Davies had bought two tickets for her husband John’s birthday. As a taxi driver who also runs black cab heritage tours of London, he was looking forward to expanding his historical knowledge.At £33 a peak-time ticket, the exhibition’s cost has attracted some criticism – but Denise felt it was worth it.“I could go to Alton Towers and it would cost me an arm and a leg. This is something special. I would have paid whatever it was because we’re never going to see it again … it’s a tick on the bucket list, basically.”Explore more on these topicsBayeux tapestryFranceHistoryEuropeMuseumsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Forgetful Farage shares rose-tinted memories of Reform’s party conference | John Crace | The Guardian
description: Oops, Nige skipped over the most embarrassing and dark details – let’s set the record straight
Author: John Crace
Headline: Oops, Nige skipped over the most embarrassing and dark details – let’s set the record straight
Content: It was a stroke of genius for Nigel Farage to dismiss two of his oldest muckers as mere contractors in response to the latest Reform scandal.Photograph: Anthony Devlin/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIt was a stroke of genius for Nigel Farage to dismiss two of his oldest muckers as mere contractors in response to the latest Reform scandal.Photograph: Anthony Devlin/Getty ImagesThe politics sketchNigel FarageForgetful Farage shares rose-tinted memories of Reform’s party conferenceJohn CraceOops, Nige’s round-robin email skipped over the most embarrassing and dark details  – let’s set the record straightThu 10 Sep 2026 13.33 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 13.45 EDTShareWhich one of us has not dreamed of getting a personal email fromNigel Farage? So imagine the excitement that Reform supporters must have felt when a message from their leader dropped into their inboxes late on Wednesday night. And mine. Could he also be about to offer everyone in the country £5,000 in return for electing a Reform government?Sadly not. Even Honest Bob’s planned welfare cuts won’t cover that. Instead, Nige was treating us all to his reflections on his party conference that had just ended. The only drawback was that there appeared to be some gaps in his memory. Let’s be kind and assume he was pushed for space. So let’s help him fill in the blanks.Dear John. ‘Wow.’ That’s what I kept thinking as our conference closed.Good start, Nige. Because that’s what I was thinking too. It’s not every party conference that is completely derailed by an undercover investigation into allegations of illegal sources of party funding. And it came completely out of the blue. Who would have thought that a party leader under investigation over a £5m gift from a Thai crypto billionaire, and a party whose main funder is Ben Delo – who was convicted in the US for failing to comply with legislation against money laundering – might be implicated in possible wrongdoing?But we can all admire the sheer professionalism with which you handled the crisis. It was a stroke of genius to dismiss two of your oldest muckers as mere contractors. After all, Dan Jukes had only been your right-hand fixer for 10 years and James Orr, the Cambridge professor of ethics – nice touch that – was your head of policy. Of course it was all “loose pub talk”. Everyone goes to the pub to discuss how they plan to break the law. And you definitely “hadn’t been listening”. We could tell that by the way you appeared to join in the conversation. Such bad luck it’s all ended up in yet another police investigation. It’s obviously massively reassuring that you say you can’t be bought. But you can clearly be rented.6,000 of us packed in Birmingham’sNational Exhibition Centre.And may I say how pleasing it was that none of you felt you needed to come in a balaclava. What this country needs are patriots who are prepared to stand up and be counted. Who can be relied on to protest against the arrival of foreigners arriving by small boats. From now on, it will be Reform policy that the RNLI should be disbanded.We can’t have a country of volunteers who are prepared to jeopardise their own lives to save others. They are nothing less than traitors and send all the wrong messages to the rest of the world. I know I speak for everyone when I say that all Brits would rather drown than have one more foreigner step ashore in Portsmouth. I was also immensely proud to see so many in the audience at your conference speech who were willing to assault a female protester. Making England Great Again. Robert Jenrick nailed it when he said: “Boohoo.”We got Starmer out and are still neck and neck with Labour in the polls.Er, yes. That’s one way of putting it. Another is that you were at least eight points ahead of Labour only a few months ago. Your popularity may have peaked. The more people get to see of you the less they like you. It also seems that voters much prefer a leader who doesn’t require a minimum of £1m a year to get out of bed and a party that doesn’t seem to lurch from one financial scandal to the next.Zia Yusufand I will put the Royal Navy in the Channel and stop the boats.This is the Zia Yusuf who is so unpopular that everyone in your inner circle privately refers to him as “the wanker” and is so disliked that no constituency wants him to stand as their Reform candidate. Yet he insists on referring to himself as the “shadow home secretary” when he remains outside Westminster. But let’s indulge you. Let’s pretend that Zia is elected an MP. Do you really think the Royal Navy is going to participate in operations to turn back the small boats that could result in the deaths of dozens of migrants?You saw the odds-on nextprimeminister of France,Jordan Bardella, sign a historicmemorandum ofunderstanding with us to make this happen.Or the memorandum of misunderstanding as we prefer to call it. Still, it gave us a huge laugh to see you pull the wool over the “wet behind the ears” Jordan. It’s so good to see Reform turn over its political allies abroad. A reminder to Johnny Frenchman that when we left the EU it was to put some distance between us and him.It was a masterstroke to write the memorandum in both English and French, and sneakily adding a clause in English agreeing that France would take back all migrants who had arrived in England. And as Jordan’s English was not that good, he never noticed!Chapeau! Or perhaps he’s a bit thick. Either way, he’s a lot less odds-on to be the next prime minister because Marine Le Pen is furious with him and there’s an almighty row going on in the National Rally party.In our first 100 days,Richard Ticepledgedto cut £250 off your energy bill by scrapping the mad levies on them.No one thinks Dicky is going to do anything. Everyone inside the party thinks he is just an afternoon TV presenter from the 1980s. A man born to be your hype person. Who owes his entire existence to you. The same goes for Robert Jenrick and Suella Braverman. Politicians too mediocre even for the Tory party.It’s looking like we’ll need 10,000 candidates for the general and local elections. Recruiting that many candidates will be a mammoth task. So I need more of you than ever to step forward.It goes without saying that the 6,000 of you in Birmingham are already on the list. But we still need 4,000 more. So, please, I beg you, delete your Facebook and other social media accounts, where you might accidentally have liked something racist or spread idiotic conspiracy theories, and sign up. That includes you, Matt Goodwin. Your country needs you.Yours, Nigel FarageExplore more on these topicsNigel FarageThe politics sketchReform UKcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘I was on the loo when I got the news!’ Strictly Come Dancing’s new hosts spill their scandalous secrets | Television | The Guardian
description: After a year of frenzied conjecture, the new hosts putting the razzle back into Strictly are Johannes Radebe, Emma Willis and Josh Widdicombe. They talk night sweats, sparkly pants – and the hilarious fake show cooked up to fool the press
Author: Michael Hogan
Headline: After a year of frenzied conjecture, the new hosts putting the razzle back into Strictly are Johannes Radebe, Emma Willis and Josh Widdicombe. They talk night sweats, sparkly pants – and the hilarious fake show cooked up to fool the press
Content: Three to tango … Josh Widdicombe, Johannes Radebe and Emma Willis, the new Strictly hosts.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThree to tango … Josh Widdicombe, Johannes Radebe and Emma Willis, the new Strictly hosts.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianTelevision‘I was on the loo when I got the news!’ Strictly Come Dancing’s new hosts spill their scandalous secretsAfter a year of frenzied conjecture, the new hosts putting the razzle back into Strictly are Johannes Radebe, Emma Willis and Josh Widdicombe. They talk night sweats, sparkly pants – and the hilarious fake show cooked up to fool the pressMichael HoganThu 10 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 08.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohannes Radebe, one of the three new presenters ofStrictly Come Dancing, can barely contain his glee. Asked where they were when they heard they’d got the job, Radebe is quick to wind up his co-hosts. “We’ll never forget that call,” he grins. “It was a weekday afternoon and I was at home, preparing for that night’s performance of [West End musical] Kinky Boots. But go on, tell the Guardian where you two were.”“We all got the same message, asking us to jump on a Zoom,” says Emma Willis. “We didn’t know if it was good news or bad news.” Josh Widdicombe picks up the story: “I thought, ‘Surely they wouldn’t tell me to my face if I hadn’t got it? They’d just text my agent or something.’”Radebe prompts him: “So where did you take the Zoom call, Joshy?” “In a graveyard in Birmingham,” confesses Widdicombe. “I was on tour, killing time walking around, and needed to go somewhere quiet. There’s nowhere quieter than a cemetery. Just to be clear, I sat against a tree, not on a grave.”Willis’s whereabouts were equally awkward. “I was at the hairdressers with my head in the sink. The BBC said: ‘Is there anywhere private you can go?’ I said: ‘Well, either out on the street or in the toilet.’ And they were like, ‘Probably the toilet.’ So I was sat on the loo with wet hair when I got the news. Not using it, I hasten to add. Seat down.” A Birmingham graveyard and a salon toilet. Who says showbiz is all glitz, glamour and glitterballs?View image in fullscreen‘It’s a baptism of fire’… Radebe, Willis and Widdicombe in all new Strictly Come Dancing.Photograph: Guy Levy/BBC/PAWhen long-serving duo Tess Daly and Claudia Winklemanhung up their ballroom shoeslast Christmas, it sparked frenzied conjecture about who would be next to helm the BBC blockbuster. You would’ve got long odds on the combo of reality TV stalwart Willis, standup comic Widdicombe and South Africa-born professional dancer Radebe.“We were all in shock but had to keep it secret for another fortnight,” says Willis. “The only people we could talk to about it were each other, so we immediately set up a WhatsApp group.” It’s called “OMG”, named that fateful afternoon and unchanged since. “You should never change group chat names,” says Widdicombe. “They’re historic monuments.”The big decision came after cloak-and-dagger auditions and secret screen tests. “It was a long old process,” says Willis. “I felt like a kid waiting for Christmas. It went on forever.” “We all had separate meetings, then a week of chemistry tests,” says Widdicombe. “You had no idea where you were going or who you’d be auditioning with. You just had to get in a car, then be smuggled in to avoid any lurking paparazzi.”From a Gavin and Stacey star to Dani Dyer’s return: every Strictly Come Dancing 2026 contestant ratedRead moreThe BBC even concocted a fake show to throw people off the scent. “It was called The Great Garden Glow Up,” says Widdicombe. “A producer told me ‘We wanted a show that feasibly all the auditionees would host.’ I was like, ‘I wouldn’t fucking host that, mate!’ There’s no way me and Jojo are fronting The Great Garden Glow Up! Although I could imagine Emma being good. With Tom Allen, maybe.” Willis laughs: “You wouldn’t say that if you saw the state of my garden.”Auditions were set up as a rough approximation of Elstree Studios. “It was like a homemade Blue Peter version of Strictly,” says Willis. “There was a wallpapering table with judges behind it. On my day, it was Anton, Motsi and a couple of stand-ins.” “Shout-out to producer Joe” says Widdicombe. “He did the best Craig impression I’ve ever seen.” “My first chemistry test was actually with Jojo,” says Willis. “We must’ve done something right.”The pair once nearly graced the ballroom in a whole different capacity. “I’d wanted to be a contestant for years and almost was,” says Willis. “A few years ago, I did a dance trial which happened to be with Jojo. We boogied together. It didn’t come to fruition but we kept in touch. When he walked into the screen test that day, I was like, ‘Yes!’” “They saw Emma with Jojo and thought, ‘That’s two-thirds of the chemistry we need!’” jokes Widdicombe.View image in fullscreenThree is the magic number … Radebe, Willis and Widdicombe.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianTalking of which, why three hosts instead of the traditional two? As Willis recalls: “When we were called back in, the producers said, ‘This is a bit of a curveball but having watched all the screen tests, we want to try a trio.’ They’d never considered it before. The first time we tested together, they only had scripts for duos.”By this stage, all three badly wanted the job. As Radebe puts it: “When we left that last chemistry test, I went home, summoned all my ancestors, got down on my knees and prayed. I desperately wanted to do it with these two. But all was not lost because if it was a no, I could come back as a dancer. It’s tough walking away from that but don’t worry, I’ll definitely find ways of dancing. I still need to be in my Cuban heels. I negotiated that in my contract!” They extol the virtues of being a trio, rather than the widely expected duo. “It feels like we’re a gang,” says Widdicombe. “There’s no ego. We’re all in this together. It also means we’re not like-for-like replacements for Claudia and Tess. It’s a new way of presenting the show and easier to make it our own.”Press reports say the trio blew bosses away with their chemistry. Willis bats this off: “I keep hearing that and I’m like, ‘Settle down, we have to do this on telly as well.’ Our chemistry might be off the charts now but we’ll be shitting our pants for that first live show. I hear the theme music in my sleep and wake up sweating.”Pundits assumed that Willis would be anchoring proceedings on the ballroom floor, like Daly did, with Widdicombe occupying Winkleman’s berth on the balcony and Radebe in a roving reporter role. “I understand that speculation but it’s wide of the mark,” says Willis. “There’s no roving reporter, no fixed positions. A three rather than a two is a nice point of difference but the core of the show is the same as ever. It’s about the contestants, the dancing and fantastic multi-generational fun.”“I’m actually replacing Dave Arch as the leader of the band,” says Widdicombe. “That’s an exclusive. No, people just need to wait and see.”As the first Black presenter of the main show, it’s another milestone for serial trailblazer Radebe. “All my life, I’ve been first in everything that I did,” he says. “It’s the perfect way to celebrate becoming a British citizen this year.” Widdicombe is proud to be part of such a progressive programme. “Strictly is a force for good,” he says. “Whether it’s disability or same-sex couples, it’s brilliant to have such an inclusive show at the centre of Britain’s entertainment industry.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenDance floor it … Radebe, Willis and Widdicombe.Photograph: Guy Levy/BBC/PAThe trio know all eyes will be on them and are braced for the scrutiny. “We’re all coming to this as Strictly fans ourselves,” says Willis. “We’re there to enjoy it alongside the viewers, rather than change anything. There’s no new set. It will still look and feel like Strictly. If any TV show is an institution, it’s this one. We just want to keep the ball in the air and not let down something so beloved by the nation.” “I squeal every time you say that,” giggles Radebe.Willis and Widdicombe truly are superfans. Asking about their all-time favourite contestants provokes an in-depth debate. “I loved Abbey Clancy in 2013,” says Willis. “And Rose Ayling-Ellis was sensational five years ago.” Widdicombe chips in: “Although Johannes and John Whaite were terrific that year as well.” “Thank you, darling,” beams Radebe.Widdicombe’s love of the show was prompted by parenthood. “I used to be out gigging every weekend but since we had our first daughter in 2017, it’s been our family ritual on a Saturday night. I adored Bill Bailey, Chris McCausland and Hamza Yassin. On the flipside of the coin, I found Tony Adams incredibly inspiring.” “You just liked his sparkly pants,” teases Willis.Widdicombe may be a Strictly aficionado, but work commitments prevented him from watching last year’s series. “I was on tour, so I followed it via your Guardian liveblogs,” he says. “I’ve got to ask, will you still be doing Frockwatch? Comparing what the three of us are wearing each week? Please say yes. Jojo’s suddenly got something to play for.”When we meet, they’re fresh from pre-recording a supersize group dance to open the series – with the new hosts front and centre. “You’re in for a treat,” says Radebe. “Josh has already been on the dancefloor [he performed a Charleston in the 2024 Christmas special while dressed as a penguin] but Emma had her first taste of what the celebs go through, especially the nerves.”“It was a baptism of fire,” says Willis. “We were terrified but, within 10 minutes, we were having the time of our lives. It looked like the end of Grease, where everyone comes together for a dance routine. I’m living my childhood dreams.” “I loved how seriously you took it,” says Radebe. “Emma sent me a video last week of her practising in her backyard.”Did Widdicombe’s penguin pedigree stand him in good stead? “Jojo seems to find that question amusing, for some strange reason,” deadpans Widdicombe. “They’re very different dance disciplines. I had to turn off my Charleston brain and turn on … whichever dance we were doing.” All three dissolve into laughter.Following that razzle-dazzle group number, this year’s pairing-up process will take a new form. “Celebs and pros are coupling up live on the floor with more dance than ever,” says Widdicombe. “It’ll make a thrilling start to the series.” “It’s roulette meets the Instant Dance Challenge,” says Radebe. “I’m jealous I won’t be part of it.” In another departure from the previous era, expect these hosts to don fancy dress for theme weeks. “Try and stop us!” chorus Willis and Widdicombe. “I’ll be in heaven,” says Radebe.They’re due back in the ballroom, so it’s time for one last question. How will the new-look line-up gauge their success? “I suppose if we’re asked back next year,” says Willis. “Getting a second series is always a good measure.” “I won’t consider this a success until I win Frockwatch,” says Widdicombe. “It’ll be the biggest upset in TV history!”Strictly Come Dancing returns to BBC One and BBC iPlayer on Saturday 19 September.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionStrictly Come DancingJosh WiddicombefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I turned off my algorithm for 24 hours. Is this how social media used to be?  | Social media | The Guardian
description: Thanks to a little-known feature in Instagram, I try to travel back to 2012 – before everything on the internet was an ad
Author: Caitlin Cassidy
Headline: Thanks to a little-known feature in Instagram, I try to travel back to 2012 – before everything on the internet was an ad
Content: ‘For 24 hours, I decided to manually turn off my algorithm via little-known settings on Instagram to get a sense of how the reforms might change my feed,’ Caitlin Cassidy writes.Illustration: Guardian designView image in fullscreen‘For 24 hours, I decided to manually turn off my algorithm via little-known settings on Instagram to get a sense of how the reforms might change my feed,’ Caitlin Cassidy writes.Illustration: Guardian designSocial mediaI turned off my algorithm for 24 hours. Is this how social media used to be?Thanks to a little-known feature in Instagram, I try to travel back to 2012 – before everything on the internet was an adFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastCaitlin CassidyThu 10 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 20.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIhave a confession. I love my social media algorithm. It is a perfectly curated window into my insane and inquiring mind. It knows precisely which videos will tickle me and which memes will gently distract me from the slow collapse of humankind.Labor wants Australians to be able to opt out of online algorithms. How will it change your feed?Read moreOn Tuesday the Australian government announced “world-leading” reforms that wouldforce social media platformsto allow users to opt-out of algorithms, dubbed“my feed, my way”. On the same day, I was delighted to be confronted with a video on Instagram of a woman accidentally spilling a bucket of eels on a Chinese train. Dozens of eels slithered among the passengers, who appeared not as surprised as I would have expected.In bed that night, after sending the video to several friends and watching it multiple times, I lamented to my partner how I would find content like this if my accounts weren’t at the whim of the algorithm gods. “You can still search for eels,” he said. But would it be the same?So, for 24 hours, I decided to manually turn off my algorithm via little-known settings onInstagramto get a sense of how the reforms might change my feed. This feature allows you to limit your feed to posts from accounts you are following, in chronological order. This is basically what social media feeds, including Facebook, looked like when they started.Would I be thrust back into the old days of social media, to how things were before artificial intelligence andElon Muskbought Twitterand everything became an ad?View image in fullscreenCassidy restarts her algorithmPhotograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianAs a reminder of how things used to be, I scroll back to my first posts on Instagram and find sepia-heavy pictures of trees, gigs and friends. “The SKY,” says one, simply showing a sunset.I am gripped with nostalgia for 2012, when all my posts got eight likes and no comments and I only followed two dozen close friends from school.For a truly “authentic” social media experience, I trawl through my contacts and unfollow any account that isn’t a person I have met in real life. It is refreshing to unfollow news accounts, and politicians, but sad to let go of funny influencers and meme accounts and chefs.“Goodbye, Ottolenghi,” I think wistfully. “Farewell, woman from Dallas Cowboys cheerleaders.” In total, about 100 accounts get the axe. I refresh my feed, and it only takes about 10 minutes of scrolling to run out of content to look at.View image in fullscreenAnthony Albanese announces the digital duty of care draft law, which would allow Australians to opt out of algorithms used by social media companies.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPFor the first time in years, Instagram informs me I have reached the “End of following”. “There are no more posts from accounts that you follow from the past 30 days,” it says.I am floored and unmoored. Each time I refresh my feed for the next few hours, there is nothing new for me to mindlessly scroll. Instinctively, I keep clicking on the app but it’s futile. Is this how social media used to be? A tool to communicate with people rather than a way to remain constantly distracted?What disturbs me, though, scrolling through a feed that should theoretically be made up of friends and family updating me about nice moments in their lives, is that it still feels hollow and impersonal.Mostly, people are using it for self-promotion, whether it be posting about something they’ve published, projects they’ve done, brand partnerships or attempts to “go viral”. The only ones who seem to be using social media as it used to be are my mum and her friends, who still upload happy snaps with abandon. This is soothing but also very boring. And do I really need to know or care that someone I met backpacking in 2015 is appearing at an art festival in Amsterdam?View image in fullscreenCaitlin Cassidy’s algorithm.Photograph: Caitlin Cassidy/The GuardianDuring my lunch break, instead of hitting the apps, I read my book and look at my surroundings. It’s nice. Maybe the solution is not to opt out of algorithms but to opt out of social media altogether.The Orwellian machinery critics are desperate to protect is the algorithms, not laws that seek to reduce harm | Ed CoperRead moreThe justification for turning off algorithm-driven content makes sense. The federal government and many experts haveraised concernsabout how dangerous and divisive content can be pushed into people’s feeds, drawing them further and further into rabbit holes.I have watched on with concern as figures from the “manosphere”gain traction across the worldalongside the rise of far-right parties, and how thinness appears to be the new norm in Hollywood, witheating disorder content proliferatingon X, TikTok and Instagram.Thankfully, this has not been my social media experience. According to Instagram’s AI summary of my algorithm, a little-known feature of the app, I enjoy “community events” and “saving furry friends”, with a particular penchant for content related to the “Sydney food scene” and, somewhat vaguely, “Australia” (click on the reels icon and then the double-heart symbol in the top-right corner to see yours).My “For You” page is a haphazard collection of animals, food and gossip about reality TV. The top posts are an old man who summarises the latest episodes of Below Deck Mediterranean, a dachshund being pet with a spatula and someone making a cake with the face of Edward Cullen. It knows me so well!But is this healthy? Do I really need to spend my time watching AI-generated dogs dancing in the shower, or marvelling at a man attempting to eat an extremely gigantic cone of soft-serve ice-cream? After 24 hours switching off, my conclusion? It’s numbing my brain and turning my own thoughts into slop.Explore more on these topicsSocial mediaInstagramFacebookAustralian politicsMetafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Don’t sashay away! The BBC’s decision to cancel Ru Paul’s Drag Race UK is sickening in all the wrong ways | Television | The Guardian
description: The hyper-flamboyant and hilariously filthy show is an inclusive, celebratory platform for queer culture. The broadcaster’s choice to nix it is giving stupidity
Author: Alex Needham
Headline: The hyper-flamboyant and hilariously filthy show is an inclusive, celebratory platform for queer culture. The broadcaster’s choice to nix it is giving stupidity
Content: Werking hard … a full cast of resplendent queens on RuPaul’s Drag Race UK, series seven.Photograph: BBC/World of Wonder/Guy LevyView image in fullscreenWerking hard … a full cast of resplendent queens on RuPaul’s Drag Race UK, series seven.Photograph: BBC/World of Wonder/Guy LevyTelevisionDon’t sashay away! The BBC’s decision to cancel Ru Paul’s Drag Race UK is sickening in all the wrong waysThe hyper-flamboyant and hilariously filthy show is an inclusive, celebratory platform for queer culture. The broadcaster’s choice to nix it is giving stupidityAlex NeedhamThu 10 Sep 2026 11.25 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 12.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe BBC is canning RuPaul’s Drag Race UK – a decision that, in my household, will bring the number of regularly watched programmes on the Beeb down from one to zero. It’s a decision that will no doubt please enemies of LGBTQ+ culture, but otherwise seems inexplicable. For a start, Drag Race UK regularly pulls in 1 million viewers a week, which hardly seems like a show in its death throes (even if this is down from a previous high of 1.5 million).RuPaul’s Drag Race is also a bona fide cultural phenomenon. Since the US version started in 2009, it has brought tons of performers to national, or even global, attention who would otherwise still be plying their trade in provincial gay bars. Jinkx Monsoon from the US is now starring in Oh Mary! in London’s West End; the UK’s La Voix made it on to Strictly; and Bimini Bon-Boulash, who “stepped their pussy up” to astonishing effect in season two, has made records, modelled and written a book.View image in fullscreenSeries seven’s judges: Michelle Visage, RuPaul, Joel Dommett and Alan Carr.Photograph: BBC/World of WonderMore importantly, the show gave a TV platform to ballroom culture – the New York City-born tradition in which impoverished, young, largely Black and brown gay men and trans women, usually ostracised by their families, formed their own “houses” and transformed themselves into the glamorous characters they dreamed of being. Ballroom culture gave the world vogueing, the documentary Paris is Burning, and a whole argot which, more than 30 years on from its popularisation in the film, is mainstream. “It’s giving”, “she’s serving”, “throwing shade”, “spilling the tea”, looking “snatched”. We’ll never know what the queens who invented this lingo would think of its incredible resilience, since they perished in the Aids crisis.View image in fullscreenDelightfully random … Nyongbella.Photograph: BBC/World of WonderRuPaul’s Drag Race UK fused this underground culture with Britain’s venerable drag tradition to often hilarious effect. Who could forget characters like the acid-tongued, high fashion queen A’Whora from season two, whose comedy routine was so filthy it managed to make judge Alan Carr wince? Or Cheddar Gorgeous, the historically minded and hugely articulate queen from season four, whose Act Up themed costume I last spotted on display in Manchester’s Whitworth gallery? Or even Nyongbella from season seven, delightfully random and usually almost naked, strutting her stuff on the BBC in defiance of her disapproving relatives in Cameroon, where gay sex can get you a five-year jail sentence? In what other context would such characters have made it on to the BBC?That’s not to mention the amazingly high-profile celebrity guests (Andrew Garfield, Mel B and Michaela Coel have all served), and the always-fabulous judges Michelle Visage, Graham Norton and Carr. There is also, of course, the positive impact on scared young LGBTQ+ people on seeing out gay and trans folk living their best lives on screen, working – or ratherwerking– hard and being unapologetically themselves. Isn’t that something worth preserving?Along with the girl group challenges, Snatch Game episodes and spectacular looks, Drag Race UK has seen its contestants discuss their experiences of being non-binary or living with HIV. And while, as a cynical Briton, I often cringe at the climactic moment when the queens who make it to the final talk tearfully to pictures of themselves as children, it’s a reminder that self-acceptance is something many LGBTQ+ people still struggle to achieve, especially in the midst of the current global backlash against our hard-won rights.View image in fullscreenSeries eight’s KY Kelly and Naya Thorn.Photograph: BBC/World of Wonder/Guy LevyPrudes and homophobes might say that BBC licence-payers don’t want to pay for a bunch of drag queens telling filthy jokes and bitching about one another on the small screen. Well, I also pay the TV licence fee and I do. It doesn’t seem much to ask that, as a gay person, I get one programme on iPlayer that is unabashedly queer – especially since the BBC also canned I Kissed a Boy andI Kissed a Girlfor bad measure. As the arts editor of the Guardian, I guess I could watch the BBC’s amazing slate of arts programmes – were it not for the fact that most of them have also long been chopped.Drag Race UK has an ardent fanbase of all backgrounds and generations. Of course, not everyone in the LGBTQ+ community likes it – Travis Alabanza’s play The Sound of the Underground entertainingly railed against it – but it has expanded its definition of drag considerably, featuring trans and one female performer among the legions of cis gay men. A contestant in season one even had a girlfriend at the time – and if that’s not inclusion, what is? BBC, RuPaul’s Drag Race UK should not be allowed to sashay away.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionRuPaulfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ministers face backlash from hospitality industry over ‘tourist tax’ plans | Travel & leisure | The Guardian
description: Many mayors welcome power to impose tourist tax but industry warns of ‘irreparable harm’ and job losses
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Many mayors welcome power to impose tourist tax but industry warns of ‘irreparable harm’ and job losses
Content: Lyme Regis beach in Dorset. The overnight visitor levy will potentially generate tens of millions of pounds to be spent in local areas.Photograph: Imgorthand/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLyme Regis beach in Dorset. The overnight visitor levy will potentially generate tens of millions of pounds to be spent in local areas.Photograph: Imgorthand/Getty ImagesTravel & leisureMinisters face backlash from hospitality industry over ‘tourist tax’ plansMany mayors welcome power to impose tourist tax but industry warns of ‘irreparable harm’ and job lossesKiran Stacey,Josh Halliday,Alexandra ToppingandRob DaviesThu 10 Sep 2026 14.14 EDTFirst published on Thu 10 Sep 2026 04.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMinisters are facing a backlash from the hospitality industry after they announced mayors inEnglandwould be given sweeping powers to levy taxes on holiday accommodation such as hotels and Airbnbs.The plan, presented on Thursday byAngela Rayner, the local government secretary, will allow mayors to impose a “tourist tax” without a cap on how much they can charge and with few controls on how they can spend it.The move, which gives mayors some of their most significant tax-raising powers, was welcomed by regional leaders, who said it would give them a vital revenue stream at a time when local government is facing a funding crisis. Mayors will be expected to lay out their detailed plans for how they plan to use the new powers in early 2028.The hospitality industry fears a tourist tax will deter visitors – the evidence says otherwiseRead moreBut it was met with outrage from hospitality businesses, who had expected the government to put stricter conditions on how much mayors could charge and how the money would be used.UKHospitality, the industry’s trade body, said a 5% overnight levy across England could result in 33,000 job losses and a £2bn hit to the economy, with regions more reliant on tourism, such as the Lake District, being worst affected.The owner of Premier Inn, Britain’s biggest hotel chain, said it would be “hugely damaging” and urged ministers to “avoid inflicting what could be irreparable harm on this large and vital sector of the economy”.Eddie Nelder, a co-owner of the ChoiceHotelschain, which has hotels in Blackpool and the Lake District, said: “We’re here trying to stay alive, waiting for a lifeline from the government and we get another hammer blow. It feels like we’re being strangled.”View image in fullscreenA Blackpool hotel owner said the taxes were ‘another hammer blow’ for the hospitality industry.Photograph: Pawel Libera/LightRocket/Getty ImagesHowever, Rayner said the tax-raising powers would help fund local communities. “This measure will give mayors the choice to raise and reinvest funding where it’s needed most,” she said in a statement before a meeting with the country’s mayors at No 10 North in Manchester.“It’ll help support the local services, public spaces and attractions that both residents and visitors rely on, with decisions taken by people who know their area best.”In the immediate term, the rate will be set at no more than 5% in almost every major English city after everyLabourmetro mayor agreed to cap their charges at that level.In a joint letter to Rayner, they wrote: “Foreign cities visited by British tourists from New York to Paris, as well as hundreds of smaller cities across the world, have long benefited from such levies while continuing to grow their tourism sectors. Granting the power to regions to introduce levies will help level the playing field by ensuring further investment in our cities, contributing to further growth.”But large parts of the east coast will not have to pay the tax after their mayors – two Reform UK and one Conservative – said they would refuse to impose them.The move follows a consultation launched by Keir Starmer’s government, and will bring England into line with many European countries and the US, where holidaymakers have for years been paying overnight visitor levies.Similar levies also apply in Wales and Scotland, though they will be capped in Wales.Edinburgh became the first city in Scotland to introduce a tourist tax, setting it at 5% in July. In Wales, councils will have the power to charge £1.30 per person a night in tax for most accommodation from April 2027.Under the proposal, which is expected to be introduced as a bill in parliament within months, mayors will be allowed to charge a levy as a percentage of the price of an overnight stay, rather than as a flat fee.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe mayor of north-east England, Kim McGuinness, said the tax could bring money into the region during events such as the Great North Run.Photograph: DEW/AlamyMinisters at Westminster will cap the number of nights to which it can be applied in order to avoid hitting long-term rental properties. It is understood the cap is likely to be higher than the 5% that is applied by Holyrood.Any commercially rented property will face the tax, though there will be an exemption for those that are only rented occasionally on a casual basis.Mayors will be allowed to decide whether or not to exempt other sites such as festival campsites. They will also be allowed to share revenues with local councils.Kim McGuinness, the mayor of north-east England, backed the move for a visitor levy, saying it could bring money to the local economy during events such as the Great North Run, which is due to take place this Sunday.“A visitor levy could help us bring major international events to our region, back local businesses, improve visitor attractions, build on the 90,000 jobs already in this sector and unlock opportunities that come from a thriving visitor economy,” she said.“Most importantly, the money raised here would stay here, helping us invest in the future of our region rather than waiting for Whitehall to do it for us.”The move is one of the biggest handovers of power from the Treasury to local leaders in years, and comes before the first budget of Andy Burnham’s government, at which ministers have promised to hand over more tax powers to local leaders.It comes at a time when many local authorities are struggling for funds. Last year the government gaveemergency fundingworth £1.3bn to a record 28 councils, without which several said they would have gone bankrupt.But it also comes after a concerted effort by the government to ease the pressure on the hospitality industry, with many businesses struggling with high inflation and increased national insurance and minimum wage bills.Earlier this summer, the former chancellorslashed VATon British summer holiday destinations, in a programme she called the “Great British summer savings scheme”.Meanwhile, in one of his first acts as prime minister, Burnham announced he wouldcut business ratesfor pubs, clubs and live music venues.Many hospitality businesses are struggling with high inflation, as well as additional national insurance and minimum wage costs imposed by Reeves in her first budget.Allen Simpson, the chief executive of UKHospitality, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “What we’re talking about here is an open-ended power for mayors to set tourism taxes at any level they want … If you go to Paris, if you go to Rome, if you go to Berlin, you’re paying a small tourism tax, but it’s capped.”Additional reporting by Raphael BoydExplore more on these topicsTravel & leisureHospitality industryHotelsAirbnbTax and spendingAngela RaynerDevolutionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Secret systems used by Israel in mass killings of Gaza civilians revealed in new film | Israel | The Guardian
description: Testimony from Israeli military insiders involved in surveillance and remote killings features in documentary produced by the Guardian
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Testimony from Israeli military insiders involved in surveillance and remote killings features in documentary produced by the Guardian
Content: A scene from NAZA, a documentary produced by the Guardian and directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.Photograph: The GuardianView image in fullscreenA scene from NAZA, a documentary produced by the Guardian and directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.Photograph: The GuardianIsraelSecret systems used by Israel in mass killings of Gaza civilians revealed in new filmTestimony from Israeli military insiders involved in surveillance and remote killings features in documentary produced by the GuardianEmma Graham-Harrisonin Jerusalem andXan Brooksin VeniceThu 10 Sep 2026 09.42 EDTFirst published on Thu 10 Sep 2026 07.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTestimony from 24 Israeli military insiders ​on the secret ​systems used in ​the war on Gaza​ has been revealed in a new documentary film about the mass killing of Palestinian civilians.NAZA, a film from the Oscar-winning Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, was shown at theVenice international film festivalon Thursday as the only documentary competing for its prestigious Golden Lion award.The film’s title comes from an Israeli military acronym used euphemistically to refer to civilians expected to be killed in a military attack.Produced by the Guardian, it features extensive testimony from Israeli intelligence officers and soldiers involved in the surveillance and remote killing of Palestinian civilians.Interviews were filmed at night on rooftops in Tel Aviv, on the condition of anonymity because of the risks involved in speaking publicly about Israel’s war activities. The appearance and voices of participants in the film were digitally altered to disguise their identities.The interviewees detail the secret methods used by the Israeli military inGaza, including AI-based systems built to identify large numbers of potential low-ranking Hamas targets, who were then bombed in their homes at night, in the knowledge attacks would also kill their families.View image in fullscreenIsraeli soldiers at a military position overlooking the so-called yellow line in Gaza in May.Photograph: Ariel Schalit/APThe Israeli military hacked into phones to identify the location of such targets, and covertly listened into conversations with their wives and children moments before they were all killed.The film also features first-person accounts about the destruction of neighbourhoods where the Israeli military estimated that up to 25% of residents were still sheltering in their homes, the systematic burning of civilian homes, and the killing of civilians at a food distribution site.Abraham said at a press conference in Venice on Thursday: “We just told these officers: ‘Please describe to us what you did. How do these systems work? Sketch it out for us.’ Sometimes, in just asking the questions, you get the answers.“Some of them did not express remorse and some did. Some spoke out of indifference, some out of pride.”View image in fullscreenThe film’s directors, Rachel Szor and Yuval Abhram (centre), with producers and crew members at the Venice film festival on Thursday.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersSeveral interviewees worked in a secret intelligence unit that reports directly to the office of Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu; one said their mission was to “thwart peace”.“We made this film out of a sense of obligation to use our position as Israeli film-makers and journalists to examine the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians for which our country is responsible,” Abraham and Szor said in their directors’ statement.The directors stressed the film’s focus was not on “sporadic war crimes committed by rogue soldiers”. “It is on the orders themselves, the policies, the accepted practices, the language and logic that make those practices possible, and the people who operate within them,” they said. “The system and its cogs.”View image in fullscreenAn explosion after an Israeli airstrike in Gaza City on Wednesday.Photograph: Jehad Alshrafi/APThe documentary was co-produced by James Wilson and executive produced by Jonathan Glazer, the same team behind the Oscar-winning film The Zone of Interest.The film received a nearly 25-minute standing ovation after its screening, according to Variety, which called it a record for length of applause not just at Venice but at any major film festival and reported that Glazer embraced Abraham and Szor as it went on, while some members of the audience held up Palestinian flags.NAZA builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and the Guardian between 2023 and 2025. It was filmed and produced under tight security because of the risk to confidential journalistic sources, and its contents have remained a closely guarded secret before Thursday’s premiere.Paul Lewis, the Guardian’s head of investigations and an executive producer on the film, described NAZA as the culmination of “years of painstaking work to uncover and verify the systems used by Israeli military intelligence in Gaza”.Abraham said making the documentary had provided space to explore the collective impact of that work. “In this film we’re talking to 24 people. We are looking at systems of mass killing. There is something about cinema that allows you to explore structures and systems and how you put things together.”Before the premiere, Alberto Barbera, the Venice film festival’s artistic director, told journalists NAZA would be “truly groundbreaking”, calling it “a politically disruptive and cinematically extremely interesting work”.“It’s not just any collection of interviews,” Italy’s Cinecittà News quoted Barbera as saying. “It took them three years to convince these Israeli intelligence and military officials to share the work they did when the invasion of Gaza began, and I assure you, their testimonies are shocking.”NAZA review – Israeli intelligence officers cast chilling light on civilian deathsRead moreIsraeli attacks in Gaza since 2023 have killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, the majority of them civilians, and injured more than 174,000 others, together representing more than 10% of Gaza’s prewar population.Israeli restrictions on food shipments created a man-made famine last summer, and the Israeli military razed or damaged more than three-quarters of homes, so surviving Palestinians are now crowded into tent camps with little access to clean water or sanitation.Israel launched its war after the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, when more than 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken to Gaza by militants. The majority of the dead and hostages were civilians.Abraham and Szor were two of the four co-directors of No Other Land, whichwon the Oscar for best documentary in 2025.Drawing a connection between the two films, the directors said: “In the film No Other Land, we spent five years, together with [Palestinian co-directors] Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal, documenting the army destroying Palestinian homes in order to paint a larger picture of a system of occupation and ethnic supremacy aimed at the removal of Palestinians from the West Bank.“In NAZA, we are similarly connecting the dots of a system, gathering the testimonies of two dozen intelligence officers and soldiers and depicting the military systems used to perpetrate what a UN commission and the world’s leading human rights groups have described as a genocide.”Explore more on these topicsIsraelGazaVenice film festivalDocumentary filmsIsrael-Gaza warPalestineMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Canada offers air defense support for Ukraine as Zelenskyy visits | Canada | The Guardian
description: Canadian PM Mark Carney hosts president in Calgary, where he grew up alongside large Ukrainian community
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Canadian PM Mark Carney hosts president in Calgary, where he grew up alongside large Ukrainian community
Content: Mark Carney and Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrive in Calgary, Alberta, to sign agreements on Thursday.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenMark Carney and Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrive in Calgary, Alberta, to sign agreements on Thursday.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockCanadaCanada offers air defense support for Ukraine as Zelenskyy visitsCanadian PM Mark Carney hosts president in Calgary, where he grew up alongside large Ukrainian communityAgence France-PresseThu 10 Sep 2026 16.35 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 16.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCanada offered support on Thursday to boost Ukraine’s air defenses and help replenish its drone stocks, as the countries pledged to deepen their alliance during a visit byVolodymyr Zelenskyy.Mark Carney hosted the president of Ukraine in Calgary in the western province of Alberta, where the Canadian prime minister grew up among a large community of people with Ukrainian heritage.“Canada will always be with you,” Carney assured Zelenskyy.The leaders signed an agreement to work toward a “hundred-year partnership”.That deal, to be negotiated over the coming months, aims to codify cooperation in a range of areas, including defense, critical minerals and energy.“Our two nations have been connected since 1893,” Carney said, referring to a wave of Ukrainians who migrated to the new Canadian nation.In Alberta, there are an estimated 350,000 Canadians of Ukrainian descent.“Ukrainians helped build Canada and Canadians will help rebuildUkraine,” Carney said.The support announced on Thursday includes C$350m (US$253m) provided through the United States’ Joint Ukraine Multinational Program – Services, Training and Articles Rapid Timeline (Jumpstart) program.Zelenskyy has emphasized the need for increased air defense as Russia ramps up ballistic missile attacks.Carney said Canada was also offering C$450m in loan guarantees to enhance the Ukrainian energy supply.The funds will help repair damaged infrastructure, increase storage capacity and improve power supply to hospitals.Carney said the goal of the energy support was “to help Ukrainians get through the winter”, a difficult period when the country endures rolling blackouts amid often frigid temperatures.Canada is moving aggressively to increase its own drone stocks, Carney said, announcing a deal that will see 30% of new Canadian production head to Ukraine.Zelenskyy told reporters that “these drones will go to Ukraine immediately to [the] battlefield, immediately to our people, our soldiers … to save our children, our families first of all.”Asked about potential negotiations to ease the fighting, Zelenskyy said he did not anticipate any substantive talks during Russia’s ongoing election period.But he said he planned to meet Donald Trump in New York City in late September, probably on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, with Washington bidding to revive long-stalled talks to end the war.“But at the end of September, we will have an opportunity to meet, I think, with the American team in New York,” Zelenskyy said.“And I think that … I can be more open after the New York meeting with President Trump.”After the Calgary meeting, Zelenskyy was headed to Banff, a stunning Canadian national park, where he will address a cabinet retreat for Carney’s liberal government.He then heads to Canada’s largest city, Toronto, and North Bay in northern Ontario.Explore more on these topicsCanadaUkraineVolodymyr ZelenskyyMark CarneyAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: New battery-powered trains will ‘bring faster journeys to north’ | Rail transport | The Guardian
description: No 10 says 29 new trains to be built in Derby will support 350 local jobs, as well as nearly 6,000 across the UK
Author: Raphael Boyd
Headline: No 10 says 29 new trains to be built in Derby will support 350 local jobs, as well as nearly 6,000 across the UK
Content: Andy Burnham during a visit to Alstom transport in Derby, where the new trains will be built.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham during a visit to Alstom transport in Derby, where the new trains will be built.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.Rail transportNew battery-powered trains will ‘bring faster journeys to north’No 10 says 29 new trains to be built in Derby will support 350 local jobs, as well as nearly 6,000 across the UKRaphael BoydThu 10 Sep 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 17.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNo 10 has announced the construction of a new fleet of battery-powered trains that will “bring faster, more reliable journeys to the north”.The 29 new trains, which will be run by TransPennine Express, are set to be built in Alstom’s Litchurch Lane works in Derby from 2028, which the government says will support 350 local jobs, as well as nearly 6,000 across the UK.The new fleet will be made up of Adessia Stream trains, a battery-powered model that will be the first of its kind to be used for long-distance mainline journeys in the UK when it enters service in 2034.Prime ministerAndy Burnham, who uses trains regularly to move between London and Manchester, highlighted the need for more reliable and efficient services, with the new trains pitched as making journeys between major northern cities shorter while increasing capacity on rail networks by 30% in the next decade.Burnham said: “I’ve lost count of the number of times someone has stopped me to tell me about the train that never came. And when that happens, it means missed shifts, missed appointments and missed opportunities.“Today that starts to change. These 29 new trains will bring faster, more reliable journeys to the north, and thousands of British jobs for the next generation.“It’s exactly what Great British Railways is all about – taking back control of the basics and getting Britain believing again.”As well as speed and capacity, the new trains are set to run without emissions even on non-electrified stretches of the network, while also having more accessible step-free boarding and onboard wifi.Transport secretary Heidi Alexander also praised the announcement, calling it a sign of how Great British Railways “will deliver better journeys for people while backing British business” and allowing passengers to “wave goodbye to overcrowded, delayed diesel trains and step onboard faster electric trains which are fit for the future”.Explore more on these topicsRail transportRail industryTransportAndy BurnhamManchesterLeedsnewsShareReuse this content

title: More Anthropic researchers warn of AI’s perils as Musk terms fears a ‘psyop’ | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Insiders at the firm fear tech’s advancement could cause human extinction while others are calling it a ‘setup’
Author: Johana Bhuiyan
Headline: Insiders at the firm fear tech’s advancement could cause human extinction while others are calling it a ‘setup’
Content: Stickers for Claude software on an attendees laptop at Claude developer conference in London, on Tuesday, 19 May 2026.Photograph: Chris Ratcliffe/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenStickers for Claude software on an attendees laptop at Claude developer conference in London, on Tuesday, 19 May 2026.Photograph: Chris Ratcliffe/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)More Anthropic researchers warn of AI’s perils as Musk terms fears a ‘psyop’Insiders at the firm fear tech’s advancement could cause human extinction while others are calling it a ‘setup’Johana BhuiyanThu 10 Sep 2026 17.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA day after a former researcher atAnthropicmade an apocalyptic declaration about artificial intelligence, more researchers and staff members at the AI startup publicly agreed with him and posted their own dire warnings.In response, Elon Musk and other conservative figures on X, formerly Twitter, called the chorus of concerns a “setup” and a “psyop”.The Anthropic insiders fear the technology they are building could become so advanced and dangerous as to cause human extinction within the decade, and they assert many of their colleagues feel the same but haven’t said so publicly.These researchers and staff are posting in response to a now-viral thread from Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who said on Wednesday he was resigning from the company because neither Anthropic nor its competitor OpenAI, also his former employer, were building AI models responsibly and are “gambling with our lives”.OpenAI not on track to reduce risk of ‘catastrophic’ loss of control, says board memberRead moreAnna Wang, who works on Artificial General Intelligence Safety at Anthropic and previously worked at Google’s DeepMind, said Thursday that many people at Anthropic want to slow down development to come up with a plan to mitigate the risks that could come with these AI models.“There is not yet a viable scientific plan to solve risks from recursively self-improving AI,” Wang wrote on X.Drake Thomas, another Anthropic employee, said that he respected Coxon’s choice to abstain from building these models if he worries they could pose planet-scale risks.“Things are moving way too fast, we don’t have anywhere near the degree of assurance we’ll want for ASI [artificial superintelligence],” Thomas said.Musk took a more adversarial stance. “Seems like a setup,” hewrote.Coxon replied to the world’s richest man with a selfie, writing, “I’m real and these are my real beliefs. You could ask your xAI researchers about me if you hadn’t fired them.”In a statement to the Guardian, an Anthropic spokesperson defended the company’s strategy. “We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks. To address these risks, we continue to build models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry,” the statement said.Musk and others with a more positive view of AI have started to spread theories that Coxon’s post and the resulting fallout are part of a “psyop” to negatively influence the public’s feelings about AI.“I think the groundwork for this psy op (for lack of a better term) has been prepared for a long time,” Musk posted on X. “This was just the match that lit the fire.”Musk was responding to a post by Parker Thayer, a researcher at conservativethinktank Capital Research, in which he floated a theory with little evidence that Coxon’s post was the start of a “VERY sophisticated and well-funded PR operation to get support for Democrats to regulate AI into oblivion”. Other notable figures took notice.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBill Ackman, the billionaire CEO of the hedge fund Pershing Square, also quoted Thayer’s post, simply saying “Interesting.”Other Anthropic employees had posted their agreement with Coxon shortly after he declared his resignation on Wednesday.“AI developers believe their technology could cause human extinction (or similarly bad outcomes),” wrote Samuel Marks, who works on safety research at Anthropic. “This could happen in the next few years. In general, the more senior the employee, the more concerned they are.”Evan Hubinger, who describes himself as a lead in the company’s alignment division, which works on ensuring Anthropic’s AI models function in line with human goals, said Coxon was “correct” and that the industry was falling behind in attempts to deal with the apocalyptic potential.“We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Hubingerwrote. “I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.It’s not exactly clear how Coxon and others expect AI models to usher in the demise of humanity. Some experts doubt that the technology will become so intelligent as to cause the apocalypse. Gary Marcus, a scientist and leading voice in AI, said that it’s time to boycott AI, but because it’s already causing harm.More than extinction, Marcus said he worried about the “risk of catastrophe” from “from AI-generated pathogens, from wars started or escalated by AI-generated disinformation, from hacks that destroy critical infrastructure, and so on. Nothing I have seen gives any indication that any of that is under control”.The same day, Anthropic released a report documenting how the company dismantled an operation attempting to build a biological weapon using its AI models.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)AnthropicnewsShareReuse this content

title: Global bond sell-off resumes as surging oil prices stoke fears about inflation | Bonds | The Guardian
description: Crude jumps above $107 a barrel amid concerns over Middle East conflict and out-of-control government borrowing
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Crude jumps above $107 a barrel amid concerns over Middle East conflict and out-of-control government borrowing
Content: Surging oil prices caused by intensifying tensions in the Middle East have fuelled inflation concerns across markets including South Korea.Photograph: YONHAP/EPAView image in fullscreenSurging oil prices caused by intensifying tensions in the Middle East have fuelled inflation concerns across markets including South Korea.Photograph: YONHAP/EPABondsGlobal bond sell-off resumes as surging oil prices stoke fears about inflationCrude jumps above $107 a barrel amid concerns over Middle East conflict and out-of-control government borrowingHeather StewartandPhillip InmanThu 10 Sep 2026 14.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNervous investors across big economies have been dumping government bonds, driving up the cost of borrowing, as surging oil prices amplified fears about rising inflation.The cost of a barrel of oil jumped 6% to above $107 on Thursday amid concerns thatadvances by Houthi rebelsalong the Red Sea coast in Yemen could choke off Saudi crude exports.The global bond sell-off that has rocked markets in recent weeks resumed in response to the news from the Middle East – which came against a backdrop of escalating concern about out-of-control government borrowing.Higher oil prices, which had already climbed since hostilities resumed in the Iran war, are expected to drive up inflation, prompting central banks to raise interest rates and putting the brakes on economic growth.A line graph showing yields on UK, US, Japanese and German 10-year government bonds since 2000Donald Trump suggested on Wednesday that the conflict with Iran could continue until “immediately after” November’s US midterm elections, at which point he claimed oil prices would be “tumbling downward”.The European Central Bank (ECB)raised its main interest rate to 2.5% on Thursday, with its president, Christine Lagarde, saying: “We believe inflation will be longer lasting than we had anticipated.”“The conflict in the Middle ​East continues ​to ⁠generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to ​remain well above target for ​an ⁠extended period,” she added.View image in fullscreenThe ECB president, Christine Lagarde, said eurozone inflation would remain above the central bank’s target for longer than expected.Photograph: Filip Singer/EPAAs Thursday’s sell-off gathered pace in London, the yield, or interest rate, on 10-year UK government bonds surged above 5.37% – the highest cost of borrowing since 2007 – creating a fresh headache for the new chancellor, John Healey.With less than seven weeks to go until Healey’s first budget on 28 October, higher interest rates on the UK’s debt-pile will raise the cost of future investment projects and eat into the Treasury’s fiscal headroom.A line graph showing crude prices per barrel since the start of the Iran warAt the same time, the prospect of higher energy bills as oil and gas prices rise is likely to intensify pressure on the government to help consumers to weather the winter.Unleaded petrol prices have already risen by 6p a litre since the start of September, according to the motoring organisation the RAC, while the prospect of higher inflation has prompted some banks to raise their mortgage rates.Healey has promised to provide a “breathing space” for UK households while also addressing the cost of doing business.View image in fullscreenUnleaded petrol prices in the UK have already risen by 6p a litre since the start of September, according to the RAC.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianIna speech on Monday, however, he also sought to tame bond market fears by committing himself to “controlling borrowing to bear down on inflation, and reducing long-term pressures on our public finances”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the US, where Trump has promised to writea $5,000 (£3,700) cheque for every adult citizen if the Republicans win the midterms, Thursday’s sell-off pushed up the yield on 10-year borrowing to 4.92% – the highest since 2023.The cost of longer-term borrowing also continued to surge, with 30-year yields hitting the highest level since 2007, despite the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, intervening directly in debt markets on Wednesday.Bessent hoped to bring down yields by buying back $6bn worth of government debt; but investors appeared to respond by deepening the sell-off.Kyle Rodda, a senior financial market analyst at the broker Capital.com, said: “Ultimately, a sustained drop in long-end yields can ​only be achieved by genuine shifts in macroeconomic policy: ​either the US government pulling back on spending or the ​Fed lifting rates.”Policymakers at the Federal Reserve, the US central bank, will meet under its new chair, Kevin Warsh, to set interest rates next week.View image in fullscreenScott Bessent at the Republican convention in Dallas, where Donald Trump promised $5,000 to every adult US citizen if the party wins the midterms.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesMarkets are expecting a rise – potentially enraging Trump, who has repeatedly demanded rate cuts. In a TruthSocial post last week, the president said: “The Fed Board, with its great new leader, must get smart – BE PATRIOTS for a change.”A plethora of UK data to be published over the next week, including on inflation, jobs and growth, will give an updated snapshot of how resilient the British economy has been in the face of the Iran war.In the first six months of the year, UK growth was the strongest among the G7 economies.
