This was despite higher-than-expected oil prices and the absence of hoped-for rate cuts.Bank of England policymakers will also meet next week, but are expected to leave the UK’s key interest rate on hold at 3.75% for the time being as they continue to monitor the impact of higher oil prices.Explore more on these topicsBondsGovernment borrowingUS Government borrowingOilInflationEuropean Central BankInterest ratesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Former PE teacher faces lengthy jail term for sexually abusing pupils | England | The Guardian
description: Bronwen James, 30, admitted offences against two girls at schools in Wiltshire and Hampshire, and found guilty of charges involving boy
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Bronwen James, 30, admitted offences against two girls at schools in Wiltshire and Hampshire, and found guilty of charges involving boy
Content: Bronwen James arrives at Winchester crown court on Thursday. The Crown Prosecution Services praised the teenagers she targeted for coming forward.Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PAView image in fullscreenBronwen James arrives at Winchester crown court on Thursday. The Crown Prosecution Services praised the teenagers she targeted for coming forward.Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PAEnglandFormer PE teacher faces lengthy jail term for sexually abusing pupilsBronwen James, 30, admitted offences against two girls at schools in Wiltshire  and Hampshire, and found guilty of charges involving boySteven MorrisThu 10 Sep 2026 13.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA former PE teacher is facing a lengthy jail sentence for grooming and sexually abusing three pupils at two schools.Bronwen James, 30, admitted offences against two girls at schools inHampshireand Wiltshire and was found guilty by a jury of charges involving a boy.The Crown Prosecution Service described James’s crimes as “a sustained pattern of predatory behaviour against children in her care” and praised the teenagers she targeted for coming forward.Judge James Bromige asked for reports to be prepared on James so that he could assess the danger she posed when sentencing her later this year. Her defence team said she knew she faced a significant jail sentence.During her trial at Winchester crown court, jurors were told that James, from Chippenham inWiltshire, flirted with a 16-year-old boy in class at a school in Southampton.They began exchanging Snapchat messages and arranged for her to drive him to a promenade, where they kissed in her car.Later they went to her house where they cuddled while watching the Wimbledon tennis championships on the television before going to her bedroom where they had sex. She told him she loved him and wanted him to move away with her.Edward Culver, prosecuting, told the trial the school was made aware of the incident after another student showed a teacher some text messages apparently sent between the James and the complainant.He said: “They suggested a sexually charged relationship. He [the boy] was named as ‘number 8’ in the messages as a cover. She acted not only in an unprofessional and overfamiliar way, but failed to recognise any boundaries, exploiting her position to engage in sexual activity with one of her young students.”In a police interview, the boy said he had been “groomed” by the defendant.James was convicted of three counts of sexual activity with a child by a person in a position of trust.Before the trial, James pleaded guilty to offences against two girls. One was a pupil at the same Southampton school as the boy, the other attended a school in Wiltshire that James had also taught at.The offences included sexual activity with a child, sexual communication with a child and making an indecent photograph of a child. The victims were 13 and 14 at the time.During legal argument, which can now be reported, it also emerged that at the start of her career, James received a warning while she was teaching at the private Seaford college in West Sussex for giving her personal mobile number to a pupil.Bethany Adams, of the CPS, said: “Bronwen James was trusted to educate and protect children. Instead, she used that trust to groom and sexually abuse three students.“James manipulated her victims with calculated precision, exploiting her position of authority to isolate them and normalise the abuse.“This was not a lapse in judgment; it was a sustained pattern of predatory behaviour against children in her care.“The courage shown by James’s victims in coming forward has been instrumental in securing this conviction. I hope it gives them, and their families, some measure of justice.”Explore more on these topicsEnglandWiltshireHampshirenewsShareReuse this content

title: Esther Rantzen now ‘too physically fragile’ to end her life in Switzerland | Esther Rantzen | The Guardian
description: Broadcaster, 86, had intended to end her life in Swiss clinic after being diagnosed with terminal lung cancer in 2023
Author: Raphael Boyd
Headline: Broadcaster, 86, had intended to end her life in Swiss clinic after being diagnosed with terminal lung cancer in 2023
Content: Esther Rantzen pictured in 2024.Photograph: Cheese Scientist/AlamyView image in fullscreenEsther Rantzen pictured in 2024.Photograph: Cheese Scientist/AlamyEsther RantzenEsther Rantzen now ‘too physically fragile’ to end her life in SwitzerlandBroadcaster, 86, had intended to end her life in Swiss clinic after being diagnosed with terminal lung cancer in 2023Raphael BoydThu 10 Sep 2026 16.04 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEsther Rantzen has said she is no longer able to travel to Switzerland to end her life because she has become “too physically fragile”.Rantzen, who presented the TV current affairs programme That’s Life! for 21 years and founded the youth support charity Childline, had intended to end her life in a Dignitas assisted dying clinic inSwitzerlandafter being diagnosed with terminal lung cancer in 2023.The broadcaster, 86, said in a statement on Thursday that her quality of life had deteriorated since her diagnosis, and that she was ready to end her life but was no longer able to make the journey despite having joined Dignitas about a year after learning she was terminally ill.Rantzen said: “Unfortunately, when I was strong enough to make the flight and go to Dignitas, my life was not unbearably painful, indeed, I was able to relax in my beloved cottage in the New Forest.“And by the time life did become unbearable, I was too physically fragile to make the journey and go through the Dignitas process.“So even though I had spent the money and made the plans, I was not ready to end my life back then, and did not realise that would be my last chance.”Assisted dying remains illegal in the UK, though a bill that would allow it in certain circumstances is being revisited.Rantzen is a vocal supporter of the bill,which is due to have a second reading in parliament on Friday, and has criticised the current laws that prevent people in her situation from legally ending their lives, calling the rules “messy and cruel”.Legalised assisted dying in the UK has been the topic of intensive debate since Kim Leadbeater’s bill was introduced to parliament in October 2024.A June 2025 vote in the Commons saw the bill progress by 314 votes to 291, with both sides receiving votes from MPs from Labour, the Conservatives and the Liberal Democrats.If the bill passes, the UK would join European countries such as Austria, Belgium, the Netherlands, Spain and Switzerland, as well as Australia, Canada and the US, where it is legal in 13 states.Advocates for the bill have claimed it will enable terminally ill people to enjoy a dignified end to their lives and allow them to die before their health declines too much.Those against it, however, argue the criteria put forward could change after the law is passed and that the quality of palliative care could decline.Explore more on these topicsEsther RantzenAssisted dyingSwitzerlandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump promise of $5,000 for US citizens after midterms decried as ‘bribery’ | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Critics react to bid for Republican votes with incredulity and point to potential $1.2tn cost atop existing national debt
Author: George Chidi
Headline: Critics react to bid for Republican votes with incredulity and point to potential $1.2tn cost atop existing national debt
Content: Donald Trump at the Republican national midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, on Wednesday.Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump at the Republican national midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, on Wednesday.Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpTrump promise of $5,000 for US citizens after midterms decried as ‘bribery’Critics react to bid for Republican votes with incredulity and point to potential $1.2tn cost atop existing national debtGeorge ChidiThu 10 Sep 2026 12.13 EDTFirst published on Thu 10 Sep 2026 10.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump’s promise of a $5,000 “Trump dividend” for every US citizen if Republicans retain control of the US Congress in November’s midterm elections has sparked incredulity and accusations of bribery.“If theRepublicanswin, you win with us and you get $5,000,” Trump said during the unprecedented Republican midterm convention in Dallas. “It will be called the Trump dividend.”It comes amid extreme concern over the US national debt, whichexceeded $40tn for the first timein August.US citizens will receive $5,000 if Republicans win midterms, Trump claims in lengthy convention speechRead moreSpeaking toPolitico, Chip Roy, the Republican US representative from Texas, sounded skeptical. “Well – I would like to know how they would plan to pay for … back of envelope … well over $1tn,” he said.In the moments after Trump made the announcement, Marc Goldwein of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget wrote on X that “this would cost about $1.2 TRILLION in just one year. That’s more than ALL THREE ROUNDS of COVID relief checks, despite no recessions. The result would be a huge spike in the deficit, and almost certainly in the inflation rate.”The US has roughly 240 million adult citizens, suggesting the cost of $1.2tn. The federal government spent about $7tn in fiscal year 2025, with about $2tn taken on as debt.“The 10-year [treasury bond is] approaching 5%,” Goldwein said on Thursday morning. “Inflation is not under control. We spend more on interest than we spend on defense or on Medicare at this point. Social security is six years from insolvency. Just about the last thing we need is to borrow another trillion dollars to send checks to everybody.”12:11Is Trump’s $5,000 midterm pledge a new low? - The LatestSpending like this risked an economic sugar high followed by a recessionary crash, he said. But Goldwein was most concerned about what might happen if Trump’s gambit is effective.“If this works, the lesson for every future politician is going to be: if you want to win an election, promise a trillion dollars. And multiply a trillion dollars times the number of elections we have coming up, that is a recipe for bankruptcy.”Democratic political leaders reacted with blunt condemnation.“After making you sicker and poorer with his war, Donald Trump now wants to buy your vote with $5,000 in taxpayer-funded blood money,” the California governor, Gavin Newsom, said. “The most corrupt man ever to occupy the Oval Office.”The Democratic National Committee (DNC) pointed to Trump’s record on similar pledges, from $5,000 stimulus checks as a result of the work of the so-called department of government efficiency (Doge) to $2,000 stimulus checks from revenue from tariffs.“Donald Trump and Republicans are once again offering empty promises to Americans,” said Kendall Witmer, the committee’s rapid response director. “The only people reaping the benefits of Trump’s economy are himself, his family, and his ultra-rich elite donors. Meanwhile, working families get nothing except sky-high receipts at the grocery store and the pump, unaffordable healthcare premiums, and wages that aren’t keeping up with inflation.”The Bipartisan Policy Center has beentrackingtariff revenue since Trump began raising rates in 2025. As of 8 September, the US has collected about $210bn in tariff and excise tax revenue in 2026. At a rate of $21bn a month, the US federal government would have to collect tariffs for nearly five years to cover a $5,000 payment, assuming every dollar of tariff revenue went to the payment, and discounting tariff payments refunded to retailers in legal challenges.Peter Schiff, chief economist for Euro Pacific Asset Management, said that Trump’s pledge had already begun rippling through financial markets.“Even though bond investors know that, even in the unlikely event Republicans retain control of the House, Trump’s promise to borrow over $1 trillion more to buy votes won’t be kept,” Schiff wrote in a post on X. “The promise itself is so reckless that they’re dumping Treasuries, sending yields to new highs …“Making his promise even worse, Trump referred to his $5,000 bribes as ‘dividends’, as if his policies had been so successful that the US now has surpluses to share. Instead, his reckless policies have produced massive deficits. Trump needs to send Americans bills, not checks.”JD Vance appeared towalk backTrump’s pledge, suggesting that the benefit would be means-tested.But the US senator Bernie Moreno, an Ohio Republican, promised support for Trump’s idea. “I will get a bill ready so that we can get the Trump Dividend passed immediately after the November 3rd election,” Moreno wrote on X.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpUS midterm elections 2026RepublicansUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: The hospitality industry fears a tourist tax will deter visitors – the evidence says otherwise | Hospitality industry | The Guardian
description: Studies from hotspots across Europe that have introduced levies suggest they have no impact on visitor numbers
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: Studies from hotspots across Europe that have introduced levies suggest they have no impact on visitor numbers
Content: A study found that Manchester’s hotels have seen no reduced occupancy since an overnight visitor levy was introduced in 2023.Photograph: Mark Waugh/AlamyView image in fullscreenA study found that Manchester’s hotels have seen no reduced occupancy since an overnight visitor levy was introduced in 2023.Photograph: Mark Waugh/AlamyHospitality industryAnalysisThe hospitality industry fears a tourist tax will deter visitors – the evidence says otherwiseJosh HallidayNorth of England editorStudies from hotspots across Europe that have introduced levies suggest they have no impact on visitor numbersThu 10 Sep 2026 12.37 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareIf you wandered down Las Ramblas or lazed on a beach in the Balearics this summer, you probably paid a tourist tax for the privilege. In fact, if you enjoyed any of Europe’s beauty spots in recent years, it is likely that an overnight levy was added to your bill.Britons have become used to paying these fees abroad but ministers have shied away from introducing them in the UK. The furious response from UK hospitality bosses helps to explain why.The trade body UKHospitalityestimatesthat a 5% tax on overnight stays in England would result in 12m fewer visits and 33,000 job losses, piling further pressure on an industrybattling an increase in taxes and employment costs, as well as the effects of war, Covid and Brexit.Tourists in England face nightly levy on hotel and Airbnb-style stays under new plansRead moreIn places like the Lake District and the Yorkshire Dales, which rely heavily on tourism, businesses are concerned that visitors will instead go to other parts of the country that choose not to impose such a levy.Large parts of England’s east coast, for example – from the seaside resort of Skegness to the town of Hartlepool – are expected to remain levy-free after their mayors, from Reform UK and the Conservative party, opposed the proposals on Thursday.But are overnight levies a success? The evidence suggests that it depends what mayors want to achieve, but they could be very lucrative.They were introduced in cities including Amsterdam, Barcelona and Venice as a way to prevent over-tourism. But there is little evidence they kept visitors at bay: trips to all three destinations have risen consistently over the past decade (despiteAmsterdam charging an additional 12.5% for an overnight stay, believed to be the most expensive tourist tax in Europe).In April 2023, Manchester became the first place in the UK to introduce an overnight visitor levy, charging £1 per room per night in the city centre. Astudypublished in the journal Tourism Management in 2025 found that the tax had had “no significant impact” on the occupancy of hotels in the city.In sharp contrast to the vocal opposition of national trade bodies, inManchesterit was hospitality businesses that introduced the levy through a business improvement district.Local leaders say the £1-a-night levy has raised £10.5m in its first three years of operation, with the revenue ringfenced for cultural projects such as the Brit awards and Mobo awards, both hosted in Manchester this year.When Labour MPs visit Liverpool for their party conference later this month, they too will be paying a tourist tax: a £2-a-night charge was introduced by its hospitality firms last June, raising more than £2m for projects in sports, culture and conferencing.Councils in Scotland already have the power to introduce local overnight levies, with Wales following suit next April.Only Edinburgh has taken the plunge so far, introducing a 5% tourist tax on 24 July, although Cardiff, Glasgow and three other regions of Scotland are expected to follow next year.Allen Simpson, chief executive of UKHospitality, said on Thursday that Edinburgh’s new charge was “already having damaging effects” on the city.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHowever, Edinburgh Tourism Action Group, which represents the city’s tourism industry, told the Guardian it was “too early to draw any meaningful conclusions” on its impact. It said many of the cities that had adopted the scheme, including Manchester, had “not experienced a decline in visitor numbers” as a result.While there is little detailed international research on the economic impact of tourist taxes,a studyby Bangor University in Wales in 2024 found no evidence to suggest they deter visitors.Researchers found they had been introduced in 125 destinations and 26 countries across Europe by 2019, with exceptions mainly in the Nordics and Baltic region. The modest nightly charges were being used to fund hundreds of millions of pounds worth of public projects, they found.In the Balaeric Islands, for example, the tourism tax had funded €263m (£226m) worth of projects since 2016, including social housing and scientific research.Zoë Billingham, the chief executive of IPPR North, a thinktank which has campaigned for a tourist tax, said it was wrong to assume that the entire hospitality industry was against the move, pointing to Manchester and Liverpool, where local businesses led the charge.She added: “With climate change and other uncertainties in the world, I would expect visitor numbers in the UK to increase – that’s not just domestic holidays, but also people from other countries coming here. This is a real way to share in the benefits of tourism growth in this country.”Henri Murison, chief executive of the business lobby group Northern Powerhouse Partnership, said there was little evidence tourists would be put off by an extra few pounds on their hotel bill.“The current system, where all the tax paid by businesses goes to central government and none of it benefits the destination, is wrong. It’s just wrong,” he said.Explore more on these topicsHospitality industryManchesteranalysisShareReuse this content

title: Alex Winter: ‘Michael Winner was the most erudite sociopath I’ve ever met’ | Movies | The Guardian
description: The Bill & Ted actor on Keanu Reeves, whether there will be a fourth instalment and nights out in Brixton with the Death Wish director
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: The Bill & Ted actor on Keanu Reeves, whether there will be a fourth instalment and nights out in Brixton with the Death Wish director
Content: Alex Winter photographed in Toronto in 2025.Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images for IMDbView image in fullscreenAlex Winter photographed in Toronto in 2025.Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images for IMDbFilm & Music reader interviewMoviesInterviewAlex Winter: ‘Michael Winner was the most erudite sociopath I’ve ever met’As told toRich PelleyThe Bill & Ted actor answers your questions about working with Keanu Reeves, whether there will be a fourth instalment and nights out in Brixton with the Death Wish directorThu 10 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou were born inLondonbut grew up inAmerica. When do you feel most British?DonarudoToranpuThe UK is still my second home. I’ve worked there a lot as an adult. When I’m back in London, I like walking on Hampstead Heath, so I would say that’s where I feel most at home.Having playedMarkoinThe Lost Boysand thenJohn PolidoriinHaunted Summer, have you been tempted to take on another vampire-related role? And was getting staked to death while you were sleeping a bit of a disappointing end for Marko – what would have been your preferred way of going out in style? Death by stereo, perhaps?Finbarre and MoreorLesPaulI’d love to do another vampire movie. I love those characters. They’re interesting and great fun to play. There are some really good vampire movies – I’m grateful I was in one that has, for some reason that none of us can figure out, really stood the test of time. And I love Marko’s death. As an actor, the first time you get staked is the most memorable.View image in fullscreenKeanu Reeves and Alex Winter in Bill & Ted’s Bogus Journey (1994).Photograph: Cinematic/AlamyWhichKeanu Reeveswas the most fun to work with: inWaiting for GodotonBroadway; asTed “Theodore” Loganto yourBill S Preston, EsqinBill & Ted; or as mutantOrtiz the Dog Boywhen you directed him inFreaked? And following Waiting for Godot, what wildly inappropriate classic should Bill & Ted tackle next?FioreSebek and GunHarpI just love performing with Keanu. The funny thing is we both play bass, so all through the first Bill & Ted, whenever we weren’t shooting, we’d be jamming. Keanu and I both have theatre backgrounds and have studied Shakespeare, so I’d like to do some Shakespeare, maybe something like Measure for Measure. There’s a few that we’ve discussed. I’m not sure if we’ll get there, but who knows? Never say never.My kids (six andnine) have just discoveredBen 10in all its incarnations and I saw you directed the live-action versions. If you could choose the powers of any of the aliens in theOmnitrix, which would it be and why?LethalLiaisonHeatblast was my favourite. He’s a powerful fire character. My children were obsessed with Ben 10 at the time, and we worked on those together, which was something I don’t often get to do, so it was a lovely experience. I met my wife on that project too. She was running Cartoon Network studios at the time.Alex Winter on fame, AI and reuniting with Keanu Reeves: ‘Sometimes we’re on a groove and go, ‘God damn, that was good!’Read moreMichael Winnerdirected you in your first film,Death Wish 3. Say something nice about him – and where did yougo out drinking when you were filming it in London?ExFi and OttoMaddoxI can absolutely say something nice about Michael Winner. He was the most erudite sociopath I’ve ever met. That’s a compliment. We used to drink in Brixton, largely. One of the people working on the show – I think he may have been involved in some criminal activity, so maybe the less said about him the better – owned a club there. They would close it and we would hang out there all night. I was 19 when I made Death Wish 3. It was a very fun, formidable summer.You’ve made documentaries aboutNapster, the dark web, blockchain and YouTube. Which part of the internet scares you most these days?ZenchiThe hasty, greed-oriented rush into the AI space is the most frightening thing happening right now. That’s not to say all AI is bad, but a lot of the people running the AI companies areverybad. So what scares me the most is the tech oligarch takeover that’s occurring in so many areas of business, politics and civic culture.View image in fullscreenFrank Zappa at the Amougies Festival in Belgium, October 1969.Photograph: Philippe Gras/AlamyAfter directing yourFrank Zappa documentary, for those, like me, who’ve been immune to his charms, can you recommend a Zappa track or album?HenleyRegattaI didn’t make the doc as a big fan. I made it because I was very interested in Frank Zappa as a way into looking at American culture and artistic culture. He’s a really good doc subject: someone who decided to live their life in a purely artistic way, and what the consequences of that were. If you want the quintessential Zappa album – unless you are just never going to like him – it’s impossible not to enjoy Hot Rats. I’m also very partial to the album he made at the very end of his life, The Yellow Shark, which is almost a classical, jazz-oriented album.The Bill & Ted movies feel like a beautiful, optimistic tribute to the idea that music created by ordinary people will save the world. Do you think it still could?venusdenicoI do think that good art will always help the world. It’s not the only thing. But I do think that music and other art forms absolutely help the planet and help humanity.View image in fullscreenReeves and Winter with William Sadler as the Grim Reaper, aka Death, in Bogus Journey (1991).Photograph: RGR Collection/AlamyThanks for that wonderful ending toBill & Ted Face the Music. Will there be a Bill & Ted4?brucevayne1000Keanu and I would love to make a fourth movie. I think the stars have to align in a number of areas for that to happen. But we love playing these characters. We kind ofareBill and Ted. We started playing the characters so young, I don’t really think they exist without us. We defined the characters from the very beginning, so I don’t think it really matters how old we are. It becomes a question of how long can you act, and I think one can act until one is no longer breathing. I really hope they don’t do a reboot. I don’t really want anyone else to play Bill, because IamBill. That would be a disaster.Alex Winter: ‘I had extreme PTSD for many, many years. That will wreak havoc’Read moreIf you had access to Bill & Ted’s phone booth, which non-bogus historical figures would you visit?TeeDubyaBeeI would like to go back to ancient Greece. I would love to meet Euripides or Aeschylus. Or go to Shakespeare’s time. The future too. What is going to happen? Will there be a planet? I’d be curious to go 40 or 50 years into the future and have a look at whether we pulled ourselves out of this climate disaster we’re falling into, which I believe we will. I’m not a nihilist. But I’d be curious to see how we did it.If you could“melvin”anyone in real life – as Bill & Ted do toDeathinBogus Journey– who would it be?Dr_J_A_ZoidbergI grew up in the US, and I did not grow up with “melvin”. I grew up with “wedgie”. It must be a coastal thing. Maybe on the west coast they say “melvin”? In the midwest and the east coast they definitely say wedgie. Anyway, who would I most like to melvin or wedgie?
