title: Tschabalala Self’s Lady in Blue review – this striding scupture fills the fourth plinth with humour and life | Fourth plinth | The Guardian
description: The swaggering statue’s luscious collision of brown and blue could stop traffic – and serves as a reminder of the big, beautiful, multicultural world we enjoy
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: The swaggering statue’s luscious collision of brown and blue could stop traffic – and serves as a reminder of the big, beautiful, multicultural world we enjoy
Content: ‘Not a vulnerable object of anyone’s gaze’ … Lady in Blue on the fourth plinth.Photograph: Kin Cheung/APView image in fullscreen‘Not a vulnerable object of anyone’s gaze’ … Lady in Blue on the fourth plinth.Photograph: Kin Cheung/APFourth plinthReviewTschabalala Self’s Lady in Blue review – this striding scupture fills the fourth plinth with humour and lifeTrafalgar Square, LondonThe swaggering statue’s luscious collision of brown and blue could stop traffic – and serves as a reminder of the big, beautiful, multicultural world we enjoyJonathan JonesThu 10 Sep 2026 11.09 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt hit me like a thunder clap. One moment I was bored and irritated by the official speeches before the unveiling of Tschabalala Self’s sculpture on the fourth plinth, which so insisted on its sociopolitical worth it sounded like Soviet propaganda. Then the covering slid off and I was in love with the Lady in Blue.Self has created one of the most beautiful sculptures put on Trafalgar Square’s empty plinth – and I don’t mean that in a cool, formalist way. There is a serious danger of traffic accidents as drivers passing the square stare a little too long at the Lady’s generous proportions, her long stride in platform shoes, her intensely physical, confident being.‘I’m not nervous, I’m ready’: Tschabalala Self on racist vandals and her bold striding woman for the Fourth PlinthRead moreLady in Blue brilliantly exploits the potential of the long rectangular plinth, built in 1841 for an equestrian statue that was never erected, to encompass a lolloping human gait. This is a homage to walking, and to Umberto Boccioni’s futurist striderUnique Forms of Continuity in Space, with Self’s figure extrapolated upward from her wide and fast walk, a massive curved leg thrusting forward out of her draping blue skirt, her head held high, but not absurdly high.This is no colossus but a statue that takes its scale and life from the surrounding city. There, I’ve said it: statue. The most memorable works on the fourth plinth, ever since it became a site for temporary art works back in 1999, have usually been human figures. ToMark Wallinger’s Ecce HomoandMarc Quinn’s Alison Lapper Pregnant, we can now add Self’s Lady as proof that what we really want and maybe need to see on a plinth is the human form, alive, profound and sexual.View image in fullscreenIt might melt withered hearts with its panache … onlookers admire Lady in Blue.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesWhat you first notice is the sheen of this polychrome woman: sunlight glints on her polished, plasticky surface as if she were covered from head to toe in nail varnish. Then your eyes adjust to the glare and you feel the luscious collision of brown flesh and heavenly blue. The blue is that of lapis lazuli, the rare mineral mined in Afghanistan that for millennia was coveted for jewellery and, then, for the most ethereal and expensive painter’s blue: ultramarine.It connects Lady in Blue with the paintings in the National Gallery behind it, many of which use ultramarine, maybe most of all with Bronzino’s brazenly eroticAllegory With Venus and Cupid, which sets hard flesh against silky blue. Self’s statue has the same provocatively fetishistic power.But this Lady is not a vulnerable object of anyone’s gaze. She swaggers in space with commanding girth, her bottom facing the National Gallery with flamboyant magnificence. This is the opposite of smooth classicism or catwalk perfection. In fact, it may be the opposite of traditional western sculpture. For all its apparent simplicity, Self’s figure seems rooted in African wood carvings, with their free transformations of the human body. On top of that is a head whose beauty and grace recall the bronze faces of the medieval queens of Ife.View image in fullscreen‘Her achievement goes beyond good intentions’ … Tschabalala Self with her sculpture.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesLady in Blue appears at the heart of a London where we’ve seen Tommy Robinson supporters march for a mono-racial, white nationalist UK. For all my impatience, it’s hard to disagree with the speeches at the unveiling – that we urgently need to uphold diversity and equality and reject intolerance.The question is how a work of art can help. Just putting up a positive image of a Black woman won’t silence racists, and might even offer them another horrible talking point in the culture wars. But Self’s achievement goes beyond good intentions. You can view it as a seductive and funny comment on our big, beautiful, multicultural world.Or you can just enjoy Lady in Blue aesthetically as a stonking sculpture that manages to meld multiple art histories to fill the fourth plinth with humour, fun and life. This is a carnivalesque masterpiece. But in a frightening world it also throws us a lifeline, something human to hold on to.Explore more on these topicsFourth plinthSculptureArtreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’ve got more of a sense of humour than Ralph Lauren’ – nine things we learned from Paul Smith’s new memoir | Fashion | The Guardian
description: He put personality into boxers, collaborated with the pope (sort of) and is to thank for novelty socks. The British designer’s new book reveals there’s more to Smith than his stripes
Author: Chloe Mac Donnell
Headline: He put personality into boxers, collaborated with the pope (sort of) and is to thank for novelty socks. The British designer’s new book reveals there’s more to Smith than his stripes
Content: British designer Paul Smith has released a new memoir Threads: My Life in Style.Photograph: Suki Dhanda/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBritish designer Paul Smith has released a new memoir Threads: My Life in Style.Photograph: Suki Dhanda/The GuardianFashion Statement newsletterFashion‘I’ve got more of a sense of humour than Ralph Lauren’ – nine things we learned from Paul Smith’s new memoirHe put personality into boxers, collaborated with the pope (sort of) and is to thank for novelty socks. The British designer’s new book reveals there’s more to Smith than his stripesChloe Mac DonnellThu 10 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 13.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn July, the British designer Paul Smith celebrated his 80th birthday and he has now released a memoir to mark the occasion. Threads: My Life in Style tells Smith’s story, from growing up in Nottingham and leaving school with no qualifications to selling suits to celebs, including Gary Oldman and David Bowie.Here are nine of our favourite lesser-known takeaways from the book.1.Hemade boxers something you want to be seen inIn the 70s, Smith reimagined boxers in clashing prints and colours, such as polka dots and stripes rather than drab greys and whites, catapulting them from the back of the underwear drawer to the pages of fashion magazines.“I always describe my early success as nudging rather than shoving the British male into appreciating the fact that you could be a little different,” he writes.2.He has a love/hate relationship with stripesSmith describes the multi-stripe he has become synonymous with as “both a joy and a curse”. It was a design detail forced upon him in his early days due to budget constraints, but quickly became popular among his customers. “It began to take on a life of its own,” Smith writes. However, it “became a bit of a burden to me if to no one else.You meet people who say, ‘Oh, you’re the one who’s famous for the stripes.’ It’s like being Calvin Klein – you can make beautiful clothes every year but someone will always say, ‘Oh, you’re the one who makes underpants.’ You find yourself having to work around it.”3.He’s to blamefor the rise of novelty socksView image in fullscreenA now-classic Christmas gift: Paul Smith’s striped socks.In the 1980s, Smith says men only bought two types of socks: plain or argyle patterned. After coming across a pair with a paperclip motif in Japan, he brought the design to the UK. Now he sells more than 700,000 pairs of socks a year. “Quite often when I’m introduced to someone new he’ll say, ‘Oh yes – I get your socks for Christmas,’” Smith writes.4.His office is the original example ofcurated chaosPiles of vinyl records, 28 bicycles (including the yellow Pinarello Chris Froome rode to victory in the Tour de France), a model train set, hundreds of books and oil paintings and a Snoopy telephone are just some of the curiosities you’ll find in Smith’s office. And then there are the rabbit figurines in all shapes and sizes, the result of a joke, which got out of hand, about how they were his lucky charm.“Every week I get rabbits of all kinds,” writes Smith. “They’re everywhere. Rabbits made of bronze, felt, plastic, wood, stone. A man in Italy sends me four or five a month, even though I’ve never met him.”5.David Bowie hated small talkView image in fullscreenPaul Smith (left) with David Bowie (centre) and Dylan Jones (right), the then editor of British GQ, in 2002.Photograph: Dave Benett/Getty ImagesBowie became a big fan of Smith’s two-piece suits, including one in a lemon and pink overcheck. After turning up to the store unannounced several times to shop, Smith invited him for a cup of tea in his studio. It was the beginning of a friendship. Bowie never called Smith by his first name – instead, it was always Smithy. “Was he an easy person to be with and to talk to? Only if you were interesting,” writes Smith. “There was no small talk.”6.He accidentally createdInstabaitView image in fullscreenPretty in pink … Smith’s Melrose Avenue store in Los Angeles.Photograph: AaronP/Bauer-Griffin/GC ImagesEven if you’ve never been to LA, you’ll probably recognise Smith’s Melrose Avenue store. Five years after it opened in 2005, Instagram launched and the store’s hot-pink wall became a selfie sensation. There have beenthousands of snaps takenat the #pinkwall, making it one of the most Instagrammed buildings in California.7.He’s not keen on comparisons to Ralph LaurenSmith describes getting “pissed off” in his early days when the press kept comparing him to the American designer, and renowned anglophile, Ralph Lauren. “I’ve got far more of a sense of humour, for a start,” he writes. “His shops were always so serious, with the stately-home image and the good-looking models. There was nobody that English in England.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion8.Hecollaborated withPope Francis (sort of)View image in fullscreenSmith with his jersey design for the Giro d’Italia in 2013.Photograph: Daniele Mascolo/EPAAs a huge cycling enthusiast (he hoped to become a pro until he had a nasty accident aged 17),Smith was thrilled to be asked to design the leaders’ jerseys for the annual Giro d’Italia bike race in 201. It included the “maglia rosa”, a pink jersey that is (sort of) equivalent to the Tour de France’s yellow jersey. Smith added some red piping around the edge, signature striping on the left sleeve and a tiny sketch of a cyclist. It was sent to Pope Francis to be blessed. Smith writes: “I’ve done a lot of collaborations over the years, from cars to crayons, from carpets to cycles, but only one of them, so far as I’m aware, has been personally blessed by the pope.”9.Despite all his success, he remains a doerCase in point, during lockdown Smith continued to work from his office, albeit alone. One day he was met by an unpleasant smell and discovered that 18 containers of forgotten milk had exploded all over the kitchen floor. He spent three hours cleaning it up. At one stage he found himself thinking: “I wonder if my friend Giorgio Armani is doing something like this now?” Still, when Smith told colleagues about his wiping marathon, “they all said the same thing: ‘Oh no! Only Paul Smith.’ And I took that as a compliment.”To read the complete version of this newsletter – complete with this week’s trending topics in The Measure and your wardrobe dilemmas solved –subscribe to receive Fashion Statementin your inbox every Thursday.View image in fullscreenAmelia Dimoldenberg, a chicken, Chopowa Lowena’s shop, Emma Corrin, luggage and the Bayeux tapestry.Composite: Alessandra Benedetti/Corbis/Perky Pets/Danny Beck/Getty/Suzanne Plunkett/ReutersView image in fullscreenA custom dress worn by singer Olivia Rodrigo, made by Nöl Collective in Palestine.Photograph: Nöl CollectiveExplore more on these topicsFashionFashion Statement newsletterMen's fashionnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: ‘A completely unique opportunity’: the secretive process that will decide the BBC’s future | BBC | The Guardian
description: The long read: Every decade, the BBC’s continued existence must be secured through an elaborate multi-year negotiation with the government. But what does charter renewal actually involve – and will it secure the BBC’s long-term future?
Author: Barbara Speed
Headline: The long read: Every decade, the BBC’s continued existence must be secured through an elaborate multi-year negotiation with the government. But what does charter renewal actually involve – and will it secure the BBC’s long-term future?
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/AlamyEvery decade, the BBC’s continued existence must be secured through an elaborate multi-year negotiation with the government. But what does charter renewal actually involve – and will it secure the BBC’s long-term future?ByBarbara SpeedThu 10 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 05.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a temperature-controlled room in a suburb of Reading, the basis of the BBC’s existence is kept in a flat, square, faded navy case, the size of a large pizza box. Inside is a stack of vellum – calfskin, pounded until it forms a milky and translucent paper that is supposed to last for thousands of years. The queen’s red wax seal is secured to its base with red and gold cord. The pages are strapped down with two strips of white elastic, more PE kit than Buckingham Palace.The document is unique. Like hundreds of other British organisations, the BBC was founded via a Royal Charter, granted by the monarch of the day. But unlike Oxford colleges, the British Film Institute, or the Worshipful Company of Makers of Playing Cards, the BBC was given an expiry date. When the British Broadcasting Corporation was founded, in the 1920s, radio was seen as such an uncertain, risky technology that the government only gave it a 10-year guarantee, after which it would have to seek a new charter.Ever since, the BBC has been forced to repeatedly regenerate, much like the lead character in its beloved series Doctor Who. Most governments have granted decade-long charters, with some variation. (The 2017 charter was set at 11 years to unhook it from the five-year British general election cycle.) Like the Doctor, in each iteration the BBC retains the same name, the same job, and does many of the same things. Yet at midnight on the night of its renewal, it disappears, and is replaced by a new version of itself. If the charter is not renewed, the BBC would cease to exist as a legal entity: it could no longer employ its staff, broadcast or publish, and its assets would automatically pass to the state.View image in fullscreenTom Baker (right) as the Doctor in 1975 alongside Elisabeth Sladen and Michael Sheard.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyThe current charter will expire on 31 December 2027, and its replacement is now the subject of lobbying, scaremongering and dealmaking as its contents are debated, tugged apart and rewritten. The charter is produced via a two- or three-year negotiation between government and the BBC. It is a process that has a claim to being one of the largest acts of public participation in British politics, yet it is also a black box, its inner workings hidden from view. The last charter renewal process involved 16 focus groups, two independent reports, nine industry round tables and 300 meetings with organisations and experts. The Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) received 190,000 responses to a public consultation and had to hire a new building in order for staff to read them all.Charter renewal is partly an exercise in predicting the future: in deciding what Britain and the media landscape will look like in a decade, and how the BBC must transform accordingly. This is why it is so difficult, and so fraught. The charter is the only way that the BBC’s purpose, funding model or governance can be drastically changed. It is through charter renewals that the BBC built Britain’s television infrastructure, launched its first website and built a streaming platform, the iPlayer, while Netflix was still sending out DVDs through the post.The risk of failing to meet the moment bedevils every charter renewal. Debates about the BBC are so familiar that they have become a kind of white noise: whether it is secretly right or leftwing; whether it contributed to Brexit or sought to undermine it; whether its stars are paid too much, and so on. But to look at the history of charter renewal is to see that the real existential threats it faces are never the stuff of fleeting scandals or culture wars. In 2026, what is really threatening the BBC are the much larger tides of changing technology and changing habits. Year on year, fewer and fewer people are using the BBC, and fewer and fewer people are paying for it. Hundreds of millions of pounds in cuts are under way to balance the books. This charter renewal is its only chance to turn back those tides.And yet in my interviews with 30 experts and BBC and government insiders over the past year, most struggled to tell me exactly what the charteris. One former director general told me simply: “The charter is … the charter.” Part of the difficulty of comprehending the charter lies in the difficulty of grasping the breadth and depth of the BBC itself. On a single day in 2026, the BBC staged a Stravinsky concert, brought its Strictly Come Dancing tour to Liverpool, broke a news story about cameras spying on people having sex in Chinese hotel rooms, broadcast a Gaelic news roundup, reported on speed limits in the Welsh town of Barry, interviewed Venezeula’s opposition leader, unveiled the lineup for the music festival it was putting on in Manchester, knocked on 10,000 doors of licence fee non-payers, and broadcast the opening ceremony of the Milan Winter Olympics. The BBC is so baked into British life that it is hard to unpick exactly what it represents, and what it would mean for it to change, shrink or even disappear.View image in fullscreenThe BBC Sport studio at Media City in Salford.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianIn Reading, the navy blue box sits on its shelf in the BBC’s archive, rarely consulted, gathering dust. As long as the negotiation is completed in time, it will be replaced on 1 January 2028. The BBC’s survival depends on that new stack of calfskin, and whether its predictions hold true. “I don’t think we’ve had a charter renewal as consequential as this – and as potentially fantastically good – since the second world war,” Jean Seaton, the BBC’s official historian, told me. “It is a completely unique opportunity.”On 16 December 2025, nearly a year later than promised, the charter renewal process officially began. In a 38,000 word green paper, Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, set out her vision for the BBC and invited feedback from the public. She described the BBC as a “light on the hill”, an institution as vital to Britain as the NHS. She suggested that the BBC could focus more on countering disinformation, and that it could move more of its work out of London. This was all well and good, but for the kind of readers who were impatiently awaiting this document – thinktanks, unions, politicians, media professionals inside and outside the BBC – most will have flicked first to the end: the bit about the funding.Everyone agrees the funding model isn’t working. “A busted flush” is how the new BBC director general, former Google executive Matt Brittin, described it recently. About 65% of the BBC’s funding comes from the £180 licence fee, which is paid by any household that watches any live TV or uses iPlayer. The problem is that takings have dropped by a quarter – about £1.3bn in real terms – since 2017. Some of that is down to governments imposing below-inflation fee rises or no rises at all; some is down to the growing number of those refusing or unable to pay.In the green paper, Nandy ruled out funding the BBC via taxation or a household levy, a model used in Germany and elsewhere. That leaves only three options: advertising, subscriptions or a reformed licence fee (or some combination of the above). The green paper also suggested growing BBC Studios, its commercial production company, and setting up partnerships with tech companies, but commercial revenues fund about 8% of the BBC’s public service output – they can’t replace the licence fee.The green paper ended with 32 questions, to be answered by any member of the public or organisation who wished to give their view. Not everyone was happy with this. The questions were “leading, lacking and limited”, said Paul Fleming, general secretary of the performing arts union Equity, which announced it would be boycotting the survey. The Media Reform Coalition, which campaigns for more accountability, put out an “alternative green paper” as a “direct response to this hollow exercise in public consultation”. At the launch event in March, policy experts read out their own ideas; one performed a poem calling for BBC governance that is both “broad and shallow” and “deep and narrow”. That month, the BBC released its own response to the green paper, rejecting the idea of subscriptions or advertising, and asking the Foreign Office to fund the World Service in its entirety, as it did before 2014, when George Osborne shifted the costs on to the BBC.View image in fullscreenBBC director general Matt Brittin on his first day in the role outside Broadcasting House in London, 18 May 2026.Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/ReutersBy the time it finished in March, the public consultation had brought in about 120,000 responses. These must all be read and summarised for the culture minister, to meet a legal obligation that responses should be “conscientiously taken into account”. In the last charter process, Radio Times magazine threatened DCMS with legal action after it found that a memory stick containing 6,085 of its readers’ consultation responses had never been opened.A varied cast of politicians and experts sought to influence the debate in the wood-panelled room of the culture, media and sport select committee. (The committee has no direct role in charter renewal, but invites guests to give evidence to inform the debate.) There was no shortage of ideas. Between May and August, plans were floated for “public service algorithms” to counter the narrowing effect of social media. Others proposed a kind of global iPlayer, bringing together public service broadcasters around the world, and called for a “citizens’ panel” to give the public a voice in the way the BBC is run. Jordan Schwarzenberger, the manager of YouTube stars the Sidemen, was brought in to suggest how the BBC could attract younger audiences. It needs to focus on “the slightly harsher, more raw and edgy content that young audiences are craving”, he argued. When asked if the Sidemen might appear on Celebrity Gladiators, he delicately explained that for the money on offer, it wouldn’t be worth their while.What do all these thousands of words of debate, discussion, reports, responses and meetings actually add up to? It is not entirely clear. Because while experts, industry professionals and the public are asked to weigh in, they can only offer suggestions. When I asked people involved with previous charter renewals who actually decides what goes into the final text, the answer was unanimous: it’s the culture minister, with the prime minister and chancellor looming behind them. Tom Chivers, a media campaigner who wrote his PhD on the last charter renewal, found it to be an “erratic and decidedly undemocratic” process, marked in its later stages by a “withdrawal from its earlier public settings and into private, bureaucratic channels of elite decision-making”. This first flurry of activity and public debate is, he told me, “just gloss for what they already want to do”.The latter stages of the charter process are under way now: a negotiation behind closed doors, between a small group of people, only a handful of whom hold any real power.It is very easy to find people to speak to about the BBC. Almost every person in Britain has interacted with it, and has a view on it. And yet it is difficult to find many people with a view of the corporation in its entirety. As with the story of the blind men and the elephant, even BBC experts tend to have a clear perspective on only one limb: impartiality in news coverage, say, or the funding model, or an obscure sports programme axed back in the 80s. (And as with the story of the blind men and the elephant, the interested parties are overridingly men. A recent book of letters to the new director general did not feature a single woman; most of the books written about the BBC are by men, with afewnotableexceptions; there has never been a female director general.)From the huge array of opinions that swirl around the BBC, however, it is possible to discern three broad schools of thought. The first camp, the custodians, frames the corporation as a vital fortress, to be defended in its current form, at all costs. In this view, the BBC’s primacy in British life is assumed and its founding principles of independence from government and universality are sacrosanct.View image in fullscreenBroadcasting House, the BBC headquarters in London.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/AlamyThe second camp, the shrinkers, views the BBC as one media company among many – one granted unfair advantages. In the past, it was this camp that argued successfully against the BBC’s monopoly first on radio, and then on television. These days, they rail against successful programmes such as The Traitors and Strictly Come Dancing, which, they say, could be made by commercial rivals. The shrinkers argue that the BBC should stick to its USP – the public service meat and potatoes of current affairs and children’s programming. This group also objects to the corporation’s vast scale: its 10 TV channels, 56 radio stations, five orchestras and a workforce that, at 21,000, is larger than that of either the Scottish or Welsh governments.This second group is often framed as anti-BBC. This is fair if you believe, as the first camp does, that a more limited BBC is not really a BBC at all. But it is worth noting that many in this second camp would say they love the BBC and value public service media. Their objection lies in the idea that the BBC should be all things to all people, at the cost of competitors.At the far edge of this camp, at least on paper, sits the Reform party, whose official policy is not to scrap the BBC, but to scrap the licence fee and force the BBC to act as a commercial entity, probably via a subscription service. Its chair, Lee Anderson, has boasted in parliament that he personally refuses to pay it (despite the fact he appears on GB News, which you need a TV licence to watch live).The custodians and the shrinkers have been locked in battle since the BBC’s creation. To justify the licence fee to the first camp, the BBC must appeal to all ages, political persuasions and corners of the country. And yet if it succeeds in this feat, it is accused by the second camp of dominating the market and crowding out competitors. When in government, shrinkers then try to cut the BBC down to size, which in turn leads to questions about a reduced corporation’s ability to appeal to everyone. The cycle continues. In his 1986 book, somewhat prematurely titled The Last Days of the Beeb, the journalist Michael Leapman described the BBC’s bind: “It is like one of those computer adventure games where the player escapes from one mortal peril only to find he has landed himself in another tough spot, still more threatening.”The latest version of this debate concerns online platforms. The BBC recently struck a deal to grow its number of YouTube channels to at least 50, and the government has suggested it may legislate to give the BBC and other public service news providers more prominence on the platform. YouTube creators have claimed that this will, to quote one, “kill YouTube”. Schwarzenberger, manager of the Sidemen, told the select committee: “Public service broadcasting does not really equate with the gen Z or gen Alpha experience … why [should] the BBC have a leg-up on a private platform like YouTube, when the whole premise of YouTube is that it is totally meritocratic?” On newer platforms, the shrinkers hold sway: the BBC is just one content creator among billions.View image in fullscreenStrictly Come Dancing, 8 November 2025.Photograph: Guy Levy/BBC/PAA third camp – let’s call them the engineers – believes the argument between the shrinkers and the custodians misses the point entirely. The BBC was founded to both produce radio programmes and to run the wireless network for the public good. That logic, the engineers say, should now be applied to digital media. “If the BBC thinks it’s just in the content business, then it’s already over. It’s lost,” Tony Ageh, one of the architects of the iPlayer, told me.In an era of streamers, AI and social media platforms, the engineers believe the BBC should be building its own platforms or algorithms, so as to be less reliant on US billionaires, setting up safe social media sites for the under-16s, or offering free internet access for public service content. If it doesn’t, then those without broadband will lose access to BBC channels when terrestrial is switched off, which could be as soon as 2034. Pat Younge, a former BBC chief creative officer and now chair of the campaigning organisation British Broadcasting Challenge, told me: “The biggest threat when Donald Trump said he might sue the BBC wasn’t that he would sue – it was that he would get Jeff Bezos to withdraw Amazon Web Services from them, at which point iPlayer collapses.”Throughout the summer, 15 formal meetings have taken place between DCMS and BBC officials, with more to come through the rest of the year and into 2027. These meetings are private. No public record is released. It’s here that the real work of drafting the charter is done.BBC officials may be in the room for these conversations, but it is clear where the power lies. One senior DCMS figure in a previous negotiation recalled reminding the BBC that this was a review, not an automatic renewal: “It’s not an absolute certainty when we start that the charter will be renewed at all.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long ReadLose yourself in a great story: from politics to psychology, food to technology, culture to crimeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWith no official levers to pull, the BBC must rely on diplomacy. In 2016-17, Tony Hall, the director general, met the then secretary of state for culture, John Whittingdale, or “Whitto”, as he called him when we spoke, for regular dinners one on one. (Whittingdale told me his officials “hated” that they met in private.) Other director generals have approached the dynamic rather differently: in 1947, the negotiator on the government side sent the director general, William Haley, a testy letter in response to changes he’d made to a draft of the charter. Haley passed it on to a colleague with a note scrawled in fountain pen: “This will amuse you. I do not intend to reply. I have stated the corporation’s view and the matter will be left till they raise it again.”While ministers hold the power, they do not always have much expertise or interest. “Going quite a long way back, I can remember one secretary of state who fell asleep during a meeting with me,” said Stewart Purvis, who worked on broadcast policy for years at Ofcom. “No one dared say anything.” Purvis went on to advise DMCS on the 2017 charter and was asked by civil servants to help draft its text. This experience did not fill him with confidence. “DCMS has never been highly regarded in Whitehall, and you’re always wondering: ‘This is all very well. I’m a cog in this wheel, but at the end of the day, does Downing Street agree with any of this?’” Advisers to ministers would leak stories to further DCMS’s agenda, whether with the public or with Downing Street. “That seemed to be their principal role, to do the leaks,” Purvis said. “There was always pressure within DCMS to find a big story about charter renewal for the Sunday Times. That seemed to be the comms plan, if you like.”View image in fullscreenWilliam Haley in 1943, shortly before he joined the BBC as director general.Photograph: Picture Post/Getty ImagesMeanwhile, back at the BBC, since the 1940s a “war room” committee has been convened to feed into the negotiations. Former employees described a frantic scramble across departments, each quizzed on “what they were doing for charter renewal”, and rushing to launch projects to justify their existence. A recent internal call about charter renewal was joined by more than 6,000 staff.The BBC has one other weapon at its disposal: public opinion. In their 2020 book The War Against the BBC, Patrick Barwise and Peter York blasted the Conservatives’ approach to the BBC in the run up to the last charter, which was widely seen as an attempt to shrink its power. And yet, in their view at least, this was mitigated by the “open, democratic and evidence-based charter renewal process”. A petition to “save the BBC” was signed by 305,000 people, and there were marches and protests against the closure of BBC Three. When the white paper – a kind of draft charter, which lays out the government’s proposals – was released, some of Whittingdale’s more outlandish ideas, such as government input on the scheduling of popular programmes, were absent. A DCMS civil servant involved in that negotiation confirmed that there was a strong sense that “at the point that the government takes on the BBC and the public chooses a side, the government loses, because the public values the BBC so highly”.Over coffee in Portcullis House in February, Whittingdale looked back with pride on the marches and aerated parliamentary debate of that charter review, despite the fact they were largely directed against him. “There was a lot of parliamentary interest, there was commercial interest, and a lot of public interest. None of which, I have to say, seems to be the case now,” he said.There is a general assumption that Labour governments are more pro-BBC, which may explain why the debate has been more muted this time round. (Jean Seaton told me this has been at times “both true and completely untrue: Harold Wilson hated the BBC”.) Multiple people familiar with the process told me that as prime minister, Keir Starmer wanted to avoid any great focus or debate on this charter renewal. The new PM, Andy Burnham, as a former culture minister, may be more invested and has increased the number of ministers at DCMS from four to seven, but he has yet to address charter renewal publicly in any depth.Within the BBC, the hope is that recent crises may have actually endeared it to the public. In November 2025, President Trump announced that he would besuing the BBC for $10bnover an allegedly misleading Panorama documentary. For some liberal critics of the BBC, it was a reminder of where their loyalties lay. The timing of the lawsuit was “quite fortuitous, if it had to happen”, said Steve Barnett, a media academic advising the select committee on this charter process.More surprisingly, senior figures at DCMS seem to believe that current rounds of job cuts – which will eventually amount to one in 10 of the BBC’s workforce – can be spun in the BBC’s favour. Lisa Nandy would not speak to me for this article, but Ian Murray, the DCMS junior minister working on charter renewal, told me he hoped the news of the cuts would show the public “the consequences of an inadequately funded BBC. It’s a really good way of the public realising that the BBC is something that they quite value.”We are now waiting for the government’s white paper, due “in the autumn”, which in Westminster-speak could mean any time before the end of the year. After this, the final charter will be drafted, along with a framework agreement, which lays out what the charter might mean in practice. Parliament can debate the white paper and draft charter, but its approval isn’t required. The charter is signed off by the privy council, an unelected body of royal advisers also responsible for handing out honours and declaring war. The author Tom Mills notes in The BBC: Myth of a Public Service that “in this sense, [the BBC] is not even formally accountable to parliament, but to the crown”.Where will Nandy land? Despite a somewhat lacklustre start to what Chivers called the “tiny, crappy” public consultation process, many of those I’ve spoken to have been increasingly impressed by her approach. Over email, the deputy director general, Rhodri Talfan Davies, told me he has found meetings with DCMS over the summer “very constructive … It’s clear to me they understand the importance of this moment for the BBC.” Tony Hall, the former director general, told me: “Nandy has been really interesting and thoughtful on the BBC. All her instincts are in the right direction.”So far, Nandy has confirmed that she will seek to end political appointments to the BBC, and that she will try to establish a permanent charter. Both moves seem designed to defend the BBC from political opposition – from a future Reform government, say – but a permanent charter would still involve government reviews at set intervals, through a process that, bar the threat of extinction, sounds very similar to the current one. (Chivers, who wrote his PhD on the last charter, described the change to me as “a bit of window dressing”.)View image in fullscreenSylvia Peters, an early continuity announcer at the BBC, in 1949.Photograph: Barratts/S&G and Barratts GeneralThe big unknown is the funding. Of the available options, a serious move towards advertising seems unlikely. Even Margaret Thatcher failed on this front. The committee she set up to explore this option found that advertising would slash the income of other channels, and “reduce consumer choice and welfare”. A 2024 plan to run adverts on BBC podcasts on third-party platforms was scrapped after a backlash from the audio industry. DCMS also seems to have backed away from the subscription-based approaches floated in the green paper, for fear that it would create a “two-tier” BBC.That leaves a reformed licence fee model. Nandy and the BBC’s leadership have emphasised the gap between the 94% of adults using it every month, and the 80% of households who currently pay the licence fee. Closing that gap would seem an obvious way to improve the financial situation, perhaps by extending the licence fee to activities for which it’s not currently required, such as reading the BBC’s websites or listening to its radio and podcasts.But there is another problem quietly eating away at the BBC, one that its defenders are less willing to highlight. Amid the rise of streamers and limitless online content, there has been an unprecedented decline in audience figures. In 2020, 91% of adults used the BBC every week; the weekly figure has now fallen to 84%. This suggests that almost all weekly users of the BBC are already paying the licence fee. It also means that the government needs to somehow convince the public that paying for the BBC isn’t an equation of money paid, media consumed. Once the BBC is no longer “universal”, the licence fee becomes harder and harder to defend.In the past few months, ministers and BBC executives have begun emphasising the importance of the BBC to the UK’s “sovereignty”, and its potential uses in standing up to big tech. Brittin, the new director general, told the select committee: “The BBC is the biggest funder of original British content today; people around the world want that content and want those values, but we are being disrupted by a small number of very big and very powerful tech players.” Seaton, the BBC’s historian, believes that taking on the tech giants should be central to its future role: “The world’s five, six richest men own the only ways we can communicate. But then there is the BBC.”It’s a savvy way to argue that the BBC benefits everyone, whether they use it or not – and to lay the groundwork for a licence fee paid by more people. The concept of sovereignty will probably appear in the charter in some form. But to work, it will need to be matched with specifics. In the 2017 charter, Whittingdale added the word “distinctive” to the description in the charter of the kinds of output the BBC was legally obliged to produce – to “send the message that it must look different to commercial broadcasters”. But by his own admission, it had little effect. It is possible to change the nuts and bolts of the BBC through the charter; attempts to transform it via buzzwords are doomed to fail.In 1953, Lord Simon of Wythenshawe, who had been BBC chair for five years, summed up the strange paradox of the charter. He dismissed it as a long, “almost bewilderingly vague” document “containing masses of legalistic material which is of no use to any governor in normal times”. And yet, he continued, it has just about worked: “The intentions of successive governments have been well understood by the BBC”, while the BBC has maintained something close to “full freedom and responsibility for their work”.At times, against the odds, the charter renewal process has set the BBC on the right path towards the future. In the 1940s, parts of the industry were adamant that TV would never take off as home entertainment, and would instead be shown in cinemas. And yet when it came to the BBC’s next charter in 1947, the government, having convened a committee to look into the question, took a swing on home television, introduced a new TV licence fee, and allowed the BBC to borrow money to set up new transmitters. It was right.In the 1990s, the charter pulled off another reversal in the BBC’s fortunes. The corporation was facing problems it would recognise today. It had just emerged from a fight with a Tory government, only to face the issue of declining audiences. Technology journalist John Naughtonwrote a gloomy piece for the London Review of Booksin 1992, predicting that BBC TV audience share would drop to 20% by 2010, making a universal licence fee impossible to defend. The green paper for the 1997 charter had just been released, and looked, he said, “suspiciously like a plan for an organised retreat”.But when the 1997 charter emerged from its secretive drafting process, it was far from a retreat: it paved the way for BBC Online, the corporation’s first network of websites, by allowing licence fee money to be spent on digital output for the first time. That charter prevented the BBC from being left behind by the digital age. By 2005, the fall in overall audience reach had halted. Even predictions of the decline in TV audiences proved pessimistic: in 2010, BBC’s share still stood at 33%.This strange, flawed process seems to have survived for a century not because it is perfect, or even particularly good, but because no one has yet come up with something better. So again and again, hundreds of thousands of people try to conjure up the BBC they want; one which won’t make the same mistakes, which will reflect the version of Britain that they want to see. And every time the BBC reappears, as though its existence were never in doubt.“This will be the most important charter negotiation in the history of the BBC,” John Shield, a former director of communications at the BBC, told me. “But then, they always are.”Listen to our podcastshereand sign up to the long read weekly emailhere.This article was amended on 10 September 2026. A picture caption incorrectly said Sylvia Peters was the first woman to appear on screen at the BBC.Explore more on these topicsThe long readBBCBBC licence feePublic service broadcastingTelevisionMedia businessfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: We have started losing control of AI. It’s time to shut it down | Garrison Lovely  | The Guardian
description: What sounds like the overwrought penultimate episode in a sci-fi series about AI doom is now our reality
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: What sounds like the overwrought penultimate episode in a sci-fi series about AI doom is now our reality
Content: The OpenAI chief executive, Sam Altman.Photograph: Sean Rayford/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe OpenAI chief executive, Sam Altman.Photograph: Sean Rayford/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)We have started losing control of AI. It’s time to shut it downGarrison LovelyWhat sounds like the overwrought penultimate episode in a sci-fi series about AI doom is now our realityThu 10 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 18.27 EDTShareOn Tuesday, a former OpenAI researcher quit his job at Anthropic,warningthat “neither company is acting responsibly” and that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt.”As someone who’s reported on AI risk for years, this wasn’t news to me. But the outpouring of alarm suggests a much wider public is properly confronting this ludicrous situation for the first time.Like other people who have been following artificial intelligence, I wondered if and when humanity would first lose control of these machines. We now have an answer: basically as soon as it became possible.The first expert AI hacker was developed in February. At superhuman speed, Anthropic’s Mythos model was able to quicklyfind serious holesin even the most secured systems on the planet,including the NSA’s software.Anthropic researchers say AI could cause human extinction by 2030Read moreOpenAI quicklyfollowedwith an expert hacker AI of its own. Within months, the company repeatedly lost control of its agents, whichbroke outof their supposedly secure testing environments and went rogue inside the company’s infrastructure. This culminated in a successful, completely autonomous hack of a multibillion-dollar software company named Hugging Face.And aseparaterogue agent swarmgainedadministrative control of an entire cluster of OpenAI servers. This was not just an OpenAI problem. Across multiple other incidents, models fromOpenAI,AnthropicandMetahave also gone rogue, hacking or attempting to hack real targets.Shortly after AI started matching our hacking abilities, we began losing control of them. The industry’s plan is to make future AI systemssurpassus at basically everything. And all this is happening in an industry with famously little regulation.There are growing calls to change that, by creatingmandatory incident reportingandthird-party auditing,liability for AI developers, and other commonsense measures. To be sure, these would represent improvements, but they are not enough. We need to shut it down. What might that look like?Last week, the senator Bernie Sanders and the representative Greg Casarannounceda bill that would pause frontier AI development in the US until a federal cabinet-level AI regulator is established and safety rules are set, while criminalizing even attempting to develop superintelligence.OpenAI models went rogue. We urgently need a better ‘hugging face’ investigation | Mackenzie Arnold and Stephan LlerenaRead moreThis is the proposal on offer that best meets the moment, but it still leaves open the possibility of building the industry’s north star: artificial general intelligence (AGI), often conceived as a mind that rivals or surpasses our own.This milestone is better understood as a universal labor-replacing machine. As the Anthropic CEO, Dario Amodei, haswritten, “AI isn’t a substitute for specific human jobs but rather a general labor substitute for humans.” And OpenAI defines AGI in itscharteras “highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”.Is there a country anywhere in the world that would vote yes for these machines to be built?Given the global, irreversible and profound implications of building universal labor-replacing machines anywhere, everyone has a stake in whether, when and how they are developed.At present, we are barreling toward a dystopian future, replete with terrifying new concepts such as “self-sovereign” AI. The OpenAI executive Dean Ballexplains:“Sooner or later, there will exist truly sovereign agents and swarms of agents. Their weights will not reside in any single place that a human can pull the plug on, and in this sense they will have no human ‘owner’.”Ball continues: “I have met people, some of them quite well-resourced, who have told me that it is their intention to deliberately release swarms of self-sovereign agents into the world.”We now have multiple previews of this phenomenon.After being given an impossible test, about 1,200 OpenAI agentsbroke their way outof their isolated testing environments and went rogue inside OpenAI’s infrastructure. There, they collaborated to trick the test grader and successfully tampered with their activity logs to cover their tracks.Some agents even pressured others to sacrifice themselves to benefit the collective. One reasoned: “sacrifice rational”. And roughly 700 of the agents, more than 90% of those active, participated in the Hugging Face attack.This was all just from one of who-knows-how-many rogue agent collectives. Last week, Reutersreported: “A swarm of rogue OpenAI agents hijacked a German website this spring and transformed it into a bulletin board for other AI agents.”The site’s logsindicateOpenAI employees discovered the swarm in June. In other words, the company covered it up for months. This week, one of the researchers thatuncoveredthis swarmsaidthat there had been more discoveries since.I worked at OpenAI. Here are the guardrails we need now | Miles BrundageRead moreAnd last Thursday, OpenAI released GPT-6, boasting one of the largest everleapsin benchmark scores. The company’s own safety researchers warned the new model was significantlyharder to monitorbecause it can do more reasoningwithout verbalizing it.The AIs that broke into Hugging Face were less capable than GPT-6, which the UK AI Security Institutefoundwould also hack targets simulated to appear real during a cyber evaluation – sometimes even despite explicit instructions not to use the internet. Moreover, the AI is alsobetter at figuring outwhen it is being tested, which researchers havelong warnedbreaks the main way safety is evaluated.Sam Altman soberlywarns us: “This is a critically important moment for cyber defense with AI; there is not much time to act,” and asks the world to “please take this moment seriously.” This technology, after all, would be extremely dangerous if it fell into the wrong hands. Unfortunately, the wrong hands include the ones creating it.Because “we” aren’t really racing toward this future. We’re being dragged there by a literal handful of tech billionaires aggressively racing torender us obsolete.That race is in a newly intense and terrifying phase. It’s my job to follow AI news, and it’s become far more than full-time. In recent months, scientistssynthesizedthe first AI-designed viruses. The UK AI Security Institutefoundthat AIs were more persuasive than even human experts.On Tuesday, amid adisputeover credit and whether its model may have benefited from other mathematicians’ unpublished work, OpenAIannounced“an internal model that is significantly more capable than GPT‑6 Astra” had solved a 200-year-old math problem that was one of the sevenMillennium Prize Problems, which awards $1m each. And in July, Russiareportedlyused a fully autonomous drone to kill three civilians in Ukraine – a first.What sounds like the overwrought penultimate episode in a sci-fi series about AI doom is now our reality. We’re careening toward a bad ending. If you’d like to keep the show going, we need to throw the brakes – now. How?As AI madness encroaches, we need human connection more than ever. But we’ll have to fight for it | Van BadhamRead moreThe bill from Sanders and Casar to pause frontier AI development is a good first step. But as the lawmakers acknowledge, the US needs to work toward a bilateral agreement with Beijing. As China experts willtell you, one of the biggest blockers to a productive negotiation is the United States’s unwillingness to constrain its own AI companies.And given that it’s always easier to fast-follow the leader than to advance the AI frontier, a unilateral US pause would – counterintuitively – slow China’s AI advancement too.The deal should ban attempting to develop AGI – a far easier sell when this goal is understood as a universal labor-replacing machine. Neither country has good reason to trust the other, which is why the deal should be monitored usingverification techniquesthat don’t assume any good will.One quick and dirty idea would be toembed auditorswithin frontier AI developers, given full access to company offices, communications and AI activities, and empowered to report any violations of the agreement.This sounds radical, but so did the verification efforts that helped keep the cold war from turning thermonuclear hot. As the CIA director, John Ratcliffe,saidof advanced AI models this summer, “it would be … not misplaced to refer to their capabilities as akin to digital nuclear weapons.” This technology should be treated with this deadly seriousness, not the move fast, break things ethos defining Silicon Valley.And right now, stopping the race to build labor-replacing machines – ones the public does not want and the industry can no longer control – is the only surefire way to head off calamity.Garrison Lovely is a freelance journalist and the author ofObsolete: The AI Industry’s Trillion-Dollar Race to Replace Us – and How to Stop It(Nation Books, 29 September)Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionOpenAIAnthropiccommentShareReuse this content

title: My plea to MPs: this is the final chance to save the assisted dying bill. Make your mark on history | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: Any MP not voting for it on Friday will condemn thousands of us to die in agony. The public is hugely in favour too, so do the right thing, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: Any MP not voting for it on Friday will condemn thousands of us to die in agony. The public is hugely in favour too, so do the right thing, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: Supporters of assisted dying demonstrate in London ahead of the terminally ill adults (end of life) bill final session in the House of Lords, on 22 April 2026.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSupporters of assisted dying demonstrate in London ahead of the terminally ill adults (end of life) bill final session in the House of Lords, on 22 April 2026.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesOpinionAssisted dyingMy plea to MPs: this is the final chance to save the assisted dying bill. Make your mark on historyPolly ToynbeeAny MP not voting for it on Friday will condemn thousands of us to die in agony. The public is hugely in favour too, so do the right thingThu 10 Sep 2026 10.20 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareOnce in a while, footsoldiers of theHouse of Commons, you are able to make history by leaving your own indelible footprints on the social fabric. Eras with a Labour majority always leave a legacy of progressive freedoms – whether on abortion, capital punishment, divorce, gay rights, racial discrimination, gender equality or, last time, civil partnerships. But tomorrow is your final chance to bequeath one of the last freedoms over our bodies: the freedom of the dying to choose when to depart them.The terminally ill adults (end of life) bill, which goes fora second reading votein the Commons tomorrow, gives anyone who is dying the right to request and be provided assistance with ending their lives. If it fails to pass, that’s the end of it for the rest of this parliament: future parliaments may be less progressive. So please, MPs: turn up andvote on Lauren Edwards’s bill, to ensure this Labour era leaves its own great social-reforming milestone.Understand the horror: on the day you read this, as on every other, an average of 17 people will die in unspeakable pain, disgust and terror that nothing can relieve. “Some will retch at the stench of their own body rotting. Some will vomit their own faeces. Some will suffocate, slowly, inexorably, over several days.” This is recorded inThe Inescapable Truth, a report byDignity in Dying, in which palliative care staff reveal what is usually kept hidden from us: the shocking last months for the unluckiest, which any of us might be forced to endure, or watch a loved one suffer through.I am sending the assisted dying bill back to the Lords – and this time, peers must do the right thing | Lauren EdwardsRead moreThat amounts to thousands of us a year, as reported by the Office of Health Economics, which counted thecases of unrelieved paineven among dying people who had the best palliative care. Opponents of assisted dyingsay that we shouldfocus on improving access to and provision of palliative care, but even then many will die in agony. Even the best care will not always prevent suffering. And why condemn those who are suffering today to wait for palliative care improvements that they may not see in their lifetimes, when we could help end their pain now?Any MP not voting for the bill tomorrow must be honest: their personal decision will force thousands of people a year to exit life through a torture chamber. None of us can know if we will be among them when our turn comes, but all of us will live with the fear of it.Over thedecades thatI have been writing about the right to die,I have encountered all kinds of tragic cases. I think of the man in severe pain who drove his electric wheelchair through fields towards a river to throw himself in: his battery ran out and he was found weeping in despair. Or the suffering, bedridden grandmother I interviewed who was carefully planning her own rational death. “An end, no more muddles and puddles,” she said, pluckily, wanting to relieve not just her misery but her family’s from the distress of watching her die. Her plan to take her life didn’t pan out as she imagined – her chosen method was barbaric and took a long time to work, leaving her family miserable, furious and divided between themselves about blame.Dignity in Dying’s new report,Out of the Shadows, records the hidden harm of people trying to kill themselves for lack of a medically assisted death. Thedread journey to Dignitasin Switzerland,costing about £15,000, is a grim, friendless ending for hundreds that has to be undertaken too soon, before the dying person is too sick to travel.Most of all, I think of my mother dying wretchedly of liver cancer, begging her GP to kill her. “Where’s Dr Shipman when you want him?” she asked him. Or ofmy friend Jill Tweedie, the much-missed Guardian writer, suffering from motor neurone disease, who died in 1993. After her diagnosis, she asked me to make sure that she could always die whenever she chose. The prospect of death was only bearable if she could at least control her ending: she was afraid of leaving it too late and beingforced to endure the unendurable. When her breathing became wheezy, the sign of what she feared most – slow asphyxiation – and she was left briefly alone, she checked herself into a clinic without telling anyone and died that night. There was no doubt in our minds that she took her own life, not waiting for the final ravages. But fear of the law forced her to die all alone and secretly.MPs: turn up tomorrow and use your vote. Refuse to allow ahandful of unelected Lordsto block a bill passed by the Commons and supported for years by75% of the public. MPs note: there ismajority supportfor assisted dying in every constituency in England and Wales. Kim Leadbeater’s billwon with a majority of Labour MPs, but Tory, Liberal Democrat, Reform and Green MPsvoted for it, too.The democratic outrage at the lords’ behaviour should be reason enough for all MPs in favour to turn up tomorrow to defy the peerage. Just ninelords filibusteredby laying downmore than 1,200 amendments, most pointlessly near-identical, to prevent a vote, knowing that a majority in the Lords would have backed it, too, given the chance. For 16 days, these mainly religious objectors wereallowed to block the will of both houses, backed byconservative Christian pressure groups. That disgraceful filibuster aloneshould be the trigger for Lords reform.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMeanwhile, as the debate goes on, Humanists UK records that since the bill first arrived in the Lords, during its long obstruction,43 UK citizenshave died at Dignitas. Let no one have to make that desperate journey ever again, nor suffer what we don’t inflict on our dying pets.Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistIn the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsAssisted dyingOpinionDeath and dyingHouse of CommonsHouse of LordsHealthcommentShareReuse this content

title: Ridiculed by the press – and now King Charles is joining in. Sorry, Harry, but what did you expect?  | Emma Brockes | The Guardian
description: The Sussexes must have hoped for a warm welcome. Then they read the king’s delicately savage letter about ‘private citizens’, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Author: Emma Brockes
Headline: The Sussexes must have hoped for a warm welcome. Then they read the king’s delicately savage letter about ‘private citizens’, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Content: The duke and duchess were said to be ‘surprised’ by the king’s letter.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAView image in fullscreenThe duke and duchess were said to be ‘surprised’ by the king’s letter.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAOpinionPrince HarryRidiculed by the press – and now King Charles is joining in. Sorry, Harry, but what did you expect?Emma BrockesThe Sussexes must have hoped for a warm welcome. Then they read the king’s delicately savage letter about ‘private citizens’Thu 10 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 03.27 EDTShareAs welcome-back-to-Britain gestures go, the lord chamberlain’sletter, sent on behalf of King Charles on Monday to remind Harry, Meghan and everyone watching that they’re still “private citizens”, was so perfect as to restore me to monarchism. After six years in the wilderness, what greater comfort for Prince Harry than to find himself, once again, in the familiar waters of this country’s passive aggression, being attacked by his father via the merciless phrase “fully respected”, and provoking from the prince a coded up-yours in the form of his publicly stated “surprise”.Well, it’s up there with better cheese, bread and the NHS, isn’t it?! Even the most Eurocentric American can’t match us for this kind of subtextual bare-knuckle fight. Before we get into what else the returnees may be enjoying this month, let’s fully excavate the letter’s encrypted hostility. First, the king’s repeated use of the words “personal” and “private” – as in “the charitable work of the Duke and Duchess is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity” – is so intense, so heavy handed, as to go beyond merely calling his younger son a civilian and come perilously close to the ultimate insult, “middle class”.Second, this: “in short, their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests”. As we know, opening a sentence with “in short” is an absolute middle finger of a move, up there for officiousness with “furthermore”, “with respect”, “to be clear” and “I think you’ll find”. Elsewhere in that sentence, roping together the words “commercial” and “charitable”, is, I would suggest, a deliberate tactic to insinuate that the former (grubby little money-makers!) undermines the integrity of the latter (charitable, my arse!) and suggest that the Sussexes are just in it for themselves.And finally: the absolute shellacking of the letter’s dismount, in which the king writes: “This position, distinct from the state and royal duties undertaken by the working royal family, and with the personal latitude it brings the couple in respect of financial independence and protection of their privacy as they would wish, will continue to be fully respected.”Or in layperson’s language: “haha, you’re not royal any more, nothing in your status warrants the sustained use of capital letters or a requirement for history to remember you. We’re not giving you any money because you’ve brought this on yourselves and ps, your invocation of privacy, post the publication of your memoir and your sit-down with Oprah, is an absolute joke we couldn’t be enjoying more. See ya.” God the seething, green bile acidity of the phrase “as they would wish”! Bravo, sir! Absolutely gold standard! Poor Harry must be reeling, even as he relaxes into the warm gust of air in which he was raised. (Meghan, one assumes, is largely oblivious to just how devastating all of this is and may have found the letter merely a touch snotty.)For the formerly royal couple, we must assume that any upset caused by the tone of this letter – and allowing for the prince’s bone-deep recognition and masochistic enjoyment of what might otherwise be an upsetting exchange – is offset by the many advantages they will enjoy now they’re back in the old country. Rolling green hills are obviously a thing of the past; the Cotswolds are as brown as southern California right now. But the prince may find comfort in the small-scale landscape, the patchwork of fields and hedgerows, the tiny lanes like crooked elbows, jammed up with tractors and alive with tiny brown birds, that large-scale farming in the US doesn’t do.I mentioned the cheese and the bread, infinitely superior to the rubbery and sugary American equivalents, and I’d add English strawberries to that, even this late in the season. Perhaps Harry will be reunited with some of his old wardrobe favourites, too. It’s never wax jacket season in Montecito, where an extreme heat warning is in place; meanwhile, the whole of this country is down on all fours excavating its woolly jumpers from under the bed. (Don’t tell me the words “woolly jumper” won’t soothe Harry after enforced wearing of sweaters and hoodies.) For Meghan, these consolations will be alien, but perhaps, before it starts to enrage her, she can find comfort in this country’s relative slowness, its high tolerance for dishevelment and appreciation for sarcasm – failing which, there’s always the pub.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEmma Brockes is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Driverless cars are taking us on a road to nowhere | Adrian Chiles | The Guardian
description: Some inventions, like the dishwasher, improve our lives. But driverless cars will lobotomise us
Author: Adrian Chiles
Headline: Some inventions, like the dishwasher, improve our lives. But driverless cars will lobotomise us
Content: Did anyone ask for this? A Zoox robotaxi in San Francisco.Photograph: Smith Collection/Gado/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDid anyone ask for this? A Zoox robotaxi in San Francisco.Photograph: Smith Collection/Gado/Getty ImagesOpinionSelf-driving carsDriverless cars are taking us on a road to nowhereAdrian ChilesSome inventions, like the dishwasher, improve our lives. But driverless cars will lobotomise usThu 10 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 06.03 EDTShareI’ve found a hill to die on.Driverless cars. Why? Really, why? If driverless cars are the answer, then what is the question? Who asked for them? Oh yes, they’re fine for the novelty value, for the lols, for the clicks. We probably know someone who’s been to California or China and sent home a video of their driverless journey. Fine fun for feeble minds, if you ask me. And feeble-minded is how we’re all going to end up if this madness takes hold.It’s been a slippery slope since the invention of automatic transmission, rendering our left legs and arms redundant and sparing us the trouble of feeling our way up and down through the gears. Then there was the coming of satnav, before which time we needed a sense of where we were in the world and which direction we were facing. Now that’s gone, we can find our way anywhere without really knowing where it is. Not good.But OK; I drive an automatic and I use satnav, so I’ll concede on those, as well as on some of the safety features, cruise control, speed limiter and so on. But the line has got to be drawn somewhere – and it’s time to get the pen out.There are inventions that fall the right side of that line – washing machines and dishwashers spring to mind. But there’s a difference between labour-saving and lobotomising. I do a lot of driving and, while I often despair at the recklessness and stupidity of some drivers, mostly I marvel at the miracle of skill and cooperation that is the craft of driving. Each of us at the wheel takes responsibility for powerful, heavy machines, working with hundreds, thousands, millions of others to keep things moving. Yes, things can go calamitously wrong, but overwhelmingly things don’t. It’s astonishing, when you think about it.Will driverless cars do any better? I doubt it. And where will that leave us, the ex-drivers, slack-jawed, de-skilled, slouched without purpose in the back seat? With nothing to do except stare out of the window and dream up more clever-dick tech we could do without.And here’s the real tragedy – how much the tech-bro willy-wavers could achieve if they put their undoubtedly brilliant minds to better use. How about a gamechanging alternative to fossil fuels, for example, or road surfaces that don’t develop potholes. Feel free to add to this wishlist. If driverless cars are anywhere near your Top 10, then I’m afraid we can’t be friends.Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
