title: The UK’s sanctions on Israeli settlements are a great victory – but must be only the beginning | Em Hilton | The Guardian
description: The change in policy is a direct result of sustained pressure from activists and organisers across the Palestine movement. But what comes next, asks Jewish writer and organiser Em Hilton
Author: Em Hilton
Headline: The change in policy is a direct result of sustained pressure from activists and organisers across the Palestine movement. But what comes next, asks Jewish writer and organiser Em Hilton
Content: A view of the Israeli settlement of Ma’ale Adumim in the occupied West Bank, 8 September 2026.Photograph: Ohad Zwigenberg/APView image in fullscreenA view of the Israeli settlement of Ma’ale Adumim in the occupied West Bank, 8 September 2026.Photograph: Ohad Zwigenberg/APOpinionWest BankThe UK’s sanctions on Israeli settlements are a great victory – but must be only the beginningEm HiltonThe change in policy is a direct result of sustained pressure from activists and organisers across the Palestine movement. But what comes next?Thu 10 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 08.34 EDTShareThe announcement on Tuesday by the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, of animport ban on goodsfrom illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories, as well as a comprehensive sanctions regime, is a hard-won victory for the Palestine solidarity movement.This is not simply a change of heart by the government: it is a direct result of sustained pressure from activists and organisers across the Palestine movement, who have consistently held the government’s feet to the fire over itscomplicity in the atrocitiesbeing committed in Gaza and the West Bank. Miliband’s announcement shows us what organised and persistent campaigning can achieve, and inspires confidence that movements can force political change.Over the past three years, Palestine has become a political and electoral challenge for the Labour party, as well as a fundamental issue of public conscience. This move signals a political reset in the UK government’s foreign policy approach to Israel. But as the UN special rapporteur Francesca Albanese has said, a ban on goods from settlements must be part of a“true paradigm shift”; the government can, and must, go further.There has already been sustained backlash at the move, with the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee,accusing Miliband of “Jew hate”on the Today programme. As a Jewish campaigner, let me be clear: holding Israel to account for its human rights violations in the West Bank is not antisemitic. To conflate the actions of violent settlers and the Israeli government with Jewish people everywhere makes us accountable for the actions of those who do not represent us.There is also warranted scepticism about the Labour government’s commitment to holding Israel accountable. But an “all or nothing” approach would be a mistake, when there is so much that can be built on here. We can certainly retain our anger at the government’s complicity. No sanction can offset the foreign policy decisions made by the former prime minister Keir Starmer and former foreign secretary David Lammy, therepression of domestic pro-Palestine advocacy, or the sheer loss of life. But we must balance this with cautious optimism that the political tide is turning.Political victories are mobilising – they fuel the belief that collective action can work. So now is the time to push at the open door. But what comes next? How do we ensure that accountability for Israel’s oppression of Palestinians is not limited to the settlements, but builds momentum for further meaningful action in support of Palestinian human rights?First, we should demand that these trade sanctions are enforced and expanded. Eleven nations, includingCanada and France, have joined the UK in these measures; we must call for further coordination and alignment with other western governments.The necessary next step is a full arms embargo and an end to cooperation with Israeli security forces – to truly have teeth, these sanctions must not take with one hand and then give with another. Miliband has said that “we’ve already suspended over 30 arms licences used by the IDF in Gaza. That suspension remains fully in place”, and that the government will “now also refuse all licence applications for arms and other exports that materially contribute to the occupation”. Butcomponents of F-35 jetscontinue to be exported to Israel and used for operations in Gaza, as are surveillance technologies such as drones and radar made in the UK byElbit Systems. This is a total dereliction of duty by the British government.Miliband’s announcements were a necessary reminder that a just political future is possible and, within it, a reckoning with past crimes. As a campaigner, I have borne witness to Israel’s most egregious human rights violations: I have documented Israeli settlers committing pogroms against the community of Al-Mufaqara, sat in Palestinian villages threatened with home demolitions and army raids, and witnessed the ongoing daily misery of Israel’s apartheid policies. This has all strengthened my motivation to see the end of the Israeli occupation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis announcement is the beginning, not the end, of the road. It is a hopeful indication of what happens when collective power is translated into political change. We must sit with the idea that Palestinians will see some justice and reprieve from relentless destruction and displacement. I hope I’m not wrong.Em Hilton is a Jewish writer and organiser. She is the co-founder of Na’amod: UK Jews Against Israeli Occupation, and the policy director at Diaspora AllianceExplore more on these topicsWest BankOpinionIsraelMiddle East and north AfricaPalestineGazaForeign policyEd MilibandcommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s comments on the Falkland Islands reflect a fractured US-UK relationship | Ted Widmer | The Guardian
description: President suggested US might not help UK if Argentina tried to seize Falklands – a new low for UK-US ‘special relationship’
Author: Ted Widmer
Headline: President suggested US might not help UK if Argentina tried to seize Falklands – a new low for UK-US ‘special relationship’
Content: ‘In 1941, Churchill and Franklin D Roosevelt articulated the shared UK-US values in their famous Atlantic charter.’Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPAView image in fullscreen‘In 1941, Churchill and Franklin D Roosevelt articulated the shared UK-US values in their famous Atlantic charter.’Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPAOpinionDonald TrumpTrump’s comments on the Falkland Islands reflect a fractured US-UK relationshipTed WidmerPresident suggested US might not help UK if Argentina tried to seize Falklands – a new low for UK-US ‘special relationship’Thu 10 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 11.05 EDTShareLast week,Donald Trumpsuggested in an interview with the British TV channel GB News that he might not help the UK if Argentina tried again to seize theFalkland Islands. It was a new low for UK-US relations.The “special relationship” (Winston Churchill’s phrase) was never perfect, but the UK helped the US on countless occasions, from Korea to Iraq to Afghanistan. The US often stood by the UK as well – although not during the Suez Crisis of 1956, but Ronald Reagan’s government provided significant intelligence and logistics support to Britain during the dust-up over the Falklands in 1982. That relationship is fading fast.Trump characteristically turned the conversation toward a grievance, and his disappointment with the UK’s initial reluctance to provide support for the Iran war launched on 28 February by Israel and the United States.With no friends left to burn, Trump is running out of diplomatic ammunition | Rafael BehrRead moreThat reluctance was fairly easy to understand at the time, given that the White House refused to consultNatoallies as it planned its sneak attack, and the goals of the war were (and remain) imprecise and inconsistent.It should be added that Nato is a defensive alliance, designed to resist a Russian invasion from the east, not support a US invasion from the west, to seize Greenland from a Nato ally. Further, Nato has no business in the Middle East. The words “North Atlantic” inside “North Atlantic Treaty Organization” make it clear that Nato is all about Europe, bringing North American troops (including both Canadians and Americans) into an interlocking defense structure with European partners.That includes roughly 80,000 US troops stationed in Europe, a strategic fact of the highest order, one that would suggest careful vetting of remarks about a Nato ally like the United Kingdom. Roughly 10,000 of those troops arebased in the UK, in fact.Emboldened by Trump’s careless remarks, the president of Argentina, Javier Milei (a fan of Margaret Thatcher), delivered a windy speech about “the winds of change”, designed to shore up his sinking popularity, approximately 37% in July. Hehintedthat the US would back Argentina if it were to renew its territorial ambitions, and called the UK a nation “in decline”.Those tremors deepened early this week, as the UK’s announcement of sanctions on Israeli settlers released a predictable explosion from theTrump administration, and Israeli threats to recognize Argentinean sovereignty in the Falklands.The UK will survive Milei’s speech, which stemmed from Trump’s unfocused complaints, and the surreal fabrications that get so much attention yet contribute so little knowledge. The diplomatic flare-up will fade, but memories will linger of Trump’s poorly chosen words, and the ease with which he chose to abandon Britain – on British television, no less.It’s also another stark reminder of how foreign the themes of democratic aspiration are to the 47th president. Were Argentina to seize the Falklands, it would overturn the result of a very democratic election, the 2013referendumin which 99.8% of the islanders chose to remain connected to the UK. More than 90% voted; of 1,517 votes cast, a whopping 1,513 were for remain. That’s the voice of the people speaking.Democratic presidents have never had a problem talking about democracy. Similarly, most Republican presidents have understood this language. Nixon was not gifted in this way, and George W Bush got many things wrong – Iraq above all – but he seemed to mean it when he spoke of the yearnings of peoples to be free.Trump’s Nato remarks rang hollow – but he recognizes something real | Christopher S ChivvisRead moreRonald Reagan could achieve poetry at times, as he spoke of those suffering behind the Iron Curtain, and in other autocracies, and meditated on how the US had historically given hope to the world’s disenfranchised. In his 1989 farewell address, he argued: “She’s still a beacon, still a magnet for all who must have freedom, for all the pilgrims from all the lost places who are hurtling through the darkness, toward home.”It’s impossible to imagine these words being spoken from today’s Oval Office, just as it would be difficult to find a president more alienated from the goals of genuine self-determination.In 1941, Churchill and Franklin D Roosevelt articulated the shared UK-US values in their famous Atlantic charter – a statement about their commitment to democracy, free trade and peace.A year later, they issued an anniversary statement about their shared goals and values. It offers wistful reading at a time when the language of great ideals appears to be woefully dated:“When victory comes, we shall stand shoulder-to-shoulder in seeking to nourish the great ideals for which we fight. It is a worthwhile battle. It will be so recognised through all the ages, even amid the unfortunate peoples who follow false gods today. We reaffirm our principles. They will bring us to a happier world.”Ted Widmer is a former White House speechwriter, and the author of an anthology, American Speeches. His most recent book is The Living Declaration: A Biography of America’s Founding Text (Library of America)Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionFalkland IslandsArgentinaNatoUS foreign policyTrump administrationRonald ReagancommentShareReuse this content

title: Nine years after Daphne Caruana Galizia’s murder, Europe must finally address Malta’s culture of impunity | Pieter Omtzigt and Emanuel Delia | The Guardian
description: Much of the corruption exposed by this brave woman remains unpunished. Brussels must carry on her work and demand reform, say Pieter Omtzigt of the Council of Europe and campaigner Emanuel Delia
Author: Emanuel Delia
Headline: Much of the corruption exposed by this brave woman remains unpunished. Brussels must carry on her work and demand reform, say Pieter Omtzigt of the Council of Europe and campaigner Emanuel Delia
Content: Protest called by Daphne Caruana Galizia's family and civic movements outside the office of the prime minister in Valletta, Malta, 29 November 2019.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenProtest called by Daphne Caruana Galizia's family and civic movements outside the office of the prime minister in Valletta, Malta, 29 November 2019.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionDaphne Caruana GaliziaNine years after Daphne Caruana Galizia’s murder, Europe must finally address Malta’s culture of impunityPieter OmtzigtandEmanuel DeliaMuch of the corruption exposed by this brave woman remains unpunished. Brussels must carry on her work and demand reformThu 10 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 04.53 EDTShareNine years ago, Daphne Caruana Galizia, Malta’s foremost investigative journalist, wasassassinated by a car bomboutside her home. The men who carried out the killing have been convicted or admitted their involvement. Nobody has been convicted of commissioning her murder.Last week, a jury acquitted Yorgen Fenech, one of Malta’s most prominent businessmen, of complicity in the assassination and criminal association.We have followed this case from different places: one of us from Malta, as a journalist and civil society activist campaigning for accountability after Daphne’s assassination; the other served as the Council of Europe’s rapporteur scrutinising the investigation and Malta’s failures of the rule of law.We were shocked by the verdict, but we respect it.The jurors decided, by eight votes to one, that Fenech’s guilt had not been proved beyond reasonable doubt. We are not asking for their verdict to be disregarded or reversed by political pressure.But the verdict does not erase what the trial exposed.Fenech admitted that he knew of the murder plan before Daphne was killed and that, while the plan was still live, hegave €50,000 to Melvin Theuma, the middleman who recruited the killers. Fenech said the money was intended to reimburse Theuma for money already paid and to persuade him to stop the assassination. He also admitted hepassed confidential information about the police investigationto Theuma and gave him further sums of money. He told the court he was blackmailed by Theuma.But Fenech denied commissioning or financing the murder. His explanation was that he had been acting out of misplaced loyalty to Keith Schembri, then chief of staff to Malta’s prime minister and one of his closest friends.The picture is appalling. A businessman at the heart of Malta’s economic establishment, the prime minister’s closest aide and the man organising the murder of the country’s most prominent investigative journalist were moving within the same small circle.Daphne had spent the last years of her life investigating precisely this proximity between political power, private wealth and people willing to operate outside the law.The Maltese government itself commissioned an independent public inquiry into her assassination. It concluded in 2021 that the state had created a culture of impunity and an atmosphere in which her murder became possible. Five years later, most of its recommendations remain unimplemented. Nor has there been anything approaching adequate accountability for the corruption Daphne was investigating.There are uncomfortable precedents. In Russia, people were convicted for their roles in the murders of journalist Anna Politkovskaya and opposition politician Boris Nemtsov. But the European court of human rights found that the authorities had failed adequately to identify and pursue those who actually commissioned the killings.Malta is not Russia, but it is the case that convicting the people who carried out a murder cannot be the end of the state’s responsibility if whoever commissioned the crime remains unidentified and unpunished. This should concern Brussels as much as Valletta.View image in fullscreenYorgen Fenech after being found not quilty of the murder of Daphne Caruana Galizia, 2 September 2026.Photograph: Matthew Mirabelli/AFP/Getty ImagesMalta’s failures do not stop at its coastline. A licence to conduct business in Malta, with limited government supervision, is effectively a licence to conduct business across theEuropean Union. Weak enforcement in one member state creates opportunities throughout the union.This is why impunity in Malta is not merely a Maltese problem.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOn Wednesday, the parliamentary assembly of the Council of Europe (Pace) returned formally to Daphne’s case. Its committee on legal affairs and human rights heard evidence from Daphne’s son Matthew Caruana Galizia and her sister Corinne Vella. Shami Chakrabarti, the committee’s rapporteur, is preparing a new report, entitled Justice delayed: the unfinished implementation of theDaphne Caruana Galiziacase. Her mandate includes examining the implementation of the public inquiry’s recommendations and Malta’s compliance with Council of Europe standards on the rule of law and press freedom.The timing could hardly be more important. Even Pace’s own monitoring committee, while recognising reforms undertaken since 2019, concluded that they addressed only part of the deficiencies and that comprehensive reform of Malta’s democratic institutions and system of checks and balances remained necessary.Malta’s prime minister, Robert Abela, should meet Chakrabarti at the earliest opportunity and give her work the Maltese government’s full cooperation. But the Council of Europe should go further.Pace has a monitoring committee specifically charged with examining whether member states are meeting their obligations to democracy, human rights and the rule of law. Malta has already been examined by that committee, which raised concerns about corruption, checks and balances, parliamentary oversight and the continuing culture of impunity. The events of the past week strengthen the case for renewed, comprehensive scrutiny of the state of the rule of law in Malta.Sabotage, leaks and political ties: the story of the Daphne Caruana Galizia murder trialRead moreEurope owes something to Daphne and to her family, who have spent nearly nine years fighting for truths the state should have established without requiring their persistence. But there is also a matter of European self-interest. The EU and the Council of Europe cannot afford pockets within their borders where serious corruption goes unpunished and political and economic power can frustrate accountability.The jury has decided that the prosecution did not prove Yorgen Fenech criminally responsible for Daphne Caruana Galizia’s murder. That judgment must be respected. It cannot become an answer to everything else.Nearly nine years after Daphne was assassinated, nobody has been convicted of ordering her murder. Much of the corruption she exposed remains unpunished. Most of the reforms recommended by the public inquiry remain undone. It is high time for Europe to start paying attention again.Pieter Omtzigt is a former Dutch MP who served as the Council of Europe parliamentary assembly’s rapporteur on the assassination of Daphne Caruana Galizia and the rule of law in Malta. Emanuel Delia is a Maltese journalist and co-founder of Repubblika, a civil society organisation campaigning for rule of law and accountability in MaltaDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on the prisons crisis: moving men into women’s jails is not the answer | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Kneejerk reactions to overcrowding will do more harm than good. Ministers should focus on probation
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Kneejerk reactions to overcrowding will do more harm than good. Ministers should focus on probation
Content: An officer patrols the B-wing at Wakefield prison, West Yorkshire.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenAn officer patrols the B-wing at Wakefield prison, West Yorkshire.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyOpinionPrisons and probationThe Guardian view on the prisons crisis: moving men into women’s jails is not the answerEditorialKneejerk reactions to overcrowding will do more harm than good. Ministers should focus on probationThu 10 Sep 2026 13.35 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 14.21 EDTShareIt is not hard to see why ministers are consideringconvertingparts of the women’s prison estate for use by men. While Andy Burnham’s decision to narrow the early-release scheme was born of political necessity, it has made an already acute capacity problem worse. Excluding manslaughter and further sexual offences cut projected early releases from6,000 to 4,500. The family of PC Andrew Harper, who was killed on duty in 2019, welcomed the assurance that his killers would not be released early. But the change leftovercrowdedEnglish and Welsh jails with even less room.The government is trying to innovate. Last week it was announced that£110m will be spenton creating new cells in existing jails, by converting underused spaces such as storage and laundry areas. Deportations are to be speeded up, if foreign governments can be persuaded to cooperate. There is an overdue and welcome commitment to examine how indeterminate imprisonment for public protection sentences can be phased out.But nobody believes that these schemes will be enough. Demand for places will continue to outstrip supply, while continued overcrowding risks worseninggrave existing problemsincluding endemic drug use, high rates of recidivism, violence and low staff morale (which undermines recruitment and retention).Most of the criminals who the public is anxious to see locked up are violent men. At the same time, there is a growing consensus that it would be better if some of the roughly 3,300 female prisoners in England (Wales has no women’s prison) served their sentences in the community. Most women are imprisoned for non-violent offences and pose no threat to public safety. Two out of three have been victims of domestic abuse; one in three have a child under 10. More than a quarter are on remand, so have not even been sentenced. The social and financial costs of locking them up are shockingly high.It is good to see these arguments gaining traction. Alandmark reviewby Jean Corston proposed the replacement of women’s jails with smaller local custodial centres nearly 20 years ago. But rushing to close a women’s prison, or part of one, in order to free up space for men would be damaging, as experts have pointed out. Female prisoners are held separately from men primarily for reasons of safety. Already, because there are so few female prisons, women are more likely than men to be held a long way from home. A report by the charity Women in Prison on theclosure of Holloway prisonin 2016 described it as a “deeply harmful process” owing to the disruption it caused.The Tories bear a heavy responsibility for prisons’ calamitous state. Criminal justice budgets were singled out for huge cuts under austerity because voters would be unlikely to notice – at least initially. The failed privatisation of the probation service was a disaster. But after two years in office, Labour must focus on the future, and explain to voters why locking people up in squalid, drug-riddled buildings is so wasteful. If they are serious about community alternatives, as plans to shrink the women’s estate would suggest, they need to show that this is more than a kneejerk reaction to overcrowding.Probationcannot be an afterthought: in early 2026, more offenders returned to prison on recall than were released from custody. Mr Burnham’s ministers need a new slogan: probation, probation, probation.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on falling birthrates: cash alone cannot buy belonging | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Young people still want partners and children. Governments must address the insecurity and isolation preventing them from building families
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Young people still want partners and children. Governments must address the insecurity and isolation preventing them from building families
Content: UN data shows global fertility fell from 5.3 births per woman in 1963 to 2.2 in 2023.Photograph: Tuan Tran/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenUN data shows global fertility fell from 5.3 births per woman in 1963 to 2.2 in 2023.Photograph: Tuan Tran/Getty ImagesOpinionPopulationThe Guardian view on falling birthrates: cash alone cannot buy belongingEditorialYoung people still want partners and children. Governments must address the insecurity and isolation preventing them from building familiesThu 10 Sep 2026 13.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 14.25 EDTShareWhy are people in one of the world’s richest, safest countries having so few children? Singapore isaskingthat question. In 2000, its fertility rate matched America’s at 1.6 children per woman. By 2025, it had dropped to 0.87 – almost half theUS rate. Singapore’s leaders, worried about population collapse, have reached for the chequebook. Each child, including those born to unmarried parents, will get$55,000in government support by the time they turn 17. Yet a quarter of Singaporeans say they do not intend to have children. Wealth and security, clearly, don’t guarantee more babies.UNdatashows that global fertility fell from 5.3 births per woman in 1963 to 2.2 in 2023. But this masks a growing divide. In some poor sub-Saharan African countries there are around six births per woman. Compare this withEngland and Wales, where the figure is just 1.39. More than half of the world – including a billion women in India and China – have a fertility rate below the global 2.1 “replacement level” needed to sustain populations without migration. But even in poor countries with high mortality rates and consequently higher replacement rates, births outpace deaths. In Nigeria, for example, the fertility rate of 4.4 exceeds its replacement rate of2.6 children per woman.To understand this phenomenon, the UN asked 100,000 18- to 39-year-olds from 73 nations their views on relationships and having children. Theresults, released in July, were striking: two-thirds said they want to marry or live with a partner. Those who did not have children overwhelmingly wanted them. Yet about a quarter of those aged 25 to 39 said they wanted a partner but were single and not dating – a status reported more by men than women. More than half said the biggest barriers to a durable relationship were economic constraints. Young people want partnership and parenthood, but questioned achieving the “emotional and financial” stability needed for a shared life.The Nordic region – consisting of five states and three territories – is viewed as a good place to have children thanks to generous parental leave and subsidised childcare. Yetfertility rateshave fallen by up to third since 2010, against 12% across the EU. The Polish sociologist Anna Gromadawrotein the Guardian that despite her country’s economic success, its fertility rate was 1.05. While the state transfers cash worth 10% of themedian wagefor every child born each month, Poland’s population is shrinking. Prof Gromada argues that people are not just deciding against children; many never form lasting relationships in which the question arises. Almost half of under-30s are single. Cash paid after a family exists cannot create the togetherness needed for a family in the first place.The world is not running out of people. The UNexpectstoday’s 8.2 billion people to become 10.3 billion by the mid-2080s. What is emerging is a demographic divide between ageing, shrinking rich societies and population growth in poorer ones. Getting richer seems to mean lower fertility. The baby bust may indicate a wealthy country’s failure to reproduce itself socially as well as biologically. People ask not only whether they can afford children, but whether they fit in, can trust each other and believe in a future. This loss of confident belonging poses questions that politics across the rich world has yet to tackle.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: What internal exclusion really means for school pupils | Secondary schools | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to a report that said use of the disciplinary measure had almost tripled in England’s secondary schools
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to a report that said use of the disciplinary measure had almost tripled in England’s secondary schools
Content: ‘Imagine if, at work today, you had to commit at all times to looking at the boss (never out of the window or at the floor).’Photograph: monkeybusinessimages/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreen‘Imagine if, at work today, you had to commit at all times to looking at the boss (never out of the window or at the floor).’Photograph: monkeybusinessimages/Getty Images/iStockphotoSecondary schoolsLettersWhat internal exclusion really means for school pupilsReaders respond to a report that said use of the disciplinary measure had almost tripled in England’s secondary schoolsThu 10 Sep 2026 12.13 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 12.30 EDTShareYour article quotes Tom Bennett, “a leading expert in behaviour management”, suggesting that internal exclusions are “a form of inclusion” (‘Internal exclusion’ of England secondary school students almost triples in three years, 3 September). That does not reflect my own experience. If a student is internally excluded, it must be as a last resort. I spent several months in the isolation room at my secondary school, and it didn’t feel inclusive to me.Like many of the students disproportionately affected by internal exclusion, I was from a disadvantaged background. I also had undiagnosed dyslexia. For me, internal exclusion meant I was unable to learn alongside other students – I’d simply get a printed handout from a teacher of the lesson notes and was told to read them.I finished my education in a pupil referral unit, but was able to go on to college thanks to the support of one of my teachers, who also mentored me. I am now in my final year of studying neuroscience at university, and I am working as a youth adviser with Lewis Hamilton’s charity,Mission 44.We are calling for internal exclusion to be properly recorded and scrutinised, alongside suspensions and permanent exclusions.Schools must also have sufficient resources and clear guidance on what good internal exclusion looks like, as well as how to address the causes of poor behaviour, so they can intervene before a young person reaches crisis point and is removed from the classroom.Faysal YusufLondonYou have to experience being in a classroom when significant disruption takes place. It is devastating. It wrecks the learning of the pupils who want to learn. It ruins the confidence of teachers who want to impart a love of their subject and enable their pupils to progress. It takes up valuable senior leadership time when a pupil has to be extracted. Dysregulated and verbally or physically disruptive children are not the product of schools. They are often the product of severely challenged family units.In such cases, internal isolation, as a strategy, has the best outcome. Pupils and teachers can resume learning and teaching in a calm atmosphere. The internally isolated pupil has a chance to recognise what triggered their outburst, and can resume learning in a fresh classroom climate that can include attention to their specific needs. And they are still safe on the school premises.Authorities and commentators should therefore not start to demonise internal isolations in schools without examining the deep-rooted socioeconomic and political causes behind them.Jo WestFormer secondary school headteacher, Virginia Water, SurreyImagine if, at work today, you had to commit at all times to looking at the boss (never out of the window or at the floor), to nodding, to walking corridors in silence and to asking questions at least five times a day. Pupils in secondary schools can be banished to internal detention for failing to do these things, among other reasons.The government’s special educational needs and disabilities reforms are based on making mainstream schools more inclusive. To achieve that, it must accept that the tyranny of rigid, non-evidenced rules does not work for 21st-century children. That doesn’t mean a reduction in standards – it means better and less harmful interventions to manage behaviour.Jane HarrisVice-chair, Disabled Children’s PartnershipWe were pleased to see you draw the public’s attention to the new data showing that poorer pupils and those with special educational needs and disabilities are disproportionately affected by internal exclusions in secondary schools.We are very concerned that the government remains mute on this and is not doing more to promote practices that are trauma-informed and grounded in modern neuroscience. Some schools are already managing to do this, investing in staff training to use relational and restorative approaches that balance both high challenge and high support. Plenty of organisations are ready to provide this training.But real change needs leadership from the very top of government. Too often, poor behaviour is still seen as deliberate defiance for its own sake. We need to see it instead as a symptom of a system that fails to promote empathy, understanding and taking responsibility for how our actions affect others.Ben HarperPeacebuilding in schools coordinator, Quakers in BritainHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Highs and lows of Keir Starmer’s time in office | Keir Starmer | The Guardian
description: Letters: Warren Brown lists some of the former PM’s achievements, but Stuart Finegan signals deep disappointment with his legacy
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Warren Brown lists some of the former PM’s achievements, but Stuart Finegan signals deep disappointment with his legacy
Content: ‘Keir Starmer too often appeared willing to abandon commitments when they became politically inconvenient.’Photograph: ITV via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Keir Starmer too often appeared willing to abandon commitments when they became politically inconvenient.’Photograph: ITV via Getty ImagesKeir StarmerLettersHighs and lows of Keir Starmer’s time in officeWarren Brownlists some of the former PM’s achievements, butStuart Finegansignals deep disappointment with his legacyThu 10 Sep 2026 12.13 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 12.30 EDTShareZoe Williams may be right to describe Keir Starmer as a poor politician, but what did we expect (Farewell Keir Starmer, a terrible politician whom we desperately wanted to be something more, 2 September)? After 14 years of economic stagnation and a succession of career politicians as prime minister, we had a leader who previously had a proper job and career outside politics. Starmer’s legacy might be to demonstrate why we need to invest in a better cadre of skilled professional politicians.Those still pining for Starmer may remind us of achievements such as removing the two-child limit on universal benefit, more free school meals, Best Start family hubs, greater employment rights, increases in the minimum wage, renters’ rights, more GPs, lower waiting lists, the Hillsborough law, better relations with Europe etc. But they shouldn’t bother – no one was listening then, and they certainly aren’t now.However, history might record his period in office as the first time the cabinet were nearly all state-educated – a massive achievement, for which he deserves our gratitude.Warren BrownIlkley, West YorkshireZoe Williams rightly highlights the deep disappointment many people feel about Keir Starmer’s political legacy. For a politician who promised principle and integrity, he too often appeared willing to abandon commitments when they became politically inconvenient.His stance on Israel’s war in Gaza remains one of the clearest examples. Rather than showing moral leadership and clearly condemning the suffering of Palestinian civilians, Starmer seemed reluctant to challenge Israel’s actions, leaving many questioning where his principles truly lay.Equally troubling was his approach to criticism. Many longstandingLaboursupporters, including elderly members who opposed the war, felt ignored or dismissed. Leadership requires engagement with dissent, not contempt for it.Starmer also struggled to connect with the public. In an age that values truth and conviction, he often appeared scripted and detached. It frequently felt as though he was delivering the conclusions of advisers rather than expressing his own beliefs.Beyond returning Labour to government, it is difficult to identify a lasting achievement. He may ultimately be remembered not as a leader, but as a manager of other people’s ideas.Stuart FineganLewes, East SussexHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Vauxhall factory closure shows that capitalism is alive and well in Luton | Automotive industry | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to Aditya Chakrabortty’s article about the closure of the Vauxhall plant
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to Aditya Chakrabortty’s article about the closure of the Vauxhall plant
Content: ‘Producing goods on the cheap and selling for the maximum price is why the car plant is now in Turkey.’Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Producing goods on the cheap and selling for the maximum price is why the car plant is now in Turkey.’Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianAutomotive industryLettersVauxhall factory closure shows that capitalism is alive and well in LutonReaders respond to Aditya Chakrabortty’s article about the closure of the Vauxhall plantThu 10 Sep 2026 12.13 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 12.30 EDTShareThe closure of the Vauxhall plant in Luton is not the failure of capitalism but its success (‘Capitalism is dying’: in Luton, these former car workers have a moral tale for our times, 4 September). Producing goods on the cheap and selling for the highest price is why the car plant is now in Turkey. Zero-hours contracts, child labour and governments unable to protect workers are global symptoms. To reverse this we need to own production – nationalise. Marx was right.Jonathan HauxwellCrosshills, North YorkshireTo the former Vauxhall worker who believes “capitalism is dying”: no, it is alive and well. Unfortunately, you have paid the price for it.Ian OsborneWichenford, WorcestershireAditya Chakrabortty writes of the plight of people trying to find work in Luton after Vauxhall’s closure. In nearby Bedford last Thursday, nearly all the jobs in an employment agency window paid the minimum wage. How are people supposed to live?Shayne Mary MitchellCambridgeA solution for Luton would be to set up a drone factory in the old Vauxhall works. It would count as investment and defence spending, and bring back employment.Nick FloyerChiswick, LondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Sailors on the USS Abraham Lincoln had it a lot easier than Nelson’s crews | US military | The Guardian
description: Letters: American sailors who were at sea for 286 days really have nothing to complain about, insists Chris Hardy
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: American sailors who were at sea for 286 days really have nothing to complain about, insists Chris Hardy
Content: An 1850 lithograph of the Battle of Trafalgar.Photograph: Fototeca Storica Nazionale./Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn 1850 lithograph of the Battle of Trafalgar.Photograph: Fototeca Storica Nazionale./Getty ImagesUS militaryLettersSailors on the USS Abraham Lincoln had it a lot easier than Nelson’s crewsAmerican sailors who were at sea for 286 days really have nothing to complain about, insistsChris HardyThu 10 Sep 2026 12.13 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 12.30 EDTShareYou report (4 September) that sailors from the USS Abraham Lincoln spent a “record uninterrupted 286 days at sea”. That’s nowhere near a record: Nelson and his fleet blockaded Toulon for two years, 1803-05, without going ashore.The American sailors complain about the food on their carrier; Nelson’s ships were exposed to terrible weather in which they pitched and rolled violently, and were cold, wet and plagued by rats. No electricity, let alone fridges; they ate salt pork and rock-hard bread full of weevils, drank green water, and every so often fought a battle or sailed to the Caribbean and back.Apparently the Americans are behaving respectably in the red-light port of Pattaya, Thailand. That’s another difference: the British sailors certainly did not when they came back to Portsmouth and were given two years’ pay in cash.Chris HardyWest Wittering, West SussexHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Sesko soars as Manchester United surge past Sabah on Champions League return | Champions League | The Guardian
description: Matheus Cunha, Bruno Fernandes and Lisandro Martínez were also on target in Manchester United’s 4-0 win against Sabah in the Champions League
Author: David Hytner
Headline: Matheus Cunha, Bruno Fernandes and Lisandro Martínez were also on target in Manchester United’s 4-0 win against Sabah in the Champions League
Content: Benjamin Sesko celebrates after scoring Manchester United’s third goal before half-time.Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenBenjamin Sesko celebrates after scoring Manchester United’s third goal before half-time.Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/ReutersChampions LeagueSesko soars as Manchester United surge past Sabah on Champions League returnDavid Hytnerat Old TraffordThu 10 Sep 2026 17.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was a night for romance given the astonishing story that Sabah brought with them to Old Trafford for their Champions League debut. This is a club that did not even exist a decade ago and nobody saw their bolt to the title in Azerbaijan coming last season; in 2024-25, they had finished 41 points off the top. The job that their manager, Valdas Dambrauskas,has done since taking overin the summer of last year is extraordinary.It was also a night for cold, hard reality.Manchester Unitedwere back in Europe’s elite competition after a two-year hiatus and in need of something to soothe them after the trauma of their last-gasp coughing up of two points in last Sunday’s Premier League draw at Everton. And before the extremely serious business of the derby here against Manchester City on Sunday. They got it on the back of a first-half performance that burned slowly before catching fire.Sabah were game. United were clinical. It was Matheus Cunha who broke the deadlock midway through the first half and the defining moments came at the end of the period when Bruno Fernandes and Benjamin Sesko sent United into half-time with a three-goal cushion. Lisandro Martínez added the fourth late on. It was a case of job done for Michael Carrick, no wobbles. Now for City.Mickels miss a turning point as latest stop in Sabah’s odyssey ends with regret | Jamie JacksonRead moreUnited had wanted to put their best foot forward when they heard theChampions Leaguearia after the chaos and embarrassment of their previous involvement in the competition. Erik ten Hag was the manager in 2023-24 and his team finished bottom of their group with four points, starting and ending with losses to Bayern Munich. It was what happened in between times against Galatasaray and Copenhagen that still causes a few shudders. It was a period when United panicked uncontrollably when they had a lead. When the defensive gifts from them came in crazy clusters.Carrick took no chances with his starting XI. There was minimal rotation in the midfield and front line, save for a first start of the season for Sesko in the No 9 position. It was easy to think that the manager wanted to groove Youri Tielemans and Kobbie Mainoo in central midfield before the City game.United looked to Fernandes to get them going. As always. There were intelligent runs from him; incision about his passes, that wonderful disguise on some of them. The breakthrough goal stemmed from him chasing a high ball over the top that looked like a lost cause only for him to keep it in play. It was what happened next that quickened United pulses. When Sabah gave the ball away cheaply to Bryan Mbeumo, United moved quickly over to the left. Patrick Dorgu crossed and Cunha’s finish was clean.Quick GuideGabriel, 15, stars with hat-trick for United in Youth League debutShowManchester United's JJ Gabriel (pictured) marked his Uefa Youth League debut with a hat-trick against Sabah aged just 15. The attacker is tipped as a future star and made his first appearance for the first team off the bench in last month’s friendly against Atlético Madrid.Gabriel has yet to make Michael Carrick’s squad for a competitive match but the teenager, who turns 16 next month, continues to knock on the door. He sparkled for the Under-19s in Thursday’s 5-0 win against Sabah in the Youth League in front of director of football Jason Wilcox, director of recruitment Christopher Vivell and first-team coach Travis Binnion.Amir Ibragimov and Jacob Watson scored early goals in Leigh, where Gabriel added another in a dominant first half.Gabriel scored two more late in the second half to claim the match ball against the Azerbaijani visitors, who did not manage a shot on a day that United mustered 44 attempts.PAPhotograph: Zohaib Alam/Manchester UnitedWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Sabah lined up in a 4-3-3 formation; no bus parking. They wanted to ask questions of a United defence that had a makeshift feel about it. There was assurance on the ball from them, the desire to carry it forward. And a huge chance in the 35th minute when Kaheem Parris crossed to the back post. Joy-Lance Mickels was clear of Noussair Mazraoui only to put the header wide. The angle was not favourable. It did not entirely excuse him.View image in fullscreenMatheus Cunha opens the scoring with a smart finish in the first half.Photograph: Stu Forster/Getty ImagesSabah were harshly treated by the half-time scoreline, even though United played on the front foot and created openings. It was the one-two punch in the closing stages of the first period that changed everything. Fernandes – who else? – made a sidefoot finish look easy after Tielemans had burst on a Cunha pass inside, spun and teed him up. The third followed a first time pass by Fernandes into Mbeumo, who got Sesko clean though. The Sabah backline was high. Sesko went around the goalkeeper to score. He never looked like missing.There was a lovely scene 90 ­minutes before kick-off when some of the Sabah players wandered around the pitch, the stadium virtually empty, phones out to capture the quiet before the storm, the sheer scale of Old Trafford. They wore wide smiles. They were determined not to be overawed when it got started. The performance of the strolling central midfielder, Ivan Lepinjica, was certainly impressive. They were just too loose at the back.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUnited played some slick stuff at times, Mainoo and ­Fernandes ever involved. When Carrick’s ­pass-and-move game clicks, it is easy to feel the ­possibility. ­Imposing it against the higher-­profile teams is the name of the game. ­Starting against City.Fenerbahce coach resigns after draw with Roma – but president insists he will stayRead moreMason Mount was introduced at half-time for his first football of the season – “It was great to get Mason back on the pitch,” Carrick later said – with Tielemans coming off, his work done. The Belgian could be pleased with his impact. Carrick was always going to withdraw other likely starters against City, such as Mainoo. Sesko came off with him on 64 minutes and was warmly applauded. After his goal at Everton on Sunday, has he done enough to make the XI for the derby?Carrick added: “We always push for more. Results-wise it hasn’t been the start we wanted, but performance-wise there are a lot of things we were looking for. The clean sheet was important tonight. Collectively as a team we have done a lot of good things and that is why we are excited what this season can bring.”His side controlled the second half. The jeopardy was long gone. The fourth goal summed up Sabah’s travails in their defensive third. It was a scooped free-kick by Fernandes for Joshua Zirkzee, on as a substitute, and when his backheel hit Aden ­McCarthy, the Sabah goalkeeper, Stas Pokatilov, lost his bearings, the ball caught under his feet. It was a tap-in for Martínez. The substitute, Orphé Mbina, headed high for Sabah at the very end. There was to be no fairytale goal.Explore more on these topicsChampions LeagueManchester UnitedSabahEuropean club footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Clearlake Capital close on buying out Chelsea co-owners Todd Boehly and Mark Walter | Chelsea | The Guardian
description: The deal would see Todd Boehly and Mark Walter make a profit on their investment and value the club at around £5bn
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: The deal would see Todd Boehly and Mark Walter make a profit on their investment and value the club at around £5bn
Content: Clearlake are already 61.5% shareholders of Chelsea.Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenClearlake are already 61.5% shareholders of Chelsea.Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesChelseaClearlake Capital close on buying out Chelsea co-owners Todd Boehly and Mark WalterDeal would value club at around £5bnWalter is seeking to raise funds to pay off insurersMatt HughesandJacob SteinbergThu 10 Sep 2026 16.49 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChelsea’s majority owners, Clearlake Capital, are closing in on an agreement to buy out co-owners Todd Boehly and Mark Walter in a deal that would see the pair make a profit on their investment and value the club at around £5bn.On-off discussions between the two ownership groups over a potential sale have been taking place for the last two years, but intensified last month as a result of Mark Walter seeking to raise funds to pay off insurers following a US federal investigation over alleged tax fraud.Chelsea’s 2016-17 Premier League title should be given to Spurs, says PochettinoRead moreWalter, Boehly and Swiss billionaire Hansjörg Wyss all own 12.8% of Chelsea following their joint £2.5bn purchase of the club with Clearlake from Roman Abramovich four years ago, in a deal in which the new owners commit to spending a further £1.75bn on the club.Under the terms of their ownership agreement, none of Chelsea’s shareholders can sell to a third party without the consent of their partners giving Clearlake, whose investment is managed by Behdad Eghbali and José E Feliciano, an exclusive option to purchase Boehly and Walter’s stakes.In a statement issued to Bloomberg a spokesperson for Walter confirmed that he is seeking a sale with an agreement close. Boehly is also expected to sell as he is a long-time investment partner of Walters. Wyss’s position is unconfirmed.“This potential transaction values Mark Walter’s stake in Chelsea Football Club at a premium to his initial investment and is another successful sports investment for him,” a spokesperson for Walter said.“After this exit, Mr Walter intends to make future sports-related investments. “Walter did not initiate the proposed transaction to sell his interest, which has been in the works for quite some time.”As 61.5% shareholders, Clearlake already had day-to-day operational control at Chelsea managed by Eghbali, and were due to make their own appointment as chairman to replace Boehly next year, but taking complete control will ease internal tensions at the club and should smooth decision making.The most immediate impact of the impending ownership change is likely to be felt in Chelsea’s plans for a new stadium, as Eghbali has clashed with Boehly over whether the club should seek to redevelop Stamford Bridge or seek an alternative site elsewhere.Walter is being investigated by the US Department of Justice over $21bn in loans which it has been alleged were not disclosed to state insurance regulators, and led to the sudden sale of assets to pay down some of the loans.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe American insurance and sports investor last month sold his 85% stake in the Los Angeles Lakers to Josh ⁠Kushner and Bob Iger in a deal that valued the NBA franchise at around £9bn.Walter’s holding company, TWG Global, subsequently issued a statement saying that the company “is not looking to sell its sports assets at ‘fire sale’ prices”.Representatives for Boehly and Clearlake declined to comment.Explore more on these topicsChelseaBusinessnewsShareReuse this content

title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Nicolas Jackson is ready to impress, Spurs are scrambled and the 199th Manchester derby takes place at Old Trafford
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Nicolas Jackson is ready to impress, Spurs are scrambled and the 199th Manchester derby takes place at Old Trafford
Content: Brentford's Vitaly Janelt, Hull City's Oli McBurnie, Aston Villa's Nicolas Jackson.Composite: Getty, ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBrentford's Vitaly Janelt, Hull City's Oli McBurnie, Aston Villa's Nicolas Jackson.Composite: Getty, ShutterstockTen things to look out for this weekendPremier LeaguePremier League: 10 things to look out for this weekendNicolas Jackson is ready to impress, Spurs are scrambled and the 199th Manchester derby takes place at Old TraffordPremier League top scorers 2026-27: who is leading race for the golden boot?Guardian sportThu 10 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 19.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google1Ton up for hard-working McBurnieWith 10 top-flight goal contributions between them across three games already this season, the Chelsea trio of Morgan Rogers, João Pedro and Cole Palmer are the early pace-setters for the Premier League’s most prolific, fluid and high octane attacking unit. But on the occasion of his 100thPremier Leagueappearance, a scruffier and more ungainly unit will be hoping to steal their thunder, as high-flying Hull try to register a top-flight win against Chelsea for the very first time. Yet to score this season but with a couple of near-misses to his name, what Oli McBurnie has thus far lacked in goal contributions he has more than made up for with selfless graft and off-the-ball grunt work, making a total mockery of Steve Clarke’s decision not to include him in Scotland’s World Cup squad. The Hull striker ought to prove a real handful for a decidedly porous home defence, and a goal would be a fitting way to mark a century of Premier League appearances. Chelsea have not won any of their past four league matches against promoted opposition and given Hull’s blistering start to the season, victory on Saturday seems anything but a foregone conclusion.Barry GlendenningChelsea v Hull, Saturday 3pm (all times BST)Chart showing duels won in the Premier League in 2026‑272Arbeloa must trust process as Iraola once didThis might be an opportune moment for Álvaro Arbeloa to meet Andoni Iraola, though perhaps not his Liverpool team. With three defeats from his first three Premier League games as Fulham head coach, and seven goals conceded, questions are already being asked over the former Liverpool defender’s ambitious approach. Just as they were when Iraola failed to win any of his first nine league games in charge ofBournemouth. Trust yourself and the process, might be the Liverpool head coach’s advice if asked. Fulham have been creative under Arbeloa but are easily exposed defensively. Liverpool, starting to click in attack under their new manager, have the assets to exploit Fulham’s weaknesses and subject Arbeloa to an uncomfortable Anfield return. Iraola’s wide options could be reduced, however, with Bradley Barcola suffering cramp on Wednesday – his first start since France’s World Cup semi-final loss – and Cody Gakpo nursing a minor injury.Andy HunterLiverpool v Fulham, Saturday 3pm3Doucouré eagerly waiting Palace returnCheick Doucouré has had a rotten run of luck with injuries. Just when the Mali midfielder looked as if he was ready to make a firstCrystal Palaceappearance since January 2025 in Tuesday’s Carabao Cup win over Middlesbrough, he was taken ill. Pierre Sage revealed last week that Doucouré looked as if he had “given him one million dollars” when he was informed he would be part of the matchday squad at Fulham, where Palace got off the mark with a 3-2 victory. Sage has confirmed that the 26-year-old, who has been sidelined with two serious knee injuries but was once a transfer target for Liverpool, could be involved against Ipswich at Selhurst Park on Saturday. Whenever he does return it is sure to be a heartwarming moment.Ed AaronsCrystal Palace v Ipswich, Saturday 3pmView image in fullscreenCheick Doucouré returned to the Crystal Palace squad for last weekend’s trip to Fulham.Photograph: James Fearn/Getty Images4Cherries must end late lapsesThe midfield battle betweenBrentfordand Bournemouth will be crucial on Saturday with Vitaly Janelt and Mamadou Sangaré setting the tempo for Keith Andrews’ physical side. Brentford top the Premier League for aerial duels won (22.3 per 90 mins), interceptions (11.3 per 90), and fouls committed (16.3 per 90). “They defend well as a team, their high pressing is good,” said Bournemouth’s Marco Rose, who is hoping to guide his side to a first Premier League victory of the season. “Their transition, they have fast players. They have quality everywhere on the pitch, and every situation.” Rose’s answer for Brentford’s aggressiveness should be Alex Scott, who leads his team for interceptions and has drawn nine fouls so far this campaign – the fourth-highest tally in the league. Late drama could also be the deciding factor at the Vitality Stadium. Despite leading in all three of their opening league fixtures, Bournemouth have picked up just two points and four of their five goals conceded have arrived from the 84th minute onwards. History favours their opponents too, as the Cherries have failed to win any of their eight top-flight meetings with the Bees.Yara El-ShabouryBournemouth v Brentford, Saturday 3pmChart showing Premier League stats per game in 2026-27 for aerial duels won, fouls and interceptions5Jackson ready to fill Watkins’ Villa bootsA summer of change at Aston Villa inevitably prompted plenty of noise but most of their new signings were long-standing targets, none more so than Nicolas Jackson. Unai Emery kickstarted Jackson’s career at Villarreal and after reuniting at Villa, the Senegal striker registered hisfirst goal at Club Bruggeon Tuesday after his initial £47.5m move. Jackson has replaced Ollie Watkins, who proved a reliable source of goals across six straight top-flight seasons, and the early evidence has been encouraging. “I had a couple of fights with him when he was at Chelsea so when he first came in I thought: ‘What’s he going to be like?’ but he’s a brilliant guy,” said the Villa captain, John McGinn. “There’s a lot of expectation with the transfer fee but he’s going to be a huge player for us.”Ben FisherAston Villa vNottingham Forest, Saturday 3pm6Signs of early season panic at SpursOnly the most pessimistic home fans at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium will be gripped by anything resembling the kind of dread, anxiety and outright terror that accompaniedEverton’s visit on the final day of last season, but the return of David Moyes’ side so early in the current campaign will still make for nervous viewing. With no goals and just one point on the board after three league games, fan faith in Roberto De Zerbi – and the hundreds of millions of pounds lavished upon new signings – has created a prevailing presumption that Tottenham will soon start firing on at least some, if not all, cylinders. In Everton, Spurs welcome a team whose record in this corner of north London is worse than any other top-flight side. Should they fail to beat a team who have taken just seven points from the past 51 available to them away at Tottenham, the sounds of early but outright mutiny are likely to be audible from the stands.BGTottenham vEverton, Saturday 5.30pmChart showing expected goals per non-penalty shot in 2026-277Stadium of Light to give Guimarães hot receptionOld acquaintance will be renewed at the Stadium of Light on Saturday evening. While Sunderland’s captain and midfield anchor, Granit Xhaka, needs no introduction to his former north London public, the home centre-half Dan Ballard is a former Arsenal youth captain who joined the Gunners’ academy at the age of eight. Then there is Bruno Guimarães. Newcastle’s former captain can expect a hot reception as his new side aim to extend their season-opening run of five straight wins (including the Community Shield). “Arsenal are flying, they’re one of the best teams in Europe,” says Régis Le Bris, Sunderland’s manager. “It will be challenging but I’m very excited to experience this situation again.” Thanks to goals from Ballard and Brian Brobbey, Le Bris choreographed a2-2 Premier League drawagainst Mikel Arteta’s side on Wearside last November. “When you face a strong opponent you can become a bit shy but the most important thing is to be ourselves,” says Le Bris. “Arsenal are so adaptive they will find solutions, so we must be flexible.”Louise TaylorSunderland v Arsenal, Saturday 8pmView image in fullscreenBruno Guimarães returns to the northeast as Arsenal visit Sunderland on Saturday night.Photograph: David Price/Arsenal FC/Getty Images8Coventry adding points to performances?One of three teams, along with Aston Villa and Tottenham, yet to score a top-flight goal this season, Coventry were extremely unfortunate not to break their duck atManchester Citylast weekend. Having narrowly avoided handing Frank Lampard’s side an early opener, it took a string of excellent saves from Gianluigi Donnarumma to ensure City took three points at the death. “They played really well against Manchester City and created a lot of chances,” said Fabian Hürzeler, who takes his Brighton team to the CBS Arena on Sunday afternoon. Having been scathing in his criticism of his own side’s lack of energy and intensity in their woeful first-half performance against Leeds, the German will be aware that a similarly lethargic performance from his team is unlikely to go unpunished. Particularly away from home against a promoted team that may be firing blanks, but visibly grew in confidence with each passing minute of their defeat to one of the league’s best teams.BGCoventry v Brighton, Sunday 2pmChart showing goals below expected goals in 2026-279Contrasting Manchester teams face off in derbyManchester derby No 199 features a fascinating showdown between two young managers operating in the sport’s rarefied air: Michael Carrick, 45, who bids to guide Manchester United to an 82nd victory in the fixture, and Enzo Maresca, 46, who aims for Manchester City’s 63rd. As the great Pep Guardiola’s successor, the visiting Italian can be delighted at his team’s perfect record from their four games under him since the Community Shield. Carrick, though, should be disappointed at the return from an opening three matches as United’s permanent manager: adefeat at Hullanddraw at Everton, with the5-2 home win over Ipswichsandwiched between. United fans will protest beforehand about the club’s approach to eradicating ticket touting, the occasion should be particularly spicy and vibrant.Jamie JacksonManchester United v Manchester City, Sunday 4.30pmView image in fullscreenManchester United supporters protested ticket touts earlier in the season and will do so again before the Manchester derby.Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/Reuters10Battle of the goalkeepers at Elland RoadTwo teams unbeaten in the Premier League this season, two German managers in the dugouts and a Monday night goalkeeping beauty contest at Elland Road. While Daniel Farke welcomes his compatriot, Matthias Jaissle, to West Yorkshire for the first time, James Trafford – the £40m England keeper Newcastle tried to sign on three separate occasions – will be in goal for Leeds. The visitors eventually turned their attentions to the £26m Czechia goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek, who arrived on Tyneside from Braga in July. So far at least, Jaissle is delighted by the 24-year-old’s performances. “Lukas is an amazing signing who has been amazing,” said Eddie Howe’s successor. “Coming to the Premier League and dealing with the pressure is not easy and, as a keeper, that pressure is something else. I like Lukas a lot. He’s so calm but so mature as well. There’s not even a hint of nervousness. He gives the whole team confidence. That helps a lot.”LTLeeds v Newcastle, Monday 8pmPosTeamPGDPts1Man City3592Arsenal3593Hull3374Chelsea3165Brentford3356Liverpool3257Newcastle3258Everton3259Leeds31510Brighton33411Man Utd31412Sunderland30413Crystal Palace3-4314Ipswich3-4315AFC Bournemouth3-1216Nottm Forest3-1217Aston Villa3-5118Tottenham Hotspur3-5119Fulham3-3020Coventry3-50Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueTen things to look out for this weekendManchester CityArsenalHull CityChelseaBrentfordLiverpoolfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: England’s Dan Lawrence delighted with form as Pakistan focus on the future | England v Pakistan 2026 | The Guardian
description: Dan Lawrence missed out on a century but said he was ‘really happy’ with recent displays, while Pakistan’s batting coach hailed his team’s potential
Author: Simon Burnton
Headline: Dan Lawrence missed out on a century but said he was ‘really happy’ with recent displays, while Pakistan’s batting coach hailed his team’s potential
Content: Dan Lawrence said, ‘I feel like I’ve got a lot to offer English cricket,’ after scoring his third half-century in four innings.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAView image in fullscreenDan Lawrence said, ‘I feel like I’ve got a lot to offer English cricket,’ after scoring his third half-century in four innings.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAEngland v Pakistan 2026England’s Dan Lawrence delighted with form as Pakistan focus on the futureLawrence rues missed ton but ‘really happy’ with displaysTourists’ batting coach hails potential of new playersSimon Burntonat EdgbastonThu 10 Sep 2026 14.54 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA few hours after his yelp of frustration echoed around Edgbaston, an innings of 65 and the growing conviction that “I was going to make a really big score” ended when he chased a wide delivery and played on, Dan Lawrence’s emotions had settled into something approaching contentment. England had taken a firm grip on the game, Pakistanending the second daystill 268 away from making them bat again with eight wickets remaining, and Lawrence, having posted three half-centuries in four Test innings this summer, is finally delivering on his obvious potential in an England shirt.“I’m obviously gutted I didn’t kick on,” he said. “I felt like I was playing really nicely and it was a really good surface to bat on against a tiring attack at that stage. I thought I was going to make a really big score, but it wasn’t meant to be. But I’m really happy with how I’ve played [this summer].skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEngland bat Pakistan out of third Test before Robinson moves in for the killRead more“I always knew deep down that my ability was good enough to play at this level, even though I hadn’t necessarily shown it in my first stint playing. That was obviously a tough time, when I got dropped from the team [in 2022], and all I was concentrating on was trying to score big runs in county cricket and get myself in, because I feel like I’ve got a lot to offer English cricket.”Pakistan are also confident about their potential, even if at this stage it seems unlikely to be realised on this tour. “There’s a lot of class in this dressing room,” said Michael Smith, who was appointed batting coach last month. “There’s a lot of serious players here. It would be nice for them to show the rest of the UK, and the people back in Pakistan, what they’ve still got. Because we’ve got no doubt that it’s there.”The tourists’ batting has been poor throughout the series – they are yet to score as many as 200 runs in an innings – but Smith is content that the right players are learning the right lessons for the future. “A lot of our players, it’s their first tour of England,” Smith said. “I suppose we might not see the sort of success we want to see now, but hopefully if a lot of these players are back on our next UK tour, we’ll really see an upward trend. I think that’s the time to really judge them.“Let’s not worry about what’s happening here. We’ve got some really exciting players and potential is exceptionally high. It’s just how quickly we can get them to that level, especially playing outside of Pakistan. That’s going to be a big challenge and it’s something we’re really excited about.”Explore more on these topicsEngland v Pakistan 2026England cricket teamPakistan cricket teamCricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: Brave new world: Ultimate Championship brings glowing javelins and $10m prize fund to track and field | Athletics | The Guardian
description: New event aims to revolutionise the sport with promises of bigger prize money and a greater role for athletes
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: New event aims to revolutionise the sport with promises of bigger prize money and a greater role for athletes
Content: Noah Lyles at the Ultimate Championship’s launch, where he enjoyed a stint as a DJ.Photograph: Dénes Erdős/APView image in fullscreenNoah Lyles at the Ultimate Championship’s launch, where he enjoyed a stint as a DJ.Photograph: Dénes Erdős/APAthleticsBrave new world: Ultimate Championship brings glowing javelins and $10m prize fund to track and fieldNew event aims to revolutionise the sport with promises of bigger prize money and a greater role for athletesSean Inglein BudapestThu 10 Sep 2026 13.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTrack and field’s brave new world begins in Budapest on Friday night. The action will be fast-paced and slick, with augmented reality showing athletes’ win percentages and javelins and hammers that glow, making them easier to see on a black infield. In the space of 48 hours, a top sprinter could earn $337,500 (£250,000) for just over a minute’s work.It is all part of the newWorld AthleticsUltimate Championship, a three-day event with a prize fund of $10m which is designed to pit the best against the best, and kick off a minor revolution in the sport.‘I’m not a robot’: Josh Kerr primed to peak against arch rival IngebrigtsenRead moreWhen Usain Bolt, who is a global ambassador for the event, was told that anyone who wins the 100m, 200m and mixed 4x100m relay here will walk away £250,000 richer, he smiled – and recalled a conversation he had just recently had with another legendary Jamaican sprinter, Asafa Powell.“I was chatting to Asafa before I came here and we were like: ‘Jeez, we missed out on a big cash prize,’” he said. “I won a fair few championships and it still doesn’t add up to all that cash. I am sad I missed out on it, but I’m happy for the athletes.”The idea is the brainchild of WorldAthleticspresident, Sebastian Coe, and chief executive, Jon Ridgeon. But this is just the start of plans to make the sport richer – and more popular.“We will deliver magnetic indelible moments that will travel around all four corners of the globe, and I think we will see a compelling glimpse into the future and the potential of this sport, which at its best is untouchable,” said Coe.“We also want this championship to be an incubator for change. As a proud Sheffielder, I would describe it as a blast furnace, ultimately shaping what our sport will look like going forward. And we want to take some of these innovations into the world championships and Olympic Games.”View image in fullscreenKeely Hodgkinson savours the red carpet treatment.Photograph: Ben Stansall/AFP/Getty ImagesSo what could be next? The Guardian can reveal there is growing clamour for Coe to stay on at WorldAthleticsin some capacity when his presidency ends in September 2027. One plan being discussed is for Coe to lead a new commercial arm, which aims to sell World Athletics’ own rights for the first time and add substantial external investment and revenues.Such a move could come about because at the end of 2029, World Athletics’ commercial contract with the sports marketing agency Dentsu, which is worth around £14m a year, will end.While it has been a happy relationship, the current deal means that even if World Athletics wants to use footage from its own world championships at its own awards ceremony it has to pay Dentsu.But in three years’ time World Athletics will have control of its commercial and broadcast rights for the first time in three decades, allowing it to explore fresh options on how best to fund the sport.It is understood that Coe, who has transformed the governance and fortunes of World Athletics since taking over from the corrupt Lamine Diack regime in 2015, is undecided as to whether he would take on such a role.In a statement to the Guardian, World Athletics said: “At the end of 2029, most of World Athletics’ commercial contracts and broadcast relationships will come to an end, as will our current contract with Dentsu, who has owned our commercial rights since 2014, and we will be in a position to sell our own rights from 2030 onwards.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenBritain’s Amy Hunt poses for a photo after the lane draft for the women’s 200m semi-finals.Photograph: Shaun Botterill/Getty Images“With that in mind, our executive board has spent the last 18 months looking at the commercial structures we need to create and determining the best way to increase revenue so we can accelerate growth in our sport over the coming years.“We are making consequential progress in an area that obviously requires detailed consultation throughout our organisation and across our sport.”Another sign of athletics’ strength is that the BBC has significantly scaled up its operation here because the viewing figures were so strong at the European championships, with more than four million watching at peak times.In total 381 top athletes from 65 federations will compete in Budapest, with the winner of each race getting $150,000 and even the eighth-place finisher walking away with $10,000.Another change is that athletes have been involved in the planning and presentation of the event, with the Olympic 100m champion, Noah Lyles, even acting as a DJ. It started with a red carpet introduction on Thursday with several athletes, including the pole vault star Mondo Duplantis and 800m Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson, wearing jackets and dresses that wouldn’t have been out of place at the Oscars.One sign of the relaxed atmosphere came when Hodgkinson was asked by a member of the press whether she was 100% fit after a minor hamstring niggle at the European championships in Birmingham. “None of your business,” she replied, smiling.Explore more on these topicsAthleticsSebastian CoeWorld AthleticsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: World Rugby floats plans for Six Nations match in US but England unlikely to participate | Rugby union | The Guardian
description: World Rugby wants a Six Nations match to be staged in the US and has offered financial incentives to the unions to do so
Author: Gerard Meagher
Headline: World Rugby wants a Six Nations match to be staged in the US and has offered financial incentives to the unions to do so
Content: Around 85% of the RFU’s revenues come from England men’s fixtures at Twickenham.Photograph: Peter Nicholls/ReutersView image in fullscreenAround 85% of the RFU’s revenues come from England men’s fixtures at Twickenham.Photograph: Peter Nicholls/ReutersRugby unionWorld Rugby floats plans for Six Nations match in US but England unlikely to participateGoverning body floating staging Ireland v Italy in USWorld Rugby eyes commercial value in American fixturesGerard MeagherThu 10 Sep 2026 13.32 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWorld Rugby wants aSix Nationsmatch to be staged in the US and has offered financial incentives to the unions to do so – but England have effectively ruled themselves out on the grounds that fixtures at Twickenham are too lucrative.The US will stage the 2031 World Cup and World Rugby is seeking to capitalise commercially despite mounting fears over the parlous state of rugby union in the host country. As a result, the governing body is desperate to raise interest in the sport’s profile by staging high-profile matches Stateside, with Baltimore hosting the fourth Test between South Africa and New Zealand on Saturday.A failed attempt was made to attract the British & Irish Lions to stop in Las Vegas on the way to Australia in 2025, thoughEngland did face the USA in Washingtonthat summer while the All Blacks and Irelandmet in Chicago last autumn. The 2030 finals weekend of the Nations Championship has also been slated for the United States.Taking a Six Nations match to America would be an altogether more significant move given how financially valuable home championship fixtures can be to the competing unions.
