But World Rugby is willing to help bridge the shortfall and has floated Ireland v Italy as a potential fixture, given the number of expats from each country on the east coast.View image in fullscreenJack Crowley kicks a penalty in Ireland’s match against New Zealand in Chicago in 2025. Ireland could be tempted to play a Six Nations match in the US.Photograph: Erin Hooley/APEngland can generate around £10m from a Six Nations home match and men’s fixtures at Twickenham account for about 85% of the Rugby Football Union’s revenues. It is understood that taking a championship fixture to the US is considered very unlikely by insiders, all the more so due to its naming rights deal with Allianz – which stipulates a certain number of matches at Twickenham – and the likely consternation that would arise among fans and debenture holders. Insiders also point to how the RFU owns its home stadium whereas New Zealand and South Africa do not.If there was appetite among the other unions, however, the Six Nations committee would have to agree as would the tournament broadcasters, though ITV’s recent £1.6bn takeover by Sky, which is owned by the US telecoms giant Comcast, may help in that regard.“In terms of the matchday economics, [South Africa v New Zealand] is like a Six Nations match,” the World Rugby chief executive, Alan Gilpin, told the Telegraph. “It starts to show that [financial return] is not the barrier. So if there is the appetite to take some of these big matches in the future to the US, we can now.“We completely understand [the] need for rugby to continue to drive more economic sustainability. Any of those unions [could] go and look at a match that they would have had at home and say, ‘Right, can I at least match, if not better my own economics by partnering with World Rugby and taking that match to the US?’”Explore more on these topicsRugby unionEngland rugby union teamRugby Football UnionSix NationsSport politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘She’s buzzing’: Charley Hull to face world No 1 Nelly Korda in Solheim Cup opener | Solheim Cup | The Guardian
description: The opening foursomes of the Solheim Cup on Friday will see Europe’s Charley Hull and Lottie Woad take on USA’s Nelly Korda and Allisen Corpuz
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: The opening foursomes of the Solheim Cup on Friday will see Europe’s Charley Hull and Lottie Woad take on USA’s Nelly Korda and Allisen Corpuz
Content: Charley Hull walks through a crowd of supporters at the opening ceremony of the Solheim Cup.Photograph: Kate McShane/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCharley Hull walks through a crowd of supporters at the opening ceremony of the Solheim Cup.Photograph: Kate McShane/Getty ImagesSolheim Cup‘She’s buzzing’: Charley Hull to face world No 1 Nelly Korda in Solheim Cup openerHull will partner debutant Lottie Woad for EuropeUSA seeking to retain trophy they won in 2024Ewan Murrayat Bernardus GolfThu 10 Sep 2026 13.07 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGalleries at the 20th Solheim Cup have been granted a blockbuster start with Nelly Korda and Charley Hull to face off in Friday morning’s foursomes. The meeting of Korda, the world No 1, and Hull, Europe’s star turn, should ensure an electric opening in the Netherlands as the USA seek to retain the trophywon in Virginia two years ago. Korda nudged out Hull at theUS Women’s Openin June.Hull will partner theSolheim Cupdebutant Lottie Woad against the formidable USA pairing of Korda and Allisen Corpuz to begin the tournament. Nanna Koerstz Madsen and Céline Boutier will represent Europe in match two, where they will take on Alison Lee and Lauren Coughlin. Esther Henseleit and Leona Maguire have been selected for the hosts in the penultimate match, with Andrea Lee and Lindy Duncan in opposition. The foursomes will conclude with Europe’s Swedish duo of Maja Stark and Linn Grant facing Rose Zhang and Jennifer Kupcho.Solheim Cup vice-captain denies Charley Hull’s late arrival due to ‘drinks’Read more“She’s been buzzing, she’s been so excited,” said Europe’s captain Anna Nordqvist of Hull. “Her and Lottie have got to play quite a bit on tour this year, so I think they were both very excited to be paired with each other.”Angela Stanford, the USA captain, said Korda and Corpuz had “earned the right” to lead their team out. “I feel like if I didn’t put those two out, I would be questioned,” Stanford added. “I feel like the whole world knew that they were coming.”In a peculiar moment as the captains completed the last of their pre-tournament media duties, Nordqvist asserted every player on each team had to play on day one as per an agreement. Stanford looked bemused by the suggestion. The actual ruling, which was later clarified, says players must appear in at least one session before Sunday. Nordqvist must hope her misstep – or misunderstanding – is not a sign of things to come.The USA have won only once on European soil since 2007, when they triumphed in 2015. Eleven years have passed since “Gimme-gate” but Alison Lee’s reappearance in a United States team in Europe gives cause to reflect upon the chaos that unfolded in Germany. “It was a shell-shocking week for me,” Lee recalls.This weekend, Lee will be the sole playing survivor from the US contingent in 2015. Back then, aged 20, she picked up her ball before the supposed formality of a concession from Europe. Suzann Pettersen seized upon the moment, claiming the hole for Europe amid tears and ferocious backlash. The USA had the last laugh, winning the Solheim Cup by one point as Pettersen spent the evening sobbing in a hotel room.View image in fullscreenAlison Lee, pictured during her practice round on Thursday, said it was “a huge goal” to be back in Europe competing in the Solheim Cup.Photograph: Maddie Meyer/Getty Images“I had been thrown into a team where I didn’t really know anyone very well,” says Lee. “I just felt really grateful that the team around me, the US team, were just so supportive of me. They had my back and they were so welcoming.“All that stuff happened on Sunday morning because there was a delay and we had to finish the Saturday afternoon session in the morning. So we had a couple hours before singles where we all came together and I was very rattled, obviously, with everything that happened. I think everyone just saw me as a little sister and they just really cared for me. They not only wanted to win, for the US, but we wanted to win for each other. And so I feel like that meant a lot.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I was so young. I remember just being on the team was such a cool thing to be a part of. Less than a year before that, I was watching them all on TV so I was a little scared to be on the team, to be honest. Winning was super special.”Pettersen’s redemption came in 2019, when sheholed the winning putt for Europe at Gleneaglesbefore announcing her retirement. Lee represented the US in Virginia two years ago but always had a return trip to Europe in her thoughts. “I feel really proud of myself,” Lee adds. “It was a huge goal to be here and I didn’t think it was in reach.“I took some time off last year, I had my son who is 16 months old now. I knew it would be challenging to try and make this team and it was a hard, hard journey, but I did everything I could to make it here. To be able to make the team on my own this year just meant a lot.”The US team will wear commemorative pin badges on Friday as a means of marking the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks.Explore more on these topicsSolheim CupGolfUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: French FA accuses Infantino of ‘seriously damaging’ football as it withdraws support | Gianni Infantino | The Guardian
description: The French Football Federation’s president, Philippe Diallo, has strongly criticised his Fifa counterpart, saying ‘trust has been broken’
Author: Raphaël Jucobin
Headline: The French Football Federation’s president, Philippe Diallo, has strongly criticised his Fifa counterpart, saying ‘trust has been broken’
Content: Gianni Infantino was accused by the French federation’s president of behaving in a ‘unilateral and opaque fashion’.Photograph: Kacper Pempel/ReutersView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino was accused by the French federation’s president of behaving in a ‘unilateral and opaque fashion’.Photograph: Kacper Pempel/ReutersGianni InfantinoFrench FA accuses Infantino of ‘seriously damaging’ football as it withdraws support‘Image and unity’ of game affected, FFF president saysIt will consult sacked former Fifa official Kevin LamourRaphaël Jucobinin ParisThu 10 Sep 2026 13.03 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe French Football Federation’s president, Philippe Diallo, saidGianni Infantinohad “seriously damaged the image and the unity of football” as he announced the end of France’s support for the Fifa president’s re-election.The FFF’s executive committee unanimously voted on Thursday to withdraw its backing, which had been formalised at the end of June. Diallo referred to “events during the World Cup” which had “flagrantly gone against the way we believe our sport should be run” and to Infantino’sWorld Cup sell-off plan,which was revealed in July andscrappedafter a widespread backlash.Infantino installs loyalist to oversee Caribbean as he splits Fifa managementRead moreDuring the World Cup the suspension of the US forward Folarin Balogun wasoverturnedby Fifa after lobbying from Donald Trump. The US presidentsaid he called Infantinoto recommend that Balogun be allowed to play. Fifa has said the decision taken by its disciplinary committee was“a balanced measure”and “based on an explicit provision of the applicable regulations”.Diallo outlined the reasons for the loss in confidence: “From July onwards, the conditions which led to us to support his candidacy had been disrupted. Does the withdrawal of the [sell-off] project solve the issue? I don’t think so. His initiatives during and after theWorld Cuphave seriously damaged the image and the unity of football. As a result, we believe that trust has been broken.”Diallo said of the initial decision to support Infantino: “It would be wrong to say that certain developments in football were not made under his mandate.” But he added: “When you are making changes to the game itself, in a unilateral and opaque fashion to sell our shared asset, that changes our appreciation.“France is one of the founding members ofFifa, and as such we have a historical legitimacy to intervene when we feel that Fifa and its president are deviating from our vision of how world football should be run. We also have sporting legitimacy, as one of the top three teams in the world rankings over the last 10 years. We wanted to make it clear that we refuse to go in a direction which does not correspond to the general interest of our sport.”When reports of the sell-off project came to light, the FFF expressed “doubts and deep concerns”. Uefa threatened a boycott of Fifa competitions andseveral European countries, including Wales and England, withdrew their support for Infantino but the FFF had not until Thursday publicly disavowed him.Diallo indicated France would play an active part in Uefa’s search for an alternative candidate for the Fifa presidency before the 18 November deadline. The election will take place in March during Fifa’s next congress.Before then, Diallo said, the FFF would reach out to figures it considers experts in “transparency and good governance” in football and beyond as part of France’s “contribution to the debate”, as it pushes for “far-reaching reform” of Fifa.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe cited Kevin Lamour, the former Fifa chief operating officer whowas dismissedafter criticising the sell-off plan, as one of the people the FFF would look to consult.Fifa was approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsGianni InfantinoFifaFootball politicsWorld CupWorld Cup 2026Sport politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It was all hands on deck’: how the CIA responded to 9/11 | September 11 2001 | The Guardian
description: Veterans recall chaos and confusion as the attacks unfolded – followed by a ‘war on terror’ that left agency with a tarnished reputation
Author: Robert Tait
Headline: Veterans recall chaos and confusion as the attacks unfolded – followed by a ‘war on terror’ that left agency with a tarnished reputation
Content: The CIA director, George Tenet, with senior Bush administration staff at the presidential emergency operations center after the attacks of 9/11.Photograph: David Bohrer/US National Archives via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe CIA director, George Tenet, with senior Bush administration staff at the presidential emergency operations center after the attacks of 9/11.Photograph: David Bohrer/US National Archives via Getty ImagesSeptember 11 2001‘It was all hands on deck’: how the CIA responded to 9/11Veterans recall chaos and confusion as the attacks unfolded – followed by a ‘war on terror’ that left agency with a tarnished reputationRobert Taitin WashingtonThu 10 Sep 2026 14.11 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 17.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA generation of spies had lost an enemy but not yet found a role. Then came 9/11.A decade after the dissolution of the Soviet Union, al-Qaida’s devastating attacks on New York and Washington on 11 September 2001 announced to the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) that the long era of battling communism, for which it had been founded, was officially at an end.It was to be replaced by a no-holds-barred “war on terror” that would leave the CIA with a soiled reputation overfalsified intelligencethat led to the invasion and occupation of Iraq, and anextraordinary renditionprogram in which suspects were subjected to “enhanced interrogations” at secret sites that official US inquiries subsequently defined as torture.The US intelligence community was dramatically transformed after two planes flew into the World Trade Center, a third smashed into the Pentagon, and a fourth crashed in the Pennsylvania countryside after passengers overcame the hijackers.Accounts of what unfolded inside the CIA’s headquarters in Langley, Virginia, suggests an organization unprepared for the drastically changed world the attacks ushered in, despite an awareness among some in the intelligence community that al-Qaida and its leader,Osama bin Laden, represented a clear and present danger.Margaret Henoch, then a counter-intelligence officer with little knowledge of terrorism, recalls confusion, chaos and an initial lack of direction from senior leadership as staff struggled to process what seemed like a bolt from a clear blue sky on that balmy late summer day.“One of my officers came in and said to me: ‘A plane just ran into the World Trade Center,’” she said. To this day, Henoch – who had previously been stationed in Vienna, where she focused on the International Atomic Energy Agency and nuclear threats – is haunted by the apparent vacuum that followed.View image in fullscreenSmoke pours over the lower Manhattan skyline on 9/11.Photograph: Brad Rickerby/ReutersAbout 40 minutes after the first attack, with no clear direction from the top of CIA, she decided to go up to the seventh floor, which accommodated the agency’s senior figures, including its then director,George Tenet.To her surprise, the area was deserted, apart from three assistants.“It was reasonable that they would have moved those guys someplace else,” said Henoch. “What was unreasonable, in my humble opinion, was that no one thought about all those people sitting in that building. Because if the Pentagon was hit, there was a chance that we, too, were a target – and it would be nice to believe that the people who left the building rapidly had a thought for all those who worked for them.“It was not clear that they did.”The Guardian contacted Tenet, now working in the private sector, for comment. In an emailed response, Bill Harlow, the CIA’s public affairs director at the time of the attacks, cited details in the 2007 memoir, At the Center of the Storm, which he co-wrote with Tenet, and said orders were issued for the majority of the staff to leave the building at “about 10am” – nearly an hour after the second plane struck at 9.03am.Harlow added: “We were aware at the time of intelligence gathered around 1995-96 of terrorist desires to attack CIA HQ with an airplane.“Director Tenet and the senior leadership moved to another building on the compound that presented a lower profile and would have a greater chance of survival if we were hit by a plane.“Notably, a decision was made that the personnel of the counter-terrorism center remained in the original headquarters building throughout that day … accepting the risk. The senior leadership team returned to the headquarters in the middle of the afternoon on 9/11.”‘I had a briefing on who the hell al-Qaida was’Some time afterwards, an order was given for the thousands of personnel in the building to evacuate. Some, including Henoch, were told to relocate to alternative sites to address the emergency.But by the time of that instruction, nearby roads were choked with traffic as commuters returned home from Washington DC after being released from work early. That prevented agency staff from departing, and triggered fears that they could be sitting ducks for the doomed fourth plane, which was already known to be in the air.“Large segments of the CIA operating staff were trapped,” Henoch said. “One guy, who was senior to me, was standing next to me in the car park and he said, ‘I have served in multiple war zones. I was a combat soldier in Vietnam and I’m going to die in the parking lot of the CIA.’”The dysfunctional scene was soon replaced by one of much greater conviction – leading to permanent changes in US intelligence.“I just remember loads of cable traffic coming in that said: it’s got to be al-Qaida,” said Henoch. “It wasn’t my world, so I had to have a quick briefing on who the hell al-Qaida was, because I just didn’t know anything about it.“The change was immediate. The next morning, everybody at the Central Intelligence Agency had to know who they were, and how it intersected with everything you were doing.”Steven Cash, a former CIA counter-terrorism officer who had left the agency to join the staff of the US Senate intelligence committee six months beforehand, faults the CIA’s pre-9/11 terrorism strategy as being too narrowly focused “looking to find bad guys” while neglecting the “political dimension”.View image in fullscreenOsama bin Laden in Afghanistan in April 1998.Photograph: AP“There was an emphasis on looking at terrorists as if they were a motorcycle gang,” said Cash, who had specialized on the Lebanese Shia group Hezbollah, a close ally of Iran. “A decision was made in the first [George HW] Bush administration to take terrorism away from the people who looked at geographic areas and separate it out. [It was] illustrative of a mistaken way of looking at the world, because terrorists don’t exist in a vacuum.”Cash moved on to focus on the Balkans before leaving the agency, but still harboured guilt after the attacks. “Was this our fault? Did we fail? That kind of guilt felt, at least for me, really personal.”Cash had been on Capitol Hill, attending a committee meeting, when news of the attacks filtered through. “Somebody said, put on the TV and we saw the second plane hit,” he said. “And then they started evacuating the building.“It was a mess. People were in the hall screaming, running around. The third plane had hit the Pentagon by that point, because we could see smoke across the National Mall.”The following day, Cash and his then boss, the late Democratic senator Dianne Feinstein, visited CIA headquarters and found a mood of determined resolve. “It was all hands on deck. The people I knew were getting deployed very quickly to Afghanistan,” he recalled. “These people are pros. They didn’t care whether they were blamed or not. They wanted to do something.“I have a little bit of survivor guilt here. Maybe I should have been shipped out to Afghanistan.”Political pressureOn their visit to CIA headquarters on 12 September, senators asked agency operatives what legislation and resources they would need to respond to the attacks of the previous day, according to Cash.Two early – and controversial – results were the USA Patriot Act of 2001, which expanded law enforcement and surveillance powers, and the Homeland Security Act of the following year, creating the US Department of Homeland Security, which houses agencies including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).Later changes established theOffice of the Director of National Intelligence, with the goal of coordinating 18 different intelligence bodies and eliminating the lack of coordination widely held to blame for warning signs of the 9/11 plot going unheeded.“DNI was formed to make sure that we actually share everything with everybody. We don’t just keep it inside CIA,” said Susan Miller, a retired CIA counter-intelligence officer.View image in fullscreenGeorge Bush with the CIA director, George Tenet, speaker of the House, Dennis Hastert, defense secretary, Donald Rumsfeld, and Senate majority leader, Tom Daschle, on 12 September 2001.Photograph: Mark Wilson/Getty Images“What’s really cool is we’ve changed how we do things across the board, not just for terrorism. It’s really improved things. There was no coordination before.”Yet the reaction to the attacks changed intelligence in another way – by making it more susceptible to political pressure, asPresident George W Bush’sadministration searched for information that could be used to justify an invasion of Iraq to topple Saddam Hussein.In September 2002, Henoch – who had previously studied Russian weapons capabilities working at the Stanford Research Institute – was asked to assess intelligence provided by an Iraqi defector codenamed Curveball, who had sought asylum in Germany, and provided its intelligence agency with what he said was proof of Saddam’s biological weapons program.She quickly concluded the claims were fabricated, and passed her conclusions up the chain of command. They were not well received. When Colin Powell, the then US secretary of state, visited the CIA months later to review the agency’s intelligence on Iraq, Henoch and her fellow doubters were not informed. Powell’s subsequent speech to the United Nations security council in February 2003, in which he made the case for war, relied heavily on Curveball’s testimony – despite Henoch’s insistence when the address was checked with her and other officers beforehand that his assertions were not credible.“We took a look at the Powell speech and I said: ‘You can’t use this. We think this is garbage,” she said. “I did write somewhere – I can’t remember on what page – ‘How can you send someone to die for something like this? No one ever answered that for me.“The next thing I heard was, ‘Well, when we get in there, we’ll find something.’”View image in fullscreenTariq Aziz, Izzat Ibrahim and Taha Yassin Ramadan with Saddam Hussein, far right, in Baghdad in July 2002.Photograph: INA/Getty ImagesAfter the invasion, inspectorsfound no evidence of biological weapons.Curveball was later debunkedas a fraud.Miller, too, encountered the administration’s zeal for intelligence that could justify invading Iraq when she was posted to Prague as CIA station chief in 2002. Czech intelligence had investigated – and, initially, tentatively confirmed – a claim that one of the 9/11 ringleaders,Mohammed Atta, had travelled to Praguethe previous year and met an Iraqi embassy official, Ahmad Samir al-Ani, months before the attacks.The report was seized on by the hawkish US vice-president, Dick Cheney, as evidence of Saddam’s possible links to the attacks, thus providing another justification for war. ButCzech intelligence officials retreatedfrom their earlier stance, and the CIA concluded there was no evidence that the meeting happened.Nevertheless, Donald Rumsfeld, then the US defense secretary, brazenly tried to revive it when Miller briefed him – along with George W Bush and Condoleezza Rice, the national security adviser – when they visited the Czech capital for a Nato summit in 2002.View image in fullscreenColin Powell, Condoleezza Rice and Donald Rumsfeld with President Bush at the Prague Nato summit.Photograph: Brooks Kraft/Corbis/Getty Images“‘Young lady, you forgot about this other thing’,” Rumsfeld told Miller, she said. “I played dumb and said: ‘What other thing?’ He replied: ‘Mohammed Atta was here in Prague meeting the Iraqi consul.’“Bush was looking really uncomfortable and Condi was looking straight ahead. I simply said, ‘Mr President, Madam Secretary, and Mr Rumsfeld, the CIA, the Czech service and I don’t make things up. We give you the facts, and the fact is that he was not here.’“Bush and Rice nodded in acceptance and the ambassador supported me. But Rumsfeld threw his pen down in disgust.”The invasion the neocons cravedWhether the supposed meeting happened or not, Rumsfeld and his neoconservative allies got the invasion they craved – leading to a protracted conflict that tarnished the CIA’s reputation and whose length, along with the coinciding US-led military campaign in Afghanistan, spurred popular opposition to “forever wars”.Despite the blow to the agency’s standing, Cash insisted that its intelligence-gathering and functioning radically improved, thanks to the changes instituted after the attacks. “We have improved our intelligence capabilities significantly from what they were before 9/11,” he said, citing the success in preventing repeat attacks on US soil.View image in fullscreenThe CIA seal at headquarters in Langley.Photograph: Dennis Brack/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesBut with the Trump administration now engaged in a war with Iran, roiling the Middle East, such security could no longer be guaranteed, he believes.“I’m not saying it was a great time,” Cash said, of the CIA’s record in the months and years after September 2001. “But the sense of purpose of being at a place in history where we – as a group, as a society – can do something, was pretty intoxicating.“I was very proud to have been part of it. It sucked – but proud to have been part of it. And I think everything we’re seeing now is the antithesis of that.”Explore more on these topicsSeptember 11 2001CIAnewsShareReuse this content

title: Shabana Mahmood urges police to curb far-right, anti-migrant protests | Far right | The Guardian
description: Home secretary tells officers to make ‘full use’ of their powers after masked vigilantes cause weekend of chaos
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Home secretary tells officers to make ‘full use’ of their powers after masked vigilantes cause weekend of chaos
Content: Mahmood’s move raises the possibility that Hampshire police will insist that protesters due to meet in Portsmouth at 12.30pm on Saturday will be ordered to take off any face coverings.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMahmood’s move raises the possibility that Hampshire police will insist that protesters due to meet in Portsmouth at 12.30pm on Saturday will be ordered to take off any face coverings.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesFar rightShabana Mahmood urges police to curb far-right, anti-migrant protestsHome secretary tells officers to make ‘full use’ of their powers after masked vigilantes cause weekend of chaosRajeev SyalHome affairs editorThu 10 Sep 2026 12.51 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 17.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShabana Mahmood has urged police to curb the activities of far-right, anti-migrant groups which have “obvious malign intent” after a weekend of chaos caused by balaclava-wearing vigilantes.In a meeting on Thursday, the home secretary told senior officers to make “full use” of their powers, including bans on face coverings, afterpolice were assaulted and ports were disruptedin Kent and Hampshire.She signalled the need for “strong deterrence” and improved intelligence in light of new tactics being deployed by groups such asPatriot Platform, led by the convicted kidnapper Daniel Thomas, which helped to organise the protests.Far-right port protests: police told to improve intelligence gatheringRead moreMahmood told the officers: “These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious malign intent being communicated to our residents. This makes it different from other protests, so we need to make sure we are learning lessons.”The Home Office and police were criticised in the aftermath of the weekend for failing to take a hard line on the far right. Environmental campaigners and civil liberties groups have complained that there appears to be a “two-tier” approach, with peaceful climate protesters prosecuted more aggressively than far-right agitators.Police in Dover on Saturday and then Portsmouth on Sunday were taken by surprise when hundreds of protesters wearing black clothes and face masks massed to oppose what they say is illegal immigration via small boats.Both protests are believed by police to have been far-right inspired, with evidence emerging that those behind them were determined to avoid detection.Thursday’s online meeting was held ahead of this weekend, when further disruption is predicted to take place.Mahmood told senior officers to make better use of intelligence to ensure they have the correct resources and expertise in place, and made clear the government’s expectation that police should make full use of the powers at their disposal to ensure anyone who is committing a criminal offence is dealt with “robustly”.The home secretary urged police to make full use of digital evidence, including body-worn video, facial recognition technology, CCTV, ANPR and other intelligence products to identify offenders.The move raises the possibility that Hampshire police will insist that protesters due to meet in Portsmouth at 12.30pm on Saturday will be ordered to take off any face coverings.Forces have planned an “enhanced and coordinated approach to intelligence gathering and operational planning” ahead of the weekend – laying the groundwork for a more proactive response.Labour’s Crime and Policing Act, which took effect in April, gave police powers to create mask-free zones at protests, backed by fines of up to £1,000 or one month’s imprisonment, or both.The power only applies to people who are trying to conceal their identity, rather than those covering their face for reasons of religion, health or work, and officers must take reasonable steps to notify the public of the restriction.Saturday’s protests in Dover, which Thomas claimed to have organised, blocked the town’s roads for several hours, disrupting traffic heading to and from the port.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKent police initially claimed that they had no warning of the Dover protest. That claim fell apart when the force admitted there were warning calls to police on Friday evening which were not acted upon.After a dinghy carrying 120 asylum seekers was rescued on Sunday near the Solent, about 200 black-clad men gathered at Eastney Marina. Protesters blocked roads, leading to alleged assaults on several officers. No one was arrested at either demonstration.Patriot Platform has attempted to bring together disparate local “patriot” groups rather than construct a single hierarchical organisation.In a further development, RNLI volunteers and staff have been warned not to wear the charity’s branding because of the “unacceptable abuse” they have faced from anti-migrant protesters.The charity has issued security advicesince the protests in Dover and Portsmouth, which saw its workers targeted for bringing some small boat migrants ashore.This week, footage posted on social media showed volunteers being labelled as “traitors” after helping to look after people who had arrived in a dinghy in Portsmouth. Protests have been held at RNLI sites, including on Wednesday, when a small anti-migrant gathering was held at the RNLI College in Poole, Dorset.Commenting after the meeting, the deputy chief constable Andy Mariner, the NPCC lead for public order, said: “Policing is continually assessing and preparing for protests and any potential impact on public safety. This includes working closely with local forces, specialist teams, communities and partners, monitoring publicly available information, and ensuring the right resources are available where needed.“We have stepped up this activity this week at a national level, supporting local forces to ensure we have the right information, support and operational capacity in place to respond should we need to.“This includes ensuring commanders are ready to use every power at our disposal, from arrests and dispersal orders to more recent powers which can help police manage protests, where it is proportionate and necessary to do so.”Explore more on these topicsFar rightShabana MahmoodnewsShareReuse this content

title: Lindsay Clancy’s lawyer asks judge to find her not guilty after mistrial | Massachusetts | The Guardian
description: Kevin Reddington says prosecution did not offer evidence that client’s killing of her children constituted murder
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Kevin Reddington says prosecution did not offer evidence that client’s killing of her children constituted murder
Content: Lindsay Clancy's defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, speaks to the press after a mistrial in Plymouth, Massachusetts, on 4 September.Photograph: Joseph Prezioso/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLindsay Clancy's defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, speaks to the press after a mistrial in Plymouth, Massachusetts, on 4 September.Photograph: Joseph Prezioso/AFP/Getty ImagesMassachusettsLindsay Clancy’s lawyer asks judge to find her not guilty after mistrialKevin Reddington says prosecution did not offer evidence that client’s killing of her children constituted murderReutersThu 10 Sep 2026 16.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLindsay Clancy’s lawyer on Thursday asked the judge who oversaw theMassachusettswoman’s murder trial to declare her not guilty of murder by reason of insanity, saying prosecutors had failed to ⁠prove that, despite being mentally ill, ⁠she knew killing her ​three young children would be wrong.Defense attorney Kevin Reddington made the request to Judge William Sullivan six days after the trial ended in a deadlock, and as a fourth member of ⁠the 12-member jury went public to describe how a single juror had prevented the panel from reaching a unanimous verdict.The jury in Plymouth, Massachusetts, deliberated for seven days before Sullivan on Friday declared a mistrial, following repeated ⁠reports by the jury that it was deadlocked.Prosecutors have yet to say if they plan to retry Clancy. But Reddington argued that ​Sullivan should decide the matter himself, saying prosecutors during the ‌six-week trial did not present evidence ‌that would allow a jury to find her guilty on the first-degree murder charges she faces.Reddington argued that even the prosecution’s expert witnesses ‌agreed Clancy suffered from a serious mental illness at the time, and he said the evidence at most showed that she retained the ability to perform familiar tasks, not that she could appreciate the wrongfulness of her actions.“No rational jury could find beyond a reasonable doubt that she had no mental disease or defense when the Commonwealth’s own proof established that she did,” Reddington wrote in the motion, referring to the prosecution.Lindsay Clancy murder trial ends in dramatic deadlock – what comes next?Read moreHe asked the judge to hear arguments on his motion during a hearing scheduled ‌for 29 September. A spokesperson for the Plymouth county district attorney, Timothy Cruz, did not respond to a request for comment.Clancy, 36, has admitted to strangling her three children with exercise bands on 24 January 2023, in ​the basement of their home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury. She then cut herself with a knife and jumped from a second-story window in an attempt to end her own life that left her paralyzed.Reddington at trial sought to convince jurors she should be found not guilty by reason of insanity, known in Massachusetts as lack of criminal responsibility, saying she suffered from postpartum psychosis when she killed Cora, ⁠five; Dawson, three; and eight-month-old Callan.In his motion, Reddington said that 11 of the 12 jurors ​had been prepared to find her not guilty ​by reason of lack of criminal responsibility but ​could not return a verdict due to a holdout who despite acknowledging having reasonable doubt would not agree ​to find her not guilty.Explore more on these topicsMassachusettsUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Four people in hospital after stabbing in south-east London | London | The Guardian
description: Seven people arrested following ‘altercation’ on Bromley High Street on Thursday afternoon
Author: Emine Sinmaz
Headline: Seven people arrested following ‘altercation’ on Bromley High Street on Thursday afternoon
Content: A police statement said: ‘Officers attended the scene alongside the London ambulance service and London’s air ambulance and found four men with stab wounds.’Photograph: James Manning/PAView image in fullscreenA police statement said: ‘Officers attended the scene alongside the London ambulance service and London’s air ambulance and found four men with stab wounds.’Photograph: James Manning/PALondonFour people in hospital after stabbing in south-east LondonSeven people arrested following ‘altercation’ on Bromley High Street on Thursday afternoonEmine SinmazandKevin RawlinsonThu 10 Sep 2026 14.07 EDTFirst published on Thu 10 Sep 2026 12.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSeven people have been arrested after four men were stabbed in south-eastLondon, the Metropolitan police said.Officers were called to reports of “an altercation” on Bromley High Street at 2.15pm and found four men with stab wounds, the force added.In a statement, it said: “Officers attended the scene alongside the London ambulance service and London’s air ambulance and found four men with stab wounds. Three of them were taken to hospital where they are receiving treatment for non-life-threatening injuries. One is in critical condition.View image in fullscreenForensic investigators at the scene on Thursday afternoon.Photograph: James Manning/PA“Seven men were arrested and they all remain in custody. Police inquiries continue and there is not believed to be any wider threat to the public.”A cordon was in place at the scene on Thursday, with police, as well as community support officers, standing around the perimeter. Forensics officers dressed in blue overalls and a crime scene photographer were coming and going from a branch of KFC, where locals said the incident occurred, and there were evidence markers visible on the floor.Abandoned food could still be seen on the tables as evening drew in, suggestive of the haste in which people left the restaurant amid the incident. “I heard a really loud bang and people running from KFC,” said George Ioannou, who was working in Antonio’s Male Grooming next door to the KFC.“An elderly woman ran into the shop and I had to lock the door to shelter her until it calmed down. She was crying. About five minutes later, we heard the sirens.” Other shop workers nearby said the incident was quick and that it was over in moments.The KFC has an alleyway down one side – along which people ran as they passed the male grooming shop – and faces on to Bromley’s High Street. Part of the latter was still closed to the public on Thursday evening. It is a busy thoroughfare, with a large shopping centre at one end and a train station taking commuters between Kent, south-east London and the capital’s centre at the other. Those and the parade of shops lining the high street draw large numbers of people from the surrounding area. About 15 bus routes were diverted, including the 61, 208 and 119.The London ambulance service said ambulance crews, a paramedic in a fast-response car, an incident response officer, an advanced paramedic and London’s air ambulance were dispatched to the scene.Four patients were treated at the scene before being taken to hospital, the service added.The Bromley and Biggin Hill MP Peter Fortune said: “I am aware of the incident on Bromley High Street this afternoon and I know that residents will have safety concerns. The police are in attendance and have made a number of arrests. I will remain in close contact with the police as they continue to investigate this incident.”A picture shared on social media on Thursday afternoon appeared to show a section of Bromley High Street cordoned off, with an emergency vehicle on site. The Met asked anyone with information to contact the police on 101.Explore more on these topicsLondonCrimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Florida sues Netflix over misleading parents over minors’ data collection | Florida | The Guardian
description: Lawsuit brought by James Uthmeier, the attorney general, marks latest action by the state against big tech companies
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Lawsuit brought by James Uthmeier, the attorney general, marks latest action by the state against big tech companies
Content: Netflix’s corporate office in Los Angeles, California.Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNetflix’s corporate office in Los Angeles, California.Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty ImagesFloridaFlorida sues Netflix over misleading parents over minors’ data collectionLawsuit brought by James Uthmeier, the attorney general, marks latest action by the state against big tech companiesMarina DunbarThu 10 Sep 2026 16.11 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 16.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFlorida officials filed a lawsuit againstNetflix, accusing the streaming giant of misleading parents about its collection of minors’ data and using features that encourage children to “binge watch” content.The lawsuit, filed Wednesday and led by James Uthmeier, the RepublicanFloridaattorney general, marks the latest action by Florida against major technology companies. The red-leaning state has taken an increasingly aggressive approach toward big tech, particularly during the rise of artificial intelligence (AI).“Netflix told Florida families they could pay a monthly fee to escape big tech surveillance. That was false,” Uthmeier said in astatement. “Netflix collected detailed data on children and families, designed its product to keep kids watching, and then commercialized that information to launch the advertising business it promised never to build.“Parents, not corporate executives, direct the upbringing of their children. Netflix should expect to be held accountable,” he added.In a statement shared with The Guardian, a spokesperson for Netflix said: “Netflix takes our members’ privacy seriously. We comply with privacy and data‑protection laws everywhere we operate and have dedicated safeguards in place for kids who watch content on Netflix. This lawsuit lacks merit and we intend to vigorously defend the matter in court.”In the66-page lawsuit, Florida accuses Netflix of carrying out a “years-long bait-and-switch” that has “led the company right to where it promised never to be: addicting children and families to its platform, mining those users for data, and then converting that data into lucrative intelligence for global advertising juggernauts”.The lawsuit claims Netflix opened Floridians’ data to commercial data brokers and advertising platforms after it launched advertisements in November 2022, allegedly allowing advertisers to “target Floridians by life stage, income, and household composition”. The complaint says Netflix failed to obtain the consent required under Florida law.It emphasizes that Netflix has in the past made a point to distinguish itself from tech companies that offer “free” services in exchange for data collection such as Google, Facebook, and Amazon, but claims that Netflix has failed to live up to its promises to not track and monetize data similar to other tech companies.Netflix provides members with its updated privacy statement and terms of use annually, according to the streaming service. Those terms lay out the company’s advertising and privacy practices, along with users’ rights and available controls. It also offers parental controls that allow parents to filter or block content.The Florida case follows a lawsuit filed earlier this year by Texas officials accusing Netflix ofspying on childrenand designing its platform to be addictive.Uthmeier has also filed lawsuitsagainst OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT,and TikTokthis year. He recently kept Florida out of amulti-state settlementinvolving Meta, saying the $17bn agreement was “not enough to punish” the company over allegations that it failed to protect minor users.“We’re going to send a message to big tech companies. If you hurt our kids, you are going to have to pay for it,” Uthmeier said whileannouncingthe Netflix lawsuit on Wednesday. “And so, in this lawsuit, we will be seeking billions of damages.”Explore more on these topicsFloridaNetflixLaw (US)newsShareReuse this content

title: UK ministers explore raising price of water for industrial users amid shortages | Water | The Guardian
description: Environment Agency says talks under way about increasing prices for industrial users to try to reduce poor water management
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: Environment Agency says talks under way about increasing prices for industrial users to try to reduce poor water management
Content: Woodhead reservoir near Glossop, England, in August.Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWoodhead reservoir near Glossop, England, in August.Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty ImagesWaterUK ministers explore raising price of water for industrial users amid shortagesEnvironment Agency says talks under way about increasing prices for industrial users to try to reduce poor water managementPippa NeillEnvironment reporterThu 10 Sep 2026 07.14 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMinisters are exploring making water more expensive for some users, in the face of severe supply shortages.Despite the UK being a famously wet country, theprecarious natureof the water supply has been made particularly acute this summer, with almost three-quarters of England and all of Walesin droughtand 27 million people facing restrictions on their water use.As the climate crisis worsens and demand for water increases, theEnvironment Agencyhas estimated that, without action, England’s water supply could be short by 5bn litres a day by 2055.Helen Wakeham, the director of water at the Environment Agency, said that to plug this severe and growing gap, the value of water needed to increase.“If someone wants an abstraction licence from the Environment Agency, what they pay for is the cost of producing the licence. They don’t pay anything towards the value of that water,” she said.While millions of households in England are payingrecord levelsfor their water bills, Wakeham said that, for big industrial customers, the more water they used, the less they paid.There was a “lively conversation” going on about whether we could “completely reframe the way we value and pay for water”.“It’s the beginning of a conversation, but ministers have asked us to look at the value of water and how our abstraction licensing system works,” she said.The Guardianrecently revealedthat less than 1% of businesses in England use more water than the daily needs of 10 million people. Some of these businesses, which include oil refineries, chemical plants and paper mills, face no requirements to cut their consumption.With the government committed to make England an AI superpower, there are also questions about where water-hungry datacentres will get their resources from. Water UK, the body representing the UK water industry, warned theUK would not have enough waterfor future datacentres.“The reason datacentres are water-hungry is because water is so cheap,” said Wakeham.View image in fullscreenAn aerial view of the depleted Chew reservoir in Oldham, England, in August.Photograph: Brook Mitchell/Getty ImagesDr Doug Parr, Greenpeace UK’s chief scientist and policy adviser, said: “Every day, people are doing their bit to save water, but they are being hit with higher bills and hosepipe bans while big business gets cheap water access. At a time when the country is facing water stress due to climate change, it is absurd that major companies have access to water that is cheaper for them, per litre, the more they use. This has to change. The whole abstraction policy and licensing needs to be rewritten from a blank sheet of paper to make it fit for a country facing summer droughts and a biodiversity crisis.”Environment Agency permitting means datacentres are required to use drinking water only. Jon Chappell, the trade body’s deputy director, said this was “unforgivable” and a “genuine failing of government”.WaterUK has estimated that datacentres in England use 6.6m litres of drinking water every day. With the government’s ambition to triple datacentre capacity by 2030, this could increase to 19.8m litres a day.Wakeham agreed there was an issue with drinking water being used for cooling and industrial supply, and said the agency was “working with the government to look at different ways of pricing and valuing water to make sure that the right water goes to the right places”. She said this could result in water becoming more expensive for industrial users.“The overarching message is that water is so cheap that often it’s not managed, because it’s cheaper just to use more water,” Wakeham said.A Defra spokesperson said: “We’ve all felt the impact of extreme weather this year. With millions of households facing hosepipe bans and farmers dealing with drought, it’s only right that we take a closer look at industrial water use too, to ensure we’re using our water resources wisely.“We want to keep bills as low as possible for consumers and make sure industry uses less drinking-quality water where it isn’t needed, while making it easier to reuse water so every drop counts. The water system in this country is broken. That’s why we’re delivering the biggest reform in a generation, so water is there for the people who need it.”Explore more on these topicsWaterEnvironment AgencyWater industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Canada helped save the bald eagle from near extinction in the US – does the White House know? | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: The White House posted a photo of bald eagle attacking a Canada goose – but it was Canada that played a critical role in the recovery of the raptor in the US
Author: Leyland Cecco
Headline: The White House posted a photo of bald eagle attacking a Canada goose – but it was Canada that played a critical role in the recovery of the raptor in the US
Content: As many as half a million bald eagles once thrived before the European settlement of North America.Photograph: Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAs many as half a million bald eagles once thrived before the European settlement of North America.Photograph: Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpCanada helped save the bald eagle from near extinction in the US – does the White House know?The White House posted a photo of bald eagle attacking a Canada goose to send a message – but it was Canada that played a critical role in the recovery of the bird in the USLeyland Ceccoin TorontoThu 10 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 14.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn late August, the White House posted a real photograph on social media of a bald eagle standing atop the limp neck of aCanadagoose.The raptor presses the goose’s face into the grey winter slush. With its stark white head and brilliant yellow talons, the eagle looks victorious and defiant.As trade talks failed and tensions between Canada and the US rose, the image, viewed millions of times, apparently proved irresistible to the social media handlers at the White House for sending a clear message: the United States could not be challenged by Canada.But experts say the bald eagle, long prized by Americans as a symbol even before becoming the country’s national bird in 2024, came perilously close to disappearing from much of the country – and that it was neighbouring Canada that played a critical role in its recovery, even going as far as to fly juvenile eagles south by plane to return them to US skies.As many as half a million bald eagles once thrived before the European settlement of North America, near large bodies of open water, where they feasted on the abundant fish and nested in towering trees.View image in fullscreenThe eagle’s hulking, majestic presence left an imprint on the founders of the modern United States.Photograph: Mark Peterson/Corbis/Getty ImagesThe eagle’s hulking, majestic presence left an imprint on the founders of the modern United States, who placed the bird on the Great Seal of the United States in 1782. (The use of the word “bald” doesn’t not mean hairless. Instead, it comes derives from the Middle English word “balde” or “balled” whichmeans marked by a whiteblaze)But crisis struck, as rapidly expanding settlements put eagles on a collision course with humans. “Bald eagles were seen by some as competitors for fish resources and a threat to their livestock and wild game by others,” said David Bird, a professor emeritus of wildlife biology at McGill University in Montreal. “None of those things turned out to be true in the end.”Officials initially offered 50 cents for a pair of eagle feet, later raising the bounty to $2 by 1949. More than 100,000 bald eagles were killed under the bounty program until it was discontinued in 1953.View image in fullscreenIn birds of prey, the result of DDT was devastating: eggshells became so thin and brittle that many eggs broke before they could hatch.Photograph: Andrew Lichtenstein/Corbis/Getty ImagesMeanwhile, a synthetic chemical compound was having an unexpected effect on wildlife. DDT, first produced on a large scale to combat malaria and then widely applied after the second world war to fight pests, was accumulating in the fatty tissues of animals – particularly in predators at the top of the food chain. In birds of prey, the result was devastating: eggshells became so thin and brittle that many eggs broke before they could hatch. The effectsinspired Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring, the 1962 book that helped catalyse the modern environmental movement.“If we are going to live so intimately with these chemicals eating and drinking them, taking them into the very marrow of our bones – we had better know something about their nature and their power,” she wrote. The pesticide was eventually banned in 1972.Bird said the “the double whammy” of bounties and reproductive collapse put immense pressure on bald eagles. In 1963, only 417 breeding pairs remained in the lower 48 states.Desperate biologists and officials turned to Canada. While DDT had ravaged much of the population in the US, the pesticide had been used less extensively north of the border.View image in fullscreenA doctor examining the X-ray of a bald eagle, in 1972.Photograph: Denver Post/Getty ImagesA 1983 media reportprofiled Operation Eaglet, a complex logistical effort that required cars, float planes and biologists in order to help repopulate the US. The CBC reporter called the effort a “courtesy of Canadian goodwill”. In one instance, the team collected eight baby eagles from northern Manitoba, where experts believed roughly 3,000 birds remained, and sent one each to Pennsylvania and New Jersey, with the remaining six bound for Massachusetts, where they would make “a tremendous difference”, as project leader Jack Swedberg told the CBC, because “currently we don’t have any”.The mission relied on a technique called “hacking”, in which eaglets were raised in controlled environments, out of sight of people, in order to prevent imprinting on humans and associating their caregivers with food. Over the years, 88 eagles were brought to Pennsylvania from the province of Saskatchewan. Thestate now has300 breeding pairs.View image in fullscreenBill Clinton meets Challenger, to celebrate the success of the Endangered Species Act by announcing action to remove the American bald eagle from the endangered species list, on 2 July 1999 in the Rose Garden.Photograph: Georges De Keerle/Getty ImagesEven thelocation of the photographused by the White House reflects the unlikely recovery of the population. The image was captured by Derek Stoll in New York state, which by the 1970s had justa single breeding pair.“You’re not allowed to import bald eagles. So there was a population in Canada, but we are not allowed to bring bald eagles into the United States,” Darryl McGrath, the Albany-based author of Flight Paths,said during a 2016 lecture. “So we couldn’t get the eagle chicks for this hacking project – we couldn’t get them from Canada, even though Canada was very willing to help us out.” Instead, New York relied on other states, including Alaska, until laws concerning the transport of endangered species were amended.Other eagles were sourced for the US from the coastal provinces of British Columbia and Nova Scotia, including 36 from Cape Breton sent to repopulate New Jersey and Massachusetts.Bird says that the peopletrading memes about the eagle and the goosemay not know the shared history of a key conservation success story. But he points out that even if Canada geese look like easy prey for an eagle – and they can be – they are also “formidable” birds with powerful club-like wings.And he notes that another beloved Canadian bird – which adorns Canada’s one-dollar coin – should similarly not be underestimated.View image in fullscreenLincoln the bald eagle during the UFC Freedom 250 ceremonial weigh-in, in Washington DC on 13 June.Photograph: Chris Unger/Zuffa LLCIn 2020 an eaglewas found floating lifelessly in a Maine lake. A necropsy confirmed what experts suspected – the eagle threatened a common loon and its chick.“It stabbed the eagle through the heart with its beak,” said Bird, adding that given the current political climate, the symbolism was “hard to ignore”.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpTrump tariffsCanadaMark CarneyAmericasTariffsUS politicsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Climate solutions most likely to reach ‘positive tipping points’ revealed by scientists | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: Global shift towards clean electricity could trigger ‘cascade’ of progress, helping reduce air pollution, cut waste and revive oceans
Author: Matthew Pearce
Headline: Global shift towards clean electricity could trigger ‘cascade’ of progress, helping reduce air pollution, cut waste and revive oceans
Content: The report identified clean electricity as the ‘highest-leverage’ transition, as cheaper solar and wind power could accelerate change beyond the energy sector.Photograph: Dave Donaldson/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe report identified clean electricity as the ‘highest-leverage’ transition, as cheaper solar and wind power could accelerate change beyond the energy sector.Photograph: Dave Donaldson/AlamyClimate crisisClimate solutions most likely to reach ‘positive tipping points’ revealed by scientistsGlobal shift towards clean electricity could trigger ‘cascade’ of progress, helping reduce air pollution, cut waste and revive oceansMatthew PearceThu 10 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 05.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA rapid global shift to clean electricity could trigger a “cascade” of progress towards repairing the damage to the planet by the climate crisis, according to a report identifying the environmental solutions most likely to bring about change.The analysis focuses on “positive tipping points” – thresholds beyond which a sustainable technology or practice becomes increasingly cheap, widespread or politically popular, allowing progress to become self-propelling.It identifies clean electricity as the “highest-leverage” transition, because cheaper solar and wind power can accelerate change far beyond the energy sector. Clean power improves the economics of electric vehicles, heat pumps and cleaner industrial processes, while reducingair pollutionand stimulating further demand for renewable electricity.Removing CO2 from atmosphere vital to avoid catastrophic tipping points, leading scientist saysRead moreThereportbuilds on the work ofProf Tim Lenton, the founding director of the University of Exeter’s Global Systems Institute, who has studied climate tipping points since the 1990s.Steve Smith, the report’s author and a research fellow at the University of Exeter, said: “The cascade of clean energy that we’re seeing now is just doing so much more than anybody expected even 10 years ago.”Solar and wind power have already crossed positive tipping points in many major markets, Smith said, as growing deployment has reduced costs, attracted investment and driven further expansion.The report, produced by the University of Exeter with theEarthshot prize, applies tipping point science to 51 priority areas across five environmental goals: protecting nature, cleaning the air, reviving oceans, eliminating waste and tackling the climate crisis.Smith said positive tipping points could be understood as the beneficial counterpart todangerous climate thresholds, such as the collapse of ice sheets or the death of coral reefs.“Tipping points can also work in our favour,” he said. The rapid growth of solar power, wind power and electric vehicles, as well as the recovery of some natural systems, showed beneficial change could accelerate after reaching a critical threshold.However, the transition to clean power is being impeded by slow planning and grid expansion, particularly in wealthier economies, and a severe lack of investment elsewhere. Africa receives less than 2% of global clean energy investment despite possessing 60% of the world’s best solar resources, according to the report.Research cited in the analysissuggests coordinated policies supporting clean power, transport and heating could bring forward tipping points in those sectors by between two and eight years. Progress in one sector makes the others easier by increasing demand for clean electricity, encouraging investment and driving costs down further.Transforming global commodity supply chains is identified as another high-impact intervention. A relatively small number of companies, banks and regulators control trade in commodities including beef, soy, palm oil, timber, cocoa and coffee, which together drive much of the world’s tropical deforestation.Aligning the policies of large markets such as the EU, China, UK and US could make deforestation-free products the global norm, the report said. If regulators, producers and financial institutions adopted common standards, companies could find it increasingly difficult to sell or finance goods linked to forest destruction.“You need to be able to align not just the producers, but also the policymakers, the wholesalers, the consumers, the banks, the insurance companies, and get everybody working and doing the same thing,” Smith said.Clean cooking and household energy are also close to tipping points in some countries, as pay-as-you-go business models and decentralised solar power make cleaner technologies more affordable and accessible. About 2.1 billion people still rely on solid fuels for cooking, exposing them to harmful indoor air pollution, with women and children suffering disproportionately.Smith also singled out cuttingmethaneemissions as one of the quickest ways to alter the course of global heating. Methane is responsible for about 30% of the warming experienced so far but remains in the atmosphere for only about 12 years.“Methane abatementis one of the fastest levers we have available for limiting peak warming,” he said. Satellites and drones can now expose methane leaks that were previously invisible, allowing relatively inexpensive interventions to affect the temperature trajectory within a decade.The report argues that climate adaptation could also become self-reinforcing. When flood defences, early-warning systems and resilient infrastructure are shown to reduce losses, they can lower insurance and borrowing costs, attract investors and make further investment more attractive.But finance is frequently working in the opposite direction. About $7.3tn (£5.4tn) flows each year to activities that degrade nature, compared with about $220bn for nature-based solutions,according to UN figurescited in the report.“For every £1 invested in protecting nature, you’ve got £30 spent trying to degrade it,” Smith said. “So that’s a political choice and it’s not a lack of finance. It’s where it’s used.”Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisShareReuse this content

title: Climate ‘feedback loops’ could worsen global warming by 30%, study finds | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: Emissions of planet-heating methane and CO2 from natural sources are worsening the climate crisis, paper says
Author: Oliver Milman
Headline: Emissions of planet-heating methane and CO2 from natural sources are worsening the climate crisis, paper says
Content: Fiercer wildfires in drying forests are occurring globally, as seen in this image from Indonesia in August 2026.Photograph: Mast Irham/EPAView image in fullscreenFiercer wildfires in drying forests are occurring globally, as seen in this image from Indonesia in August 2026.Photograph: Mast Irham/EPAClimate crisisClimate ‘feedback loops’ could worsen global warming by 30%, study findsEmissions of planet-heating methane and CO2 from natural sources are worsening the climate crisis, paper saysOliver MilmanThu 10 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRising global temperatures caused by the burning of fossil fuels are transforming the world’s forests, wetlands and tundra to the point they are releasing emissions that could further worsen global heating by as much as 30%, a new study has found.As the world heats up, permafrost in the high latitudes is thawing, fiercer wildfires are burning in drying forests and wetlands and lakes are warming. All of these changes are themselves causing the release of planet-heating methane and carbon dioxide locked in trees and soils, therefore worsening the climate crisis, the paper states.While scientists have long known of these “feedback loops” that amplify the impact of direct pollution from burning coal, oil and gas, the emissions from natural sources are largely unaccounted for in climate projections.This additional heating is however significant, researchers found, with emissions from natural sources set to amplify global heating by 20% to 30% by the end of this century. This would add an estimated 0.2C to 0.4C to the global average temperature by this time, depending on the overall action taken by countries to combat the climate crisis.View image in fullscreenFumaroles are seen in an area of cultivated cattail swamps to mitigate air pollution threat at the Salton Sea on 19 February 2021 near Calipatria, California.Photograph: David McNew/Getty ImagesEven small fractions of temperature change across the global climate can greatly change the risk of severe and deadly heatwaves, floods, drought and other impacts.The United Nationslast week concededthe international pact to constraint the global temperature rise to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels will be breached in the next few years, causing climate impacts such as this summer’s recordheatwavesandwildfiresto “strike faster, hit harder and last longer.”Yet the increase in the world’s fever will likely be even larger than most projections currently account for, the new research warns, as they do not factor in the methane and CO2 that will spew from permafrost, wetlands, freshwaters and wildfires – the four areas the paper analyzed.“This hidden multiplier is missing from the models guiding climate policy, so those models are likely underestimating how much warming is coming – and overestimating how much carbon we can still afford to emit,” said Sam Abernethy, a scientist atSpark Climate Solutionswho led theresearch, published in Environmental Research Letters.The disruption of the world’s carbon cycles is now being seen in “real time”, said Rob Jackson, a Stanford University scientist and study co-author. “The results are a wake-up call, and it’s imperative that they be included in the next generation of climate policies,” he added. “Failure to do so will make meeting the world’s climate goals less and less likely.”There has been long-standing concern that should global heating melt enough of the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets, thaw enough permafrost, warp crucial ocean currents and turn the Amazon rainforest into a savannah, the world will career past a series of catastrophic tipping points where the climate system spins wildly outside any sort of restraining human influence.The planet is getting closer to such a “point of no return” where this runaway global heating becomes reality,a separate study earlier this year warned.View image in fullscreenSevere erosion of the permafrost tundra in the Yukon Delta, Alaska in 2019. According to scientists emissions from natural sources set to amplify global heating by 20% to 30% by the end of this century.Photograph: Mark Ralston/AFP/Getty ImagesThis latest paper makes clear that action by countries to cut fossil fuel pollution will still lessen the amount of additional emissions that come from landscapes. Under the most optimistic climate scenario where emissions are cut quickly, natural sources will add 0.2C of warming, the paper found. Under a worse case higher emissions scenario, 0.4C will likely be added.Current policies put in place by governments are likely to see the global temperature rise to 2.6C above pre-industrial times,according to Climate Action Tracker. This will likely cause severe disruption and hardship to billions of people through sea level rise, crop losses and other consequences.“One of the most troubling aspects of climate change is that warming can trigger natural processes that cause still more warming,” said Bill Ripple, an ecologist at Oregon State University who helped author the research earlier this year on runaway heating. He was not involved in the new paper, which he called “important”.“This does not mean that a Hothouse Earth trajectory is inevitable, but it provides another warning about the possibility of reinforcing feedbacks that can amplify the warming humans initiate,” he said.“The paper also reminds us why every fraction of a degree matters. The more we warm the planet, the more we risk activating natural processes that add still more greenhouse gases to the atmosphere. This makes rapid reductions in fossil fuel emissions even more urgent.”Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisFossil fuelsEnergynewsShareReuse this content

title: Ryanair will dispute passenger’s claim he was sucked out of window | Ryanair | The Guardian
description: CEO Michael O’Leary tells reporters the businessman was sucked ‘towards’ but not ‘out of’ the opening
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: CEO Michael O’Leary tells reporters the businessman was sucked ‘towards’ but not ‘out of’ the opening
Content: The smashed window of the Ryanair aircraft seen after it made an emergency landing in July. Michael O’Leary said he was ‘not trying to downplay’ the incident.Photograph: Despoina Papapavlou/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe smashed window of the Ryanair aircraft seen after it made an emergency landing in July. Michael O’Leary said he was ‘not trying to downplay’ the incident.Photograph: Despoina Papapavlou/ReutersRyanairRyanair will dispute passenger’s claim he was sucked out of windowCEO Michael O’Leary tells reporters the businessman was sucked ‘towards’ but not out of the openingGwyn TophamTransport correspondentThu 10 Sep 2026 08.10 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRyanair has said it will be “disputing” that any part of a passenger’s body was sucked outside when a window on one of its aircraft broke while in flight.US investigators are examiningthe incidentwhich left Ljubisa Karović, 61, severely injured when the window beside him shattered on a Ryanair flight from Greece to Germany in July.Karović’s lawyer said the Serbian businessman was hauled back in after his head and right arm were sucked through the window of the Boeing 737 owing to the sudden depressurisation.However, Ryanair’s chief executive, Michael O’Leary, said the airline would be “disputing” that account, telling reporters after the airline’s annual general meeting (AGM) in Dublin on Thursday that Karović was “certainly sucked towards the window, but he didn’t get out the window”.The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) in the US is leading the accident investigation, alongside Boeing, engine manufacturer GE, and Ryanair.O’Leary said: “He wasn’t partially out the window. Part of his face didn’t get out the window. We don’t think any part of his body got out the window, but he was certainly sucked in very dramatic circumstances towards the window.”View image in fullscreenMichael O’Leary disputed the account of the air traffic control provider Nats over the reasons for the latest air traffic control failure on Tuesday.Photograph: Kuba Stężycki/ReutersHe said the passenger had been “belted into the seat”, adding: “We will be certainly at the end of the process disputing that he or any part of his anatomy will bend out the window.”O’Leary said he was “not trying to downplay it” and the airline would “have to await the outcome of the NTSB report”.In aninterview with the Guardian, Karović said he believed his seatbelt had kept him in the plane as he blacked out, while his wife, Svetlana, said one passenger played a crucial part in his rescue, as she watched her husband “half in and out of the plane”.She said the unknown male passenger, believed to be Albanian, “did all he could to bring him in and then tried to block the window, first with a bag that was immediately sucked out and then with a suitcase, which worked”.Ryanair warns air fares in Europe will jump next year if oil price stays highRead moreMeanwhile, about a third of shareholders at the AGM voted against O’Leary’s latest pay deal, worth €150m (£129m). The package, agreed over the summer, would give him options on 10m shares if he hits profit and share price targets, and stays at the helm of the Irish carrier until 2032.Ryanair said it would later publish the results of the votes, which approved the deal by about 2-1.O’Leary also continued to dispute the account of the British air traffic control provider National Air Traffic Services (Nats) over the reasons for the latestfailure on Tuesday, which disrupted travel for hundreds of thousands of passengers flying in and out of the UK and cancelled more than 2,100 flights.Martin Rolfe, the Nats boss, told the BBC on Tuesday: “This will be something we haven’t seen in more than 50 years of operation.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionContinuing his long vendetta against Rolfe, O’Leary accused him of “telling lies to save his own skin”.A Ryanair spokesperson said Nats told a call with its teams on Tuesday that the reason was a “spurious flight plan”. A separate flight plan problemcaused an outage in 2023.Nats said the problem occurred in its flight processing system but was not the same fault as those that caused outages and mass disruption in 2023 and 2025.Speaking in the Commons on Thursday, the aviation minister, Keir Mather, said Nats had “experienced an issue with its flight processing system at its Swanwick centre affecting the data that was available to controllers”.He said the fix “took time as the systems needed to be tested to ensure that they had fully recovered and operations could safely return to normal”. Nats, he added, had “confirmed that it was a technical issue and it does not believe it to be cyber-related”.Nats is due to submit a report next week while ministers have instructed the Civil Aviation Authority to conduct an independent review.O’Leary stoked further outrage by comparing his competitors to “rapists”, a term he has used for some rivals since the 2000s but less often publicly in recent times.He told reporters people were “desperate to get to Ryanair’s low fares because they can’t afford to fly with the high-fare rapists around Europe”. After repeating the “high-fare rapists” comments, and when challenged whether this was appropriate language, O’Leary told reporters: “Absolutely.”Explore more on these topicsRyanairAirline industryMichael O'LearyAir transportIrelandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sacha Baron Cohen lined up for Quentin Tarantino’s West End playwriting debut | Theatre | The Guardian
description: The Ali G and Borat creator is reported to be taking the lead in The Popinjay Cavalier, a swashbuckling comedy Tarantino is developing for early 2027
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: The Ali G and Borat creator is reported to be taking the lead in The Popinjay Cavalier, a swashbuckling comedy Tarantino is developing for early 2027
Content: ‘Armed with techniques that still get me into trouble’ … Sacha Baron Cohen.Photograph: Christopher Polk/Variety/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Armed with techniques that still get me into trouble’ … Sacha Baron Cohen.Photograph: Christopher Polk/Variety/Getty ImagesTheatreSacha Baron Cohen lined up for Quentin Tarantino’s West End playwriting debutThe Ali G and Borat creator is reported to be taking the lead in The Popinjay Cavalier, a swashbuckling comedy Tarantino is developing for early 2027Chris WiegandStage editorThu 10 Sep 2026 13.04 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 13.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHe will soon be seen resuming his old Staines rudeboy persona in the filmAli G: Who Iz I?, but Sacha Baron Cohen may also be eyeing a new departure – on stage.The actor will reportedly star inQuentin Tarantino’s first play, The Popinjay Cavalier, which is billed as a“rambunctious comedy of deception and disguise” and a “sweeping celebration of theatre and its heightened romance”, set in 1830s Europe.According to Deadline, Baron Cohen will play the swashbuckling title character in the play, which Tarantino will also direct.The Popinjay Cavalier, presented by Sonia Friedman Productions and Sony Pictures Entertainment, was announced in March and has a planned opening date of early 2027, in a West End theatre yet to be confirmed.
