Tarantino, who now lives in Tel Aviv, said last year that he would move to England with his family to work on the play and that it would take up between 18 and 24 months of his life.View image in fullscreenQuentin Tarantino in 2023.Photograph: Jacopo M Raule/Getty Images for Belles Rives GroupIn July, Friedman told the Sunday Times that Tarantino was “very theatre literate”, and that “the most refreshing thing about him, which not all writers and directors have, is his interest in the audience experience. He wants the audience to have the best freaking night out in the theatre they’ve had all year.”Baron Cohen, who took his successful TV characters such as Ali G and Borat from the small to the big screen with huge success, has not yet had a leading role in a major stage production. He trained with the French clown guru Philippe Gaulier. When Gaulier died earlier this year,the actor told the Guardian: “If I hadn’t crossed paths with him, I’d probably be doing something terribly sensible. Instead, I chose comedy – entirely because he believed in me, pushed me, and armed me with techniques that still get me into trouble.”Tarantino cast Baron Cohen in a small role in his 2012 western Django Unchained but the actorlater saidthat he withdrew from the production in order to star in Tom Hooper’s film version ofLes Misérables, based on the long-running West End musical.Ali G: Who Iz I? is released next month. Publicists for Baron Cohen and The Popinjay Cavalier did not confirm the casting when contacted.Explore more on these topicsTheatreWest EndSacha Baron CohenQuentin TarantinoComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)newsShareReuse this content

title: English winemakers expect ‘vintage year’ after record-breaking summer heat | England | The Guardian
description: Hot weather means sweeter grapes, but outlook gloomier for beermakers, as drought diminishes barley harvest
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Hot weather means sweeter grapes, but outlook gloomier for beermakers, as drought diminishes barley harvest
Content: Nyetimber vineyard in West Chiltington.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNyetimber vineyard in West Chiltington.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesEnglandEnglish winemakers expect ‘vintage year’ after record-breaking summer heatHot weather means sweeter grapes, but outlook gloomier for beermakers, as drought diminishes barley harvestHelena HortonThu 10 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEnglish sparkling winemakers expect their earliest grape harvest and a “vintage year” after a scorching summer quickly ripened grapes.However, beer sellers have warned of a potential shortage after record-breaking temperatures and a drought hitting much ofEnglandhas caused poor yields of barley.Nyetimber, which was the first producer in England to grow pinot noir, chardonnay and pinot meunier exclusively for sparkling wine, has 11 vineyards in West Sussex, Kent and Hampshire.It has announced it will begin picking grapes on 14 September for this year’s harvest, the earliest since the company planted its first vines in 1988. The winemaker’s next earliest harvest was in 2018, when the first grape was picked on 19 September.Nyetimber said this harvest, for which it has recruited 500 pickers, will yield almost 2,500 tonnes of grapes, which could result in more than 1.5 million bottles of sparkling wine being produced from the 2026 vintage.‘It’s a sun trap’: climate crisis brings boomtime for British wineRead moreBecause of the late spring frosts, it is expected the harvest will be slightly smaller than usual, but that the large number of sunny days this year will have concentrated the sugar in the grapes, meaning 2026 could be a vintage year. The company’s first vintage was Blanc de Blancs 1992, which won numerous wine prizes.Nyetimber’s head winemaker, Cherie Spriggs, said: “This year brings another unprecedented vintage as we begin harvesting earlier than ever. We are excited to taste the fruits of our labour, which as always has come with certain challenges: late spring frosts that affected almost 30% and the summer drought, which has decreased the size of certain berries. However, the hot and sunny weather has helped to balance out these factors, giving us strong potential for fantastic wine quality.”Though winemakers are celebrating, the outlook is gloomier for beer aficionados. Lisa Hogan, who runs the Diddly Squat Farm in Oxfordshire with her partner, the TV presenterJeremy Clarkson, has said there may be “less beer all around” after extreme weather led to a poor barley harvest.View image in fullscreenDiddly Squat Farm in Chipping Norton, Oxfordshire is run by Hogan and Clarkson.Photograph: Stephen Dorey/AlamyThis summer was theUK’s hottest on record,according to provisional Met Office data. In England, temperatures peaked at 38.1C (100.1F) at Kew Gardens in London on 13 August, and June had already been confirmed as the country’shottest since records began in 1884.Scientists have said these heatwaves are only possible because of the climate crisis, driven by burning fossil fuels. August was thejoint hottest monthever recorded around the world, with global temperatures reaching 1.65C above preindustrial levels, scientists said on Thursday, amid warnings of further heating on the way.European heatwave is worst ever and impossible without climate crisis, scientists sayRead moreHogan and Clarkson make Hawkstone Lager on their farm, which has been made famous by the Amazon show Clarkson’s Farm.Hogan said: “I think a lot of barley farmers suffered … And funnily enough, last year our yields were terrible, but the quality was better. This year, after a second year of dry weather, both the harvest and its quality have suffered.” She said farmers were struggling to irrigate crops, leading to poor yields.TheAgricultureand Horticulture Development Board has said the barley harvest could be the worst on record and said yields were running 19% below the five-year average last month.Hogan added that other countries are facing similar difficulties: “It is a struggle because if you have another bad harvest, you won’t be able to supplement, say, by getting grain in from Poland. So, we just have to pay a higher cost, and then we have to try not to pass that on to the customer.”Explore more on these topicsEnglandWineBeerClimate crisisExtreme heatFossil fuelsFarmingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Two arrested in London on suspicion of aiding Iran’s foreign intelligence | UK news | The Guardian
description: Arrests of woman, 42, and man, 60, follow Met search of addresses in north and north-west London
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Arrests of woman, 42, and man, 60, follow Met search of addresses in north and north-west London
Content: The Met said the investigation is not linked to attacks at buildings and venues linked to Jewish and Iranian communities in London.Photograph: Kin Cheung/APView image in fullscreenThe Met said the investigation is not linked to attacks at buildings and venues linked to Jewish and Iranian communities in London.Photograph: Kin Cheung/APUK newsTwo arrested in London on suspicion of aiding Iran’s foreign intelligenceArrests of woman, 42, and man, 60, follow Met search of addresses in north and north-west LondonPress AssociationThu 10 Sep 2026 09.54 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man and a woman have been arrested by counter-terrorism police in London on suspicion of assisting Iran’s foreign intelligence service.The arrests of the 42-year-old woman and 60-year-old man were made after searches at addresses in north and north-west London on 24 June, the Metropolitan police said.A third property was also searched in north-west London on 9 September after their arrest under the National Security Act (NSA).The investigation is not linked to attacks at buildings and venues linked to Jewish and Iranian communities in London, the force added.It is also not thought to be linked to any activity or events linked to the Jewish high holy days period.The man and woman have been released on conditional bail until a date in October.Commander Helen Flanagan, the head of counter-terrorism policing London, said: “We know that news of these arrests will come as a concern to some members of the public, but I want to stress that we do not believe there to be any imminent threat to the wider public in connection with this matter.“We’ve seen a marked increase in the tempo of our work linked to national security and state threats over the past year and this investigation is a continuation of that.“As we’ve shown here, if we suspect any activity could threaten the safety of the UK or the public, then we will not hesitate to take action.“I would also like to remind the public that the overall terrorism threat level is at severe, so we continue to ask for everyone’s support through being vigilant, and if you see or hear anything that doesn’t look right, then please, trust your instincts, and report it to us.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Houthis seize key Yemeni port of Mocha in drive to take control of Red Sea coast | Houthis | The Guardian
description: Iran and its proxies move closer to full control of two shipping chokepoints as regional conflict widens
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Iran and its proxies move closer to full control of two shipping chokepoints as regional conflict widens
Content: Fighters loyal to the Houthis take part in a recruitment drive in Sana’a on Thursday.Photograph: Mohammed Huwais/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFighters loyal to the Houthis take part in a recruitment drive in Sana’a on Thursday.Photograph: Mohammed Huwais/AFP/Getty ImagesHouthisHouthis seize key Yemeni port of Mocha in drive to take control of Red Sea coastIran and its proxies move closer to full control of two shipping chokepoints as regional conflict widensExplained: why the fighting in Yemen matters globallyPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorThu 10 Sep 2026 07.39 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHouthi forces inYemenare making a concerted drive to take over the country’s Red Sea coast fully, claiming control of the key port of Mocha in the most serious wave of fighting with the Saudi-backed government in years, bringing the Iran-aligned group closer to full control of a key shipping route.Seizure of the coast and some of the islands in the sea would be a strategic disaster forSaudi Arabiaand the US, taking Iran and its proxies closer to full control of two choke points for western shipping on opposite sides of the Arabian peninsula: the Bab al-Mandab at the southern end of the Red Sea and the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.Observers have said a reduction in hostilities – the most intense since the UN-sponsored ceasefire of April 2022 put an end to major military exchanges – now seems unlikely in what is seen as an attempt by theHouthisto open a second front in the Iran-US war, alongside the battle for control of Hormuz.Baraa Shiban,the Royal United Services Institute’s(Rusi) Yemen specialist, a London-based security thinktank, said the situation in the country was spiralling out of control, adding that the UN-recognised Yemeni government was opening new fronts against the Houthis in the hope of putting more pressure on their forces than they could withstand. But in the past 48 hours the Houthis had major advances south, down Yemen’s west coast, taking them closer to the high ground overlooking the narrow Bab al-Mandab strait.View image in fullscreenA screen grab from video footage released by Saudi-backed forces shows a rocket being fired during fighting in Taiz province.Photograph: Yemen National Resistance Forces/AFP/Getty ImagesThe fighting has also raised questions about whether Saudi Arabia, which on Thursday launched as many as 40 airstrikes on Houthi targets, will activate the Mecca defence agreement and ask its co-signatories, Pakistan and Turkey, to send forces. The pact is designed to be defensive in nature and believed unlikely to apply to Saudi military activities in Yemen.A map showing the area of Yemen controlled by Houthi forcesBy taking control of more of the Red Sea coast south of the port of Hodeidah, the Houthis’ aim is to use a new lever to put pressure on Saudi Arabia and the US to agree a deal that lifts the US blockade on Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf. Donald Trump on Wednesday acknowledged he did not expect the war withIranto end before the US midterm elections at the start of November.The latest phase in the escalation began when Houthis attacked energy installations and southern cities in Saudi Arabia using drones and ballistic missiles. In response, the kingdom’s military forces launched at least 15 strikes between 3 and 7 September.View image in fullscreenThe aftermath of Houthi strikes on Mocha last month. The rebel group claims it now controls the port.Photograph: Al Joumhouriya TV/ReutersThe conflict data monitor Acled estimated there were 276 fatalities over the five-day period alone. The fighting has continued, with the Houthis claiming control of Mocha in Taiz province, as well as the inland city of Hays and the Khalid ibn al-Walid camp, the largest military base in the region. One Houthi-linked estimate suggested its forces had gained control of more than 2,320 sq miles (6,000 sq km) of land.The commander of the Yemeni government forces, Maj Gen Tareq Saleh, admitted he had organised a strategic retreat south of Mocha in order to regroup in a secure location. “The armed forces in the western coast paid a heavy price – martyrs and wounded – over the past days as they confronted the Houthi attack planned by Iran, and supported by it,” he said. Analysts claimed that the effectiveness of Yemen’s government forces was weakened by internal divisions, as well as external pressure from Saudi Arabia.View image in fullscreenA satellite image shows smoke billowing from an Aramco oil depot near the Saudi city of Abha after a Houthi attack.Photograph: Planet Labs/AFP/Getty ImagesThe latter, meanwhile, continues to take advantage of its air superiority to attack Houthi positions, though government sources acknowledged Houthi ground advances along the coast and their missile strikes on the strategic Red Sea islands of Zuqar and Hanish.The clashes have raged across Yemen, including Ad Dali, al-Bayda, Marib, Shabwah, al-Jawf, Hodeidah, and Taiz. In the initial days of the renewed conflict the Houthis were forced back in some areas as battles on multiple fronts overstretched their resources and fighter numbers.The Houthis will be hoping political divisions inside the Yemeni government, reflected in a lack of an integrated military, will slowly give them the upper hand. The United Arab Emirates, previously a powerful player in southern Yemen where it backed the separatist forces of the Southern Transitional Council, withdrew its financial and military support at the turn of the year. The southern forces have refused to fight outside their own region.View image in fullscreenA screen grab from video footage released by the Saudi-backed forces shows a fighter firing at Houthi forces in Taiz province.Photograph: Yemen National Resistance Forces/AFP/Getty Images“A reduction in hostilities anytime soon seems unlikely, as both sides continue to escalate with the goal of inflicting enough damage to the other side to force a compromise,” said Sherwan Hindreen Ali, a Yemen analyst for Acled. “In terms of military capability, both sides are more equal compared to the immediate period prior to the 2022 ceasefire when the Houthis had the upper hand.”He added: “Fighting will remain focused on the fronts of the Red Sea coast in Hodeidah and Taiz, where both the Houthis and the Saudi Arabia-Yemen government have a vested interest in claiming the whole territory to deprive the other side of effective control of the strait of Bab al-Mandab.”The head of the Houthis’ national delegating negotiating team, Muhammad Abdul Salam, insisted non-Saudi commercial shipping would not be attacked.The fighting has contributed to the price of oil rising above $100 a barrel after weeks when it was trading closer to $80.View image in fullscreenFootage reportedly shows Houthi attacks on Saudi-backed forces in al-Jawf province.Photograph: Ansarullah Media Centre/AFP/Getty ImagesThe escalation to this week’s all-out violence has been a slow process. It began after a senior delegation of the Houthi group, which has long been in a complex alliance with Iran, flew to Tehran for the funeral of the Iranian supreme leader Ali Khamenei in July, returning in an Iranian plane that the Saudis refused to land in rebel-controlled Sana’a.The Saudis instead bombed the runway, leading the Houthis to announce a Red Sea naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in what the Yemeni group described as a blockade for a blockade. The 20 July announcement of the blockade was followed by a strike on Saudi Arabia’s Jazan refinery on 25 July and on a tanker off Yanbu on 24 August.Saudi Arabia has become reliant on the Red Sea route for trade after Iran throttled shipping through the strait of Hormuz as a result of US-Israeli attacks.Explore more on these topicsHouthisYemenSaudi ArabiaIranMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Secret son revelation ignites bitter succession dispute in Ugandan kingdom | Uganda | The Guardian
description: Family of late King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV reject committee’s choice of cousin and TV presenter as new monarch
Author: Carlos Mureithi
Headline: Family of late King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV reject committee’s choice of cousin and TV presenter as new monarch
Content: Mourners including Princess Ruth Komuntale (second left) and the Queen Mother Best Kemigisa Akiiki (right) at Entebbe International airport, where they  received the coffin containing the body of King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV.Photograph: Abubaker Lubowa/ReutersView image in fullscreenMourners including Princess Ruth Komuntale (second left) and the Queen Mother Best Kemigisa Akiiki (right) at Entebbe International airport, where they  received the coffin containing the body of King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV.Photograph: Abubaker Lubowa/ReutersUgandaSecret son revelation ignites bitter succession dispute in Ugandan kingdomFamily of late King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV reject committee’s choice of cousin and TV presenter as new monarchCarlos Mureithiin Nairobi and agenciesThu 10 Sep 2026 13.29 EDTFirst published on Thu 10 Sep 2026 11.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA traditional Ugandan kingdom has become engulfed in a bitter succession dispute after the family of a king who recently died rejected the selection of a television news anchor as his successor.King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who became the world’s youngest reigning monarch when he took the throne in the kingdom of Tooro in 1995 at the age of three, died on 27 August in the US, where he was receiving cancer treatment.View image in fullscreenKing Oyo Nyimba, aged 13, sits between his mother Best Kemigisha and an unidentified adviser during celebrations marking his first decade in power in Fort Portal, Uganda.Photograph: ReutersOn Wednesday, the royal clan’s succession committee announced it had chosen Oyo’s cousin Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, a news anchor and editor at the public broadcaster UBC, as crown prince.However, at a press conference held later the same day, Oyo’s sister, Princess Ruth Nsemere Komuntale, said that according to her brother’s will, a son whose existence had not been publicly known until his death should succeed him.View image in fullscreenPrincess Ruth Komuntale waiting to receive the body of her brother, the late King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, at Entebbe International airport last week.Photograph: Hajarah Nalwadda/Getty ImagesThe kingdom’s ‌spokesperson shared a section of the document, which says: “I hereby declare and direct that if, at the date of my death, I am survived by a son lawfully recognised as my biological son, I appoint him as my heir to the throne of the kingdom of Tooro.”In a statement on Thursday, Oyo’s mother, Queen Mother Best Kemigisa Akiiki, denounced a “self-appointed group of clan members” who had selected a new king despite having had the will read to them hours earlier.She also claimed that the royal family had been put under house arrest. Troops had “removed the royal guards without notice, and ... were deployed around the palace,” she said. “We cannot leave or receive people freely.”View image in fullscreenA portrait of the late king on the red carpet at Entebbe International airport.Photograph: Hajarah Nalwadda/Getty ImagesOyo was unmarried and was not known to have any children. The Tooro kingdom’s prime minister, Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki, revealed the existence of a son ina social media poston 27 August when announcing Oyo’s death.“His majesty leaves behind a prince as his heir, whose identity will be formally revealed at the appropriate time, in accordance with the traditions and customs of Tooro kingdom,” he said.Another contender had been Prince George Desmond-Kamurasi, who plays for the London amateur football club South East Dons. According to the committee, the goalkeeper had declined the offer of the throne because of his other responsibilities.The Tooro king is selected by a succession committee appointed by the royal clan. A committee member told the local NTV station that a royal child must be officially introduced to elders in order to be considered for leadership.View image in fullscreenQueen Mother Best Kemigisa Akiiki waiting to receive the body of her son at Entebbe International airport.Photograph: Hajarah Nalwadda/Getty ImagesAndrew Mwenda, ⁠a prominent Ugandan journalist and relative of the royal family, wrote on X on Thursday that Oyo’s ​family had not been able to produce a photo ​of the purported son, and declined to disclose ​details about the family of the boy’s mother. He added that, in Tooro, a king’s son could only succeed ​him if he were born to ‌a queen officially married ​to the king.The prime minister ​called for restraint on Thursday. “There will be time to examine the will, to hear those advancing a different position, and to consider our customs, the applicable law and the proper institutions through which succession should be determined,” he said ina social media post.“That process should take place calmly and credibly, not through competing announcements, confrontation, or attempts to establish facts on the ground while our king still awaits burial.”View image in fullscreenUganda’s president, Yoweri Museveni, lays a wreath on the casket of the king at Entebbe International airport.Photograph: Hajarah Nalwadda/Getty ImagesEdward, a popular TV news presenter, is the son of Prince Christopher Paul Kijanangoma and a grandson of the former king George David Rukidi III.Oyo, who was crowned after his father’s death, will be buried on Saturday at the Karambi royal tombs in the kingdom’s capital of Fort Portal in western Uganda.Uganda has several ancient kingdoms that lack formal sovereignty, but whose leaders are revered as symbols of tradition and wield vast social influence. Tooro is one of five that are recognised by the government. Their monarchs have no political authority and are legally barred from engaging in partisan politics.In 1967 Uganda’s then president, Milton Obote, abolished the kingdoms, saying he wanted to unify the country. They were restored bythe current president, Yoweri Museveni, in 1993.View image in fullscreenThe casket of the late king arrives at Entebbe International airport.Photograph: Hajarah Nalwadda/Getty ImagesThe Tooro are the latest African royal family to become mired in a succession dispute. King Misuzulu Sinqobile kaZwelithini, the reigning king of the Zulu people in South Africa, waited 15 months for his coronation after the death of his father because of a bitter feud involving accusations offorgery and poisoning.Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsUgandaAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Malta warned of corruption crisis after ‘utter disbelief’ over Daphne Caruana Galizia verdict | Daphne Caruana Galizia | The Guardian
description: Labour peer tells Council of Europe inquiry failure to implement legal protections still putting journalists at risk
Author: Juliette Garside
Headline: Labour peer tells Council of Europe inquiry failure to implement legal protections still putting journalists at risk
Content: A demonstrator holding up the Maltese flag in the capital Valletta after the acquittal of Yorgen Fenech last week.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersView image in fullscreenA demonstrator holding up the Maltese flag in the capital Valletta after the acquittal of Yorgen Fenech last week.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersDaphne Caruana GaliziaMalta warned of corruption crisis after ‘utter disbelief’ over Daphne Caruana Galizia verdictLabour peer tells Council of Europe inquiry failure to implement legal protections still putting journalists at riskJuliette GarsideThu 10 Sep 2026 08.17 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMalta is vulnerable to “repeated instances of high-level corruption” unless it strengthens the rule of law and protections for journalists, the Labour peer Shami Chakrabarti said at the opening of an inquiry into judicial failures following the death ofDaphne Caruana Galizia.Chakrabarti, a member of the House of Lords and former director of the human rights group Liberty, has been named special rapporteur for aCouncil of Europeinvestigation into the fallout from the assassination of the anti-corruption journalist, who died in a car bombing in October 2017.Malta is in turmoil after theacquittal of a wealthy and politically influential businessman, Yorgen Fenech, of any involvement in Caruana Galizia’s murder.Fenech denies paying a middleman €150,000 to have her killed.At the inquiry’s first hearing, on Wednesday, Chakrabarti said the verdict had “staggered many throughout Maltese society and beyond.View image in fullscreenShami Chakrabarti: ‘Atmosphere of utter disbelief at how the jury could have reached such a decision’.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PA“It’s now almost nine years since the assassination that struck at the very heart of Maltese public life but a mastermind has not yet been held accountable,” she added.The first witnesses on Wednesday were the journalist’s eldest son, Matthew Caruana Galizia, and her sister Corinne Vella, who questioned the verdict, which dismissed both charges against Fenech by an 8-1 majority.Sabotage, leaks and political ties: the story of the Daphne Caruana Galizia murder trialRead moreMatthew Caruana Galizia told members of the council’s committee on legal affairs and human rights: “The Maltese public have seen all of the evidence against the accused, and the vast majority were convinced of his complicity in the murder. And this is why there is this atmosphere of utter disbelief at how the jury could have reached such a decision.”Malta’s state prosecutor is understood to be preparing an appeal, with the aim of securing a retrial.The Council ofEurope, founded in 1949 after the second world war, created the European convention on human rights. It is led by an assembly drawn from members of the parliaments of its 46 member states.During the hearing, representatives expressed shock and concern about the verdict, calling for the European parliament and the European Commission to intervene. Iulian Bulai, a Romanian centre-right politician, suggested the EU could withhold funds from Malta. The procedure, known as the rule of law conditionality mechanism, was first used in 2022, against Hungary.“If there is such huge problem in matter of rule of law and a function of the Maltese institutions, the EU should apply a similar procedure on increasing pressure for reform,” said Bulai. He said the procedure had “functioned in other cases … So why shouldn’t it function in Malta’s case?”View image in fullscreenDaphne Caruana Galizia pictured in 2011.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersMalta, the EU’s smallest member state, with a population of 600,000, is a net recipient of EU money. Analysis suggests that since joining the block 22 years ago, the island has received €2.4bn more in subsidies than it has paid in.Chakrabarti said she would look at why Malta had failed to implement many of the recommendations from a public inquiry held after the murder.“Thetargeted assassination of a journalistin the middle of investigating high-level corruption sent a chill down the spine of everyone who cares about democratic values,” she said. “Many claim that the legal and policy changes needed to protect journalists to combat corruption and ensure the independent functioning of justice have not been carried out.“I’m extremely concerned by the apparent absence of reforms in critical areas which make Malta vulnerable to repeated instances of high-level corruption and limit the press freedom which should hold it in check.”View image in fullscreenYorgen Fenech leaving the courthouse in Valetta on 2 September after his acquittal.Photograph: Kevin Schembri Orland/APThe public inquiry found although there had been no evidence that the Maltese state had a direct role in the murder, the state bore responsibility for creating a climate of impunity.It recommended Italian-style anti-mafia laws, and making the hindrance of police investigations and abuse of office a crime for public officials. These measures have yet to be implemented.Chakrabarti compared the Caruana Galizia case to miscarriages of justice in the UK, where officials had been involved in coverups, citing the mismanagement of Grenfell Tower, the Post Office scandal and the Hillsborough football stadium disaster. She said her inquiry, titledJustice delayed: the unfinished implementation of the Daphne Caruana Galizia case, was likely to conclude in a year.Vella said fear that serious crimes could go unpunished had increased since the verdict. “Before the verdict was given, we lived in a country where a journalist was killed, but there was a chance of ending impunity. That disappeared as soon as the verdict was out.”She said journalists who had continued to investigate corruption allegations involving former members of Malta’s government “felt uneasy walking to their own cars following that verdict”.Explore more on these topicsDaphne Caruana GaliziaMaltaJournalist safetyCouncil of EuropeEuropeHuman rightsHouse of LordsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Japan seeks change to new UN world map over Russia 'misconception' | Japan | The Guardian
description: The new ‘true-scale’ map shrinks Europe and North America while enlarging Africa – and depicts the disputed Kuril islands as ruled by Moscow
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The new ‘true-scale’ map shrinks Europe and North America while enlarging Africa – and depicts the disputed Kuril islands as ruled by Moscow
Content: Japan was among the 164 UN members who voted in favour of the new Equal Earth map.Illustration: equal-earth.comView image in fullscreenJapan was among the 164 UN members who voted in favour of the new Equal Earth map.Illustration: equal-earth.comJapanJapan seeks change to new UN world map over Russia 'misconception'The new ‘true-scale’ map shrinks Europe and North America while enlarging Africa – and depicts the disputed Kuril islands as ruled by MoscowAgence France-Presse in TokyoThu 10 Sep 2026 08.55 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 17.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJapan has asked for the revision of a new world map adopted by the UN because it said it made the disputed Kuril islands appear to belong toRussia.The UN general assembly voted on Friday to adopt the new map, which makes the African continent larger while also shrinking North America andEurope, drawing condemnation from the US.UN votes to adopt new world map that shows Africa’s true scaleRead moreJapan was among the 164 UN members that supported the resolution, but has now taken issue with it because it shows the Kurils, known inJapanas the Northern Territories, in the same colour as Russia.Ukraine last week abstained in the UN vote on the map as it showed occupied Crimea in a different colour to the rest of the country, which its representatives at the UNwarned opens a “Pandora’s box” violating the UN charter and international law.Japanese government spokesperson Minoru Kihara on Thursday said the new map – known as the Equal Earth cartographic projection – “contained a depiction contradicting the Japanese government’s position”.“We lodged a protest with the map site’s operator through our diplomatic channel to demand the correction of this depiction,” Kihara told reporters.He declined to say when the issue was brought to government’s attention but said Japan “needs to prevent misconceptions of our territories and geographical names from spreading”.The disputed islands were seized in 1945 by the former Soviet Union, which then expelled the Japanese population.View image in fullscreenThe disputed Kuril islands, top right.Photograph: equal-earth.comRelations between Japan and Russia soured significantly last month, when the Russian president, Vladimir Putin,made a surprise visitto the disputed islands for the first time.Japan swiftly summoned Moscow’s ambassador, with the prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, saying Putin’s visit “offends the sentiments of the Japanese people”, adding that it was “absolutely unacceptable”.She said the islands were “an inherent part of Japan’s territory, both historically and under international law”.Moscow quickly hit back, saying it “categorically” rejects such statements, “which we consider politically inappropriate, insulting and, of course, legally unfounded”.The UN said the new map aimed to present “a more accurate representation” of continental landmasses than was portrayed by more traditional Mercator projections.Ukraine was last week among six countries that abstained in the voteExplore more on these topicsJapanUnited NationsRussiaAsia PacificEuropeMapsnewsShareReuse
