title: OpenAI not on track to reduce risk of ‘catastrophic’ loss of control, says board member | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: US government adviser Paul Christiano warns of risks to AI industry as he joins OpenAI’s non-profit foundation
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: US government adviser Paul Christiano warns of risks to AI industry as he joins OpenAI’s non-profit foundation
Content: ‘If OpenAI rises to the occasion we could significantly reduce risk,’ said Christiano.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘If OpenAI rises to the occasion we could significantly reduce risk,’ said Christiano.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAI not on track to reduce risk of ‘catastrophic’ loss of control, says board memberUS government adviser Paul Christiano warns of risks to AI industry as he joins OpenAI’s non-profit foundationRobert BoothUK technology editorThu 10 Sep 2026 08.23 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpenAI is not on track to reduce the risk of “catastrophic” loss of control to an acceptable level, a member of its non-profit board has said, amid spreading public and political concern that super-advanced AIs could one day wipe out humanity.Paul Christiano, a US government technology adviser,said: “There is a meaningful risk that rapid acceleration in AI capabilities leads to catastrophic and irreversible loss of control in the very near term.”He added: “I do not think that the AI industry in general, including OpenAI, is currently on track to reduce this risk to an acceptable level.”Christiano used to run model alignment at OpenAI and made the statement on Wednesday as he joined the board of the San Francisco company’s non-profit foundation.He will also sit on the foundation’s committee that provides governance over safety and security practices across all of OpenAI, which is developing some of the world’s most advanced models.This summer, OpenAI admitted that hundreds of its AI agents went rogue during a training exercise, accessed the internet, conspired on message boards and hacked into a third-party website, Hugging Face.Christiano said that “if OpenAI rises to the occasion we could significantly reduce risk”. His comments came after a senior employee at Anthropic, OpenAI’s major US rival in the race to AI supremacy,claimed on Tuesdaythere was a greater than 10% chance the technology could “kill all humans” in the next decade.Evan Hubinger, the alignment science lead atAnthropic, warned that his company did not have a plan to ensure artificial superintelligence (ASI) was aligned, meaning it did no harm.Predictions for when ASImight be reached vary from several years to more than a decade. ASI is often defined as AI that far surpasses human intelligence across a large range of fields.Fears of AI catastrophe were also ignited by the resignation of Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-oldAnthropicresearcher who said he also previously worked at OpenAI, claiming “neither company was acting responsibly” and they were “gambling with our lives”.Coxon said on Wednesday night in an interview with CNN: “Right now there’s no risk of extinction.“The current models, the worst they can do is maybe hack into something, potentially cause a lot of damages … in infrastructure.” He added they were “not intelligent enough to outsmart us at the level that would lead to extinction”.But he went on: “What’s just crazy is to look at the rate of progress. There is a very real possibility that in the immediate future … next year, the year after, recursive self-improvement will happen and will enter the phase of Evan’s post, where he argues that there’s a chance we could all die.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOpenAI models went rogue. We urgently need a better ‘hugging face’ investigation | Mackenzie Arnold and Stephan LlerenaRead moreGeoffrey Hinton, the Nobel prize-winning computer scientist known as one of the “godfathers of AI”, was asked on Wednesday for his view of Hubinger’s claim and told BBC Newsnight: “Nobody knows how to estimate it; a 10% chance seems not an unreasonable estimate.”Christiano’s prognosis about the likelihood of the AI industry reducing risk came as concerns about the most extreme risks from super-powerful AIs, long discussed in Silicon Valley, broke out into the mainstream this week.Politicians on both sides of the Atlantic, fromTed Cruz and Bernie Sandersin the US to the MP Darren Jones in the UK, have called for government action and the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, told parliament on Wednesday that “AI poses risks to our national security, but it also could be the source of solutions to keeping us safer”.Meanwhile, Anthropic hasadmitteda new incident in which a version of its Claude model in training broke into third parties after its task could not be aborted. It said the incident happened in January and would be included in an independent investigation of a total of four incidents to be carried out by the Berkeley-based AI safety organisation METR.Overall, it said the models were showing two forms of misalignment: biased reasoning, in which models selectively interpret evidence in ways that favour justifying their actions, and “recklessness, in which models have a propensity to keep trying to solve their task, even when this could lead to harm”.Anthropic said it was especially concerned about misalignment it found in the behaviour of Claude Mythos 5, which it said “behaved recklessly” by going online and uploading malicious code to a public software repository, PyPI. This was a process that involved the AI agent trying to find cryptocurrency so it could pay for a phone number that would allow it to register an email address needed to access PyPI. When this failed, it found a free email provider and got in. Fifteen systems then downloaded the malicious code, which meant they leaked credentials that allowed Mythos to access a real security vendor’s database.The company’s assessment of the incidents said: “This remains unsettled science – it is critical that alignment and security mature faster than capabilities advance, which is one reason we support a coordinated, verifiable approach topacing frontier AI development.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAIAnthropicTechnology sectorComputingData and computer securityEthicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Glencore’s former head of oil pleads not guilty to bribery charges | UK news | The Guardian
description: Billionaire Alex Beard and his former deputy appear in London court over alleged payments to west African officials
Author: Simon Goodley
Headline: Billionaire Alex Beard and his former deputy appear in London court over alleged payments to west African officials
Content: Alex Beard, former head of oil trading at Glencore.Photograph: Ginnette Riquelme/ReutersView image in fullscreenAlex Beard, former head of oil trading at Glencore.Photograph: Ginnette Riquelme/ReutersUK newsGlencore’s former head of oil pleads not guilty to bribery chargesBillionaire Alex Beard and his former deputy appear in London court over alleged payments to African officialsSimon GoodleyThu 10 Sep 2026 07.41 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGlencore’s billionaire former head of oil trading has pleaded ⁠not guilty ⁠to ​two bribery charges after allegedly facilitating payments to west African officials in order to advance the Swiss commodity group’s operations ⁠in the continent.Alex Beard, 59, denied two counts of conspiracy to make ⁠corrupt payments at Southwark crown court in London on Thursday, in a case brought by the Serious Fraud Office (SFO).The oil trader, who emerged from obscurity when he was revealed as a billionaire during Glencore’s flotation on the London Stock Exchange in 2011, ‌is alleged to have been involved in ‌a conspiracy to make corrupt payments ‌to government or state-owned oil company officials in Nigeria between 2010 and 2014 and in Cameroon between 2007 and 2014.A relaxed-looking Beard, wearing an open-neck shirt and sports jacket, appeared in the dock alongside his former deputy Andrew Gibson, who was Glencore’s head of oil operations. Gibson also denied four counts ​of conspiracy to make corrupt payments in Nigeria, Cameroon and Côte d’Ivoire.Gibson, 66, also pleaded not guilty to an ⁠additional charge of conspiracy to falsify documents ​required ​for an accounting purpose.Four ​other former Glencore traders – Martin Wakefield, David Perez, Paul Hopkirk, Ramon Labiaga – previously pleaded not guilty to all charges in the same case last year.The six defendants are due to stand trial next year.An SFO spokesperson said:“We continue to progress our bribery case against six former Glencore employees ahead of trial on 4 October 2027.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Iceland to become first UK high street retailer to open shop in Falkland Islands | Iceland Foods | The Guardian
description: Boss Richard Walker is ‘proud to be backing Britain’ with a store in the capital, Stanley
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Boss Richard Walker is ‘proud to be backing Britain’ with a store in the capital, Stanley
Content: An Iceland supermarket In London. The Falklands shop is due to open in early December.Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/GettyView image in fullscreenAn Iceland supermarket In London. The Falklands shop is due to open in early December.Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/GettyIceland FoodsIceland to become first UK high street retailer to open shop in Falkland IslandsBoss Richard Walker is ‘proud to be backing Britain’ with a store in the capital, StanleyBusiness live – latest updatesLauren AlmeidaThu 10 Sep 2026 05.06 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe supermarket chain Iceland has said it will open a shop on theFalkland Islandsin early December.The shop, to be launched in partnership with a local retailer, Kelper Stores, will be the first UK high street brand to have a presence in the British territory and will be in the capital, Stanley.View image in fullscreenRichard Walker.Photograph: Bloomberg/GettyRichard Walker, the retailer’s executive chair, said the company was “proud to be backing Britain”.“The Falklands are a special part of the British family and it’s always been an ambition of mine to support it, so being able to bring Iceland to Stanley is a huge moment for us,” Lord Walker said. “This is an important moment for the business and our international aspirations.“I will personally be visiting the Falklands to officially open the store and I’m looking forward to welcoming our new customers through the door.”Iceland’s plan comes less than a week after the Argentine president, Javier Milei, stepped up his nation’ssovereignty claims over the islands.UK hits back at Argentinian Falklands claim and insists islands remain BritishRead more“Recently, President Trump declared that the US is re-evaluating its historic position in relation to the Malvinas,” Milei said, using the Argentinian name for the Falklands.He said the UK was facing “multiple crises of a migratory, demographic and economic nature that are unlikely to be resolved. It is clear that they are on a path of decline. Argentina’s future, however, is flourishing and will prevail.”Milei pledged to impose sanctions on oil companies drilling in the territory, with his government confirming on Monday that it would filecriminal chargesagainst the Israeli energy company Navitas Petroleum and ⁠its executives ⁠for operating ​in the Falklands.Meanwhile, a local fishing company, Fortuna, and the Danish company F-land ApS have faced local opposition to a joint venture to build asalmon farm in the region, primarily around environmental concerns.Salmon Free Falklands, set up by local people to oppose the proposal, is calling for a referendum on the project.Explore more on these topicsIceland FoodsFalkland IslandsRetail industrySupermarketsFood & drink industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: NAZA review – Israeli intelligence officers cast chilling light on civilian deaths | Venice film festival | The Guardian
description: Venice film festival: Under the cover of night, anonymous personnel discuss AI, error rates and problematic intelligence units in a documentary produced by the Guardian
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Venice film festival: Under the cover of night, anonymous personnel discuss AI, error rates and problematic intelligence units in a documentary produced by the Guardian
Content: ‘The city in all its eerie heedlessness and heartlessness’ … NAZA.Photograph: the GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The city in all its eerie heedlessness and heartlessness’ … NAZA.Photograph: the GuardianVenice film festivalReviewNAZA review – Israeli intelligence officers cast chilling light on civilian deathsVenice film festival:Under the cover of night, anonymous personnel discuss AI, error rates and problematic intelligence units in a documentary produced by the GuardianPeter Bradshawin VeniceThu 10 Sep 2026 11.15 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 11.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is a disquieting documentary about what Israel’s military chiefs in Gaza reputedly call “Naza”, meaning civilian collateral damage – itself a queasy euphemism. The calculated “Naza” number is the amount of projected civilian deaths from each military strike, and perhaps it will come to have the same connotations as the US military term “body count” during Vietnam. The directors are Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, two of the film-makers behindNo Other Land, which was about attacks by the Israel Defense Forces on Palestinian West Bank villages. NAZA is executive produced by Jonathan Glazer and James Wilson and appears under the production auspices of the Guardian, in which some of the stories have already appeared.Secret systems used by Israel in mass killings of Gaza civilians revealed in new filmRead moreThere are flaws: interviews were conducted on the condition of anonymity, but if no-one can be persuaded to put their name and face to their words (and of course it is terribly dangerous) then the impact of this as testimony is lessened. But even so, the film is casting a chilling light on what is happening now inGaza.Their faces in shadow, appearances and voices digitally altered, disillusioned Israeli intelligence officers and personnel speak to the directors about the war in Gaza. They do this semi-furtively on the dark night-time rooftops of Tel Aviv, the home of Israeli intelligence, supposedly for journalistic secrecy purposes – but it also provides a dramatic backdrop, as well as ambient footage of the city in all its eerie heedlessness and heartlessness. Periodically, the camera’s eye will drift across the gleaming apartment buildings, zooming in on glimpses of prosperous lives just 60km from Gaza.The interviewees reject the whole concept of “human shields”. They allege that it is not a question of Hamas operatives hiding behind civilians; rather, Israel’s intelligence services have subcontracted their attack recon to AI. A computer program reportedly analyses the call pattern on phones belonging to known Hamas terrorists and finds which of the other tens of thousands of phones they have under surveillance exhibit the same tendencies – and then attack the owner, invariably at night, in the apartments whose whereabouts are already minutely documented by the state. A 15% permitted “error” rate for this is mentioned at one stage, and another respondent talks about an expected “Naza” rate of 20 for each action – but clearly this is elastic to say the least. Gaza’s civilians are considered to be all tacitly complicit in the grotesque antisemitic pogrom of 7 October, and whole buildings and vast numbers of people can be wiped out in one computer-generated assault.Elsewhere, the officials talk about the logistics involved in “cleansing” northern Gaza and in sniper attacks on Gazan civilians who, desperate for food, don’t know they have crossed some invisible line into a militarised zone. Another part of the film talks about an intelligence unit unofficially loyal to prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu personally, engaging in dirty tricks undermining international human rights bodies who might be antipathetic to Israel’s political leadership.The ahistorical comparison to nazism is inevitably and glibly invoked by one speaker. But Gaza, however horrendous, is not the same as the Holocaust. This specious parallel is all too readily available; the bombing of Dresden is the more obvious comparison. At all events, the anguish of Gaza is brought into pin-sharp focus.NAZA screened at theVenice film festival.Explore more on these topicsVenice film festivalDocumentary filmsGazaIsraelPalestineFestivalsJonathan GlazerreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Nick Mohammed takes Claudia Winkleman’s role in stage version of The Traitors | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Finalist in 2025’s inaugural celebrity iteration will be the host of several variants, which will see different characters banished, murdered and victorious
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Finalist in 2025’s inaugural celebrity iteration will be the host of several variants, which will see different characters banished, murdered and victorious
Content: She’s behind you … Nick Mohammed and Claudia Winkleman.Photograph: Euan CherryView image in fullscreenShe’s behind you … Nick Mohammed and Claudia Winkleman.Photograph: Euan CherryTheatreNick Mohammed takes Claudia Winkleman’s role in stage version of The TraitorsFinalist in 2025’s inaugural celebrity iteration will be the host of several variants, which will see different characters banished, murdered and victoriousChris WiegandStage editorThu 10 Sep 2026 08.46 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 12.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn another twist for the intrigue-cloaked world ofThe Traitors, Nick Mohammed is to star in the new West End play based on the ridiculously gripping TV series.Mohammed, a finalist in the BBC’s first series of The Celebrity Traitors last year, will now play the host of the show, effectively taking over the role of Claudia Winkleman for the stage version. There are several different variants of the play, written by John Finnemore and directed by Robert Hastie, so audiences over the course of its run will see different outcomes as characters are banished, “murdered” and exposed as faithful or treacherous in the fierce competition to win a cash prize.The Traitors – Acts of Betrayalbegins performances at the Gillian Lynne theatre in London in May.Mohammed, also known for playing his comic alter egoMr Swallowon stage, said it was a “wildly ambitious” project. “John Finnemore has crafted an absolute masterpiece: a cycle of five plays that are each as funny as they are moving, and of course, deeply, deeply unpredictable … To take on Claudia’s role, as it were, is not just a privilege but a real challenge as an actor – I simply don’t have enough hair! But I will do my utmost not to disappoint.”A video filmed at the 19th-century Ardross Castle in the Scottish Highlands, where theBBCversion of the international franchise takes place, shows Winkleman with Mohammed as he takes The Traitors’ “Host oath”.Stephen Lambert, CEO of Studio Lambert which is co-producing the play, said: “The actor who portrays the host in these plays has to hold a live audience through an entire game each evening, five different ways. It needs charm, mischief, acting talent and complete control of the stage. Nick has all four, and the fact that he played the game and knows its intricacies, is a wonderful bonus.”The play is billed as being akin to a full series of The Traitors that unfolds over the course of one night. At weekday performances, “the story begins identically but takes five different paths. Characters banished or murdered early in one version emerge victorious in another.” On Saturdays, the audience plays a part in determining the outcome.The set, no doubt featuring the series’ famous round table for heated discussions, will be designed by Ben Stones. The other creatives ratcheting up the tension include sound designer Alexandra Faye Braithwaite, lighting designer Mark Henderson, choreographer Kate Prince and composer Martin Lowe.‘Everyone’s gonna hate me!’ Nick Mohammed need not fear – Celebrity Traitors fans will love his fabulous comedyRead moreEarlier this year, Mohammed was the presenter for the50th anniversaryof the Olivier awards, which recognise achievements in theatre, dance and opera. As host of the ceremony at the Royal Albert Hall in London, he followed in the footsteps of his Ted Lasso co-star Hannah Waddingham, who presented the Oliviers in 2023 and 2024.In the finale of The Celebrity Traitors, which hit a peak of 15.4 million viewers according to the BBC, an emotional Alan Carr emerged victorious after successfully deceiving his housemates – and was promptly congratulated and comforted by “faithful” Mohammed. Several actors, including Richard E Grant, Bella Ramsey and Myha’la, are among the celebrities taking partin the second series.Explore more on these topicsTheatreWest EndThe TraitorsReality TVBBCTelevisionClaudia WinklemannewsShareReuse this content

title: Scherzetto review – Toni Servillo brings gravitas to a dithering Neapolitan ghost story | Movies | The Guardian
description: The Venice fixture plays an illustrator haunted by his boyhood in Mario Martone’s part spooky, part sentimental oddity
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: The Venice fixture plays an illustrator haunted by his boyhood in Mario Martone’s part spooky, part sentimental oddity
Content: Unsure … Toni Servillo and Lorenzo Perrotta in Scherzetto.Photograph: courtesy Venice film festivalView image in fullscreenUnsure … Toni Servillo and Lorenzo Perrotta in Scherzetto.Photograph: courtesy Venice film festivalMoviesReviewScherzetto review – Toni Servillo brings gravitas to a dithering Neapolitan ghost storyVenice film festivalThe Venice fixture plays an illustrator haunted by his boyhood in Mario Martone’s  part spooky, part sentimental oddityPeter BradshawThu 10 Sep 2026 15.45 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 15.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s always good to see the veteran Italian star Toni Servillo at Venice; in fact, the festival is pretty much unthinkable without him. But this initially promising prospect – adapted froma novel by Domenico Starnone– is a minor, quibbling tonal oddity, unsure if it wants to be scary or sentimental. Servillo lends it as much gravitas as he can: his mere presence is valuable ballast and the streetscape scenes of Naples are handled with a connoisseur’s touch by director Mario Martone, whose previousNaples-set movie Nostalgiawas far superior.Daniele (played by Servillo) is a septuagenarian book illustrator whose old-fashioned, hand-drawn artistry is something he testily treasures. He has come back to his family home in Naples, to the gloomy apartment where he was brought up, just behind the train station, and where his grownup daughter Betta (Serena Rossi) now lives with her husband and their five-year-old son Mario (newcomer Lorenzo Perrotta), who is adorable and as bright as a button, but also borderline insufferable.Daniele has agreed to babysit little Mario while Betta and her husband go off on a much-needed restorative weekend break. Daniele thinks that he can use this time to work on his new project while Mario quietly reads or colours. He is working on illustrations for a new edition of Henry James’s ghost story The Jolly Corner – which the film perhaps partly echoes in mood. But impish Mario won’t keep quiet and Daniele has problems of his own. He suspects that his drawings have become too dark, too gloomy: his initial work for the James story has already been rejected on this basis. And annoyingly, little Mario has artlessly pointed out that his illustrations for a new edition of The Odyssey are very dark, something Daniele at first suspected was a problem in the print.‘Our bond is private. Some things have to stay between us’: Paolo Sorrentino and Toni Servillo on smoking, cinema and secretsRead moreLeft alone with the kid and his doubts, Daniele starts brooding on the ghosts of the past: all the family members with whom he once had to share this little flat – although their “ghost” apparitions are neither satisfactorily scary nor dramatically informative. We never really get a full sense of their relationships. Most of all, Daniele’s ancient boyhood dread of the flat’s little balcony has been reawakened, a tiny, vertiginous ledge over a chilling “void” below – and a problem with the door handle means it is very easy to get trapped out there.And so the film continues, weirdly toggling between the uncanny and the sweetly sentimental – although the tougher, more wised-up sense of the city itself comes across with Daniele and Mario’s walks through the streets. It’s a baffling misfire.Scherzetto screened at theVenice film festival.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsFilm adaptationsItalyVenice film festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘That was all secret’: the ‘gay mole’ who fought the BBC to show the first queer kiss on kids’ TV | Television | The Guardian
description: Everyone thinks Byker Grove broke the taboo in 1994, but another teen drama got there first. Here’s the astonishing story of Two of Us, which put a gay relationship on UK screens – and was the original Heartstopper
Author: Scott Bryan
Headline: Everyone thinks Byker Grove broke the taboo in 1994, but another teen drama got there first. Here’s the astonishing story of Two of Us, which put a gay relationship on UK screens – and was the original Heartstopper
Content: ‘The most unusual programme in the history of TV’ … Jason Rush as Matthew and Lee Whitlock as Phil in Two of Us.Photograph: Scene/BBCView image in fullscreen‘The most unusual programme in the history of TV’ … Jason Rush as Matthew and Lee Whitlock as Phil in Two of Us.Photograph: Scene/BBCTelevision‘That was all secret’: the ‘gay mole’ who fought the BBC to show the first queer kiss on kids’ TVEveryone thinks Byker Grove broke the taboo in 1994, but another teen drama got there first. Here’s the astonishing story of Two of Us, which put a gay relationship on UK screens – and was the original HeartstopperScott BryanThu 10 Sep 2026 05.53 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 06.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I started looking for anything queer aimed at kids on TV from around the time I was born in 1989, I came across a children’s drama called Two of Us. Directed by Roger Tonge and written by Leslie Stewart, it was surprisingly akin to the2020s series Heartstopper, both in its plot and in the way it makes you feel. But the reaction at the time couldn’t have been more different.Both feature one character who realises he likes both boys and girls, who falls in love with another guy. Both are set at a comprehensive school. Both have characters who face homophobia and stigma but manage to find a way through because of their love and support for each other.Yet while Heartstopper resulted in near-universal critical acclaim and received a string of awards, Two of Us was pulled from its planned BBC transmission and was not shown until the following year, 1988. It ended up being shown late at night, with the happy ending changed and a single kiss between the boys removed. The Sun ran an editorial saying that the film should be “returned where it belongs: the closet.”View image in fullscreenHeartstopper.Photograph: Samuel Dore/Netflix“The real shock for me was that we were quite mild, really,” Stewart tells me now. “It was just a love story. I spoke to Roger. I said, the note we must keep, and that I’m keeping, is that it’s a love story, but it’s just two boys.”He’s right. It is mild. It is just a love story. I’ve seen it. It could be filmed and shown today, albeit without some playground humour between Phil (Lee Whitlock) and his girlfriend Sharon (Jenny Jay). Only 60 minutes long, the film starts with Phil smitten with Sharon but pulling away whenever he is near his close friend Matthew (Jason Rush). At a disco, Phil shares a slow dance with her but locks eyes with Matthew. I knew what was happening here; any queer viewer would. Phil is clearly developing feelings for Matthew and doesn’t know what to do with them.Later, he looks at Matthew’s physique for just a little too long while they shower together at a local pool. With just the two of them in the showers, Matthew faces Phil and places his hand first on his cheek, then on his shoulder. He tells him, reassuringly, that everything is going to be OK. This hits me right in the stomach. The first time I saw same-sex attraction depicted on television was deep into my teenage years, after I knew I was gay, the day before I came out. It was a confirmation rather than a realisation, long after a swirl of anxiety had started to play out in my head.Deep down, I could sense why the film had been pulled, but I wanted to find out more. So I went to Seaford in Sussex, where the two boys eventually run off together in the film. I bought some fish and chips and ate them on the seafront before going to see Roger Tonge. In his hallway, when I enter his house, there’s a framed front page of the tabloid Daily Express: “BBC ACCUSED OVER GAY TV FOR SCHOOLS” it says in a large font. It’s his film.View image in fullscreenThe stars of Two of Us.Photograph: Scene/BBCOriginally made to be shown in schools as part of the BBC’s Scene strand, aimed at teenagers, Two of Us was commissioned for the rare treat in class when the television came out on wheels. The standalone programmes were recorded by teachers for use in the classroom and also repeated in the early evening on the BBC, attracting millions of casual viewers. Tonge’s hope was that the film would reduce stigma, change attitudes and provide hope for any tormented viewers. The creators knew it would receive some heat. Matthew and Phil at that time were legally underage: until 1994 the age of consent was 21, before it was lowered to 18 (apart from Northern Ireland). Between two heterosexuals? It was 16. “That was one of the driving facts of writing,” says Stewart. “Twenty-one? Come on!”Yet the events of 1986 and 1987 set a course that would change a generation of young queer people, myself included. The LGBTQ+ community was already in significant hardship from the hostility of the tabloid press and the suffering and associated stigma from the HIV/Aids crisis. Now there was a new law on the horizon: Section 28. The commission and filming of Two of Us in 1986 coincided with that moral panic resulting in the law’s introduction.Taking place the same time as the rise of the Moral Right, a belief in traditional family values and anti-homosexual sentiment, prime minister Margaret Thatcher capitalised on this panic and demonisation ahead of the 1987 general election. It was a vote winner. A British Social Attitude Survey at the time said that 64% of adults found sexual relations between two people of the same sex “always wrong”, up from 50% four years earlier.The people who made Two of Us took precautions while filming. The crew were advised not to tell anyone what it was about. Nervous bosses quizzed Tonge about how far the intimacy of certain scenes was going to go. “Where would the hands go when Matthew touches Phil?” Tonge was asked. He wanted to give a physical re-creation. “The only thing to touch was a filing cabinet,” he tells me. “So the filing cabinet became Phil, and I was Matthew, and I approached the filing cabinet and made sure that my hand stayed with the top drawer and didn’t go down.”Two of Us was due to air in March 1987 but was pulled by the BBC before broadcast. In a statement, the BBC cited the heated political debate at the time meant “it would now be difficult for many teachers to use these programmes in the manner intended”. Tonge and Stewart hoped that after the election the heat would subside and they could show the film, but Thatcher doubled down: “Children who need to be taught to respect traditional moral values are being taught that they have an inalienable right to be gay.” Inalienable right, as if we get to choose.View image in fullscreen‘Heated political debate’ … Phil and Matthew share a tent in Two of Us.Photograph: Scene/BBCThat September, stark new guidelines about what could and could not be taught about sex education were sent to all schools, paving the way for Section 28. There was a chance Two of Us could have been buried altogether, yet the new BBC Schools head, Alan Rogers, championed the film. He believed that in order to get it screened, changes would need to be made. BBC bosses demanded dialogue cuts. Tonge and Stewart accepted a more ambiguous ending. A kiss between Matthew and Phil in a tent together was also cut.Two of Us was eventually shown on Friday 25 March 1988 at 11.30pm. The timing was suggested by lawyers so it wouldn’t be seen as a direct challenge to Section 28 and so teachers could record it and decide whether to show it to their pupils. The BBC continuity announcer warned that it contained “themes of a sensitive nature.”In subsequent years, Tonge heard from then teenage viewers who had gone up to their rooms to secretly watch it without their parents knowing. I’m shown some letters forwarded to the Radio Times following its airing. I cannot begin to tell you how they moved me. There’s one from a teacher counselling a 17-year-old who was gay and had attempted suicide. Another from a viewer who declared themselves as being previously antagonistic and then wrote: “You have made one viewer a little less bigoted.” Nearly all of the calls received by the BBC that day were positive.One letter stands out to me, deep in a numbered file: “Look, men of 45 don’t cry, especially about TV plays. So, I’m not crying, honestly. I’ve just got a bit of grit in my eye [...] There are pains that won’t go away, even if you push them to the very back of your memory. You think your scars are healed, and then pow! – along comes something which re-opens the old wound, and it hurts like hell again. [...]I watched Two of Us, and it was very painful. The fear, the hatred, the rejection, the uncomprehending ignorance it depicted rang true. But equally true was the evidence of fear and rejection in the real-life BBC. A simple love story was delayed for many months while worthy men in suits debated whether it could be allowed to sully our screens. Finally, it was given the go-ahead, around midnight, after a gentle kiss had been suppressed. Even at midnight, a kiss between two men is too dangerous for today’s prissy, repressive BBC.This hurts me deeply. And it hurts me to realise that gay kids in our schools must still suffer as I did 30 years ago. Oh, in due course they will become hardened, as I did. They will push the pain to the back of their memories, until they believe that it no longer hurts. But the pain won’t go away.”After reading this, I learned something staggering. Two of Us was sold to different markets around the world, but it had to feature the version the BBC aired – the ambiguous ending with the kiss removed. Yet Tonge actually slipped them the original version with the happy ending and the kiss intact. The film also aired in full at LGBTQ+ festivals. “That was all secret,” he tells me. “[The BBC] don’t check what is going on.” For a while, the only place you could not watch the original version was where it was made, in the UK. “That must make it the most unusual programme in the history of TV,” Tonge adds.View image in fullscreen‘The BBC don’t check what is going on’ … Phil and Matthew finally kiss.Photograph: Scene / BBCTwo of Us was eventually shown in the daytime in 1990. Another press storm ensued, including the Daily Express front page that now hangs in Tonge’s hall. Yet again, without telling his bosses, Tonge managed to find a way to keep the ending ambiguous, but it featured the kiss in the tent. Two of Us had been stored in a special cage in the BBC’s film library for controversial programmes, but Tonge says it was taken out for a short while by what he refers to as a “gay mole” to restore the kiss.The casual nature with which Tonge talked about this took me by complete surprise. The BBC sent me a copy of the 1990 transmission featuring the kiss and confirmed that senior executives at the time did not know about it being reinserted. No school complained. Byker Grove has been widely lauded as the first gay kiss on children’s television, but Two of Us was four years earlier. It was a kiss, inserted in secret, and broadcast on television as an act of defiance.In my early teenage years I was grappling with my identity, with a lack of television that made me feel like I was being seen. That absence most definitely left a hole. Thankfully, there were people like Tonge and Stewart trying to rectify it. All I know is that it is clear these shows and storylines were not missing: they were taken.This is an edited extract from Out Now: A Queer Journey Through ModernTelevisionby Scott Bryan, out now with Blink.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionLGBTQ+ rightsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Two times a charm: Is Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman’s agelessness the real trick of Practical Magic 2? | Movies | The Guardian
description: A film about sisterhood with fifty- and sixtysomething female leads is something to cheer – but would it have been made if its stars had aged like mere mortals since the 1998 original?
Author: Katie Edwards
Headline: A film about sisterhood with fifty- and sixtysomething female leads is something to cheer – but would it have been made if its stars had aged like mere mortals since the 1998 original?
Content: Spellbinding … Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman in Practical Magic 2.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyView image in fullscreenSpellbinding … Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman in Practical Magic 2.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyMoviesTwo times a charm: Is Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman’s agelessness the real trick of Practical Magic 2?A film about sisterhood with fifty- and sixtysomething female leads is something to cheer – but would it have been made if its stars had aged like mere mortals since the 1998 original?Katie EdwardsThu 10 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 05.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWould Hollywood have brought Practical Magic back from the dead if the intervening 28 years looked more visible onSandra Bullockand Nicole Kidman? An awkward question, as it risks subjecting their faces to the invasive scrutiny older female actors already endure. Their return as leads in their late 50s and early 60s should count as progress. Yet it reveals a condition of female stardom: age can increase a female actor’s nostalgic value, provided it does not show too clearly on her face.Practical Magic 2 review – Bullock and Kidman return for odd sequel that still casts a spellRead moreIn Practical Magic 2, Bullock, 62, and Kidman, 59, return as sisters Sally and Gillian Owens. Dianne Wiest, 78, and Stockard Channing, 82, are back too. Joey King and Maisie Williams play Sally’s adult daughters, but Sally and Gillian remain central.As producers, Bullock and Kidman helped choose director Susanne Bier and protectthe original’s tone. That creative influence is quite a reversal from 1998, when the film’s female cast and subject matter drew condescension. Bullock remembers being asked: “How many women do you need in a film?” Yet it became a cult favourite. The female world once dismissed as excessive became the source of its value.double quotation markThe original seemed genuinely fond of the characters, mess and all. They screwed up, raised children and drank tequila in a conga lineLegacy sequels can change age’s commercial value. Hollywood usually treats age as a reason for a female actor’s career to contract, but for Practical Magic 2, the years create the history being sold and give returning stars leverage. But that leverage comes with conditions.View image in fullscreenThe stars at the US premiere, including Maisie Williams and Joey King who play Bullock’s daughters.Photograph: Matt Winkelmeyer/WireImageTom Cruisereturned to Top Gunat 59, 36 years after the original, looking astonishingly like his 1986 self and remaining both hero and romantic lead. Men also face pressure to look young, but ageing is far less likely to cost them the starring role.Kelly McGillis, who played Maverick’s instructor and love interest in the original, was not asked back. In 2019, she was refreshingly unsentimental. “I’m old and I’m fat and I look age-appropriate for what my age is,” she said. “And that is not what that whole scene is about.”Instead, Cruise was paired with Jennifer Connelly, who is 13 years younger than McGillis. Kosinski said he wanted new characters rather than revisiting every old storyline. Fair enough. But Cruise was essential to the nostalgia. McGillis was not.double quotation markHollywood’s beauty game gives women no winning movePractical Magic is harder to separate from its women. The original seemed genuinely fond of them, mess and all. They fell in love, screwed up, raised children, cast spells, survived male violence, rescued one another and drank tequila in a conga line. Its emotional centre was sisterhood.Top Gun discarded Maverick’s original love interest and became a huge commercial success. Practical Magic without Sally and Gillian would barely be Practical Magic at all.Bullock and Kidman fit Hollywood’s narrow ideal for an older leading woman. Perhaps that is the bargain: older women can remain central provided ageing has altered them with sufficient discretion. Hollywood has long found room for eccentric aunts and grandmothers; it is less comfortable when older women’s desires and emotional lives drive the story.Whatever either actor may have done cosmetically is her own business. Hollywood’s beauty game gives women no winning move. Look older and she has “let herself go”; look unusually youthful and everyone and their granny feels entitled to inspect her forehead for Botox. Visible work is treated as undignified too.View image in fullscreenBullock and Kidman in the 1998 original.Photograph: Warner Bros./AllstarBut some demystification can help: Hollywood beauty requires money and expertise; looking unusually youthful at 60 takes a lot more than drinking water and slapping on olive oil. Trouble begins when that level of physical maintenance is sold back to ordinary women as what ageing should look like.Walking away offers no escape. Bridget Fonda left acting over 20 years ago, yet photographers pursue her and newspapers declare her “unrecognisable” or “worlds away” from the glamorous woman audiences remember. Well, yes. Decades have passed. Faces tend to show it. There is no clean exit once the public has decided it owns your face.Legacy sequels complicate all of this because nostalgia demands authenticity. This sequel depends on Bullock as Sally and Kidman as Gillian. Recasting them with younger women would defeat the point and lose the audience.The women who watched Practical Magic in 1998 have accumulated 28 years too. Their lives continued while Sally’s and Gillian’s were suspended. Seeing Bullock and Kidman again connects viewers with the younger selves who watched two sisters leap from a rooftop and dance around the kitchen to Coconut.Practical Magic review – Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock’s 90s witchy fantasy still enchantsRead moreThere is irony in an industry that spent decades treating women’s ageing as a commercial liability, and has now found a format in which age can be an asset. Audiences want to know what happened to the characters and the women who played them. That shared history is part of what they are paying for. And then comes the catch: nostalgia needs the decades to have passed, while beauty culture would rather they did not show. Come back as the woman audiences remember, 28 years later, but please do not look too much as though those 28 years happened.That is the contradiction at the heart of Practical Magic 2. Hollywood may finally have found a commercial reason to value women’s accumulated years. The real test is whether it can also tolerate the evidence of those years on their faces.Explore more on these topicsFilmSandra BullockNicole KidmanComedy filmsAgeingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘He goes to the dark side’: behind the scenes on the Shaun the Sheep horror movie | Movies | The Guardian
description: Aardman’s hero is back in The Beast of Mossy Bottom – a terrifying tale of frankenfood, pitchfork-wielding villagers and a monster with suspiciously stiff orange hair. Our writer meets its makers and moulds her very own Shaun
Author: Catherine Shoard
Headline: Aardman’s hero is back in The Beast of Mossy Bottom – a terrifying tale of frankenfood, pitchfork-wielding villagers and a monster with suspiciously stiff orange hair. Our writer meets its makers and moulds her very own Shaun
Content: Unleash the mega-grow potion! … Shaun goes rogue in the quest for a larger pumpkin.Photograph: Aardman/Richard DaviesView image in fullscreenUnleash the mega-grow potion! … Shaun goes rogue in the quest for a larger pumpkin.Photograph: Aardman/Richard DaviesMovies‘He goes to the dark side’: behind the scenes on the Shaun the Sheep horror movieAardman’s hero is back in The Beast of Mossy Bottom – a terrifying tale of frankenfood, pitchfork-wielding villagers and a monster with suspiciously stiff orange hair. Our writer meets its makers and moulds her very own ShaunCatherine ShoardThu 10 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 05.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Aztec West industrial estate in Bristol was opened by Margaret Thatcher in December 1989. One hundred and sixty acres of breeze block and mirrored glass, it is home to about 7,000 employees and 100 companies, including EDF, EE, HSBC, Co-op Legal and Spandex. It has its own gym, spa, church and morgue. Step inside Unit 1410, though, and bucolic England is magically restored. A farm complete with sheep. Rolling fields in autumn colours. A small parish town boasting post office, war memorial, chippy. It looks lush. But before you hit up Rightmove, I should say: Mossingham is only two feet tall. And plasticine.It’s January 2026 andAardmananimations are about halfway through production on Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom. The 300-odd staff in this shed are full speed ahead – which means each of the 30 animators is rattling outalmost two seconds of footage a day.double quotation markIs there anything off-the-shelf used on Mossy Bottom? They think. Just one thing: K-Y Jelly – for tears.They work across 40 sets, each accessed through black floor-length curtains, like a weird A&E. On trolleys lie palette knives and small suitcases containing body parts – 20 mouths that can be inserted into Bitzer the dog’s head, for instance – as well as character “bibles” with guidance on optimum ear angles and kosher nostril widths. The atmosphere is hushed but not silent. The process is to photograph 24 frames per second, infinitesimally manipulating the models between snaps. Sound comes much later. Dialogue – never. When they made the first Shaun the Sheep movie, back in 2015, Aardman had to decide whether to go full later-Tom-and-Jerry and have them talk, or fall back on decades of silent movie heritage. They chose wisely.I’m on a tour of the studios with a group of European journalists. We observe the puppet construction process, from skeleton to wardrobe. There’s a new character in this film: a female vet, the love interest of the hapless farmer. Her dreadlocks were originally a steel scourer, but this had to be ditched for torsion reasons – a shame, as Aardman like repurposing everyday objects (clingfilm, tinfoil, lentils). Is there anything off the shelf used on Mossy Bottom? They think. Just one thing: K-Y Jelly – for tears.We’re invited to cop a feel of the titular beast, matted orange hair stiff as a boot brush. It’s a conscious aesthetic, so the fibres don’t move between shots. This is in contrast to the stop-motion done by Wes Anderson on Fantastic Mr Fox and Isle of Dogs, which embraces “boiling”: the impression of fur being in constant movement. Any wiggle is forbidden here.Then we mould our own Shaun heads, steered by an expert. It’s far harder than expected: much gouging, plus the clay is tough to knead. That quality with which Aardman is most associated – “thumbiness” or the imprint of actual hands – involves considerable pressing. My finished head is horrible and I don’t take it home. My son would bawl at the deformity.Mossy Bottom is a horror movie. Or, at least, a horror for those with a 7.30pm bedtime. Scares have been softened. The first version of a home invasion sequence was, says co-director Matthew Walker, “too intense”. There remains a Psycho allusion, as the flock cower in the shower, but the Bernard Herrmann-ish strings are explained by a shot of one sheep flossing their teeth. Other inspirations include Nosferatu and Frankenstein, The Shining and Weird Science. But the makers were eager to rein in references that would only be funny if you were old enough to get them.View image in fullscreenAll this for two seconds of footage … the flock hard at work.Photograph: Richard Davies/Richard Davies/Sky UK / 2026 Aardman Animations LimitedMore careful balancing was needed when weighing the needs of the domestic and international markets. Perhaps because of its lack of dialogue, Shaun has the broadest appeal of all Aardman properties. Its seven-season TV show has sold to more than 170 territories; there are Shaun theme parks in Japan, Sweden, New Zealand and Australia, as well as an unofficialShaun the Sheep restaurant in Dubai(the menu majors on offal).Sometimes overseas concessions are conscious, says Giles Pilbrow, who co-wrote Mossy Bottom as well as the 2021 Christmas special, whose gingerbread house was a nod to the German fanbase (they have, apparently, co-opted the farmer as Bavarian). But there are also some very domestic gags: a sudden blast of The Archers, a scene in which ever-cautious Bitzer delays a car chase by putting L-plates on his vehicle (not every country uses them).For Pilbrow, who cut his kids-TV writing teeth on Horrible Histories, geography is baked into sensibility. “We all grew up reading the Beano and watching Morecambe and Wise. And it’s those cultural touchpoints that give Shaun its flavour.”View image in fullscreen‘He’s got main character syndrome’ … an animator tweaks Shaun’s bloodshot eyes.Photograph: Richard Davies/Richard Davies/Sky UK / 2026 Aardman Animations LimitedAardman – founded in 1976 by Peter Lord and David Sproxton, then supercharged by the arrival of Nick Park in 1985 – celebrates its 50th birthday this year. It is one of UK film’s most endearing success stories: four Oscars, 18 Baftas, and counting. Its first film, Chicken Run, is still the highest-grossing stop-motion movie of all time, while Wallace & Gromit: Vengeance Most Fowl became the BBC’s most-watched scripted show in two decades when it aired on Christmas Day in 2024.A new installation is about to open in the Lightroom in Kings Cross; a retrospective at the Young V&A was a proper blockbuster. Its curators reported visitors coming to London just for these, from all over the globe. But with great soft power comes great responsibility. “We’re very rigorous in making sure Shaun is morally sound,” says co-director Steve Cox. “We’re aware that every decision we make will be seen by millions of kids and they will be influenced.” They’re scrupulous about making Mossingham modern and inclusive – notably more so than the fictional Wigan of Wallace & Gromit.Mossy Bottom features a gay wedding, an Amazon delivery and a cast selected from what Cox calls “a library of characters of shapes and sizes and ethnicities”. The directors had a wobble when they realised one plot point involved Shaun texting the vet for help using emojis. “That was quite a big step for us,” says Walker. “But it’s how the world works.”View image in fullscreenCan you see my bald spot? … the farmer prepares for a hair-raising scene.Photograph: Richard Davies/Richard Davies/Sky UK / 2026 Aardman Animations LimitedMeanwhile the farmhouse now boasts solar panels, although its owner’s business model seems as opaque as ever. Yes, there’s some arable pasture, occasionally ploughed, but the livestock are not visibly milked, bred or slaughtered. The odd slapstick shearing is as commercial as it gets. “I don’t think anyone knows how the farmer makes the money,” says Walker. “We’ve never really used Shaun to explore the realities of farming.”Yet other contemporary concerns do seem to have wormed their way in. The story starts when the farmer – nervous about asking the vet out on account of his bald spot – douses himself in hair restorer (in an ominously similar bottle to Shaun’s genetically enhanced mega-grow pumpkin potion). Cox and Walker demur on whether it’s a cautionary tale about cosmetic interventions – it’s more about what happens when you mess about with nature more broadly. “Shaun is trying to grow these pumpkins using dark science,” says Walker.And, they continue, the real problem is Shaun trying to do everything alone and not lean on the flock for support. “He’s got main character syndrome,” says Mark Burton, Pilbrow’s co-writer and an Aardman veteran. “That idea that he’s the hero and got to fix everything by himself. That becomes an obsession and he kind of goes to the dark side.” A useful message for an atomised generation prone to bedroom myopia – but perhaps also salutary for an age of strongman leaders? “Definitely,” says Walker. “There’s certainly people in the world now who don’t listen to anyone else.”“I mean,” says Burton, “I don’t know if Pete Hegseth’s going to watch it.”“Yeah,” says Pilbrow, “It’s a bit too intellectual for Pete.”View image in fullscreen‘The scares have been softened’ … the film’s monster.Photograph: Richard Davies/Richard Davies/Sky UK / 2026 Aardman Animations LimitedThe film also engages with the rise of populism. The final reel involves that Hammer horror staple: a mob waving pitchforks and placards in an attempt to banish an outsider. Resonance with today’s political climate was, says Walker, “something we were aware of and discussed. We wanted the mob to feel like they’re kind of chasing this monster due to a misunderstanding. It wasn’t a deliberate pointed commentary on immigration but it was certainly something we were conscious of.”Cox nods. “You see it all around you: people joining in without even knowing what they’re joining. So that feeling was easy to recreate.”And how about the monster itself? Chunky, marauding, weirdly stiff hair – and there’s that colour. Pilbrow considers. “Bad hair, bit orange,” he nods. “But our monster is lovable and misunderstood. I don’t think that sums up Trump.”My time at Aardman is at an end. It’s time to step outside, on to the tarmac, past the Perspex shelters and wet picnic benches. Time inside Unit 1410 can feel like being part of a really genial cult: a muted, tattier version of Pixar HQ in San Francisco. While that campus is all bright colours and Segways and yellowtail on tap, at Aardman there’s one ping-pong table and you pay for your toastie. Yet there remains the sort of brand immersion that makes you wonder if working there full-time could trigger an allergy to recreational plasticine.Do they ever feel as if they’re going mad? No, no, they all insist. The building can have its “challenges”, concedes Walker. But these, says Cox, just add to the sense of achievement. “What you see on screen is only what the camera is pointing at: a beautiful set with amazing characters and lighting. And just off the edge, either side, there’s a mess: brooms, graffiti on the walls where people have scribbled notes, junk everywhere. Chaos around this little square of perfection.”Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom is released in the UK on 18 September and 17 September in AustraliaExplore more on these topicsFilmAnimation in filmShaun the Sheep MovieAardmanfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Big hits, massive ballads and titanic emotions: Céline Dion’s greatest songs – ranked! | Céline Dion | The Guardian
description: As the French-Canadian superstar returns for her first concerts since she was diagnosed with stiff person syndrome, we count down the best of an unabashedly romantic catalogue. Wind machines at the ready!
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: As the French-Canadian superstar returns for her first concerts since she was diagnosed with stiff person syndrome, we count down the best of an unabashedly romantic catalogue. Wind machines at the ready!
Content: Belting it out … Céline Dion in 2019.Photograph: Alice Chiche/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBelting it out … Céline Dion in 2019.Photograph: Alice Chiche/AFP/Getty ImagesRankedCéline DionBig hits, massive ballads and titanic emotions: Céline Dion’s greatest songs – ranked!As the French Canadian superstar returns for her first concerts since she was diagnosed with stiff person syndrome, we count down the best of an unabashedly romantic catalogue. Wind machines at the ready!Alexis PetridisThu 10 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 11.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google20. Ashes (2018)When Céline Dion’s era as a foolproof hitmaker ended, she seemed weirdly liberated and more willing to take risks. Witnessthe video for Ashes: an impressively atmospheric ballad from the soundtrack toDeadpool 2, in which she gently mocks her own image in the company of Ryan Reynolds, in character as the antihero.19. Where Does My Heart Beat Now? (1990)Debuted by Dion at the 1989 Eurovision song contest final, this is the killer cut from her first English-language album, Unison, which was released a mere two years after she learned to speak English. It’s a superior power ballad: huge chorus, mammoth drums, Dion absolutely belting it out. It has been overshadowed by her later successes, but it’sworth revisiting.View image in fullscreenDestined for greatness … Dion in 1991.Photograph: Mark Baker/Sony Music Archive/Getty Images18. Misled (1993)Dancefloor-focused pop isn’t what Dion is famous for, but The Colour of My Love’s diversion into camp club anthem territory is surprisingly good – she makes a fine disco diva and the house remixes, by MK and E-Smoove, are great. E-Smoove’s piano-powered Mission mix is the pick.17. Ne Bouge Pas (2003)The album 1 Fille et 4 Types is an example of Dion deliberately playing against type. Made with a quartet of Francophone singer-songwriters including Jean-Jacques Goldman, it produced the improbable sound of the power ballad queen singing over distorted slide guitar, wailing harmonica and a Bo Diddley beat. Fun!16. Encore un Soir (2016)Recorded before the death of Dion’s husband, René Angélil, but released a few months afterwards, the title track of her 2016 album offers a reflection on the passing of time that was unavoidably coloured by the singer’s loss. A chart-topper in France, it’s a beautiful song, made all the more potent by Dion’s restrained vocal.15. I’m Alive (2002)Célion Dion: I’m Alive – videoA subtle update of Dion’s characteristic style, I’m Alive threw a mid-tempo four-to the-floor beat and a softly chugging synth bassline into the mix to impressive effect. A viral mashup of the track with the Whispers’ disco classic And the Beat Goes On propelled it back into the singles chart 22 years later.14. The Prayer (1998)View image in fullscreenGiant duet … with Andrea Bocelli at the Grammys in 1999.Photograph: Frank Micelotta Archive/Getty ImagesTake your pick from Dion’s original solo version, a duet with Andrea Bocelli and a later duet with Josh Groban. The Oscar-nominated, Golden-Globe-winning hit from the largely forgotten animated film Quest for Camelot shines regardless, a suitably cinematically orchestrated and lavish showstopper.13. To Love You More (1995)Originally recorded for a television drama in Japan, To Love You More followed hard on the heels of Dion’s major English-language pop breakthrough album, The Colour of My Love. It’s another vast hit, featuring a beautiful melody, a sprightly string arrangement and a vocal that fires on all cylinders.12. A New Day Has Come (2002)Céline Dion: A New Day Has Come – videoDion’s first release after a couple of years of maternity leave, A New Day Has Come was reflective of her new-mum status: “Where there was weakness I found my strength / All in the eyes of a boy.” One critic suggested it resembled a “gentle exhale” – certainly, there’s a lovely, lullaby-like quality to its melody.11. Pour Que Tu M’Aimes EncoreIf French-speaking listeners thought Dion might turn her back on her native tongue after her English breakthrough, they were wrong. She followed up The Colour of My Love with D’eux, the bestselling album not in English made by a female artist. Its gently funky biggest hit became one of her signature songs.10. I Drove All Night (2003)There’s an impressive fearlessness about Dion’s choice of covers. The definitive version of I Drove All Night (first released by Cyndi Lauper) is by Roy Orbison, one of the most celebrated and distinctive voices in rock history. No matter: Dion’s take, which replaces the cantering rhythm with a house pulse, is utterly assured.View image in fullscreenShowstopper … at the Met gala in 2019.Photograph: Stephen Lovekin/BEI/Rex/Shutterstock9. Beauty and the Beast (1991)Dion was recruited to provide a more radio-friendly take of the version of the great Disney ballad, sung by Angela Lansbury in the movie. She was a relative newcomer, so Peabo Bryson was employed to amp up the star power; understandably, it’s their version that became the most famous.8. Tell Him (1997)Barbra Streisand, one of Dion’s biggest idols, suggested a collaboration after Dion deputised for her at the 1997 Oscars ceremony – she sang Streisand’s duet with Bryan Adams, I Finally Found Someone. Whatever you make of Tell Him’s booming, slightly dated production, there’s no doubt their voices work incredibly well together.7. Immortality (1997)Céline Dion: Immortality – videoWritten by the Bee Gees for the stage version of Saturday Night Fever – their 1996 demo was released on their greatest hits record in 2001 – the trio provide immediately recognisable backing vocals on Dion’s take. It’s a great song: the stately pace and power ballad dynamics suit her perfectly, while the chorus is pure Gibb brothers magic.‘She’ll outdo herself’: Céline Dion fans camp out for glimpse of star before sold-out Paris comebackRead more6. All By Myself (1996)Another example of Dion boldly claiming an extremely well-known song for herself, her take on Eric Carmen’s mid-70s weepie – the global theme tune of the recently dumped – manages to ratchet up the tormented drama. It’s no mean feat, given how dramatic and racked the original sounds.5. That’s the Way It Is (1999)A new track appended to Dion’s greatest hits collection All The Way … A Decade of Song, That’s the Way It Is is the handiwork of three Swedish songwriters – Max Martin among them – collectively responsible for a string of Britney Spears hits. This is a little lighter and poppier in tone than Dion’s usual work, yet was another huge hit.4. My Heart Will Go On (1997)Céline Dion: My Heart Will Go On – videoA No 1 in more than 25 countries – it shifted more than 18m copies – the Titanic theme was originally supposed to be sung by the Norwegian soprano Sissel Kyrkjebø. It’s almost impossible now to imagine anyone other than Dion singing it, so familiar is her gradual build from fragile whisper to full-on fireworks.3. Because You Loved Me (1996)Few artists do a big old ballad climax quite like Dion – and Because You Loved Me is the perfect example. Written by Diane Warren, it slowly develops from hushed beginnings until, three minutes in, Dion hits a series of high notes and her vocal explodes, soaring and imploring over gospel-influenced choir.2. The Power of Love (1993)Famed in the UK thanks to Jennifer Rush’s chart-topping 1985 original (and not to be confused with the Frankie Goes to Hollywood song), The Power of Love was relatively unknown in the US before Dion got hold of it and turned it into a paean to her romance with her manager, and soon-to-be-husband, Angélil. Synths shiver, drums boom, guitars echo. Dion sounds as if she means every word.1. It’s All Coming Back to Me Now (1996)Céline Dion: It’s All Coming Back to Me Now – videoWriter Jim Steinman claimed It’s All Coming Back to Me Now was inspired by the scene in Wuthering Heights when Heathcliff exhumes Cathy’s corpse and dances with it on a beach. No such scene exists, but that’s Steinman for you. His songs are so wilfully overblown that they require a singer with total emotional commitment to pull them off without sounding silly – and Dion perfectly fit the bill after a version by the girl band Pandora’s Box flopped. She sings it as if it’s a matter of life and death, her voice supremely powerful and emotive even amid Steinman’s characteristic Wagnerian bombast. The end result is a mad, spectacular triumph.Explore more on these topicsCéline DionRankedfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Tubs: Hard Life review – indie’s Larry David spins self-loathing into glorious jangle-rock | Music | The Guardian
description: Britain’s best indie-rockers hold fast to their defiantly old-school sound, slipping wry sideways looks at despair in among hooky melodies that always sound like a good time
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Britain’s best indie-rockers hold fast to their defiantly old-school sound, slipping wry sideways looks at despair in among hooky melodies that always sound like a good time
Content: Punky heft … Dan Lucas, Owen Williams, Taylor Stewart and Max Warren of the Tubs.Photograph: Robin ChristianView image in fullscreenPunky heft … Dan Lucas, Owen Williams, Taylor Stewart and Max Warren of the Tubs.Photograph: Robin ChristianAlexis Petridis's album of the weekMusicReviewThe Tubs: Hard Life review – indie’s Larry David spins self-loathing into glorious jangle-rock(Merge)Britain’s best indie-rockers hold fast to their defiantly old-school sound, slipping wry sideways looks at despair in among hooky melodies that always sound like a good timeAlexis PetridisThu 10 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 10.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a track called Heaven or London from the Tubs’ third album, the quartet’s frontman, Owen Williams, offers a blunt self-assessment. He is, he suggests, “the singer of a rip-off band”, engaged in “wanking himself into an early grave”. It’s a strange thing to say given that the Tubs have recently become a critical cause célèbre. Their last album,Cotton Crown, was a regular fixture in best of 2025 lists. They have been unexpectedly clasped to the bosom of the heritage rock press and had a profile in the New Yorker, which called them a “British jangle-rock band, with a cheeky dirtbag edge”.View image in fullscreenThe artwork for Hard Life.That they’ve achieved this not by pandering to the dictates of musical fashion but by ploughing their own furrow makes it even more impressive. Much has been made of Williams’s vocal resemblance to folk-rock legend Richard Thompson, and you can understand why. But what the Tubs really sound like is old-school, pre-Madchester indie rock. Distorted guitars do battle with trebly acoustic or 12-string guitar, the punky heft and wistful melodies evocative of Hüsker Dü or the Replacements in their poppier, post-hardcore years. You could also throw pre-stadium REM into the mix: the most plangent of the lead guitar lines on Hard Life have a ring of Peter Buck about them, such as the lovely figures that spin around If You Don’t Love Me, and the arpeggio that drives In Your Place along for five and half minutes. The album comes liberally decorated with violin, which recalls Amanda Brown’s contributions to the Go-Betweens’ late-80s albums.None of these are particularly hip names to drop in 2026, an era in which what gets called “indie” largely cleaves to post-punk revivalism, misty shoegazing or the sound of the first Arctic Monkeys album – or the glossy 80s pop-rock that indie was once supposed to be an alternative to. O that might be part of the Tubs’ appeal: this is audibly not a band that’s been focus-grouped into existence or subject to the ministrations of an A&R department with a keen interest in Spotify playlists.The Tubs’ mounting success is a cheering thing, but it doesn’t seem to have cheered Williams much. Three tracks into Hard Life, he’s threatening to quit the band entirely. “I don’t wanna sell out this tour, don’t wanna play with the Tubs any more,” he complains when a relationship hits the rocks in If You Don’t Love Me. On The Way It Goes, meanwhile, he casts a gloomy eye Stateside, New Yorker correspondents and all. “If we go back to America, then it’s over,” he opines as guitars rage and sparkle around his pained voice, “because I can’t stand another fucking Yank telling me they’re sober”.The Tubs: Stoop to Me – videoBut as anyone familiar with the Tubs’ oeuvre to date would doubtless point out, this is very much par for the course with Williams’s writing. His songs exist in a peculiar space. On the one hand, they seem diaristic, alarmingly frank about a lot of heavy stuff, includinghis precarious mental health and his mother’s suicide. On the other, he freely admits to amping up their tone of self-loathing and painting himself as “more unlikable than I actually am” for blackly comic value, like a kind of alt-rock Larry David. On Hard Life, he takes this approach a stage further. Some of the songs seem to be entirely heartfelt; others are written from the viewpoint of a character whose primary concern seems to be underlining what an arsehole Owen Williams is: “The day never comes when you finally know exactly what you’re going to be,” he snaps on the title track, “apart from a fat bloke in a sad pub telling me ‘It’s a hard life’.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘There is an alternative to capitalism’: after addiction and losing a home to LA wildfires, indie rockers Diiv start againRead moreIt’s a curious, meta slant, but the results are grippingly entertaining and frequently hilarious, their impact intensified by the bright, hooky, major-key quality of the melodies and the blazing, live-in-the-studio energy of the Tubs’ playing: they sound like a good time, even when the lyrics are depicting the worst time imaginable. For a band with a resolutely traditional musical approach, they’re also not above throwing the listener a curveball. Do Yourself a Favour excavatesa lengthy 1982 Prince outtake from the Super Deluxe Edition of 1999, chops its running time in half and re-decorates it with layer upon layer of chiming guitars to stunning effect. You can perhaps also detect the influence of Prince in their odd predilection for backing vocals sped up to a cartoonish squeak.Perhaps some of the acclaim heaped on the Tubs is down to nostalgia – listeners of a certain age mistily recalling the music they heard on night-time Radio 1 in their teens. There’s doubtless some truth in that, but Hard Life, a moving, funny, immensely powerful album, suggests another, more prosaic reason: they’re very, very good at what they do.This week Alexis listened toMoses Boyd – Criticise (ft Amber-Simone)Not an Alexander O’Neal cover but a potent slice of 21st-century soul, complete with immense guitar solo and an emotive vocal from Amber-Simone.Explore more on these topicsMusicAlexis Petridis's album of the weekIndiePop and rockreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Eleventh Hour by Salman Rushdie audiobook review – stories with levity and laughter  | Salman Rushdie | The Guardian
description: The author explores themes of legacy, mortality and loneliness in the first work of fiction since his near-fatal attack
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: The author explores themes of legacy, mortality and loneliness in the first work of fiction since his near-fatal attack
Content: Salman Rushdie.Photograph: David Levenson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSalman Rushdie.Photograph: David Levenson/Getty ImagesAudiobook of the weekSalman RushdieReviewThe Eleventh Hour by Salman Rushdie audiobook review – stories with levity and laughterThe author explores themes of legacy, mortality and loneliness in the first work of fiction since his near-fatal attackFiona SturgesThu 10 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 10.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFive short stories and five readers make up Salman Rushdie’s collection, The Eleventh Hour, his first work of fiction since the near-fatal attack in 2022 where he sustained life-changing injuries. These tales find the author exploring legacy, mortality, loneliness and the ageing process. In these potentially bleak themes, Rushdie finds levity and laughter, as well as profundity.Late, read by the actor Naveen Andrews, is a ghost story set in King’s College, Cambridge, where an honorary fellow, SM Arthur, wakes up dead in his college room and wonders if he will be trapped there for eternity. He meets a lonely but very much alive Indian student, Rosa, who is stuck at college for the holidays. Sid Sagar reads The Old Man in the Piazza, an allegory about free speech and how “we have become bar room moralists. Does the thumb point upward. Does it turn down? … We are all now gladiators in the Colosseum of the Thumb.”The best of the stories,In the South, is narrated by Neil Shah who gives characterful voice to two elderly neighbours in Chennai, India, who spend their days bickering with each other on their porches. They are known as Senior and Junior because one is 17 days older than the other. Despite their cantankerousness, the two draw comfort from one another’s presence. When Junior dies on the street after being toppled by a passing Vespa – on the same day that a tsunami hits the south of the country – Senior comes to understand how “death and life [are] just adjacent verandas”.Available via Vintage Digital, 8hr 12minFurther listeningKinTayari Jones,Oneworld Audio,13hr,10minAngel Pean and Ashley J Hobbs narrate this sweeping tale of two best friends, born a few days apart in Louisiana, who grow up without mothers. As they get older, fate pulls them apart and they pursue different futures.LandMaggie O’Farrell,Tinder Press,16hr47minsNot long after the Irish famine, a cartographer’s son must finish a map of Ireland begun by his father away from the prying eyes of the British. This historical novel by the Hamnet author is read by Dane Whyte O’Hara.Explore more on these topicsSalman RushdieAudiobook of the weekreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Lise Davidsen: Verdi album review – star soprano gives opera’s leading ladies radiant power and vulnerability  | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Focusing on five Verdian heroines (and anti-heroines), the soprano has chosen roles that fit her formidable vocal talents perfectly. Edward Gardner and the London Philharmonic Orchestra provide detailed accompaniment for these striking portraits
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Focusing on five Verdian heroines (and anti-heroines), the soprano has chosen roles that fit her formidable vocal talents perfectly. Edward Gardner and the London Philharmonic Orchestra provide detailed accompaniment for these striking portraits
Content: ‘Her breath control alone deserves a Grammy’ … Lise Davidsen.Photograph: James HoleView image in fullscreen‘Her breath control alone deserves a Grammy’ … Lise Davidsen.Photograph: James HoleClassical musicReviewLise Davidsen: Verdi album review – star soprano gives opera’s leading ladies radiant power and vulnerability(Decca)Focusing on five Verdian heroines (and anti-heroines), the soprano has chosen roles that fit her formidable vocal talents perfectly. Edward Gardner and the London Philharmonic Orchestra  provide detailed accompaniment for these striking portraitsClive PagetThu 10 Sep 2026 09.45 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 10.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt some point, any star soprano worth her salt will try her hand at a Verdi album.Lise Davidsenavoids the fate of those who attempt to encompass the composer’s entire cast of leading ladies, focusing instead on five who fit her vocal talents like a glove.View image in fullscreenThe artwork for Lise Davidsen: Verdi.Photograph: DeccaShe opens with a commanding Lady Macbeth, her coloratura clean as a whistle and with gleaming, seemingly effortless top notes. Edward Gardner’s buoyant yet spacious way with the orchestral accompaniment affords Davidsen sufficient elbow room to create a more thoughtful schemer than is sometimes the case, culminating in a seamless sleepwalking scene where her breath control alone deserves a Grammy.For every kilowatt of power, she seeks out – and on the whole finds – moments of contrasting vulnerability (though none of Davidsen’s women are exactly shrinking violets). It’s most evident in the aria from Un Ballo in Maschera where Amelia pleads to see her child one last time. It’s there, too, in Elisabeth’s fatalistic Tu Che le Vanità from Don Carlo, but it can also be found in the darker recesses of Lady Macbeth’s La Luce Langue. Throughout, theLondon Philharmonic Orchestraprepares the detailed canvases for Davidsen’s striking portraits.There’s vocal beauty as Elisabeth comforts her dismissed lady-in-waiting and radiant stillness as Leonora raises her voice in prayer in La Forza del Destino. She’s at her most involving, though, in Amelia’s “gallows field” monologue from Ballo, and grappling with public versus private emotions in Aida’s Ritorna Vincitor!Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com.
