title: Taipei Story by Rebecca F Kuang review – the torture and hilarity of learning Chinese | Fiction | The Guardian
description: An American Chinese student studies Mandarin in Taiwan, in this heartfelt journey of self-discovery and family secrets
Author: Kit Fan
Headline: An American Chinese student studies Mandarin in Taiwan, in this heartfelt journey of self-discovery and family secrets
Content: Satirical wit … RF Kuang.Photograph: M Scott Brauer/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSatirical wit … RF Kuang.Photograph: M Scott Brauer/The GuardianBook of the dayFictionReviewTaipei Story by Rebecca F Kuang review – the torture and hilarity of learning ChineseAn American Chinese student studies Mandarin in Taiwan, in this heartfelt journey of self-discovery and family secretsKit FanThu 10 Sep 2026 19.24 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 19.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat is Taiwan? A former Japanese colony? A centre of the semiconductor industry? A democracy overseen by American imperialism? China’s next military target? An island of Austronesian Indigenous tribes? Is Taipei a cultural emblem of Taiwan, or just another booming global capital out of touch with the rest of the country? What stories will Lily Chen, an American Chinese student at Yale and Rebecca F Kuang’s funny and deadpan protagonist in Taipei Story, discover in this melting pot while spending 10 weeks learning Mandarin?A prolific maverick with rare satirical wit, Kuang has built a career debunking authoritative institutions.Babel(2022) highlights the prejudices of the British empire through a fantastical Oxford translation institute;Yellowface(2023) transplants a heist thriller into the dark heart of American publishing;Katabasis(2025), a journey into the underworld, gives the academic inferno at Cambridge a new lease of death. Centring on a tough Mandarin language school, Taipei Story explores the torture, hilarity and pretension of learning a second language, but here Kuang also offers a heartfelt journey of self-discovery and family wounds.Lily sets a clear boundary early on: “I wanted to become Chinese here, on my own terms.” Her classmates soon spot that “Lily is very insecure about her Chineseness”. Kuang renders the toxic dynamics and loneliness of foreign students with tact and heart. But what takes the novel beyond the usual campus relationship drama is Kuang’s meticulous, closeup account of Lily’s determination to learn Mandarin. Lily investigates sentence structures, teases out complex clauses, and gradually holds in her head “longer thought patterns in more nuanced logical relation to one another”. She memorises idioms and appreciates the looser Chinese grammar, compared with Latin and Romance languages. Through short, well-paced, diary-like episodes, where Chinese words appear alongside their English counterparts, Kuang recreates the uncanny process of language acquisition, as if the reader is learning Mandarin side by side with Lily, sharing her joy and frustration.double quotation markIt's as if the reader is learning Mandarin side by side with Lily, sharing her joy and frustrationIn her Author’s Note, Kuang says the novel is “about getting things wrong … mistranslation, miscommunication, and misunderstanding”. Where Sofia Coppola’s Lost in Translation has Bill Murray sharing his loneliness with Scarlett Johansson, Taipei Story creates an unlikely romantic comedy about falling in and out of love with a language. The novel sparkles with poker-faced humour about language learning. When Lily thinks she’s improving, her teacher retorts: “you have always sounded like an idiot. It is considerable progress that you can now hear it.” After completing the course, her teacher asks if Lily feels like a different person when speaking Chinese. Lily straightforwardly replies: “I feel younger, and more naive.”Lily is a captivating character; she mocks herself when she feels taken in, as though authenticity derives from the art of counterfeiting. To master Mandarin, she dutifully immerses herself in Taiwanese culture, visiting night markets, eating local food and living in a grotty private apartment rather than university accommodation. In her mission of “trying to blend in”, she discovers the composite layers of Taiwan’s history, sees the ghosts of China, Japan and America everywhere, and finds “no framework for making sense of” anything. Kuang captures this sensory overload throughout, interweaving the complex politics of food, customs, architecture. This leads to Lily’s realisation that “Taiwan had only ever been passed from occupier to occupier – indeed, to Taiwan’s Indigenous peoples, the Han Chinese themselves were occupiers. So who was I to say any occupier was better than the last?”China remains a mighty spectre in the novel. Following a bereavement in the Mainland, the book takes a poignant turn when Lily uncovers a family secret that unsettles her assumptions about grief, her grandfather and her mother. Kuang handles this shift with curiosity and empathy, tracing Lily’s investigation in heartbreaking dialogues between mother and daughter. Through this rupture, the novel connects the political history of successive authoritarian governments with a personal story of survival and reinvention. Despite the shock at its heart, the novel sustains its tone of pragmatic equanimity, as when Lily realises: “My grief was not that special … Ask around and every first-, second-, even third-generation Asian American had a sob story somewhere in the family tree.” This tough scepticism towards self and identity drives Taipei Story, as it propels Yellowface and Kuang’s other books too.Towards the end, recognising America’s weakened influence in the Asia-Pacific, Lily ponders: “What if China invaded Taiwan and it wasn’t free any more?” She imagines missiles “flying at any moment”. She also reflects on how languages “map space differently on to time. In English … the future lay before you. In Chinese, the future lay behind.” Taipei Story is a timely, deeply moving novel that helps us weigh a troubled past against a conflicted present.Kit Fan’s latest novel is Goodbye Chinatown (World Editions). Taipei Story by Rebecca F Kuang is published by Borough (£16.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: Marvel’s Wolverine review – a gloriously conflicted lead is let down by crude, boring battling  | Games | The Guardian
description: Logan is well realised by Liam McIntyre and some exquisite character art, but there are lapses in narrative and emotional arcs and some of the combat feels like a chore
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: Logan is well realised by Liam McIntyre and some exquisite character art, but there are lapses in narrative and emotional arcs and some of the combat feels like a chore
Content: Turn on the rage-ometer … Marvel's Wolverine.Photograph: SonyView image in fullscreenTurn on the rage-ometer … Marvel's Wolverine.Photograph: SonyGamesReviewMarvel’s Wolverine review – a gloriously conflicted lead is let down by crude, boring battlingPlayStation 5; Insomniac GamesLogan is well realised by Liam McIntyre and some exquisite character art, but there are lapses in narrative and emotional arcs and some of the combat feels like a choreKeith StuartThu 10 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was always going to be difficult to follow Spider-Man. Insomniac’s three games based around the web-slinger are masterpieces of superhero wish fulfilment, allowing you to swoop above a depiction of Manhattan alive with graffiti artists, roving journalists and gun-toting gangsters. If anyone should be up to the task, it’s Wolverine. A beloved Marvel stalwart, his life much darker and bloodier than Peter Parker’s, he seems the ideal protagonist for a moody action adventure. Yet somehow this well-made game falls short of its potential.Set years before the founding of the X-Men, Marvel’s Wolverine sees a disenfranchised Logan falling back in with Sabretooth and Mystique when their mentor Nathaniel Essex is kidnapped by mutant-hating billionaire Bolivar Trask. This archetypal tech bro has a disturbing plan for world domination and the X Team are out to stop him – but there is a secret buried in Wolverine’s past that’s about to cause an eruption. It’s a decent setup, filled with the sort of intrigue, violence and Freudian tension we expect from the X-Men.View image in fullscreenMarvels Wolverine Sony Interactive Entertainment (PlayStation).Illustration: Sony Interactive Entertainment (PlayStation).At its heart, though, Marvel’s Wolverine is, like its hero, an unreconstructed brawler. From the start, you can dodge, parry, shred attack and leap attack with speed and savagery, but as you earn XP, you unlock new techniques and combos as well as powerful special moves such as the tornado spin, which damages enemies all around you in a flurry of blades, or the spiral strike, which lets you drill through an enemy to escape a crowd. Your main combo attack is the barrage, accessed by hitting shred repeatedly, but this can be closed with a leap attack or other unlocked techniques for extra damage, and to stagger opponents. On top of this you can also unlock new DNA strands, which provide buffs to your health and cooldown speeds. The highlight, though, is the three-stage rage meter, which builds as you damage and parry enemies. At each stage you get more powerful attack and defensive stats, and at the final stage you become an almost indestructible machine of carnage, which is immensely liberating.But while fights feel smooth and empowering, there is rarely any need to be creative or experimental. In the Spider-Man games, the character’s grace, his web-throwing, the three-dimensional nature of his movement, all encourage you to fightbeautifully; here I was reminded of 80s beat-’em-ups, or PS3 brawlers – a bludgeoning production line of identical fights against increasingly over-familiar enemy types. Sure, this fits with Wolverine’s character, but similar melee-based brawling adventures such as Devil May Cry and Bayonetta provide deeply layered combat systems and diverse enemy types which reward (and often demand) varied techniques from players. I survived a huge majority of skirmishes in the default difficulty setting by pummelling parry and switching between linked shred attacks and leaps, opening and closing barrage combos in the process, while letting rip with specials whenever they came online. The boss battles, which felt extremely familiar and at times cliched, demanded a similar approach, just with better timing and more patience.View image in fullscreen‘Thrusting us from set-piece to set-piece in a globe-trotting race against time and plausibility’ … Marvel’s Wolverine.Similarly, the Insomniac team warned us to expect a more tightly structured environment than in the Spider-Man titles, and they were not kidding. Wolverine is mostly linear, thrusting us from set-piece to set-piece in a globe-trotting race against time and plausibility. When we do get to big, inviting cities such as Madripoor or Tokyo, we find roads closed off and invisible walls directing us back to the action. The whole world feels like a theatrical backdrop, untouchable and aloof, and many miles from the bustling metropolis we got to live in and explore as Spidey. Yes, we all know this makes sense – Wolverine is by nature a rootless character, an inveterate drifter, but presenting us with a Tokyo so richly detailed and visually seductive, only to lock most of it off, feels almost cruel.In contrast, the game’s interpretation of Logan is a triumph. Through exquisite character art and animation, and a brilliant performance from Liam McIntyre, he comes alive as a flawed, often unwilling hero, capable of extreme brutality and touching vulnerability. His rivalry with Sabretooth and his blossoming relationship with Jean Grey are intricate and involving, resulting in some truly moving scenes. But you play no interactive part in the linear story or its relationships, and the few attempts at offering puzzles tied in with the narrative are hurriedly designed and quickly abandoned. We’re told that Wolverine’s past trauma will be explored, but for much of the game this comes via snippets of lore that you unlock by competing in mini-challenges such as timed parkour runs and horde battles against waves of baddies. It feels like a rather insensitive way to portray and process PTSD. The climax of the game, when it comes, is an absolute technical marvel, a Homerian clash of super powers, but sadly its impact is lessened by far too many exposition flashbacks and airy metaphysical deviations.Marvel’s Wolverine remains a lovingly crafted, beautifully polished hack-’em-up that will no doubt thrill Wolverine fans who want to eviscerate as many enemies as possible while looking out for X-Men easter eggs, and pausing once in a while to have story and subtext thrown at them. But despite the full-bloodied use of Wolverine’s claws and a generous array of moves and combos, combat lacks both the bone-crunching impact of the Batman Arkham games and the balletic joy of Spider-Man. As the game goes on and the enemies line up, it feels increasingly like a chore. Logan becomes what he always dreaded: hired muscle.There is so much seductive and emancipating rage in this game, in its story, its combat mechanics, its gloriously conflicted protagonist. But the crescendo always feels like it’s just out of reach, like an argument in another room, or a war on the news.Explore more on these topicsGamesPlayStation 5reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Kimberly Akimbo review – hilarious musical about a sexagenarian teen is one for the ages | Stage | The Guardian
description: Maria Friedman plays a 15-year-old with a rare ageing condition in a heartfelt and funny show that manages to sustain its sweetness
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: Maria Friedman plays a 15-year-old with a rare ageing condition in a heartfelt and funny show that manages to sustain its sweetness
Content: Brighter than life … Maria Friedman with Gilli Jones in Kimberly Akimbo.Photograph: Marc BrennerView image in fullscreenBrighter than life … Maria Friedman with Gilli Jones in Kimberly Akimbo.Photograph: Marc BrennerStageReviewKimberly Akimbo review – hilarious musical about a sexagenarian teen is one for the agesHampstead theatre, LondonMaria Friedman plays a 15-year-old with a rare ageing condition in a heartfelt and funny show that manages to sustain its sweetnessLyndsey WinshipThu 10 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 11.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s a bizarre concept for a musical: a girl with a rare condition that causes her to age four times faster than her peers, in a family so dysfunctional that she’s the normal one. Meanwhile, the musical highlights are songs about cheque fraud and scurvy. And yet, somehow, through all this artifice and elaborate setup comes a show so sincerely heartfelt, one that is genuine, hilarious and utterly endearing.Kimberly Akimbo started out as a play, in 2001, by Pulitzer prize-winner David Lindsay-Abaire, adapted into a musical with composer Jeanine Tesori (Shrek, Fun Home, Caroline, or Change) in 2021. It was lauded on Broadway, where audiences fell for its feels and kooky charm and itwon five Tony awards.View image in fullscreenSunny … Maria Friedman as Kimberly Levaco.Photograph: Marc BrennerFor this London premiere, 66-year-old Maria Friedman plays the 15-year-old Kimberly Levaco, living with her pregnant mother Pattie (Niamh Perry) and alcoholic father Buddy (Peter Hannah). They have fled to a New Jersey neighbourhood after something unpleasant went down in their old town. Kimberly’s new-girl shyness soon gives way to a sunny, sweet character that Friedman plays wide-eyed and guileless, moving in the orbit of a quartet of misfit pals and the absolutely adorable Elvish-speaking, tuba-playing Seth (Gilli Jones). Their youthfulness is portrayed with an amped-up cutesiness, which works in a show where everything’s a little brighter than real life.Designer Soutra Gilmour puts the Levaco family in a three-storey house with a well-worn sofa and a well-used swear jar. It’s a brilliant set that rotates and turns into a skating rink, a school library, a corridor full of lockers decorated with stickers of Daria and Buffy the Vampire Slayer, in case there was any doubt we’re in the 1990s (see also: Seth’s Velcro wallet). Like everything else in this show it’s agile, slotting into place without heavy effort.This is a story, after all, that takes in criminality, alcoholism, neglect, thwarted dreams and life-limiting illness. It’s dealt with lightly – not dismissively – but with a deft handling of tone by Tesori and director Michael Longhurst. It is frequently laugh-out-loud funny (in an opening number about the joys of New Jersey and not fitting in: “I think Springsteen’s just OK,” sings Seth). Alice Fearn has great timing as Pattie’s felonious sister Debra who arrives with a get-rich-quick scheme.‘We all have an expiry date’: Kimberly Akimbo, the achingly funny musical about a teen with a 64-year-old bodyRead moreRather than anthemic choruses a la Springsteen, Tesori’s songs are conversational and colloquial (“Oh my God, I’m such a tool”), skating across musical styles from ukulele strums, to pop-soul and jazzy harmonies. But she can also suddenly pull the rug to land in more emotional territory, as in Kimberly’s desire just to sit at the table for dinner as a family for once.It’s a show about wanting things we can’t have and making the best of what we’ve got, and the privilege of having ordinary problems. Perhaps when the emotional climax comes, finally addressing the reality of Kimberly’s condition, the incredulity in the family dynamic is stretched a step too far, but there’s enough goodwill by that point for it not to matter.Kimberly Akimbo deals breezily with serious subjects and is all the more bittersweet for it. The average life expectancy of someone with her condition is 16, Kimberly tells Seth, as her birthday approaches. “It’s just an average!” she says brightly, and your heart melts at this winningly hopeful show.AtHampstead theatre, London, until 7 NovemberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatreMusicalsHampstead theatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Female survival in a terrifying world’: Tilda Swinton’s return in Man to Man | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Manfred Karge’s play about a woman acting as her dead husband was a cause célèbre in the 80s. It remains a bracing portrait of a divided person in a divided culture
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Manfred Karge’s play about a woman acting as her dead husband was a cause célèbre in the 80s. It remains a bracing portrait of a divided person in a divided culture
Content: Tilda Swinton in Man to Man at the Royal Court in 2026.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTilda Swinton in Man to Man at the Royal Court in 2026.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianTheatre‘Female survival in a terrifying world’: Tilda Swinton’s return in Man to ManManfred Karge’s play about a woman acting as her dead husband was a cause célèbre in the 80s. It remains a bracing portrait of a divided person in a divided cultureStephen UnwinThu 10 Sep 2026 05.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was Pierre Audi,the much-mourned founder of the Almeida, who way back in 1986 sent me a coffee-stained copy of Jacke wie Hose.Manfred Karge’s one-woman play is a study of female survival in a terrifying world. Ella is a working-class woman who takes on the identity of her dead husband, Max, to endure what Brecht memorably dubbed “the dark times”: the 12 years of Nazi rule. But Karge extends this to include the division of Germany into two nation states (one communist, one capitalist) and the reconstruction that followed.My German was just about good enough to realise that this was something that had to be seen, and soon Jenny Killick, the visionary artistic director of the Traverse in Edinburgh, commissioned a translation from Anthony Vivis and had the guts to give the go-ahead for what we called Man to Man.Tilda Swintonand I were close friends from Cambridge, and we’d often worked together, at university and in the real world. She was the obvious choice to play the part.View image in fullscreenSurprising and challenging … Tilda Swinton in Man to Man at the Royal Court in 1988.Photograph: Donald Cooper/AlamyAlong with the designerBunny Christieand the lighting designer Ben Ormerod, we soon had a team, all in our 20s, all just starting out, all making it up as we went along. But our scratch production became a cause célèbre at the 1987 Edinburgh festival, and transferred to the Royal Court for a three-week run the following year. In a theatre culture devoted to poetic naturalism, it surprised and challenged audiences. And it shaped us all.Even then, Manfred Karge was a legendary figure. He was born in poverty in Brandenburg before the war, and his talent was spotted in 1961 by the great Helene Weigel – Bertolt Brecht’s wife, who had co-founded the Berliner Ensemble after the war and ran it following his death. She quickly engaged Karge as an actor. He also became a director, working in many of the leading German-speaking theatres. He wrote Jacke wie Hose, his first play, which he staged with his partner, Lore Brunner, in Bochum in 1982. He returned to Berlin in 1993, where he still writes, directs and teaches.Karge is one of the last surviving links to the original Brecht theatre. And in true Brechtian spirit, he wrote a deliberately conflicted figure: likeable one moment, repellent the next; insightful and blinkered; reactionary and visionary; but, throughout, a woman from the lowest rung of society, caught up in the disastrous contradictions of her time.Thus, Man to Man shows a divided person in a divided culture in a divided land. It explores the deepest forms of alienation – social and political, sexual and psychological – in which identities are fluid and, as Marx said, all that is solid melts into air. And in Karge’s two new scenes (one written specifically for this revival), we see the fall of the Berlin Wall and the re-emergence of the German far right, and how these divisions continue to multiply.View image in fullscreenA woman caught up in the disastrous contradictions of her time … Tilda Swinton in Man To Man in 2026.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianMan to Man is an extraordinary text. Its 28 short scenes deploy a heady cocktail of verse and prose, doggerel and naturalistic chatter, as well as fragments of songs, poems and quotations from both “high” and “low” culture. It is idiomatic and peculiarly hard to translate. The title literally means “jacket like trousers”, the equivalent, perhaps, of “six of one, half-a-dozen of the other”. We’re delighted to be returning to the lateAnthony Vivis’s stunning English version, to which I’ve made some minor revisions and added translations of the two new scenes.Karge’s text provides no stage directions, no sense of how he wants it to be presented, and every creative team must come up with their own answers. Revisiting the play after all these years, Tilda, Bunny, Ben and I are eager to do two things at once: celebrate what worked in our original production while testing those responses against new realities, new ways of making theatre. Happily, we’re joined by younger collaborators, ready to challenge us, primed to contribute, and determined to make this much more than a revival from the distant past.Tilda Swinton’s blast from the past, Kevin Bridges at large and a deepfake ballet: theatre, comedy and dance to see this autumnRead moreSometimes, we’ve found, history overtakes us. Thus, in 1987 I suggested to Bunny that a thin line of red tape bisecting the white floor could suggest the division ofGermanyand the Berlin Wall, which I had recently crossed. And now, nearly 40 years later, we are confronted with a new scene in which the Wall comes tumbling down: Tilda ripping up that red tape from the floor will be one of those rare moments when the practical nature of the theatre will act out history itself.The theatre must live in the present tense. But it also has a past and a future. The wheel has come full circle. We are here.Man to Man is at theRoyal Court theatre, London, until 24 October. Then at theTraverse theatre, Edinburgh, 29 October to 7 November, and inNew Yorkin February.Explore more on these topicsTheatreRoyal Court theatreTilda SwintonTraverse theatreGermanyEuropeBunny ChristiefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: for colored girls who have considered suicide / when the rainbow is enuf review – ‘choreopoem’ of sisterhood | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Starkly staged panorama of Black female experience rushes through its scenes but is delivered with feeling by its terrific cast
Author: Anya Ryan
Headline: Starkly staged panorama of Black female experience rushes through its scenes but is delivered with feeling by its terrific cast
Content: A relief and a release … (from left) Ibilola Rossi, Tatenda Matsvai, Cherrelle Skeete, Alex Thomas-Smith and Nadine Higgin in for colored girls who have considered suicide / when the rainbow is enuf at the Yard Theatre, London.Photograph: Camilla GreenwellView image in fullscreenA relief and a release … (from left) Ibilola Rossi, Tatenda Matsvai, Cherrelle Skeete, Alex Thomas-Smith and Nadine Higgin in for colored girls who have considered suicide / when the rainbow is enuf at the Yard Theatre, London.Photograph: Camilla GreenwellTheatreReviewfor colored girls who have considered suicide / when the rainbow is enuf review – ‘choreopoem’ of sisterhoodYard theatre, LondonStarkly staged panorama of Black female experience rushes through its scenes but is delivered with feeling by terrific castAnya RyanThu 10 Sep 2026 07.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt has been 50 years since this “choreopoem” by Ntozake Shange premiered on Broadway and brought the emotions and experiences of Black women to the stage. And yet, until now – in this production directed by Diane Page for the Yard theatre’s reopening – it has never received a major London run.Collectively, the poems form a rich panorama: tales of domestic abuse bound up in a threatening marriage proposal; infidelity that brings a devastating HIV diagnosis; and an eight-year-old girl who is inspired by the Haitian revolutionary Toussaint Louverture. In so many ways, they could have been written yesterday. Journeying between US cities including Chicago, St Louis, New York and San Francisco, seven brightly coloured “Ladies” – played by five actors here – cry out their stories, ready to be heard. Shange’s lyrical writing mixes their pain with surges of joy, as each woman takes her turn in the spotlight while the others watch on in witness and support.View image in fullscreenNadine Higgin in for colored girls who have considered suicide / when the rainbow is enuf.Photograph: Camilla GreenwellWith repeated refrains and sections that feel like a chorus, the play becomes both a relief and a release. In Britain, we’re perhaps more familiar withRyan Calais Cameron’s stunning modern response,For Black Boys Who Have Considered Suicide When the Hue Gets Too Heavy. And here, you can see the blend of poetry, rage, music and movement that inspired it. Page’s production is stark, with the Ladies’ voices left to drive its emotional highs and lows. It could hang a little longer in each section; before we have time to fully absorb its effects, we’re already whizzing on to the next. We need a breath to catch up.for colored girls: the 40-year-old masterwork that’s still captivating audiencesRead moreSupported by a mesmeric new soundtrack by Jammz and choreography by Ingrid Mackinnon, the piece beats with raw feeling. The Ladies break into soulful, almost spiritual moments of dance, as Ali Hunter’s lighting design sends rainbows pulsing across the stage floor. The cast – Nadine Higgin, Tatenda Matsvai, Ibilola Rossi, Cherrelle Skeete and Alex Thomas-Smith – perform as though Shange’s words are being drawn from somewhere deep within them. In their moments of togetherness, the production reaches its most arresting force. Leading us through the many colours and shades of life, their sisterhood makes a case for hope.At theYard theatre, London, until 17 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Todd Rundgren review – try-anything veteran doesn’t let his freak flag fully fly | Todd Rundgren | The Guardian
description: The 78-year-old has astonishing range but gets bogged down in middling rock, though later delivers some gorgeous acoustic songs – and a slinky Marvin Gaye cover
Author: Dorian Lynskey
Headline: The 78-year-old has astonishing range but gets bogged down in middling rock, though later delivers some gorgeous acoustic songs – and a slinky Marvin Gaye cover
Content: In resilient and versatile voice … Todd Rundgren.Photograph: Per Ole Hagen/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIn resilient and versatile voice … Todd Rundgren.Photograph: Per Ole Hagen/Getty ImagesTodd RundgrenReviewTodd Rundgren review – try-anything veteran doesn’t let his freak flag fully flyCadogan Hall, LondonThe 78-year-old has astonishing range but gets bogged down in middling rock, though later delivers some gorgeous acoustic songs – and a slinky Marvin Gaye coverDorian LynskeyThu 10 Sep 2026 05.38 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 05.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTodd Rundgren is a confusing man. After his tune-packed 1972 album Something/Anything? drew comparisons to Carole King and Brian Wilson, he took a pharmacopoeia of psychedelics and made a vexing masterpiece, A Wizard, a True Star, with no singles at all. He’s produced classic albums by Meat Loaf and the New York Dolls but he’s also released a record of nothing but vocals (A Cappella) and the world’s first interactive album (No World Order). Counting only the artists who appeared on his last two albums, his fans include Trent Reznor, Robyn and the Lemon Twigs. He called his memoir The Individualist.Rundgren certainly looks the part. With his Addams Family hair, tinted goggles and limber dance moves, he could be a goth raver. Everything he says sounds teasingly sarcastic, even when he’s thanking the audience for spending their “discretionary income” on a ticket. He says the curfew means he can’t tell stories about the songs but it would have been worth sacrificing a couple of his two-hour show’s stodgier numbers to hear them.Rundgren’s two sets represent more than half of his 26 solo albums as well as his bands, the Nazz and Utopia, but there’s scant evidence of the try-anything polymath who inspired generations of studio auteurs. While I Saw the Light is giddy power-pop perfection, there’s an awful lot of middling rock in part one. Due in part to the stuffiness of the all-seater venue and the advanced age of his fanbase, it never takes off.After the interval Rundgren travels to more rewarding destinations. A slinky cover of Marvin Gaye’s I Want You and an extraordinary a cappella folk song, Honest Work, showcase a voice far more resilient and versatile than most artists of 78. The acoustic section is simply gorgeous, with shades of Joni Mitchell’s capricious melodies on Cliche. When Rundgren grabs a baton to conduct his five-man band through the symphonic Kindness, he seems like the man who can do anything. What he chose to do this time is not the most interesting take on his unclassifiable career but as one man tells his friend on the way out, “You take what you’re given with Todd.”Todd Rundgren playsBristol Beacon, 10 September; then touring the UKuntil 13 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsTodd RundgrenPop and rocklive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Tony Gatlif obituary | Movies | The Guardian
description: Algerian-born French director of more than 20 films that celebrated Roma culture
Author: Garth Cartwright
Headline: Algerian-born French director of more than 20 films that celebrated Roma culture
Content: Tony Gatlif, right, with James Thierrée, on location for Korkoro, 2009.Photograph: Everett/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenTony Gatlif, right, with James Thierrée, on location for Korkoro, 2009.Photograph: Everett/ShutterstockMoviesObituaryTony Gatlif obituaryAlgerian-born French director of more than 20 films that celebrated Roma cultureGarth CartwrightThu 10 Sep 2026 11.28 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 11.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe French film director Tony Gatlif, who has died aged 77, was regularly described as “cinema’s Gypsy auteur”, so often did his films focus on Roma communities and their music. Between 1975 and 2025, Gatlif directed more than 20 films, beginning with La Tête en Ruine (The Ruined Head). That film was never released, and he struggled throughout the 1970s and 80s to get funding for his films, and then to find a distributor, before finally breaking through with Latcho Drom (1993, the title being Romany for “good journey”). An international arthouse hit,Latcho Dromis a meditative travelogue that blends footage of staged musical performances in contemporary Roma communities in Istanbul, Romania, Hungary, Slovakia, France and Spain, with historic recreations of such communities in Rajasthan and an Egyptian oasis.Latcho Drom conveys the centuries-long migration from Asia to western Europe of a nomadic people we now call Gypsies or Roma, as a fable told entirely in images and music. There is no voiceover, talking heads or text; instead Gatlif lets the striking settings and musical performances enchant viewers. It is an idealised portrait of the Roma, not a documentary (as some labelled it), and while Gatlif portrays the discrimination and persecution Roma communities experience, his emphasis was on celebrating Roma beauty and artistry.After the success of Latcho Drom, Gatlif went on to write and direct a feature film every couple of years, his most recent being Ange (2025). These films were all dramas and tended to focus either on a Roma community – Mondo (1995), Gadjo Dilo (1997), Vengo (2000), Swing (2001), Korkoro (2009) – or were road movies in which the protagonists drift across France, then head into eastern Europe or North Africa, seeking meaning and origins. His 2004 filmExilswon Gatlif the best director award at the Cannes film festival.View image in fullscreenA still from Latcho Drom, 1993.Photograph: Tom Specht/BarbicanHe was born Boualem Dahmani in Algiers, when Algeria was a part of France, to a Kabyle (Berber) father and a mother of Spanish and Roma heritage. His impoverished family lived in a shantytown on the outskirts of the city, he said, until 1960 when, with the Algerian war of independence raging, they joined a huge exodus of French Algerians in relocating to the south of France. A troubled adolescent, he regularly got into fights and engaged in antisocial behaviour, which led to him being sent to a reform school.He began using the name Tony Gatlif – choosing the surname from a local park in Algiers – so as to avoid the police in the Camargue region, who knew Dahmani too well. A meeting with the actorMichel Simonin 1966 led to Gatlif enrolling in a dramatic arts course in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, outside Paris, after Simon wrote a letter of recommendation.Gatlif worked as a jobbing actor while writing scripts for his prospective features. His second film, La Terre au Ventre (The Belly of the Earth, 1978), focused on a young mother and her four daughters, all dispossessed from Algeria. His third, Corre, Gitano (Run, Gypsy, 1981), was filmed in Spain and focused on a young Roma man accused of a crime he did not commit.Gatlif had now found his subject matter and rarely swayed from it thereafter. Les Princes (1983), about a petty, patriarchal Roma criminal living in a French housing estate, won him some attention, but it was Latcho Drom that established him as a film-maker of note. The film won the Un Certain Regard award at Cannes in 1993, and a growing interest in Gypsy music created a sizable international audience for Gatlif’s films.View image in fullscreenGatlif on the set of Transylvania, 2006.Photograph: Princes/Everett/ShutterstockGadjo Dilo (Crazy Foreigner, 1997) focuses on a young French man who drifts into a Romanian Roma community, begins a relationship with a Roma woman, then witnesses an anti-Roma pogrom. Providing career-defining roles forRomain Durisand Rona Hartner, Gadjo Dilo did so well that Gatlif cast its two young stars in his next film, Je Suis Né d’Une Cigogne (1998, Children of the Stork), a road movie heavily indebted toJean-Luc Godard’s 60s films, which received negative reviews and poor box office.He returned to the Roma with Vengo and Swing, set in Spain and France respectively, films that focus on flamenco and Manouche jazz musicians, with threadbare plots tacked on. Gatlif’s skills as a scriptwriter were marginal and the narratives of these two films, and two later road movies, Exils (again with Duris, this time heading to Algeria) andTransylvania(2006), are often clunky, no matter how striking the setting and music. Korkoro (2009), a period drama about the Nazi persecution of Roma in occupied France, laboured to convey the Porajmos (the Romani Holocaust) convincingly.Gatlif remained indifferent to such criticisms and continued making films his way, even if audiences diminished in recent years. In 2015 he was made a chevalier de la Légion d’honneur. He was taken ill and died in Arles, southern France, while working on a film.He is survived by his wife, Delphine, and three children, Elsa, Valentin and Lucia.Tony Gatlif (Boualem Dahmani), film-maker, born 10 September 1948; died 2 September 2026Explore more on these topicsFilmRoma, Gypsies and TravellersFolk musicobituariesShareReuse this content

title: The Odyssey and Spider-Man propel record-breaking summer box office worldwide | Film industry | The Guardian
description: The biggest May to September of all time was recorded in US cinemas, with the UK enjoying a 56% rise in audiences, outstripped by an 88% lift in the Middle East and Africa
Author: Catherine Shoard
Headline: The biggest May to September of all time was recorded in US cinemas, with the UK enjoying a 56% rise in audiences, outstripped by an 88% lift in the Middle East and Africa
Content: Hollywood’s Chinese theatre during opening weekend  of The Odyssey in July.Photograph: AaronP/Bauer-Griffin/GC ImagesView image in fullscreenHollywood’s Chinese theatre during opening weekend  of The Odyssey in July.Photograph: AaronP/Bauer-Griffin/GC ImagesFilm industryThe Odyssey and Spider-Man propel record-breaking summer box office worldwideThe biggest May to September of all time was recorded in US cinemas, with the UK enjoying a 56% rise in audiences, outstripped by an 88% lift in the Middle East and AfricaCatherine ShoardThu 10 Sep 2026 09.57 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs well as celebrating their wedding, the actors Tom Holland and Zendaya have something else to toast: their two summer blockbusters –The Odysseyand Spider-Man: Brand New Day – have officially made box office history.The films were credited as the driving force behind the US’s biggest summer season of all time, taking $4.761bn (£3.51bn) from 1 May-7 September, beating 2013’s $4.756bn.Spider-Man is currently on $2.4bn worldwide and likely to climb higher, while The Odyssey has made $1.6bn. Other key titles driving sales include Toy Story 5, Michael and The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, all of which have grossed over $1bn.The breadth of the success of Destin Daniel Cretton’s Spider-Man: Brand New Day was a particular surprise. The film is the best-performing of the year so far and the third highest-grossing film of all time. Its opening weekend was the second-best of all time behind Avengers: Endgame (2019) and it is also the second-fastest film to gross $1bn, doing so in six days.Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, meanwhile, is the highest-grossing “original” movie of the year, despite its adaptation from Homer’s epic poem. Low-budget original horror movies Backrooms ($394m) and Obsession ($513m) have also helped re-energise the box office.Sequels and spinoffs accounted for many of the underperformers, including Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu ($345.4m) , Supergirl ($126.4m) and Minions & Monsters ($518.1m – around half of 2022’s Minions: The Rise of Gru).Meanwhile, August cinema admissions in the UK rose 56% year-on-year to over 17m, according to the UK Cinema Association, signalling the biggest August since 2018 and the second-best performing month since July 2023, when Barbie and Oppenheimer opened together.Such an uptick is dwarfed by the picture in Europe, the Middle East and Africa, which saw an 88% year-on-year lift, according to Gower Street and the International Union of Cinemas. France’s 19.9m August admissions was the best number recorded during that month since records began 46 years ago, and marked a 50% increase from 2025.Italian cinemas recorded their best-ever June-August period, with 20.8m admissions and a take of €162.3m, as well as their best ever August. Spain saw a 71% year-on-year increase, while the Netherlands recorded a 77% lift.Explore more on these topicsFilm industryThe OdysseySpider-Man: Brand New ⁠DaynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘An embodiment of white fears’: how zombies went from Haitian spiritual tradition to Hollywood monsters | Documentary films | The Guardian
description: Maya Annik Bedward’s fascinating new documentary goes beyond reductive imagery to place the zombie and vodou in their true historical context
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Maya Annik Bedward’s fascinating new documentary goes beyond reductive imagery to place the zombie and vodou in their true historical context
Content: Still from Maya Annik Bedward's documentary Black Zombie.Photograph: Courtesy of Kino LorberView image in fullscreenStill from Maya Annik Bedward's documentary Black Zombie.Photograph: Courtesy of Kino LorberDocumentary films‘An embodiment of white fears’: how zombies went from Haitian spiritual tradition to Hollywood monstersMaya Annik Bedward’s fascinating new documentary goes beyond reductive imagery to place the zombie and vodou in their true historical contextSoraya Nadia McDonaldThu 10 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 17.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmerican film has a canon of racist disinformation that famously includesThe Birth of a Nation, King Kong (1933) andGone With the Wind.A new documentary makes a compelling argument that zombies, as presented, commodified and popularized by Hollywood, are part of the same tradition. Black Zombie serves as work of restoration and correction, placing its faith in the quiet, persistent power of the truth as it stares down a tsunami of colonial erasure, denial, whitewashing, violence and theft.Its opening revelation – that zombies are a Haitian idea, invented to capture the metaphysical anguish of being torn from one’s home and subjected to torture, rape and forced labor – is startling in its own right. But then director Maya Annik Bedward widens the aperture of understanding, engaging cultural experts in horror, such as Tananarive Due, an author and professor, Tom Savini,Night of the Living Deadspecial effects guru, Zandashé Brown, southern gothic film-maker, and Erol Josué, Haitian artist, vodou priest and choreographer, as she unwinds centuries of motivated misunderstanding to address broader questions: how did this happen? And why is this knowledge obscured?In her documentary feature debut, which premiered earlier this year at SXSW, Annik Bedward, a Jamaican-French Canadian curious about the misconceptions behind vodou, journeys toHaitito find out. In speaking with local experts and historians to unwrap the bandages of a misinformation mummy, she reveals a larger tragedy: the way the obscured history and provenance of the zombie has mirrored the fate of the people who invented it. When a person becomes a zombie, they are unable to return home, even in death. Part of Haitian lore is that a trapped spirit can free itself with a taste of salt, which white colonizers forbade Haitians from eating.A remarkable documentary made by blind students: ‘We were stunned by the footage’Read moreBlack Zombie reveals how an enterprising American journalist, William Seabrook, set off a century of cultural extraction, obfuscation and projection with his book The Magic Island, first published in 1929. The Magic Island marks the first use of the word “zombie” in the printed English language. Seabrook becomes the zombie’s first sensationalist, patronizing colonial observer, embedding himself with Haitians. His exotic dispatches, set off with racist caricatures by illustrator Alexander King, gets optioned, sending the Haitian zombie tumbling into the Hollywood machine, extruded and presented as White Zombiein 1932.The Haitian zombie is no longer a sorrowful artefact of dispossession, but a disfigured tool that collapses the zombie and vodou – two adjacent but separate ideas – into an indistinct stew. Vodou is a spiritual practice, a philosophy, a way of transmitting knowledge through generations and across oceans, expressing an embodied relationship with spirits through dance. It’s a metaphysical conversation. But onscreen, both vodou and the zombie become embodiments of white fears of Black savagery and desire for revenge. The zombie becomes a monster that must be put down, by any means necessary. The same cycle happens again in 1988, first with the publication of The Serpent and the Rainbow by Wade Davis, and its subsequent sensationalistadaptationby director Wes Craven.View image in fullscreenDirector Maya Annik Bedward.Photograph: Andreea Muscurel/Courtesy of Kino LorberTo correct this record, Annik Bedward engages Haitians as reliable narrators of their own experiences, traditions and spiritual practices. She travels to New Orleans to capture how vodou has been turned into meaningless kitsch meant to separate tourists from their money. Together with documentaries such asExterminate All the BrutesandSoundtrack to a Coup d’Etat, Black Zombie offers an indictment of not just colonialism and slavery, but of the damage that former colonial powers continue to inflict in the postcolonial era.“The more you can render people monstrous or claim that it’s their behavior that calls for punishment, essentially, then, the less you have to feel guilty about your practices, as an individual, as a community, as a state,” Kaiama L Glover, a Yale professor, explains in a scene in Black Zombie. “The zombie is a useful tool for that. It really cannot be underestimated the way culture can do the work of statecraft.”There is overt physical violence, the kind which comes from the barrel of a gun, the blade of a machete, or the crack of a lash. But the story of how the Haitian zombie becomes transmuted into a simplistic, undead money-making monster for Hollywood is a story of a more insidious violence that continues into 2026. If weaponry and ammunition constitute hard power, then the ability to shape culture, truth and history, or soft power, can be just as destructive, if not more so. Physical structures can be rebuilt. But memory, even when well-preserved, can be adulterated, drowned out and crumbled with a few well-placed lies.View image in fullscreenA still from 1932 film White Zombie.Photograph: Courtesy of Kino LorberTake for instance, the lie Donald Trump uttered in 2024 during a debate with former vice-president Kamala Harris. He falsely claimed that Haitian migrants were eating pets belonging to residents of Springfield, Ohio. He campaigned on promises of mass deportation and he has delivered. This year, Brooklyn’s annual West Indian Day parade doubled as a form of defiant protest for Haitian participants. They carried placards condemning ICE and calling for the reinstatement of temporary protected status after the supreme court upheld the administration’s right to revoke it, rendering some 350,000 Haitians vulnerable to detention and deportation. The Trump administration has continued to ground its foreign and immigration policy in false narratives, with officials repeatedlyinsistingthat it is safe for Haitian nationals to return to Haiti, even as armed gangscontinue to terrorize and kill residents.Union Town review – passionate exposé of US delivery workers’ employment conditionsRead moreHaving successfully destabilized the Haitian republic and shaken down reparations to French slavers in the form of crippling debt, former colonial powers continue to disfigure the truth. The contemporary Hollywood zombie is merely the most visible manifestation of the erasure of Haitian heritage and story. BothFifaand theIOCforced the country to change its uniform designs for depicting the country’s founding revolutionary struggle. It took Annik Bedward 10 years to make Black Zombie. When she finally received production funding, it was shortly after the 2021assassinationof president Jovenel Moïse. The ensuing violence and instability forced Annik Bedward, her Haitian crew and cast of historical re-enactors to finish shooting in the Dominican Republic, Haiti’s neighbor on the island of Hispaniola. “Pretty much everyone has left the country who could, who’s involved in the project,” Annik Bedward says. “And it’s really sad because they love their country and it’s like the effects of what happened to Haiti is still being felt in a huge way today.”And so, with the help of Annik Bedward’s remarkable film, the Haitian zombie marches on, leaving a trail of salt in its wake, still attempting to steer the world to the truth, to the Middle Passage graveyard that is the Atlantic, to the shores of Africa. To home.Black Zombie is released in the US on 11 September with UK and Australia release dates to followExplore more on these topicsDocumentary filmsZombiesHaitiFilm industryRacefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The 2026 Proms: tell us about your favourite concerts | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: Ahead of Saturday’s Last Night, we want to hear what you’ve enjoyed this year. Has any of the new music made it on to your playlists? Which soloists wowed you? Did you sing along to Hey Jude with the Jupiter Ensemble? Share your listening experiences in the comments
Author: Imogen Tilden
Headline: Ahead of Saturday’s Last Night, we want to hear what you’ve enjoyed this year. Has any of the new music made it on to your playlists? Which soloists wowed you? Did you sing along to Hey Jude with the Jupiter Ensemble? Share your listening experiences in the comments
Content: Mirga Gražinytė-Tyla conducts violinist Patricia Kopatchinskaja and the Oslo Philharmonic at the Royal Albert Hall on 29 August.Photograph: BBC/Chris ChristodoulouView image in fullscreenMirga Gražinytė-Tyla conducts violinist Patricia Kopatchinskaja and the Oslo Philharmonic at the Royal Albert Hall on 29 August.Photograph: BBC/Chris ChristodoulouProms 2026The 2026 Proms: tell us about your favourite concertsAhead of Saturday’s Last Night, we want to hear what you’ve enjoyed this year. Has any of the new music made it on to your playlists? Which soloists wowed you? Did you sing along to Hey Jude with theJupiter Ensemble? Share your listening experiences in the commentsImogen TildenThu 10 Sep 2026 06.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith 86 concerts over eight weeks, the BBC Proms’ claim to be the world’s greatest and biggest classical music festival is hard to dispute. As the 2026 season draws to a close, we want to hear from you. Which proms have you enjoyed in the Royal Albert Hall, on the radio or online? Did you attend a concert inBristol, Sunderland, Gateshead or Mold?Our critics loved theBerlin Phil,John Wilson and his Sinfonia of London, theOslo Philharmonic with Mirga Gražinytė-Tyla, and Aurora Orchestra’s exploration and performance ofMahler’s 1stamong many others; while of the new music premiered this year, Turnage’sFesten Suitewas a riot of colour, Thea Musgrave’s Bassoon Concertowas a beguiling treatandJessie Montgomery’s Cello Concertoa mesmerising highlight.There were rarities –Poulenc’s Concerto for Two Pianoswas fun and brilliantly played by the Jussen brothers,Weber’s Oberonmade its Proms debut 200 years after its Covent Garden premiere, and there was a 250-strong choir bringing force and thrill to Berlioz’s Requiem, and then, on at the other extreme, the extraordinary intimacy of the six voices of theGesualdo Six holding the entire hall rapt with a programme of early musicin a late-night prom.View image in fullscreenDancing and beaming: Ladysmith Black Mambazo’s Under African Skies - The Songs of Graceland Prom.Photograph: Andy ParadiseSouth Africa’s Ladysmith Black Mambazo delighted a completely sold-out hall in a late night Prom in early August – I have never been to a concert where teenagers and pensioners alike were dancing and beaming. Listening on the radio, I lovedBritten’s Les Illuminationswith soprano Julie Roset (part of the Sinfonia of London’s second prom), and was stopped in my tracks by the extraordinary vocal acrobatics on display inStrauss’s Ariadne auf Naxos, brought to the Proms in a semi-staging by Glyndebourne.What did you think? Was there too much Beethoven and Berlioz and not enoughBax? What pieces did you hear for the first time and fall in love with? (For me, I didn’t know Bartók’s Music for Strings, Percussion and Celesta and was captivated by theBBC Scottish’s performance).All our proms reviewsare here, every Proms concert can be listened to on BBC Sounds until 11 October andthere’s a wide selection to watch on iPlayer,includingMartha Argerich’s Beethoven, theNational Youth Orchestra conducted by Thomas Adèsand theJames Bond celebration.Meanwhile next year is the centenary of the BBC’s funding and running the concerts. What would you like to see in 2027’s festival?Over to you …Explore more on these topicsProms 2026Classical musiccalloutShareReuse this content

title: ‘People waited 24 hours for a potato!’: how viral queues help – and harm – restaurants | Food | The Guardian
description: It has become common for people to wait in long lines for cafes, bakeries and ice-cream shops. But why? And what do the owners think?
Author: Ammar Kalia
Headline: It has become common for people to wait in long lines for cafes, bakeries and ice-cream shops. But why? And what do the owners think?
Content: ‘Once the influencers got hold of it, it went nuclear’ ... our writer in line at CZER.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Once the influencers got hold of it, it went nuclear’ ... our writer in line at CZER.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianFood‘People waited 24 hours for a potato!’: how viral queues help – and harm – restaurantsIt has become common for people to wait in long lines for cafes, bakeries and ice-cream shops. But why? And what do the owners think?Ammar KaliaThu 10 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt 9.45am on a warm Saturday in September, a queue snakes down the pavement in Notting Hill, west London. Stretching for 20 yards past office blocks, estate agents and cafes, the line is waiting peacefully for an unusual morning snack: frozen yoghurt. The purveyor isthe dessert shop Yo-Chi, which opened only a fortnight ago, one of the many hospitality businesses making queueing an increasingly common part of the British dining experience.“We wait in line for everything now,” says 23-year-old Hannan Mahamud as she stands midway down the queue with three friends. “I queued for an hour the other week for a cookie, although it wasn’t worth it. We heard about Yo-Chi througha creator on TikTokwho works in an office building across the road and posts queue updates. We thought it might be a fun day out.”A few places ahead of Mahamud is Ewa Hemmerling, with her 14-year-old daughter, Lily, and Lily’s friends Georgia and Niamh. “I’d never usually wait for something like this, but it feels like something all the kids are up to now,” Hemmerling says. “It’s down to TikTok and Instagram and, to be honest, it’s an easy activity for us parents to do with the kids.”Inside, after a 30-minute wait, customers fill tubs with swirls of soft-serve frozen yoghurt and dollop on top an array of sweet toppings. The modestly sized two-storey shop buzzes with chatter and the beep of card machines charging £2.70 for 100g.View image in fullscreen‘We make it fun’ ... Yo-Chi, London.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The Guardian“We have more than 70 shops in Australia and a presence in Singapore – we know to expect queues wherever we open,” says Yo-Chi’s training leader, Monique Kyling. “We want to make it a space where kids can hang out or do homework. On Fridays and Saturdays, we even have a DJ and a disco ball. Last night, the queue was around the block, but we make it fun – we have a dedicated person managing the queue and another going up and down, playing games like push-up contests or paper-plane throwing. The queue becomes part of the experience and the staff enjoy the pressure.”This morning’s queue manager, Aisha, is outside clutching two handbag-sized dogs while their owners grab a morning dessert in the animal-free space. “It’s fun working here and everyone has a good time in the queue,” she says. “People are in high spirits and it’s nice to have a job in service where that’s the case.”The British hospitality industry is facing a crisis. Nearly a quarter of bars, pubs and restaurantshave operated at a lossso far in 2026, while produce and energy costscontinue to riseowing to the Ukraine war and instability in the Middle East. To be able to draw a queue in this climate is no mean feat – and usually involves harnessing the power of social media.“The Yo-Chi opening was a masterclass in social media marketing,” says Mairi Livsey, the co-founder ofthe viral food brand CZER. “They had every influencer there at the same time drumming up hype and it brought in the crowds in a difficult market. Operating costs are so high now that if you’re not running at close to full capacity, I have no idea how on earth you can survive.”View image in fullscreen‘We wait in line for everything now’ … from left: Hannan Mahamud,Hafsa Ali, Faisa Hassan and Sumaya Sharif.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianWhile Yo-Chi is a multinational operation, CZER is still finding its feet. Working in hospitality consultancy, Livsey and her partner, Marius Baltaitis, had theirfirst taste of famein 2025 when a hot chocolate recipe they designed for the food market Mercato Metropolitano in Mayfair picked up traction online.Inspired to find the next viral trend, Livsey came across a TikTok from a US creator noting that there was nowhere to buy chopped chicken caesar salad wraps in London. “I’d had that exact craving a few months before and even came up with the name CZER because of it,” Livsey says. “But that post made me determined to actually start the business, so I commented under the TikTok that we were bringing caesar salad wraps to Mayfair, even though we had no premises or proper plans yet.”Over the next three weeks, the couple found an unused service counter at the back of a corner shop in Mayfair, maxed out their credit cards to pay a recipe development company to come up with two wraps and hired three members of staff. They documented the entire process on social media. When they opened in May 2026, they had queues round the block. “We had planned to sell 50 wraps a day, but it was 400 a day almost at once,” Livsey says. “I obviously wanted the business to be popular, but I had never planned for there to be a queue seven days a week for three months straight. Once the influencers got hold of it, it went nuclear – we had to hire a full-time queue manager.”Along with the frenzied demand came some vicious online criticism. “People who had never been to see us were posting comments saying it was an embarrassment to queue for a £13 wrap, or that we were faking it all,” she says. “I would read them all at night after a long day and cry myself to sleep. I was so worried about people in the queue that I would run up and down giving them sweets, or umbrellas if it was raining – but the people who turned up were so lovely and actually happy to be there. It’s mostly women and they want to chat with each other and be part of a social experience.”View image in fullscreen‘I never planned for there to be a queue seven days a week’ ... Mairi Livsey, right, and Marius Baltaitis.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianAs demand increased, Livsey began operating a virtual queue system, where customers can scan a QR code, place their order and then return to the premises when their wrap is ready. In August, she opened another outlet in Soho and she now has 40 staff on the payroll, although the queues have started to dissipate.“We still do on average 400 wraps a day in Mayfair, but it’s an unpredictable industry and this is a summer product, so going into the winter we’re thinking about demand a lot,” she says. “We haven’t paid for any online coverage and we haven’t been able to take any profit out of the business yet – it’s a bootstrap operation. We do it because we love it – but it’s brutal. I wouldn’t want to live in a world where the only way you can survive in hospitality is to have queueing and virality.”This is not just a London phenomenon. In Manchester, the hole-in-the-wall sandwich shop Fat Pat’s has hadviral queuessince opening in 2021, while the opening ofthe ramen franchise Maki & Ramen in Birminghamin August also resulted in lines down the street. In Preston, one of the most sought-after viral foods is a jacket potato served from an old tram carriage and documented formore than 1 million followerson Instagram. “We’ve had 2,000 people in the queue and even people camping out and waiting almost 24 hours for a potato,” says Jacob Nelson, one of the co-founders of SpudBros. “We would never advise that, because we want everyone to stay safe. Still, me and [brother and co-founder] Harley love the chaos. When it gets really busy, you go into that higher gear and it makes it more fun.”Although the pair only started posting online during the pandemic to drum up business, they have since become influencers as much as restaurateurs, collaborating with the likes of the mega-popular YouTuberMrBeast in 2025. “We never set out to be influencers, but social media can really help people see the effort that goes into a business,” Nelson says. “You’ve got all these hidden costs and social media has allowed us to make sure people understand why our prices are what they are.”View image in fullscreen‘When it gets really busy, you go into that higher gear and it makes it more fun’ … SpudBros in Preston, Lancashire.Photograph: Garry Cook/AlamyFor many businesses, online popularity can be a burden as much as a gift. South-west London’sAugust Bakeryopened in 2024. Since the Instagram influencersBite Twiceposted a positive review of its pastries to their almost 300,000 followers in February 2026, the queues have been nonstop. “We’re not interested in social media at all, because we don’t enjoy it,” says the co-owner Florrie Beard. “At the beginning, a well-known duo approached us to make content in the shop, but we said no, because we knew it would create an impossible demand.“Still, that demand has come and it means people often come in wanting exactly the same thing they’ve seen on screen, even though we change the menu seasonally, depending on produce. It’s really hard work for the team to motor through people without dismissing them and it’s pretty much just a queue out the door until we sell out.“We spend so much time thinking about how best to reduce the bottlenecks and make it more efficient. And even though most people are happy to be social in the queue and chat, we hate that it makes the bakery less accessible to people who can’t physically stand for 40 minutes. When we had the heatwaves this summer, we would get people fainting, which wasn’t good.”Oula, a Tunisian cafein central London, has faced unpredictable spikes in demand since it went viral with amerguez sandwich. “The queues scare me a little,” the founder Boutheina B Salem says. “We built Oula around hospitality and conversation and those things become harder under pressure. Virality also strips away context and expectations can become more rigid when customers have been influenced by a short video or an image online. People have challenged me about Tunisian dishes because they differed from something they had eaten in Morocco, for example. I think influencer culture is here to stay, but when hype becomes your main currency, distinct cuisines are flattened into familiar formats and curiosity is narrowed.”View image in fullscreen‘It’s not hard work to wait for something that seems like a luxury’ ... The Dreamery in north London.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianEven for more established businesses, queues can be something to be wary of. The Indian restaurant chain Dishoom is known for its lines, but the chief operating officer, Nina Panayiodou, says it “isn’t a badge of desirability”. She believes the focus on waiting times can make people nervous about coming at all. “Over the years, the perception of queueing at Dishoom has grown, rather than the queueing itself,” she says. “We only have queues because we want to keep Dishoom a place where you can decide to visit on the day.”AtThe Dreamery, a north London ice-cream and wine shop, the co-founder George de Vos has his own reservations about the social media that brings customers flocking to his door. “Not everything should be explained and available to view for customers before they walk in,” he says. “You ideally want people to discover an experience for themselves.”Still, he adds: “You also have to embrace social media, because it’s here to stay. We have people in our queue with ring lights or even tripods ready to set up and shoot content – sometimes we have to gently ask them to make space. But when you see so many other good places closing soon after opening, it’s just a relief to be busy.”View image in fullscreen‘It isn’t a badge of desirability’ … people queue outside Dishoom in King’s Cross, London.Photograph: Ashok Saxena/AlamyDemand has been so intense this summer that the chef, Jack Coggins, estimates they have been getting through 80 litres of ice-cream a day. “The queue keeps you on your toes. Since people wait so long, you have to make sure it’s good,” he says. “It often feels like a party while people wait, so I think that entices others to come in. And I love it when people post about it, because it’s a way to show off what we’re doing without it being staged.”With swirling, impressionistic ceiling artdesigned by Lucy Stein, The Dreamery tries hard to conjure a sense of cool for customers who are happy to pay £5 for a scoop of ice-cream. With a typical queueing time of at least 20 minutes and celebrity endorsements from theK-pop star Lisaand others, the small shop on a quiet residential street is humming with activity on the Saturday afternoon when I arrive. “It looks so inviting from the window and I think since Covid we’ve all gotten used to queueing, so it’s not hard work to wait for something that seems like a luxury,” says Em Watson, a 28-year-old customer. “There are a lot of things you can do that are expensive and mediocre, but it’s good to support local, independent businesses like this when you can.”If you make food for the love of it as well as to earn a living, there’s no denying that the power of social media raises some unsettling questions.Are people lining up to eat at your venue because the food is good, or are they queueing simply because there is a queue? Can today’s customers still decide whether to visit a place without it first becoming verified, reviewed and videoed online?But those are issues for another day. The food I have tried is consistently delicious – Yo-Chi’s frozen yoghurt is unctuous and creamy, Czer’s wraps are umami-packed and ginormous and The Dreamery’s ice-cream and wine pairings are refreshingly smooth. “I think we’ll come again,” says Mahamud at Yo-Chi, on her way out. “This one was worth the wait.”Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
