title: My mother-in-law buys overly girly clothes for my daughter. I try to be gracious but it kills me – do I tell her to stop? | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: There’s a risk in trying to get our girls away from frilly skirts that we swing all the way to a different kind of enforcement, advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith writes
Author: Eleanor Gordon-Smith
Headline: There’s a risk in trying to get our girls away from frilly skirts that we swing all the way to a different kind of enforcement, advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith writes
Content: ‘The bigger issue is that your mother-in-law is treading on a parenting preference of yours,’ Eleanor Gordon-Smith writes. Painting: Cornelia, Mother of the Gracchi, Pointing to Her Children as Her Treasures by Angelica Kauffman.Photograph: Public domain via Wikimedia CommonsView image in fullscreen‘The bigger issue is that your mother-in-law is treading on a parenting preference of yours,’ Eleanor Gordon-Smith writes. Painting: Cornelia, Mother of the Gracchi, Pointing to Her Children as Her Treasures by Angelica Kauffman.Photograph: Public domain via Wikimedia CommonsLeading questionsAustralian lifestyleMy mother-in-law buys overly girly clothes for my daughter. I try to be gracious but it kills me – do I tell her to stop?There’s a risk in trying to get our girls away from frilly skirts that we swing all the way to a different kind of enforcement, advice columnistEleanor Gordon-SmithwritesRead moreLeading questionsEleanor Gordon-SmithThu 10 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 20.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI am the motherof a six-year-old girl, and I have relatively progressive views about gender. Amongother things, I try to give my daughter a choice of clothes that are practical – T-shirts, leggings – and that tend to be unisex in colour scheme. There are no overly fussy and frilly skirts and dresses in pink and sparkles in her wardrobe. As much as possible, I try to buynon-sweatshop brands. These choices are part of a world system of values I want to show my daughter – that being a “girl” is so much more than just wearing a frilly dress; that we can have well-made things without contributing to the suffering of others.My mother-in-law, on the other hand, loves buying these sorts of clothes forher granddaughter. She is a kind and caring woman, and this is one of her love languages. These clothes are often gauche, overly feminine, expensive and poorly made.I try my best to be gracious in accepting these things but it kills me to pass them to my daughter to wear. I feelas though she is enforcing these specific views on gender, through fashion, on my daughter, that don’t align with how I want to raise her. As a result, my mother-in-law becomes hurt that I’m not dressing my daughter in these ugly froufrou clothes; and I feel guilty about wasting her time and money.Should I be upfront with her about what clothes I do and don’t want her to buy for my daughter? Or am I overthinkingit and should let this slide?Eleanor says:For what it’s worth, to be defined by rejecting something is still to be defined by it. “Overly feminine”, “ugly froufrou”; these are still judgments about how to be a girl well.I completely share your taste here, so I point this out from right next to you in the trenches of thinking about femininity and pink and frills for young girls. It took me so long to work out that just as the firm belief that womenmustbe “girly” is freighted with all kinds of sexism, the firm belief that we mustn’t is freighted with other generalisations, too – some no less sexist. For instance, “if feminine, vapid”. (Why, when I need to seem serious at work, do I dress more like a man?)I don’t get along with my sister-in-law. Should I try to address the dynamic? | Leading questionsRead moreThis isn’t to say your careful selection of your daughter’s wardrobe is wrong. It’s a wonderful counterbalance to all the nonsense that the world will expect her to love. But there’s a slight risk that in trying to get our girls away from “you must love frilly skirts and pink”, we swing all the way to a different kind of enforcement: “you mustn’t love frilly skirts and pink”. And that’s the seeds of a complex: the clues that clothing is somehow grave, contains rules, is something you can get wrong.I think the bigger issue is that your mother-in-law is treading on a parenting preference of yours. She’s either not noticing or not minding the gulf between your tastes in things to buy your daughter. Neither is very thoughtful of the fact that this is your child.Perhaps she feels your rejection of her taste is judgmental. But presumably she doesn’t like some things you like, and she wouldn’t want you to infer that, as a result, she thinks you’re bad or wrong. So it needn’t mean that when you don’t sharehertaste, either. That may be a useful way of framing things: we’re just different. No need to fear that. Your taste just isn’t hers, and you’re the parent.Could you perhaps redirect some of this impulse to buy things? If it’s a love language, could it be more exciting for her to buy stuff your daughter is actually interested in – equipment for a hobby, toys, stationery? Or objects that can express a bit of your mother-in-law’s taste but that your daughter doesn’t have to wear, and that are more likely to be made ethically – like a kind of food, a local treat, a decoration? Could you nudge her towards at least buying costumes for playing make-believe – so they don’t seem to say that this is how girlsshoulddress, all the time?This strategy is a bit cheekier, but you could also say you’re trying to not let your daughter get too used to expensive things and lots of presents. That way it’s not aboutwhatyour mother-in-law gives: you could ask her to focus instead on teaching her things, or making things together. That may make her feel less rejected while still meaning you don’t have to come home with a bag full of taffeta.I so understand trying to teach your daughter important values through her clothes and consumer choices. Perhaps one lesson you can model is that Mum and Grandma have different ideas about important things, and that’s OK.Ask Eleanor a questionShare your questionTell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose. For alternative ways to get in touch securely please see ourtips guide.NameWhat is your question for Eleanor?Email addressYour contact details are helpful so we can contact you for more information. They will only be seen by the Guardian.By submitting your response, you are agreeing to share your details with us for this feature.SubmitShow moreExplore more on these topicsAustralian lifestyleLeading questionsParents and parentingFamilyGrandparents and grandparentingGenderfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The best office chairs in the UK for all-day comfort and support, tested | Working from home | The Guardian
description: After months of testing and countless hours seated, our endurance sitter picked the best office chairs for every budget
Author: Stuart Andrews
Headline: After months of testing and countless hours seated, our endurance sitter picked the best office chairs for every budget
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterWorking from homeReviewThe best office chairs in the UK for all-day comfort and support, testedAfter months of testing and countless hours seated, our endurance sitter picked the best office chairs for every budgetThe best gaming chairs – testedStuart AndrewsThu 10 Sep 2026 10.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat’s the most important thing when you’re spending hours in front of a computer? Is it having the fastest internet? The sharpest screen? The perfect keyboard? No. When you’re spending most of your day on your bottom, the most crucial element is what’s directly underneath.With a good office chair, you can handle a long working day without any feelings of discomfort. With a bad one, you can expect backache, neck ache, tender glutes and assorted nagging pains. Who wants to return to work when the last day left you feeling achy and decrepit?Many decent chairs are available, and while you don’t want to go cheap, you also don’t have to spend a fortune. I’ve spent months testing nine to find the best office chairs – including some lower-cost alternatives – to help you make a better choice.At a glanceWhy you should trust meI’m a hard-working writer who spends long days (and often nights) sitting at a desk. I’m prone to spending even more time at my desk after working hours, playing video games and working on personal projects. Basically, I’m a world-class endurance sitter, and I demand a lot from my office chair.I’m also an experienced reviewer, covering consumer technology, PC hardware, ergonomic office accessories and a wide range of home and garden products. I’ve got a strong idea of what works, what is going to drive you crazy, and what you need to think about before you buy.How I testedView image in fullscreenEach chair was used for at least five hours daily for up to a fortnight.Photograph: Stuart Andrews/The GuardianI’d like to say I spent hours running automated pressure and wear simulations, but in truth, I simply spent a lot of time sitting on each chair. I assembled each model where assembly was required, noting any issues with the process, the supplied instructions and the fixtures and fittings provided. I then spent up to a fortnight using each as my everyday office chair across two testing periods, sitting in blocks of up to five hours, two or three times a day.I also roped in my wife for further testing. She’s a freelance illustrator and similarly inclined to spending long days at her desk. We rotated the chairs between us, occasionally bickering over who got to sit in the most comfortable option and who would be hit with the chair with the immovable backrest and less cushioning.I also put each office chair’s adjustments through their paces to see what could and couldn’t be moved, checked for safety issues and noted any mechanisms that didn’t feel built to last. When we’d finished with a chair, it was dispatched back to the manufacturer, or a branch of Devon charityHospiscare, so that it could go on living a useful life at someone else’s desk.The best office chairsView image in fullscreen‘Compact and attractive’: the Habitat Beck.Photograph: Stuart Andrews/The GuardianBest office chair overall:Slouch Task OneSlouchTask One, with arms£294£294 at SlouchWhat we loveVery comfortable; good range of adjustmentsWhat we don’t loveForward tilt an optional extra; hard armrestsView image in fullscreenFrom £294 (with arms) at SlouchThe Slouch Task One may not have the wow factor of the Herman Miller Aeron featured below, but it still gives you everything you’d want from an office chair. It comes semi-assembled, but the base, gas lift and back all needed to be put together and bolted into place before use. It’s a quick 20-minute job with very clear instructions, complete with videos to help. Once assembled, it feels solid, with none of the cheap plastics or creaky fittings found on the budget chairs.It looks good, too, in a choice of black or light grey for the frame and seats in beige, charcoal, pink, light grey, off-white and blue. Most importantly, it’s hugely comfortable, making light work of even the most epic working days.Why we love itSlouch has got the seat spot on, with enough padding to keep your posterior from encountering any hard surfaces, and a moulded shape that holds up well under pressure. The mesh backrest keeps the spine upright while allowing for a degree of tilt, with a four-stage lock and synchronised mechanism to keep you balanced.Just about everything is adjustable, from the seat height and depth to the tension of the backrest, the height and position of the arms and the placement of the lumbar support. The gas lift has a smooth action that makes it easy to get the height right. Slouch also offers the chair with a choice of casters, covering soft and hard floors (though there is an additional cost of £19 for the hard floor option).It’s a shame that…you have to pay £39 extra if you want a forward seat-tilt mechanism, although it’s still a bargain compared with most other chairs. Some may hanker for more padding on the soft-feel armrests or find the colour options bland.Dimensions:70 x 65 x 108cm(WDH)Seat depth and height:42-48cm; 42-54cmAdjustments:seat depth, seat height, arm height and position, back-tilt tension, lumbar supportSlouchTask One, with arms£294£294 at SlouchWhat we loveVery comfortable; good range of adjustmentsWhat we don’t loveForward tilt an optional extra; hard armrestsBest budget office chair:Habitat BeckHabitatBeck£98£98 at ArgosWhat we loveCompact, cheap and fairly stylishWhat we don’t loveNot comfortable enough for all-day useView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Stuart Andrews/The Guardian£98 at ArgosHabitat’s chair does a good job of fitting into your average home-office setup. It’s compact and attractive, with a white frame, a pink mesh backrest and a sunny light orange seat. Clear instructions make it easy to assemble – I had it ready within 15 minutes – and it feels solid once that’s done. There are, sadly, no adjustments for the back or armrests, but the seat height can rise from 44cm to 52cm, and it tilts backwards and forwards as you move.Why we love itIt’s less than £100, but the Beck looks and feels like a more expensive chair. The seat has better cushioning than you’ll find on other budget options, and it’s neither too soft nor too firm. You may want more support from below for all-day working, but it’s fine for a few hours here and there. The tilt mechanism is also more responsive than on some cheap models, though the fixed back means you don’t get the same flexibility as on the Slouch, Herman Miller and Ikea chairs.The Beck is a great chair for slouching at your desk while you’re engaged in deep thought or otherwise procrastinating, but not so great when you’re sitting up and trying to get work done. The backrest feels slanted backwards, suggesting a relaxed posture rather than the more ergonomic vertical stance.It’s a shame that …the back isn’t adjustable, and neither is the seat depth or the height of the armrests, so you’re stuck with what you’ve got. If it were my own money, I’d really try to find the extra to get the Slouch.Dimensions:65 x 60 x 92cm (WDH)Seat depth and height:48cm; 44-52cmAdjustments:seat height, back-tilt tension, tilt lockHabitatBeck£98£98 at ArgosWhat we loveCompact, cheap and fairly stylishWhat we don’t loveNot comfortable enough for all-day useBest office chair for all-day comfort:Herman Miller AeronHerman MillerAeronfrom£1,065.75£1,065.75 at Herman Miller£1,399 at John LewisWhat we loveHighly adjustable; great support for long hoursWhat we don’t loveBig and heavy; premium price tagView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Stuart Andrews/The GuardianFrom £1,065.75 at Herman Miller£1,399 at John LewisThe Aeron is a high-end office design classic, and you only need to sit on one for an hour or two to understand why. Counterintuitively, the mesh seat is gentler on the glutes than any conventional padded effort, sloping down and curving off to support your thighs at just the right angle without digging in behind the knee. You can’t even feel the hard plastic edge at the front, which is where so many copycats fall down. It looks and feels like the seating equivalent of an executive saloon car, mixing tough plastics with the occasional bit of chrome.Why we love itIt comes already built, so there’s no pain there, and it’s incredibly adjustable. It’s the only chair where I needed to refer to the instructions to figure out all the controls. However, once you spend an hour or so tweaking all the heights, depths and angles, it fits the body like a glove, effortlessly tilting forwards and backwards in perfect synchronisation as you move.If you absolutely have to spend long days and nights beavering away to hit a deadline, this is the chair to do it in. While getting up to move and stretch is recommended, your back and neck won’t be accusing you of torture when you do finally get away. Make sure you buy it in the right size, with smaller and larger A and C options as well as the standard B fit.It’s a shame that …it’s big and heavy, so best for an established office space; you don’t want to lug this big galoot around. Really, though, the only reason not to buy it is the price. It’s arguably worth it even so, but it is a serious investment.Dimensions (size B):66 x 60 x 109cm (WDH)Seat depth and height:46cm; 45-58cmAdjustments:seat height, arm height and position, back-tilt tension, tilt limiter, lumbar supportHerman MillerAeronfrom£1,065.75£1,065.75 at Herman Miller£1,399 at John LewisWhat we loveHighly adjustable; great support for long hoursWhat we don’t loveBig and heavy; premium price tagBest office chair for reclining:Boulies MasterBouliesMasterfrom£289.99£289.99 at Boulies£309.99 at AmazonWhat we loveSpacious, firm and supportive with an epic reclineWhat we don’t loveNoisy mechanisms; lightweight leversView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Stuart Andrews/The Guardian£289.99 at Boulies£309.99 at AmazonThe Boulies Master takes its cues from gaming chairs, although its materials and sports-car flourishes are relatively restrained. Fittingly, there’s a certain level of challenge in putting it together, with most components needing to be attached to the basic frame and a surprising number of bolts to screw in.Why we love itThe effort is worth it. The cushioning is a little firmer than you’ll find on most office chairs, but there’s plenty of it, and I didn’t find the chair wearing by the end of a hard day. You can quickly adjust the seat height, the back-tilt tension and the position of the lumbar support, while a little lever near the backrest on the right allows you to recline unnervingly close to horizontal, which might be ideal for catching 40 winks if it doesn’t bring back bad memories of the dentist. The arms have a soft surface and are moulded for comfort, and I was pleasantly surprised that I didn’t get hot in it during work hours or long periods gaming.It’s a shame that …the seat-height and tilt-tension levers feel slightly flimsy when you try to pull them up, as if they might give before allowing any adjustment. The recline control makes a loud noise when engaged or disengaged, and there’s no way to adjust the seat depth.Dimensions:76 x 71 x 127.2cm (WDH)Seat depth and height:48cm, 46-53cmAdjustments:seat height, arm height and position, back-tilt tension, tilt angle, lumbar supportBouliesMasterfrom£289.99£289.99 at Boulies£309.99 at AmazonWhat we loveSpacious, firm and supportive with an epic reclineWhat we don’t loveNoisy mechanisms; lightweight leversBest office chair for adjustable style:Steelcase GestureSteelcaseGesturefrom£1,089£1,089 at Steelcase£1,089 at AmazonWhat we loveStylish design; intuitive adjustmentsWhat we don’t loveYou really have to like a firm seat cushionView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Stuart Andrews/The Guardian£1,089 from Steelcase£1,089 at AmazonSteelcase’s chair is a looker, more compact and elegant than most office chairs, but without any compromise on the ergonomics. There’s only minimal assembly before you can get seated, and it feels like it’s been thoughtfully designed and expertly engineered. The plastics and materials feel premium, and every mechanism works smoothly. It’s available as a chair or in a taller stool version, and in many different fabrics and colours, with or without a headrest.Why we love itIt’s not just the looks that impress: it’s comfortable, too. The seat and rear cushion are on the firm side, but provide excellent support over long periods without putting excessive pressure on your body. It’s also highly adjustable, with intuitive controls that make it easy to find the right position. You can slide the seat backwards and forwards or set the maximum tilt with a quick turn of a knob or flick of a lever, while the armrests are just as easy to raise, lower or change angle. The tilt mechanism feels smooth, making it easy to lean back and pause for thought.It’s a shame that …the firm cushions won’t be for everyone. Both my wife and I found it comfortable, but your mileage may vary. I’m also unsure how well the Gesture would suit larger builds, as its seat feels narrower and less forgiving than those on the Slouch or Boulies chairs.Dimensions:66 x 62.5 x 104cm (WDH)Seat depth and height:41-47.5cm, 42-52cmAdjustments:seat height, seat depth, arm height, width and angle, back-tilt tension, adjustable backstopSteelcaseGesturefrom£1,089£1,089 at Steelcase£1,089 at AmazonWhat we loveStylish design; intuitive adjustmentsWhat we don’t loveYou really have to like a firm seat cushionThe best of the restLiberNovo Omni ProLiberNovoOmni Profrom£1,191£1,191 at LiberNovo£1,191 at AmazonWhat we loveGreat back support; comfortable recliningWhat we don’t loveSome gimmicky features; complex assemblyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Stuart Andrews/The Guardian£1,191 at LiberNovo£1,191 at AmazonBest for:hi-tech featuresLiberNovo’s hi-tech office chair is easily the most feature-packed I’ve tested. While the seat-height, armrest and backrest adjustments are manual, motors adjust the shape of the flexible lumbar support, and you can use the buttons on the armrest to get this just right. The seat and backrest can recline through five positions between 105 and 160 degrees, with an optional two-level footrest to support your feet under the desk or while you’re lying back and stretching.On top of that, there’s an automatic lumbar-stretch function to get your spine moving if you’ve been sitting for too long, plus a built-in fan to cool the seat. The chair as a whole is hugely adjustable and supportive, with everything tilting in perfect synchronisation every time you lean back. It’s powered by a rechargeable battery that charges through a USB-C port, but I haven’t had to recharge it in around six weeks of use.It didn’t make the final cut because …while it’s an excellent office chair, it’s also expensive. I’m not sure the stretch function and motorised adjustments add much in terms of day-to-day comfort, either. It still takes a lot of fiddling to get the right fit, and I found the Steelcase and Herman Miller chairs more easygoing on my bum and thighs during long working days. It’s also one of the most complex chairs to assemble, with a whole bunch of different parts to be locked and bolted into place.Dimensions:79 x 65.5 x 132.5cm (WDH);seat depth and height:45-48cm, 48.5-59.5cm;adjustments:seat height, arm height and position, back-tilt tension, tilt angle, lumbar support, neck support height, tilt and depthLiberNovoOmni Profrom£1,191£1,191 at LiberNovo£1,191 at AmazonWhat we loveGreat back support; comfortable recliningWhat we don’t loveSome gimmicky features; complex assemblyIkea HattefjällIkeaHattefjäll£199£199 at IkeaWhat we loveVery stylish; synchronised tiltWhat we don’t loveThin and hard seat cushion; tiny leversView image in fullscreen£199 at IkeaBest for:cool Scandinavian looksWith its elegant frame, sleek seat and backrest and choice of tasteful fabrics, the Hattefjäll is ideal for the stylish home office. You’ll feel like you’re working in an upmarket consultancy, even when you’ve rolled up in your fading T-shirt and jogging bottoms. It has a synchronised tilt mechanism, just like the more expensive chairs, and you can tweak the height of the backrest, the height and width of the armrest, and lock the tilt to enhance your comfort. It’s among the most ergonomic options at this price.It didn’t make the final cut because …the levers to adjust the height and tilt are too small, making these adjustments tricky, and we had an issue with our test sample where the bolts and slits to attach one arm didn’t quite align. Most of all, the seat’s too thin and uncomfortably firm. Do our Swedish friends have something against cushioning?Dimensions:68 x 68 x 114cm (WDH);seat depth and height:40cm; 46-56cm;adjustments:seat height, seat depth, arm height and position, backrest height, back-tilt tension, tilt lock, lumbar supportIkeaHattefjäll£199£199 at IkeaWhat we loveVery stylish; synchronised tiltWhat we don’t loveThin and hard seat cushion; tiny leversWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenBack it up: adjustable support can make a big difference over a long working day.Photograph: Stuart Andrews/The GuardianWhat makes a good office chair?Comfort, above all else. And that means more than how a chair feels when you first sit down; it’s about how it supports your body and your posture over longer periods. The seat and backrest should cushion your weight and relieve pressure on your back, sides and buttocks, while offering enough adjustment to help you maintain a good working position. Ideally, your feet should sit flat on the floor close to the desk, withyour thighs roughly horizontal and your back straight as much as possible. Your arms should rest parallel to your desk, with your hands at the appropriate height, supported by the armrests if your chair has them. Chairs that can help you achieve this position will be far more comfortable over a full day of sitting.Should I go for mesh or foam?With the success of the Herman Miller Aeron chair helping to popularise mesh office chairs, there are more chairs at every price point featuring mesh backs, and even budget chairs featuring mesh seats. Mesh backrests and seats allow more air to circulate around your body, which can help you stay cool in summer while still providing ample support. However, plenty fall short when it comes to support, with some even sagging after just a few months. Others have hard surfaces near the front or edges that can dig into the backs of your knees.Foam seats can also be very comfortable, while newer materials and designs do a better job of staying cool and allowing airflow underneath and behind you. But thin or overly soft cushions can fail to provide enough padding, making the hard surfaces beneath all too noticeable.What adjustments should I look for?The more adjustments available – from seat depth, seat height, arm height and so on – the easier it is to achieve the support you need. Look for adjustable lumbar support, too, which can help keep your lower back comfortable and supported throughout the day.A tilt can also be helpful, especially if you spend long hours at your desk. It allows you to push back or lean forward in your seat, with the chair continuing to support your lower back. However, if the tilt action is too loose or allows too much uncontrolled backwards movement, it can make it harder to maintain a good working posture. The best office chairs offer synchronised tilt, where the seat and backrest tilt independently but move in unison to provide support as you move backwards and forwards. Just remember: there’s no substitute for getting out of your chair and stretching, preferably forfive or so minutesevery hour.What safety features do I need?All office chairs have to meet relevant fire-safety requirements – the charities we’ve spoken to won’t even accept our used chairs without the certifying sticker or label attached. It’s also worth checking for rough edges or sharp points that might poke you as you move around, and mechanisms that might trap a finger as you lean forward or back. Perhaps the most important safety feature, though, is not to skimp on a chair you’ll spend hours in every day. You’re likely to regret it in the long run.For more, read our guide to thebest gaming chairsand thebest backpacks for work, travel and wild adventuresStuart Andrews is ajournalist with more than three decades of experience in computing and consumer tech. When he’s not messing around with PCs, laptops and projectors, he’s trying to tame his post-apocalyptic garden with the latest cordless gadgets. title: How I Shop with Laura Jackson: ‘Once you have a water filter, you can’t go back’ | Celebrity | The Guardian
description: Always wondered what everyday stuff celebrities buy, where they shop for food, and the basic they scrimp on? The creative director talks 80s knitwear, joyful knickers and a love of Boots with the Filter
Author: Lily Smith
Headline: Always wondered what everyday stuff celebrities buy, where they shop for food, and the basic they scrimp on? The creative director talks 80s knitwear, joyful knickers and a love of Boots with the Filter
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Jordan CarterView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Jordan CarterGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.How I shopCelebrityInterviewHow I Shop with Laura Jackson: ‘Once you have a water filter, you can’t go back’As told toLily SmithAlways wondered what everyday stuff celebrities buy, where they shop for food, and the basic they scrimp on? The creative director talks 80s knitwear, joyful knickers and a love of Boots with the FilterHow I Shop with Millie MackintoshThu 10 Sep 2026 05.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLaura Jackson is a creative director and broadcaster who works across design, food and culture. She co-founded the homewares websiteGlassettein 2021 and later founded the skincare brand Rocco. Her broadcasting career spans television, radio and digital.Jackson launched a collection with British jewellery brandAstley Clarkein September 2026, featuring gemstones, celestial motifs and tarot symbolism.What’s the last treat you bought for yourself?A bunch of cosmos from the market on the way home. Completely worth it: I’ve put them in individual stem vases dotted around the house. You can’t beat a bunch of fresh flowers; they instantly lift your mood.View image in fullscreenIn bloom: fresh flowers are the go-to pick-me-up.Photograph: hawk111/Getty Images/iStockphotoWhere do you buy your food?I do a big weekly shop online from Ocado, but I’m lucky to work offBroadway marketin east London, where there are great delis. Bread from a bakery, eggs from somewhere I actually trust. I also like Pesky Fish and the Ethical Butcher.View image in fullscreenGive us our deli bread: London’s Broadway market is a brilliant source of fresh loaves.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesShop OcadoShop Pesky FishShop the Ethical ButcherWhat’s the best present you’ve given?A photobook. There’s something about them that a phone gallery will never be able to replicate: the weight of them in your hands, flicking through pages instead of swiping, knowing every single photo was chosen on purpose. I’ll spend hours going through pictures, narrowing them down, getting the order right, because I want it to actually tell a story, not just be a random collection of moments.In a world where everything’s so instant and disposable, a gift that forces you to slow down is one worth spending a little more time on.View image in fullscreenPicture perfect: a photobook turns favourite memories into something to keep.Photograph: Manu Vega/Getty Images… and the best present you’ve received?For our wedding, we received books from all our guests filled with handwritten notes – proper, heartfelt, personal messages. There’s something so special about someone sitting down and actually writing something for you. It’s the kind of gift that genuinely gets more precious with time.What’s your favourite online store?I love the Newt in Somerset. It’s my go-to for gift buying, and it always puts together great curated selections. It has a brilliant home and garden section, and I buy itscordialsover and over again.View image in fullscreenA Taste of the Newt hamperShop the Newt’s online storeWhat’s your favourite bricks-and-mortar shop?I love my local Boots in Westfield. I have shopped at Boots since I was a kid, and I’m in there so much that the staff know me. I bring my empties there to recycle and love discovering new brands and products.View image in fullscreenBoots on the ground: Laura Jackson has been shopping at the store since she was a child.What’s the gadget you use most often?My Berkey water filter sits on the counter and gets used throughout the day. It sounds unglamorous, but once you have one, you genuinely can’t go back. The water tastes completely different, and it’s great for a busy house like mine.View image in fullscreenBig Berkey water filter£250 at WaterFilterShopWhat’s the purchase you regret the most?When you first buy a house, it’s normal to get overexcited and want to pick up things instantly, but I’ve learned to take my time and understand the space, how the light works, how it’s used before making a decision on buying something. It’s the same with my wardrobe: I have to sit on something for a while before I reach for my purse.What’s the thing/s you get delivered?Not hugely exciting to some, but the joy I get when myMinimlorder arrives … from shampoo to laundry detergent to bubble bath, these products are so good, and they last so long, even with three kids.View image in fullscreenMiniml body wash + bubble bath Uplifting pink grapefruit, 400ml£3.99 at Miniml£4 at AmazonFor more, check out our review ofthe best eco-friendly laundry detergentsWhere do you buy your underwear?Comfort first, always. For everyday, you can’t go wrong with M&S. But I’ve recently fallen a bit in love with Fruity Booty, particularly its bridal range. It’s so fun and joyful and just makes you feel good. I said to my husband, maybe it’s time to renew our vows, just so I have an excuse to wear it all … he’s yet to respond to that one.Shop lingerie at M&SShop bridal lingerie at Fruity BootyWhat would you buy with £20?A really good candle or the best bunch of flowers I could find from the local market.View image in fullscreenDaylesford geranium leaf candleskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFrom £22 at Daylesford£22 at Ocado… and £200?View image in fullscreenReclaim the day: Laura Jackson would head to a salvage yard with £200 to spend.Photograph: mtreasure/Getty ImagesI’d head straight to a market or a reclamation yard and see what found me. That budget can get you something genuinely special.What’s your ‘saved search’ on eBay/Vinted?VintageMissoniknitwear, the real stuff from the 70s and 80s. The colours, the patterns, the quality. You find it occasionally if you’re patient enough, and when you do, it feels like an absolute victory. We’re giving the studio office a little revamp, so my saved searches are a bit all over the place: vintage desk lamps, interesting shelving, office chairs.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Emilie/Vestiaire CollectiveShop vintage Missoni Knitwear Vestiaire CollectiveShop vintage Missoni on eBayWhat item do you buy on repeat?Good olive oil, Greek yoghurt, fresh fruit and flowers. Every single week without fail. My kitchen doesn’t function without them.View image in fullscreenLaura getsolivethe good stuff on repeat.Photograph: Laura Reid/Getty ImagesHow do you make your coffee at home?A cafetière, always, and good quality coffee, freshly ground. We have a busy house, and I often work from home, so a big pot in the morning makes early starts easier. We have a huge 1-litre Bodum cafetière at the office and at home. It looks great on the shelf and in the middle of a messy desk. I love Hard Lines coffee or Union.View image in fullscreenBodum 1lCaffettierafrenchpress coffee maker£40 at Wolf & BadgerFor more, read our guide to thebest cafetièresView image in fullscreenHard Lines coffeeShop coffee at Hard LinesView image in fullscreenUnion coffeeShop coffee at UnionShop Union coffee at AmazonWhat’s your biggest splurge?Travel, without question. I’d rather spend money on a really special trip, somewhere that genuinely shifts your perspective, than on things.And what everyday item do you scrimp on?Mechanical pencils. I love them, and they don’t cost much at all. I’m a chronic list-maker and note-taker. I love Muji, or a multipack from the supermarket does the job perfectly well.View image in fullscreenMuji mechanical pencil with eraser£2.50 at MujiView image in fullscreenBic mechanical pencil set, five£3 at Ocado£3 at AmazonAnd what’s your greatest vintage find?The cabinetry in our kitchen, reclaimed from a church and restored to become the centrepiece of the whole room. Every single person who comes to the house asks about it. It has more character than anything you could ever buy new, and the story behind it is half the reason I love it so much.For more, read How I Shop withMillie MackintoshandFred Sirieix.
