title: The start of autumn is the perfect time to turn to retro comfort food | Food | The Guardian
description: As the autumn nights draw in, I’m craving elevated classics that remind me of childhood. It’s all about fish fingers, pies, sausages and eggs – and chips with everything
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: As the autumn nights draw in, I’m craving elevated classics that remind me of childhood. It’s all about fish fingers, pies, sausages and eggs – and chips with everything
Content: Stanley Tucci’s Calabrian eggs poached in tomato sauce.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The GuardianView image in fullscreenStanley Tucci’s Calabrian eggs poached in tomato sauce.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.FeastFoodThe start of autumn is the perfect time to turn to retro comfort foodAs the colder nights draw in, I’m craving elevated classics that remind me of childhood. It’s all about fish fingers, pies, sausages and eggs – and chips with everythingSign up here for our weekly food newsletter, FeastFelicity CloakeThu 10 Sep 2026 09.17 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 09.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLast weekend, my family congregated at a restaurant in Edinburgh to celebrate my parents’ diamond wedding anniversary. Good though the meal was, the farewell lunch my mum prepared the next day sparked more in the way of fond reminiscence. With her retro feast of chicken kiev, oven chips and peas, we could almost have been back around our kitchen table 30 years ago (in those days, though, my mum wouldneverhave allowed the younger generation to add ketchup).It’s also the kind of meal that feels apt for the change of season, for the first weeks back at school or work, when everyone’s finding their feet and wants something easy and familiar. Thomasina Miers’fish fingers and mushy peasfit the bill, too, as does Rowley Leigh’sfish pieand Tim Hayward’s nan’scorned beef, with yet more chips and peas. If all that’s too much of a good thing,my own corned beef hashmight appeal instead? For a more specifically Scottish take on that combination, I love Colman Andrews’ idea of adding black pudding toclassic mince and tatties(Rachel Roddy’shearty cheese and chip omelette, meanwhile, would have been brilliant if we’d actually had any chips left over – time may move on, but teenagers don’t change).View image in fullscreenThomasina Miers’ fish fingers and mushy peas.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The GuardianIn the same vein, Angela Hartnett’s take onsausage and beanshas a bit more of an Italian feel than the kind we used to eat from a tin, and Rachel’s richsausage ragulooks a cut above our own 1990s spag bol; also on the Italian theme, Stanley Tucci’s father’seggs in tomato sauce(pictured top). But he and Rachel may wish to look away at the mention of Chris Russell’s1960s-style spaghetti with fried eggs; perhaps a little less authentic, but no less delicious.Although Chinese restaurants were an occasional treat, I’m not sure we ever ate fried rice at home, but Allegra McEvedy’sversatile recipefeels cut from the same simple, satisfying cloth. As does Kay Plunkett-Hogge’spad krapow mooand Meera Sodha’sbuttery mustard greens with corn roti. Likewise, though it didn’t feature in my childhood, Jacob Kenedy’s grandmother’s recipe forsauerkraut and pork bakesounds intriguing enough to become part of my adult repertoire.We had rhubarb crumble for pudding on that Sunday, but on a weekday, you might prefer a quick and easy bowl of sliced bananas and cold custard. That said, if you have more time on your hands, Ruby Tandoh has a rather fancybaked version, or you could even – whisper it – opt for a dish of butterscotch Angel Delight. Sadly, it seems we don’t have a recipe for a homemade version of the latter (though Claire Ptak’sbutterscotch creamlooks like a rather decadent substitute) – once I’ve unpacked from my trip, it might well prove a new project for a new term. Watch this space.My week in foodView image in fullscreenIce shortbread sandwiches are the cousins of the linzer cookie.Photograph: Ekaterina Smirnova/AlamyTakes the biscuit|Iced shortbread sandwiches, or empire biscuits, are rarely seen outside Scotland, despite the fact thatthese cousins of the linzer cookiewere known throughout the UK as German biscuits until the outbreak of the first world war (and continue to carry that name in Northern Ireland, or so I’m told). If they’ve been renamed once, it seems reasonable to suggest that they might be so again … In any case, I had such an enjoyable example from theBoardwalk Beach Clubat Silverknowes, in Edinburgh, that I’m determined tohave a go myself.Plum job|My icebox is full of plums, and one of the benefits of living alone is that I am quite sure no one has eaten them; in fact, I love them so much that I am miserly about their consumption. The čačanska najbolja and golden transparent gages I bought fromthe National Fruit Collection at Brogdalein Kent are too good not to eat from the hand, but the Welsh denbigh cooking variety proved delicious in an oat and plum knickerbocker recipe from Jeremy Lee’s new book,Kitchening. I’m also so tempted by the pork and plum meatballs in Ed Smith’s latestRocket & Squash newsletterthat I might seek out more punnets before they disappear for another year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFeastRecipes from all our star cooks, seasonal eating ideas and restaurant reviews. Get our best food writing every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSlop for dinner|I’m not alone in finding the uncanny imagesproliferating in food advertisingless than appetising. But I was, perhaps naively, startled to discover that AI has made its way on to our plates, too. According toa piece in the New Yorker(£), some pretty high-end restaurants are using it for inspiration, to generate “images and ideas foreign to classically trained chefs by pulling ingredient pairings and plating ideas from across the world”. Given that posters and flyers are already starting to look the same, I find this a bleak prospect for our palates.More retro delights|I was recently given 15 issues of theFanny and Johnnie Cradock Cookery Programme, “from concept to the last sprig of garnish”. Originally published in weekly parts during the early 1970s, it was found by a friend in a Suffolk charity shop. As anyone familiar with Fanny’s work might guess, the food styling is what caught her eye (sauteed pigeon breasts accessorised by wings in full feather, anyone?), but a cursory glance reveals greater treasure within, from W Somerset Maugham’s cook’s recipe for avocado ice-cream to a striking egg dish entitled L’oeuf monstrueux, or How to Show Off Very Easily. I’m looking forward to cooking my way through it, albeit selectively. In the meantime, I’m reminded of Cradock’s book Coping With Christmas, recently reissued and for which I wrote a foreword. If you happen to be in the mood for an utterly OTT celebration this year, I note that it is currentlyon offer online at a rather insulting 40% off.If you want to read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive Feast in your inbox every Thursday.Explore more on these topicsFoodFeastAutumn food and drinkFruitEggsStanley TucciVegetablesMeatnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: How to choose the perfect wine for aperitivo hour | Wine | The Guardian
description: Whether you go for traditional champagne or sherry, or branch out with muscadet and picpoul, an appetite-whetting glass of wine will set you up for the evening ahead
Author: Mina Holland
Headline: Whether you go for traditional champagne or sherry, or branch out with muscadet and picpoul, an appetite-whetting glass of wine will set you up for the evening ahead
Content: Typically, an aperitif is light and crisp, which explains why sparkling wines are common choices.Photograph: AzmanL/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTypically, an aperitif is light and crisp, which explains why sparkling wines are common choices.Photograph: AzmanL/Getty ImagesWineHow to choose the perfect wine for aperitivo hourWhether you go for traditional champagne or sherry, or branch out with muscadet and picpoul, an appetite-whetting glass of wine will set you up for the evening aheadMina HollandThu 10 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBeginnings are important. As a writer, I’m all too aware of this: from the right introduction, the rest tends to flow. The same logic applies to drinks: a good beginning eases proceedings. For this reason, I am unbendingly particular about how I take my morning coffee and, if I’m drinking, what form an evening’s aperitif should take. Life’s too short for bad beverages, after all.An aperitif is arguably less a specific drink than an appetite-whetting moment with a glass of something. But what? Typically, when it comes to wine, an aperitif will be light and crisp, with any fruit character at the more green or citrussy end of the spectrum. Brioche-y sparkling wine, be that champagne, crémant or something English, and dry sherry such as fino and manzanilla, with their savoury notes, are traditional choices to ready your palate for food.One of my favourite wine discoveries of the past year or so has beenBodegas Alvearin the Montilla-Moriles region of Andalusia, which produces wines made exclusively with pedro ximénez (PX), a grape famous for producing the darkest, stickiest sherries out there. Its Tres Miradas cuvée in today’s pick is a unique dry white wine made with old vine PX grown in chalky soils; it has a light sherry note thanks to being aged under a layer of natural yeast (flor), but it is both fresh and structured, making for the sort of high-impact aperitif I’m after.Wines from maritime climates, particularly cooler ones, tend to be a safe bet, too, bringing the salinity and minerality I’m looking for to stimulate appetite. A txakoli from Spain’s Basque region, say, with punchy, citrus-apple notes and a touch of spritz to surprise the palate. Muscadet, made from the melon de bourgogne grape in the westernmost Loire, is another great, unsung white: crisp, affordable and a fine aperitif. Take a road trip along the northern French coast, and you’ll be spoiled for pre-dinner deals on a plate of oysters and a glass of this stuff. It’s often bottledsur lie– that is, with dead yeast cells that give the wine a rounder, almost bready flavour that works particularly well as an aperitif.Ocado has several available, with some for less than a tenner.There is also a breed of aperitif wine that both readies you for a meal and sees you all the way through it. Muscadet and its southern French cousin picpoul de pinet do this, as do albariño and zesty bourgogne aligoté, which usually has that Burgundian butteriness that can be hard to leave behind. Pale rosé is also a classic aperitif choice, as happy on its own as with a plate of crudites or a bowl of peanuts. The Pink Flamingo rosé in my pick, made in Europe’s largest organic vineyard in the Camargue wetlands west of Marseille, has a coastal freshness that I’d happily enjoy before, during and after a meal. After all, endings are as important as beginnings.Six wines that work brilliantly as aperitifsOliver Dubois Muscadet 2023/4£10.50 (with “mix six”) Majestic, 12%. A straightforwardly crowd-pleasing muscadet: lean, green and a great price.Pink Flamingo Organic Camargue Rosé£12.50 Waitrose, 12%. You’ll never want aperitif hour to end, nor does it have to. This peachy-pink, daisy-fresh number is food friendly, too.Rezabal Txakoli 2025£13.50 The Wine Society, 11%. Make your aperitif a Basque one with this energetic and petillant txakoli.Alvear Tres Miradas2022£17.50 The Whisky Exchange, ?13%. Green orchard fruit meets almonds and sourdough.Fortnum’s Muscadet Sur Lie Domaine de la Morinière £12.95, 11.5%. A lovely example of a muscadet aged on the lees. Lemony, saline and richly textured.Crémant de Loire, Domaine Catherine et Pierre Breton NV£23.40 Sip Wines, 13%. Possibly the perfect crémant, combining 40% red grapes with chenin blanc for a fizz that’s as generous as it’s refreshing.Explore more on these topicsWineFoodFrench food and drinkSpanish food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for a not-sachertorte | Cake | The Guardian
description: A chocolate cake inspired by the Sacher hotel in Vienna’s trademark creation and emulated by a local Roman pasticceria
Author: Rachel Roddy
Headline: A chocolate cake inspired by the Sacher hotel in Vienna’s trademark creation and emulated by a local Roman pasticceria
Content: Rachel Roddy’s not-sachertorte.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The Guardian.View image in fullscreenRachel Roddy’s not-sachertorte.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The Guardian.A kitchen in RomeCakeRachel Roddy’s recipe for a not-sachertorteA chocolate cake inspired by the Sacher hotel in Vienna’s trademark creation and emulated by a local Roman pasticceriaRachel RoddyThu 10 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis column began two years ago, almost to the day, when I made a birthday cake for a friend. “I don’t mind,” was her reply when I first asked what sort of cake she would like. But then, a few minutes later, she said: “Hang on, I mean chocolate with glossy icing. Like the mini ones they make atBarberini.”Barberini is a local bar and cake shop, and the mini cakes she was referring to are their sacher (inspired bysachertorte, of course) – chocolate sponge cakes with a heart of apricot jam and a glossy, chocolate glaze. At Barberini, each one is the size of a single draughts piece, but deep, so not quite two bites but slightly too big for one, unless you open your mouth very wide. “You mean sachertorte?” I said. “That would be great,” was her reply, before changing the subject to I can’t remember what. Walking home, I regretted asking.According to the Sacher hotelwebsite, its sachertorte (perhaps the world’s most famous cake) is still handmade using Franz Sacher’s original recipe. It also provides a recipe – a wonderful, quite complicated, anxiety-inducing recipe. It is also an approximate one, with a note in capital letters and highlighted red explaining that the original recipe must remain a tightly kept secret. I have never felt so relieved at not being given a recipe.It also meant Barberini must be approximating, so I would, too. I would approximate by using my own faithful chocolate sponge recipe, which is inspired byNigella Lawson’s faithful and tender sponge cake, filling it with my homemade peach jam and topping it with an enthusiastic attempt at the hotel’s approximate glaze recipe. I would make a not-sachertorte.“Make sure he doesn’t disgrace me tonight,” is, according to legend, what Prince Metternich said on discovering it was apprentice pastry chef Franz Sacher who was charged with making the impressive cake. I certainly worried that my glaze would be a disgrace as I poured it over the surface of the cake, both two years ago and again twice this week. My anxiety was unfounded: while not nearly as smooth as Barbarini’s (let alone the Sacher hotel’s), the results were smooth enough.The last bit of advice is from the Sacher hotel’s website, which notes that slices of sachertorte are best enjoyed with a dollop of unsweetened whipped cream. Slices of not-sachertorte are, too.Chocolate cake with peach jam and chocolate glaze – a not sachertorte recipeServes8-12200g plain flour200g caster sugar1 tsp baking powder½ tsp bicarbonate of soda40g cocoa powder175g soft unsalted butter,plus extra for greasing2 large eggs2 tsp vanilla extract150ml soured or single cream150g-200g peach or apricot jam200g caster sugar150gdark chocolate(at least 70% cocoa), choppedUnsweetened whipped cream, to serveHeat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4 and grease and line two 20cm cake tins, ideally with removable bases.Working in a large bowl, mix the flour, sugar, baking powder, bicarb and cocoa. In another bowl, beat the butter, eggs, vanilla and cream, until combined and creamy, then add to the flour bowl, beating well until smooth. (This can also be done in reverse – that is, wet first, then dry – in a food processor.)Divide the batter between the lined tins and bake for 25-35 minutes, or until a stand of spaghetti inserted into the centre comes out clean. Once out of the oven, wait 15 minutes, then invert the cakes on to a cooling rack – don’t worry about any cracks; the icing will cover that. Once the cakes are cool, sandwich them together using the jam.Next, make the glaze. Working in a small pan, heat the sugar and 125ml water, boiling hard and stirring constantly, for four minutes, until the sugar has dissolved. Take off the heat and leave cool for five minutes – this is really important – then gradually adding the chopped chocolate, stirring until it forms a thick, shiny glaze.Once the glaze is lukewarm and thick but not stiff, pour it over the cake (still on the wire rack so the glaze can drip through) and use a flat knife dipped in warm water to smooth it. Leave the glaze to set completely, then carefully transfer the cake to a plate, cut and serve with whipped cream.Explore more on these topicsCakeA kitchen in RomeFoodChocolateDessertBakingItalian food and drinkrecipesShareReuse this content

title: You be the judge: should my son finish bottles and packets before opening new ones? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Jasper stands accused of being wasteful but feels aggrieved that Mindy says he’s being lazy. Is this a race to the bottom? You decide
Author: Georgina Lawton
Headline: Jasper stands accused of being wasteful but feels aggrieved that Mindy says he’s being lazy. Is this a race to the bottom? You decide
Content: Illustration: Igor Bastidas/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Igor Bastidas/The GuardianYou be the judgeLife and styleYou be the judge: should my son finish bottles and packets before opening new ones?Jasper stands accused of being wasteful but feels aggrieved that Mindy says he’s being lazy. Is this a race to the bottom? You decideFind out how to get a disagreement settled or become a jurorInterviews byGeorgina LawtonThu 10 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 09.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheprosecution:Mindydouble quotation markOpening new products when old ones aren’t empty is wasteful – and he does it to avoid cleaning upMy son Jasper, who is 21, has a very annoying habit: he loves to leave the last bit in every bottle, jar and box. There are bottles of ketchup, shampoo and face cream, all with a tiny amount in, left around the house.Jasper thinks that by not finishing off the last of something he is doing me and his father, Dave, a favour. I find it annoying as I’m the one who then washes the bottles and takes them out to the recycling. He’s shirking the responsibility of disposing of them himself. Jasper says: “I left the last bit for you.” But it’s just laziness.double quotation markLeaving such a small amount of anything isn’t generous … these little scraps left everywhere drive me absolutely pottyAt dinner, Jasper will get a new bottle of sauce out of the fridge instead of finishing off the one with a tiny bit left. He loves opening a new packet or a new bottle. He does the same with cereal – he’ll leave tiny crumbs in the bottom and open a new box. He also leaves the heel of the bread.I’ve tried explaining to him that leaving such a small amount of anything isn’t actually generous, but I know that’s not the real reason he does it. He just likes everything to be fresh and new. I don’t like the idea of opening a new packet or bottle of something if there’s still some of the old one left. I find it wasteful. I’d rather he used it up, rinsed the bottle and put it in the recycling, instead of leaving it for someone else to deal with. The little scraps left everywhere drive me absolutely potty.Jasper’s habits create more work for me. He gets to feel as though he has been good, while I’m the one finishing things and disposing of the containers. If I don’t do it, we end up with several versions of the same product cluttering up the cupboards and fridge.Dave thinks I should just let it go and Jasper thinks I’m being fussy. He says I can just throw things away or use them myself, but I don’t want it to become my job. Sometimes Jasper helps with the recycling, but he could do more chores. I think that if you finish something, or get close enough that nobody else can reasonably use it, you should take responsibility for getting rid of the container, too.You be the judge – send us your domestic disputesRead moreThe defence: Jasperdouble quotation markIf I want fresh cereal or enough sauce for my dinner, I’m always going to open a new containerI think Mum is making me sound more calculating than I am. I’m not deliberately leaving tiny amounts of things because I want her to clean up after me. I don’t like using the last bit of something, especially when there’s a new one available.If there are two bottles of ketchup in the fridge and one has been squeezed to death, I don’t want to spend five minutes trying to get the last drop out when there’s a full bottle next to it. It doesn’t make much difference whether we use the last bit or not. Either way, that new bottle is going to get opened.I sometimes say: “I left the last bit for you,” but I’m partially joking. Mum acts like I’ve left her some enormous task, but all she has to do is either use it or throw it away. I don’t think rinsing out a ketchup bottle is a major chore.double quotation markObviously I should clean up after myself, but we all have habits that annoy the people we live withSometimes I think a bottle is empty, whereas Mum can see there’s still something in there. But often, with things like ketchup or hot sauce, there isn’t enough to go with my dinner, so I’d rather open a new jar or bottle. If I threw away shampoo or face cream containers that still had some left, Mum would probably tell me I was being wasteful. It feels as if I can’t win.She is right that I like opening new things. Fresh bread is obviously nicer than the last crust, and I’d rather have cereal from a new box than eat the crumbs at the bottom of an old one. I don’t think that makes me selfish.I do understand her point about clutter. If I open a new bottle when there’s still an old one, I can see how we end up with lots of nearly empty containers. I could be better at throwing things away and recycling. But I think Mum could also stop treating every almost empty container as evidence that I’m lazy.Obviously I should clean up after myself, but we all have habits that annoy the people we live with. I’ll make more of an effort to finish nearly empty containers or throw them away. But if I want a fresh box of cereal or enough sauce for my dinner, I’m always going to open a new one.Names have been changedskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe jury of Guardian readersWho could criticise Jasper for opening new ketchup if he had helpfully rinsed and recycled the old bottle? I empathise with his need for enough sauce with dinner, but he is shirking the chore here and needs to recognise that there are some jobs no one likes to do.Lois, 31If it’s such a small job, Jasper, why don’t you do it yourself? Time to grow up. That said, Mindy can solve this problem by not providing so much – if there’s no fresh ketchup until the old bottle is washed, he’ll soon learn what’s worth the squeeze.Neil, 34Maybe it is a generational thing – I was taught to squeeze the last toothpaste out of the tube. But Mindy is correct, if he’s part-finished it and left it, he should also dispose of it.John,70Washing out jars and emptying cereal crumbs before putting the containers in the recycling bin may be a pain, but why should Mindy do it all the time? Why doesn’t Jasper recycle them and then open a new pack?Margaret, 73How many nearly empty bottles would Jasper leave cluttering up the fridge if Mindy didn’t step in? In the name of reducing household mess and food waste, Jasper needs to clean up his act.Noa, 32Now you be the judgeIn our online poll, tell us: should Jasper finish things off and clean up his act?The poll closes on Wednesday 16 September at 9am BSTLast week’s resultsWe asked whether Robin should stop letting therecycling pile up.94% of you said yes – Robin is guilty6% of you said no – Robin is not guiltyExplore more on these topicsLife and styleYou be the judgefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Pixel 11 Pro review: Google’s best pocket camera goes customisable | Pixel | The Guardian
description: Solid battery life, snappy performance and quality software make for a great smaller phone with a killer camera
Author: Samuel Gibbs
Headline: Solid battery life, snappy performance and quality software make for a great smaller phone with a killer camera
Content: The Pixel 11 Pro doesn’t break the mould, but Google’s top smaller phone shows you don’t have to have a massive screen to have the best camera.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Pixel 11 Pro doesn’t break the mould, but Google’s top smaller phone shows you don’t have to have a massive screen to have the best camera.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.PixelReviewPixel 11 Pro review: Google’s best pocket camera goes customisableSolid battery life, snappy performance and quality software make for a great smaller phone with a killer cameraSamuel GibbsConsumer technology editorThu 10 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGoogle’s latest Pro phone is out to prove it has the best camera on a smartphone while embracing customisation, allowing you to change the look and feel of your photos far beyond simple filters even if that means making them technically worse.ThePixel11 Pro packs the best of Google’s hardware and software into a still-pocketable and easy to handle frame, instantly making it a contender for best smaller phone of the year.Being smaller doesn’t make it cheap. The 11 Pro sits above the regular £879Pixel 11and costs from £1,079 (€1,199/$1,099/A$1,849) – £80 (€100/$100/A$150) more than last year, with double the storage but less memory owing to thecost of RAMageddon.Little has changed on the outside for thePro Pixelsinseveral years. The new model is 0.1mm smaller in all directions and 3g lighter but has the same size 6.3in OLED screen, same polished aluminium and glass body and a large camera bar sticking out the back. It is an attractive design that has aged well.The temperature sensor fromprevious Pixel Pro generations, which always felt like a gimmick, has been replaced by a coloured HiLight LED that works as a camera flash and notification light. The LED glows when you talk to Gemini or pulses with one of five colours when your favourite contact calls. But it doesn’t work for notifications of any other kind, so is a wasted opportunity.View image in fullscreenThe HiLight LED swirls different colours when you talk to Gemini, but only when the phone is face down, which is not something I’ve ever wanted to do.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe 11 Pro has the same Tensor G6 chip as the regular Pixel 11 and has 12 or 16GB of RAM depending on the storage version. It can’t match the raw performance of the topQualcommor Apple chips for games but is snappy in day-to-day tasks.Battery life is just shy of two days with the screen actively used for about seven hours across a mix of wifi and 5G for browsing, messaging apps and photos. This is a bit behind theregular Pixel 11but should see out even the heaviest of use days with some left in the tank. Most people will need to charge the 11 Pro every other day for general use.SpecificationsScreen:6.3in 120Hz QHD+ OLED (495ppi)Processor:Google Tensor G6RAM:12 or 16GBStorage:256, 512GB or 1TBOperating system:Android17Camera:50MP + 48MP UW + 48MP 5x tele; 42MP selfieConnectivity:5G, eSIM, wifi 7, UWB, NFC, Bluetooth 6, Thread and GNSSWater resistance:IP68 (1.5m for 30 minutes)Dimensions:152.7 x 71.9 x 8.4mmWeight:204gQuality Android 17 experience and AIView image in fullscreenA fast and accurate ultrasonic fingerprint scanner and solid camera-based face recognition make the Pixel feel responsive.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe 11 Pro runs the same Google version of Android 17 asthe regular Pixel 11and will be supported untilAugust 2033with operating system and security updates, making it one of the longest-lasting devices available.It’s a polished experience with smooth animations, nice touches of haptic feedback across the system and enough customisation to make it yours. But as with other Pixel devices, the phone is a showcase for Google’s most advanced AI tools that are littered throughout the software.The 11 Pro comes with six months ofGoogle AI Pro subscription, which gives you access toGemini Omnito generate surprisingly good eight-second videos, higher AI usage limits, 5TB of cloud storage and Google Health Premium.But the most interesting tools are the local AI ones, including thenew Rambler voice dictation featurein Gboard, which produces fully formed succinct sentences and paragraphs from your ramblings, removing unnecessary pauses, ums, ers and deviations. Gemini’s proactive assistance has also improved with more time-saving suggestions, although it only works in certain apps and not WhatsApp, Signal or other third-party apps.CameraView image in fullscreenThe camera app has lots of optional tools for making the best of your photos, from standard modes to AI framing guidance.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe reason you buy a Pixel Pro is for the camera. The 11 Pro has a very good 42-megapixel selfie camera on the front and a similar winning triple camera system on the rear from last year: a 50MP wide, 48MP ultra wide and a 48MP 5x telephoto camera.All three cameras capture really fantastic photos across a range of lighting conditions with very little effort. The wide and telephoto cameras now capture more light and slightly better detail, but the biggest boost is the new Instant Night Sight. It dramatically speeds up low-light photos by up to 4.5 times, which makes taking great shots in very dark scenes a lot easier.The 5x telephoto camera manages a very good 10x crop zoom before stretching up to 120x magnification, first with a very good traditional digital zoom to 30x then using local generative AI to go beyond. The camera keeps the regular digital zoom image and the one processed by AI to add back lost detail, which can be remarkable or filled with artefacts.Magic Capturetakes video and photos automatically with just one button for point-and-shoot recording, which works well for events such as a birthday party.ButCamera Looksis the most interesting feature for getting creative with photography. It allows you to modify how the camera processes your photos, starting with subtle changes such as darker shadows and ranging to more distinctive looks such as “minimal”, which reduces the computational photography processing for a more raw photo. Other options include “digi”, which replicates the look of olddigital cameras that have become popular, and “velvet”, which mimics the look of some film cameras. Each look can be further customised, allowing great creative licence.The Pixel shoots great video with lots ofstabilisation and processing toolsincluding the new “Creator Suite”, which captures clips straight into a folder for storyboarding and trimming, with a teleprompter, framing for social media and speed enhancement.SustainabilityView image in fullscreenThe phone takes about 90 minutes to fully charge using a 30W or greater power adaptor (not included) hitting 54% in half an hour. It also supports 25W Qi2.2 wireless charging.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe batteryis rated to lastin excess of 1,000 full-charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity. The phone is repairable by Google, third-party shops or self-repairwith manualsandparts available.The Pixel 11 Pro contains 31% recycled materials by weight. The company breaks down thephone’s environmental impactin its report and willrecycle old devicesfor free.PriceThe Google Pixel 11 Pro costs from£1,079(€1,199/$1,099/A$1,849) in a choice of four colours.For comparison, the Pixel 11 costs£879, Pixel 11 Pro XL costs£1,279, Pixel 11 Pro Fold costs from£1,799, thePixel 10acosts£499, theSamsung Galaxy S26costs£879, theSamsung Galaxy S26 Ultracosts£1,279and theApple iPhone 17 Procosts£1,099.VerdictThe Pixel 11 Pro is a refinement of multiple generations of Google’s Pro phones rather than an outright revolution, but that’s no bad thing.It is one of the very best smaller phones, packing all the top-end hardware, cameras and AI features of Google’s most biggest and expensive model into a slightly cheaper and more pocketable form. You buy a Pro Pixel for the camera, which doesn’t disappoint with arguably the best photography on a phone at the moment.The ability to customise the processing of your photos goes far beyond rivals for interesting creative potential. The dramatically faster Night Sight is also a significant improvement.Gemini’s proactive tools show great potential but depend on using the right apps. The supercharged Rambler voice dictation system is fantastic, and there are many other little AI tools that are useful from time to time.With just shy of two days battery life, a decent chip and quality software, the Pixel 11 Pro is a great pocketable phone. It just isn’t a massive upgrade on the already excellent Pixel 11 or recent Pixel Pro models.Pros:great camera with extended zoom and extensive customisation, seven years of software updates, excellent screen, impressive dictation and local AI features, Qi2 wireless charging and magnetic accessory support, good battery life, great size, fast fingerprint and face recognition, six months of Google AI Pro included.Cons:quite expensive, less memory on cheapest model than before, face unlock option not as secure as Face ID, raw performance and battery life short of best-in-class, no physical sim card slot in the US, not a massive upgrade.Explore more on these topicsPixelAndroidGoogleMobile phonesAlphabetreviewsShareReuse this content

title: A scientist said bananas ‘kill’ the benefit of blueberries. Is that true? | Well actually | The Guardian
description: Can blending these popular fruits in a smoothie adversely affect the berries’ nutritional benefits? Experts weigh in
Author: Adrienne Matei
Headline: Can blending these popular fruits in a smoothie adversely affect the berries’ nutritional benefits? Experts weigh in
Content: Could the common, beloved mash-up of blueberries and bananas really be a bad match, as Dr Rhonda Patrick said?Photograph: PavelKant/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenCould the common, beloved mash-up of blueberries and bananas really be a bad match, as Dr Rhonda Patrick said?Photograph: PavelKant/Getty Images/iStockphotoWell actuallyA scientist said bananas ‘kill’ the benefit of blueberries. Is that true?Can blending these popular fruits in a smoothie adversely affect the berries’ nutritional benefits? Experts weigh inAdrienne MateiThu 10 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 12.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis year was shaping up to be a banner year for bananas: they were lauded as “2026’s big viral taste”, landed pride of place as Prada’s newlip balmflavor, and were even deemed “the next pumpkin spice”.But this summer, the Mel Robbins Podcast featured Dr Rhonda Patrick, a biomedical scientist, who said that adding banana to a blueberry smoothie could adversely affect the nutritional benefits of the berries.Could the beloved mashup of blueberries and bananas really be a bad match?What is the claim about bananas affecting the nutritional value of blueberries?Cutting down on ultra-processed foods isn’t easy. Here are eight tips that worked for my familyRead morePatrick’s claim involved an enzyme called polyphenol oxidase, which appears in bananas, and polyphenols, an umbrella term for a diverse family of antioxidant compounds found in plants – including blueberries.“Polyphenol oxidase, it’s essentially an enzyme that’s breaking down the polyphenols. And there have now been studies … showing if you add bananas to blueberries, you’re not getting as many polyphenols. In fact, it’s quite a bit lower. So the banana is killing the benefit,” shesaid.The most likely source for Patrick’s claim is a 2023studythat explored how polyphenol oxidase affected the body’s absorption of particular polyphenols called flavanols.The study found that participants who drank banana smoothies with added flavanol had lower blood levels of these antioxidants than those who drank mixed-berry smoothies with the same additive.Does this study support the banana-blueberry claim?There are a few reasons not to rely too heavily on this study for this specific claim.First of all, the researchers “never, ever made a smoothie with bananas and blueberries together”, says Dr Joe Schwarcz, a science communicator and director of McGill University’s office for science and society.Further, the study “only had eight subjects … not a big enough number to have significant conclusions”, says Schwarcz.But zooming out to the effects of polyphenol oxidase on flavanols, “there is a statistical difference in the amount of polyphenols that may be present in your smoothie as the result of the banana,” says Schwarcz.I reached out to Patrick at her health content company, FoundMyFitness, to clarify her claim. A spokesperson, Dan (their full name was not provided on request), responded by email: “The fact that this enzyme breaks down some polyphenols is essentially beyond reproach and not dependent on any one study she cites.”A body of research does support that polyphenol oxidase influences the antioxidative capacity of different compounds in fruit and vegetables in variousdifferent ways.Graphic with three lines of text that say, in bold, ‘Well Actually’, then ‘Read more on living a good life in a complex world,’ then a pinkish-lavender pill-shaped button with white letters that say ‘More from this section’But context is important. Blueberries contain several types of polyphenols. Anthocyanins, which are responsible for the color of blueberries, are proportionally more significant and abundant in the fruit than flavanols, says Schwarcz.Anthocyanins areassociatedwith a range of potential health benefits, including reduced risk of overall mortality, cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes.Thus, what this study measured was “not even the important compounds of blueberries”, says Schwarcz.Finally, this study was funded by the Mars company – and the flavanols used in this project were derived from cocoa.“And it just so happens that [Mars] sells flavanol supplements” and chocolate, which contains flavanols, says Schwarcz.Can nutrients actually ‘cancel each other out’?Yes, they can. “Nutrient interactions in food are actually quite common,” says Alyssa Northrop, a registered dietitian based in Minneapolis.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Some nutrients enhance the absorption of other nutrients, like vitamin C and iron. Others can reduce absorption, such as the oxalates in spinach, which bind to calcium and reduce its bioavailability.”But in the grand scheme of your diet, Northrop says you shouldn’t lose sleep over such interactions.“Rather than trying to micromanage every food combination, I encourage people to focus on the bigger picture: eat a varied diet with plenty of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, nuts, seeds and other nutrient-dense foods to meet your body’s needs,” she says.Eating too few fruits and vegetables is a bigger concern than optimizing polyphenol absorption from every smoothie, says Northrop.“Most of us aren’t consuming the recommended five servings of fruits and vegetables daily. If adding a banana makes a berry smoothie more delicious and encourages someone to eat more fruit, I see that as a win,” she says.“Bananas are often added to smoothies for their natural sweetness and unique texture that can make the smoothie thick and creamy,” says Sheri Gaw, a registered dietitian nutritionist based in the San Francisco Bay Area. Furthermore, bananas are easily accessible, inexpensive and healthy. Theycontainpotassium, vitamin B6, vitamin C, manganese and magnesium, along with about 3 grams of fiber per medium fruit.Should we be worried about not getting enough polyphenols?Polyphenol-rich foods have been associated with a range of potential health benefits, including supporting cardiovascular and metabolic health, promoting a healthy gut microbiome, and helping prevent chronic diseases, says Northrop.Evidencesuggests that consuming between 400 and 600mg of flavanols daily fromfoodssuch as green tea, cocoa and apples may support cardiometabolic health, including potential improvements in blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar regulation.Experts say we need to eat 30 plants a week. This is how I faredRead moreBut unlike with vitamin and mineral deficiencies, which can cause distinct negative health effects, “we don’t know the physiological effects of polyphenol insufficiency on health. Polyphenols are not considered essential nutrients, and there isn’t an established recommended daily intake for total polyphenols,” Northrop says.If you’re really worried about your berry smoothie’s flavanol levels, add fruit that is lower in polyphenol oxidase than banana, such as mango or pineapple.Or, experiment with different ingredients. “Oats, yogurt, silken tofu, kefir, avocado and frozen cauliflower are popular smoothie add-ins that can offer a similar creamy thickness as a banana,” Gaw adds.Do I really need to stop putting bananas in my berry smoothie?“In the context of your overall diet,” the interplay of bananas and berries is “insignificant”, says Schwarcz. Overall, it’s good to eat a variety of fruits, and we benefit from their varied antioxidant compounds.Schwarcz has seen the idea of focusing on a specific food component and its impact on human health bubble up in nutrition literature for years.“Your health is a very complex business of nutrition, of genetics, of your activity levels. And to try to make a big deal out of whether you put a banana in your smoothie or not – it’s just scientific nonsense,” he says. “It makes no practical difference in your life.”Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyHealthFruitFoodHealth & wellbeingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ralph Lauren proves the American dream still sells at New York fashion week | New York fashion week | The Guardian
description: Designer mixes burnt-out velvet and shredded denim with a mythology that keeps getting more profitable
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: Designer mixes burnt-out velvet and shredded denim with a mythology that keeps getting more profitable
Content: Models on the catwalk during the Ralph Lauren spring 2027 collection show.Photograph: Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenModels on the catwalk during the Ralph Lauren spring 2027 collection show.Photograph: Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty ImagesNew York fashion weekRalph Lauren proves the American dream still sells at New York fashion weekDesigner mixes burnt-out velvet and shredded denim with a mythology that keeps getting more profitableJess Cartner-Morleyin New YorkThu 10 Sep 2026 08.59 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe opening show of fashion’s month of catwalks was not on the official schedule, but Viola Davis and Cynthia Erivo were snuggled on to celebrity-packed benches in a cathedral-sized marble hall where tapestry-hung walls and a gilded coffered ceiling framed a view over lower Manhattan.Ralph Lauren, 86, took his bow at the end of this women’s wear show casually dressed in a varsity jacket spelling outNew York. In an industry obsessed with youth and novelty, Lauren is more relevant than ever in his ninth decade.Preppy polo players, timeless tuxedos and … fishing rods: the history of the Ralph Lauren catwalk – in picturesRead moreHe described the show as “irreverent”. Velvet evening wear was burnt out to show a little skin beneath. There were shredded, low-slung jeans – take note, jeans-wearers everywhere – and a wink to the extra-wide ties that started his empire 59 years ago.The spray-painted brocade gowns and lush embroidered evening coats on this catwalk will be giddily expensive, but the energy propelling the brand comes from a much broader audience.View image in fullscreenRalph and Ricky Lauren. The designer took his bow at the end of this show casually dressed in a varsity jacket spelling out New York.Photograph: Dia Dipasupil/Getty ImagesGen Z has rediscovered Ralph Lauren, and its Polo shirts, rugby shirts and baseball caps are cool again, a renaissance that shows up emphatically on the balance sheet. This year the fashion house reached its highest ever annual revenue figure of $8.1bn (£6bn) – a rise of 15% on the previous year.Ralph Lauren has a genius for marketing that feels like mythology. The 1920s-coded cocktail dresses nod to Gatsby’s lawn; the denim to cowboy ranches. There are college jocks and Upper East Side socialites. Born Ralph Lifshitz, the son of Jewish immigrants from Belarus, the designer has invented a fantasy America, borrowing from English aristocracy and from classic westerns; from Native American craft and Waspish New England; from country clubs and jazz clubs.He has taken the contradictions of the US – old money and the frontier, east coast establishment and wild west freedom – and made them look as if they belong together.This world is not real, but it is visually coherent, and has proved to be universally seductive whether you are shopping for a baseball cap or a ballgown. It is this sleight-of-hand – selling the fantasy, not the actual product – that has enabled Lauren to remain aspirational to the 1% while making a ton of money in the malls.In a statement, Lauren described his latest collection as “the freedom and fun of creating a style that is truly personal”. Experimental fabric techniques gave the impression of a design studio that still knows how to have fun.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenLauren described his latest collection as ‘the freedom and fun of creating a style that is truly personal’.Photograph: Caitlin Ochs/ReutersGrand gowns were laundered with a “spritz and tumble” method that gave a louche rumple to their glide along the catwalk. Lauren was this week announced as a nominee for American menswear designer of the year, and his tailoring heritage showed up in two sharp trouser suits, tailored for women in an Italian menswear workshop.The swagger of the show was a fitting curtain-raiser to aNew York fashion weekthat opens with more confidence than in recent seasons, as designers gravitate toward a US market that is a bright spot in a troubled global luxury industry.Fellow grandee Tommy Hilfiger will stage a show at the Plaza Hotel, with Michael Kors setting up his catwalk at the Museum of Modern Art. The Diane von Furstenberg brand returns with its first show in a decade when new designer Henry Zankov shows his debut, and London-based, New York-born Conner Ives makes his home-town debut.Explore more on these topicsNew York fashion weekFashion weeksFashion industryNew YorknewsShareReuse this content

title: Make tracks: 8 of the UK’s best walking and cycling trails on former railway lines | Travel | The Guardian
description: Repurposed railway lines make accessible and family-friendly walking and cycling routes. Here are some of the best, from Somerset to the Highlands of Scotland
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Repurposed railway lines make accessible and family-friendly walking and cycling routes. Here are some of the best, from Somerset to the Highlands of Scotland
Content: The Headstone Viaduct on the Monsal Trail in the Peak District.Photograph: Lankowsky/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Headstone Viaduct on the Monsal Trail in the Peak District.Photograph: Lankowsky/AlamyGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.TravelMake tracks: 8 of the UK’s best walking and cycling trails on former railway linesRepurposed railway lines make accessible and family-friendly walking and cycling routes. Here are some of the best, from Somerset to the Highlands of ScotlandAnnabelle ThorpeThu 10 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheMonsal Trail,Peak District,DerbyshireStart/finishCoombs Road in Bakewellto Blackwell Mill inChee Dale, but there are lots of access points along the wayDistance8.5 milesCycle, hike or ride a horse along the Monsal Trail to explore a swathe of Derbyshire’s industrial history. This former stretch of the Midland Railway line winds past the imposing structures of two 18th-century cotton mills, through illuminated railway tunnels and over the Headstone Viaduct, which gives glorious views of the River Wye and Monsal Dale below. Interpretation and listening panels along the route explain the area’s history, geology and wildlife, while a short detour on to Monsal Head offers a panoramic view of the viaduct itself. Pause here for lunch or a pint atthe Monsal, or stop in atHassop Station Cafe, which offers bike rental alongside hefty sandwiches, homemade cakes and wood-fired pizza at weekends.monsaltrail.org.ukThe Strawberry Line,SomersetView image in fullscreenCycling on the Strawberry Line at Shute Shelve railway tunnel.Photograph: Joe Dunckley/AlamyStart/finishYattonrailwaystationto the old (unused)CheddarrailwaystationDistance10.7 milesNamed for the fruity cargo that trains once carried from the strawberry fields up to London, this flat, accessible route – shared by walkers, cyclists and wheelchair users – knits together former railway stations, cider orchards and small, historic towns. Direct trains run from Bristol to Yatton, where the not-for-profit, community-runStrawberry Line Cafeserves hearty breakfasts and homemade cakes, while next door theStrawberry Line Cycle Projectoffers bike hire and accessories such as child seats. The route runs through wildlife-rich wetlands, open grazing land and lush valleys, while the medieval square at Axbridge gives an insight into the region’s rich history, dating back to the 10th century, when it was a busy commercial centre. Settle in at theAlmshouse Teashop, in a building almost 600 years old, for freshly made soup and sweet treats, before setting off again.thestrawberryline.org.ukThe Mawddach Trail,Gwynedd,WalesView image in fullscreenThe toll bridge at Penmaenpool, over the Mawddach.Photograph: Henry Ciechanowicz/AlamyStart/finishMarian Mawr car parkinDolgellautoBarmouthviaductDistance9.5 milesMostly running alongside the Mawddach estuary, this tranquil trail is a great choice for birders, with peregrine falcons and buzzards whirling above, and curlews and oystercatchers in the salt marshes. The wide, even surface also makes it ideal for wheelchairs and mobility scooters, and there are several joining points along the trail, meaning you can walk or bike as little or as far as you like. Just next to the 150-year-old Penmaenpool wooden toll bridge, theGeorge III hotel and puboffers sweeping estuary views and classic pub food (including particularly fine pies), or pick up picnic supplies fromFork, Cork and Feathersin Dolgellau, which has a cold counter crammed with cured meats, cheeses and other local produce. There are seats and picnic tables dotted all the way along the trail.mawddachtrail.co.ukThe Cuckoo Trail,East SussexView image in fullscreenThe Cuckoo Trail.Photograph: Johan Siebke/AlamyStart/finishStation Road in HeathfieldtoHampden Park in EastbourneDistance14 milesA great choice for a family adventure, this mostly flat trail has five augmented reality “story stops” along the way – where, with just a quick scan of the QR code, children can interact with animated wildlife characters, solve puzzles and take a selfie with a grumpy badger. There are sculptures too, including carved wooden seats made from oak trees that fell during the great storm of 1987 and steel sculptures that act as mileposts.Cuckoo Shack Cafe, part of Priory Court Farm in Polegate, is set right on the trail and offers homemade-cakes, sandwiches and excellent coffee, but it is only open at weekends and during school holidays. Otherwise, a quick diversion into Hailsham offers a clutch of places to eat, including Neapolitan street food and wood-fired pizza atRustico.wealden.gov.ukThe Flitch Way, EssexView image in fullscreenThe former Rayne railway station, near Braintree.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyStart/finishBraintree station to Start Hill,near Bishop’s StortfordDistance15 milesDiscover a tranquil side of Essex by following this rural trail along the edge of the former royal hunting ground ofHatfield Forest– where fallow deer roam between the ancient oak trees – andGreat Notley Country Park, where families can take advantage of the 1.2km play trail, with slides, forts and swings. The main refreshment stop is 2 miles along the trail from Braintree at the Rayne Station centre, which combines theBooking Hall Cafewith the free-to-enterRailway Carriage Museum, a visitor centre and toilets. For something more sustaining (and a pint or two), theLion and Lambpub is just a short detour off the trail, in the pretty village of Little Canfield. Keep an eye out for kestrels and buzzards, plus brown hares dashing out of the hedgerows.explore-essex.comThe Wirral Way, Merseysideand CheshireView image in fullscreenThurstaston beach.Photograph: David Chapman/AlamyStart/finishWest Kirbyrailway station to Hootonrailway stationDistance12.2 milesOne of the first converted railway lines in England, the Wirral Way is now a dramatically beautiful coastal path running along the Wirral Peninsula. It takes in theWirral Country Park, whereWirral Way Bikesoffers cycle hire for adults and kids (including ebikes), and clifftop picnic spots have gorgeous views over the Dee estuary. Take a detour down the cliffs to Thurstaston beach for a spot of fossil hunting or a quick paddle, and pause at Hadlow Road station, which has been preserved in all its 1950s glory (when the passenger service stopped) as an open museum; it also operates as an information point for the trail. Time your walk or ride for sunset, when the mudflats glow rose-pink and gold as the sun drops below the Clwydian Hills, and take the short connecting path down to theHarp Inn, Little Neston, set directly on the estuary, for a sundowner to go with the view.visitcheshire.comThe Crab and Winkle Way, KentView image in fullscreenRewilded bison on the Blean.Photograph: Donovan Wright/PAStart/finishCanterbury West station to Whitstable HarbourDistance7.5 milesFollowing the route of one of the earliest railway lines, built in 1830, this hiking and cycling trail passes throughthe Blean, a large swathe of ancient woodland, home to the 13th-century church of St Cosmus and St Damian, and an RSPB reserve. It’s also home to Europe’s first free-roaming bison, introduced as part of arewilding initiativein 2022 by the Kent Wildlife Trust and Wildwood Trust. There’s not really anywhere en route to stop and eat, so either pick up treats for a picnic at theGoods Shedin Canterbury (an indoor farmers market, closed mondays) or save yourself for oysters and a glass of fizz at theWhitstable Oyster Company, right on the beach.explorekent.orgThe Dava Way,Moray and Highland, ScotlandView image in fullscreenThe collie dog memorial on the Dava Way.Photograph: John Bracegirdle/AlamyStart/finishMannachie Avenue in Forres to Dulicht Bridge in Grantown-on-SpeyDistance24 milesUnusually for a rail trail, the Dava Way includes a stiff climb from the Moray Firth up overDava Moorto the Dava Summit, at 320 metres (1,050ft), before heading back down to Grantown-on-Spey, following the Highland Railway line that operated for over a century, from 1863 to 1965. The ascent is well worth it for the spectacular views across the Moray Firth to Sutherland in the north, and south to the Cromdale Hills and the Cairngorms, while the ride back down is a breeze. TheDivie Viaduct, built in 1863, is the most famous landmark along the way, while the Halfway Hut is a restored shelter that makes a perfect spot for a picnic, with old photographs and route info on the walls (not for overnight stays).davaway.org.ukExplore more on these topicsTravelUnited Kingdom holidaysWalkingWalking holidaysCycling holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Scots are the kindest people on earth!’ Meet the Americans moving to Scotland | Scotland | The Guardian
description: Since Donald Trump’s re-election in 2024, there has been a 63% rise in Americans renting properties in Scotland. Politics is one reason – but there are many other surprising motivations …
Author: Anita Chaudhuri
Headline: Since Donald Trump’s re-election in 2024, there has been a 63% rise in Americans renting properties in Scotland. Politics is one reason – but there are many other surprising motivations …
Content: ‘I’ve never felt a longing to move back to the US’ … Hailey Beaupre, in the historic cloisters at Glasgow University.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I’ve never felt a longing to move back to the US’ … Hailey Beaupre, in the historic cloisters at Glasgow University.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianScotland‘Scots are the kindest people on earth!’ Meet the Americans moving to ScotlandSince Donald Trump’s re-election in 2024, there has been a 63% rise in Americans renting properties in Scotland. Politics is one reason – but there are many other surprising motivations …Anita ChaudhuriThu 10 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 08.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFour years ago, when Tammi Gaw, a 50-year-old property adviser, moved from Washington DC to Glasgow with her Scottish partner, friends and family laughed at her. “People back home kept asking me: ‘Ha ha, why would you want to move toScotland, where it rains all the time?’ Now those same people are asking me: ‘Hey, how do I move there?’”They are not alone.According to data from Rightmove, 28% of inquiries from Americans about buying a home in the UK are about Scotland, a larger number than for London. Anda recent surveyfrom lettings platform Goodlord reported a 63% rise in the number of Americans renting properties in Scotland since Donald Trump’s re-election in November 2024.But Gaw, a member of Democrats Abroad, believes that disenchantment with the current administration does not fully explain Scotland’s appeal. She also cites the feelgood factor created by the more than 20,000 Scottish football fans who descended on Massachusetts for the World Cup this summer, winning over Bostonians with their pranks and bagpipe parades, enriching local bar owners and even bagging up their rubbish: “The Tartan Army put on a better marketing campaign for their country than any funded programme by the government. People now view Scotland as a very fun option.”There are other, more hard-headed reasons for Scotland’s allure. “I advise people across all income brackets,” says Gaw. “Some are planning ahead. For example, they want Scottish residency so that, later, their children can get free university tuition fees.”She mentions the NHS as another draw. Although most people moving to the UK on a family or skilled worker visa have to payan annual immigration health surcharge of £1,035, this is considered a bargain by those familiar with American health insurance plans. “The cost was less than the basic monthly premiums in the US, before all the other deductibles and charges,” says Gaw. She suggests that Scotland has a particular advantage for those with longstanding health conditions because prescriptions are free for all in Scotland.View image in fullscreen‘People view Scotland as a fun option’ … Tammi Gaw, who moved from Washington to Glasgow, at the Clydeside distillery in Glasgow.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianPolitics and practicalities aside, a cursory glance at social media reveals another, less obvious, reason for some of this Caledonian clamour – the long-running fantasy series Outlander, in which a former second world war military nurse, Claire Randall, is transported to the 18th-century Highlands, where she falls in love with Jamie Fraser, a warrior. The series features scenic locations including the Devil’s Pulpit in Finnich Glen and the standing stones at Calanais. “Plans for the evening: watch Outlander. Knit Outlander shawl. Dream of moving to Scotland,” readsa typical post. “Just back from Scotland and did a few Outlander filming locations. Cried my eyes out for a couple of days after returning home. Need to move to the Scottish Highlands!”reads another.Someone who knows more than most about the Outlander effect is Hailey Beaupre, 28, who runs the tour companySassenach Historian. She became obsessed while still a student in New Hampshire, binge-watching the series, reading the books by Diana Gabaldon on which it is based and booking a whirlwind trip to Scotland.“I attended an Outlander tour where we drove to Midhope Castle [the derelict 15th-century castle near South Queensferry was one of the locations in the series]. It was like a switch in my head flipped. I said aloud: “I’m going to move to Scotland and I’m going to do tours like this for a living.”Beaupre now describes what happened next as “either a breakdown or a breakthrough”, depending on how you look at it. “I broke up with my boyfriend, I hired a therapist and I changed my degree from education to history, all in the space of a week.”Her resolve to relocate remained unwavering, despite challenges. Her first attempt, enrolling on a course at Dundee University in March 2020, lasted three days before she was repatriated because of Covid. That same week, her best friend died. “Outlander, and the dream of moving to Scotland, gave me something to believe in, something to reach for during that difficult time. I would not still be here without it.”Eventually, she completed a master’s at the University of Aberdeen, got a job as a tour guide and set up her own company. She now lives in Glasgow’s thriving Southside with her Scottish husband. “Honestly, I’ve never felt homesick or a longing to move back to the US. Scots are the kindest people on earth. You meet them in the pub and they’ll give you a hug and buy you a pint. I’ve never once felt unwelcome here. The thing that people say to me most often is: ‘I’ve lived here all my life but you probably know more about Scotland than I do.’”As a Scot myself, I must hang my head in shame on that front. I have only the sketchiest grasp of Highland clearances, rebellions and clans, based solely on school textbooks that were more dreary than dreamy. But when it comes to today’s Scotland, it seems doubtful that anyone who has previously only lived in the US would have a clue about the reality.Few Americans appear to be rushing to move to any of the less scenic areas of the Central Belt. Take the former shipbuilding town of Greenock, for example, where thecouncil recently announced that it has been actively encouraging migrants to move thereas a remedy for depopulation. And no one mentions that other Scottish screen hit, Trainspotting, in their relocation fantasies. Scotland has its fair share of social and economic problems, and not everyone is delighted by the influx of wealthy Trump refugees. “There is already a housing crisis in many of those longed-for areas due to second homes, holiday lets etc,” vents one poster on Threads. “People who pay over the odds for their dream homes push out younger folk from those areas, reducing services. Scotland is not a retirement village.”On the other hand, social media and newspaper headlines are inflating the scale of the American inundation. Getting a visa is not easy without a British parent or an employer willing to sponsor you. Looking more closely at the increase in demand for rentals, the number of properties involved is tiny: from265 in 2024 to 431 this year. Plus, Scotland needs skilled workers, and many coming to the country are filling vital roles in remote areas with falling populations.View image in fullscreen‘It started with whisky porridge for breakfast’ … American Corey Kinnan, at Redcastle on the Black Isle peninsula, Inverness, where he moved with his wife and child.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEleven years ago, American photographerCorey Kinnan, 44, and his wife went on holiday to Scotland for the first time. “We only had a week, because like many people in the US, we had limited vacation time. But during those days, we fell in love with the country. There was this one day in particular that started with whisky porridge for breakfast, then a tour of Balvenie distillery in Speyside, then an afternoon on the dunes at Lossiemouth, and in the evening a ceilidh. It was so appealing seeing a community coming together like that, in a way that doesn’t really happen in the US any more. Afterwards, my wife and I agreed that it was the most amazing day of our lives. We decided to sell our home in Maine and relocate.”But turning the dream into reality was not easy. It took the couple 10 years to get there, and it was only possible because Kinnan’s wife, an obstetrician, got a job in Inverness. Now with a young son in tow, they bought a house in the Black Isle, a remote but scenic peninsula.“Arriving there in the December was a bit of a depression,” admits Kinnan. Their bed was in transit. They couldn’t even buy a sofa because, without any credit history, they couldn’t apply for a credit card. It was all a long way from whisky porridge.Gradually, though, they began to find their feet, buoyed by the landscape that had lured them there in the first place. “New colleagues generously loaned us furniture and made us feel welcome. And, when you cross over the Kessock Bridge into the Black Isle, seeing the mountains in the background and a red kite flies over your car, it feels like the best place on Earth,” Kinnan says.Having to restart his photography business in a new country has proved tough, though. “I’ve had to adapt what I do, from only selling landscape prints to offering portrait shoots to people honeymooning or celebrating anniversaries in the area. That has become a big trend now, and one I’m grateful for.” He also stumbled upon Dingwall Camera Club, which he says has been a social lifeline as well as a boon for professional networking. “We don’t have anything like that back home. It’s yet another reason why our hope is to live here permanently. We want to contribute to our community and make Scotland a better place. Not that I am suggesting that it needs any improving,” he adds hastily.Melody Sandona, a 66-year-old corporate meeting planner, also relocated to the Highlands in August 2025, when she got a remote-working transfer to her company’s European office. She has dual citizenship because of her Mancunian mother, and had travelled to the UK to visit family for most of her life. Yet she only ventured into Scotland after she turned 60. “I had an old friend who lived in Edinburgh and she invited me to come for a visit. I fell in love with the country on that trip. I had always planned on moving to the UK at some point; on that trip I decided to move from Colorado to Scotland.”A perhaps over romantic view of the country prompted her to rent a stone cottage in a village on the Kyle of Lochalsh. The nearby village of Plockton is a location best known as the eerie setting for the film The Wicker Man. “My younger son was with me for the first six months and it was very cold and miserable.” Fortunately, Sandona lived next door to the local library and the two librarians took her under their wing and welcomed her warmly into the community.“But just before Christmas last year, my Edinburgh friend paid me a visit. ‘What are you doing here? This is a dump!’ I mean, it was charming, but bleak. Anyway, she has a beautiful big home and insisted I move into her spare room. So, there are three women living there now, in this wonderful Golden Girls setup. We have a great time. I feel so at peace here.”Sandona finds the cost of living is far cheaper than in the US. “I was spending $200 [£150] a month on cellphone service, $2,000 on health insurance and $1,000 a month on groceries. I’m never going back to the US – this is it for me. It’s been the best thing I’ve ever done in my life.”View image in fullscreen‘I want to buy a kilt, but I don’t know if I’m really allowed to wear one’ … Ryan Forber, formerly a firefighter in Nashville, stands in front of the Forth rail bridge in Fife.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianFor Ryan Forber, a 46-year-old firefighter from Nashville, the decision to move with his family to Kirkcaldy in January was political and practical. “My brother-in-law is from Edinburgh, and we visited two summers ago. Since the first Trump administration, my wife and I had been having a conversation about leaving. I felt that there was only so much you could do with activism and voting. At some point you have to just be like Albert Einstein and get out,” he says, referring to the scientist’s decision to renounce his German citizenship and move to the US in 1933.Unfortunately, there isn’t a formal programme for American firefighters to join the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service, so for the family to secure a skilled worker visa, it was necessary for his wife, a vet, to find a job. “She got responses to her application within 48 hours,” says Forber, still sounding amazed. “It was lightning fast.”It took a lot of energy and resources to make the move, though. “We sold everything we owned, including our home. I’m really aware that this isn’t an option for everyone. When you factor in all the costs, it’s a very expensive thing to do.”Since the move, they have settled happily into the local community. Forber says he likes the slower pace of life, being able to cycle to school with his son on the back of his e-bike and being recognised by local people. “Scotland is a much safer place to bring up a child,” he says. “School shootings and gun violence have always been a concern of mine. I went to high school in Littleton, Colorado, at the time of theColumbine shooting, though I attended a different school. It was earth-shattering.”Forber cites everyday joys and frustrations about his new life – missing his beloved Girl Scout Cookies, the slog of getting a UK driving licence, “though I’ve learned to love roundabouts”, the great pub culture, football and Scottish beer. The main challenge has been finding work as a firefighter. “I feel that I’m stuck in a system where I have to apply from scratch, along with all the kids who are just starting out. I could run rings round them, but I’m not even getting a call back. I really miss the camaraderie of the job as well.”What advice would he give to his compatriots thinking about making a similar move? “It’s not all green pastures and golf courses. Keep an open mind. Just because you watched Braveheart as a kid does not mean you understand the country or its traditions. For example, I sort of want to buy a kilt, but then I don’t know if I’m really allowed to wear one. My Scottish friends tell me I should get one. But I’m dragging my feet. I’ve got until next January to decide.”Why next January?“Our first Burns Night,” he says. Spoken like a true Scot.Explore more on these topicsScotlandfeaturesShareReuse this content

Author: Martin Belam

She wants to know which TV show is changing its name following Donald Trump's recent splurge of renaming things?South Park is becoming South AmericaThe Simpsons is becoming The AmericansFamily Guy is becoming American GuyBeavis and Butt-Head is becoming Beavis and Maga-HeadReveal9.This week's other guest feline is Pepper, another cat that lives at the Oakside Stadium in Barkingside. However, Najidi Storm (pictured, left) has brought eternal shame on his bloodline by becoming the shortest-priced loser in British racing history. What were his odds of winning the Cleansing Service Group Novice Stakes at Goodwood, which he did not, in fact, win?1-251-331-501-1,057Reveal11.The city of Malibu, California, has ordered the evacuation of more than 30 properties after a large sinkhole (pictured) opened in a house reported to be owned by which actor?Jared LetoEric RobertsEdward NortonNicolas CageReveal12.Which band are somewhat aggrieved that the child of one of their former sound engineers is auctioning off an archive of more than 100 hours of their recordings?BlurColdplayOasisSparksReveal13.The Thursday quiz regrets to inform you that Liz Truss has been at it again, this time 'relaunching' her podcast on which channel?Mike Graham’s YouTube channel, UKLiveJulia Hartley-Brewer's YouTube channel, JuliaLiveDan Wootton's YouTube channel, OutspokenGary Barlow's massive son's YouTube channel, GiantTVReveal14.It is little Alex Horne's birthday today. Happy birthday Alex! Your time starts now! When was Taskmaster first broadcast in the UK?2009201220152018Reveal15.And finally … the Angry People in Local Newspapers Facebook page would call them 'pencil-necked desk jockeys at the council', but what have officials in Conservative-led Westminster council decided to ban in Soho?Card-only retail outletsDelivery e-bikesVertical drinkingFeral hogsRevealIf you really do think there has been an egregious error in one of the questions or answers – and can show your working and are absolutely 100% positive you aren’t attempting to factcheck a joke – you can complain about it in the comments below.
