title: Country diary: A little garden mystery – why are the wood mice hoarding opium seeds? | Wildlife | The Guardian
description: Allendale, Northumberland: My late-flowering poppies have lit up the garden, and it’s not only me who’s taken an interest
Author: Susie White
Headline: Allendale, Northumberland: My late-flowering poppies have lit up the garden, and it’s not only me who’s taken an interest
Content: A wood mouse has taken an interest in the poppies in Susie White’s garden.Photograph: Arterra/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA wood mouse has taken an interest in the poppies in Susie White’s garden.Photograph: Arterra/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesCountry diaryWildlifeCountry diary: A little garden mystery – why are the wood mice hoarding opium seeds?Allendale, Northumberland:My late-flowering poppies have lit up the garden, and it’s not only me who’s taken an interestSusie WhiteThu 10 Sep 2026 00.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe opium poppies have now set seed, their leaves rattling like crisp packets, the vents beneath their pod lids open for the seeds to be scattered. Dotted throughout my flower borders, adding stature to the vegetable garden,Papaver somniferumis the breadseed poppy, its large, floppy petals unpredictable in colour: pale lilac, purple, pink or sometimes with fringed petals. The unexpected brings a freedom and a randomness to the garden.Those blue-grey seeds are sprinkled on bagels and bread, baked into cakes or ground as a thickener for curries, adding protein, plant fats and trace elements such as manganese. But in its unripe state this is the plant that gives opium, a two-sided drug, both medicinal and destructive as a sedative – its specific namesomniferummeans sleep-bringing.View image in fullscreenPoppy in the paving with a chewed stem.Photograph: Susie WhiteIt is when the petals fall off, leaving a plump, unripe capsule the colour of celadon, that the opium is extracted. Damage the pod or break off a poppy stem, and a white, milky latex oozes out. It is this that contains a mixture of opiate alkaloids including morphine, heroin and codeine, something wildlife would normally avoid.These poppies are also the source of a mystery in my garden. I’m sitting on the terrace in the late afternoon sun, feeling the absence of the swallows, when a wood mouse scampers past. It runs lightly up the stalk of a poppy, one that I’ve been enjoying for its late flowering. Speedily severing a stem, the mouse carries a pod several times the size of its own head, and manoeuvres it with difficulty into a hidden store in the drystone wall.Curious to know if the alkaloids take their toll, I set a nightly wildlife camera. Several times the mouse goes back, eyes large in the momentary light, tail curling round a stalk. There’s a rustle of foliage and the sound of chewing before a heavy seedpod drops to the ground.Bemused, I try some research. The general opinion is that unripe poppies would spoil when cached, that immature seeds have fewer nutrients, and that even a small amount of latex would be toxic to the mouse. I haven’t seen the field mouse since, but then maybe it has chosen something else to harvest.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsWildlifeCountry diaryPlantsWild flowersRural affairsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘They poison the population’: Swedish Muslims challenge far right ahead of election | Sweden | The Guardian
description: Ask-a-Muslim campaign takes to streets as country faces prospect of extremists entering highest levels of government
Author: Ashifa Kassam
Headline: Ask-a-Muslim campaign takes to streets as country faces prospect of extremists entering highest levels of government
Content: Kashif Virk, an imam in Malmö, is seeking to challenge people’s ideas about Islam with his Ask-a-Muslim campaign.Photograph: Emma Larsson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenKashif Virk, an imam in Malmö, is seeking to challenge people’s ideas about Islam with his Ask-a-Muslim campaign.Photograph: Emma Larsson/The GuardianSweden‘They poison the population’: Swedish Muslims challenge far right ahead of electionAsk-a-Muslim campaign takes to streets as country faces prospect of extremists entering highest levels of governmentAshifa Kassamin Malmö and StockholmThu 10 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 13.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNot far from one of Scandinavia’s biggest shopping malls, Kashif Virk stood on the pavement, handing out flyers and smiling at those who passed by. On a cloudy Tuesday afternoon, the Swedish-born imam had taken to the street to invite people to ask him anything they had ever wanted to know aboutIslam.For years, Sweden’s far right has peddled its own, distorted view of Islam, portraying it as being at odds with Swedish values. The Ask-a-Muslim – orFråga en Muslim–campaign, conceived by Virk in 2017, was his way of fighting back.With the help of dozens of volunteers from theAhmadi Muslim community, the campaign had called in at more than 150 farmers markets, squares and city centres, inviting strangers to strike up a conversation in hopes of dispelling myths and shedding light on Islam.“We have some radical parties and people are genuinely afraid about Islam,” said Virk. “Sometimes people get very rude. But most people in Sweden are lovely, friendly and interested – they want to learn more.”View image in fullscreenThe team at Mahmood mosque in Malmö.Photograph: Emma Larsson/The GuardianAhead of Sweden’s general election on Sunday, polls show the centre-left opposition has a narrow lead, suggesting that the rightwing minority-run coalition supported by the far-right Sweden Democrats could be ousted.Such a result would not only be significant for the Scandinavian country; it could also reassure mainstream voters acrossEuropethat far-right forces such as the Sweden Democrats or Germany’s Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) – triumphant after its best showing in a state election last weekend – are not inevitably on the rise.But even so, the Swedish polls have narrowed slightly in recent weeks, making many nervous, particularly as the right-leaning ruling coalition hasfor the first timesaid it would offer ministerial posts to the far right if it wins. Those who have borne the brunt of the far right’s time propping up the government worry that Sweden, long held up as a leading light when it comes to equality and freedom, may have been irrevocably changed, regardless of what happens on Sunday.“It’s a kind of Pandora’s box that has been opened,” said Munir Niazi, who has long worked with Virk on the Ask-a-Muslim campaign.During the government of the centre-right prime minister Ulf Kristersson, the far-right Sweden Democrats haveused their leverageto steer policies on migration and crime, seizing on the spotlight to spread rhetoric linking the two and scapegoating migrants, Muslims and other minorities for all that ails the country.View image in fullscreenMunir Niazi, who also works on the Ask-a-Muslim campaign, with Virk (right) at the mosque.Photograph: Emma Larsson/The GuardianThe result had shifted Sweden’s national conversation to the right, said Niazi. “In the past four years, the biggest opposition party, the Social Democrats, have slowly adopted and even voted with the right wing on migration, on crime. In the near future, at least, we don’t see the country going back to the policies of the 80s and 90s.”Virk nodded in agreement. “We see, unfortunately, that everybody plays the anti-Islam card when they need it.”The repercussions have been felt widely. Last year, a gunman killed 10 people in the Swedish city of Örebro,most of whomhad an immigrant background. Across Sweden, mosques have regularly been vandalised and in 2023 the country grappled with aspate of protestsin which copies of the Qur’an were burned or otherwise damaged.Speaking to commuters in Malmö making their way through Hyllie station, many said the politics had started to feel deeply personal, as though their existence in Sweden was a political battleground.“When the far right talk about my religion and my hijab, it feels like they’re talking about an animal,” said one nurse, 46, who asked not to be named.View image in fullscreenIn 2023 the country grappled with protests where copies of the Qur’an were burned or otherwise damaged.Photograph: Jonas Gratzer/Getty ImagesOriginally from Lebanon, she had settled in Sweden in 1999. “The older people in the hospital say that myself and other immigrants have helped to build Sweden – why doesn’t the far right see this?”Sitting in a nearby park, Onyango, 42, said the atmosphere in Sweden had become “horrible” for migrants amid the far right’s steady increase in influence. “I feel like they poison the population,” he said. “They’ve created an environment where if you’re not a Swede, you are scared.”The hostile rhetoric, coupled with efforts by the government to tighten the rules around migration, had left the Kenyan national devising a backup plan despite nine years spent in the country and a good job working with supply chains. “You start thinking maybe I need to have an apartment in Kenya and set aside some money, just in case,” he said.Sitting next to him, his friend Waithira, 30, nodded in agreement. “Before you wanted to invest here, buy an apartment here, start a business. But now you start thinking twice,” she said. “We don’t know what the future holds, but it’s a bit less attractive than before.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the southern reaches of Stockholm’s Södermalm district, Jonna Mannberg and Isaac Kuehnle-Nelson recalled how in 2015, about 1,700 people from across the country spontaneously turned up at the city’s central station, eager to welcome and help settle Syrian and Afghan asylum seekers as they arrived.In the 11 years since, the initiative, formalised into Refugees Welcome Stockholm, had unwittingly become a shorthand for the changes sweeping Sweden. “We’ve gone from being an organisation that was at the forefront of public political dialogue in Sweden to being a smaller organisation where our funding and ability to reach out have shrunk significantly,” said Kuehnle-Nelson.They had watched as policy stances once reserved for the far right became mainstream, from aslashing of refugeequotas from 5,000 to 900 people a year, to allowing residency permits to be revoked over the vaguely defined criteria of “bad behaviour”.“In 2015, people were met with open arms. We had the prime minister say: ‘My Europe doesn’t build walls,’” said Mannberg. “But the harsh reality is that we still have the same people that we were dealing with in 2015. We’re still with them in 2026 and they have not received legal status yet.”View image in fullscreenThe far-right Sweden Democrats have leverage in the Swedish parliament since their support is needed by the ruling coalition.Photograph: Tom Little/ReutersThe psychological toll was laid bare during a recent programming course for young, undocumented asylum seekers. “There were days when many were unable to attend because they couldn’t get out of bed,” she said. “To have physically healthy, 20-year-old guys who have been so pushed down by life that they were unable to leave their beds, unable to see any future for themselves, that’s a really hard thing.”Among those caught up in the crackdown on asylum seekers was an undocumented 14-year-old who, despite being born in Sweden, was facing deportation to Armenia, along with his single-parent mother and his younger brother. “It’s like hell. I’ve been here my whole life,” he told the Guardian. “I feel Swedish.”His parents had come to Sweden as political asylum claimants, but their separation resulted in the claim becoming mired in bureaucracy. While there had been a visa category that might have given the family another chance of continuing the lives they had built in Sweden, it was scrapped recently by the rightwing government.Instead, the order looms over them, clouding the life of a child who had sung in a church choir and dreamed of a future as a civil engineer in Sweden. “It feels horrible,” he said, pointing out that he had never been to Armenia, did not speak the language and was terrified about the possibility of being forced to complete its mandatory military service.The changes to immigration policy, includingrecently introduced rulesbarring most asylum seekers from accessing permanent residency, were an example of how the political conversation in Sweden had been transformed by the far right’s time as power-brokers, said journalist Bilan Osman.“There’s a lot of proposals in Swedish politics today that we couldn’t even imagine 10 years ago,” she said, citing the tens of thousands of eurosbeing offeredto migrants to return home as an example. “People would have said: ‘You’re a lunatic.’ Now it’s like: ‘Let’s discuss it.’”Osman had long researched rightwing extremism, tracking the movement as they created their own media outlets capable of reaching new audiences. What emerged was a steady normalisation of their discourse, blaming migrants and minorities for Sweden’s social and economic ills, while the fallout of the country’ssoaringinequality levels was largely overlooked.The resulting rhetoric had pushed some to the margins, recasting Sweden as a place where some belonged and others were made to feel as though they did not. It was a marked shift that would probably have long-lasting consequences, she said, citing Swedish Muslims, who make up an estimated 8% of the population, as an example.“I think we are at a breaking point right now in Sweden, where the main question is: ‘Is there a future for Muslims in this country?’” said Osman. “If we continue to have these kinds of discussions, I think a lot of Muslims will feel that there is not a future here. And that’s sad.”Explore more on these topicsSwedenIslamReligionEuropeMigrationThe far rightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Secret son revelation ignites bitter succession dispute in Ugandan kingdom | Uganda | The Guardian
description: Family of late King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV reject committee’s choice of cousin and TV presenter as new monarch
Author: Carlos Mureithi
Headline: Family of late King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV reject committee’s choice of cousin and TV presenter as new monarch
Content: Mourners including Princess Ruth Komuntale (second left) and the Queen Mother Best Kemigisa Akiiki (right) at Entebbe International airport, where they  received the coffin containing the body of King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV.Photograph: Abubaker Lubowa/ReutersView image in fullscreenMourners including Princess Ruth Komuntale (second left) and the Queen Mother Best Kemigisa Akiiki (right) at Entebbe International airport, where they  received the coffin containing the body of King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV.Photograph: Abubaker Lubowa/ReutersUgandaSecret son revelation ignites bitter succession dispute in Ugandan kingdomFamily of late King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV reject committee’s choice of cousin and TV presenter as new monarchCarlos Mureithiin Nairobi and agenciesThu 10 Sep 2026 13.29 EDTFirst published on Thu 10 Sep 2026 11.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA traditional Ugandan kingdom has become engulfed in a bitter succession dispute after the family of a king who recently died rejected the selection of a television news anchor as his successor.King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who became the world’s youngest reigning monarch when he took the throne in the kingdom of Tooro in 1995 at the age of three, died on 27 August in the US, where he was receiving cancer treatment.View image in fullscreenKing Oyo Nyimba, aged 13, sits between his mother Best Kemigisha and an unidentified adviser during celebrations marking his first decade in power in Fort Portal, Uganda.Photograph: ReutersOn Wednesday, the royal clan’s succession committee announced it had chosen Oyo’s cousin Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, a news anchor and editor at the public broadcaster UBC, as crown prince.However, at a press conference held later the same day, Oyo’s sister, Princess Ruth Nsemere Komuntale, said that according to her brother’s will, a son whose existence had not been publicly known until his death should succeed him.View image in fullscreenPrincess Ruth Komuntale waiting to receive the body of her brother, the late King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, at Entebbe International airport last week.Photograph: Hajarah Nalwadda/Getty ImagesThe kingdom’s ‌spokesperson shared a section of the document, which says: “I hereby declare and direct that if, at the date of my death, I am survived by a son lawfully recognised as my biological son, I appoint him as my heir to the throne of the kingdom of Tooro.”In a statement on Thursday, Oyo’s mother, Queen Mother Best Kemigisa Akiiki, denounced a “self-appointed group of clan members” who had selected a new king despite having had the will read to them hours earlier.She also claimed that the royal family had been put under house arrest. Troops had “removed the royal guards without notice, and ... were deployed around the palace,” she said. “We cannot leave or receive people freely.”View image in fullscreenA portrait of the late king on the red carpet at Entebbe International airport.Photograph: Hajarah Nalwadda/Getty ImagesOyo was unmarried and was not known to have any children. The Tooro kingdom’s prime minister, Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki, revealed the existence of a son ina social media poston 27 August when announcing Oyo’s death.“His majesty leaves behind a prince as his heir, whose identity will be formally revealed at the appropriate time, in accordance with the traditions and customs of Tooro kingdom,” he said.Another contender had been Prince George Desmond-Kamurasi, who plays for the London amateur football club South East Dons. According to the committee, the goalkeeper had declined the offer of the throne because of his other responsibilities.The Tooro king is selected by a succession committee appointed by the royal clan. A committee member told the local NTV station that a royal child must be officially introduced to elders in order to be considered for leadership.View image in fullscreenQueen Mother Best Kemigisa Akiiki waiting to receive the body of her son at Entebbe International airport.Photograph: Hajarah Nalwadda/Getty ImagesAndrew Mwenda, ⁠a prominent Ugandan journalist and relative of the royal family, wrote on X on Thursday that Oyo’s ​family had not been able to produce a photo ​of the purported son, and declined to disclose ​details about the family of the boy’s mother. He added that, in Tooro, a king’s son could only succeed ​him if he were born to ‌a queen officially married ​to the king.The prime minister ​called for restraint on Thursday. “There will be time to examine the will, to hear those advancing a different position, and to consider our customs, the applicable law and the proper institutions through which succession should be determined,” he said ina social media post.“That process should take place calmly and credibly, not through competing announcements, confrontation, or attempts to establish facts on the ground while our king still awaits burial.”View image in fullscreenUganda’s president, Yoweri Museveni, lays a wreath on the casket of the king at Entebbe International airport.Photograph: Hajarah Nalwadda/Getty ImagesEdward, a popular TV news presenter, is the son of Prince Christopher Paul Kijanangoma and a grandson of the former king George David Rukidi III.Oyo, who was crowned after his father’s death, will be buried on Saturday at the Karambi royal tombs in the kingdom’s capital of Fort Portal in western Uganda.Uganda has several ancient kingdoms that lack formal sovereignty, but whose leaders are revered as symbols of tradition and wield vast social influence. Tooro is one of five that are recognised by the government. Their monarchs have no political authority and are legally barred from engaging in partisan politics.In 1967 Uganda’s then president, Milton Obote, abolished the kingdoms, saying he wanted to unify the country. They were restored bythe current president, Yoweri Museveni, in 1993.View image in fullscreenThe casket of the late king arrives at Entebbe International airport.Photograph: Hajarah Nalwadda/Getty ImagesThe Tooro are the latest African royal family to become mired in a succession dispute. King Misuzulu Sinqobile kaZwelithini, the reigning king of the Zulu people in South Africa, waited 15 months for his coronation after the death of his father because of a bitter feud involving accusations offorgery and poisoning.Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsUgandaAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Canada offers air defense support for Ukraine as Zelenskyy visits | Canada | The Guardian
description: Canadian PM Mark Carney hosts president in Calgary, where he grew up alongside large Ukrainian community
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Canadian PM Mark Carney hosts president in Calgary, where he grew up alongside large Ukrainian community
Content: Mark Carney and Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrive in Calgary, Alberta, to sign agreements on Thursday.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenMark Carney and Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrive in Calgary, Alberta, to sign agreements on Thursday.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockCanadaCanada offers air defense support for Ukraine as Zelenskyy visitsCanadian PM Mark Carney hosts president in Calgary, where he grew up alongside large Ukrainian communityAgence France-PresseThu 10 Sep 2026 16.35 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 16.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCanada offered support on Thursday to boost Ukraine’s air defenses and help replenish its drone stocks, as the countries pledged to deepen their alliance during a visit byVolodymyr Zelenskyy.Mark Carney hosted the president of Ukraine in Calgary in the western province of Alberta, where the Canadian prime minister grew up among a large community of people with Ukrainian heritage.“Canada will always be with you,” Carney assured Zelenskyy.The leaders signed an agreement to work toward a “hundred-year partnership”.That deal, to be negotiated over the coming months, aims to codify cooperation in a range of areas, including defense, critical minerals and energy.“Our two nations have been connected since 1893,” Carney said, referring to a wave of Ukrainians who migrated to the new Canadian nation.In Alberta, there are an estimated 350,000 Canadians of Ukrainian descent.“Ukrainians helped build Canada and Canadians will help rebuildUkraine,” Carney said.The support announced on Thursday includes C$350m (US$253m) provided through the United States’ Joint Ukraine Multinational Program – Services, Training and Articles Rapid Timeline (Jumpstart) program.Zelenskyy has emphasized the need for increased air defense as Russia ramps up ballistic missile attacks.Carney said Canada was also offering C$450m in loan guarantees to enhance the Ukrainian energy supply.The funds will help repair damaged infrastructure, increase storage capacity and improve power supply to hospitals.Carney said the goal of the energy support was “to help Ukrainians get through the winter”, a difficult period when the country endures rolling blackouts amid often frigid temperatures.Canada is moving aggressively to increase its own drone stocks, Carney said, announcing a deal that will see 30% of new Canadian production head to Ukraine.Zelenskyy told reporters that “these drones will go to Ukraine immediately to [the] battlefield, immediately to our people, our soldiers … to save our children, our families first of all.”Asked about potential negotiations to ease the fighting, Zelenskyy said he did not anticipate any substantive talks during Russia’s ongoing election period.But he said he planned to meet Donald Trump in New York City in late September, probably on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, with Washington bidding to revive long-stalled talks to end the war.“But at the end of September, we will have an opportunity to meet, I think, with the American team in New York,” Zelenskyy said.“And I think that … I can be more open after the New York meeting with President Trump.”After the Calgary meeting, Zelenskyy was headed to Banff, a stunning Canadian national park, where he will address a cabinet retreat for Carney’s liberal government.He then heads to Canada’s largest city, Toronto, and North Bay in northern Ontario.Explore more on these topicsCanadaUkraineVolodymyr ZelenskyyMark CarneyAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Rubio signals shift to working with allies to fight drug trade as latest boat strike kills three | Marco Rubio | The Guardian
description: Rubio visits Ecuador and welcomes cooperation after campaign of unilateral strikes on alleged ‘narco-terrorists’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Rubio visits Ecuador and welcomes cooperation after campaign of unilateral strikes on alleged ‘narco-terrorists’
Content: Marco Rubio outside the US embassy in Quito on Wednesday.Photograph: Dolores Ochoa/ReutersView image in fullscreenMarco Rubio outside the US embassy in Quito on Wednesday.Photograph: Dolores Ochoa/ReutersMarco RubioRubio signals shift to working with allies to fight drug trade as latest boat strike kills threeRubio visits Ecuador and welcomes cooperation after campaign of unilateral strikes on alleged ‘narco-terrorists’Associated PressWed 9 Sep 2026 21.02 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 14.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US secretary of state,Marco Rubio, gave new clarity on the approach toward combating drug trafficking in Latin American waters, saying the Trump administration was focused on working with allied countries and aligning with their laws but insisted the military would “still blow up ships if need be”.The public acknowledgment of a shift in US strategy comes a year after Washington began a campaign of unilateral deadly strikes against those it calls “narco-terrorists” operating boats in international waters.Late Wednesday, US Southern Commandannounced the latest such strikein the Caribbean Sea, saying it killed three people. That brought the number of people who have been killed in boat strikes by the US military to at least 230 in 69 strikes.Still, the Trump administration is focused on building agreements for joint operations with allied countries in the region, including Colombia andEcuador, that comply with their laws in their waters.“I think its an incredible advance for the first time to have countries that are willing to participate in these efforts in their territorial waters,” Rubio told reporters on a trip to the Ecuadorian capital, Quito.“The important point is that these routes are being disrupted. These routes are being ended,” he added.He said the decision is “a strike-by-strike or operation-by-operation determination” that depends on the threat and location of the boat.Recent US interdictions in Latin American waters are unlike the Trump administration’s initial strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats that began in September 2025. People onboard floating refueling stations said to be supporting drug trafficking have been removed and transferred to Ecuadorian authorities. Then theUS militaryblows up the vessels.The shift comes after a series of strikes on boats over the year on people the Trump administration accused of being “narco-terrorists” without providing evidence.Rubio’s comments came during a three-country tour of South America aimed at boosting security cooperation with conservative leaders who have cozied up to Donald Trump.Explore more on these topicsMarco RubioUS foreign policyEcuadorUS militaryDrugs tradeAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Japan seeks change to new UN world map over Russia 'misconception' | Japan | The Guardian
description: The new ‘true-scale’ map shrinks Europe and North America while enlarging Africa – and depicts the disputed Kuril islands as ruled by Moscow
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The new ‘true-scale’ map shrinks Europe and North America while enlarging Africa – and depicts the disputed Kuril islands as ruled by Moscow
Content: Japan was among the 164 UN members who voted in favour of the new Equal Earth map.Illustration: equal-earth.comView image in fullscreenJapan was among the 164 UN members who voted in favour of the new Equal Earth map.Illustration: equal-earth.comJapanJapan seeks change to new UN world map over Russia 'misconception'The new ‘true-scale’ map shrinks Europe and North America while enlarging Africa – and depicts the disputed Kuril islands as ruled by MoscowAgence France-Presse in TokyoThu 10 Sep 2026 08.55 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 17.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJapan has asked for the revision of a new world map adopted by the UN because it said it made the disputed Kuril islands appear to belong toRussia.The UN general assembly voted on Friday to adopt the new map, which makes the African continent larger while also shrinking North America andEurope, drawing condemnation from the US.UN votes to adopt new world map that shows Africa’s true scaleRead moreJapan was among the 164 UN members that supported the resolution, but has now taken issue with it because it shows the Kurils, known inJapanas the Northern Territories, in the same colour as Russia.Ukraine last week abstained in the UN vote on the map as it showed occupied Crimea in a different colour to the rest of the country, which its representatives at the UNwarned opens a “Pandora’s box” violating the UN charter and international law.Japanese government spokesperson Minoru Kihara on Thursday said the new map – known as the Equal Earth cartographic projection – “contained a depiction contradicting the Japanese government’s position”.“We lodged a protest with the map site’s operator through our diplomatic channel to demand the correction of this depiction,” Kihara told reporters.He declined to say when the issue was brought to government’s attention but said Japan “needs to prevent misconceptions of our territories and geographical names from spreading”.The disputed islands were seized in 1945 by the former Soviet Union, which then expelled the Japanese population.View image in fullscreenThe disputed Kuril islands, top right.Photograph: equal-earth.comRelations between Japan and Russia soured significantly last month, when the Russian president, Vladimir Putin,made a surprise visitto the disputed islands for the first time.Japan swiftly summoned Moscow’s ambassador, with the prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, saying Putin’s visit “offends the sentiments of the Japanese people”, adding that it was “absolutely unacceptable”.She said the islands were “an inherent part of Japan’s territory, both historically and under international law”.Moscow quickly hit back, saying it “categorically” rejects such statements, “which we consider politically inappropriate, insulting and, of course, legally unfounded”.The UN said the new map aimed to present “a more accurate representation” of continental landmasses than was portrayed by more traditional Mercator projections.Ukraine was last week among six countries that abstained in the voteExplore more on these topicsJapanUnited NationsRussiaAsia PacificEuropeMapsnewsShareReuse title: Wall Street Journal publisher convicted in Hong Kong of deterring reporter from union role | Hong Kong | The Guardian
description: Dow Jones convicted of one count of deterring Selina Cheng from role at Hong Kong Journalist Association but cleared of second charge
Author: Danny Vincent
Headline: Dow Jones convicted of one count of deterring Selina Cheng from role at Hong Kong Journalist Association but cleared of second charge
Content: Selina Cheng says she was told her termination from the WSJ was officially due to restructuring.Photograph: Tyrone Siu/ReutersView image in fullscreenSelina Cheng says she was told her termination from the WSJ was officially due to restructuring.Photograph: Tyrone Siu/ReutersHong KongWall Street Journal publisher convicted in Hong Kong of deterring reporter from union roleDow Jones convicted of one count of deterring Selina Cheng from role at Hong Kong Journalist Association but cleared of second chargeDanny Vincentin Hong KongThu 10 Sep 2026 01.57 EDTFirst published on Thu 10 Sep 2026 01.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Hong Kong court has convicted the publisher of theWall Street Journalof deterring a reporter from taking up a trade union role, in a case that raised concerns about press freedom in the city.The newspaperdismissed Selina Chengjust weeks after she was appointed chair of the Hong Kong Journalist Association (HKJA) in 2024. She was told at the time her termination was officially due to restructuring.Outside court on Thursday, Cheng said: “If reporters’ employment rights are not sufficiently safeguarded, or when their rights are violated and not enforced in law, then we can no longer work safely as reporters.”Principal magistrate David Cheung ruled that Dow Jones Publishing, the parent company of the Wall Street journal, was guilty of “preventing or deterring an employee from exercising trade union rights,” but acquitted it of “dismissing or discriminating against an employee because she exercised those rights.”Cheng, who covered China’s automobiles and energy sectors for the WSJ, said her editor had told her that employees should not be seen as advocating for press freedom in “places like Hong Kong”, saying it could be perceived as a conflict of interest. She alleged her employer had attempted to prevent her from taking up a role in the union.‘She’s not afraid of anyone’: the prison writings of one of Hong Kong’s last outspoken democracy activistsRead moreShe said the company told her that she needed to seek the firm’s approval for outside activities and requested her to leave her then-board position at the association.Cheng launched the private prosecution against Dow Jones Publishing after losing her job in July 2024, weeks after taking up the position as chair of the union.The company pleaded not guilty to both charges, which each carry a maximum fine of HK$100,000 (about $12,750).Sentencing is expected to be handed down at a later date.During the trial, the defence argued that Cheng was terminated because of redundancy and that the prosecution had not sufficiently proved that the firm’s management instructed Cheng’s supervisor. The defence also accused Cheng of acting in bad faith in a previous hearing.But magistrate David Cheung said that Cheng’s termination “was motivated by wrongful and unjustified application of their code of conduct” when it insisted Cheng needed to seek prior approval to stand as chair of HKJA.Cheung said he accepted Cheng’s explanation, describing the former WSJ reporter as “honest and reliable”, adding she and was clearly motivated by “the wish to see justice”.Cheng’s termination alarmed journalists, who are already operating in an increasingly restricted media environment in the city, where foreign outlets have traditionally faced less pressure than local news outlets.“The WSJ set a very bad precedent by punishing an employee who was exercising her constitutionally protected rights in Hong Kong,” said Eric Lai, a senior fellow at the Georgetown Center for Asian Law.The WSJ maintained there was no link between Cheng’s role in the Hong Kong union and her termination. At the time of Cheng’s dismissal, it issued a statement saying: “The Wall Street Journal has been and continues to be a fierce and vocal advocate for press freedom in Hong Kong and around the world.”HKJA is the oldest journalist union in Hong Kong. It was established in 1968 and is registered as a trade union representing journalists and workers in news. It has faced increasing pressure since the introduction of aBeijing-imposed national security lawin 2020.Hong Kong has fallen sharply in global press freedom rankings since the law’s introduction. In 2019 Reporters Without Borders ranked the city 73rd in the world. By 2026 it had fallen 67 places to 140th out of 180 countries and territories.Explore more on these topicsHong KongWall Street JournalCensorshipChinaAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Deadly Philippines ferry fire triggers search for scores of missing | Philippines | The Guardian
description: Multiple search and rescue vessels deployed after blaze off Palawan island leaves at least five dead, says coast guard
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Multiple search and rescue vessels deployed after blaze off Palawan island leaves at least five dead, says coast guard
Content: 0:46Philippines ferry fire leaves at least five dead and scores missing – videoPhilippinesDeadly Philippines ferry fire triggers search for scores of missingMultiple search and rescue vessels deployed after blaze off Palawan island leaves at least five dead, says coast guardReutersThu 10 Sep 2026 01.54 EDTFirst published on Wed 9 Sep 2026 22.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA large-scale ⁠search and rescue operation ​is under way off the western Philippine island of Palawan on Thursday after a passenger ferry caught fire, killing five people and leaving ⁠scores of passengers missing.The Philippine coast guard said multiple vessels and other assets were searching for survivors as rescue teams used drift-modelling tools ⁠to identify areas where people may have been carried by currents.Based on the vessel’s manifest, the ​number of survivors – currently at 43 – and ‌the fatalities reported so ‌far, authorities estimated that more than 80 people remained unaccounted for, although the figures could still change.Coast ‌guard spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said rescuers could not yet enter the M/V June Aster, with the search hampered by thick smoke still billowing from the ferry and concerns about extreme heat and the risk of explosions.Drone footage released by the coast guard showed the blackened ferry surrounded by clear blue-green waters, with the vessel still generating smoke hours after the ‌fire broke out on Wednesday night.View image in fullscreenSmoke rising from the burnt passenger ferry M/V June Aster off Palawan province, Philippines, on Thursday.Photograph: Philippine coast guard /EPACayabyab said the vessel’s manifest listed a total of 117 passengers and 17 crew members. The ferry had departed from Baseco ​in Manila and was bound for Coron, a popular tourist destination in Palawan known for its diving sites, beaches and island-hopping attractions.Biodiversity fears as human-bred hybrid fish integrate into Philippines lakeRead moreAmong the 43 people rescued were two Chilean nationals, said Aileen Ausente, a spokesperson for the coast guard in Palawan, adding that air assets were on standby to help with rescue operations, ⁠weather permitting.The burned ferry had drifted farther from its original location overnight, ​carried by currents and winds, ​adding to the challenges facing rescuers, ​Cayabyab said.View image in fullscreenA survivor is helped off a small boat after being rescued from the burning ferry.Photograph: Philippine coast guard/APThe cause of the fire is under investigation.Ferry travel is a ​common mode of ‌transport in thePhilippines, ​an archipelago of ​more than 7,600 islands, where millions of people rely on boats to travel between provinces.The country has a patchy maritime safety record, and many previous ferry disasters have been linked to overcrowding, rough weather and lax enforcement of safety regulations.Explore more on these topicsPhilippinesAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: North Korea has built new uranium facility to expand nuclear arsenal, UN agency says | North Korea | The Guardian
description: The International Atomic Energy Agency voices ‘serious concerns’ over expansion of Yongbyon facility to enrich uranium
Author: Justin McCurry
Headline: The International Atomic Energy Agency voices ‘serious concerns’ over expansion of Yongbyon facility to enrich uranium
Content: Kim Jong-un tours a nuclear facility in June. The IAEA says North Korea has built a new facility capable of enriching weapons grade uranium.Photograph: KCNA VIA KNS/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKim Jong-un tours a nuclear facility in June. The IAEA says North Korea has built a new facility capable of enriching weapons grade uranium.Photograph: KCNA VIA KNS/AFP/Getty ImagesNorth KoreaNorth Korea has built new uranium facility to expand nuclear arsenal, UN agency saysThe International Atomic Energy Agency voices ‘serious concerns’ over expansion of Yongbyon facility to enrich uraniumJustin McCurryin TokyoThu 10 Sep 2026 01.08 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 01.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has voiced “serious concern” over evidence thatNorth Koreahas built a facility capable of enriching weapons-grade uranium to bolster its nuclear arsenal.The new building, located at the the country’s main Yongbyon nuclear facility, can house up to 28 centrifuge cascades – machinery commonly used to enrich uranium – according to a report by the nuclear watchdog released this week.The regime has also expanded operations at an enrichment site in Kangson, near the capital Pyongyang, according to the report, which was based on analysis of satellite imagery and open-source material, including photographs published by the country’s state media.North Korea’s ‘exponential’ nuclear program: why Kim Jong-un is racing to expand his arsenalRead moreThe IAEA, whose inspectors wereexpelled from North Korea in 2009, identified the Yongbyon building as the site’s second uranium ‌enrichment facility after comparing satellite images taken during its construction with media photographs of a visit in early June by the country’s leader,Kim Jong-un.View image in fullscreenA satellite image from 4 September shows the nuclear material production factory in Yongbyon.Photograph: 2026 Planet Labs PBC/ReutersDuring his visit, Kim claimed the North’s capacity to produce weapons-grade nuclear materialhad more than doubled over the past five years, according to state media, promising “vast future plans to exponentially strengthen the country’s nuclear forces”.Citing a 2025 analysis by the James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies in the US, South Korea’s Chosun Daily said the potential 28 cascades comprising 4,592 centrifuges at the Yongbyon facility could yield about 85 kg of weapons-grade highly enriched uranium a year – enough to build three or four additional warheads.In a statement released this week, the IAEA’s director general, Rafael Grossi, said: “The ongoing operation of enrichment facilities at Kangson and Yongbyon and the reported further expansion of [North Korea’s] production of weapons-grade nuclear material is a cause for serious concern.”“The continuation and further development” of North Korea’s nuclear programme are “clear violations of relevant UN security council resolutions and are deeply regrettable”, he added.South Korea’s defence minister, Ahn Gyu-back, said in August that the North possessed between 80 and 120 nuclear warheads – a much higher number than the 57 cited by Donald Trump the same month. The South Korean figure was based on estimates by private research organisations, Ahn told lawmakers, adding that the country’s military could not confirm the numbers.North Korea has made rapid progress in itsballistic missileand nuclear programmes in recent years, as it demands international recognition as a legitimate nuclear state.North Korea has conducted multiple long-range missile tests since 2017, the year it lasttested a nuclear weapon. In a report submitted to the UN security council in 2020, international experts said the North had “probably developed nuclear devices to fit into the warheads of its ballistic missiles”.Explore more on these topicsNorth KoreaKim Jong-unInternational Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA)Nuclear weaponsAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Woolworths increased prices of at least four ‘family staples’ during ‘Price Freeze’ promotion | Woolworths | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Analysis shows cost of chicken fillets, potatoes and donuts rose during supermarket giant’s three-month promotion
Author: Catie McLeod
Headline: Exclusive: Analysis shows cost of chicken fillets, potatoes and donuts rose during supermarket giant’s three-month promotion
Content: Woolworths increased the prices of at least four key products during its ‘Price Freeze’ promotion, pricing data reveals.Photograph: Loren Elliott/ReutersView image in fullscreenWoolworths increased the prices of at least four key products during its ‘Price Freeze’ promotion, pricing data reveals.Photograph: Loren Elliott/ReutersWoolworthsWoolworths increased prices of at least four ‘family staples’ during ‘Price Freeze’ promotionExclusive:Analysis shows cost of chicken fillets, potatoes and donuts rose during supermarket giant’s three-month promotionFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastCatie McLeodConsumer affairs reporterThu 10 Sep 2026 18.05 EDTFirst published on Thu 10 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWoolworths raised prices for popular items – including a 33% mark up on chicken fillets – within days of promising to freeze prices on 300 “family staples” for three months to help customers with the cost of living.Pricing data, compiled by comparison website CW Scanner and provided to Guardian Australia, shows the supermarket chain increasing the prices of at least four key products after starting the three-month “Price Freeze” promotion on 1 May.The supermarket nearly doubled the price of a 420g can of Woolworths “Mexican Style 3 Bean Mix” during the promotional period – from 60c to $1 on 17 June – the data shows. Woolworths dropped the price back to 60c on 17 August.Woolworths posts $1.14bn profit in cost-of-living crisis – but CEO says it’s not thanks to rising shelf pricesRead moreWoolworths has justified the increases because it regarded the previous prices as promotional prices, rather than the “standard shelf price” for each product.A Woolworths spokesperson said that the end of a temporary promotion did not represent a shelf price increase.“The Price Freeze gave our customers the certainty that they would not pay more than the shelf price on 300 popular products for three months – and we delivered on that,” the spokesperson said.When theprice freeze was announced, the Woolworths chief executive officer, Amanda Bardwell, said the supermarket wanted to help customers who were concerned about how inflation driven by the war on Iran was affecting household budgets.“That’s why, for the next three months, we’re freezing the shelf price on 300 staples that families rely on most, like eggs, chicken breast fillets, pasta, beef sausages and nappies,” Bardwell said in a press release on 30 April.“It’s our promise that the shelf price you see on these items today is the most you’ll pay for the next three months. We’ll invest to absorb any extra costs that are agreed with suppliers on these products to make that happen.”Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailProf Jana Bowden, a marketing expert and chair of ethics at Macquarie University’s business school, said raising prices after claiming they had been fixed was “akin to not delivering on the everyday consumer’s interpretation of a ‘price freeze’ promise”.“How is the consumer expected to know what the start prices were before the campaign or even after the campaign started?” Bowden said.“No consumer walks into a supermarket with the insights of how the prices for the hundreds of products that they buy vary over a day, week, month or year – nor should they have to.”The analysis comes at a time of high scrutiny of the pricing tactics used byWoolworths– and rivalColes– after landmark court cases involving both companies.Woolworths is awaiting the verdict inthe federal court casebrought against it by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC), with the watchdog alleging the supermarket misled shoppers with effectively fake discounts on its “Prices Dropped” campaign.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPrices unfrozenDuring its price freeze period, Woolworths increased the retail price of 350g packs of RSPCA-approved chicken breast fillets by 33%.While a customer would have paid $9 for the chicken breast fillets on 29 April, the price increased to $12 on 5 May. It then alternated between $9 and $12 twice more during the “Price Freeze”.But, after the promotional period ended, the price dropped to $4.20 on 17 August.Before the promotion, Woolworths’ 2kg bags of washed potatoes had consistently followed a routine high-low pricing pattern alternating between $6 and $8. This appears to have occurred during the promotional period, with CW Scanner data showing they cost customers $6 on 29 April, before the price went up to $8 on 6 May.The price of a 12-pack of the supermarket’s own-brand fresh cinnamon donuts was increased from $3 to $3.50 on 6 May. It was reduced to $3 again on 18 August.Choice’s senior campaigns and policy adviser, Bea Sherwood, said the advocacy group regularly heard from consumers who said they were confused by the pricing tickets they saw on supermarket shelves.“Prices have changed so much over recent years and we’re seeing them continuously increase, so having an understanding of what a regular shelf price is is not something we can expect consumers to stay on top of,” Sherwood said.“When Woolworths or Coles say something is a standard price, we don’t have the transparency to understand how they’ve come to that.”Explore more on these topicsWoolworthsSupermarketsConsumer affairsBusinessnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I don’t want to be here’: Andrew Hastie was a reluctant but ‘straightforward’ witness in the Ben Roberts-Smith defamation case | Andrew Hastie | The Guardian
description: The Liberal MP and former SAS soldier is under attack from One Nation after complying with a subpoena to give evidence in the failed 2022 civil case
Author: Ben Doherty
Headline: The Liberal MP and former SAS soldier is under attack from One Nation after complying with a subpoena to give evidence in the failed 2022 civil case
Content: Andrew Hastie leaving the federal court in 2022 after giving evidence as part of the Ben Roberts-Smith defamation trial.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPView image in fullscreenAndrew Hastie leaving the federal court in 2022 after giving evidence as part of the Ben Roberts-Smith defamation trial.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPAndrew HastieAnalysis‘I don’t want to be here’: Andrew Hastie was a reluctant but ‘straightforward’ witness in the Ben Roberts-Smith defamation caseBen DohertyThe Liberal MP and former SAS soldier is under attack from One Nation after complying with a subpoena to give evidence in the failed 2022 civil caseFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastThu 10 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 16.42 EDTShare“I don’t dislike Mr Roberts-Smith at all. I pity Mr Roberts-Smith. I pity this whole process. I don’t want to be here.”Andrew Hastie was a reluctant witness in theBen Roberts-Smithdefamation case. Hastie appeared only under force of subpoena in 2022: compelled to attend court, obliged to swear an oath, and to tell “the whole truth and nothing but the truth”.His was an unhappy (of many) visit to the witness box. But it brought with it an additional scrutiny: he was, at the time of the case, not only a member of parliament, but the assistant minister for defence. Of the dozens of former SAS soldiers compelled to give evidence to the defamation case – many resentfully – Hastie was the only one named and photographed, the only one not afforded the protection of being a “sensitive witness”.In his judgment, Justice Anthony Besanko was approbative: “Mr Hastie was an honest and straightforward witness.” Three times, in fact, he characterised the former officer, now MP, as “straightforward” in his testimony.Andrew Hastie accuses Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce of being ‘lying cowards’ over One Nation ‘traitor’ cartoonRead moreOf Hastie’s former comrade who brought the defamation case – Victoria Cross recipient Ben Roberts-Smith – Besanko was equally forthright, but less complimentary.“[Roberts-Smith] was not an honest and reliable witness.“In each case, [his] motive for the lie is the realisation of guilt and a fear of the truth.”Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereNow, for his testimony, Hastie has been referred to as a “gutless maggot” and a “traitor” in a cartoon posted online by Pauline Hanson’s One Nation party. Hanson, personally, said she would prefer to call Hastie a “wanker”.‘Blooding’Membership of “the regiment” – the SAS – is famously clandestine. Roberts-Smith and Hastie are perhaps its best-known former members. The pair’s service, while contemporaneous, was not tightly aligned. They are not close.Hastie, an officer, has written he remembers hisfirst encounter with Roberts-Smith– the corporal ordering officer candidates into push-ups in a dead-of-night training exercise. Hetold the federal court there was a “widespread view”across the SAS that Roberts-Smith was a bully.Before the federal court, Hastie was asked to testify as to his recollection of an operation on a compound in a village known as Syachow in October 2012. It was his only operation in Afghanistan alongside Roberts-Smith.It was alleged before the federal court that on that mission Roberts-Smith ordered a subordinate soldier – known as Person 66 – to execute an unarmed prisoner in a so-called “blooding” incident.Hastie did not shy away from recounting details of the event in his testimony.Person 66, too, was subpoenaed to appear in court. He refused to answer a question about whether he’d been on operation in Afghanistan with Roberts-Smith as his patrol commander.“Person 66 objected to giving an answer to that question on the ground that it may tend to prove that he had committed the offence of the war crime of murder,” Besanko wrote in his judgment.On those grounds, Besanko could not find the allegation proved.Asked directly whether he ordered Person 66 to kill an unarmed prisoner, Roberts-Smith told the court: “I did not.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHastie told the court he once held Robert-Smith in “very high regard”.“I am no longer proud of Mr Roberts-Smith.”‘Shoot him’The alleged incident at Syahchow is one of the five war crimes murders with which Roberts-Smith has since been criminally charged.The statement of facts before the court reads that two PUCs – Persons Under Control – werehors de combatafter an SAS raid on a compound. The two prisoners were handcuffed and blindfolded at the cessation of the raid.Jacqui Lambie calls Pauline Hanson an ‘angry little woman’ after One Nation cartoon calling Andrew Hastie a traitorRead more“Roberts-Smith cut the handcuffs from PUC 1 who was in front of Person 66, removed PUC 1’s blindfold and pushed him to the ground. PUC 1 fell backwards and put his hand in front of his face with his palms facing outwards. Roberts-Smith said ‘shoot him’.“Person 66 believed this to be an order from Roberts-Smith. Person 66 was two metres away from PUC 1. Person 66 paused for a moment and then shot PUC 1 two to three times in the chest, killing him.”The statement of facts states: “Person 66 has admitted their role in this incident.”Roberts-Smith’s case is now before the courts. He has consistently and vigorously denied the allegations against him.“For the past 10 years, my family and I have been subject to a campaign to convince Australians that I’ve acted improperly in my service in Afghanistan,” Roberts-Smith said in a statement after he was charged.“As I’ve always maintained, I categorically deny all of these allegations, and while I would’ve preferred these charges not be brought, I will be taking the opportunity to finally clear my name.“I have never run from a fight in my life. I will never give up, and I will always be in the fight.”Explore more on these topicsAndrew HastiePauline HansonBen Roberts-SmithAustralian politicsOne NationanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Grace Tame apologises for comments labelling rape of Israeli women during Hamas attacks ‘propaganda’ | Grace Tame | The Guardian
description: The former Australian of the Year said she stood with survivors of sexual violence ‘everywhere’ and ‘no matter who they are’
Author: Adeshola Ore
Headline: The former Australian of the Year said she stood with survivors of sexual violence ‘everywhere’ and ‘no matter who they are’
Content: Former Australian of the Year Grace Tame issued an apology in an Instagram video on Thursday.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPView image in fullscreenFormer Australian of the Year Grace Tame issued an apology in an Instagram video on Thursday.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPGrace TameGrace Tame apologises for comments labelling rape of Israeli women during Hamas attacks ‘propaganda’The former Australian of the Year said she stood with survivors of sexual violence ‘everywhere’ and ‘no matter who they are’Get ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAdeshola OreThu 10 Sep 2026 04.22 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 04.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGrace Tame has apologised for her comments labelling the rape of Israeli women by Hamas during the 7 October attacks as “propaganda” and “debunked”, saying her words were “misinterpreted”.The former Australian of the Year issued the apology in an Instagram video on Thursday. The comments were made in an ABC interview about Israel and Gaza in March.In the video, Tame said she stood with survivors of sexual violence “everywhere, no matter who they are”.“There’s something I’ve wanted to clarify for a while, which I regret not clarifying sooner. I stand with survivors of sexual violence everywhere, no matter who they are”, she said.“Comments I made on ABC radio in March this year were misinterpreted to mean that I disbelieve Israeli survivors of sexual violence. This is not the case. I always have, and always will stand with survivors of sexual violence,” she said.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailTame said Human Rights Watch had been unable to find evidence to support the claim that Israeli women were raped en masse on 7 October 2023.“However, I do not deny the legitimate accusations of rape made by individual Israeli women, including accounts of gang-rape,” she said.“I do not hate Israelis. I do not hate Jewish people. I abhor the crimes of the State of Israel.“I believe Israeli survivors, I believe Jewish survivors, as I believe all survivors. While the intention of my remarks was not to imply otherwise, I acknowledge and sincerely apologise for any harm their mischaracterisation has caused.”Lynda Ben-Menashe, the president of the National Council of Jewish Women Australia, lashed Tame’s statement, saying it was not an apology.“She called Israeli women’s widely proven claims of sexual violence ‘debunked propaganda,’ which added insult to their injury, and fanned the flames of incitement against all Jewish women – and men in this country,” she said in a statement.“Saying she’s sorry for how people interpreted her words is not an apology. It neither rehabilitates her nor reverses the damage her original words did to us.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the March interview, Tame was asked whether she had expressed outrage about Israeli women who were sexually assaulted during the 7 October attacks.She said: “I’m not going to sink to the level of entertaining any kind of propaganda” and that “those things have been debunked”.In 2024, the United Nation’s special envoy on sexual violence in conflict concluded there were “reasonable grounds” to believesexual assaults including rape and gang-rape in several placestook place during the 7 October attacks by Hamas.Tame’s comments drew a rebuke from the Israeli embassy in Canberra, with a social media post accusing her of losing her “moral compass”.The ABC’s ombudsman’s office said it received145 complaints after Tame’s interview, while a further four raised “distinct but similar matters”.Explore more on these topicsGrace TameIsrael-Gaza warAustralian Broadcasting CorporationAustralian medianewsShareReuse this content

title: RSL says One Nation’s Hastie ‘slur’ was an ‘attack on every veteran’s service’ – as it happened | Australia news | The Guardian
description: This blog is now closed
Author: Achol Arok
Headline: This blog is now closed
Content: 02.26 EDTRSL Australia says calling a veteran a traitor is a ‘slur’Sarah Basford CanalesAustralia’s largest veteran support group has warned calling veterans traitors is a “slur” and an attack on every veteran’s service.It follows a bitter rift between the Liberal frontbencherAndrew Hastieand theOne Nationleader,Pauline Hanson, after the latter refused to apologise for a cartoon her party published that labelled Hastie a “traitor”.In a statement this afternoon, the Returned & Services League of Australia, better known as RSL Australia, said using the word sends a “corrosive message to the wider veteran community” that “your service can be recast as betrayal the moment it’s politically convenient”.The statement said:double quotation markThe recent comments from Senator Hanson towards Andrew Hastie MP go beyond political disagreement.This may have begun as a political dispute between Senator Hanson and Mr Hastie, however, when a person’s military service is used as the punchline, when the word ‘traitor’ is thrown at someone who has worn the uniform and deployed on operations, that stops being politics and starts being an attack on every veteran’s service.Veterans don’t stop being accountable to their oath once they leave the ADF. Branding a former soldier a ‘traitor’ sends a corrosive message to the wider veteran community: that your service can be recast as betrayal the moment it’s politically convenient.RSL Australia asks all sides of politics to keep that distinction. Calling a veteran a traitor is a slur, and it deserves to be treated as one regardless of who it’s aimed at or how it’s dressed up.”Read more:Jacqui Lambie calls Pauline Hanson an ‘angry little woman’ after One Nation cartoon calling Andrew Hastie a traitorRead moreShareUpdated at03.08 EDT

title: Orthodox church sends medieval prince’s remains to Russian troops in Ukraine | Russia | The Guardian
description: Part of Dmitry Donskoy’s right hand sent to ‘spiritually strengthen’ soldiers
Author: Pjotr Sauer
Headline: Part of Dmitry Donskoy’s right hand sent to ‘spiritually strengthen’ soldiers
Content: The relic was first brought on Tuesday to the Saur-Mogila war memorial in the Russian-occupied Donetsk region of Ukraine.Photograph: Yaroslav Chingaev/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe relic was first brought on Tuesday to the Saur-Mogila war memorial in the Russian-occupied Donetsk region of Ukraine.Photograph: Yaroslav Chingaev/ReutersRussiaOrthodox church sends medieval prince’s remains to Russian troops in UkrainePart of Dmitry Donskoy’s right hand sent to ‘spiritually strengthen’ soldiersPjotr SauerThu 10 Sep 2026 11.12 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 15.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Russian Orthodox church has sent a fragment of a medieval warrior prince’s remains to troops fighting inUkraine, saying the relic would “spiritually strengthen” soldiers and help them achieve victory.A reliquary containing part of the right hand of Dmitry Donskoy, the 14th-century prince revered inRussiafor his victory over the Mongolian Golden Horde in 1380, has been taken to Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and is now being transported along the frontline.The Russian Orthodox church said in a statement: “The holy commander is going to where the fate of the fatherland is being decided today, so that he may invisibly take his place in the same battle ranks as our defenders.”The relic was first brought on Tuesday to the Saur-Mogila war memorial in the Russian-occupied Donetsk region of Ukraine, where senior Orthodox clergy held a prayer service alongside representatives of the Russian military.The Russian-installed Metropolitan Vladimir of Donetsk and Mariupol said its presence would help soldiers and civilians “mobilise their strength” and secure victory over the enemy.‘Miserable and impossible’: food scarce in Kyiv as Russia targets supply chainsRead moreThe relic’s journey is the latest example of the Russian Orthodox church’s rabid embrace of the Kremlin’s war in Ukraine, which Patriarch Kirill, its leader, has repeatedly portrayed in religious terms.Since Vladimir Putin launched the full-scale invasion in February 2022, the church hierarchy has become deeply embedded in the Russian war effort. Priests have been sent to military units and occupied territories, while churches across Russia have been instructed to recite prayers asking God to grant victory.Donskoy’s relics were first formally uncovered only last month during restoration work at the Cathedral of the Archangel inside the Kremlin, where generations of Russian princes and tsars are buried.Putin, who has grown increasingly close to the Russian Orthodox church over his more than two decades in power, personally attended the ceremony marking the unearthing.Critics have accused the church of breaking with religious protocol by opening Donskoy’s centuries-old tomb. The location of the prince’s burial had long been known, but the church had previously made no attempt to exhume his remains after he was canonised in 1988.Alexander Zanemonets, an Orthodox priest and historian based outside Russia, said the decision to uncover the relics almost four decades after Donskoy’s canonisation appeared driven by the demands of wartime patriotism.He wrote in apiece for the Carnegie thinktank: “By the fifth year of war, the church leadership in Moscow began to wonder what else it could do to show its support for what Russia terms its ‘special military operation’.”Zanemonets said the portrayal of Donskoy as a defender of the homeland fitted neatly with the Kremlin’s insistence that Russia was defending itself rather than conducting a war of aggression against its neighbour.Earlier this year, relics of Alexander Nevsky, another medieval prince and military hero revered by the Russian Orthodox church, were also sent to the front.Explore more on these topicsRussiaUkraineReligionEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Russia’s actions have strengthened European case for boosting defence spending, says Nato chief – as it happened | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Mark Rutte said that Europeans ‘increasingly understand’ the need for their countries to take ‘greater responsibility for our own security’
Author: Jakub Krupa
Headline: Mark Rutte said that Europeans ‘increasingly understand’ the need for their countries to take ‘greater responsibility for our own security’
Content: 06.01 EDTRussia's actions are 'reckless, dangerous and a threat to life,' Nato's Rutte warns, but says they only strengthen resolve to help UkraineIn his speech,Rutterepeatedly praises Germany’s role within Nato, and then eventually gets to his stark assessment of the situation inUkraine– and Europe.He says:“Russia’s brutal attacks against Ukraine are unrelenting.Russia is suffering enormous losses, now estimated atmore than 40,000 killed or seriously wounded every month.Think about it for a moment. Over 40,000 every month.Despite those heavy losses,Putin shows no willingness to bring the war to an end.Instead,Russia repeatedly strikes Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine, often targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure, and at the same time,the list of Russia’s malign hybrid activities across Europe grows longer and longer:cyber-attacks, sabotage, arson, airspace violations, drone incidents.…The latest hostile actions by Russia are reckless, dangerous and a threat to life.But we are not intimidated. We know these are the tactics of a desperate regime that is failing to meet its objectives in Ukraine. Putin thinks he can divide us, destabilise us and weaken our support for Ukraine. But he will fail. These malicious actions are having the opposite effect.”Share

title: Much of Europe already levies a tourist tax – a nice little earner for Italian hotspots | Italy | The Guardian
description: While England makes its first foray into unfamiliar territory, it’s proved a boon for Italy’s cash-strapped municipalities
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: While England makes its first foray into unfamiliar territory, it’s proved a boon for Italy’s cash-strapped municipalities
Content: An overnight levy or tourist tax is a serious earner for popular Italian destinations, with Rome alone making more than €200m in 2024.Photograph: Andreas Solaro/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn overnight levy or tourist tax is a serious earner for popular Italian destinations, with Rome alone making more than €200m in 2024.Photograph: Andreas Solaro/AFP/Getty ImagesItalyAnalysisMuch of Europe already levies a tourist tax – a nice little earner for Italian hotspotsAngela Giuffridain RomeWhile England makes its first foray into unfamiliar territory, it’s proved a boon for Italy’s cash-strapped municipalitiesThu 10 Sep 2026 09.57 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareA nightly tourist tax may beunfamiliar territory in the UK, but countries in continental Europe have been cashing in on these kinds of levies for decades.Tourists usually need to pay the tax on the day they check out of a hotel or holiday let, and are often surprised by an extra fee on top of their accommodation costs.Among the earliest introductions of a tourist tax was in Austria in 1842, specifically targeting those who stayed in spa and wellness retreats.Similar measures were later implemented in France,Italy, Germany and Switzerland as a way to prevent the inhabitants of towns hosting such high-end resorts from paying for costs incurred by wealthy visitors.Italy’s tourist tax structure has gone through various changes. During Benito Mussolini’s fascist regime, it was broadened to include any town or city classified as a tourist destination.The tax was then completely abolished for the World Cup in 1990 as Italy embraced more visitors, only to be brought back in nationally in 2011, with Rome becoming the first city to reintroduce the levy.Depending on the destination, and sometimes the hotel type, the nightly fee typically ranges from between €1 (£0.86) and €10 per person, although guests of five-star hotels in Milan pay €12.Venice has also had an entrance fee in place since 2024, although that is only targeted at day-trippers.The overnight levy is a serious earner for popular Italian destinations. In 2024, Rome made €222.4m, followed by Milan (€109.3m), Florence (€82.9m) and Venice (€38.9m), according to data from Siope, the finance ministry’s tracker of public money flows.The revenues are supposed to be spent on local services, especially in towns and cities buckling under the pressure of overtourism, or on maintaining monuments. However, the reality is that cash-strapped municipalities use it for other expenses.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“All municipalities want the fee because they need the money,” said Gianluca De Gaetano, the manager of the Rome unit for Federalberghi, the hotels’ association.Tourists mostly just absorb the payment, even if begrudgingly. “They tend to complain when they find that the services in a city are not up to par, especially if they’ve already paid a lot for their accommodation,” said De Gaetano.Explore more on these topicsItalyEuropeTravel & leisureHospitality industryTax and spendingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Primark to launch home delivery service despite ‘challenging’ market | Primark | The Guardian
description: Chain has long avoided deliveries in Great Britain but says a shift now offers ‘opportunity for profitable growth’
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Chain has long avoided deliveries in Great Britain but says a shift now offers ‘opportunity for profitable growth’
Content: Primark expects slightly higher quarterly sales in the UK and Ireland but a drop of more than 4% on the continent.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPrimark expects slightly higher quarterly sales in the UK and Ireland but a drop of more than 4% on the continent.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianPrimarkPrimark to launch home delivery service despite ‘challenging’ marketChain has long avoided deliveries in Great Britain but says a shift now offers ‘opportunity for profitable growth’Business live – latest updatesLauren AlmeidaThu 10 Sep 2026 09.31 EDTFirst published on Thu 10 Sep 2026 03.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePrimark will offer home delivery in Great Britain for the first time as the fast-fashion retailer seeks to revive flagging sales.The company, which already offers a click and collect service, has long avoided home delivery, arguing that its low prices made it too difficult to absorb the cost of packing and shipping orders.However, the clothing chain, which willspin off from its owner Associated British Foods (ABF) next year, disclosed on Thursday that it had acquired an automated fulfilment facility in Sheffield and would offer home delivery “in the future” in the UK, except for Northern Ireland.“Primark’s digital maturity, including the success of click and collect, and online market developments, mean there is now the opportunity for profitable growth through the home delivery channel,” it said in a statement.The push into home delivery came as the company told investors that it expected Primark’s sales to drop 3% ⁠in its quarter ended on 12 September, with ​the UK and ​Ireland up 0.4% ​but continentalEuropedown 4.3%.George Weston, the chief executive of ABF, said Primark’s trading in Europe “remained challenging”, but the initial customer reaction to its “iconic value” campaign – in which it cut prices across hundreds of autumn and winter products – had been encouraging.Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at the broker AJ Bell, said Primark, faced with slowing sales, “clearly had no choice but to adapt to the modern retail world” and adopt online delivery.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPrimark to split from food business despite warning of Iran war impactRead moreShares in ABF, which is listed on the London Stock Exchange, fell by almost 10% on Thursday, taking its year-to-date fall to 14%.Analysts at the broker Jefferies, an investment bank, said Primark looked particularly vulnerable as it started its final quarter of the year.“In an environment with rising concerns over both the health of the consumer and of industry input cost challenges, Primark continues to be among the most disadvantageously positioned clothing retailers,” they said.The news comes asPrimark prepares to split from its parent company ABF, the owner of Twinings tea and Kingsmill bread. The demerger, which is likely to complete in December 2027, is expected to create two new FTSE 100 companies, with analysts predicting that Primark could be valued at as much as £9bn, and the food business £4bn.Weston, a member of the billionaire family that controls ABF and who is the long-term chief executive of the group, is to lead the food business after the demerger.Eoin Tonge, an experienced former ABF, Marks & Spencer and Greencore finance director, will remain as chief executive of Primark.The fashion chain, which wasfounded by Arthur Ryanunder its Irish brand name, Penneys, in Dublin in 1969, opened its first shop in Britain in 1974, in Derby. It employs more than 80,000 people around the world.Explore more on these topicsPrimarkRetail industryAssociated British FoodsEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Malta warned of corruption crisis after ‘utter disbelief’ over Daphne Caruana Galizia verdict | Daphne Caruana Galizia | The Guardian
description: Labour peer tells Council of Europe inquiry failure to implement legal protections still putting journalists at risk
Author: Juliette Garside
Headline: Labour peer tells Council of Europe inquiry failure to implement legal protections still putting journalists at risk
Content: A demonstrator holding up the Maltese flag in the capital Valletta after the acquittal of Yorgen Fenech last week.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersView image in fullscreenA demonstrator holding up the Maltese flag in the capital Valletta after the acquittal of Yorgen Fenech last week.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersDaphne Caruana GaliziaMalta warned of corruption crisis after ‘utter disbelief’ over Daphne Caruana Galizia verdictLabour peer tells Council of Europe inquiry failure to implement legal protections still putting journalists at riskJuliette GarsideThu 10 Sep 2026 08.17 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMalta is vulnerable to “repeated instances of high-level corruption” unless it strengthens the rule of law and protections for journalists, the Labour peer Shami Chakrabarti said at the opening of an inquiry into judicial failures following the death ofDaphne Caruana Galizia.Chakrabarti, a member of the House of Lords and former director of the human rights group Liberty, has been named special rapporteur for aCouncil of Europeinvestigation into the fallout from the assassination of the anti-corruption journalist, who died in a car bombing in October 2017.Malta is in turmoil after theacquittal of a wealthy and politically influential businessman, Yorgen Fenech, of any involvement in Caruana Galizia’s murder.Fenech denies paying a middleman €150,000 to have her killed.At the inquiry’s first hearing, on Wednesday, Chakrabarti said the verdict had “staggered many throughout Maltese society and beyond.View image in fullscreenShami Chakrabarti: ‘Atmosphere of utter disbelief at how the jury could have reached such a decision’.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PA“It’s now almost nine years since the assassination that struck at the very heart of Maltese public life but a mastermind has not yet been held accountable,” she added.The first witnesses on Wednesday were the journalist’s eldest son,
