Matthew Caruana Galizia, and her sister Corinne Vella, who questioned the verdict, which dismissed both charges against Fenech by an 8-1 majority.Sabotage, leaks and political ties: the story of the Daphne Caruana Galizia murder trialRead moreMatthew Caruana Galizia told members of the council’s committee on legal affairs and human rights: “The Maltese public have seen all of the evidence against the accused, and the vast majority were convinced of his complicity in the murder. And this is why there is this atmosphere of utter disbelief at how the jury could have reached such a decision.”Malta’s state prosecutor is understood to be preparing an appeal, with the aim of securing a retrial.The Council ofEurope, founded in 1949 after the second world war, created the European convention on human rights. It is led by an assembly drawn from members of the parliaments of its 46 member states.During the hearing, representatives expressed shock and concern about the verdict, calling for the European parliament and the European Commission to intervene. Iulian Bulai, a Romanian centre-right politician, suggested the EU could withhold funds from Malta. The procedure, known as the rule of law conditionality mechanism, was first used in 2022, against Hungary.“If there is such huge problem in matter of rule of law and a function of the Maltese institutions, the EU should apply a similar procedure on increasing pressure for reform,” said Bulai. He said the procedure had “functioned in other cases … So why shouldn’t it function in Malta’s case?”View image in fullscreenDaphne Caruana Galizia pictured in 2011.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersMalta, the EU’s smallest member state, with a population of 600,000, is a net recipient of EU money. Analysis suggests that since joining the block 22 years ago, the island has received €2.4bn more in subsidies than it has paid in.Chakrabarti said she would look at why Malta had failed to implement many of the recommendations from a public inquiry held after the murder.“Thetargeted assassination of a journalistin the middle of investigating high-level corruption sent a chill down the spine of everyone who cares about democratic values,” she said. “Many claim that the legal and policy changes needed to protect journalists to combat corruption and ensure the independent functioning of justice have not been carried out.“I’m extremely concerned by the apparent absence of reforms in critical areas which make Malta vulnerable to repeated instances of high-level corruption and limit the press freedom which should hold it in check.”View image in fullscreenYorgen Fenech leaving the courthouse in Valetta on 2 September after his acquittal.Photograph: Kevin Schembri Orland/APThe public inquiry found although there had been no evidence that the Maltese state had a direct role in the murder, the state bore responsibility for creating a climate of impunity.It recommended Italian-style anti-mafia laws, and making the hindrance of police investigations and abuse of office a crime for public officials. These measures have yet to be implemented.Chakrabarti compared the Caruana Galizia case to miscarriages of justice in the UK, where officials had been involved in coverups, citing the mismanagement of Grenfell Tower, the Post Office scandal and the Hillsborough football stadium disaster. She said her inquiry, titledJustice delayed: the unfinished implementation of the Daphne Caruana Galizia case, was likely to conclude in a year.Vella said fear that serious crimes could go unpunished had increased since the verdict. “Before the verdict was given, we lived in a country where a journalist was killed, but there was a chance of ending impunity. That disappeared as soon as the verdict was out.”She said journalists who had continued to investigate corruption allegations involving former members of Malta’s government “felt uneasy walking to their own cars following that verdict”.Explore more on these topicsDaphne Caruana GaliziaMaltaJournalist safetyCouncil of EuropeEuropeHuman rightsHouse of LordsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Secret systems used by Israel in mass killings of Gaza civilians revealed in new film | Israel | The Guardian
description: Testimony from Israeli military insiders involved in surveillance and remote killings features in documentary produced by the Guardian
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Testimony from Israeli military insiders involved in surveillance and remote killings features in documentary produced by the Guardian
Content: A scene from NAZA, a documentary produced by the Guardian and directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.Photograph: The GuardianView image in fullscreenA scene from NAZA, a documentary produced by the Guardian and directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.Photograph: The GuardianIsraelSecret systems used by Israel in mass killings of Gaza civilians revealed in new filmTestimony from Israeli military insiders involved in surveillance and remote killings features in documentary produced by the GuardianEmma Graham-Harrisonin Jerusalem andXan Brooksin VeniceThu 10 Sep 2026 09.42 EDTFirst published on Thu 10 Sep 2026 07.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTestimony from 24 Israeli military insiders ​on the secret ​systems used in ​the war on Gaza​ has been revealed in a new documentary film about the mass killing of Palestinian civilians.NAZA, a film from the Oscar-winning Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, was shown at theVenice international film festivalon Thursday as the only documentary competing for its prestigious Golden Lion award.The film’s title comes from an Israeli military acronym used euphemistically to refer to civilians expected to be killed in a military attack.Produced by the Guardian, it features extensive testimony from Israeli intelligence officers and soldiers involved in the surveillance and remote killing of Palestinian civilians.Interviews were filmed at night on rooftops in Tel Aviv, on the condition of anonymity because of the risks involved in speaking publicly about Israel’s war activities. The appearance and voices of participants in the film were digitally altered to disguise their identities.The interviewees detail the secret methods used by the Israeli military inGaza, including AI-based systems built to identify large numbers of potential low-ranking Hamas targets, who were then bombed in their homes at night, in the knowledge attacks would also kill their families.View image in fullscreenIsraeli soldiers at a military position overlooking the so-called yellow line in Gaza in May.Photograph: Ariel Schalit/APThe Israeli military hacked into phones to identify the location of such targets, and covertly listened into conversations with their wives and children moments before they were all killed.The film also features first-person accounts about the destruction of neighbourhoods where the Israeli military estimated that up to 25% of residents were still sheltering in their homes, the systematic burning of civilian homes, and the killing of civilians at a food distribution site.Abraham said at a press conference in Venice on Thursday: “We just told these officers: ‘Please describe to us what you did. How do these systems work? Sketch it out for us.’ Sometimes, in just asking the questions, you get the answers.“Some of them did not express remorse and some did. Some spoke out of indifference, some out of pride.”View image in fullscreenThe film’s directors, Rachel Szor and Yuval Abhram (centre), with producers and crew members at the Venice film festival on Thursday.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersSeveral interviewees worked in a secret intelligence unit that reports directly to the office of Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu; one said their mission was to “thwart peace”.“We made this film out of a sense of obligation to use our position as Israeli film-makers and journalists to examine the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians for which our country is responsible,” Abraham and Szor said in their directors’ statement.The directors stressed the film’s focus was not on “sporadic war crimes committed by rogue soldiers”. “It is on the orders themselves, the policies, the accepted practices, the language and logic that make those practices possible, and the people who operate within them,” they said. “The system and its cogs.”View image in fullscreenAn explosion after an Israeli airstrike in Gaza City on Wednesday.Photograph: Jehad Alshrafi/APThe documentary was co-produced by James Wilson and executive produced by Jonathan Glazer, the same team behind the Oscar-winning film The Zone of Interest.The film received a nearly 25-minute standing ovation after its screening, according to Variety, which called it a record for length of applause not just at Venice but at any major film festival and reported that Glazer embraced Abraham and Szor as it went on, while some members of the audience held up Palestinian flags.NAZA builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and the Guardian between 2023 and 2025. It was filmed and produced under tight security because of the risk to confidential journalistic sources, and its contents have remained a closely guarded secret before Thursday’s premiere.Paul Lewis, the Guardian’s head of investigations and an executive producer on the film, described NAZA as the culmination of “years of painstaking work to uncover and verify the systems used by Israeli military intelligence in Gaza”.Abraham said making the documentary had provided space to explore the collective impact of that work. “In this film we’re talking to 24 people. We are looking at systems of mass killing. There is something about cinema that allows you to explore structures and systems and how you put things together.”Before the premiere, Alberto Barbera, the Venice film festival’s artistic director, told journalists NAZA would be “truly groundbreaking”, calling it “a politically disruptive and cinematically extremely interesting work”.“It’s not just any collection of interviews,” Italy’s Cinecittà News quoted Barbera as saying. “It took them three years to convince these Israeli intelligence and military officials to share the work they did when the invasion of Gaza began, and I assure you, their testimonies are shocking.”NAZA review – Israeli intelligence officers cast chilling light on civilian deathsRead moreIsraeli attacks in Gaza since 2023 have killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, the majority of them civilians, and injured more than 174,000 others, together representing more than 10% of Gaza’s prewar population.Israeli restrictions on food shipments created a man-made famine last summer, and the Israeli military razed or damaged more than three-quarters of homes, so surviving Palestinians are now crowded into tent camps with little access to clean water or sanitation.Israel launched its war after the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, when more than 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken to Gaza by militants. The majority of the dead and hostages were civilians.Abraham and Szor were two of the four co-directors of No Other Land, whichwon the Oscar for best documentary in 2025.Drawing a connection between the two films, the directors said: “In the film No Other Land, we spent five years, together with [Palestinian co-directors] Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal, documenting the army destroying Palestinian homes in order to paint a larger picture of a system of occupation and ethnic supremacy aimed at the removal of Palestinians from the West Bank.“In NAZA, we are similarly connecting the dots of a system, gathering the testimonies of two dozen intelligence officers and soldiers and depicting the military systems used to perpetrate what a UN commission and the world’s leading human rights groups have described as a genocide.”Explore more on these topicsIsraelGazaVenice film festivalDocumentary filmsIsrael-Gaza warPalestineMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Houthis seize key Yemeni port of Mocha in drive to take control of Red Sea coast | Houthis | The Guardian
description: Iran and its proxies move closer to full control of two shipping chokepoints as regional conflict widens
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Iran and its proxies move closer to full control of two shipping chokepoints as regional conflict widens
Content: Fighters loyal to the Houthis take part in a recruitment drive in Sana’a on Thursday.Photograph: Mohammed Huwais/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFighters loyal to the Houthis take part in a recruitment drive in Sana’a on Thursday.Photograph: Mohammed Huwais/AFP/Getty ImagesHouthisHouthis seize key Yemeni port of Mocha in drive to take control of Red Sea coastIran and its proxies move closer to full control of two shipping chokepoints as regional conflict widensExplained: why the fighting in Yemen matters globallyPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorThu 10 Sep 2026 07.39 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHouthi forces inYemenare making a concerted drive to take over the country’s Red Sea coast fully, claiming control of the key port of Mocha in the most serious wave of fighting with the Saudi-backed government in years, bringing the Iran-aligned group closer to full control of a key shipping route.Seizure of the coast and some of the islands in the sea would be a strategic disaster forSaudi Arabiaand the US, taking Iran and its proxies closer to full control of two choke points for western shipping on opposite sides of the Arabian peninsula: the Bab al-Mandab at the southern end of the Red Sea and the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.Observers have said a reduction in hostilities – the most intense since the UN-sponsored ceasefire of April 2022 put an end to major military exchanges – now seems unlikely in what is seen as an attempt by theHouthisto open a second front in the Iran-US war, alongside the battle for control of Hormuz.Baraa Shiban,the Royal United Services Institute’s(Rusi) Yemen specialist, a London-based security thinktank, said the situation in the country was spiralling out of control, adding that the UN-recognised Yemeni government was opening new fronts against the Houthis in the hope of putting more pressure on their forces than they could withstand. But in the past 48 hours the Houthis had major advances south, down Yemen’s west coast, taking them closer to the high ground overlooking the narrow Bab al-Mandab strait.View image in fullscreenA screen grab from video footage released by Saudi-backed forces shows a rocket being fired during fighting in Taiz province.Photograph: Yemen National Resistance Forces/AFP/Getty ImagesThe fighting has also raised questions about whether Saudi Arabia, which on Thursday launched as many as 40 airstrikes on Houthi targets, will activate the Mecca defence agreement and ask its co-signatories, Pakistan and Turkey, to send forces. The pact is designed to be defensive in nature and believed unlikely to apply to Saudi military activities in Yemen.A map showing the area of Yemen controlled by Houthi forcesBy taking control of more of the Red Sea coast south of the port of Hodeidah, the Houthis’ aim is to use a new lever to put pressure on Saudi Arabia and the US to agree a deal that lifts the US blockade on Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf. Donald Trump on Wednesday acknowledged he did not expect the war withIranto end before the US midterm elections at the start of November.The latest phase in the escalation began when Houthis attacked energy installations and southern cities in Saudi Arabia using drones and ballistic missiles. In response, the kingdom’s military forces launched at least 15 strikes between 3 and 7 September.View image in fullscreenThe aftermath of Houthi strikes on Mocha last month. The rebel group claims it now controls the port.Photograph: Al Joumhouriya TV/ReutersThe conflict data monitor Acled estimated there were 276 fatalities over the five-day period alone. The fighting has continued, with the Houthis claiming control of Mocha in Taiz province, as well as the inland city of Hays and the Khalid ibn al-Walid camp, the largest military base in the region. One Houthi-linked estimate suggested its forces had gained control of more than 2,320 sq miles (6,000 sq km) of land.The commander of the Yemeni government forces, Maj Gen Tareq Saleh, admitted he had organised a strategic retreat south of Mocha in order to regroup in a secure location. “The armed forces in the western coast paid a heavy price – martyrs and wounded – over the past days as they confronted the Houthi attack planned by Iran, and supported by it,” he said. Analysts claimed that the effectiveness of Yemen’s government forces was weakened by internal divisions, as well as external pressure from Saudi Arabia.View image in fullscreenA satellite image shows smoke billowing from an Aramco oil depot near the Saudi city of Abha after a Houthi attack.Photograph: Planet Labs/AFP/Getty ImagesThe latter, meanwhile, continues to take advantage of its air superiority to attack Houthi positions, though government sources acknowledged Houthi ground advances along the coast and their missile strikes on the strategic Red Sea islands of Zuqar and Hanish.The clashes have raged across Yemen, including Ad Dali, al-Bayda, Marib, Shabwah, al-Jawf, Hodeidah, and Taiz. In the initial days of the renewed conflict the Houthis were forced back in some areas as battles on multiple fronts overstretched their resources and fighter numbers.The Houthis will be hoping political divisions inside the Yemeni government, reflected in a lack of an integrated military, will slowly give them the upper hand. The United Arab Emirates, previously a powerful player in southern Yemen where it backed the separatist forces of the Southern Transitional Council, withdrew its financial and military support at the turn of the year. The southern forces have refused to fight outside their own region.View image in fullscreenA screen grab from video footage released by the Saudi-backed forces shows a fighter firing at Houthi forces in Taiz province.Photograph: Yemen National Resistance Forces/AFP/Getty Images“A reduction in hostilities anytime soon seems unlikely, as both sides continue to escalate with the goal of inflicting enough damage to the other side to force a compromise,” said Sherwan Hindreen Ali, a Yemen analyst for Acled. “In terms of military capability, both sides are more equal compared to the immediate period prior to the 2022 ceasefire when the Houthis had the upper hand.”He added: “Fighting will remain focused on the fronts of the Red Sea coast in Hodeidah and Taiz, where both the Houthis and the Saudi Arabia-Yemen government have a vested interest in claiming the whole territory to deprive the other side of effective control of the strait of Bab al-Mandab.”The head of the Houthis’ national delegating negotiating team, Muhammad Abdul Salam, insisted non-Saudi commercial shipping would not be attacked.The fighting has contributed to the price of oil rising above $100 a barrel after weeks when it was trading closer to $80.View image in fullscreenFootage reportedly shows Houthi attacks on Saudi-backed forces in al-Jawf province.Photograph: Ansarullah Media Centre/AFP/Getty ImagesThe escalation to this week’s all-out violence has been a slow process. It began after a senior delegation of the Houthi group, which has long been in a complex alliance with Iran, flew to Tehran for the funeral of the Iranian supreme leader Ali Khamenei in July, returning in an Iranian plane that the Saudis refused to land in rebel-controlled Sana’a.The Saudis instead bombed the runway, leading the Houthis to announce a Red Sea naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in what the Yemeni group described as a blockade for a blockade. The 20 July announcement of the blockade was followed by a strike on Saudi Arabia’s Jazan refinery on 25 July and on a tanker off Yanbu on 24 August.Saudi Arabia has become reliant on the Red Sea route for trade after Iran throttled shipping through the strait of Hormuz as a result of US-Israeli attacks.Explore more on these topicsHouthisYemenSaudi ArabiaIranMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Tens of millions of people fail to get humanitarian aid as global system crumbles | Global development | The Guardian
description: Funding cuts in 2025 left women, children, older and displaced people hard hit, with 64m fewer people receiving aid
Author: Kaamil Ahmed
Headline: Funding cuts in 2025 left women, children, older and displaced people hard hit, with 64m fewer people receiving aid
Content: People queue for food during a severe drought in Kenya’s Turkana county in February. Global aid contributions fell by 30% between 2022 and 2025.Photograph: Patrick Ngugi/APView image in fullscreenPeople queue for food during a severe drought in Kenya’s Turkana county in February. Global aid contributions fell by 30% between 2022 and 2025.Photograph: Patrick Ngugi/APAid cutsGlobal developmentTens of millions of people fail to get humanitarian aid as global system crumblesFunding cuts in 2025 left women, children, older and displaced people hard hit, with 64m fewer people receiving aidSupported byAbout this contentKaamil AhmedThu 10 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe humanitarian aid system is crumbling as funding shrinks, pressures increase and governments not only fail to protect civilians but are increasingly responsible for endangering them, anew report warnedon Thursday as figures revealed 64 million fewer people received aid last year.With aid contributions cut by 30% between 2022 and 2025 and thousands of aid workers losing their jobs, the humanitarian system has suffered one of its biggest contractions since being formed in the post-second world war era, according to the State of the Humanitarian System 2026 report.In 2025, only those whose lives were in immediate danger became the focus, while support for longer-term issues and the ability to recover from crises was drastically scaled back.Jennifer Doherty, co-author of the report produced by the humanitarian organisation Active Learning Network for Accountability and Performance (Alnap), said: “The impacts were not felt equally. The combination of reduced funding and restrictive politics meant women, children, elderly people and displaced people were especially hardest hit.”Doherty, who said up to 23% of humanitarian staffing was estimated to have been lost in 2025, said: “Specialised services closed and targeted support became harder to sustain.”According to the report, funding fell to an estimated $33.3bn (£24.6bn) in 2025, from a peak of $47.5bn in 2022.While USAID sustained the most dramatic cuts, with a 55% reduction in 2025, there were alsocuts by other leading donors, with 13 of the top 20 reducing their aid donations last year.The report also highlighted the growing pressure from governments on how aid could be spent, such as theUS spending freezeon programmes considered driven by diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) policies.The aid cuts also meant that for the few people who did receive support, the targeted amount for each person dropped from $178 in 2021 to $90 in 2025, despite the actual needs of each person having risen to $255.An aggravating factor was that governments not only failed in their duties to protect civilians but were also often actually endangering people. States were responsible for 64% of attacks on healthcare workers and largely responsible for violence that affected aid workers through the use of airstrikes.View image in fullscreenDisplaced people receive food aid in Al-Khawkhah, in Yemen’s Hodeidah province, in July.Photograph: Khaled Ziad/AFP/Getty ImagesYemen was one of the countries badly affectedby aid cuts, with nutrition worsening and diphtheria cases rising because vaccination campaigns were suspended.Mohammed Bahashwan, Action for Humanity’s country director inYemen, said diminishing levels of aid were exacerbating the crises faced by families.“Problems are not occurring separately. A family may have lost its income, be unable to afford food, have a malnourished child and still need to travel considerable distances or pay costs they cannot afford to access healthcare,” he said.The report said there were examples of the humanitarian system mobilising to support those most in need, often led by local aid organisations, and of diaspora networks stepping in. But it also said the international system did not coordinate well with these networks and that it was often local aid organisations and staff who were worst affected by cuts.Meg Sattler, chief executive of the Vienna-based organisation Ground Truth Solutions, which carries out regular surveys of people who need aid, said there should be more focus on localisation because the international humanitarian system had not adapted fast enough orpushed back against the cuts and stipulationsimposed by the US.“We have definitely spoken to people feeling the pinch of this contraction. It is especially causing distress where aid is now considered ‘life-saving only’ and isn’t letting people do things such as send their kids to school or save to start a business – things that would help them be less reliant on aid in the future,” she said.Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentAid cutsAidUSAIDTrump administrationHumanitarian responseGlobal healthChildren's healthnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Our forefathers are coming back’: Naga people celebrate after Oxford museum agrees to return remains  | Global development | The Guardian
description: Following six years of talks, Pitt Rivers Museum will return body parts collected by British colonial administrators to north-east India
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Following six years of talks, Pitt Rivers Museum will return body parts collected by British colonial administrators to north-east India
Content: The Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford is returning 39 pieces of human remains belonging to the Naga tribes after six years of negotiations.Photograph: Pitt Rivers MuseumView image in fullscreenThe Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford is returning 39 pieces of human remains belonging to the Naga tribes after six years of negotiations.Photograph: Pitt Rivers MuseumGlobal development‘Our forefathers are coming back’: Naga people celebrate after Oxford museum agrees to return remainsFollowing six years of talks, Pitt Rivers Museum will return body parts collected by British colonial administrators to north-east IndiaSupported byAbout this contentTora AgarwalaThu 10 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnthropologists and community leaders from Nagaland, a remote state in north-easternIndiabordering Myanmar, have expressed joy and relief that human remains belonging to their ancestors that had been on display in a British museum for nearly a century are finally being returned.On Monday, thePitt Rivers Museum in Oxfordannounced that 39 pieces of human remains – including parts of skulls, a finger and a piece of skin with hair – belonging to the Naga tribes, will be returned to Nagaland after six years of negotiation between the community and the museum.For the Nagas, the repatriation is not just about “bones and ancestral remains … It is about memory returning to where it belongs,” the community said in a statement.“We are at peace,” said A Peihwang Wangsa, an Indigenous Konyak man involved in the repatriation negotiations. “Our forefathers are coming back.”Wangsa, whose ancestors’ remains are among those being returned, added that the homecoming would be a moment of “mourning and celebration”.NT Thamlong Phom, a Naga community leader from the Phom sub-tribe, said: “I feel joy, I feel blessed.“Ever since the announcement was made, my entire community has felt happy,” he said. “Our ancestors’ spirit will have a final resting place.”Thejao Vihienuo, who is also part of the repatriation discussions and went to Oxford in 2025, said he had been “angry and unhappy” to see the remains of his ancestors, which he said had been “taken in a most dubious manner”.“It was displayed as if it was a trophy, but they silently spoke of the atrocities the British committed on our people,” he said.The return caused “mixed feelings”, he said, but added: “We owe it to our ancestors to bring their remains back and put them to peaceful rest. And also to our younger generation to decolonise their minds and show that our children are not inferior to any white man.”The Nagas are a transnational Indigenous group of tribes living in India’s north-east and parts of Myanmar,once associated with headhuntingbut now predominantly Christian.The Pitt Rivers Museum, home to one of the world’s largest ethnological collections, has more than 6,500 Naga objects, 898 of which were on display. Most of the collection was “coercively” acquired by the colonial administrators James Philip Mills and John Henry Hutton.View image in fullscreenProf Dolly Kikon, a Naga anthropologist (kneeling, centre, in a red scarf) with other Naga delegates and museum staff.Photograph: Pitt Rivers MuseumThe human remains were displayed at the museum for 80 years. In 2020, they were put into storage during a revamp aimed at addressing the institution’s colonial past and how exhibiting human remains “reinforced racist and stereotypical thinking” of other cultures.The museum said in a statement: “Thirty-nine Naga ancestors will soon begin their journey home from Oxford to Nagaland.”In November, a Naga delegation will visit Oxford for a handover ceremony and the remains are expected to arrive in Nagaland before the end of the year. They will be laid to rest in a traditional community ceremony in the state capital, Kohima.The repatriation negotiations were led by representatives from all of the Naga tribes.“It has been a journey of redemption,” saidProf Dolly Kikon, a Naga anthropologist. “This shows that we are no longer victims of colonial violence. We embrace our roles as people who find redemption and healing by giving dignity and honour to a very violent past.”The negotiations started in 2020, when Kikon wrote to the museum after reading “an article in the Guardianthat they were doing an ethical review” of the collection. “They replied within 24 hours,” said Kikon.That was just the beginning of a lengthy process that soon expanded into a wider community-led campaign.The Forum for Naga Reconciliation, a community peace group, assembled a team known as Recover, Restore and Decolonise, bringing together Naga volunteers from across the region to work on the repatriation effort.View image in fullscreenMembers of the Naga delegation view the relics on display at the Pitt Rivers Museum.Photograph: Pitt Rivers Museum“They travelled to villages and organised meetings to inform people about the remains,” said Arkotong Longkumer, a Naga anthropologist who worked closely with Kikon to lead the initiative, which he described as “open and transparent”.“It was an intergenerational journey that brought together students, civil society, tribal leaders and the church,” said Longkumer, who teaches at Edinburgh University.New images reveal extent of looting at Sudan’s national museum as rooms stripped of treasuresRead moreA Naga delegation, including tribal leaders, visited Oxford in 2025 to officially register a claim to the remains.“I had never known our ancestral human remains had been taken away like that,” said Wangsa. “I felt angry when I saw them.”Laura Van Broekhoven, director of the Pitt Rivers Museum and a professor of museum studies and ethics at Oxford University, said the museum was completing paperwork to enable the return of the remains.“We will then start working towards the ceremonial aspects so we can have everything ready,” she said. “In our experience, handover ceremonies can be very emotional.”Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentIndigenous peoplesAnthropologyMuseumsHeritageBritish empireIndianewsShareReuse this content

title: New battery-powered trains will ‘bring faster journeys to north’ | Rail transport | The Guardian
description: No 10 says 29 new trains to be built in Derby will support 350 local jobs, as well as nearly 6,000 across the UK
Author: Raphael Boyd
Headline: No 10 says 29 new trains to be built in Derby will support 350 local jobs, as well as nearly 6,000 across the UK
Content: Andy Burnham during a visit to Alstom transport in Derby, where the new trains will be built.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham during a visit to Alstom transport in Derby, where the new trains will be built.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.Rail transportNew battery-powered trains will ‘bring faster journeys to north’No 10 says 29 new trains to be built in Derby will support 350 local jobs, as well as nearly 6,000 across the UKRaphael BoydThu 10 Sep 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 17.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNo 10 has announced the construction of a new fleet of battery-powered trains that will “bring faster, more reliable journeys to the north”.The 29 new trains, which will be run by TransPennine Express, are set to be built in Alstom’s Litchurch Lane works in Derby from 2028, which the government says will support 350 local jobs, as well as nearly 6,000 across the UK.The new fleet will be made up of Adessia Stream trains, a battery-powered model that will be the first of its kind to be used for long-distance mainline journeys in the UK when it enters service in 2034.Prime ministerAndy Burnham, who uses trains regularly to move between London and Manchester, highlighted the need for more reliable and efficient services, with the new trains pitched as making journeys between major northern cities shorter while increasing capacity on rail networks by 30% in the next decade.Burnham said: “I’ve lost count of the number of times someone has stopped me to tell me about the train that never came. And when that happens, it means missed shifts, missed appointments and missed opportunities.“Today that starts to change. These 29 new trains will bring faster, more reliable journeys to the north, and thousands of British jobs for the next generation.“It’s exactly what Great British Railways is all about – taking back control of the basics and getting Britain believing again.”As well as speed and capacity, the new trains are set to run without emissions even on non-electrified stretches of the network, while also having more accessible step-free boarding and onboard wifi.Transport secretary Heidi Alexander also praised the announcement, calling it a sign of how Great British Railways “will deliver better journeys for people while backing British business” and allowing passengers to “wave goodbye to overcrowded, delayed diesel trains and step onboard faster electric trains which are fit for the future”.Explore more on these topicsRail transportRail industryTransportAndy BurnhamManchesterLeedsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Esther Rantzen now ‘too physically fragile’ to end her life in Switzerland | Esther Rantzen | The Guardian
description: Broadcaster, 86, had intended to end her life in Swiss clinic after being diagnosed with terminal lung cancer in 2023
Author: Raphael Boyd
Headline: Broadcaster, 86, had intended to end her life in Swiss clinic after being diagnosed with terminal lung cancer in 2023
Content: Esther Rantzen pictured in 2024.Photograph: Cheese Scientist/AlamyView image in fullscreenEsther Rantzen pictured in 2024.Photograph: Cheese Scientist/AlamyEsther RantzenEsther Rantzen now ‘too physically fragile’ to end her life in SwitzerlandBroadcaster, 86, had intended to end her life in Swiss clinic after being diagnosed with terminal lung cancer in 2023Raphael BoydThu 10 Sep 2026 16.04 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEsther Rantzen has said she is no longer able to travel to Switzerland to end her life because she has become “too physically fragile”.Rantzen, who presented the TV current affairs programme That’s Life! for 21 years and founded the youth support charity Childline, had intended to end her life in a Dignitas assisted dying clinic inSwitzerlandafter being diagnosed with terminal lung cancer in 2023.The broadcaster, 86, said in a statement on Thursday that her quality of life had deteriorated since her diagnosis, and that she was ready to end her life but was no longer able to make the journey despite having joined Dignitas about a year after learning she was terminally ill.Rantzen said: “Unfortunately, when I was strong enough to make the flight and go to Dignitas, my life was not unbearably painful, indeed, I was able to relax in my beloved cottage in the New Forest.“And by the time life did become unbearable, I was too physically fragile to make the journey and go through the Dignitas process.“So even though I had spent the money and made the plans, I was not ready to end my life back then, and did not realise that would be my last chance.”Assisted dying remains illegal in the UK, though a bill that would allow it in certain circumstances is being revisited.Rantzen is a vocal supporter of the bill,which is due to have a second reading in parliament on Friday, and has criticised the current laws that prevent people in her situation from legally ending their lives, calling the rules “messy and cruel”.Legalised assisted dying in the UK has been the topic of intensive debate since Kim Leadbeater’s bill was introduced to parliament in October 2024.A June 2025 vote in the Commons saw the bill progress by 314 votes to 291, with both sides receiving votes from MPs from Labour, the Conservatives and the Liberal Democrats.If the bill passes, the UK would join European countries such as Austria, Belgium, the Netherlands, Spain and Switzerland, as well as Australia, Canada and the US, where it is legal in 13 states.Advocates for the bill have claimed it will enable terminally ill people to enjoy a dignified end to their lives and allow them to die before their health declines too much.Those against it, however, argue the criteria put forward could change after the law is passed and that the quality of palliative care could decline.Explore more on these topicsEsther RantzenAssisted dyingSwitzerlandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ministers face backlash from hospitality industry over ‘tourist tax’ plans | Travel & leisure | The Guardian
description: Many mayors welcome power to impose tourist tax but industry warns of ‘irreparable harm’ and job losses
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Many mayors welcome power to impose tourist tax but industry warns of ‘irreparable harm’ and job losses
Content: Lyme Regis beach in Dorset. The overnight visitor levy will potentially generate tens of millions of pounds to be spent in local areas.Photograph: Imgorthand/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLyme Regis beach in Dorset. The overnight visitor levy will potentially generate tens of millions of pounds to be spent in local areas.Photograph: Imgorthand/Getty ImagesTravel & leisureMinisters face backlash from hospitality industry over ‘tourist tax’ plansMany mayors welcome power to impose tourist tax but industry warns of ‘irreparable harm’ and job lossesKiran Stacey,Josh Halliday,Alexandra ToppingandRob DaviesThu 10 Sep 2026 14.14 EDTFirst published on Thu 10 Sep 2026 04.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMinisters are facing a backlash from the hospitality industry after they announced mayors inEnglandwould be given sweeping powers to levy taxes on holiday accommodation such as hotels and Airbnbs.The plan, presented on Thursday byAngela Rayner, the local government secretary, will allow mayors to impose a “tourist tax” without a cap on how much they can charge and with few controls on how they can spend it.The move, which gives mayors some of their most significant tax-raising powers, was welcomed by regional leaders, who said it would give them a vital revenue stream at a time when local government is facing a funding crisis. Mayors will be expected to lay out their detailed plans for how they plan to use the new powers in early 2028.The hospitality industry fears a tourist tax will deter visitors – the evidence says otherwiseRead moreBut it was met with outrage from hospitality businesses, who had expected the government to put stricter conditions on how much mayors could charge and how the money would be used.UKHospitality, the industry’s trade body, said a 5% overnight levy across England could result in 33,000 job losses and a £2bn hit to the economy, with regions more reliant on tourism, such as the Lake District, being worst affected.The owner of Premier Inn, Britain’s biggest hotel chain, said it would be “hugely damaging” and urged ministers to “avoid inflicting what could be irreparable harm on this large and vital sector of the economy”.Eddie Nelder, a co-owner of the ChoiceHotelschain, which has hotels in Blackpool and the Lake District, said: “We’re here trying to stay alive, waiting for a lifeline from the government and we get another hammer blow. It feels like we’re being strangled.”View image in fullscreenA Blackpool hotel owner said the taxes were ‘another hammer blow’ for the hospitality industry.Photograph: Pawel Libera/LightRocket/Getty ImagesHowever, Rayner said the tax-raising powers would help fund local communities. “This measure will give mayors the choice to raise and reinvest funding where it’s needed most,” she said in a statement before a meeting with the country’s mayors at No 10 North in Manchester.“It’ll help support the local services, public spaces and attractions that both residents and visitors rely on, with decisions taken by people who know their area best.”In the immediate term, the rate will be set at no more than 5% in almost every major English city after everyLabourmetro mayor agreed to cap their charges at that level.In a joint letter to Rayner, they wrote: “Foreign cities visited by British tourists from New York to Paris, as well as hundreds of smaller cities across the world, have long benefited from such levies while continuing to grow their tourism sectors. Granting the power to regions to introduce levies will help level the playing field by ensuring further investment in our cities, contributing to further growth.”But large parts of the east coast will not have to pay the tax after their mayors – two Reform UK and one Conservative – said they would refuse to impose them.The move follows a consultation launched by Keir Starmer’s government, and will bring England into line with many European countries and the US, where holidaymakers have for years been paying overnight visitor levies.Similar levies also apply in Wales and Scotland, though they will be capped in Wales.Edinburgh became the first city in Scotland to introduce a tourist tax, setting it at 5% in July. In Wales, councils will have the power to charge £1.30 per person a night in tax for most accommodation from April 2027.Under the proposal, which is expected to be introduced as a bill in parliament within months, mayors will be allowed to charge a levy as a percentage of the price of an overnight stay, rather than as a flat fee.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe mayor of north-east England, Kim McGuinness, said the tax could bring money into the region during events such as the Great North Run.Photograph: DEW/AlamyMinisters at Westminster will cap the number of nights to which it can be applied in order to avoid hitting long-term rental properties. It is understood the cap is likely to be higher than the 5% that is applied by Holyrood.Any commercially rented property will face the tax, though there will be an exemption for those that are only rented occasionally on a casual basis.Mayors will be allowed to decide whether or not to exempt other sites such as festival campsites. They will also be allowed to share revenues with local councils.Kim McGuinness, the mayor of north-east England, backed the move for a visitor levy, saying it could bring money to the local economy during events such as the Great North Run, which is due to take place this Sunday.“A visitor levy could help us bring major international events to our region, back local businesses, improve visitor attractions, build on the 90,000 jobs already in this sector and unlock opportunities that come from a thriving visitor economy,” she said.“Most importantly, the money raised here would stay here, helping us invest in the future of our region rather than waiting for Whitehall to do it for us.”The move is one of the biggest handovers of power from the Treasury to local leaders in years, and comes before the first budget of Andy Burnham’s government, at which ministers have promised to hand over more tax powers to local leaders.It comes at a time when many local authorities are struggling for funds. Last year the government gaveemergency fundingworth £1.3bn to a record 28 councils, without which several said they would have gone bankrupt.But it also comes after a concerted effort by the government to ease the pressure on the hospitality industry, with many businesses struggling with high inflation and increased national insurance and minimum wage bills.Earlier this summer, the former chancellorslashed VATon British summer holiday destinations, in a programme she called the “Great British summer savings scheme”.Meanwhile, in one of his first acts as prime minister, Burnham announced he wouldcut business ratesfor pubs, clubs and live music venues.Many hospitality businesses are struggling with high inflation, as well as additional national insurance and minimum wage costs imposed by Reeves in her first budget.Allen Simpson, the chief executive of UKHospitality, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “What we’re talking about here is an open-ended power for mayors to set tourism taxes at any level they want … If you go to Paris, if you go to Rome, if you go to Berlin, you’re paying a small tourism tax, but it’s capped.”Additional reporting by Raphael BoydExplore more on these topicsTravel & leisureHospitality industryHotelsAirbnbTax and spendingAngela RaynerDevolutionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Four people in hospital after stabbing in south-east London | London | The Guardian
description: Seven people arrested following ‘altercation’ on Bromley High Street on Thursday afternoon
Author: Emine Sinmaz
Headline: Seven people arrested following ‘altercation’ on Bromley High Street on Thursday afternoon
Content: A police statement said: ‘Officers attended the scene alongside the London ambulance service and London’s air ambulance and found four men with stab wounds.’Photograph: James Manning/PAView image in fullscreenA police statement said: ‘Officers attended the scene alongside the London ambulance service and London’s air ambulance and found four men with stab wounds.’Photograph: James Manning/PALondonFour people in hospital after stabbing in south-east LondonSeven people arrested following ‘altercation’ on Bromley High Street on Thursday afternoonEmine SinmazandKevin RawlinsonThu 10 Sep 2026 14.07 EDTFirst published on Thu 10 Sep 2026 12.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSeven people have been arrested after four men were stabbed in south-eastLondon, the Metropolitan police said.Officers were called to reports of “an altercation” on Bromley High Street at 2.15pm and found four men with stab wounds, the force added.In a statement, it said: “Officers attended the scene alongside the London ambulance service and London’s air ambulance and found four men with stab wounds. Three of them were taken to hospital where they are receiving treatment for non-life-threatening injuries. One is in critical condition.View image in fullscreenForensic investigators at the scene on Thursday afternoon.Photograph: James Manning/PA“Seven men were arrested and they all remain in custody. Police inquiries continue and there is not believed to be any wider threat to the public.”A cordon was in place at the scene on Thursday, with police, as well as community support officers, standing around the perimeter. Forensics officers dressed in blue overalls and a crime scene photographer were coming and going from a branch of KFC, where locals said the incident occurred, and there were evidence markers visible on the floor.Abandoned food could still be seen on the tables as evening drew in, suggestive of the haste in which people left the restaurant amid the incident. “I heard a really loud bang and people running from KFC,” said George Ioannou, who was working in Antonio’s Male Grooming next door to the KFC.“An elderly woman ran into the shop and I had to lock the door to shelter her until it calmed down. She was crying. About five minutes later, we heard the sirens.” Other shop workers nearby said the incident was quick and that it was over in moments.The KFC has an alleyway down one side – along which people ran as they passed the male grooming shop – and faces on to Bromley’s High Street. Part of the latter was still closed to the public on Thursday evening. It is a busy thoroughfare, with a large shopping centre at one end and a train station taking commuters between Kent, south-east London and the capital’s centre at the other. Those and the parade of shops lining the high street draw large numbers of people from the surrounding area. About 15 bus routes were diverted, including the 61, 208 and 119.The London ambulance service said ambulance crews, a paramedic in a fast-response car, an incident response officer, an advanced paramedic and London’s air ambulance were dispatched to the scene.Four patients were treated at the scene before being taken to hospital, the service added.The Bromley and Biggin Hill MP Peter Fortune said: “I am aware of the incident on Bromley High Street this afternoon and I know that residents will have safety concerns. The police are in attendance and have made a number of arrests. I will remain in close contact with the police as they continue to investigate this incident.”A picture shared on social media on Thursday afternoon appeared to show a section of Bromley High Street cordoned off, with an emergency vehicle on site. The Met asked anyone with information to contact the police on 101.Explore more on these topicsLondonCrimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Former PE teacher faces lengthy jail term for sexually abusing pupils | England | The Guardian
description: Bronwen James, 30, admitted offences against two girls at schools in Wiltshire and Hampshire, and found guilty of charges involving boy
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Bronwen James, 30, admitted offences against two girls at schools in Wiltshire and Hampshire, and found guilty of charges involving boy
Content: Bronwen James arrives at Winchester crown court on Thursday. The Crown Prosecution Services praised the teenagers she targeted for coming forward.Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PAView image in fullscreenBronwen James arrives at Winchester crown court on Thursday. The Crown Prosecution Services praised the teenagers she targeted for coming forward.Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PAEnglandFormer PE teacher faces lengthy jail term for sexually abusing pupilsBronwen James, 30, admitted offences against two girls at schools in Wiltshire  and Hampshire, and found guilty of charges involving boySteven MorrisThu 10 Sep 2026 13.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA former PE teacher is facing a lengthy jail sentence for grooming and sexually abusing three pupils at two schools.Bronwen James, 30, admitted offences against two girls at schools inHampshireand Wiltshire and was found guilty by a jury of charges involving a boy.The Crown Prosecution Service described James’s crimes as “a sustained pattern of predatory behaviour against children in her care” and praised the teenagers she targeted for coming forward.Judge James Bromige asked for reports to be prepared on James so that he could assess the danger she posed when sentencing her later this year. Her defence team said she knew she faced a significant jail sentence.During her trial at Winchester crown court, jurors were told that James, from Chippenham inWiltshire, flirted with a 16-year-old boy in class at a school in Southampton.They began exchanging Snapchat messages and arranged for her to drive him to a promenade, where they kissed in her car.Later they went to her house where they cuddled while watching the Wimbledon tennis championships on the television before going to her bedroom where they had sex. She told him she loved him and wanted him to move away with her.Edward Culver, prosecuting, told the trial the school was made aware of the incident after another student showed a teacher some text messages apparently sent between the James and the complainant.He said: “They suggested a sexually charged relationship. He [the boy] was named as ‘number 8’ in the messages as a cover. She acted not only in an unprofessional and overfamiliar way, but failed to recognise any boundaries, exploiting her position to engage in sexual activity with one of her young students.”In a police interview, the boy said he had been “groomed” by the defendant.James was convicted of three counts of sexual activity with a child by a person in a position of trust.Before the trial, James pleaded guilty to offences against two girls. One was a pupil at the same Southampton school as the boy, the other attended a school in Wiltshire that James had also taught at.The offences included sexual activity with a child, sexual communication with a child and making an indecent photograph of a child. The victims were 13 and 14 at the time.During legal argument, which can now be reported, it also emerged that at the start of her career, James received a warning while she was teaching at the private Seaford college in West Sussex for giving her personal mobile number to a pupil.Bethany Adams, of the CPS, said: “Bronwen James was trusted to educate and protect children. Instead, she used that trust to groom and sexually abuse three students.“James manipulated her victims with calculated precision, exploiting her position of authority to isolate them and normalise the abuse.“This was not a lapse in judgment; it was a sustained pattern of predatory behaviour against children in her care.“The courage shown by James’s victims in coming forward has been instrumental in securing this conviction. I hope it gives them, and their families, some measure of justice.”Explore more on these topicsEnglandWiltshireHampshirenewsShareReuse this content

title: Florida executes man in connection to Hog Trail Murders | Florida | The Guardian
description: The execution of Daniel Owen Conahan Jr makes him the state’s 15th person executed this year
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The execution of Daniel Owen Conahan Jr makes him the state’s 15th person executed this year
Content: The wing at Florida state prison that houses the execution chamber on 28 July 2026.Photograph: Douglas R Clifford/TNS/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe wing at Florida state prison that houses the execution chamber on 28 July 2026.Photograph: Douglas R Clifford/TNS/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockFloridaFlorida executes man in connection to Hog Trail MurdersThe execution of Daniel Owen Conahan Jr makes him the state’s 15th person executed this yearKeely AougaThu 10 Sep 2026 18.40 EDTFirst published on Thu 10 Sep 2026 10.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAFloridaman was executed by lethal injection on Thursday after being convicted of one of a series of suspected killings that became known as the Hog Trail Murders in the 1990s.Daniel Owen Conahan Jr, 72, was sentenced to death for the 1996 kidnapping and strangling of Richard Allen Montgomery. Authorities found Montgomery’s mutilated body in a wooded south-west Florida area where the remains of at least six people have been found over a three-year span.Conahan died at 6.12pm ET, state officials said.Florida has carried out more than half of the 24 total executions in the US this year, under Ron DeSantis, the Republican governor who leaves office in January. Conahan Jr is the 15th person executed in the state this year.Under DeSantis, Florida carried out 19 executions in 2025, setting a state record since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976.Conahan was arrested in July 1996 after local and state law enforcement officials spent more than two years investigating a series of homicides in which mutilated and decomposing bodies were discovered in a wooded area of Charlotte county, north of Fort Myers.The deaths eventually were categorized as the Hog Trail Murders because of the swampy, wooded locations where the bodies were found. The case has been featured many times over the past three decades on true-crime media content.Conahan, who maintained his innocence, was previously identified by authorities as a person of interest in the other deaths, but he was never charged. He argued that the evidence against him was circumstantial.The first body was found by hunters in February 1994, followed by at least five more bodies over the next three years. Most of the remains were severely decomposed, but investigators believed Montgomery had been dead for less than a day when he was found.Investigators eventually determined that the killer was targeting men who were unhoused.Detectives started looking into Conahan in 1996 after a man in prison for stealing Conahan’s car claimed that Conahan had lured him to a remote area and offered to pay him to pose for nude photos. The man said he drove off in the car after seeing a knife.Conahan waived his right to a jury trial and was convicted by a judge of murder and kidnapping in August 1999.The Florida supreme court last week denied Conahan’s final appeals, including one requesting additional testing on DNA collected from the victim.The petition said he has been requesting DNA testing since March 2025 of evidence collected at the scene and from Montgomery’s body to “conclusively establish that he is not responsible for the death”.Within 24 hours, the court ruled that proving Montgomery had DNA on his body from someone other than Conahan would not exonerate him.The US supreme court on Thursday denied his final appeal.Explore more on these topicsFloridaUS crimeCapital punishmentUS justice systemnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump ally resigns from post leading inquiry into alleged conspiracy against president | Trump-Russia investigation | The Guardian
description: Joe diGenova led investigation focused on intelligence assessment that Russia interfered in 2016 election
Author: Aram Roston
Headline: Joe diGenova led investigation focused on intelligence assessment that Russia interfered in 2016 election
Content: Donald Trump after he was sworn in as president on 20 January 2017, after an election a special counsel concluded Russia had interfered in.Photograph: Justin Lane/EPAView image in fullscreenDonald Trump after he was sworn in as president on 20 January 2017, after an election a special counsel concluded Russia had interfered in.Photograph: Justin Lane/EPATrump-Russia investigationTrump ally resigns from post leading inquiry into alleged conspiracy against presidentJoe diGenova led investigation focused on intelligence assessment that Russia interfered in 2016 electionAram Rostonand agenciesThu 10 Sep 2026 18.19 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA longtime ally ofDonald Trumpresigned from his post leading a Department of Justice investigation into whether former law enforcement and intelligence officials conspired against the Republican president.“Sometimes people want things done faster and that’s all you can do,” Joe diGenova said on Thursday. He appeared to be referring to concerns among other Trump loyalists that the president’s retribution cases were not moving quickly enough.“The bottom line is it takes a long time to make good cases, and you simply have to work at it,” he added. “All you can do is do the best you can under the circumstances.”The departure injects instant tumult into an investigation targeting former government officials who have investigated Trump over the last decade, including in connection with Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election and his retention of classified documents at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach, Florida.The Florida-based investigation has proceeded in fits and starts since its inception a year ago, with its contours loosely defined, though it had shown recent signs of activity with new subpoenas demanding testimony before a federal grand jury.While retribution by the justice department against Trump’s perceived adversaries has been one of the president’s highest priorities, diGenova’s comments hint at internal dissent and disagreement over the cases. He declined to say exactly why he resigned.“I’m not going to make any comments about indictments or anything else,” diGenova said. “When you’ve been a prosecutor as long as I have you know how to make cases, and it takes time. And that’s just part of the process. And sometimes that works out, and sometimes it doesn’t.”During the firstTrump administration, diGenova was a legal adviser to John Solomon, a conservative journalist who has played an official role in White House efforts to push the conspiracy allegations.In an interview later with the New York Post, diGenova responded to criticism of his management of the investigation by saying: “If you want indictments where there’s no evidence, you have an ethical problem.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat’s really behind Trump’s deference to Putin?Read moreA spokesperson for the justice department did not immediately return a message seeking comment.The 81-year-old diGenova served as the US attorney for the District of Columbia during the Reagan administration. A close Trump ally, he was brought back to the justice department in April and given responsibility for an investigation aimed at trying to establish a conspiracy against Trump.DiGenova had previously asked the then US attorney general, Pam Bondi, to appoint him to the job and had openly and repeatedly claimed Trump was the victim of an intelligence community conspiracy.But five months later, no charges have been brought, and it remains unclear whether any will be, or what information has been gathered to support any basis for the idea of a plot against Trump by the government officials who investigated him.The investigation has focused intensely on one of Trump’s chief grievances: a US intelligence community assessment that Russia had interfered on his behalf in the 2016 presidential election.The president and some of his supporters have long decried that conclusion as a “deep state” plot to undermine the legitimacy of his win. Multiple government investigations, including by a justice department special counsel and by the department’s own inspector general, have concluded that Russia interfered in sweeping fashion to help get Trump elected.The year-long investigation had proceeded in fits and starts well before diGenova’s appointment, which was announced soon after a career national security prosecutor who had been playing a key role in the investigation was replaced on the inquiry after raising doubts about its legal viability.The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsTrump-Russia investigationDonald TrumpRussiaElection interferenceTrump administrationUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: More Anthropic researchers warn of AI’s perils as Musk terms fears a ‘psyop’ | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Insiders at the firm fear tech’s advancement could cause human extinction while others are calling it a ‘setup’
Author: Johana Bhuiyan
Headline: Insiders at the firm fear tech’s advancement could cause human extinction while others are calling it a ‘setup’
Content: Stickers for Claude software on an attendees laptop at Claude developer conference in London, on Tuesday, 19 May 2026.Photograph: Chris Ratcliffe/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenStickers for Claude software on an attendees laptop at Claude developer conference in London, on Tuesday, 19 May 2026.Photograph: Chris Ratcliffe/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)More Anthropic researchers warn of AI’s perils as Musk terms fears a ‘psyop’Insiders at the firm fear tech’s advancement could cause human extinction while others are calling it a ‘setup’Johana BhuiyanThu 10 Sep 2026 17.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA day after a former researcher atAnthropicmade an apocalyptic declaration about artificial intelligence, more researchers and staff members at the AI startup publicly agreed with him and posted their own dire warnings.In response, Elon Musk and other conservative figures on X, formerly Twitter, called the chorus of concerns a “setup” and a “psyop”.The Anthropic insiders fear the technology they are building could become so advanced and dangerous as to cause human extinction within the decade, and they assert many of their colleagues feel the same but haven’t said so publicly.These researchers and staff are posting in response to a now-viral thread from Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who said on Wednesday he was resigning from the company because neither Anthropic nor its competitor OpenAI, also his former employer, were building AI models responsibly and are “gambling with our lives”.OpenAI not on track to reduce risk of ‘catastrophic’ loss of control, says board memberRead moreAnna Wang, who works on Artificial General Intelligence Safety at Anthropic and previously worked at Google’s DeepMind, said Thursday that many people at Anthropic want to slow down development to come up with a plan to mitigate the risks that could come with these AI models.“There is not yet a viable scientific plan to solve risks from recursively self-improving AI,” Wang wrote on X.Drake Thomas, another Anthropic employee, said that he respected Coxon’s choice to abstain from building these models if he worries they could pose planet-scale risks.“Things are moving way too fast, we don’t have anywhere near the degree of assurance we’ll want for ASI [artificial superintelligence],” Thomas said.Musk took a more adversarial stance. “Seems like a setup,” hewrote.Coxon replied to the world’s richest man with a selfie, writing, “I’m real and these are my real beliefs. You could ask your xAI researchers about me if you hadn’t fired them.”In a statement to the Guardian, an Anthropic spokesperson defended the company’s strategy. “We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks. To address these risks, we continue to build models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry,” the statement said.Musk and others with a more positive view of AI have started to spread theories that Coxon’s post and the resulting fallout are part of a “psyop” to negatively influence the public’s feelings about AI.“I think the groundwork for this psy op (for lack of a better term) has been prepared for a long time,” Musk posted on X. “This was just the match that lit the fire.”Musk was responding to a post by Parker Thayer, a researcher at conservativethinktank Capital Research, in which he floated a theory with little evidence that Coxon’s post was the start of a “VERY sophisticated and well-funded PR operation to get support for Democrats to regulate AI into oblivion”. Other notable figures took notice.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBill Ackman, the billionaire CEO of the hedge fund Pershing Square, also quoted Thayer’s post, simply saying “Interesting.”Other Anthropic employees had posted their agreement with Coxon shortly after he declared his resignation on Wednesday.“AI developers believe their technology could cause human extinction (or similarly bad outcomes),” wrote Samuel Marks, who works on safety research at Anthropic. “This could happen in the next few years. In general, the more senior the employee, the more concerned they are.”Evan Hubinger, who describes himself as a lead in the company’s alignment division, which works on ensuring Anthropic’s AI models function in line with human goals, said Coxon was “correct” and that the industry was falling behind in attempts to deal with the apocalyptic potential.“We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Hubingerwrote. “I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.It’s not exactly clear how Coxon and others expect AI models to usher in the demise of humanity. Some experts doubt that the technology will become so intelligent as to cause the apocalypse. Gary Marcus, a scientist and leading voice in AI, said that it’s time to boycott AI, but because it’s already causing harm.More than extinction, Marcus said he worried about the “risk of catastrophe” from “from AI-generated pathogens, from wars started or escalated by AI-generated disinformation, from hacks that destroy critical infrastructure, and so on. Nothing I have seen gives any indication that any of that is under control”.The same day, Anthropic released a report documenting how the company dismantled an operation attempting to build a biological weapon using its AI models.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)AnthropicnewsShareReuse this content

title: San Francisco mayor declares rent emergency as housing costs soar amid AI boom | San Francisco | The Guardian
description: Median rent for one-bedroom apartment in city tops $4,495 with a national median of $1,900
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: Median rent for one-bedroom apartment in city tops $4,495 with a national median of $1,900
Content: The North Beach neighborhood in San Francisco, where rents are soaring as the AI boom brings a new wave of wealth to the city.Photograph: Heather Diehl/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe North Beach neighborhood in San Francisco, where rents are soaring as the AI boom brings a new wave of wealth to the city.Photograph: Heather Diehl/Getty ImagesSan FranciscoSan Francisco mayor declares rent emergency as housing costs soar amid AI boomMedian rent for one-bedroom apartment in city tops $4,495 with a national median of $1,900Uwa Ede-OsifoThu 10 Sep 2026 17.34 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSan Francisco’s mayor, Daniel Lurie, declared a rent emergency on Thursday, proposing reforms aimed at curbing evictions and preventing rent spikes as the city grapples with soaring apartment prices.The Bay Area city, home to a large number of high-earning tech workers, has long been one of the most expensive housing and rental markets in the country.The median rent for a one-bedroom apartment in San Francisco is currently $4,495,accordingto Zumper, a rental listings site. In comparison, the national median for a one-bedroom apartment is $1,900.The ballooning rental costs have been attributed to a recent influx of wealth in the market, as artificial intelligence companies began to go public on the stock market. While demand has ratcheted up for limited housing options,San Franciscohas notoriously lagged behind other cities in approving new housing.Among Lurie’s proposed measures are caps to rent increases for rent-controlled apartments, $27m in funding to cover funding lapses from federal housing vouchers set to expire and an increase in payments to tenants who are evicted under the Ellis Act, legislation landlords can evoke when leaving the rental business.“Today, most San Franciscans feel our city is finally moving in the right direction, but many are also asking whether they can still afford to live here,” Lurie said in a statement on Thursday.“We have lived through booms before – this time, we have an opportunity to build a recovery that is broad-based and lasting, where San Franciscans can put down roots and participate in our city’s success.”Explore more on these topicsSan FranciscoHousing marketInflationHousingCaliforniaWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: Global bond sell-off resumes as surging oil prices stoke fears about inflation | Bonds | The Guardian
description: Crude jumps above $107 a barrel amid concerns over Middle East conflict and out-of-control government borrowing
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Crude jumps above $107 a barrel amid concerns over Middle East conflict and out-of-control government borrowing
Content: Surging oil prices caused by intensifying tensions in the Middle East have fuelled inflation concerns across markets including South Korea.Photograph: YONHAP/EPAView image in fullscreenSurging oil prices caused by intensifying tensions in the Middle East have fuelled inflation concerns across markets including South Korea.Photograph: YONHAP/EPABondsGlobal bond sell-off resumes as surging oil prices stoke fears about inflationCrude jumps above $107 a barrel amid concerns over Middle East conflict and out-of-control government borrowingHeather StewartandPhillip InmanThu 10 Sep 2026 14.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNervous investors across big economies have been dumping government bonds, driving up the cost of borrowing, as surging oil prices amplified fears about rising inflation.The cost of a barrel of oil jumped 6% to above $107 on Thursday amid concerns thatadvances by Houthi rebelsalong the Red Sea coast in Yemen could choke off Saudi crude exports.The global bond sell-off that has rocked markets in recent weeks resumed in response to the news from the Middle East – which came against a backdrop of escalating concern about out-of-control government borrowing.Higher oil prices, which had already climbed since hostilities resumed in the Iran war, are expected to drive up inflation, prompting central banks to raise interest rates and putting the brakes on economic growth.A line graph showing yields on UK, US, Japanese and German 10-year government bonds since 2000Donald Trump suggested on Wednesday that the conflict with Iran could continue until “immediately after” November’s US midterm elections, at which point he claimed oil prices would be “tumbling downward”.The European Central Bank (ECB)raised its main interest rate to 2.5% on Thursday, with its president, Christine Lagarde, saying: “We believe inflation will be longer lasting than we had anticipated.”“The conflict in the Middle ​East continues ​to ⁠generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to ​remain well above target for ​an ⁠extended period,” she added.View image in fullscreenThe ECB president, Christine Lagarde, said eurozone inflation would remain above the central bank’s target for longer than expected.Photograph: Filip Singer/EPAAs Thursday’s sell-off gathered pace in London, the yield, or interest rate, on 10-year UK government bonds surged above 5.37% – the highest cost of borrowing since 2007 – creating a fresh headache for the new chancellor, John Healey.With less than seven weeks to go until Healey’s first budget on 28 October, higher interest rates on the UK’s debt-pile will raise the cost of future investment projects and eat into the Treasury’s fiscal headroom.A line graph showing crude prices per barrel since the start of the Iran warAt the same time, the prospect of higher energy bills as oil and gas prices rise is likely to intensify pressure on the government to help consumers to weather the winter.Unleaded petrol prices have already risen by 6p a litre since the start of September, according to the motoring organisation the RAC, while the prospect of higher inflation has prompted some banks to raise their mortgage rates.Healey has promised to provide a “breathing space” for UK households while also addressing the cost of doing business.View image in fullscreenUnleaded petrol prices in the UK have already risen by 6p a litre since the start of September, according to the RAC.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianIna speech on Monday, however, he also sought to tame bond market fears by committing himself to “controlling borrowing to bear down on inflation, and reducing long-term pressures on our public finances”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the US, where Trump has promised to writea $5,000 (£3,700) cheque for every adult citizen if the Republicans win the midterms, Thursday’s sell-off pushed up the yield on 10-year borrowing to 4.92% – the highest since 2023.The cost of longer-term borrowing also continued to surge, with 30-year yields hitting the highest level since 2007, despite the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, intervening directly in debt markets on Wednesday.Bessent hoped to bring down yields by buying back $6bn worth of government debt; but investors appeared to respond by deepening the sell-off.Kyle Rodda, a senior financial market analyst at the broker Capital.com, said: “Ultimately, a sustained drop in long-end yields can ​only be achieved by genuine shifts in macroeconomic policy: ​either the US government pulling back on spending or the ​Fed lifting rates.”Policymakers at the Federal Reserve, the US central bank, will meet under its new chair, Kevin Warsh, to set interest rates next week.View image in fullscreenScott Bessent at the Republican convention in Dallas, where Donald Trump promised $5,000 to every adult US citizen if the party wins the midterms.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesMarkets are expecting a rise – potentially enraging Trump, who has repeatedly demanded rate cuts. In a TruthSocial post last week, the president said: “The Fed Board, with its great new leader, must get smart – BE PATRIOTS for a change.”A plethora of UK data to be published over the next week, including on inflation, jobs and growth, will give an updated snapshot of how resilient the British economy has been in the face of the Iran war.In the first six months of the year, UK growth was the strongest among the G7 economies. This was despite higher-than-expected oil prices and the absence of hoped-for rate cuts.Bank of England policymakers will also meet next week, but are expected to leave the UK’s key interest rate on hold at 3.75% for the time being as they continue to monitor the impact of higher oil prices.Explore more on these topicsBondsGovernment borrowingUS Government borrowingOilInflationEuropean Central BankInterest ratesnewsShareReuse this content

title: ECB raises interest rates to 2.5% and warns Iran war is fuelling inflation  | European Central Bank | The Guardian
description: Borrowing costs climb in Europe and oil tops $105 a barrel as bank says growing price pressures in eurozone will be ‘longer lasting than we had anticipated’
Author: Phillip Inman
