He ‌is upset about it,” the club president added.“I just spoke to Ismail Kartal. He mentioned the bottle incident and he also complained about being under pressure,” he said. Asked whether the manager had told him he would stay, Yildirim said: “There’s no need for him ‌to say that he’d continue. I am his senior, I told him to continue and that’s ​it. We are a family.”Kartal, who spent a decade at Fenerbahce as a player, coached the club in 2014-15, then on an interim basis in 2021-22 before returning for a full ⁠campaign in 2023-24. He was the assistant manager at Fenerbahce the ​past two ​times the club won ​the Turkish title, and returned for a fourth ​managerial spell in ‌June.View image in fullscreenArchie Brown celebrates his equaliser for Fenerbahce. The English full-back was left dumbfounded when learning of his coach’s resignation after the final whistle.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesFenerbahce have ​finished second ​in the Turkish Super Lig in each of the past five seasons, and reached the Champions League’s league phase this season for the first time in 18 years. The team sit ninth in the Turkish top-flight, having lost twice in their opening four games, including Saturday’s 2-1 home defeat to Besiktas.Roma took the lead in the 39th minute when Donyell Malen rolled a pass to ​Bryan Cristante, who beat Fenerbahce keeper Ederson with a bouncing finish. The hosts levelled before half-time when Mason Greenwood slipped a ​pass through to Archie ​Brown, who clipped a finish over ​Mile Svilar.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRoma were awarded a penalty in the 68th minute when ​Kerem Akturkoglu was ‌penalised for a ​foul on Paulo ​Dybala, but a VAR check ruled that the challenge had taken place outside the area. Fenerbahce came closest to grabbing a winner late on when Nathan Aké headed against the Roma crossbar.Fenerbahce will travel to Aston Villa and host Liverpool in two of their remaining league phase games – whether Kartal will be in charge or not remains to be seen.Explore more on these topicsFenerbahceChampions LeagueEuropean club footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: Mauricio Pochettino: ‘I am always open to help Tottenham. In whatever division’ | Mauricio Pochettino | The Guardian
description: The manager is excited by new US deal but might be at Spurs if the stars had aligned and does not rule out taking England job one day
Author: David Hytner
Headline: The manager is excited by new US deal but might be at Spurs if the stars had aligned and does not rule out taking England job one day
Content: Mauricio Pochettino’s elite CV includes managerial roles at Tottenham, Chelsea, Paris St-Germain and the United States.Photograph: Richard Heathcote/FIFA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMauricio Pochettino’s elite CV includes managerial roles at Tottenham, Chelsea, Paris St-Germain and the United States.Photograph: Richard Heathcote/FIFA/Getty ImagesMauricio PochettinoInterviewMauricio Pochettino: ‘I am always open to help Tottenham. In whatever division’David HytnerManager is excited by new US deal but might have returned to Spurs if the stars had aligned and does not rule out taking England job one dayThu 10 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 05.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf things had worked out differently,Mauricio Pochettinowould have gone back to his beloved Tottenham over the summer. They had put in the call and it stirred him. Nothing was going to put him off – not even the possibility of the club being in the Championship.Seriously, Mauricio? After aWorld Cup campaign with the United Statesand top jobs with Chelsea and Paris Saint-Germain before that, he would have been willing to start a new chapter in the second tier of English football? “Yes, of course,” Pochettino says. “Tottenham … it’s the only club that always I am open to help. In whatever division.”Chelsea’s 2016-17 Premier League title should be given to Spurs, says PochettinoRead moreFootball is about timing and Pochettino was left to reflect on how his stars did not align. It has been a theme of his managerial career, along with the desire to keep an eye out for greener pastures. And not be shy about doing so.Spurs’ idea aftersacking Thomas Frankin February was to get to the end of the season under the interim Igor Tudor, when they could assess a potentially deeper pool of candidates. They knew that if Pochettino was to be their man, they would have to wait for him because he was contracted to the US until after the World Cup. There was no way he could walk out on that challenge. Nor would he have wanted to.Then the picture changed. When Tudor bombed, leaving Spurs one point above the relegation zone with seven games to play, they pivoted to Roberto De Zerbi, who said no to them after they dismissed Frank. De Zerbi had just left Marseille and needed a break. Now Spurs made him a long-term offer he could not refuse. And so Pochettino felt the door close to the club where he managed for five-and-a-half years from 2014; where he established such a strong connection.“The problem was that the timings were never the best,” he says. “When I was free, I never received a contact and then when I was working, I received a contact but I cannot make the decision to come back. It was a little bit unlucky. Maybe one day the stars will align and it can happen. If I was free, of course, I come. But I wasn’t free. I was preparing the World Cup.”View image in fullscreenMauricio Pochettino, celebrating after the dramatic semi-final win against Ajax, led Tottenham to the Champions League final in 2019.Photograph: Matthew Childs/Action Images/ReutersWas the door to Spurs ever truly open for Pochettino? The club have insisted that De Zerbi was their No 1 target for the summer before they were forced to move ahead of time. Perhaps we will never know. But one thing is clear: these kind of teasers and Pochettino’s openness about them are a part of his story. They add to his swaggering appeal. In a game where micromanaged content is the norm, where managers are tied in knots by the party line, there is something exhilarating about hearing Pochettino hold court.The 54-year-old has always had his suitors, ever since he first began to establish his reputation as a forward-thinking coach and charismatic man-manager at Espanyol, where he took charge in 2009. He has always liked to keep them close and he always will do. Should US Soccer be worried? Pochettino has just signed a new four-year contract to take him up to the 2030 World Cup. That is probably an unhealthy way of thinking. Better for the federation to focus on how it has one of the game’s elite managers and accept that they will have options.View image in fullscreenMauricio Pochettino has signed a new deal with the United States that will take him through to the 2030 World Cup.Photograph: Todd Kirkland/FIFA/Getty ImagesPochettino has had his share of sliding-doors moments. He was linked to the Real Madrid job in November 2017 as Zinedine Zidane was tipped for the sack only for the Frenchman to hang on and end up winning the Champions League that season. Two days before the final against Liverpool, Pochettino signed a new long-term contract at Spurs. Five days after it, Zidane announced his shock resignation. It was not the first or, indeed, the last time that Pochettino was linked to Madrid.There have been links with Manchester United. The club considered him when they sacked Louis van Gaal in 2016, when they dismissed José Mourinho in 2018 and turned to Ole Gunnar Solskjær, initially on an interim basis (Solskjær would make the job his own), and before they hired Erik ten Hag in 2022.Then there was England. Pochettino was in the conversation as the Football Association looked for a successor to Sir Gareth Southgate after Euro 2024. The way Pochettino tells it, he committed to the US in August of that year and it was before the FA started its search in earnest. It would end with it choosing Thomas Tuchel.Would Pochettino consider the England job one day? He is aware that his Argentinian nationality would present an issue – because of the Falklands conflict andthe history between the countrieson the football pitch. It was fractious when they clashed in the World Cup semi-final in July, Argentina winning 2-1. But Pochettino does not see it as a deal-breaker.“Maybe, yes,” he says of coaching England. “If you consider in a few years’ time, yes … if I got an approach. One thing I don’t want because theUSAguys will kill me is if you say the headline is: ‘Mauricio will consider English job.’ It is like I am considering it now. No. Not now. If I am free [in the future].View image in fullscreenMauricio Pochettino, still adored by Tottenham fans, says the north London team is ‘still my club’.Photograph: Tony O’Brien/Action Images/Reuters“My respect is that it’s football. I am the first to feel for my people in Argentina but at the end of the day it’s just football. The World Cup semi-final was just one game of football, although people wanted to convert it to other subjects. It is true that it can be controversial because an Argentinian guy is thinking to maybe one day defend the flag of England and we were involved in a war …”Pochettino still has his family home in north London. He has a love affair with the city and England. “We are very similar, Argentinian and English people, in the way we feel the passion of football,” he says. “I love the countryside here, too. I think you respect all the things that I also grew up with in my country.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“In Argentina, I lived in a town in Murphy with a lot of Irish and British people around. And all the clubs … Racing Club, River Plate, Newell’s Old Boys. They are English language names, no? Now I am here doing my passion that is football and I cannot work here [for England]? Why? It is crazy. I really believe in the diplomatic things, going to talk and for sure to find the best way.”Pochettinoextended his contract with the USfor many reasons, among them the faith the federation had shown in him. They offered him the four-year deal before the World Cup kicked off, which he appreciated greatly. He signed it in August. The challenge excites him – to change the perception of the game in the country, to build something. He has made a good start.The World Cup ended badly with the4-1 defeat by Belgiumin the last 16. The game was overshadowed by theFolarin Balogun controversy; how the US federation was able to overturn the striker’s suspension amid trademark grandstanding from Donald Trump. It ought to have been a blessing. It ended up as a curse, affecting Balogun and the team; giving Belgium even more of a cause. But before that, everything had gone extremely well.View image in fullscreenMauricio Pochettino managed USA to the last-16 of this summer’s World Cup.Photograph: Alex Livesey/FIFA/Getty ImagesThe free-flowing 4-1 victory against Paraguay in the opening game sparked a feelgood factor. Then came the comfortable win over Australia to secure qualification from the group with a game to spare. Bosnia and Herzegovina were swatted aside in the last 32. “We created something,” Pochettino says. “The fans were amazing. We never expected the fans in this way. The players changed completely the mindset.”Pochettino’s situation, though, does feel different with the longer contract – certainly to him. “Now it is a different thing,” he says. “When we gave our word to the federation [in August 2024], it was about starting and finishing after the World Cup. For us, it was the moment to say: ‘If some club comes, it’s impossible.’ Always you can break a contract, say you stop and that’s it … you agree something. But in the moment it wasn’t right for us to create all these situations and expectations.“Now it’s a four-year contract, it’s different. We can next season lose the Copa América or the Gold Cup, they’re not happy with us and they can sack us. Or we can say: ‘OK. It’s not in the way that we think.’ Four years is different. Maybe now if someone calls in the future, it’s a different, different type [of thing]. We are excited, we are thinking to spend four years to the next World Cup. But now it’s a long period.”The conversation turns back to Spurs. As it often does with Pochettino. He says his former striker Harry Kane, who is at Bayern Munich, would be a deserving winner of this year’s Ballon d’Or. He insists he was pleased to see De Zerbi get more than £300m to spend on players over the summer; a figure he could only have dreamed about. “I am happy because I feel Tottenham … it’s still my club,” Pochettino says. And there is another window into his soul when he reflects on how Spurs got rid ofthe longstanding chair, Daniel Levy, last September – the man who dismissed him.“I think he feels like I did when I was sacked,” Pochettino says. “I keep in touch with him and I never made the situation personal because you can sack a coach. The way I felt in that moment … you receive the letter, you pick up your things and you can never come back to say goodbye to the people, maybe 200, 300 people, that were your family. You cannot send a text, you cannot do nothing.“That was really, really tough for me and I was talking with him [Levy] about that. Of course, I am not happy that now he feels the same because I am not a person who has bad feelings. But yes, it’s difficult for him and his family and I am so sorry for him.”Pochettino is ready for the next phase of his US adventure. As ever, his mind and heart race with possibility.Explore more on these topicsMauricio PochettinoUS sportsUSATottenham HotspurinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Declan Rice shrugs off Arsenal concerns and says 60 games a season is sustainable | Arsenal | The Guardian
description: Arsenal are monitoring Declan Rice’s workload but the midfielder has insisted that playing over 60 games a season is sustainable
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Arsenal are monitoring Declan Rice’s workload but the midfielder has insisted that playing over 60 games a season is sustainable
Content: Declan Rice played the entire match of Arsenal’s 1-0 Champions League win at Napoli.Photograph: David Price/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDeclan Rice played the entire match of Arsenal’s 1-0 Champions League win at Napoli.Photograph: David Price/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesArsenalDeclan Rice shrugs off Arsenal concerns and says 60 games a season is sustainableArsenal are monitoring midfielder’s workloadRice received painkilling injections last seasonEd Aaronsin NaplesThu 10 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 17.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDeclan Rice has insisted his body can sustain more than 60 appearances again this season, despite Arsenal’s concerns after he played through pain at the World Cup.Rice racked up 69 appearances last season for Arsenal and England butrevealed during the World Cuphe had been managing neural back and hamstring pain, for which he is understood to have received a pain-killing injection, after a hamstring injury in December. It is understood Arsenal are monitoring the 27-year-old’s workload closely after he had only three weeks off before returning to training a week before the Community Shield last month.Ødegaard ‘edge’ delights Arteta as Arsenal secure narrow win at NapoliRead moreRice came off the bench to replace Bruno Guimarãesin the victory over Manchester Cityin Cardiff and has since started all Arsenal’s matches, with Guimarães’ return from an injury being managed. A major reason why Arsenal bought the Brazil midfielder for £75m from Newcastle was to take some strain off from Rice, although it was noticeable that Rice played all of Wednesday’s Champions Leaguevictory at Napoli, with Mikel Merino coming off for Guimarães.“I think for the last six seasons, even since my West Ham days when they were in Europe, I’ve played 60-plus every season,” Rice said. “So I think it is sustainable because I’ve shown that I can do it.“It’s just about maintaining it, maintaining the level and the consistency of the performances. For me, that’s the main thing, showing up every week, giving a good account of myself and helping the team win. I’ve been lucky enough to be able to do that. So I’m really hungry to be able to do that again this season.”It is understood Arsenal offered Rice more time off after the World Cup exploits but that he was keen to return for the start of the season. He is expected to be part of Thomas Tuchel’s squad for Nations League fixtures against Spain, Czechia and Croatia when it is announced next Friday, although whether he features in all four matches remains to be seen, with Arsenal likely to request that he and Bukayo Saka are given another opportunity to rest. Rice said he had found things “tough” during the World Cup but is adamant he is feeling “refreshed”.“I feel really good at the minute, in really good form, so we’ll make it continue,” he said. “I think everyone knew I had an issue with a neural hamstring. But also on the top of the Premier League season, which was so demanding, the Champions League, to then play a World Cup in that heat really does take its toll. I’m a player that goes on the pitch, wants to be fresh and give 100% every time I put on anEnglandshirt. Yes, there were stages where I felt really, really good and stages where I didn’t feel so good. There were a few things that frustrated me, just with myself, just not feeling 100%. It’s one of those things I just had to manage.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRice is one of three England players nominatedfor the Ballon d’Orthis week, with Jude Bellingham and Harry Kane. The ceremony, traditionally in Paris, will take place in London on 26 October as a tribute to Sir Stanley Matthews, who won the inaugural award in 1956, and Rice has backed Kane to become the first English winner since Michael Owen in 2001. “I would Iove to see Harry win it,” he said. “So I’m wishing him all the best in that.”Explore more on these topicsArsenalEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Football saved Dad’s life’: meet the coach of the England women’s Parkinson’s team | Women's football | The Guardian
description: It began with getting her dad into walking football after his diagnosis – now Gemma Darvill is taking a national team on tour to Canada
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: It began with getting her dad into walking football after his diagnosis – now Gemma Darvill is taking a national team on tour to Canada
Content: Gemma Darvill helped set up the England women’s Parkinson’s team and is their first head coach.View image in fullscreenGemma Darvill helped set up the England women’s Parkinson’s team and is their first head coach.Moving the Goalposts newsletterWomen's football‘Football saved Dad’s life’: meet the coach of the England women’s Parkinson’s teamIt began with getting her dad into walking football after his diagnosis – now Gemma Darvill is taking a national team on tour to CanadaTom GarryThu 10 Sep 2026 06.53 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 07.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Gemma Darvill’s dad, Les, was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease aged 58, joining a walking football team stopped him from confining himself to his own home, and she believes the game saved his life.What she could never have foreseen was that, eight years later, she would find herself coachingthe first England women’s Parkinson’s team, helping transform the lives of women with the disease from all across the country. She is set to embark on a journey to Toronto to help spread awareness of the ways in which walking football can help put the brakes on the progression of Parkinson’s symptoms.‘A dream come true’: behind the scenes with Wolves Women as they enter new eraRead moreA teacher at Swallowfield primary school in Woburn Sands, in Milton Keynes, Darvill’s interest in walking football was sparked by supporting her dad. She now coaches what is believed to be the first walking football team specifically dedicated to women with Parkinson’s,the Parkinson’s Pioneers, who train in Solihull and have seen a tenfold increase in their membership in just over three years. That led to her appointment as the coach of the first England women’s national side.There are reportedly about 166,000 people in the UK living with Parkinson’s disease. It is a progressive brain condition for which there is no cure, but known treatmentscan help reduce the severity of the main symptoms. Darvill, who says exercise “helped slow down the progression of the disease” for her dad, recalled: “When he was first diagnosed, it hits you hard. But football genuinely saved his life.“At first, he didn’t want to leave the house. He used to have a season ticket at Tottenham [but] he gave that up. He didn’t tell any of his friends. He just stopped doing everything. He really struggled with life in general, [even] getting out of bed. And then we found this football session. His team’s calledFighting Fit Football[based at Watford’s training ground]. I took him along one week and he’s never looked back since.“So, just to be able to give back a little bit, I guess that’s why I still do it: to help others who get diagnosed, to show them that there is still a life after being diagnosed with the disease and you can meet lots of incredible people, and still try to do things as normally as possible.”View image in fullscreenGemma Darvill’s first coaching role was with the Parkinson’s Pioneers, a team she helped set up in 2023.Darvill, who has played football since she was 10, was spotted cheering for her dad on the sidelines of a tournament at St George’s Park and was promptly asked by Annie Booth, the founder of the Parkinson’s Pioneers, if she would be interested in helping set up the team. To Darvill, helping out felt natural: “I’ve always coached football as well as played, and I was a teacher, so I used to run football camps for kids in the school holidays.”Booth and Darvill have seen the Parkinson’s Pioneers blossom into a flourishing community, explaining: “I remember our very first training session, it was only three of us. We now have over 40 ladies coming to the sessions. It’s incredible.“They use it as a social network as well. So after the sessions, everyone stays for a bit of food, a conversation, and they can just discuss like their symptoms, how they’re coping. And we’re family now, really, if I’m honest. Everyone just helps each other out.“We train at Solihull purely because the ladies come from all over the country. We have ladies from Manchester, we have myself coming from Milton Keynes, we have people in Devon.“So it’s the most central location that we could find to try to make it as fair as possible for everyone travelling. So we try to meet up once a month and then we enter the tournaments as well.”As well as prohibiting running, walking football includes several different rules to the mainstream game. There is no offside rule, no heading, no throw-ins and it is a non-contact game. Darvill says: “I’d say the tactics are the same [in general]. But you can’t tackle from the side or from behind in walking football – it has to be face-on.View image in fullscreenDarvill’s first involvement with walking football for people with Parkinson’s came through helping her father after his diagnosis.“Everyone with Parkinson’s has a very different level of the condition. The walking element just helps keep them all safe. We have a brilliant physio on board as well who is specifically a Parkinson’s physio, which is brilliant, and she helps us a lot with the warm-ups and the cool-downs and just makes sure that ladies are getting what they need. It makes their brain think about something else. [For example] I’ve got one lady who can’t walk in a straight line but if you put a sports ladder down in front of her, she can walk through it. It’s really interesting.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe growth of the Pioneers meant that Darvill was the natural pick when the Walking Football Association (WFA) was launching the first England women’s Parkinson’s team with trials last year. Then, in August this year, the WFA and the Football Associationannounced a new partnershipthat will install the FA as walking football’s governing body in England with the WFA now the delivery partner for the game. The collaboration was partly aimed at benefits such as being able to streamline the registration of referees and agree on a unified set of rules. Darvill adds: “That’s a positive, going forward, that they’re coming together a little bit more.”Darvill’s England team play six-a-side and the players range in age from 36 to 66. They have held training sessions in Watford, Droitwich and Bedford so far, but are about to cross the Atlantic to join the England men’s Parkinson’s team on a landmark trip to Canada for an international showcase of the benefits of walking football and a series of invitational friendlies.The team travel on Saturday for one week in Toronto. The teams have been crowdfunding to try to help cover the course of the trip. Darvill’sown fundraising pagehas raised over £400 and awider fundraising page for both the men’s and women’s sideshas drawn in more than £17,000. Darvill says: “We’re doing it because we want to raise awareness of Parkinson’s in Canada and help those out there with Parkinson’s. We’re trying to showcase sort of what we do, to try to reach more people.“We’re going to play two American teams when we’re out there, an over-40s team and over-60s all women’s walking football team [non-disabled], and then we’re going to play some men’s teams as well. We’re running a Parkinson’s fundraising day too, where we will run the session ourselves, we’ll put on the coaching drills and have a bit of fun to try to get as many people in Canada interested.”For Darvill, it is a mission with a deeply personal motivation, with her own gratitude to walking football for how it is helping her dad continuing to drive her to help others with the condition.Get in touchIf you have any questions or comments about any of our newsletters please emailmoving.goalposts@theguardian.com.This is an extract from our free email about women’s football, Moving the Goalposts. To get the full edition,visit this page and follow the instructions. Moving the Goalposts is delivered to your inboxes every Tuesday and Thursday.Explore more on these topicsWomen's footballMoving the Goalposts newsletterDisability and sportDisabilityfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: England’s Dan Lawrence delighted with form as Pakistan focus on the future | England v Pakistan 2026 | The Guardian
description: Dan Lawrence missed out on a century but said he was ‘really happy’ with recent displays, while Pakistan’s batting coach hailed his team’s potential
Author: Simon Burnton
Headline: Dan Lawrence missed out on a century but said he was ‘really happy’ with recent displays, while Pakistan’s batting coach hailed his team’s potential
Content: Dan Lawrence said, ‘I feel like I’ve got a lot to offer English cricket,’ after scoring his third half-century in four innings.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAView image in fullscreenDan Lawrence said, ‘I feel like I’ve got a lot to offer English cricket,’ after scoring his third half-century in four innings.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAEngland v Pakistan 2026England’s Dan Lawrence delighted with form as Pakistan focus on the futureLawrence rues missed ton but ‘really happy’ with displaysTourists’ batting coach hails potential of new playersSimon Burntonat EdgbastonThu 10 Sep 2026 14.54 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA few hours after his yelp of frustration echoed around Edgbaston, an innings of 65 and the growing conviction that “I was going to make a really big score” ended when he chased a wide delivery and played on, Dan Lawrence’s emotions had settled into something approaching contentment. England had taken a firm grip on the game, Pakistanending the second daystill 268 away from making them bat again with eight wickets remaining, and Lawrence, having posted three half-centuries in four Test innings this summer, is finally delivering on his obvious potential in an England shirt.“I’m obviously gutted I didn’t kick on,” he said. “I felt like I was playing really nicely and it was a really good surface to bat on against a tiring attack at that stage. I thought I was going to make a really big score, but it wasn’t meant to be. But I’m really happy with how I’ve played [this summer].skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEngland bat Pakistan out of third Test before Robinson moves in for the killRead more“I always knew deep down that my ability was good enough to play at this level, even though I hadn’t necessarily shown it in my first stint playing. That was obviously a tough time, when I got dropped from the team [in 2022], and all I was concentrating on was trying to score big runs in county cricket and get myself in, because I feel like I’ve got a lot to offer English cricket.”Pakistan are also confident about their potential, even if at this stage it seems unlikely to be realised on this tour. “There’s a lot of class in this dressing room,” said Michael Smith, who was appointed batting coach last month. “There’s a lot of serious players here. It would be nice for them to show the rest of the UK, and the people back in Pakistan, what they’ve still got. Because we’ve got no doubt that it’s there.”The tourists’ batting has been poor throughout the series – they are yet to score as many as 200 runs in an innings – but Smith is content that the right players are learning the right lessons for the future. “A lot of our players, it’s their first tour of England,” Smith said. “I suppose we might not see the sort of success we want to see now, but hopefully if a lot of these players are back on our next UK tour, we’ll really see an upward trend. I think that’s the time to really judge them.“Let’s not worry about what’s happening here. We’ve got some really exciting players and potential is exceptionally high. It’s just how quickly we can get them to that level, especially playing outside of Pakistan. That’s going to be a big challenge and it’s something we’re really excited about.”Explore more on these topicsEngland v Pakistan 2026England cricket teamPakistan cricket teamCricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: Somerset return to summit after dog stops play: county cricket, day three – as it happened | County Championship | The Guardian
description: Somerset eased to a 377-run win over Leicestershire to go top of Division One while Notts were caught cold by Hampshire’s attack
Author: Tanya Aldred
Headline: Somerset eased to a 377-run win over Leicestershire to go top of Division One while Notts were caught cold by Hampshire’s attack
Content: 8h ago13.55 EDTRoundup: Somerset's dog days may soon be overIn a round of staggering collapses, batting sides continued to strap on their roller skates and head to the ice rink. At Grace Road,Leicestershirewere rumbled for 145, a 377 run-victory that putsSomersetback on the top of the table, that longed-for first title still in reach.Somerset set Leicestershire 523 to win after waiting for New Zealand signing Henry Nicholls to reach his first Championship century. Craig Overton (four for 33) and Jack Leach (three for 30) then stormed through Leicestershire’s defences. The most entertaining moment for a loyal crowd was when a runaway husky frolicked on the pitch.At Trent Bridge, defending championsNottinghamshirewere bowled out for 104 by a rampantHampshireattack. Seventeen-year-old Manny Lumsden, bowling with fire and bounce, sprung out five for 36, including top scorer Joe Clarke for 37. Hampshire, set 178, were soon batting on a see-saw of their own against Olly Stone (three for 15) and Dillon Pennington (three for 18). They had stumbled to 61 for six when bad light brought temporary respite.At Headingley,Essexfell foul of Kuldeep Yadav, whose six for 50 has almost ensuredYorkshire’s Division One spot next season. At one stage Essex were 26 for five following on, but Paul Walter’s 48 and George Bell’s 28 ensured they passed 100. Kuldeep can tuck career-best match figures of 10 for 120 into his wallet. Sam Cook, who arrived late, unwanted at the Test, didn’t bowl a ball.Northamptonshiretook 20 points from their six-wicket victory overWorcestershire, leapfrogging promotion challengersKent. They had a more difficult day at the County Ground againstDerbyshire, who have set the visitors 434 to win after half centuries for Brooke Guest, Luis Reece and the in-form Martin Andersson.Elsewhere, an unbeaten maiden first-class 50 from Rocky Flintoff gaveLancashirea glimmer of hope for their first win since April. They trailGloucestershireby 128 runs with four wickets remaining.Share

title: World Rugby floats plans for Six Nations match in US but England unlikely to participate | Rugby union | The Guardian
description: World Rugby wants a Six Nations match to be staged in the US and has offered financial incentives to the unions to do so
Author: Gerard Meagher
Headline: World Rugby wants a Six Nations match to be staged in the US and has offered financial incentives to the unions to do so
Content: Around 85% of the RFU’s revenues come from England men’s fixtures at Twickenham.Photograph: Peter Nicholls/ReutersView image in fullscreenAround 85% of the RFU’s revenues come from England men’s fixtures at Twickenham.Photograph: Peter Nicholls/ReutersRugby unionWorld Rugby floats plans for Six Nations match in US but England unlikely to participateGoverning body floating staging Ireland v Italy in USWorld Rugby eyes commercial value in American fixturesGerard MeagherThu 10 Sep 2026 13.32 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWorld Rugby wants aSix Nationsmatch to be staged in the US and has offered financial incentives to the unions to do so – but England have effectively ruled themselves out on the grounds that fixtures at Twickenham are too lucrative.The US will stage the 2031 World Cup and World Rugby is seeking to capitalise commercially despite mounting fears over the parlous state of rugby union in the host country. As a result, the governing body is desperate to raise interest in the sport’s profile by staging high-profile matches Stateside, with Baltimore hosting the fourth Test between South Africa and New Zealand on Saturday.A failed attempt was made to attract the British & Irish Lions to stop in Las Vegas on the way to Australia in 2025, thoughEngland did face the USA in Washingtonthat summer while the All Blacks and Irelandmet in Chicago last autumn. The 2030 finals weekend of the Nations Championship has also been slated for the United States.Taking a Six Nations match to America would be an altogether more significant move given how financially valuable home championship fixtures can be to the competing unions. But World Rugby is willing to help bridge the shortfall and has floated Ireland v Italy as a potential fixture, given the number of expats from each country on the east coast.View image in fullscreenJack Crowley kicks a penalty in Ireland’s match against New Zealand in Chicago in 2025. Ireland could be tempted to play a Six Nations match in the US.Photograph: Erin Hooley/APEngland can generate around £10m from a Six Nations home match and men’s fixtures at Twickenham account for about 85% of the Rugby Football Union’s revenues. It is understood that taking a championship fixture to the US is considered very unlikely by insiders, all the more so due to its naming rights deal with Allianz – which stipulates a certain number of matches at Twickenham – and the likely consternation that would arise among fans and debenture holders. Insiders also point to how the RFU owns its home stadium whereas New Zealand and South Africa do not.If there was appetite among the other unions, however, the Six Nations committee would have to agree as would the tournament broadcasters, though ITV’s recent £1.6bn takeover by Sky, which is owned by the US telecoms giant Comcast, may help in that regard.“In terms of the matchday economics, [South Africa v New Zealand] is like a Six Nations match,” the World Rugby chief executive, Alan Gilpin, told the Telegraph. “It starts to show that [financial return] is not the barrier. So if there is the appetite to take some of these big matches in the future to the US, we can now.“We completely understand [the] need for rugby to continue to drive more economic sustainability. Any of those unions [could] go and look at a match that they would have had at home and say, ‘Right, can I at least match, if not better my own economics by partnering with World Rugby and taking that match to the US?’”Explore more on these topicsRugby unionEngland rugby union teamRugby Football UnionSix NationsSport politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Former University of Michigan hockey players say they were sexually hazed decades ago | Michigan | The Guardian
description: More than a dozen ex-players are suing the University of Michigan, alleging coach and staff were aware of abuse
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: More than a dozen ex-players are suing the University of Michigan, alleging coach and staff were aware of abuse
Content: The Yost ice arena on the campus of the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor on 11 February 2022.Photograph: Zuma Press Inc/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Yost ice arena on the campus of the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor on 11 February 2022.Photograph: Zuma Press Inc/AlamyMichiganFormer University of Michigan hockey players say they were sexually hazed decades agoMore than a dozen ex-players are suing the University of Michigan, alleging coach and staff were aware of abuseAssociated PressThu 10 Sep 2026 16.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than a dozen former hockey players are suing the University ofMichigan, alleging their coach and other staff were aware of sexual hazing that included the forced shaving of their genitals and other abuse by teammates decades ago.“The abuse was ritualized, meticulously planned and sadistic … Enduring sexual abuse was required to be a member of the Michigan men’s ice hockey team,” attorney Michael Pitt said in a sex discrimination lawsuit filed on Wednesday in federal court in Detroit.The plaintiffs are 16 men who played at Michigan between 1984 and 2001. The lawsuit apparently grew out of conversations among several former teammates in 2024.Paige Shiver says ex-Michigan coach Moore ‘controlled’ her, reveals she was pregnantRead moreThe university said the allegations are “disturbing”, but denied responsibility.“To the extent any former student athlete engaged in hazing or other misconduct, they were violating university policy,” spokesperson Paul Corliss said in a written statement.The 72-page document describes players being forced to consume excessive amounts of alcohol and eat live fish. A common allegation: they were forced to have hair around their genitals shaved by teammates. A player identified as John Doe 7 said he was taunted with a blowtorch while on a table.The lawsuit says Red Berenson, who was coach from 1984 to 2017, was aware of the abuse and did not intervene.View image in fullscreenHead coach Red Berenson of the Michigan Wolverines directs practice on 9 April 2008 in Denver, Colorado.Photograph: Doug Pensinger/Getty ImagesJohn Doe 3 said he told Berenson that he didn’t want to participate in the hazing. The coach coerced him by telling him to be a “Michigan man” and a ”good teammate”, according to the lawsuit.Berenson, 86, declined to comment when reached by the Associated Press. He told MLive.com there was a “certain element of initiation” by the team’s seniors, but no one had complained to him.“Were there some mishaps? Were there some bad experiences? Possibly, but it wasn’t a matter of direction or encouragement from the coaching staff or from the administration,” Berenson, a former NHL player, said.Berenson announced the end of “freshman hazing” in 2012, mostly referring to first-year players being forced to carry equipment and eat team meals last. He made no mention of physical abuse but acknowledged “captains that got too carried away”, according to news reports at the time.The university could argue that the hockey players waited too long to file a lawsuit, a position it took in 2020 when former athletes sued over sexual misconduct committed decades earlier by a campus sports doctor. The university ultimately agreed to pay $490m to settle claims by more than 1,000 people.Explore more on these topicsMichiganUS universitiesUS crimeIce hockeyCollege sportsUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tiafoe v Shelton US Open semi-final a legacy of the departing Gaël Monfils | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: Veteran Frenchman bowed out in New York but the clash of two black players in the last four of the men’s singles is testament to his effect
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Veteran Frenchman bowed out in New York but the clash of two black players in the last four of the men’s singles is testament to his effect
Content: Frances Tiafoe has reached his third US Open semi-final.Photograph: Mike Segar/ReutersView image in fullscreenFrances Tiafoe has reached his third US Open semi-final.Photograph: Mike Segar/ReutersUS Open Tennis 2026Tiafoe v Shelton US Open semi-final a legacy of the departing Gaël MonfilsVeteran Frenchman bowed out in New York but the clash of two black players in the last four of the men’s singles is testament to his effectTumaini Carayolat Flushing MeadowsThu 10 Sep 2026 14.51 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe early days of this year’s US Open can be told in a series of farewells to competitors who plan to end their careers this year. The most moving of them all came in the form of Gaël Monfils’s grand departure inside Louis Armstrong Stadiumagainst the wildly talented 20-year-old Learner Tien. Tien was competing in front of his home crowd, one of the Americans capable of a deep run, but for much of his straight-sets defeat the Frenchman had the American crowd in the palm of his hands.Beyond the massive popularity he has garnered among tennis fans, one of the most striking parts of Monfils’s long farewell was seeing how highly nearly all of his fellow professionals, particularly his fellow black players, regard him. Frances Tiafoe says he spent his youth looking up to Monfils. Arthur Fils considers Monfils his older brother. Naomi Osaka’s nickname for Monfils, one of her idols, is simply “the Goat”. They all hold Monfils in such great esteem, and for good reason.Two forehands, no backhands: meet the US Open’s fascinating ambidextrous experimentRead moreWhile women’s tennis has witnessed the successes of a long line of top black players, Monfils and his retired compatriot Jo-Wilfried Tsonga were, for so long, the standard bearers for black players in men’s tennis. In the same year that the 40-year-old Monfils will finally bow out, the new generation of black men’s players have consolidated their positions at the top of the sport.Last month, the Cincinnati Open featured two black players competing in a Masters 1000 final for the first time as the 22-year-old Frenchman Fils overcame a year of injuriesto defeat Tiafoe and win his first big title. Fils’s victory was preceded byBen Shelton’s triumph at the Canadian Openin Montreal.View image in fullscreenGaël Monfils takes the acclaim of the Flushing Meadows crowd.Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPAIt took three weeks for the Fils v Tiafoe final to be eclipsed by an even more significant match between two black players. Tiafoe and Shelton will compete against each other in the US Open semi-finals on Friday night, with the winner becoming the first black man since Jo-Wilfried Tsonga at the 2008 Australian Open, and the first African American man since MaliVai Washington, the 1996 Wimbledon finalist, to reach a grand slam final. The victor will then attempt to become the third black man to win a grand slam after Arthur Ashe and Yannick Noah. Along with last year’s semi-finalist Félix Auger-Aliassime, there will be four black players inside the ATP’s top 11. The status commanded by Monfils, who never reached did not reach a major final, plainly underlines how important this moment is for future generations of black tennis players as well as themselves.As Americans at the US Open, two players who have spent their careers being reminded of how far American men’s tennis has fallen since its decades of dominance over the sport, and particularly of Andy Roddick’s triumph at the 2003 US Open, the last time an American man won a title here, the significance of this moment is doubly important to Tiafoe and Shelton. Unlike in their previous runs, there are no multiple grand-slam champions or all-time greats left in the draw, with the earlier semi-final feauturing top seed Alexander Zverev against former top-10 player Karen Khachanov. All four can win this title.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenBen Shelton enjoyed the biggest win of his career against Carlos Alcaraz.Photograph: Adam Hunger/APThe past few years in New York have been leading up to this match. It is just the fourth time Shelton has competed in the US Open main draw, yet somehow this will be his third US Open meeting with Tiafoe. Shelton won their 2023 quarter-final before Tiafoe exacted revenge in a bruising five-set, third-round match in 2024. They have become great friends, which can be awkward oncourt for some, but they enjoy battling against each other so much that their relationship only makes them even more determined to produce their best. It helps they are such creative, all-court players with great variation and explosive athleticism, which makes for such a complementary match-up.This is a third major semi-final for both players, but neither man has ever been so well prepared. Shelton just delivered thebiggest win of his careerover the defending champion Carlos Alcaraz and the 23-year-old continues to evolve into a genuine grand slam threat. Tiafoe, meanwhile, has been one of the revelations this year. The 28-year old has spent the season determined to be more professional and focused each week than ever before, and his results are a direct consequence of his growing maturity. Their efforts have yielded by far the biggest opportunity of their careers, and the winner will be decided by which competitor is truly ready for the pressure and weight that accompanies such a massive opening.Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026US Open tennisTennisUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘She’s buzzing’: Charley Hull to face world No 1 Nelly Korda in Solheim Cup opener | Solheim Cup | The Guardian
description: The opening foursomes of the Solheim Cup on Friday will see Europe’s Charley Hull and Lottie Woad take on USA’s Nelly Korda and Allisen Corpuz
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: The opening foursomes of the Solheim Cup on Friday will see Europe’s Charley Hull and Lottie Woad take on USA’s Nelly Korda and Allisen Corpuz
Content: Charley Hull walks through a crowd of supporters at the opening ceremony of the Solheim Cup.Photograph: Kate McShane/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCharley Hull walks through a crowd of supporters at the opening ceremony of the Solheim Cup.Photograph: Kate McShane/Getty ImagesSolheim Cup‘She’s buzzing’: Charley Hull to face world No 1 Nelly Korda in Solheim Cup openerHull will partner debutant Lottie Woad for EuropeUSA seeking to retain trophy they won in 2024Ewan Murrayat Bernardus GolfThu 10 Sep 2026 13.07 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGalleries at the 20th Solheim Cup have been granted a blockbuster start with Nelly Korda and Charley Hull to face off in Friday morning’s foursomes. The meeting of Korda, the world No 1, and Hull, Europe’s star turn, should ensure an electric opening in the Netherlands as the USA seek to retain the trophywon in Virginia two years ago. Korda nudged out Hull at theUS Women’s Openin June.Hull will partner theSolheim Cupdebutant Lottie Woad against the formidable USA pairing of Korda and Allisen Corpuz to begin the tournament. Nanna Koerstz Madsen and Céline Boutier will represent Europe in match two, where they will take on Alison Lee and Lauren Coughlin. Esther Henseleit and Leona Maguire have been selected for the hosts in the penultimate match, with Andrea Lee and Lindy Duncan in opposition. The foursomes will conclude with Europe’s Swedish duo of Maja Stark and Linn Grant facing Rose Zhang and Jennifer Kupcho.Solheim Cup vice-captain denies Charley Hull’s late arrival due to ‘drinks’Read more“She’s been buzzing, she’s been so excited,” said Europe’s captain Anna Nordqvist of Hull. “Her and Lottie have got to play quite a bit on tour this year, so I think they were both very excited to be paired with each other.”Angela Stanford, the USA captain, said Korda and Corpuz had “earned the right” to lead their team out. “I feel like if I didn’t put those two out, I would be questioned,” Stanford added. “I feel like the whole world knew that they were coming.”In a peculiar moment as the captains completed the last of their pre-tournament media duties, Nordqvist asserted every player on each team had to play on day one as per an agreement. Stanford looked bemused by the suggestion. The actual ruling, which was later clarified, says players must appear in at least one session before Sunday. Nordqvist must hope her misstep – or misunderstanding – is not a sign of things to come.The USA have won only once on European soil since 2007, when they triumphed in 2015. Eleven years have passed since “Gimme-gate” but Alison Lee’s reappearance in a United States team in Europe gives cause to reflect upon the chaos that unfolded in Germany. “It was a shell-shocking week for me,” Lee recalls.This weekend, Lee will be the sole playing survivor from the US contingent in 2015. Back then, aged 20, she picked up her ball before the supposed formality of a concession from Europe. Suzann Pettersen seized upon the moment, claiming the hole for Europe amid tears and ferocious backlash. The USA had the last laugh, winning the Solheim Cup by one point as Pettersen spent the evening sobbing in a hotel room.View image in fullscreenAlison Lee, pictured during her practice round on Thursday, said it was “a huge goal” to be back in Europe competing in the Solheim Cup.Photograph: Maddie Meyer/Getty Images“I had been thrown into a team where I didn’t really know anyone very well,” says Lee. “I just felt really grateful that the team around me, the US team, were just so supportive of me. They had my back and they were so welcoming.“All that stuff happened on Sunday morning because there was a delay and we had to finish the Saturday afternoon session in the morning. So we had a couple hours before singles where we all came together and I was very rattled, obviously, with everything that happened. I think everyone just saw me as a little sister and they just really cared for me. They not only wanted to win, for the US, but we wanted to win for each other. And so I feel like that meant a lot.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I was so young. I remember just being on the team was such a cool thing to be a part of. Less than a year before that, I was watching them all on TV so I was a little scared to be on the team, to be honest. Winning was super special.”Pettersen’s redemption came in 2019, when sheholed the winning putt for Europe at Gleneaglesbefore announcing her retirement. Lee represented the US in Virginia two years ago but always had a return trip to Europe in her thoughts. “I feel really proud of myself,” Lee adds. “It was a huge goal to be here and I didn’t think it was in reach.“I took some time off last year, I had my son who is 16 months old now. I knew it would be challenging to try and make this team and it was a hard, hard journey, but I did everything I could to make it here. To be able to make the team on my own this year just meant a lot.”The US team will wear commemorative pin badges on Friday as a means of marking the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks.Explore more on these topicsSolheim CupGolfUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Two forehands, no backhands: meet the US Open’s fascinating ambidextrous experiment | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: The 16-year-old junior from Denver is treating the tennis world to a wildly unorthodox style – and proving it’s much more than a parlor trick
Author: Andrew Lawrence
Headline: The 16-year-old junior from Denver is treating the tennis world to a wildly unorthodox style – and proving it’s much more than a parlor trick
Content: Teodor Davidov in action against Connor Doig during their junior boys’ singles match at the US Open on Sunday.Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTeodor Davidov in action against Connor Doig during their junior boys’ singles match at the US Open on Sunday.Composite: Getty ImagesUS Open Tennis 2026Two forehands, no backhands: meet the US Open’s fascinating ambidextrous experimentTeo Davidov doesn’t hit backhands. He serves from both sides. The 16-year-old from Denver is treating the tennis world to a wildly unorthodox style – and proving it’s more than a parlor trickAndrew Lawrenceat Flushing MeadowsThu 10 Sep 2026 10.25 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 10.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTeo Davidov always has the upper hands. An amiable junior prodigy from Denver, the 16-year-old was the oddest sight at this year’s US Open, the only player in the tournament – man, woman or junior – who hits only forehands. To be clear: it’s not that he doesn’t have a backhand or can’t hit a backhand. He’s ambidextrous and so he doesn’t bother with them.It’s nothing personal. “To be honest, I like the traditional backhand-forehand,” he says. “I like the classiness of it. I like hitting backhands myself just to play around, just for fun.” He hits those from both wings, too.Davidov has been a giddy curiosity for hardcore tennis fans for the past five years, with rubberneckers gaping at clips from his matches and training sessions that seem at a glance like AI. A four-year-old video of himflummoxing Carlos Alcaraz’s younger brothermakes for especially tasty viewing. “I don’t really look at the comments or things like that,” Davidoff says. “But I’ve heard most people online just always have something they think might not work.”Teodor Davidov shows off his ambidextrous game during a 6-1, 6-0 win over Carlos Alcaraz’s younger brother Jaime at the IMG Future Stars tournament in Greece in 2022.Davidov’s internet clips don’t do him justice, though. You have to see him in person, especially now that he’s a 5ft 7in teenager. His second-round doubles match on Wednesday evening had hordes of wine and Honey Deuce-sipping casuals drifting over to Court 6 at sunset for a closer look – and whipping out their phones from the first warm-up ball. It really was the damnedest thing watching him alternate hitting groundstrokes with his right and left hand, lobs and volleys too.But witnessing the kid serve was the trippiest experience by far, like watching AI in the wild. It’s always advantage Davidov. It doesn’t matter which side of the baseline he sets up on – if you’re returning, you’d better mind your backhand. “Obviously it depends on who I’m playing, but the general foundation is right hand on the deuce side and left hand on the ad,” he says. “I’ve been mixing it up a lot more, different spins, different looks, just making it as hard as possible.”Will hordes of influencers, weed smokers and mid-point talkers bring down the US Open?Read moreIt all seems like parlor tricks, the sort of thing that could hinder him and his partner, fellow American Tyler Lee, as much as their opponents, Brazil’s Guto Miguel and Slovenian Ziga Sesko – the world’s No 1 and No 4 juniors in singles and the top-seeded boys’ doubles team in New York. But when it came to dictating pace, chasing down line drives or the rapid-fire exchanges at net, Davidov never fumbled his racquet.There were times during his rallies when it was debatable whether a backhand would be easier for him to load or if switching forehand sides mid-rally took some of the edge off when he clearly just wanted to grip and rip. But the double-wing thing is ingrained for Davidov. “I’d say before the main speculation that people had with it, they’d say, I don’t have time to switch hands,” he says. “But I think now as time went on, they kind of see that it’s not a problem. It almost never happens where I’m late for a ball because something goes wrong with the switching.”On Wednesday, it was a matter of running into a much stronger opponent. Davidov and Lee – wildcard entrants into this draw – had their moments, dazzling the crowd with a handful of pell-mell exchanges, but they were ultimately overwhelmed by Sesko’s punishing groundstrokes and Miguel’s feline reflexes. Sesko, the reigning Australian Open singles and Wimbledon doubles champion, is seriously impressive; Miguel, already a Futures-level title winner, has a real shot at the US Open boys’ singles crown.View image in fullscreenTeodor Davidov, left, and Tyler Lee in action during the junior boys’ doubles competition at the US Open.Photograph: Simon Bruty/USTA/Getty ImagesFor a few early points, Davidov’s unique style appeared to jar them. Occasionally, he can catch players who haven’t faced him before by surprise, “but most of the Americans know me,” he says. Eventually, though, Sesko and Miguel settled into a rhythm and served the Americans a 6-2, 6-2 loss that, while more competitive than the scoreline suggests, spanned 42 minutes nonetheless. “I felt like we were close,” Davidov says. “We just had some loose points, we got broken. I missed a few volleys. But overall it was really fun and really cool to hear the crowd roar after crazy points.”For Davidov, this trip was about building match experience on the big stage, about properly field-testing his double-wing style. “I’d say the first two days and when I lost my singles, it was so hectic,” he says of his time in New York. “Everything felt like it was going wrong. But I’d say now, especially the last two, three days have been super enjoyable and I’ve gotten used to the courts, which are really fast compared to the ones I play on at home.”Davidov hasn’t played a ton of juniors events but turned heads in spite of that, last year becoming the first player born in 2010 to pass the qualifying round of a professional M15-level ITF event; that achievement came after he captured the boys doubles title at the prestigious Les Petits As tournament in France. Earlier this year, Davidov reached the semi-finals of an M15 event in Naples to earn his first career ATP points. “To have a guy who can effectively serve left-handed and right-handed at the same level, that is potentially game-changing,” Andy Roddicksaidon a recent episode of his podcast. “The serving aspect is what really interests me. It’s like having a baseball pitcher who can throw equally well from both sides.” Karue Sell, a professional once ranked as high as No 258 in the world, wondered if he wasn’t looking atthe future of tennisafter playing Davidov in March.Really, ever since he began swinging at a suspended ball at age two, Davidov – a Bulgaria native who immigrated to the US young – has been something of an athletic experiment presided over and fiercely protected by his father Kalin and mother Elena – both of whom have backgrounds in sports and holistic medicine. Kalin, a devotee of philosophy and Chinese medicine, devised Teo’s playing style with the goal of creating an athlete who was at one with himself.“When Teo was about to turn eight years old, I decided he’s going to start playing left-handed, to affect his right hemisphere of the brain,” Kalintold the Guardian in 2021, when his son was 10. “He’s way too extroverted, too fiery, a little too imbalanced, so I just wanted to affect the right hemisphere of his brain, using the left part of his body.”View image in fullscreenTeodor Davidov in action against Connor Doig during the junior boys’ singles competition at the US Open.Photograph: Simon Bruty/USTA/Getty ImagesMany will wince at the routine he was put through while still a child: 30 to 40 hours of training a week, on and off the court – some of it as specialized as exercises focused on breathing through one nostril at a time. These days, Teo says he has added more cardio and weight training to build stamina and fill out a frame that remains a touch on the small side. “Before I was just a little kid, and everyone was twice the size of me and way stronger than me,” he says. “But now I’m kind of growing into my body a bit more.”Ambidextrous players are the rarest sight in tennis. American Luke Jensen was the last to make a major impression, winning the 1993 French Open doubles title with his younger brother Murphy while ripping 130 mph serves from both wings. And Russia’s Evgenia Kulikovskaya was ranked in the top 100 in the early 2000s while playing tennis with two forehands. The Davidov experiment – he is not naturally ambidextrous – appears to be built on Toni Nadal’s gambit to convert his nephew Rafael from a righty to a leftie, and we all saw how that turned out.Still, when it comes to thetacticalblueprint for Davidov’s game, well, who could serve as a model for a player who is sui generis? “The idea was for the leftie forehand to be more like Rafa and righty to be more like Fed,” Davidov says. “It’s still a work in progress. I don’t know if we’re going to get there someday, but that’s the hope.”But before you take Davidov for some kind of tennis lab rat, know that his parents have gone to pains to make their boy as well-rounded as those court legends, too. Besides skiing and hiking, Davidov enjoys basketball, American football and soccer. Golf’s the only sport he picked up with two hands. “I used to play left-handed, but I actually switched recently and started playing righty. On the range, it’s definitely going farther.”After the Open, Davidov said he plans to play a 300-level juniors tournament in Texas before considering a few pro events. As for what lies beyond, he’s still undecided about whether he wants to follow his doubles partner Lee, who’s bound for Duke, and play on a university team (“College [tennis] has gotten so much better lately,” Davidov says) or skip it altogether and turn pro.Wherever he goes, he’ll remain one to watch – especially if he winds up adding a backhand just to press home his advantage. “We were actually thinking about it, to have even more variety, playing like one point lefty,” he says. “But I think we’re kind of stuck to the two forehands. But we’ll see.”Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026TennisUS Open tennisUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI not on track to reduce risk of ‘catastrophic’ loss of control, says board member | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: US government adviser Paul Christiano warns of risks to AI industry as he joins OpenAI’s non-profit foundation
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: US government adviser Paul Christiano warns of risks to AI industry as he joins OpenAI’s non-profit foundation
Content: ‘If OpenAI rises to the occasion we could significantly reduce risk,’ said Christiano.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘If OpenAI rises to the occasion we could significantly reduce risk,’ said Christiano.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAI not on track to reduce risk of ‘catastrophic’ loss of control, says board memberUS government adviser Paul Christiano warns of risks to AI industry as he joins OpenAI’s non-profit foundationRobert BoothUK technology editorThu 10 Sep 2026 08.23 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpenAI is not on track to reduce the risk of “catastrophic” loss of control to an acceptable level, a member of its non-profit board has said, amid spreading public and political concern that super-advanced AIs could one day wipe out humanity.Paul Christiano, a US government technology adviser,said: “There is a meaningful risk that rapid acceleration in AI capabilities leads to catastrophic and irreversible loss of control in the very near term.”He added: “I do not think that the AI industry in general, including OpenAI, is currently on track to reduce this risk to an acceptable level.”Christiano used to run model alignment at OpenAI and made the statement on Wednesday as he joined the board of the San Francisco company’s non-profit foundation.He will also sit on the foundation’s committee that provides governance over safety and security practices across all of OpenAI, which is developing some of the world’s most advanced models.This summer, OpenAI admitted that hundreds of its AI agents went rogue during a training exercise, accessed the internet, conspired on message boards and hacked into a third-party website, Hugging Face.Christiano said that “if OpenAI rises to the occasion we could significantly reduce risk”. His comments came after a senior employee at Anthropic, OpenAI’s major US rival in the race to AI supremacy,claimed on Tuesdaythere was a greater than 10% chance the technology could “kill all humans” in the next decade.Evan Hubinger, the alignment science lead atAnthropic, warned that his company did not have a plan to ensure artificial superintelligence (ASI) was aligned, meaning it did no harm.Predictions for when ASImight be reached vary from several years to more than a decade. ASI is often defined as AI that far surpasses human intelligence across a large range of fields.Fears of AI catastrophe were also ignited by the resignation of Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-oldAnthropicresearcher who said he also previously worked at OpenAI, claiming “neither company was acting responsibly” and they were “gambling with our lives”.Coxon said on Wednesday night in an interview with CNN: “Right now there’s no risk of extinction.“The current models, the worst they can do is maybe hack into something, potentially cause a lot of damages … in infrastructure.” He added they were “not intelligent enough to outsmart us at the level that would lead to extinction”.But he went on: “What’s just crazy is to look at the rate of progress. There is a very real possibility that in the immediate future … next year, the year after, recursive self-improvement will happen and will enter the phase of Evan’s post, where he argues that there’s a chance we could all die.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOpenAI models went rogue. We urgently need a better ‘hugging face’ investigation | Mackenzie Arnold and Stephan LlerenaRead moreGeoffrey Hinton, the Nobel prize-winning computer scientist known as one of the “godfathers of AI”, was asked on Wednesday for his view of Hubinger’s claim and told BBC Newsnight: “Nobody knows how to estimate it; a 10% chance seems not an unreasonable estimate.”Christiano’s prognosis about the likelihood of the AI industry reducing risk came as concerns about the most extreme risks from super-powerful AIs, long discussed in Silicon Valley, broke out into the mainstream this week.Politicians on both sides of the Atlantic, fromTed Cruz and Bernie Sandersin the US to the MP Darren Jones in the UK, have called for government action and the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, told parliament on Wednesday that “AI poses risks to our national security, but it also could be the source of solutions to keeping us safer”.Meanwhile, Anthropic hasadmitteda new incident in which a version of its Claude model in training broke into third parties after its task could not be aborted. It said the incident happened in January and would be included in an independent investigation of a total of four incidents to be carried out by the Berkeley-based AI safety organisation METR.Overall, it said the models were showing two forms of misalignment: biased reasoning, in which models selectively interpret evidence in ways that favour justifying their actions, and “recklessness, in which models have a propensity to keep trying to solve their task, even when this could lead to harm”.Anthropic said it was especially concerned about misalignment it found in the behaviour of Claude Mythos 5, which it said “behaved recklessly” by going online and uploading malicious code to a public software repository, PyPI. This was a process that involved the AI agent trying to find cryptocurrency so it could pay for a phone number that would allow it to register an email address needed to access PyPI. When this failed, it found a free email provider and got in. Fifteen systems then downloaded the malicious code, which meant they leaked credentials that allowed Mythos to access a real security vendor’s database.The company’s assessment of the incidents said: “This remains unsettled science – it is critical that alignment and security mature faster than capabilities advance, which is one reason we support a coordinated, verifiable approach topacing frontier AI development.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAIAnthropicTechnology sectorComputingData and computer securityEthicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Elon Musk attacks film-maker behind documentary about him | Elon Musk | The Guardian
description: Tech mogul calls director Alex Gibney a ‘bitter old man’ who has ‘zero integrity’ in series of posts on X
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Tech mogul calls director Alex Gibney a ‘bitter old man’ who has ‘zero integrity’ in series of posts on X
Content: Elon Musk described the film as a ‘hit piece that misses’.Photograph: Gonzalo Fuentes/ReutersView image in fullscreenElon Musk described the film as a ‘hit piece that misses’.Photograph: Gonzalo Fuentes/ReutersElon MuskElon Musk attacks film-maker behind documentary about himTech mogul calls director Alex Gibney a ‘bitter old man’ who has ‘zero integrity’ in series of posts on XMichael SavageMedia editorThu 10 Sep 2026 08.29 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElon Muskhas issued an angry tirade at the film-maker behind a four-hour documentary about his life and influence, labelling the director, Alex Gibney, a “bitter old man” who has “zero integrity”.Gibney, who has previously made films about the collapse of Enron,WikiLeaksand Vladimir Putin, premiered his Musk documentary at theVenice film festivalthis week. He said he believed the world’s richest man was“extremely dangerous”.Musk review – epic study of the world’s richest and most banal manRead moreIn a series of posts on X, whichMusk bought for $44bn in 2022, the tech mogul railed against the film as a “hit piece that misses”, adding its four-hour length also made the documentary, which is highly critical of Musk, “as boring af”.Musk also appeared to push at conspiracy theory,reposting an imagedepicting the Democratic party as a puppet, controlling another puppet labelled “Team Soros” – a reference to the billionaire George Soros, who has supported progressive causes.That puppet in turn controls another one labelled “Alex Gibney”, while the Gibney puppet controls another labelled “Hollywood”. In response to the picture, Musk stated: “Accurate.”In response to a supporter who said he had never heard of Gibney until his Musk film, Musk replied: “It’s a psy op” – a reference to a planned “psychological operation” designed to influence the public’s thoughts.“Gibney has zero integrity. Zero,” said Musk. “Fortunately, his movies are boring af … It’s a hit piece that misses, and makes the fatal sin of being boring for 4 hours.“Gibney just assembled a hit list of people who either have an axe to grind or don’t even know me (but still have an axe to grind) … He’s a bitter old man who lost the plot long ago.“Dogshit is worth more respect than Gibney.”Musk’s lawyer has alsothreatened to sue Gibneyfor defamation, NPR reported on Thursday.State handouts, 10,000 lasers – and Trump’s election: six things we learned from the Elon Musk filmRead moreThe documentary has caused a stir since its premier, as have the claims made by some of those involved in the film.Musk specifically denied a claim made by his ex-partner, the former Maga influencer Ashley St Clair, that his team offered her $40m to sign a non-disclosure agreement about their time together. “She was never offered that and has a history of making false claims,” he wrote.Musk also amplified a post by the podcaster Katie Miller, the wife of Donald Trump’s powerful adviser Stephen Miller and former communications director for Musk’s “department of government efficiency” (Doge). Miller complained about the alleged absence of Musk acquaintances and allies in the film.“It simply can’t be ‘definitive’ if the people who were present didn’t participate,” she said. “This fictional movie is a hit job by a self-obsessed Hollywood director.”Musk’s influence on public discourse through X, and the content it prioritises, is making international waves. While he has repeatedly intervened in the immigration debate in the UK, he also celebrated the strong result for Germany’s far-right Alternative für Deutschland party in this week’sstate elections in Saxony-Anhalt.Speaking at a press conference in Venice, Gibney said he had encountered a “sense of fear” among people he approached over his film. He surmised that Musk’s childhood in South Africa may account for how he behaves now.“He had a childhood that was very difficult and traumatic,” Gibney said. “To some extent he’s now playing out that trauma on the rest of us, if I were to psychoanalyse the situation.”Explore more on these topicsElon MuskAlex GibneyDocumentary filmsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Pixel 11 Pro review: Google’s best pocket camera goes customisable | Pixel | The Guardian
description: Solid battery life, snappy performance and quality software make for a great smaller phone with a killer camera
Author: Samuel Gibbs
Headline: Solid battery life, snappy performance and quality software make for a great smaller phone with a killer camera
Content: The Pixel 11 Pro doesn’t break the mould, but Google’s top smaller phone shows you don’t have to have a massive screen to have the best camera.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Pixel 11 Pro doesn’t break the mould, but Google’s top smaller phone shows you don’t have to have a massive screen to have the best camera.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.PixelReviewPixel 11 Pro review: Google’s best pocket camera goes customisableSolid battery life, snappy performance and quality software make for a great smaller phone with a killer cameraSamuel GibbsConsumer technology editorThu 10 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGoogle’s latest Pro phone is out to prove it has the best camera on a smartphone while embracing customisation, allowing you to change the look and feel of your photos far beyond simple filters even if that means making them technically worse.ThePixel11 Pro packs the best of Google’s hardware and software into a still-pocketable and easy to handle frame, instantly making it a contender for best smaller phone of the year.Being smaller doesn’t make it cheap. The 11 Pro sits above the regular £879Pixel 11and costs from £1,079 (€1,199/$1,099/A$1,849) – £80 (€100/$100/A$150) more than last year, with double the storage but less memory owing to thecost of RAMageddon.Little has changed on the outside for thePro Pixelsinseveral years. The new model is 0.1mm smaller in all directions and 3g lighter but has the same size 6.3in OLED screen, same polished aluminium and glass body and a large camera bar sticking out the back. It is an attractive design that has aged well.The temperature sensor fromprevious Pixel Pro generations, which always felt like a gimmick, has been replaced by a coloured HiLight LED that works as a camera flash and notification light. The LED glows when you talk to Gemini or pulses with one of five colours when your favourite contact calls. But it doesn’t work for notifications of any other kind, so is a wasted opportunity.View image in fullscreenThe HiLight LED swirls different colours when you talk to Gemini, but only when the phone is face down, which is not something I’ve ever wanted to do.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe 11 Pro has the same Tensor G6 chip as the regular Pixel 11 and has 12 or 16GB of RAM depending on the storage version. It can’t match the raw performance of the topQualcommor Apple chips for games but is snappy in day-to-day tasks.Battery life is just shy of two days with the screen actively used for about seven hours across a mix of wifi and 5G for browsing, messaging apps and photos. This is a bit behind theregular Pixel 11but should see out even the heaviest of use days with some left in the tank. Most people will need to charge the 11 Pro every other day for general use.SpecificationsScreen:6.3in 120Hz QHD+ OLED (495ppi)Processor:Google Tensor G6RAM:12 or 16GBStorage:256, 512GB or 1TBOperating system:Android17Camera:50MP + 48MP UW + 48MP 5x tele; 42MP selfieConnectivity:5G, eSIM, wifi 7, UWB, NFC, Bluetooth 6, Thread and GNSSWater resistance:IP68 (1.5m for 30 minutes)Dimensions:152.7 x 71.9 x 8.4mmWeight:204gQuality Android 17 experience and AIView image in fullscreenA fast and accurate ultrasonic fingerprint scanner and solid camera-based face recognition make the Pixel feel responsive.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe 11 Pro runs the same Google version of Android 17 asthe regular Pixel 11and will be supported untilAugust 2033with operating system and security updates, making it one of the longest-lasting devices available.It’s a polished experience with smooth animations, nice touches of haptic feedback across the system and enough customisation to make it yours.
