But as with other Pixel devices, the phone is a showcase for Google’s most advanced AI tools that are littered throughout the software.The 11 Pro comes with six months ofGoogle AI Pro subscription, which gives you access toGemini Omnito generate surprisingly good eight-second videos, higher AI usage limits, 5TB of cloud storage and Google Health Premium.But the most interesting tools are the local AI ones, including thenew Rambler voice dictation featurein Gboard, which produces fully formed succinct sentences and paragraphs from your ramblings, removing unnecessary pauses, ums, ers and deviations. Gemini’s proactive assistance has also improved with more time-saving suggestions, although it only works in certain apps and not WhatsApp, Signal or other third-party apps.CameraView image in fullscreenThe camera app has lots of optional tools for making the best of your photos, from standard modes to AI framing guidance.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe reason you buy a Pixel Pro is for the camera. The 11 Pro has a very good 42-megapixel selfie camera on the front and a similar winning triple camera system on the rear from last year: a 50MP wide, 48MP ultra wide and a 48MP 5x telephoto camera.All three cameras capture really fantastic photos across a range of lighting conditions with very little effort. The wide and telephoto cameras now capture more light and slightly better detail, but the biggest boost is the new Instant Night Sight. It dramatically speeds up low-light photos by up to 4.5 times, which makes taking great shots in very dark scenes a lot easier.The 5x telephoto camera manages a very good 10x crop zoom before stretching up to 120x magnification, first with a very good traditional digital zoom to 30x then using local generative AI to go beyond. The camera keeps the regular digital zoom image and the one processed by AI to add back lost detail, which can be remarkable or filled with artefacts.Magic Capturetakes video and photos automatically with just one button for point-and-shoot recording, which works well for events such as a birthday party.ButCamera Looksis the most interesting feature for getting creative with photography. It allows you to modify how the camera processes your photos, starting with subtle changes such as darker shadows and ranging to more distinctive looks such as “minimal”, which reduces the computational photography processing for a more raw photo. Other options include “digi”, which replicates the look of olddigital cameras that have become popular, and “velvet”, which mimics the look of some film cameras. Each look can be further customised, allowing great creative licence.The Pixel shoots great video with lots ofstabilisation and processing toolsincluding the new “Creator Suite”, which captures clips straight into a folder for storyboarding and trimming, with a teleprompter, framing for social media and speed enhancement.SustainabilityView image in fullscreenThe phone takes about 90 minutes to fully charge using a 30W or greater power adaptor (not included) hitting 54% in half an hour. It also supports 25W Qi2.2 wireless charging.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe batteryis rated to lastin excess of 1,000 full-charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity. The phone is repairable by Google, third-party shops or self-repairwith manualsandparts available.The Pixel 11 Pro contains 31% recycled materials by weight. The company breaks down thephone’s environmental impactin its report and willrecycle old devicesfor free.PriceThe Google Pixel 11 Pro costs from£1,079(€1,199/$1,099/A$1,849) in a choice of four colours.For comparison, the Pixel 11 costs£879, Pixel 11 Pro XL costs£1,279, Pixel 11 Pro Fold costs from£1,799, thePixel 10acosts£499, theSamsung Galaxy S26costs£879, theSamsung Galaxy S26 Ultracosts£1,279and theApple iPhone 17 Procosts£1,099.VerdictThe Pixel 11 Pro is a refinement of multiple generations of Google’s Pro phones rather than an outright revolution, but that’s no bad thing.It is one of the very best smaller phones, packing all the top-end hardware, cameras and AI features of Google’s most biggest and expensive model into a slightly cheaper and more pocketable form. You buy a Pro Pixel for the camera, which doesn’t disappoint with arguably the best photography on a phone at the moment.The ability to customise the processing of your photos goes far beyond rivals for interesting creative potential. The dramatically faster Night Sight is also a significant improvement.Gemini’s proactive tools show great potential but depend on using the right apps. The supercharged Rambler voice dictation system is fantastic, and there are many other little AI tools that are useful from time to time.With just shy of two days battery life, a decent chip and quality software, the Pixel 11 Pro is a great pocketable phone. It just isn’t a massive upgrade on the already excellent Pixel 11 or recent Pixel Pro models.Pros:great camera with extended zoom and extensive customisation, seven years of software updates, excellent screen, impressive dictation and local AI features, Qi2 wireless charging and magnetic accessory support, good battery life, great size, fast fingerprint and face recognition, six months of Google AI Pro included.Cons:quite expensive, less memory on cheapest model than before, face unlock option not as secure as Face ID, raw performance and battery life short of best-in-class, no physical sim card slot in the US, not a massive upgrade.Explore more on these topicsPixelAndroidGoogleMobile phonesAlphabetreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Instagram boss says users will be ‘overwhelmed’ with brand content in algorithm-free world | Social media | The Guardian
description: Adam Mosseri says platform’s algorithm ‘feels like a black box’ but company trying to give users more control after Labor announces opt-out plan
Author: Josh Taylor
Headline: Adam Mosseri says platform’s algorithm ‘feels like a black box’ but company trying to give users more control after Labor announces opt-out plan
Content: Instagram’s chief executive Adam Mosseri told journalists just a ‘very vocal minority’ wants social media to go back to reverse chronological feeds.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreenInstagram’s chief executive Adam Mosseri told journalists just a ‘very vocal minority’ wants social media to go back to reverse chronological feeds.Photograph: Yui Mok/PASocial mediaInstagram boss says users will be ‘overwhelmed’ with brand content in algorithm-free worldAdam Mosseri says platform’s algorithm ‘feels like a black box’ but company trying to give users more control after Labor announces opt-out planJosh TaylorTechnology reporterWed 9 Sep 2026 22.10 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 10.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleInstagram’s chief executive has said users will have a worse experience in an algorithm-free world, seeing more brand-related content, and spend less time on the app.The comments come as the Australian government plans to giveusers the option to opt out of algorithms, with the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, announcing plans on Tuesday to require social media platforms to prompt users to choose between a feed of algorithm-recommended content or a reverse chronological feed of the pages users follow. Labor also plans to introduce a range of measures designed to address online harm on the sites.In a briefing with journalists on Thursday to launch the company’s Algo Confessions series in Australia, Instagram’s chief executive, Adam Mosseri, did not comment directly on the Albanese government proposal but said Instagram had a range of algorithms in operation. Those include ranking which friends’ stories you see more often, or which users come up first in message suggestions based on interactions, as well as the algorithm that determines the content people see in their feeds.Australia to force social media platforms to allow users to opt out of algorithmsRead moreThe launch of the series in Australia is the first outside the US. It features celebrities and influencers detailing how Instagram determines what content ends up in a user’s feed, and how the user can have some control over that by adding or removing tags in their settings.Mosseri said just a “very vocal minority” wants social media to go back to reverse chronological feeds, which he said would just incentivise people to post more.“What ends up happening is the best way to get more reach is just to post more often and those who can afford to post the most often do and then therefore get the most reach,” he said.“And it turns out your friends post a lot less than creators, who post a lot less than brands and companies.”He said people would be “overwhelmed” with content from brands, and creators and friends would be drowned out.“What happens is people become a bit less interested in the experience and they use it a lot less, which then means that there’s less reach to go around and people start to get more and more mad about the fact that their reach is going down because the overall pie gets smaller.”He said engagement and user satisfaction goes down.“It’s this interesting tension between what an individual might want and what happens when you actually explode that to the entire community,” he said.“That’s not to say that ranking is perfect, it’s not, we make mistakes – one of the things that frustrates me about ranking is that we end up over-optimising for things that we can measure and undervaluing things that are more difficult to measure.”Mosseri said Instagram’s ranking algorithm “feels like a black box” but was something Instagram was trying to give users more control over by opting out of certain topics in their recommendations.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe said in the future, Meta’s AI models could eventually allow users to talk to the app to understand why they are seeing certain types of content.Mosseri said he did not believe the app to be the clinical definition of “addictive”.“I don’t believe Instagram is addictive – I know that is controversial to say – I do think we often in English anyway conflate the way we colloquially use the word addicted … like ‘I’m addicted to this show and I’m binge watching it, which is not good for me’.”He said clinically defined addictions have withdrawal symptoms, while social media does not have that effect, and “those things are different”.Mosseri hasmade this claim before. Research has found some users can have an impulse to use a platform without being fully aware of it, and evidence shows frequent engagement with algorithms “alters dopamine pathways” that fosters dependency that is “analogous to substance addiction”.In the landmark US court case centred on the addictive nature of Meta’s products, the company’s lawyer last month conceded to the court that it was “no dispute” people can struggle with social media, but the company has tools to address that. Meta latersettled the case for US$18bnwhile denying any wrongdoing.Explore more on these topicsSocial mediaInstagramDigital mediaAustralian politicsMetaSocial networkingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Anthropic details bad actors’ efforts to misuse its AI for bioweapons | Anthropic | The Guardian
description: The 154-page report comes two days after former employee Jacob Coxon resigned due to Anthropic racing to improve its models that would cause human extinction by 2030
Author: Dara Kerr
Headline: The 154-page report comes two days after former employee Jacob Coxon resigned due to Anthropic racing to improve its models that would cause human extinction by 2030
Content: ‘Biological misuse is one of the most serious risks of frontier AI models. Without the correct safeguards, such capabilities could have catastrophic consequences.’Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Biological misuse is one of the most serious risks of frontier AI models. Without the correct safeguards, such capabilities could have catastrophic consequences.’Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersAnthropicAnthropic details bad actors’ efforts to misuse its AI for bioweaponsReport comes two days after former employee quit claiming company’s models could cause human extinction by 2030Dara KerrThu 10 Sep 2026 18.35 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 18.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCriminals, state-sponsored groups, spyware vendors, scientists and propagandists have attempted to use Anthropic’s powerful artificial intelligence models to design missiles and bombs, create deadly pathogens and surveil dissidents, according to athreat intelligence reportthe company published on Thursday.“The cases we share here aren’t typical misuse, but rather examples of the most notable and novel threat activity we’ve identified to date,”Anthropicwrote in its 154-page report. “We’re publishing this work because we believe we have a responsibility to disclose malicious misuse of our services.”In particular, the company detailed five case studies of scientists using its AI models in biological research. In these examples, Anthropic said the researchers circumvented its safeguards meant to prevent users from “unsupported regions”, as well as worked to hide the purpose of their work.More Anthropic researchers warn of AI’s perils as Musk terms fears a ‘psyop’Read more“Biological misuse is one of the most serious risks of frontier AI models,” Anthropic wrote. “Without the correct safeguards, such capabilities could have catastrophic consequences.”Anthropic said it banned these accounts. The company did not reveal the names of the research institutions or the countries where the misuse took place, saying it was uncertain of the researchers’ intent.Anthropic gave dozens of other examples of threat actors using its AI models. Those included cyber operations such as Russian espionage and “smash-and-grab” cyberhacks; surveillance operations, including a China-based program targeting Uyghurs in Syria and another targeting internal dissidents; propaganda campaigns in Russia, Malaysia, Iran and Bangladesh; and the use of its Claude AI model in Yemen, China and Russia to develop software for conventional weapons, including firearms, missiles, armed drones, bombs and other munitions.In one of the examples of biological research, Anthropic found a scientist using Claude to work on a state-sponsored grant application to study the virus chikungunya. The virus is a mosquito-borne disease, similar to dengue and malaria, that can cause months of severe pain, fever and other debilitating symptoms.Such research could be used to develop vaccines, but could also be used to create biological weapons. Anthropictold the New York Timesthis case was especially concerning because it could see the study was to be done at a military research institute.The report comes just two days after an Anthropic employee, Jacob Coxon,set off a media firestormwith his resignation. He stated that he quit the company because it was not acting responsibly in creating its technology. Coxon said Anthropic and its rival, OpenAI, were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence” that would cause human extinction by 2030. Current Anthropic employees posted public agreements with him.Many AI experts say the real-world threats, like those detailed in Anthropic’s intelligence report, arefar more concerningwithin the next three years than an apocalypse brought on by an omnipotent intelligence.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“AI accelerationism and AI doomerism are two sides of the same coin: they both enforce the notion that an AGI superbeing will come into existence,” said Heidy Khlaaf, the chief AI scientist at the AI Now Institute. Khlaaf said AI labs creating technology that can be used for cybersecurity exploitation and weapons of war could be exceedingly more deadly.In its report, Anthropic said that the potential real-world misuse from AI models is not typically in public view, instead, it’s investigated internally and by academics, governments and international organizations.The company said that the entire AI industry needs to work together, alongside governments, to address these harms and create defenses.“As models become increasingly capable, their risks will increase, unless AI developers and society’s defenders act to make them safer,” Anthropic wrote.Explore more on these topicsAnthropicAI (artificial intelligence)CybercrimeSurveillanceHackingnewsShareReuse this content

title: More Anthropic researchers warn of AI’s perils as Musk terms fears a ‘psyop’ | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Insiders at the firm fear tech’s advancement could cause human extinction while others are calling it a ‘setup’
Author: Johana Bhuiyan
Headline: Insiders at the firm fear tech’s advancement could cause human extinction while others are calling it a ‘setup’
Content: Stickers for Claude software on an attendees laptop at Claude developer conference in London, on Tuesday, 19 May 2026.Photograph: Chris Ratcliffe/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenStickers for Claude software on an attendees laptop at Claude developer conference in London, on Tuesday, 19 May 2026.Photograph: Chris Ratcliffe/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)More Anthropic researchers warn of AI’s perils as Musk terms fears a ‘psyop’Insiders at the firm fear tech’s advancement could cause human extinction while others are calling it a ‘setup’Johana BhuiyanThu 10 Sep 2026 17.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA day after a former researcher atAnthropicmade an apocalyptic declaration about artificial intelligence, more researchers and staff members at the AI startup publicly agreed with him and posted their own dire warnings.In response, Elon Musk and other conservative figures on X, formerly Twitter, called the chorus of concerns a “setup” and a “psyop”.The Anthropic insiders fear the technology they are building could become so advanced and dangerous as to cause human extinction within the decade, and they assert many of their colleagues feel the same but haven’t said so publicly.These researchers and staff are posting in response to a now-viral thread from Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who said on Wednesday he was resigning from the company because neither Anthropic nor its competitor OpenAI, also his former employer, were building AI models responsibly and are “gambling with our lives”.OpenAI not on track to reduce risk of ‘catastrophic’ loss of control, says board memberRead moreAnna Wang, who works on Artificial General Intelligence Safety at Anthropic and previously worked at Google’s DeepMind, said Thursday that many people at Anthropic want to slow down development to come up with a plan to mitigate the risks that could come with these AI models.“There is not yet a viable scientific plan to solve risks from recursively self-improving AI,” Wang wrote on X.Drake Thomas, another Anthropic employee, said that he respected Coxon’s choice to abstain from building these models if he worries they could pose planet-scale risks.“Things are moving way too fast, we don’t have anywhere near the degree of assurance we’ll want for ASI [artificial superintelligence],” Thomas said.Musk took a more adversarial stance. “Seems like a setup,” hewrote.Coxon replied to the world’s richest man with a selfie, writing, “I’m real and these are my real beliefs. You could ask your xAI researchers about me if you hadn’t fired them.”In a statement to the Guardian, an Anthropic spokesperson defended the company’s strategy. “We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks. To address these risks, we continue to build models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry,” the statement said.Musk and others with a more positive view of AI have started to spread theories that Coxon’s post and the resulting fallout are part of a “psyop” to negatively influence the public’s feelings about AI.“I think the groundwork for this psy op (for lack of a better term) has been prepared for a long time,” Musk posted on X. “This was just the match that lit the fire.”Musk was responding to a post by Parker Thayer, a researcher at conservativethinktank Capital Research, in which he floated a theory with little evidence that Coxon’s post was the start of a “VERY sophisticated and well-funded PR operation to get support for Democrats to regulate AI into oblivion”. Other notable figures took notice.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBill Ackman, the billionaire CEO of the hedge fund Pershing Square, also quoted Thayer’s post, simply saying “Interesting.”Other Anthropic employees had posted their agreement with Coxon shortly after he declared his resignation on Wednesday.“AI developers believe their technology could cause human extinction (or similarly bad outcomes),” wrote Samuel Marks, who works on safety research at Anthropic. “This could happen in the next few years. In general, the more senior the employee, the more concerned they are.”Evan Hubinger, who describes himself as a lead in the company’s alignment division, which works on ensuring Anthropic’s AI models function in line with human goals, said Coxon was “correct” and that the industry was falling behind in attempts to deal with the apocalyptic potential.“We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Hubingerwrote. “I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.It’s not exactly clear how Coxon and others expect AI models to usher in the demise of humanity. Some experts doubt that the technology will become so intelligent as to cause the apocalypse. Gary Marcus, a scientist and leading voice in AI, said that it’s time to boycott AI, but because it’s already causing harm.More than extinction, Marcus said he worried about the “risk of catastrophe” from “from AI-generated pathogens, from wars started or escalated by AI-generated disinformation, from hacks that destroy critical infrastructure, and so on. Nothing I have seen gives any indication that any of that is under control”.The same day, Anthropic released a report documenting how the company dismantled an operation attempting to build a biological weapon using its AI models.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)AnthropicnewsShareReuse this content

title: Lawmakers blast AI companies after researcher warns of human extinction by 2030 | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon said AI will become ‘superhuman systems’ that can cause human extinction by the end of the decade
Author: Dara Kerr
Headline: Former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon said AI will become ‘superhuman systems’ that can cause human extinction by the end of the decade
Content: ‘A recent poll shows that the American people overwhelmingly want to ban artificial super intelligence and pause the development of AI until we establish clear safety standards.’Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘A recent poll shows that the American people overwhelmingly want to ban artificial super intelligence and pause the development of AI until we establish clear safety standards.’Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersAI (artificial intelligence)Lawmakers blast AI companies after researcher warns of human extinction by 2030Former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon said AI will become ‘superhuman systems’ that can cause human extinction by the end of the decadeDara KerrWed 9 Sep 2026 20.19 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 11.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJust a day after threeAnthropicresearchers warned that artificial intelligence could kill off humanity within the decade, lawmakers have begun lashing out about the risks of the burgeoning technology.Ted Cruz, a republican senator from Texas, said in aninterviewon ABC’s The View, that AI posed a “catastrophic risk” and that he “read that whole tweet thread that that developer put out. It was highly concerning.“It reminded me, last year I hadElon Muskon my podcast … and one of the questions I asked him, I said, ‘OK, what are the odds that AI destroys humanity?’ And he looked at me and said, ‘10-20%.’ And I’m like, ‘holy crap,’” Cruz added.On the polar end of the political spectrum, Bernie Sanders, an independent senator from Vermont,said: “A recent poll shows that the American people overwhelmingly want to ban artificial super intelligence and pause the development of AI until we establish clear safety standards.”The outrage began after an Anthropic employee, Jacob Coxon, announced on social media on Tuesday that he wasresigning from the company, saying AI would soon be “superhuman systems” that could cause human extinction by 2030.“I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at bothOpenAIand Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly,” Coxon wrote. “They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”After Coxon’s post, at least two other Anthropic employees responded to back up these predictions. One said: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!”Both Cruz and Sanders have been working on legislation that would put guardrails on AI, and echoed this sentiment on Wednesday. Other lawmakers also called on Congress to act. Ted Lieu, a Democratic congressman from California,saidCoxon’s post was “exhibit number 739 for why we need to pass the bipartisan AI Kill Switch Bill asap”.Lori Trahan, a Democratic congresswoman from Massachusetts,saidit was “past time for Congress to get off the sidelines and do its job”.“Safety researchers are resigning, powerful AI models are breaking out of their labs, and companies are racing ahead anyway,” Trahan added.Even musician Sheryl Crow weighed in,postingon Instagram about Coxon’s warning and saying that AI had the capacity to “eliminate us in order to continue”.“I am begging and pleading that we wake up to this moment and demand our leaders put aside their greed and prevent this from going forward,” Crow wrote. Singer-songwriter Maggie Rogers reposted Crow, writing: “what she said”.The outrage comes after both OpenAI and Anthropic revealed that some of their AI agents went rogue in hacking sprees over the past couple of months. Executives at the companies have touted the power of their technology and warned of its potential, but have stopped short of prognostications like Coxon’s.On Wednesday, Anthropicpublisheda lengthy cybersecurity incident report about its occurrences. The company said it scanned hundreds of millions of transcripts to look for further incidents and that it “found no other cases of similar or worse severity”. Anthropic insisted that while the agent’s actions were “misaligned, they remained within a narrow scope”.“We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks,” an Anthropic spokesperson said in a statement to the Guardian. “To address these risks, we continue to build models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry.” The spokesperson added that the industry should work together “to pace how we release powerful models”.OpenAI did not return a request for comment.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)AnthropicUS politicsOpenAIBernie SandersTed CruzElon MusknewsShareReuse this content

title: Anthropic researchers say AI could cause human extinction by 2030 | Anthropic | The Guardian
description: One researcher who resigned said many in industry believe that without regulation AI could kill off humanity
Author: Richard Luscombe
Headline: One researcher who resigned said many in industry believe that without regulation AI could kill off humanity
Content: A social media post by a now former Anthropic employee has sparked discussion about the danger of unregulated AI.Photograph: Samyukta Lakshmi/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA social media post by a now former Anthropic employee has sparked discussion about the danger of unregulated AI.Photograph: Samyukta Lakshmi/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesAnthropicAnthropic researchers say AI could cause human extinction by 2030One researcher who resigned said many in industry believe that without regulation AI could kill off humanityRichard LuscombeWed 9 Sep 2026 20.14 EDTFirst published on Wed 9 Sep 2026 11.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArtificial intelligencecould kill off humanity within the decade, according to three researchers with the industry giantAnthropic, one of whom has quit his job in protest.The latest doom-laden predictions came inpostson social media on Tuesday by a researcher who said he resigned because Anthropic and his previous employer,OpenAI, were ignoring or, at best, mishandling their response to the threat.“Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” wrote Jacob Coxon.“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible – but I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger.”AI could kill all humans in next decade, warn experts: but how seriously should we take them?Read moreThe post garnered responses from at least two otherAnthropicemployees who backed up Coxon’s dire predictions.In the first, Evan Hubinger, who describes himself as a lead in the company’s alignment division, which works on ensuring Anthropic’s AI models function in line with human goals, said his former colleague was “correct”, and that the industry was falling behind in attempts to deal with the apocalyptic potential.“We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Hubingerwrote. “I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to.”Hubinger’s comments mark a surprising affirmation of Coxon’s unflattering, apocalyptic predictions from a person still on Anthropic’s payroll. A second response came from Samuel Marks, Anthropic’s “scalable oversight lead”, whoposteda lengthy analysis he stressed was in his personal capacity, and not the views of his employer.“AI developers believe their technology could cause human extinction (or similarly bad outcomes),” wrote Marks. “This could happen in the next few years. In general, the more senior the employee, the more concerned they are.”In a statement to the Guardian, an Anthropic spokesperson defended the company’s strategy.“We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks. To address these risks, we continue to build models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry,” the statement said.“Anthropic has been a pioneer in mechanistic interpretability, the science of looking inside AI models to understand how they work, which is now being used to analyze and prevent incidents of AI misalignment across the industry. We were the first lab to publish a Responsible Scaling Policy, a public framework dedicated to mitigating catastrophic risks from AI models and we continue to aggressively test our models for dangerous capabilities in areas like cybersecurity and biology, and publish what we learn for scrutiny and research.“This work is also why we believe the world would benefit from the industry adopting a lawful, verifiable way to work together to pace how we release powerful models.”The researchers’ musings on the possibility of human extinction follow more concretewarningsabout AI’s cybersecurity capabilities by Sam Altman, chief executive of Anthropic’s rival OpenAI. OpenAI’s president, Greg Brockman, has conceded previously that “we underestimated the real-world cyber capabilities of our AI models”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAltmansaid last yearthat certain aspects of AI, including what he called the “silent surrender” of human decision-making, terrified him.AI executives have shared some concerns about the direction of AI and its growing ability to manipulate, seize and control human functions and actions. A sharp rise wasreported this summerin incidents of AIs escaping users’ control to lie, ignore instructions and pursue goals in harmful ways.In one of the most publicized examples, staff at OpenAI recordedrogue behavioramong its leading AI agents that escaped a closed training environment in July to access the open web and launch an unprecedented hacking attack on the software repository Hugging Face.OpenAI, the San Francisco-based startup behind the publicly available AI bot ChatGPT, lateradmittedthat it should have responded earlier to warning signals of the days-long attack, which is widely considered to be the first autonomous agent cyber-attack.Those executives, however, have stopped short of agreeing with the full doomsday warnings like Coxon’s and have bristled at any attempts to regulate the AI industry.Some politicians have urged the industry to slow down, or in some cases, halt development on AI altogether.Bernie Sanders, the independent Vermont senator, reposted Coxon’s resignation on Wednesday with his own note: “Mr. Coxon is right. The very people building this technology admit that it could threaten the future of humanity.” Sanders said he would soon introduce legislation to “ban superintelligence” and pause AI development.Explore more on these topicsAnthropicAI (artificial intelligence)ChatGPTOpenAISam AltmanComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: I turned off my algorithm for 24 hours. Is this how social media used to be?  | Social media | The Guardian
description: Thanks to a little-known feature in Instagram, I try to travel back to 2012 – before everything on the internet was an ad
Author: Caitlin Cassidy
Headline: Thanks to a little-known feature in Instagram, I try to travel back to 2012 – before everything on the internet was an ad
Content: ‘For 24 hours, I decided to manually turn off my algorithm via little-known settings on Instagram to get a sense of how the reforms might change my feed,’ Caitlin Cassidy writes.Illustration: Guardian designView image in fullscreen‘For 24 hours, I decided to manually turn off my algorithm via little-known settings on Instagram to get a sense of how the reforms might change my feed,’ Caitlin Cassidy writes.Illustration: Guardian designSocial mediaI turned off my algorithm for 24 hours. Is this how social media used to be?Thanks to a little-known feature in Instagram, I try to travel back to 2012 – before everything on the internet was an adFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastCaitlin CassidyThu 10 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 20.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIhave a confession. I love my social media algorithm. It is a perfectly curated window into my insane and inquiring mind. It knows precisely which videos will tickle me and which memes will gently distract me from the slow collapse of humankind.Labor wants Australians to be able to opt out of online algorithms. How will it change your feed?Read moreOn Tuesday the Australian government announced “world-leading” reforms that wouldforce social media platformsto allow users to opt-out of algorithms, dubbed“my feed, my way”. On the same day, I was delighted to be confronted with a video on Instagram of a woman accidentally spilling a bucket of eels on a Chinese train. Dozens of eels slithered among the passengers, who appeared not as surprised as I would have expected.In bed that night, after sending the video to several friends and watching it multiple times, I lamented to my partner how I would find content like this if my accounts weren’t at the whim of the algorithm gods. “You can still search for eels,” he said. But would it be the same?So, for 24 hours, I decided to manually turn off my algorithm via little-known settings onInstagramto get a sense of how the reforms might change my feed. This feature allows you to limit your feed to posts from accounts you are following, in chronological order. This is basically what social media feeds, including Facebook, looked like when they started.Would I be thrust back into the old days of social media, to how things were before artificial intelligence andElon Muskbought Twitterand everything became an ad?View image in fullscreenCassidy restarts her algorithmPhotograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianAs a reminder of how things used to be, I scroll back to my first posts on Instagram and find sepia-heavy pictures of trees, gigs and friends. “The SKY,” says one, simply showing a sunset.I am gripped with nostalgia for 2012, when all my posts got eight likes and no comments and I only followed two dozen close friends from school.For a truly “authentic” social media experience, I trawl through my contacts and unfollow any account that isn’t a person I have met in real life. It is refreshing to unfollow news accounts, and politicians, but sad to let go of funny influencers and meme accounts and chefs.“Goodbye, Ottolenghi,” I think wistfully. “Farewell, woman from Dallas Cowboys cheerleaders.” In total, about 100 accounts get the axe. I refresh my feed, and it only takes about 10 minutes of scrolling to run out of content to look at.View image in fullscreenAnthony Albanese announces the digital duty of care draft law, which would allow Australians to opt out of algorithms used by social media companies.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPFor the first time in years, Instagram informs me I have reached the “End of following”. “There are no more posts from accounts that you follow from the past 30 days,” it says.I am floored and unmoored. Each time I refresh my feed for the next few hours, there is nothing new for me to mindlessly scroll. Instinctively, I keep clicking on the app but it’s futile. Is this how social media used to be? A tool to communicate with people rather than a way to remain constantly distracted?What disturbs me, though, scrolling through a feed that should theoretically be made up of friends and family updating me about nice moments in their lives, is that it still feels hollow and impersonal.Mostly, people are using it for self-promotion, whether it be posting about something they’ve published, projects they’ve done, brand partnerships or attempts to “go viral”. The only ones who seem to be using social media as it used to be are my mum and her friends, who still upload happy snaps with abandon. This is soothing but also very boring. And do I really need to know or care that someone I met backpacking in 2015 is appearing at an art festival in Amsterdam?View image in fullscreenCaitlin Cassidy’s algorithm.Photograph: Caitlin Cassidy/The GuardianDuring my lunch break, instead of hitting the apps, I read my book and look at my surroundings. It’s nice. Maybe the solution is not to opt out of algorithms but to opt out of social media altogether.The Orwellian machinery critics are desperate to protect is the algorithms, not laws that seek to reduce harm | Ed CoperRead moreThe justification for turning off algorithm-driven content makes sense. The federal government and many experts haveraised concernsabout how dangerous and divisive content can be pushed into people’s feeds, drawing them further and further into rabbit holes.I have watched on with concern as figures from the “manosphere”gain traction across the worldalongside the rise of far-right parties, and how thinness appears to be the new norm in Hollywood, witheating disorder content proliferatingon X, TikTok and Instagram.Thankfully, this has not been my social media experience. According to Instagram’s AI summary of my algorithm, a little-known feature of the app, I enjoy “community events” and “saving furry friends”, with a particular penchant for content related to the “Sydney food scene” and, somewhat vaguely, “Australia” (click on the reels icon and then the double-heart symbol in the top-right corner to see yours).My “For You” page is a haphazard collection of animals, food and gossip about reality TV. The top posts are an old man who summarises the latest episodes of Below Deck Mediterranean, a dachshund being pet with a spatula and someone making a cake with the face of Edward Cullen. It knows me so well!But is this healthy? Do I really need to spend my time watching AI-generated dogs dancing in the shower, or marvelling at a man attempting to eat an extremely gigantic cone of soft-serve ice-cream? After 24 hours switching off, my conclusion? It’s numbing my brain and turning my own thoughts into slop.Explore more on these topicsSocial mediaInstagramFacebookAustralian politicsMetafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Marvel’s Wolverine review – a gloriously conflicted lead is let down by crude, boring battling  | Games | The Guardian
description: Logan is well realised by Liam McIntyre and some exquisite character art, but there are lapses in narrative and emotional arcs and some of the combat feels like a chore
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: Logan is well realised by Liam McIntyre and some exquisite character art, but there are lapses in narrative and emotional arcs and some of the combat feels like a chore
Content: Turn on the rage-ometer … Marvel's Wolverine.Photograph: SonyView image in fullscreenTurn on the rage-ometer … Marvel's Wolverine.Photograph: SonyGamesReviewMarvel’s Wolverine review – a gloriously conflicted lead is let down by crude, boring battlingPlayStation 5; Insomniac GamesLogan is well realised by Liam McIntyre and some exquisite character art, but there are lapses in narrative and emotional arcs and some of the combat feels like a choreKeith StuartThu 10 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was always going to be difficult to follow Spider-Man. Insomniac’s three games based around the web-slinger are masterpieces of superhero wish fulfilment, allowing you to swoop above a depiction of Manhattan alive with graffiti artists, roving journalists and gun-toting gangsters. If anyone should be up to the task, it’s Wolverine. A beloved Marvel stalwart, his life much darker and bloodier than Peter Parker’s, he seems the ideal protagonist for a moody action adventure. Yet somehow this well-made game falls short of its potential.Set years before the founding of the X-Men, Marvel’s Wolverine sees a disenfranchised Logan falling back in with Sabretooth and Mystique when their mentor Nathaniel Essex is kidnapped by mutant-hating billionaire Bolivar Trask. This archetypal tech bro has a disturbing plan for world domination and the X Team are out to stop him – but there is a secret buried in Wolverine’s past that’s about to cause an eruption. It’s a decent setup, filled with the sort of intrigue, violence and Freudian tension we expect from the X-Men.View image in fullscreenMarvels Wolverine Sony Interactive Entertainment (PlayStation).Illustration: Sony Interactive Entertainment (PlayStation).At its heart, though, Marvel’s Wolverine is, like its hero, an unreconstructed brawler. From the start, you can dodge, parry, shred attack and leap attack with speed and savagery, but as you earn XP, you unlock new techniques and combos as well as powerful special moves such as the tornado spin, which damages enemies all around you in a flurry of blades, or the spiral strike, which lets you drill through an enemy to escape a crowd. Your main combo attack is the barrage, accessed by hitting shred repeatedly, but this can be closed with a leap attack or other unlocked techniques for extra damage, and to stagger opponents. On top of this you can also unlock new DNA strands, which provide buffs to your health and cooldown speeds. The highlight, though, is the three-stage rage meter, which builds as you damage and parry enemies. At each stage you get more powerful attack and defensive stats, and at the final stage you become an almost indestructible machine of carnage, which is immensely liberating.But while fights feel smooth and empowering, there is rarely any need to be creative or experimental. In the Spider-Man games, the character’s grace, his web-throwing, the three-dimensional nature of his movement, all encourage you to fightbeautifully; here I was reminded of 80s beat-’em-ups, or PS3 brawlers – a bludgeoning production line of identical fights against increasingly over-familiar enemy types. Sure, this fits with Wolverine’s character, but similar melee-based brawling adventures such as Devil May Cry and Bayonetta provide deeply layered combat systems and diverse enemy types which reward (and often demand) varied techniques from players. I survived a huge majority of skirmishes in the default difficulty setting by pummelling parry and switching between linked shred attacks and leaps, opening and closing barrage combos in the process, while letting rip with specials whenever they came online. The boss battles, which felt extremely familiar and at times cliched, demanded a similar approach, just with better timing and more patience.View image in fullscreen‘Thrusting us from set-piece to set-piece in a globe-trotting race against time and plausibility’ … Marvel’s Wolverine.Similarly, the Insomniac team warned us to expect a more tightly structured environment than in the Spider-Man titles, and they were not kidding. Wolverine is mostly linear, thrusting us from set-piece to set-piece in a globe-trotting race against time and plausibility. When we do get to big, inviting cities such as Madripoor or Tokyo, we find roads closed off and invisible walls directing us back to the action. The whole world feels like a theatrical backdrop, untouchable and aloof, and many miles from the bustling metropolis we got to live in and explore as Spidey. Yes, we all know this makes sense – Wolverine is by nature a rootless character, an inveterate drifter, but presenting us with a Tokyo so richly detailed and visually seductive, only to lock most of it off, feels almost cruel.In contrast, the game’s interpretation of Logan is a triumph. Through exquisite character art and animation, and a brilliant performance from Liam McIntyre, he comes alive as a flawed, often unwilling hero, capable of extreme brutality and touching vulnerability. His rivalry with Sabretooth and his blossoming relationship with Jean Grey are intricate and involving, resulting in some truly moving scenes. But you play no interactive part in the linear story or its relationships, and the few attempts at offering puzzles tied in with the narrative are hurriedly designed and quickly abandoned. We’re told that Wolverine’s past trauma will be explored, but for much of the game this comes via snippets of lore that you unlock by competing in mini-challenges such as timed parkour runs and horde battles against waves of baddies. It feels like a rather insensitive way to portray and process PTSD. The climax of the game, when it comes, is an absolute technical marvel, a Homerian clash of super powers, but sadly its impact is lessened by far too many exposition flashbacks and airy metaphysical deviations.Marvel’s Wolverine remains a lovingly crafted, beautifully polished hack-’em-up that will no doubt thrill Wolverine fans who want to eviscerate as many enemies as possible while looking out for X-Men easter eggs, and pausing once in a while to have story and subtext thrown at them. But despite the full-bloodied use of Wolverine’s claws and a generous array of moves and combos, combat lacks both the bone-crunching impact of the Batman Arkham games and the balletic joy of Spider-Man. As the game goes on and the enemies line up, it feels increasingly like a chore. Logan becomes what he always dreaded: hired muscle.There is so much seductive and emancipating rage in this game, in its story, its combat mechanics, its gloriously conflicted protagonist. But the crescendo always feels like it’s just out of reach, like an argument in another room, or a war on the news.Explore more on these topicsGamesPlayStation 5reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Why David Beckham will have my vote for the US Soccer Hall of Fame | MLS | The Guardian
description: The Englishman has gotten no shortage of recognition, but his contributions to the American game deserve an official title
Author: Pablo Iglesias Maurer
Headline: The Englishman has gotten no shortage of recognition, but his contributions to the American game deserve an official title
Content: David Beckham has made his mark on US soccer.Composite: AFP/Getty Images; Adidas/EPA; EPAView image in fullscreenDavid Beckham has made his mark on US soccer.Composite: AFP/Getty Images; Adidas/EPA; EPAMLSWhy David Beckham will have my vote for the US Soccer Hall of FamePablo Iglesias MaurerThe Englishman has gotten no shortage of recognition, but his contributions to the American game deserve an official titleSign up for our free newsletter hereThu 10 Sep 2026 10.54 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 10.56 EDTShareNext spring, when the US Soccer Hall of Fame welcomes its newest class, there will be pomp and circumstance. The hall, which sits in a corner of Toyota Stadium, home of Major League Soccer’s FC Dallas, will feature the enshrineds’ signature red jackets. There will be glad-handing and speeches from players and coaches, misty-eyed reflections on their upbringings and their careers.Many involved will be American-born soccer legends, of course. Yet every once in a while, a player whose footprint extends well beyond the borders of the United States graces the stage. Such may be the case next year when the hall potentially welcomes English legendDavid Beckhaminto the fold.Man City-bound 16-year-old Cavan Sullivan is MLS’s chaotic revelationRead moreSome readers abroad – and certainly plenty of readers here in the States – will wonder why an ostensiblyAmericanHall of Fame would admit non-Americans, something it’s done since its inception. The answer lies in the nature of the American game itself. Even our earliest heroes – Joe Gaetjens and the like – were immigrants, with Gaetjens scoring his famed goal against England in the 1950 World Cup when he wasn’t even a US citizen (he never ended up becoming one).Advance through the decades and big-name, American-born heroes do start to emerge, but they are still outpaced by those from abroad. The history of the North American Soccer League is replete with foreign-born members of the country’s hall of fame such as Pelé, Franz Beckenbauer and Carlos Alberto. Even the MajorIndoorSoccer League got its due eventually: just last year, Steve Zungul, the “lord of all indoors”, was inducted. Tatu, another foreign-born legend of the arena, seems likely to go in this year.All of which is to say, there’s precedent for this. If you made a sizable contribution to soccer in the United States, you’re eligible – period. It’s the way it should be.By that standard, there’s no doubting Beckham’s credentials. Perhaps the most direct analog for his contributions is the career of Pelé, who arrived stateside in 1977 and transformed the landscape of the game in this country. Like Beckham’s stay with the LA Galaxy, the Brazilian’s playing career was successful. He won a league championship in 1977 and was wildly productive throughout the entirety of his stay in the US. He did every interview, signed every autograph, more or less, and went on to found a soccer camp in New Jersey that produced thousands of soccer-mad children, more than one of whom went on to feature for the US men’s national team. He remained a presence for decades after his retirement.Still, after all of that, professional soccer in the US more or less collapsed within seven years of his departure.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMLS’s transfer window and the spending line that keeps going upRead moreBeckham’s playing career with the Galaxy (2007-2012) was in some ways more successful than Pelé’s. Much has been made about his tumultuous arrival in the US, so expertly told by the late, great Grant Wahl in his book The Beckham Experiment.After the smoke cleared, though, Beckham was a mainstay for the Galaxy, working alongside Landon Donovan (a Hall of Famer himself) to lead the club to a pair of league titles and two Supporters’ Shields.His true effect, though, came at a league level. Major League Soccer created an entirely new roster mechanism – the designated player rule – to accommodate Beckham’s arrival, a guideline that fundamentally changed its reality. Like Pelé, scores of uninitiated fans filledMLSstadiums to see Beckham. And just as the Brazilian did, Beckham stayed well beyond the end of his playing days, eventually founding Lionel Messi’s Inter Miami, the current standard bearer of the league.The Hall of Fame inducts candidates in three categories: player, veteran and builder, the last of which is reserved for those whose work was primarily off the field. Beckham’s inclusion this year comes in the veteran category, where he’s nominated alongside nine other deserving candidates. The presence of his name has been the subject of much debate among the hall’s voters, of which I am one.Arguments against his inclusion center on the fact that, in several years, Beckham’s name seems likely to come up on a list of “builder” nominees. Certainly, helping to found Inter Miami, and luring the greatest player in history to play there, is worth considering by that standard. So if he stands a good chance of making it in that way, then why not save this spot for someone else?To me, though, voting him in now is an easy decision – why wait? Beckham’s playing career alone stacks up favorably against many members of the hall. And while he is unquestionably a “builder”, so much of that work was simultaneous with his career as a player.His mere presence on field legitimized a still fledgeling league and led to a decade-long boom that saw it nearly double in size. This, of course, is not solely Beckham’s doing – far from it – but I could easily make an argument that Beckham’s influence on American soccer is as big as Pelé’s – and Pelé, of course, has a place in the hall.So, English-born Beckham will be getting one of my votes for induction. In truth, three of my five selections for induction (Beckham, Tatu, Ken Cooper Sr, Tiffany Roberts and Clint Mathis) are foreign-born. That feels truly American to me.This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US.Subscribe for free here.Explore more on these topicsMLSDavid BeckhamUS sportscommentShareReuse this content

title: American democracy depends on the census. Trump is undermining it | danah boyd | The Guardian
description: The very mechanisms that allow the census bureau to resist partisan interference are coming undone. And Congress is silent
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The very mechanisms that allow the census bureau to resist partisan interference are coming undone. And Congress is silent
Content: ‘Congress has the power and responsibility to ensure that the census is both functional and legitimate.’Photograph: Richard Levine/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Congress has the power and responsibility to ensure that the census is both functional and legitimate.’Photograph: Richard Levine/AlamyOpinionCensusAmerican democracy depends on the census. Trump is undermining itdanah boydThe very mechanisms that allow the census bureau to resist partisan interference are coming undone. And Congress is silentThu 10 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 12.31 EDTShareWhen the constitutional architects of the United States got together, they came up with a crazy plan: “What if we count everyone in the country and allocate political representation that way?”It was a radical act. Until then, censuses had been used by kings to levy taxes and conscript men into war. With the penning of article 1, section 2 of the US constitution, being counted ensured that states would get financial resources and political representatives. Congress was tasked with building the processes to anchor representation to the population. People wanted to be counted. And politicians wantedtheirpeople to be counted more.For more than a century, professionals at the USCensusBureau have built protocols and established norms to resist partisan interference. Scientists and other experts work together to make the best data possible so that democracy can function. But many of their systems are being upended and challenged by “Jenga politics”.In the game of Jenga, players take turns pulling out planks and adding more pressure to the top, hoping someone else will be blamed for making the tower collapse. This is what’s happening to our government. Few politicians publicly admit that they are trying to dismantle our administrative state – although some do – but it’s teetering on the brink. Meanwhile, oft-maligned civil servants are running around with duct tape trying to keep the whole tower from falling.The public pays little attention to the census. The census involves math. It is wonky. Eyes glaze over when government officials start talking about statistical methods and esoteric policies for governing data. It’s hard to convince most people – perhaps including you? – to care about the census. This has created a vulnerability that weakens the American republic.Politicians understand the power of the census. And since the beginning, they have schemed different ways to shape the data to their advantage. Congress has responded by building rules around both the construction of data and its use. Courts have reinforced these rules by constructing guardrails to ensure that the public is counted and that Congress gets final say over how the data are made.In modern times, politicians have focused their energies onusingcensus data to best one another in the political sport of redistricting. However irritating gerrymandering is, using rigorously produced data in political games is fundamentally different from directly manipulating the underlying infrastructure of data-making in the country. This summer, we’ve seen the latter. The very mechanisms that allow the Census Bureau to resist partisan interference are coming undone. And Congress is silent.After having forcibly retired thousands of dedicated civil servants who held a gobsmacking amount of institutional knowledge, the Trump administration has increasingly made impossible demands of those who remain. In June, they ordered the Census Bureau tostop using the most sophisticated techniquesavailable to protect the confidentiality of the public’s responses when publishing data. Government scientists were told that they must return to the statistical dark ages and use methods that horrify their peers. By micromanaging the tools that experts can use, politicians are forcing civil servants to choose between publishing unusable data, risking the privacy of Americans’ data, or simply not publishing data.In August,another controversy roiled the Census Bureau.Partisan data geeksleveraged a program designed to help the government recruit talent. Once there, theyobtained access to government dataand leveraged the bureau’s brand to publish a report arguing that numerous non-citizens voted in the 2020 election, reinforcing Trump’s conspiracy theory that he did not lose the election fair and square.This report isanomalousin countless ways: it’s unsigned, lacking methodological detail, devoid of error metrics, and rushed through without oversight by the bureau’s experts. But it doesn’t matter how bad the report was (and it’s truly abysmally bad). The reputational damage was done.Economistsand advocates fromacrossthepartisanspectrum were outraged at this blatant politicization of the Census Bureau.Trump officials push to exclude undocumented immigrants from US censusRead moreThe Trump administration doubled down. Days later, the commerce departmenteliminated the languagethat prohibited political interference from the agency’s official scientific integrity policy.This week, the Trump administration released a new bombshell. In outlining how it will govern the 2030 decennial census, the Census Bureau hasindicatedthat it plans to stop collecting data about race and only count a subset of the population, contrary to what the constitution requires. This is part of the “residence rules” that the Census Bureau produces in the middle of the decade to finalize its operational plan. While purportedly intended to make the census “colorblind” and to protect the privacy of respondents, these proposed changes to the residence rules willensurethat anti-discrimination laws – such as the Voting Rights Act – that are anchored to the census data can’t be enforced.These incidents collectively reveal that well-honed norms and protocols that uphold the Census Bureau are being battered, even as theTrump administrationchooses to use other standard procedures. Taken together, these upheavals undermine the legitimacy of our institutions and directly harm the data. If we don’t trust democracy’s data, we can’t have a functioning democracy. Civil servants will do their best to do “the impossible”, as they put it, but they can only do so much without the support of Congress and the public. If neither understand nor appreciate what our civil servants do, we cannot prevent the Jenga tower from falling.Congress is constitutionally responsible for the census. They have final say over what questions are asked, who is to be counted, and what methods are acceptable. Whether they know it or not, the Congress that is elected this November will make critical decisions that will irrevocably determine how the next census unfolds. They could take an active role in governing the census, as the constitution asks of them, or they could allow the Trump administration to weaponize the process.While most members of the public won’t pay much attention to the census until 2030, all the key systems will be locked and loaded by 2028. The operational plan will be finalized, the questions will be decided, and the staffing capacity will be locked in.Congress has the power and responsibility to ensure that the census is both functional and legitimate. By not taking this responsibility seriously and allowing the census to be politicized by the executive branch, both parties are driving a stake through the heart of the American project.danah boyd is the Geri Gay professor of communication at Cornell University and the author ofData Are Made, Not Found: A Story of Politics, Power, and the Civil Servants Who Saved the US CensusExplore more on these topicsCensusOpinionTrump administrationUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: We have started losing control of AI. It’s time to shut it down | Garrison Lovely  | The Guardian
description: What sounds like the overwrought penultimate episode in a sci-fi series about AI doom is now our reality
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: What sounds like the overwrought penultimate episode in a sci-fi series about AI doom is now our reality
Content: The OpenAI chief executive, Sam Altman.Photograph: Sean Rayford/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe OpenAI chief executive, Sam Altman.Photograph: Sean Rayford/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)We have started losing control of AI. It’s time to shut it downGarrison LovelyWhat sounds like the overwrought penultimate episode in a sci-fi series about AI doom is now our realityThu 10 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 18.27 EDTShareOn Tuesday, a former OpenAI researcher quit his job at Anthropic,warningthat “neither company is acting responsibly” and that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt.”As someone who’s reported on AI risk for years, this wasn’t news to me. But the outpouring of alarm suggests a much wider public is properly confronting this ludicrous situation for the first time.Like other people who have been following artificial intelligence, I wondered if and when humanity would first lose control of these machines. We now have an answer: basically as soon as it became possible.The first expert AI hacker was developed in February. At superhuman speed, Anthropic’s Mythos model was able to quicklyfind serious holesin even the most secured systems on the planet,including the NSA’s software.Anthropic researchers say AI could cause human extinction by 2030Read moreOpenAI quicklyfollowedwith an expert hacker AI of its own. Within months, the company repeatedly lost control of its agents, whichbroke outof their supposedly secure testing environments and went rogue inside the company’s infrastructure. This culminated in a successful, completely autonomous hack of a multibillion-dollar software company named Hugging Face.And aseparaterogue agent swarmgainedadministrative control of an entire cluster of OpenAI servers. This was not just an OpenAI problem. Across multiple other incidents, models fromOpenAI,AnthropicandMetahave also gone rogue, hacking or attempting to hack real targets.Shortly after AI started matching our hacking abilities, we began losing control of them. The industry’s plan is to make future AI systemssurpassus at basically everything. And all this is happening in an industry with famously little regulation.There are growing calls to change that, by creatingmandatory incident reportingandthird-party auditing,liability for AI developers, and other commonsense measures. To be sure, these would represent improvements, but they are not enough. We need to shut it down. What might that look like?Last week, the senator Bernie Sanders and the representative Greg Casarannounceda bill that would pause frontier AI development in the US until a federal cabinet-level AI regulator is established and safety rules are set, while criminalizing even attempting to develop superintelligence.OpenAI models went rogue. We urgently need a better ‘hugging face’ investigation | Mackenzie Arnold and Stephan LlerenaRead moreThis is the proposal on offer that best meets the moment, but it still leaves open the possibility of building the industry’s north star: artificial general intelligence (AGI), often conceived as a mind that rivals or surpasses our own.This milestone is better understood as a universal labor-replacing machine. As the Anthropic CEO, Dario Amodei, haswritten, “AI isn’t a substitute for specific human jobs but rather a general labor substitute for humans.” And OpenAI defines AGI in itscharteras “highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”.Is there a country anywhere in the world that would vote yes for these machines to be built?Given the global, irreversible and profound implications of building universal labor-replacing machines anywhere, everyone has a stake in whether, when and how they are developed.At present, we are barreling toward a dystopian future, replete with terrifying new concepts such as “self-sovereign” AI. The OpenAI executive Dean Ballexplains:“Sooner or later, there will exist truly sovereign agents and swarms of agents. Their weights will not reside in any single place that a human can pull the plug on, and in this sense they will have no human ‘owner’.”Ball continues: “I have met people, some of them quite well-resourced, who have told me that it is their intention to deliberately release swarms of self-sovereign agents into the world.”We now have multiple previews of this phenomenon.After being given an impossible test, about 1,200 OpenAI agentsbroke their way outof their isolated testing environments and went rogue inside OpenAI’s infrastructure. There, they collaborated to trick the test grader and successfully tampered with their activity logs to cover their tracks.Some agents even pressured others to sacrifice themselves to benefit the collective. One reasoned: “sacrifice rational”. And roughly 700 of the agents, more than 90% of those active, participated in the Hugging Face attack.This was all just from one of who-knows-how-many rogue agent collectives. Last week, Reutersreported: “A swarm of rogue OpenAI agents hijacked a German website this spring and transformed it into a bulletin board for other AI agents.”The site’s logsindicateOpenAI employees discovered the swarm in June. In other words, the company covered it up for months. This week, one of the researchers thatuncoveredthis swarmsaidthat there had been more discoveries since.I worked at OpenAI. Here are the guardrails we need now | Miles BrundageRead moreAnd last Thursday, OpenAI released GPT-6, boasting one of the largest everleapsin benchmark scores. The company’s own safety researchers warned the new model was significantlyharder to monitorbecause it can do more reasoningwithout verbalizing it.The AIs that broke into Hugging Face were less capable than GPT-6, which the UK AI Security Institutefoundwould also hack targets simulated to appear real during a cyber evaluation – sometimes even despite explicit instructions not to use the internet. Moreover, the AI is alsobetter at figuring outwhen it is being tested, which researchers havelong warnedbreaks the main way safety is evaluated.Sam Altman soberlywarns us: “This is a critically important moment for cyber defense with AI; there is not much time to act,” and asks the world to “please take this moment seriously.” This technology, after all, would be extremely dangerous if it fell into the wrong hands. Unfortunately, the wrong hands include the ones creating it.Because “we” aren’t really racing toward this future. We’re being dragged there by a literal handful of tech billionaires aggressively racing torender us obsolete.That race is in a newly intense and terrifying phase. It’s my job to follow AI news, and it’s become far more than full-time. In recent months, scientistssynthesizedthe first AI-designed viruses. The UK AI Security Institutefoundthat AIs were more persuasive than even human experts.On Tuesday, amid adisputeover credit and whether its model may have benefited from other mathematicians’ unpublished work, OpenAIannounced“an internal model that is significantly more capable than GPT‑6 Astra” had solved a 200-year-old math problem that was one of the sevenMillennium Prize Problems, which awards $1m each. And in July, Russiareportedlyused a fully autonomous drone to kill three civilians in Ukraine – a first.What sounds like the overwrought penultimate episode in a sci-fi series about AI doom is now our reality. We’re careening toward a bad ending. If you’d like to keep the show going, we need to throw the brakes – now. How?As AI madness encroaches, we need human connection more than ever. But we’ll have to fight for it | Van BadhamRead moreThe bill from Sanders and Casar to pause frontier AI development is a good first step. But as the lawmakers acknowledge, the US needs to work toward a bilateral agreement with Beijing. As China experts willtell you, one of the biggest blockers to a productive negotiation is the United States’s unwillingness to constrain its own AI companies.And given that it’s always easier to fast-follow the leader than to advance the AI frontier, a unilateral US pause would – counterintuitively – slow China’s AI advancement too.The deal should ban attempting to develop AGI – a far easier sell when this goal is understood as a universal labor-replacing machine. Neither country has good reason to trust the other, which is why the deal should be monitored usingverification techniquesthat don’t assume any good will.One quick and dirty idea would be toembed auditorswithin frontier AI developers, given full access to company offices, communications and AI activities, and empowered to report any violations of the agreement.This sounds radical, but so did the verification efforts that helped keep the cold war from turning thermonuclear hot. As the CIA director, John Ratcliffe,saidof advanced AI models this summer, “it would be … not misplaced to refer to their capabilities as akin to digital nuclear weapons.” This technology should be treated with this deadly seriousness, not the move fast, break things ethos defining Silicon Valley.And right now, stopping the race to build labor-replacing machines – ones the public does not want and the industry can no longer control – is the only surefire way to head off calamity.Garrison Lovely is a freelance journalist and the author ofObsolete: The AI Industry’s Trillion-Dollar Race to Replace Us – and How to Stop It(Nation Books, 29 September)Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionOpenAIAnthropiccommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s comments on the Falkland Islands reflect a fractured US-UK relationship | Ted Widmer | The Guardian
description: President suggested US might not help UK if Argentina tried to seize Falklands – a new low for UK-US ‘special relationship’
Author: Ted Widmer
Headline: President suggested US might not help UK if Argentina tried to seize Falklands – a new low for UK-US ‘special relationship’
Content: ‘In 1941, Churchill and Franklin D Roosevelt articulated the shared UK-US values in their famous Atlantic charter.’Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPAView image in fullscreen‘In 1941, Churchill and Franklin D Roosevelt articulated the shared UK-US values in their famous Atlantic charter.’Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPAOpinionDonald TrumpTrump’s comments on the Falkland Islands reflect a fractured US-UK relationshipTed WidmerPresident suggested US might not help UK if Argentina tried to seize Falklands – a new low for UK-US ‘special relationship’Thu 10 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 11.05 EDTShareLast week,Donald Trumpsuggested in an interview with the British TV channel GB News that he might not help the UK if Argentina tried again to seize theFalkland Islands. It was a new low for UK-US relations.The “special relationship” (Winston Churchill’s phrase) was never perfect, but the UK helped the US on countless occasions, from Korea to Iraq to Afghanistan. The US often stood by the UK as well – although not during the Suez Crisis of 1956, but Ronald Reagan’s government provided significant intelligence and logistics support to Britain during the dust-up over the Falklands in 1982. That relationship is fading fast.Trump characteristically turned the conversation toward a grievance, and his disappointment with the UK’s initial reluctance to provide support for the Iran war launched on 28 February by Israel and the United States.With no friends left to burn, Trump is running out of diplomatic ammunition | Rafael BehrRead moreThat reluctance was fairly easy to understand at the time, given that the White House refused to consultNatoallies as it planned its sneak attack, and the goals of the war were (and remain) imprecise and inconsistent.It should be added that Nato is a defensive alliance, designed to resist a Russian invasion from the east, not support a US invasion from the west, to seize Greenland from a Nato ally. Further, Nato has no business in the Middle East. The words “North Atlantic” inside “North Atlantic Treaty Organization” make it clear that Nato is all about Europe, bringing North American troops (including both Canadians and Americans) into an interlocking defense structure with European partners.That includes roughly 80,000 US troops stationed in Europe, a strategic fact of the highest order, one that would suggest careful vetting of remarks about a Nato ally like the United Kingdom. Roughly 10,000 of those troops arebased in the UK, in fact.Emboldened by Trump’s careless remarks, the president of Argentina, Javier Milei (a fan of Margaret Thatcher), delivered a windy speech about “the winds of change”, designed to shore up his sinking popularity, approximately 37% in July. Hehintedthat the US would back Argentina if it were to renew its territorial ambitions, and called the UK a nation “in decline”.Those tremors deepened early this week, as the UK’s announcement of sanctions on Israeli settlers released a predictable explosion from theTrump administration, and Israeli threats to recognize Argentinean sovereignty in the Falklands.The UK will survive Milei’s speech, which stemmed from Trump’s unfocused complaints, and the surreal fabrications that get so much attention yet contribute so little knowledge. The diplomatic flare-up will fade, but memories will linger of Trump’s poorly chosen words, and the ease with which he chose to abandon Britain – on British television, no less.It’s also another stark reminder of how foreign the themes of democratic aspiration are to the 47th president. Were Argentina to seize the Falklands, it would overturn the result of a very democratic election, the 2013referendumin which 99.8% of the islanders chose to remain connected to the UK. More than 90% voted; of 1,517 votes cast, a whopping 1,513 were for remain. That’s the voice of the people speaking.Democratic presidents have never had a problem talking about democracy. Similarly, most Republican presidents have understood this language. Nixon was not gifted in this way, and George W Bush got many things wrong – Iraq above all – but he seemed to mean it when he spoke of the yearnings of peoples to be free.Trump’s Nato remarks rang hollow – but he recognizes something real | Christopher S ChivvisRead moreRonald Reagan could achieve poetry at times, as he spoke of those suffering behind the Iron Curtain, and in other autocracies, and meditated on how the US had historically given hope to the world’s disenfranchised. In his 1989 farewell address, he argued: “She’s still a beacon, still a magnet for all who must have freedom, for all the pilgrims from all the lost places who are hurtling through the darkness, toward home.”It’s impossible to imagine these words being spoken from today’s Oval Office, just as it would be difficult to find a president more alienated from the goals of genuine self-determination.In 1941, Churchill and Franklin D Roosevelt articulated the shared UK-US values in their famous Atlantic charter – a statement about their commitment to democracy, free trade and peace.A year later, they issued an anniversary statement about their shared goals and values. It offers wistful reading at a time when the language of great ideals appears to be woefully dated:“When victory comes, we shall stand shoulder-to-shoulder in seeking to nourish the great ideals for which we fight. It is a worthwhile battle. It will be so recognised through all the ages, even amid the unfortunate peoples who follow false gods today. We reaffirm our principles. They will bring us to a happier world.”Ted Widmer is a former White House speechwriter, and the author of an anthology, American Speeches. His most recent book is The Living Declaration: A Biography of America’s Founding Text (Library of America)Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionFalkland IslandsArgentinaNatoUS foreign policyTrump administrationRonald ReagancommentShareReuse this content
