title: Trump’s repeated threats to ‘wipe out’ Iran are normalizing mass violence | Mohamad Bazzi | The Guardian
description: The president’s latest warning barely registered, written off as typical behavior. But the threats have real-world consequences
Author: Mohamad Bazzi
Headline: The president’s latest warning barely registered, written off as typical behavior. But the threats have real-world consequences
Content: ‘Most western powers and leaders have become numb to the loss and suffering of Palestinians, Iranians, Lebanese and others in the Middle East.’Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPAView image in fullscreen‘Most western powers and leaders have become numb to the loss and suffering of Palestinians, Iranians, Lebanese and others in the Middle East.’Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPAOpinionUS-Israel war on IranTrump’s repeated threats to ‘wipe out’ Iran are normalizing mass violenceMohamad BazziThe president’s latest warning barely registered, written off as typical behavior. But the threats have real-world consequencesThu 10 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 12.51 EDTShareAs the US and Iran fought around the strait of Hormuz last week, Donald Trump issued one of his typical threats. In an interview with a Fox News correspondent,Trump said Iranwould be “totally wiped out as a country” if it retaliated for the latest wave of US airstrikes.That threat by the US president to wipe out another country generatedfew headlines, even during a relatively slow news week by Trump administration standards.Trump has delivered this kind of warning so frequently over the past six months of his war against Iran that it hardly registers any more. But it’s important not to normalize Trump’s threats, which are usually accompanied by promises todevastate Iran’s infrastructure– vowing to destroy bridges and power plants. Those kinds of attacks would constitutewar crimesunder international law.With no friends left to burn, Trump is running out of diplomatic ammunition | Rafael BehrRead moreThe president’s repeated vows to obliterate Iran are usually written off by other western leaders and the news media as typical of Trump’s bravado and unpredictability, but they have real-world consequences. By treating Trump’s rhetoric as normal, US and western societies are becoming more desensitized to the idea of large-scale violence – including the targeting of civilians and civilian infrastructure – as a legitimate kind of warfare. And of course, Israel’s war on Gaza has inured many in the western world towholesale atrocities, including intense aerial bombardment that leads to massive civilian casualties and displacement.Trump set the stage for apocalyptic threats against Iran weeks into the war, when it became clear that the US would not achieve the quick military victory he was hoping for. On 7 April, as he vacillated between agreeing to a ceasefire and ordering even more intense bombing, Trump ominously declared in asocial media post: “A whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again.”In the days leading up to that statement, Trump had issued a series of warnings that the US would destroy Iran’s infrastructure unless it reopened the strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s oil and liquid gas supplies flowed before Tehran effectively shut the waterway at the start of the war. On 1 April, in a primetime address from the White House,Trump threatenedto bomb Iran “back to the Stone Ages, where they belong”. On 6 April,Trump claimedthat Iran “could be taken out in one night” and said the US had a plan to destroy every bridge and power plant in the country, leaving that infrastructure “burning, exploding, and never to be used again” – a statement announcing his intention to commit war crimes.Trump set a deadline of 8pm ET on 7 April for Iranian leaders to comply with his demands. As that deadline neared, Trump shared his now infamous post on his Truth Social network that promised to erase Iran’s civilization. That threat to carry out large-scale war crimes against a country of 90 million people prompted outrage around the world,with condemnationfrom the UN secretary general and the pope. Some human rightsexperts arguedthat Trump’s statement may constitute a threat to commit genocide, which is defined by the UN’sGenocide Conventionas acts committed “with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group”.Shortly before Trump’s deadline expired, Pakistan’s prime minister announced that the US andIranhad agreed to an immediate ceasefire. But Trump never apologized or retracted his statement. And why should he feel any pressure to do so, despite the momentary outrage his words caused? In today’s world, there are no consequences for threatening – or carrying out – a genocide.Trump’s threat to obliterate Iran is partly a manifestation of a new international order that emerged over the past three years, as the USsupplied billions of dollarsin weapons and protected Israel as it carried out a genocidal war in Gaza. In his second term, Trump has behaved more erratically and like an autocrat drunk with power. But he has also taken advantage of a nascent global order, in which western leaders destroyed decades of international norms and the facade of rule of law – all to enable Israel to continue its bloodshed in Gaza, and more recently,in Lebanon.As they did with Gaza, most western powers and leaders have become numb to the loss and suffering of Palestinians, Iranians, Lebanese and others in the Middle East. And as long as this numbness and impunity continue, it will become normal for the US president to threaten wholesale destruction of societies and civilizations, as Trump has done in Iran.Let’s call Trump’s approach to Iran what it is: kindergarten diplomacy | Moustafa BayoumiRead moreWhile Trump can be dismissed as an unpredictable, or even irrational, world leader who scorns global institutions and norms – the epitome ofthe “madman theory”of US foreign policy – his predecessor Joe Biden helped paved the way for the current age of impunity we’re living in. Biden, along with other western leaders who provided unwavering support to Israel after the Hamas attacks in October 2023, defied and weakened international law in order to shield Israel long before Trump returned to office in early 2025.For 15 months, the Biden administrationundermined global institutions– including the international court of justice (ICJ) and the international criminal court (ICC) – to help Israel and its prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, avoid facing consequences for their war crimes in Gaza. Biden and other western leaders rendered international law meaningless after their inaction and obstruction in Gaza – and it was only a matter of time before Trump abandoned any pretense of lofty rhetoric about human rights and rule of law. Trump prefers to flaunt American military power and his ability to inflict massive destruction on US enemies.The normalization of Israel’s atrocities in Gaza has rippled across the world, including the expanding regional war that engulfed Iran and the US. It has also diluted international outrage at Trump’s repeated threats to destroy Iran, even within a period of months. While Trump’s apocalyptic warning in April that “a whole civilization will die” prompted global condemnation, his subsequent rhetoric has barely registered.In July,Trump claimedthat the US would bomb one Iranian bridge or power plant in retaliation for each time Iran fired at a ship in the strait of Hormuz. That kind of retaliation against civilian targets would be a war crime, but Trump has made such threats seem mundane and a normal part of warfare. At the very least, Americans and the rest of the world should call him out on it.Mohamad Bazzi is a Guardian US columnist. He is also director of the Center for Near Eastern Studies and a journalism professor at New York UniversityExplore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranOpinionDonald TrumpIranMiddle East and north AfricaUS foreign policyBiden administrationIsraelcommentShareReuse this content

title: Why all our children deserve the sanctuary of a school library no matter where in Australia they live | Nova Weetman | The Guardian
description: There is not even a legal requirement for a school to have a library, so their existence relies solely on the individual education system
Author: Nova Weetman
Headline: There is not even a legal requirement for a school to have a library, so their existence relies solely on the individual education system
Content: The library was once the centre of every school but it’s not a given any more, author Nova Weetman writes.Photograph: Andersen Ross Photography Inc/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe library was once the centre of every school but it’s not a given any more, author Nova Weetman writes.Photograph: Andersen Ross Photography Inc/Getty ImagesOpinionAustralian educationWhy all our children deserve the sanctuary of a school library no matter where in Australia they liveNova WeetmanThere is not even a legal requirement for a school to have a library, so their existence relies solely on the individual education systemThu 10 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 20.25 EDTShareAt a Catholic primary school in Melbourne’s outer-north, I began a visit by showing the students a photograph of the jar of Nova dill pickles my mum named me after. Soon we were talking about the sorts of characters I create in my books, leading them into creating their own. They were full of energy, ideas and excitement. After we finished, one of the teachers proudly showed me around the library, sunlight streaming through the window, lighting the walls of children’s artwork and book displays, and I understood then why these students were so alive to the wonder of story.Like many Australian children’s authors and illustrators, I visit a broad range of schools each year to give talks and run workshops, and it is immediately apparent when I am in a school that values the library and promotes reading culture. At these schools, the teacher-librarians will often know my books better than I do (even dressing up as my characters for a Book Week parade), and the students will ask tough narrative questions that surprise me.They will create their own stories that are complex and inventive, begging to share and building on each other’s ideas with openness and generosity. They will be encouraged by a trained teacher-librarian to find the books that work for them. Even the most reluctant student will be reading, because they will have mandated library sessions each week, taught by a professional, who can introduce them to a wide range of stories that will hopefully capture their heart.Australia’s classroom disruption among worst in world, prompting calls for ‘digital detox’Read moreThis is not just anecdotal. A2019 reviewof school libraries in South Australia found that students at schools with qualified teacher-librarians could have up to two months’ learning gain compared with students at schools without.The library was once the centre of every school, but it’s not a given any more. There is no legal requirement for a school to have a library, so their existence relies on the individual system (Catholic, public or independent) and then on the leadership to allocate funds. Qualified teacher-librarian positions have been slowly disappearing for years.A school library is a special place. It does not announce itself as a sanctuary. It just is.Growing up, my country primary school didn’t have a library. The closest public library was a drive away, so I had to rely on the visit from the weekly mobile van to borrow Sweet Dreams books (a highlight of my week). High school meant a resourced library with a trained librarian and a library card of my very own. This came with a frustrating borrowing limit, which I got around by dating a boy who would lend me his card, because I knew five books wouldn’t see me through the holidays. My high school library was where I escaped to when friendship dramas were playing out, or when I just wanted to read. It was my safe space. And I wonder sometimes if it contributed to me becoming an author. It most definitely helped make me a reader.Visiting schools means I see first-hand the alarming disparity in our education system between those that can afford week-long literature festivals versus those than can only afford a one-hour session once a year. For many state schools, the cost of a full-time librarian is prohibitive.Given that one-third of Australian studentsfail to meet literacy benchmarks, according to the latest Naplan results (worse for students from Indigenous backgrounds, lower-socioeconomic backgrounds and those from the bush), you would imagine that governments would make it a priority to adequately fund our public schools and school libraries.Teaching about respectful relationships in schools? How dare women! | First Dog on the MoonRead moreAt independent and Catholic schools, the leadership has some power to decide where to allocate funds, and all too often libraries are not the recipients. CatholicSchoolsMaitland-Newcastle has announced plans to cut teacher-librarian positions across 58 schools in the region. Teacher-librarians would be redeployed and the libraries would be run by assistants or student support officers. And while these roles are also vital, they are needed in addition to qualified teacher-librarians, not instead of them.This announcement has been met with broad industry criticism. The Australian author Kate Temple launched a petition that has received more than 12,000 signatures in a matter of days and has the backing of the Australian Coalition for SchoolLibraries, Australia Reads and the Australian Library and Information Association. The Australian School Library Association is also urging the Catholic Schools Maitland-Newcastle to reconsider.Imagine the community outrage if PE teachers were being quietly redeployed. Would we rope in unqualified people to run art classes, music lessons and language sessions to save some money on departments we no longer deem necessary? Why do we not value that which keeps us human, and mandate the employment of qualified teacher-librarians in every school, with a decent budget to buy diverse books that speak to all students?It is often argued that it is difficult to measure the value of a school library but our rising rates of illiteracy, the growing threat of AI to creativity, and the very role that story holds in teaching empathy, understanding and critical thinking, is all the proof we need.Nova Weetman is an award-winning author of books for children and young adultsExplore more on these topicsAustralian educationOpinionLibrariesSchoolsChildrencommentShareReuse this content

title: My plea to MPs: this is the final chance to save the assisted dying bill. Make your mark on history | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: Any MP not voting for it on Friday will condemn thousands of us to die in agony. The public is hugely in favour too, so do the right thing, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: Any MP not voting for it on Friday will condemn thousands of us to die in agony. The public is hugely in favour too, so do the right thing, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: Supporters of assisted dying demonstrate in London ahead of the terminally ill adults (end of life) bill final session in the House of Lords, on 22 April 2026.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSupporters of assisted dying demonstrate in London ahead of the terminally ill adults (end of life) bill final session in the House of Lords, on 22 April 2026.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesOpinionAssisted dyingMy plea to MPs: this is the final chance to save the assisted dying bill. Make your mark on historyPolly ToynbeeAny MP not voting for it on Friday will condemn thousands of us to die in agony. The public is hugely in favour too, so do the right thingThu 10 Sep 2026 10.20 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareOnce in a while, footsoldiers of theHouse of Commons, you are able to make history by leaving your own indelible footprints on the social fabric. Eras with a Labour majority always leave a legacy of progressive freedoms – whether on abortion, capital punishment, divorce, gay rights, racial discrimination, gender equality or, last time, civil partnerships. But tomorrow is your final chance to bequeath one of the last freedoms over our bodies: the freedom of the dying to choose when to depart them.The terminally ill adults (end of life) bill, which goes fora second reading votein the Commons tomorrow, gives anyone who is dying the right to request and be provided assistance with ending their lives. If it fails to pass, that’s the end of it for the rest of this parliament: future parliaments may be less progressive. So please, MPs: turn up andvote on Lauren Edwards’s bill, to ensure this Labour era leaves its own great social-reforming milestone.Understand the horror: on the day you read this, as on every other, an average of 17 people will die in unspeakable pain, disgust and terror that nothing can relieve. “Some will retch at the stench of their own body rotting. Some will vomit their own faeces. Some will suffocate, slowly, inexorably, over several days.” This is recorded inThe Inescapable Truth, a report byDignity in Dying, in which palliative care staff reveal what is usually kept hidden from us: the shocking last months for the unluckiest, which any of us might be forced to endure, or watch a loved one suffer through.I am sending the assisted dying bill back to the Lords – and this time, peers must do the right thing | Lauren EdwardsRead moreThat amounts to thousands of us a year, as reported by the Office of Health Economics, which counted thecases of unrelieved paineven among dying people who had the best palliative care. Opponents of assisted dyingsay that we shouldfocus on improving access to and provision of palliative care, but even then many will die in agony. Even the best care will not always prevent suffering. And why condemn those who are suffering today to wait for palliative care improvements that they may not see in their lifetimes, when we could help end their pain now?Any MP not voting for the bill tomorrow must be honest: their personal decision will force thousands of people a year to exit life through a torture chamber. None of us can know if we will be among them when our turn comes, but all of us will live with the fear of it.Over thedecades thatI have been writing about the right to die,I have encountered all kinds of tragic cases. I think of the man in severe pain who drove his electric wheelchair through fields towards a river to throw himself in: his battery ran out and he was found weeping in despair. Or the suffering, bedridden grandmother I interviewed who was carefully planning her own rational death. “An end, no more muddles and puddles,” she said, pluckily, wanting to relieve not just her misery but her family’s from the distress of watching her die. Her plan to take her life didn’t pan out as she imagined – her chosen method was barbaric and took a long time to work, leaving her family miserable, furious and divided between themselves about blame.Dignity in Dying’s new report,Out of the Shadows, records the hidden harm of people trying to kill themselves for lack of a medically assisted death. Thedread journey to Dignitasin Switzerland,costing about £15,000, is a grim, friendless ending for hundreds that has to be undertaken too soon, before the dying person is too sick to travel.Most of all, I think of my mother dying wretchedly of liver cancer, begging her GP to kill her. “Where’s Dr Shipman when you want him?” she asked him. Or ofmy friend Jill Tweedie, the much-missed Guardian writer, suffering from motor neurone disease, who died in 1993. After her diagnosis, she asked me to make sure that she could always die whenever she chose. The prospect of death was only bearable if she could at least control her ending: she was afraid of leaving it too late and beingforced to endure the unendurable. When her breathing became wheezy, the sign of what she feared most – slow asphyxiation – and she was left briefly alone, she checked herself into a clinic without telling anyone and died that night. There was no doubt in our minds that she took her own life, not waiting for the final ravages. But fear of the law forced her to die all alone and secretly.MPs: turn up tomorrow and use your vote. Refuse to allow ahandful of unelected Lordsto block a bill passed by the Commons and supported for years by75% of the public. MPs note: there ismajority supportfor assisted dying in every constituency in England and Wales. Kim Leadbeater’s billwon with a majority of Labour MPs, but Tory, Liberal Democrat, Reform and Green MPsvoted for it, too.The democratic outrage at the lords’ behaviour should be reason enough for all MPs in favour to turn up tomorrow to defy the peerage. Just ninelords filibusteredby laying downmore than 1,200 amendments, most pointlessly near-identical, to prevent a vote, knowing that a majority in the Lords would have backed it, too, given the chance. For 16 days, these mainly religious objectors wereallowed to block the will of both houses, backed byconservative Christian pressure groups. That disgraceful filibuster aloneshould be the trigger for Lords reform.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMeanwhile, as the debate goes on, Humanists UK records that since the bill first arrived in the Lords, during its long obstruction,43 UK citizenshave died at Dignitas. Let no one have to make that desperate journey ever again, nor suffer what we don’t inflict on our dying pets.Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistIn the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsAssisted dyingOpinionDeath and dyingHouse of CommonsHouse of LordsHealthcommentShareReuse this content

title: The UK’s sanctions on Israeli settlements are a great victory – but must be only the beginning | Em Hilton | The Guardian
description: The change in policy is a direct result of sustained pressure from activists and organisers across the Palestine movement. But what comes next, asks Jewish writer and organiser Em Hilton
Author: Em Hilton
Headline: The change in policy is a direct result of sustained pressure from activists and organisers across the Palestine movement. But what comes next, asks Jewish writer and organiser Em Hilton
Content: A view of the Israeli settlement of Ma’ale Adumim in the occupied West Bank, 8 September 2026.Photograph: Ohad Zwigenberg/APView image in fullscreenA view of the Israeli settlement of Ma’ale Adumim in the occupied West Bank, 8 September 2026.Photograph: Ohad Zwigenberg/APOpinionWest BankThe UK’s sanctions on Israeli settlements are a great victory – but must be only the beginningEm HiltonThe change in policy is a direct result of sustained pressure from activists and organisers across the Palestine movement. But what comes next?Thu 10 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 08.34 EDTShareThe announcement on Tuesday by the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, of animport ban on goodsfrom illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories, as well as a comprehensive sanctions regime, is a hard-won victory for the Palestine solidarity movement.This is not simply a change of heart by the government: it is a direct result of sustained pressure from activists and organisers across the Palestine movement, who have consistently held the government’s feet to the fire over itscomplicity in the atrocitiesbeing committed in Gaza and the West Bank. Miliband’s announcement shows us what organised and persistent campaigning can achieve, and inspires confidence that movements can force political change.Over the past three years, Palestine has become a political and electoral challenge for the Labour party, as well as a fundamental issue of public conscience. This move signals a political reset in the UK government’s foreign policy approach to Israel. But as the UN special rapporteur Francesca Albanese has said, a ban on goods from settlements must be part of a“true paradigm shift”; the government can, and must, go further.There has already been sustained backlash at the move, with the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee,accusing Miliband of “Jew hate”on the Today programme. As a Jewish campaigner, let me be clear: holding Israel to account for its human rights violations in the West Bank is not antisemitic. To conflate the actions of violent settlers and the Israeli government with Jewish people everywhere makes us accountable for the actions of those who do not represent us.There is also warranted scepticism about the Labour government’s commitment to holding Israel accountable. But an “all or nothing” approach would be a mistake, when there is so much that can be built on here. We can certainly retain our anger at the government’s complicity. No sanction can offset the foreign policy decisions made by the former prime minister Keir Starmer and former foreign secretary David Lammy, therepression of domestic pro-Palestine advocacy, or the sheer loss of life. But we must balance this with cautious optimism that the political tide is turning.Political victories are mobilising – they fuel the belief that collective action can work. So now is the time to push at the open door. But what comes next? How do we ensure that accountability for Israel’s oppression of Palestinians is not limited to the settlements, but builds momentum for further meaningful action in support of Palestinian human rights?First, we should demand that these trade sanctions are enforced and expanded. Eleven nations, includingCanada and France, have joined the UK in these measures; we must call for further coordination and alignment with other western governments.The necessary next step is a full arms embargo and an end to cooperation with Israeli security forces – to truly have teeth, these sanctions must not take with one hand and then give with another. Miliband has said that “we’ve already suspended over 30 arms licences used by the IDF in Gaza. That suspension remains fully in place”, and that the government will “now also refuse all licence applications for arms and other exports that materially contribute to the occupation”. Butcomponents of F-35 jetscontinue to be exported to Israel and used for operations in Gaza, as are surveillance technologies such as drones and radar made in the UK byElbit Systems. This is a total dereliction of duty by the British government.Miliband’s announcements were a necessary reminder that a just political future is possible and, within it, a reckoning with past crimes. As a campaigner, I have borne witness to Israel’s most egregious human rights violations: I have documented Israeli settlers committing pogroms against the community of Al-Mufaqara, sat in Palestinian villages threatened with home demolitions and army raids, and witnessed the ongoing daily misery of Israel’s apartheid policies. This has all strengthened my motivation to see the end of the Israeli occupation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis announcement is the beginning, not the end, of the road. It is a hopeful indication of what happens when collective power is translated into political change. We must sit with the idea that Palestinians will see some justice and reprieve from relentless destruction and displacement. I hope I’m not wrong.Em Hilton is a Jewish writer and organiser. She is the co-founder of Na’amod: UK Jews Against Israeli Occupation, and the policy director at Diaspora AllianceExplore more on these topicsWest BankOpinionIsraelMiddle East and north AfricaPalestineGazaForeign policyEd MilibandcommentShareReuse this content

title: Australia has recognised the state of Palestine. Now we must act to protect what settler terrorism is tearing to shreds | Ed Husic | The Guardian
description: Many Australians will question why our government won’t act when it has a chance to do so in concert with many like-minded nations
Author: Ed Husic
Headline: Many Australians will question why our government won’t act when it has a chance to do so in concert with many like-minded nations
Content: ‘We should recognise the expectations of so many Australians, who want to see action taken to see the end of suffering for innocent Palestinians,’ Labor MP Ed Husic says.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPView image in fullscreen‘We should recognise the expectations of so many Australians, who want to see action taken to see the end of suffering for innocent Palestinians,’ Labor MP Ed Husic says.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPOpinionLabor partyAustralia has recognised the state of Palestine. Now we must act to protect what settler terrorism is tearing to shredsEd HusicMany Australians will question why our government won’t act when it has a chance to do so in concert with many like-minded nationsGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastThu 10 Sep 2026 04.35 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 10.36 EDTShareRoughly 5,900 Palestinians have been completely or partially displaced by settler violence since January 2023, along with 32,000 Palestinians forcibly removed from their homes in West Bank refugee camps last year.The scale of this prompted Major General Eyal Ben-Reuven, someone who spent his life fighting forIsrael, and who recently visited the occupied West Bank, to remark: “This, what the settlers are doing here, is the real threat to Israel. This is more concerning to me than Iran, Gaza or Lebanon.”The former Israeli minister of health and retired brigadier general Ephraim Sneh said: “This is ethnic cleansing, to put it simply.” Retired air force general Asaf Agmon declared: “Once a society behaves this way – that society is doomed.”Labor friends of Palestine criticise Australia’s decision not to join sanctions on Israeli settlements in West BankRead moreOne of our most significant allies believes what’s happening in the West Bank is wrong.The UK Labour government, led by new prime minister Andy Burnham, decided enough was enough. They took action,targeting illegal settlements and settlement expansionthrough banning imports.Oddly, even before the UK formally announced their moves, our own government declared we wouldn’t embrace the same measures.I’d be misleading the parliament if I was to say I wasn’t disappointed.To justify this decision, it was said: “We have concerns about the implementation of a blanket ban and unintended consequences for Australian businesses, for Palestinians and for Israelis.”Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereBy way of contrast, it’s worth noting Australia has imposed 1,800 sanctions and strict tariffs on Russia over its illegal invasion of Ukraine, which has seen the total value of Australia’s imports from Russia drop by around 99%.And it would sound quite odd for us to say we wouldn’t impose sanctions on Russia because of the impact on Australian businesses or Ukrainians or Russians.We took action knowing it would have an impact, precisely because we wanted it to lead to change.Additionally we’ve pointed out regularly that we – as an individual nation – couldn’t possibly act on our own regarding what’s happening in the West Bank orGaza.Yet many Australians would then question why we wouldn’t act when we had a chance to do so in concert with many like-minded nations.But let me come back to the issue of impacts. Let’s look at this another way.It was former prime minister Bob Hawke who dedicated so much of himself, in such a principled and unyielding way, to ending apartheid in South Africa.As a prime minister he pushed on the world stage for comprehensive financial sanctions against South Africa, measures that were so tough, the former foreign minister Gareth Evans said they were “profoundly practically important in their economic, and ultimately, endgame political impact.”Now, imagine telling Bob Hawke not to impose bans or measures on South Africa because it would affect Australian businesses or the very South Africans resisting apartheid?Bob Hawke championed a cause that forms an important part of Labor history.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLikewise prime minister Anthony Albanese has led a government that can justifiably be proud to be part of history it has written: the first ever Australian government to recognise the state ofPalestine.But having stated the ambition, we must act to protect it.Because settler terrorism is tearing to shreds our ambition to see a state of Palestine – and we cannot sticky tape that back together with yet another statement.It’s why I have urged regularly – before and after our ALP national conference – the need for concrete action.Because the Netanyahu government will simply ride out the flurry of statements that our country or other nations issue.And we should recognise the expectations of so many Australians, who want to see action taken to see the end of suffering for innocent Palestinians.Among those Australians are many members of our own party, who joined driven by a sense of purpose, a sense of social justice. Who believe that that commitment to social justice simply does not end at our own borders.In fact I’m reminded of the words of Ben Chifley in 1949: “We have a great objective – the light on the hill – which we aim to reach by working the betterment of mankind not only here but anywhere we may give a helping hand.”I’ll end on this point.Nearly a dozen other nations agreed to join the UK in its stand this week.The only government to enthusiastically support our government’s decision not to join the UK and other nations to take a stand on settler terrorism in West Bank? The Netanyahu government.Ed Husic is the federal Labor MP for Chifley in western Sydney. title: Nine years after Daphne Caruana Galizia’s murder, Europe must finally address Malta’s culture of impunity | Pieter Omtzigt and Emanuel Delia | The Guardian
description: Much of the corruption exposed by this brave woman remains unpunished. Brussels must carry on her work and demand reform, say Pieter Omtzigt of the Council of Europe and campaigner Emanuel Delia
Author: Emanuel Delia
Headline: Much of the corruption exposed by this brave woman remains unpunished. Brussels must carry on her work and demand reform, say Pieter Omtzigt of the Council of Europe and campaigner Emanuel Delia
Content: Protest called by Daphne Caruana Galizia's family and civic movements outside the office of the prime minister in Valletta, Malta, 29 November 2019.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenProtest called by Daphne Caruana Galizia's family and civic movements outside the office of the prime minister in Valletta, Malta, 29 November 2019.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionDaphne Caruana GaliziaNine years after Daphne Caruana Galizia’s murder, Europe must finally address Malta’s culture of impunityPieter OmtzigtandEmanuel DeliaMuch of the corruption exposed by this brave woman remains unpunished. Brussels must carry on her work and demand reformThu 10 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 04.53 EDTShareNine years ago, Daphne Caruana Galizia, Malta’s foremost investigative journalist, wasassassinated by a car bomboutside her home. The men who carried out the killing have been convicted or admitted their involvement. Nobody has been convicted of commissioning her murder.Last week, a jury acquitted Yorgen Fenech, one of Malta’s most prominent businessmen, of complicity in the assassination and criminal association.We have followed this case from different places: one of us from Malta, as a journalist and civil society activist campaigning for accountability after Daphne’s assassination; the other served as the Council of Europe’s rapporteur scrutinising the investigation and Malta’s failures of the rule of law.We were shocked by the verdict, but we respect it.The jurors decided, by eight votes to one, that Fenech’s guilt had not been proved beyond reasonable doubt. We are not asking for their verdict to be disregarded or reversed by political pressure.But the verdict does not erase what the trial exposed.Fenech admitted that he knew of the murder plan before Daphne was killed and that, while the plan was still live, hegave €50,000 to Melvin Theuma, the middleman who recruited the killers. Fenech said the money was intended to reimburse Theuma for money already paid and to persuade him to stop the assassination. He also admitted hepassed confidential information about the police investigationto Theuma and gave him further sums of money. He told the court he was blackmailed by Theuma.But Fenech denied commissioning or financing the murder. His explanation was that he had been acting out of misplaced loyalty to Keith Schembri, then chief of staff to Malta’s prime minister and one of his closest friends.The picture is appalling. A businessman at the heart of Malta’s economic establishment, the prime minister’s closest aide and the man organising the murder of the country’s most prominent investigative journalist were moving within the same small circle.Daphne had spent the last years of her life investigating precisely this proximity between political power, private wealth and people willing to operate outside the law.The Maltese government itself commissioned an independent public inquiry into her assassination. It concluded in 2021 that the state had created a culture of impunity and an atmosphere in which her murder became possible. Five years later, most of its recommendations remain unimplemented. Nor has there been anything approaching adequate accountability for the corruption Daphne was investigating.There are uncomfortable precedents. In Russia, people were convicted for their roles in the murders of journalist Anna Politkovskaya and opposition politician Boris Nemtsov. But the European court of human rights found that the authorities had failed adequately to identify and pursue those who actually commissioned the killings.Malta is not Russia, but it is the case that convicting the people who carried out a murder cannot be the end of the state’s responsibility if whoever commissioned the crime remains unidentified and unpunished. This should concern Brussels as much as Valletta.View image in fullscreenYorgen Fenech after being found not quilty of the murder of Daphne Caruana Galizia, 2 September 2026.Photograph: Matthew Mirabelli/AFP/Getty ImagesMalta’s failures do not stop at its coastline. A licence to conduct business in Malta, with limited government supervision, is effectively a licence to conduct business across theEuropean Union. Weak enforcement in one member state creates opportunities throughout the union.This is why impunity in Malta is not merely a Maltese problem.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOn Wednesday, the parliamentary assembly of the Council of Europe (Pace) returned formally to Daphne’s case. Its committee on legal affairs and human rights heard evidence from Daphne’s son Matthew Caruana Galizia and her sister Corinne Vella. Shami Chakrabarti, the committee’s rapporteur, is preparing a new report, entitled Justice delayed: the unfinished implementation of theDaphne Caruana Galiziacase. Her mandate includes examining the implementation of the public inquiry’s recommendations and Malta’s compliance with Council of Europe standards on the rule of law and press freedom.The timing could hardly be more important. Even Pace’s own monitoring committee, while recognising reforms undertaken since 2019, concluded that they addressed only part of the deficiencies and that comprehensive reform of Malta’s democratic institutions and system of checks and balances remained necessary.Malta’s prime minister, Robert Abela, should meet Chakrabarti at the earliest opportunity and give her work the Maltese government’s full cooperation. But the Council of Europe should go further.Pace has a monitoring committee specifically charged with examining whether member states are meeting their obligations to democracy, human rights and the rule of law. Malta has already been examined by that committee, which raised concerns about corruption, checks and balances, parliamentary oversight and the continuing culture of impunity. The events of the past week strengthen the case for renewed, comprehensive scrutiny of the state of the rule of law in Malta.Sabotage, leaks and political ties: the story of the Daphne Caruana Galizia murder trialRead moreEurope owes something to Daphne and to her family, who have spent nearly nine years fighting for truths the state should have established without requiring their persistence. But there is also a matter of European self-interest. The EU and the Council of Europe cannot afford pockets within their borders where serious corruption goes unpunished and political and economic power can frustrate accountability.The jury has decided that the prosecution did not prove Yorgen Fenech criminally responsible for Daphne Caruana Galizia’s murder. That judgment must be respected. It cannot become an answer to everything else.Nearly nine years after Daphne was assassinated, nobody has been convicted of ordering her murder. Much of the corruption she exposed remains unpunished. Most of the reforms recommended by the public inquiry remain undone. It is high time for Europe to start paying attention again.Pieter Omtzigt is a former Dutch MP who served as the Council of Europe parliamentary assembly’s rapporteur on the assassination of Daphne Caruana Galizia and the rule of law in Malta. Emanuel Delia is a Maltese journalist and co-founder of Repubblika, a civil society organisation campaigning for rule of law and accountability in MaltaDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Ridiculed by the press – and now King Charles is joining in. Sorry, Harry, but what did you expect?  | Emma Brockes | The Guardian
description: The Sussexes must have hoped for a warm welcome. Then they read the king’s delicately savage letter about ‘private citizens’, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Author: Emma Brockes
Headline: The Sussexes must have hoped for a warm welcome. Then they read the king’s delicately savage letter about ‘private citizens’, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Content: The duke and duchess were said to be ‘surprised’ by the king’s letter.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAView image in fullscreenThe duke and duchess were said to be ‘surprised’ by the king’s letter.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAOpinionPrince HarryRidiculed by the press – and now King Charles is joining in. Sorry, Harry, but what did you expect?Emma BrockesThe Sussexes must have hoped for a warm welcome. Then they read the king’s delicately savage letter about ‘private citizens’Thu 10 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 03.27 EDTShareAs welcome-back-to-Britain gestures go, the lord chamberlain’sletter, sent on behalf of King Charles on Monday to remind Harry, Meghan and everyone watching that they’re still “private citizens”, was so perfect as to restore me to monarchism. After six years in the wilderness, what greater comfort for Prince Harry than to find himself, once again, in the familiar waters of this country’s passive aggression, being attacked by his father via the merciless phrase “fully respected”, and provoking from the prince a coded up-yours in the form of his publicly stated “surprise”.Well, it’s up there with better cheese, bread and the NHS, isn’t it?! Even the most Eurocentric American can’t match us for this kind of subtextual bare-knuckle fight. Before we get into what else the returnees may be enjoying this month, let’s fully excavate the letter’s encrypted hostility. First, the king’s repeated use of the words “personal” and “private” – as in “the charitable work of the Duke and Duchess is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity” – is so intense, so heavy handed, as to go beyond merely calling his younger son a civilian and come perilously close to the ultimate insult, “middle class”.Second, this: “in short, their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests”. As we know, opening a sentence with “in short” is an absolute middle finger of a move, up there for officiousness with “furthermore”, “with respect”, “to be clear” and “I think you’ll find”. Elsewhere in that sentence, roping together the words “commercial” and “charitable”, is, I would suggest, a deliberate tactic to insinuate that the former (grubby little money-makers!) undermines the integrity of the latter (charitable, my arse!) and suggest that the Sussexes are just in it for themselves.And finally: the absolute shellacking of the letter’s dismount, in which the king writes: “This position, distinct from the state and royal duties undertaken by the working royal family, and with the personal latitude it brings the couple in respect of financial independence and protection of their privacy as they would wish, will continue to be fully respected.”Or in layperson’s language: “haha, you’re not royal any more, nothing in your status warrants the sustained use of capital letters or a requirement for history to remember you. We’re not giving you any money because you’ve brought this on yourselves and ps, your invocation of privacy, post the publication of your memoir and your sit-down with Oprah, is an absolute joke we couldn’t be enjoying more. See ya.” God the seething, green bile acidity of the phrase “as they would wish”! Bravo, sir! Absolutely gold standard! Poor Harry must be reeling, even as he relaxes into the warm gust of air in which he was raised. (Meghan, one assumes, is largely oblivious to just how devastating all of this is and may have found the letter merely a touch snotty.)For the formerly royal couple, we must assume that any upset caused by the tone of this letter – and allowing for the prince’s bone-deep recognition and masochistic enjoyment of what might otherwise be an upsetting exchange – is offset by the many advantages they will enjoy now they’re back in the old country. Rolling green hills are obviously a thing of the past; the Cotswolds are as brown as southern California right now. But the prince may find comfort in the small-scale landscape, the patchwork of fields and hedgerows, the tiny lanes like crooked elbows, jammed up with tractors and alive with tiny brown birds, that large-scale farming in the US doesn’t do.I mentioned the cheese and the bread, infinitely superior to the rubbery and sugary American equivalents, and I’d add English strawberries to that, even this late in the season. Perhaps Harry will be reunited with some of his old wardrobe favourites, too. It’s never wax jacket season in Montecito, where an extreme heat warning is in place; meanwhile, the whole of this country is down on all fours excavating its woolly jumpers from under the bed. (Don’t tell me the words “woolly jumper” won’t soothe Harry after enforced wearing of sweaters and hoodies.) For Meghan, these consolations will be alien, but perhaps, before it starts to enrage her, she can find comfort in this country’s relative slowness, its high tolerance for dishevelment and appreciation for sarcasm – failing which, there’s always the pub.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEmma Brockes is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Is Burnham trying to appease Trump? Or Reform? What other reason is there for these North Sea oil plans? | George Monbiot | The Guardian
description: Climate catastrophe is on our doorstep – yet Labour’s impending approval of further drilling will bring more pain for negligible gains, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Author: George Monbiot
Headline: Climate catastrophe is on our doorstep – yet Labour’s impending approval of further drilling will bring more pain for negligible gains, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Content: Fossil Free London campaigners protest against North Sea drilling, London, 18 July 2026.Photograph: Jack Taylor/ReutersView image in fullscreenFossil Free London campaigners protest against North Sea drilling, London, 18 July 2026.Photograph: Jack Taylor/ReutersOpinionFossil fuelsIs Burnham trying to appease Trump? Or Reform? What other reason is there for these North Sea oil plans?George MonbiotClimate catastrophe is on our doorstep – yet Labour’s impending approval of further drilling will bring more pain for negligible gainsThu 10 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 06.51 EDTSharePinch yourself, it’s happening again. Here is a Labour government spending a vast amount of political capital to earn tiny material gains while risking huge political losses. It occurred repeatedly under Keir Starmer, and now –with the impending decisionto approve further gas and oil drilling in the North Sea – it is happening under Andy Burnham. You rack your brains to explain it, but no rational explanation comes.Burnham is studiously cryptic about his reasons.His clearest statementto date goes as follows: “There is a resource there. When people are struggling, we can’t ignore that.” Does he mean that oil and gas workers are struggling? If so, this decision will be of little use to them. The Jackdaw gasfield, likely to be approved this week, will generate a grand total of27 direct full-time jobs. The Rosebank oilfield, whose approval is likely to follow soon, will support450 UK-based jobsduring its lifetime. Yet the UK’s net zero economy directly employs300,000 people, anda further 400,000 jobsare planned. The rest of the green economyemploys more than 600,000. A just transition for fossil fuel workers, securing jobs in the green economy, is better for everyone.Or does he mean energy consumers are struggling? The gas in the Jackdaw field will make atiny contribution to our supplyand no significant difference to either ourenergy billsor ourenergy security. Switching to renewables makes usfar better offin both respects. Any oil produced by the Rosebank field isunlikely to be refined in Britain, as we no longer possess much capacity for handling oil of that kind. And as for the national accounts, a recent estimate suggests that the climate damage caused by the fields’ extra emissions wouldoutweigh any economic benefitsseveral times over.In fact, the two greatest threats to the global economy might now be climate breakdown, which, asa wide rangeof economists andeminent organisationsforecast, threatenscomprehensive economic collapse, and the AI bubble, which thegovernor of the Bank of England warnscould burst with dire consequences. Then people will really be struggling. Yet our government and others cheerfully accelerate both forces – claiming, as ever, that the industries driving them will unleash “growth”. Growth in home repossessions, perhaps.While the small amount of fossil fuel these two fields will produce allows politicians to argue that their climate impacts can be ignored, the diplomatic implications are considerable. The only chance of preventing climate catastrophe is international agreement based on mutual trust. To its credit, the UK – while falling short of what many of us would like to see – has been a leader in these efforts. But when our government refuses to leave fossil fuels in the ground, its credibility diminishes – leaving itsnegotiating position weakened.Burnham might believe this decision will get Reform UK and the Conservatives off his back. Of course it won’t. He might imagine it willappease Donald Trump, but you can’t appease Trump. Whatever you give him, he will always want more.As for the political implications, here the disparity between gain and pain becomes truly enormous. The approval of these fields is adefining issue for many Labour MPsand the voters they fear they might lose. The policy could scarcely be better designed to give the final push to voters who are minded – after so many disappointments since 2024 – to abandon Labour for a progressive alternative.If Zack Polanski, the Green party leader for England and Wales, wins the seatKeir Starmer has just vacated, this could be a major reason why. Burnham’s North Sea policy is the kind of battle Starmer’s former chief of staff Morgan McSweeney would have urged him to wage – let’sstick it to the Labour left, mwahaha – which is a major reason why Starmer is no longer prime minister.Few in power seem to understand the fire they are playing with. Last week, the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, appeared to acknowledge that we face the risk of potentially catastrophic environmental breakdown andurged usto store some extra food in our homes. The way she put it suggested that either she hasn’t grasped the magnitude of what we face, or she is trivialising the issue: “If you’ve got a store of a bit of food that can keep you going for a while before the emergency services can get to you, you’re going to be a lot better off than if you haven’t.”Right. So let’s imagine one of several possible disasters some of us havelong been warning ofarrives. As a result of harvest failures caused by climate breakdown, severe transport disruptions or – and this now looks alarmingly plausible –sudden systemic collapsein the food sector, the supermarket shelves empty, more or less overnight. We know thatthe UK government refuses, without explanation, to maintain strategic food reserves. So there are no government supplies, either. As our beans and crackers run out, the emergency services visit all29 millionof our homes. With what? Tea and sympathy? Sorry, no tea. Another slice of sympathy?Certainly, those of us who have the money and capacity to store foodshould do so: after all, no one else has our backs. But the idea that such individuated solutions would be any use in the face of a societal catastrophe is neoliberal nonsense. As always, it is the poor and excluded, with neither the cash nor the space to lay down significant supplies, who will be hit first and worst. Social breakdown would happen in days. The UK government, then, is being serious about neither the measures required to prevent climate catastrophe nor the measures required to survive it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe sense in almost every nation is of governments failing to take seriously the most serious of issues, while spending immense political resources on topics that scarcely affect our welfare (such as afew thousand peoplecrossing the Channel in small boats). Or even – as is the case with North Sea oil and gas – using their scarce political capital to make things worse for everyone, including themselves.Our government is not adoomsday cultlike the Trump government, creepily fascinated by the “end times”, as the US vice-presidentseems to be. But in terms of outcome, is there much difference?George Monbiot is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsFossil fuelsOpinionOil and gas companiesClimate crisisAndy BurnhamLabourEnergyGreenhouse gas emissionscommentShareReuse this content

title: My friend Blanche d’Alpuget often spoke to me about death. She once likened it to ‘untying a million little knots’ | Derek Rielly | The Guardian
description: The woman so pivotal in Australian literature and politics blew into my orbit in a tornado of Doris Day hair and Sophia Loren lips in the winter of 2016
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The woman so pivotal in Australian literature and politics blew into my orbit in a tornado of Doris Day hair and Sophia Loren lips in the winter of 2016
Content: Blanche d’Alpuget. ‘It wasn’t easy to disrupt Blanche but the breadth of animosity she encountered after her affair with Bob Hawke became public in late 1994 was like nothing she’d ever experienced.’Photograph: Patrick Riviere/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBlanche d’Alpuget. ‘It wasn’t easy to disrupt Blanche but the breadth of animosity she encountered after her affair with Bob Hawke became public in late 1994 was like nothing she’d ever experienced.’Photograph: Patrick Riviere/Getty ImagesOpinionBob HawkeMy friend Blanche d’Alpuget often spoke to me about death. She once likened it to ‘untying a million little knots’Derek RiellyThe woman so pivotal in Australian literature and politics blew into my orbit in a tornado of Doris Day hair and Sophia Loren lips in the winter of 2016Get ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastThu 10 Sep 2026 00.27 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 02.52 EDTShareThirty-six hoursbefore Blanche took her last breath, I negotiated the plastic tubes and mask she wore over a still beautiful face and gave her one final kiss.I wasn’t sure, then, if it was a goodbye but I knew it would be close.Who was she?Was she really, as the Sydney Morning Herald described her in an appreciation for Hazel Hawke, just “some lipsticked wraith”, a prowling blonde, the avatar for the other woman?It was a cruel fate for a woman who was so pivotal in Australian literature and politics. It wasn’t easy to disrupt Blanche but the breadth of animosity she encountered after her affair withBob Hawkebecame public in late 1994 was like nothing she’d ever experienced.About 30 years after she was photographed with Hawke at Sir Richard Kirby’s holiday house, she told me: “I was very shocked and distressed by the trolling and abuse … as opposed to simple literary criticism. I developed a great contempt, distrust and loathing of journalists.”Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailBlanche first blew into my orbit in a tornado of Doris Day hair and Sophia Loren lips in the winter of 2016, looking at least a decade younger than her 72 years, as I pursued her husband for my first book,Wednesdays with Bob. Her silk cravat and wide black sunglasses touched on the side with gold detail delivered a 70s movie-star sheen.We became friends.As she turned the corner into 80, the age when she presumed her face would suddenly collapse, as her mother’s did, and she would become a crone, I was struck by this realisation: Australia would never know the story of this woman, whose own trajectory was as compelling as that of the man whose life would come to define her.View image in fullscreenBob Hawke and Blanche D’Alpuget in 1995. ‘Her bestselling biography of Hawke, published in 1982, helped propel him into the prime ministership and thus helped change Australian politics for ever.’Photograph: Patrick Riviere/Getty ImagesBlanche d’Alpuget wasn’t just Bob Hawke’s wife. She was a fierce intellect who only saw the good in people | Craig EmersonRead moreBorn the daughter of one of Australia’s great journalists, Blanche moved to Jakarta at 22 with her first husband, Tony Pratt, where she had a front-row seat as Indonesia struggled with the bloodletting of 1965. She challenged the bolted-on moral codes of the time with her fearless writing, and her bestselling biography of Hawke, published in 1982, helped propel him into the prime ministership and thus helped changeAustralian politicsfor ever. She was still writing and living life to the full while many others of her vintage were staggering, zombie-like, along the fluorescent-lit corridors of a nursing home.And so, at the suggestion of our mutual agent, Jeanne Ryckmans, a book deal was sought and made.If Wednesdays were spent with her husband, Fridays would be with Blanche. Over the course of late 2023 and through 2024, we lunched, talked, messaged and flirted.Over several lunches, our talks had drifted to the topic of dying. It seemed, then, that everyone was dropping like flies.Death and the process of dying interested her deeply. She believed death was like walking through a fiery door but that the pain was only temporary.Blanche had seen up close what it’s like to die. She had nursed her mother through her final hours, remaining awake for days, and did an all-nighter alongside Hawke on his final day.She likened dying to “untying a million little knots”.“The soul wants to be released, but it’s held in by the body very, very strongly, and it’s an enormous effort to untie all of those knots,” she said.Regarding her final wishes, she said that her headstone was already in place next to Hawke’s at the Macquarie Park Cemetery and Crematorium in Sydney’s North Ryde.Her coffin, she told me, must be red on the inside and blue and white on the exterior. The blue represented the sky, red the colour of life and white the spirit.Blanche wanted a band to play When the Saints Go Marching In.“The more humans there are, the more love there is,” Blanche liked to say.“Love is, I believe, what distinguishes humans from the rest of the animal world or creation. Love that extends beyond one’s family and friends, beyond the blood bonds of tribe and race, to all other humans and to the rest of creation.”Derek Rielly is the author ofFridays with Blanche. His previous books are Wednesdays with Bob, a biography of the former prime minister Bob Hawke, and Gulpilil, a biography of the Australian actor and dancer David GulpililExplore more on these topicsBob HawkeOpinionAustralian politicsAustralian bookscommentShareReuse this content

title: Don’t sashay away! The BBC’s decision to cancel Ru Paul’s Drag Race UK is sickening in all the wrong ways | Television | The Guardian
description: The hyper-flamboyant and hilariously filthy show is an inclusive, celebratory platform for queer culture. The broadcaster’s choice to nix it is giving stupidity
Author: Alex Needham
Headline: The hyper-flamboyant and hilariously filthy show is an inclusive, celebratory platform for queer culture. The broadcaster’s choice to nix it is giving stupidity
Content: Werking hard … a full cast of resplendent queens on RuPaul’s Drag Race UK, series seven.Photograph: BBC/World of Wonder/Guy LevyView image in fullscreenWerking hard … a full cast of resplendent queens on RuPaul’s Drag Race UK, series seven.Photograph: BBC/World of Wonder/Guy LevyTelevisionDon’t sashay away! The BBC’s decision to cancel Ru Paul’s Drag Race UK is sickening in all the wrong waysThe hyper-flamboyant and hilariously filthy show is an inclusive, celebratory platform for queer culture. The broadcaster’s choice to nix it is giving stupidityAlex NeedhamThu 10 Sep 2026 11.25 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 12.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe BBC is canning RuPaul’s Drag Race UK – a decision that, in my household, will bring the number of regularly watched programmes on the Beeb down from one to zero. It’s a decision that will no doubt please enemies of LGBTQ+ culture, but otherwise seems inexplicable. For a start, Drag Race UK regularly pulls in 1 million viewers a week, which hardly seems like a show in its death throes (even if this is down from a previous high of 1.5 million).RuPaul’s Drag Race is also a bona fide cultural phenomenon. Since the US version started in 2009, it has brought tons of performers to national, or even global, attention who would otherwise still be plying their trade in provincial gay bars. Jinkx Monsoon from the US is now starring in Oh Mary! in London’s West End; the UK’s La Voix made it on to Strictly; and Bimini Bon-Boulash, who “stepped their pussy up” to astonishing effect in season two, has made records, modelled and written a book.View image in fullscreenSeries seven’s judges: Michelle Visage, RuPaul, Joel Dommett and Alan Carr.Photograph: BBC/World of WonderMore importantly, the show gave a TV platform to ballroom culture – the New York City-born tradition in which impoverished, young, largely Black and brown gay men and trans women, usually ostracised by their families, formed their own “houses” and transformed themselves into the glamorous characters they dreamed of being. Ballroom culture gave the world vogueing, the documentary Paris is Burning, and a whole argot which, more than 30 years on from its popularisation in the film, is mainstream. “It’s giving”, “she’s serving”, “throwing shade”, “spilling the tea”, looking “snatched”. We’ll never know what the queens who invented this lingo would think of its incredible resilience, since they perished in the Aids crisis.View image in fullscreenDelightfully random … Nyongbella.Photograph: BBC/World of WonderRuPaul’s Drag Race UK fused this underground culture with Britain’s venerable drag tradition to often hilarious effect. Who could forget characters like the acid-tongued, high fashion queen A’Whora from season two, whose comedy routine was so filthy it managed to make judge Alan Carr wince? Or Cheddar Gorgeous, the historically minded and hugely articulate queen from season four, whose Act Up themed costume I last spotted on display in Manchester’s Whitworth gallery? Or even Nyongbella from season seven, delightfully random and usually almost naked, strutting her stuff on the BBC in defiance of her disapproving relatives in Cameroon, where gay sex can get you a five-year jail sentence? In what other context would such characters have made it on to the BBC?That’s not to mention the amazingly high-profile celebrity guests (Andrew Garfield, Mel B and Michaela Coel have all served), and the always-fabulous judges Michelle Visage, Graham Norton and Carr. There is also, of course, the positive impact on scared young LGBTQ+ people on seeing out gay and trans folk living their best lives on screen, working – or ratherwerking– hard and being unapologetically themselves. Isn’t that something worth preserving?Along with the girl group challenges, Snatch Game episodes and spectacular looks, Drag Race UK has seen its contestants discuss their experiences of being non-binary or living with HIV. And while, as a cynical Briton, I often cringe at the climactic moment when the queens who make it to the final talk tearfully to pictures of themselves as children, it’s a reminder that self-acceptance is something many LGBTQ+ people still struggle to achieve, especially in the midst of the current global backlash against our hard-won rights.View image in fullscreenSeries eight’s KY Kelly and Naya Thorn.Photograph: BBC/World of Wonder/Guy LevyPrudes and homophobes might say that BBC licence-payers don’t want to pay for a bunch of drag queens telling filthy jokes and bitching about one another on the small screen. Well, I also pay the TV licence fee and I do. It doesn’t seem much to ask that, as a gay person, I get one programme on iPlayer that is unabashedly queer – especially since the BBC also canned I Kissed a Boy andI Kissed a Girlfor bad measure. As the arts editor of the Guardian, I guess I could watch the BBC’s amazing slate of arts programmes – were it not for the fact that most of them have also long been chopped.Drag Race UK has an ardent fanbase of all backgrounds and generations. Of course, not everyone in the LGBTQ+ community likes it – Travis Alabanza’s play The Sound of the Underground entertainingly railed against it – but it has expanded its definition of drag considerably, featuring trans and one female performer among the legions of cis gay men. A contestant in season one even had a girlfriend at the time – and if that’s not inclusion, what is? BBC, RuPaul’s Drag Race UK should not be allowed to sashay away.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionRuPaulfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Alex Winter: ‘Michael Winner was the most erudite sociopath I’ve ever met’ | Movies | The Guardian
description: The Bill & Ted actor on Keanu Reeves, whether there will be a fourth instalment and nights out in Brixton with the Death Wish director
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: The Bill & Ted actor on Keanu Reeves, whether there will be a fourth instalment and nights out in Brixton with the Death Wish director
Content: Alex Winter photographed in Toronto in 2025.Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images for IMDbView image in fullscreenAlex Winter photographed in Toronto in 2025.Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images for IMDbFilm & Music reader interviewMoviesInterviewAlex Winter: ‘Michael Winner was the most erudite sociopath I’ve ever met’As told toRich PelleyThe Bill & Ted actor answers your questions about working with Keanu Reeves, whether there will be a fourth instalment and nights out in Brixton with the Death Wish directorThu 10 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou were born inLondonbut grew up inAmerica. When do you feel most British?DonarudoToranpuThe UK is still my second home. I’ve worked there a lot as an adult. When I’m back in London, I like walking on Hampstead Heath, so I would say that’s where I feel most at home.Having playedMarkoinThe Lost Boysand thenJohn PolidoriinHaunted Summer, have you been tempted to take on another vampire-related role? And was getting staked to death while you were sleeping a bit of a disappointing end for Marko – what would have been your preferred way of going out in style? Death by stereo, perhaps?Finbarre and MoreorLesPaulI’d love to do another vampire movie. I love those characters. They’re interesting and great fun to play. There are some really good vampire movies – I’m grateful I was in one that has, for some reason that none of us can figure out, really stood the test of time. And I love Marko’s death. As an actor, the first time you get staked is the most memorable.View image in fullscreenKeanu Reeves and Alex Winter in Bill & Ted’s Bogus Journey (1994).Photograph: Cinematic/AlamyWhichKeanu Reeveswas the most fun to work with: inWaiting for GodotonBroadway; asTed “Theodore” Loganto yourBill S Preston, EsqinBill & Ted; or as mutantOrtiz the Dog Boywhen you directed him inFreaked? And following Waiting for Godot, what wildly inappropriate classic should Bill & Ted tackle next?FioreSebek and GunHarpI just love performing with Keanu. The funny thing is we both play bass, so all through the first Bill & Ted, whenever we weren’t shooting, we’d be jamming. Keanu and I both have theatre backgrounds and have studied Shakespeare, so I’d like to do some Shakespeare, maybe something like Measure for Measure. There’s a few that we’ve discussed. I’m not sure if we’ll get there, but who knows? Never say never.My kids (six andnine) have just discoveredBen 10in all its incarnations and I saw you directed the live-action versions. If you could choose the powers of any of the aliens in theOmnitrix, which would it be and why?LethalLiaisonHeatblast was my favourite. He’s a powerful fire character. My children were obsessed with Ben 10 at the time, and we worked on those together, which was something I don’t often get to do, so it was a lovely experience. I met my wife on that project too. She was running Cartoon Network studios at the time.Alex Winter on fame, AI and reuniting with Keanu Reeves: ‘Sometimes we’re on a groove and go, ‘God damn, that was good!’Read moreMichael Winnerdirected you in your first film,Death Wish 3. Say something nice about him – and where did yougo out drinking when you were filming it in London?ExFi and OttoMaddoxI can absolutely say something nice about Michael Winner. He was the most erudite sociopath I’ve ever met. That’s a compliment. We used to drink in Brixton, largely. One of the people working on the show – I think he may have been involved in some criminal activity, so maybe the less said about him the better – owned a club there. They would close it and we would hang out there all night. I was 19 when I made Death Wish 3. It was a very fun, formidable summer.You’ve made documentaries aboutNapster, the dark web, blockchain and YouTube. Which part of the internet scares you most these days?ZenchiThe hasty, greed-oriented rush into the AI space is the most frightening thing happening right now. That’s not to say all AI is bad, but a lot of the people running the AI companies areverybad. So what scares me the most is the tech oligarch takeover that’s occurring in so many areas of business, politics and civic culture.View image in fullscreenFrank Zappa at the Amougies Festival in Belgium, October 1969.Photograph: Philippe Gras/AlamyAfter directing yourFrank Zappa documentary, for those, like me, who’ve been immune to his charms, can you recommend a Zappa track or album?HenleyRegattaI didn’t make the doc as a big fan. I made it because I was very interested in Frank Zappa as a way into looking at American culture and artistic culture. He’s a really good doc subject: someone who decided to live their life in a purely artistic way, and what the consequences of that were. If you want the quintessential Zappa album – unless you are just never going to like him – it’s impossible not to enjoy Hot Rats. I’m also very partial to the album he made at the very end of his life, The Yellow Shark, which is almost a classical, jazz-oriented album.The Bill & Ted movies feel like a beautiful, optimistic tribute to the idea that music created by ordinary people will save the world. Do you think it still could?venusdenicoI do think that good art will always help the world. It’s not the only thing. But I do think that music and other art forms absolutely help the planet and help humanity.View image in fullscreenReeves and Winter with William Sadler as the Grim Reaper, aka Death, in Bogus Journey (1991).Photograph: RGR Collection/AlamyThanks for that wonderful ending toBill & Ted Face the Music. Will there be a Bill & Ted4?brucevayne1000Keanu and I would love to make a fourth movie. I think the stars have to align in a number of areas for that to happen. But we love playing these characters. We kind ofareBill and Ted. We started playing the characters so young, I don’t really think they exist without us. We defined the characters from the very beginning, so I don’t think it really matters how old we are. It becomes a question of how long can you act, and I think one can act until one is no longer breathing. I really hope they don’t do a reboot. I don’t really want anyone else to play Bill, because IamBill. That would be a disaster.Alex Winter: ‘I had extreme PTSD for many, many years. That will wreak havoc’Read moreIf you had access to Bill & Ted’s phone booth, which non-bogus historical figures would you visit?TeeDubyaBeeI would like to go back to ancient Greece. I would love to meet Euripides or Aeschylus. Or go to Shakespeare’s time. The future too. What is going to happen? Will there be a planet? I’d be curious to go 40 or 50 years into the future and have a look at whether we pulled ourselves out of this climate disaster we’re falling into, which I believe we will. I’m not a nihilist. But I’d be curious to see how we did it.If you could“melvin”anyone in real life – as Bill & Ted do toDeathinBogus Journey– who would it be?Dr_J_A_ZoidbergI grew up in the US, and I did not grow up with “melvin”. I grew up with “wedgie”. It must be a coastal thing. Maybe on the west coast they say “melvin”? In the midwest and the east coast they definitely say wedgie. Anyway, who would I most like to melvin or wedgie? Elon Musk.Bill & Ted’s Bogus Journey 4K UHD is out nowExplore more on these topicsFilmFilm & Music reader interviewKeanu ReevesinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Angine de Poitrine review – mind-boggling math rock mastery from freaky Québécois duo | Angine de Poitrine | The Guardian
description: The brilliantly strange band’s live show is a must-see spectacle powered by glorious noise and wild flair
Author: Alexander Abnos
Headline: The brilliantly strange band’s live show is a must-see spectacle powered by glorious noise and wild flair
Content: Khn de Poitrine of Angine de Poitrine performs in London in May.Photograph: Matthew Baker/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKhn de Poitrine of Angine de Poitrine performs in London in May.Photograph: Matthew Baker/Getty ImagesAngine de PoitrineReviewAngine de Poitrine review – mind-boggling math rock mastery from freaky Québécois duoLe Poisson Rouge, New YorkThe brilliantly strange experimental band’s live show is a must-see spectacle powered by glorious noise and wild flairAlexander AbnosThu 10 Sep 2026 14.21 EDTFirst published on Thu 10 Sep 2026 11.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheir masks light up now. To the extent there was a hard news event from Wednesday’s exhilarating sold-out New York debut ofAngine de Poitrine, that was it. The Québécois duo went viral in corners of the internet earlier this year thanks in part to their microtonal, odd-metered take on hard-driving rock, but also because of those ostentatious costumes and masks – black and white polka dot tunics and jumpsuits with oversized papier-mache faces and exaggerated features, originally featuring golden glittery eyes and signature pyramid accoutrements. The new ones have all those same things but with the added ability to light up in a bright yellow at key moments.‘We’re not Lady Gaga and Elton John’: unmasking Angine de Poitrine, the year’s buzziest, dottiest bandRead moreA small detail, to be sure, but one got the sense that the weeknight crowd was reveling in it and many others at New York’s Le Poisson Rouge (LPR) – an appropriately French-named venue given the band’s home province. Wednesday was the first of the band’s two shows at the 700-capacity basement venue renowned for its sound system and commitment to adventurous programming. Both Angine shows had been sold out for many months, ever since avideoof them playing in a French studio was uploaded to KEXP’s YouTube channel and went viral. At time of writing, the video is closing in on 20m views – a remarkable tally given that the music, by mass-appeal standards, is so magnificently odd.While their success came suddenly,Angine de Poitrinehad spent years perfecting ways of expanding small details into fully formed musical themes, using them to bring new life to the repetitious riffs that form an ever-evolving backbone of each of their lengthy songs. Added to the outfits, the masks, the double-necked guitar/bass, even their consonant-heavy song titles and stage names (Klek, drummer, and Khn, guitarist/bassist) and commitment to near-total anonymity, they have created an intoxicating mystery. Listeners are left free to wonder what this mysterious duo are playing, why it sticks in the mind like a pop song despite its timings and tunings, and how the hell they are physically able to play it with all that stuff on them.Seeing them live might have answered some of those questions, but it also raised others.
