The band’s signature sound is defined by dearth of reverb and sustain – would deadened drums and defined guitar play in a noisy concert hall? Their signature image is that of aliens who have beamed into a studio with no rough edges. Would that play once you can see the cables emerging from out the back of their costumes? With such little difference between the album and in-studio live versions of their songs, and their expert use of live looping creating few opportunities to vamp, would the live concert even be worthwhile?View image in fullscreenAngine de Poitrine performing at Le Poisson Rouge, New York, 9 September 2026.Photograph: Sachyn MitalYes, it absolutely would. The band emerged in full regalia to a roar, packed in under LPR’s low-slung ceiling. They blasted their way through Angor, the closer from Vol II, the second of their two albums, then raised the bar with Yor Zarad, another of that album’s ferocious highlights. Tamebsz, from the 2024 release Vol I followed, for the first time making use of the light-up masks to guide the audience in an especially complicated game of call-and-response. The songs had not especially changed from how they sound on their albums and in-studios. The ability to finally see the duo’s superb musicianship up close carried the show – as did the reminders that they are still human. How does a musician performing in a giant mask take a drink of water? Through special water bottles with comically long, glow-in-the-dark rubber straws.Three-quarters through, though, the perils of live performance intruded. Khn had broken a string. And when you break a string on a specially built two-necked guitar/bass with custom microtonal frettings to access notes between the western scale, well, it’s not like you can borrow somebody else’s. And given their costumes, it’s also not like you can change the string yourself without difficulty. Khnrequired the helpof a guitar tech to guide a replacement string through the back of the instrument, all while Khn himself partook in an impromptu jam with Klek using the other strings on the instrument. When that string change didn’t take, the duo figured they had delayed long enough and launched into Sarniezz – by necessity, the only time some of those signature riffs rendered a bit differently.And when they unplugged and left the stage, no encore followed, and none was demanded. Questions had either been answered, or pleasantly remained.Explore more on these topicsAngine de PoitrineExperimental musicPop and rocklive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Big hits, massive ballads and titanic emotions: Céline Dion’s greatest songs – ranked! | Céline Dion | The Guardian
description: As the French-Canadian superstar returns for her first concerts since she was diagnosed with stiff person syndrome, we count down the best of an unabashedly romantic catalogue. Wind machines at the ready!
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: As the French-Canadian superstar returns for her first concerts since she was diagnosed with stiff person syndrome, we count down the best of an unabashedly romantic catalogue. Wind machines at the ready!
Content: Belting it out … Céline Dion in 2019.Photograph: Alice Chiche/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBelting it out … Céline Dion in 2019.Photograph: Alice Chiche/AFP/Getty ImagesRankedCéline DionBig hits, massive ballads and titanic emotions: Céline Dion’s greatest songs – ranked!As the French Canadian superstar returns for her first concerts since she was diagnosed with stiff person syndrome, we count down the best of an unabashedly romantic catalogue. Wind machines at the ready!Alexis PetridisThu 10 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 11.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google20. Ashes (2018)When Céline Dion’s era as a foolproof hitmaker ended, she seemed weirdly liberated and more willing to take risks. Witnessthe video for Ashes: an impressively atmospheric ballad from the soundtrack toDeadpool 2, in which she gently mocks her own image in the company of Ryan Reynolds, in character as the antihero.19. Where Does My Heart Beat Now? (1990)Debuted by Dion at the 1989 Eurovision song contest final, this is the killer cut from her first English-language album, Unison, which was released a mere two years after she learned to speak English. It’s a superior power ballad: huge chorus, mammoth drums, Dion absolutely belting it out. It has been overshadowed by her later successes, but it’sworth revisiting.View image in fullscreenDestined for greatness … Dion in 1991.Photograph: Mark Baker/Sony Music Archive/Getty Images18. Misled (1993)Dancefloor-focused pop isn’t what Dion is famous for, but The Colour of My Love’s diversion into camp club anthem territory is surprisingly good – she makes a fine disco diva and the house remixes, by MK and E-Smoove, are great. E-Smoove’s piano-powered Mission mix is the pick.17. Ne Bouge Pas (2003)The album 1 Fille et 4 Types is an example of Dion deliberately playing against type. Made with a quartet of Francophone singer-songwriters including Jean-Jacques Goldman, it produced the improbable sound of the power ballad queen singing over distorted slide guitar, wailing harmonica and a Bo Diddley beat. Fun!16. Encore un Soir (2016)Recorded before the death of Dion’s husband, René Angélil, but released a few months afterwards, the title track of her 2016 album offers a reflection on the passing of time that was unavoidably coloured by the singer’s loss. A chart-topper in France, it’s a beautiful song, made all the more potent by Dion’s restrained vocal.15. I’m Alive (2002)Célion Dion: I’m Alive – videoA subtle update of Dion’s characteristic style, I’m Alive threw a mid-tempo four-to the-floor beat and a softly chugging synth bassline into the mix to impressive effect. A viral mashup of the track with the Whispers’ disco classic And the Beat Goes On propelled it back into the singles chart 22 years later.14. The Prayer (1998)View image in fullscreenGiant duet … with Andrea Bocelli at the Grammys in 1999.Photograph: Frank Micelotta Archive/Getty ImagesTake your pick from Dion’s original solo version, a duet with Andrea Bocelli and a later duet with Josh Groban. The Oscar-nominated, Golden-Globe-winning hit from the largely forgotten animated film Quest for Camelot shines regardless, a suitably cinematically orchestrated and lavish showstopper.13. To Love You More (1995)Originally recorded for a television drama in Japan, To Love You More followed hard on the heels of Dion’s major English-language pop breakthrough album, The Colour of My Love. It’s another vast hit, featuring a beautiful melody, a sprightly string arrangement and a vocal that fires on all cylinders.12. A New Day Has Come (2002)Céline Dion: A New Day Has Come – videoDion’s first release after a couple of years of maternity leave, A New Day Has Come was reflective of her new-mum status: “Where there was weakness I found my strength / All in the eyes of a boy.” One critic suggested it resembled a “gentle exhale” – certainly, there’s a lovely, lullaby-like quality to its melody.11. Pour Que Tu M’Aimes EncoreIf French-speaking listeners thought Dion might turn her back on her native tongue after her English breakthrough, they were wrong. She followed up The Colour of My Love with D’eux, the bestselling album not in English made by a female artist. Its gently funky biggest hit became one of her signature songs.10. I Drove All Night (2003)There’s an impressive fearlessness about Dion’s choice of covers. The definitive version of I Drove All Night (first released by Cyndi Lauper) is by Roy Orbison, one of the most celebrated and distinctive voices in rock history. No matter: Dion’s take, which replaces the cantering rhythm with a house pulse, is utterly assured.View image in fullscreenShowstopper … at the Met gala in 2019.Photograph: Stephen Lovekin/BEI/Rex/Shutterstock9. Beauty and the Beast (1991)Dion was recruited to provide a more radio-friendly take of the version of the great Disney ballad, sung by Angela Lansbury in the movie. She was a relative newcomer, so Peabo Bryson was employed to amp up the star power; understandably, it’s their version that became the most famous.8. Tell Him (1997)Barbra Streisand, one of Dion’s biggest idols, suggested a collaboration after Dion deputised for her at the 1997 Oscars ceremony – she sang Streisand’s duet with Bryan Adams, I Finally Found Someone. Whatever you make of Tell Him’s booming, slightly dated production, there’s no doubt their voices work incredibly well together.7. Immortality (1997)Céline Dion: Immortality – videoWritten by the Bee Gees for the stage version of Saturday Night Fever – their 1996 demo was released on their greatest hits record in 2001 – the trio provide immediately recognisable backing vocals on Dion’s take. It’s a great song: the stately pace and power ballad dynamics suit her perfectly, while the chorus is pure Gibb brothers magic.‘She’ll outdo herself’: Céline Dion fans camp out for glimpse of star before sold-out Paris comebackRead more6. All By Myself (1996)Another example of Dion boldly claiming an extremely well-known song for herself, her take on Eric Carmen’s mid-70s weepie – the global theme tune of the recently dumped – manages to ratchet up the tormented drama. It’s no mean feat, given how dramatic and racked the original sounds.5. That’s the Way It Is (1999)A new track appended to Dion’s greatest hits collection All The Way … A Decade of Song, That’s the Way It Is is the handiwork of three Swedish songwriters – Max Martin among them – collectively responsible for a string of Britney Spears hits. This is a little lighter and poppier in tone than Dion’s usual work, yet was another huge hit.4. My Heart Will Go On (1997)Céline Dion: My Heart Will Go On – videoA No 1 in more than 25 countries – it shifted more than 18m copies – the Titanic theme was originally supposed to be sung by the Norwegian soprano Sissel Kyrkjebø. It’s almost impossible now to imagine anyone other than Dion singing it, so familiar is her gradual build from fragile whisper to full-on fireworks.3. Because You Loved Me (1996)Few artists do a big old ballad climax quite like Dion – and Because You Loved Me is the perfect example. Written by Diane Warren, it slowly develops from hushed beginnings until, three minutes in, Dion hits a series of high notes and her vocal explodes, soaring and imploring over gospel-influenced choir.2. The Power of Love (1993)Famed in the UK thanks to Jennifer Rush’s chart-topping 1985 original (and not to be confused with the Frankie Goes to Hollywood song), The Power of Love was relatively unknown in the US before Dion got hold of it and turned it into a paean to her romance with her manager, and soon-to-be-husband, Angélil. Synths shiver, drums boom, guitars echo. Dion sounds as if she means every word.1. It’s All Coming Back to Me Now (1996)Céline Dion: It’s All Coming Back to Me Now – videoWriter Jim Steinman claimed It’s All Coming Back to Me Now was inspired by the scene in Wuthering Heights when Heathcliff exhumes Cathy’s corpse and dances with it on a beach. No such scene exists, but that’s Steinman for you. His songs are so wilfully overblown that they require a singer with total emotional commitment to pull them off without sounding silly – and Dion perfectly fit the bill after a version by the girl band Pandora’s Box flopped. She sings it as if it’s a matter of life and death, her voice supremely powerful and emotive even amid Steinman’s characteristic Wagnerian bombast. The end result is a mad, spectacular triumph.Explore more on these topicsCéline DionRankedfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: NAZA review – Israeli intelligence officers cast chilling light on civilian deaths | Venice film festival | The Guardian
description: Venice film festival: Under the cover of night, anonymous personnel discuss AI, error rates and problematic intelligence units in a documentary produced by the Guardian
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Venice film festival: Under the cover of night, anonymous personnel discuss AI, error rates and problematic intelligence units in a documentary produced by the Guardian
Content: ‘The city in all its eerie heedlessness and heartlessness’ … NAZA.Photograph: the GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The city in all its eerie heedlessness and heartlessness’ … NAZA.Photograph: the GuardianVenice film festivalReviewNAZA review – Israeli intelligence officers cast chilling light on civilian deathsVenice film festival:Under the cover of night, anonymous personnel discuss AI, error rates and problematic intelligence units in a documentary produced by the GuardianPeter Bradshawin VeniceThu 10 Sep 2026 11.15 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 11.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is a disquieting documentary about what Israel’s military chiefs in Gaza reputedly call “Naza”, meaning civilian collateral damage – itself a queasy euphemism. The calculated “Naza” number is the amount of projected civilian deaths from each military strike, and perhaps it will come to have the same connotations as the US military term “body count” during Vietnam. The directors are Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, two of the film-makers behindNo Other Land, which was about attacks by the Israel Defense Forces on Palestinian West Bank villages. NAZA is executive produced by Jonathan Glazer and James Wilson and appears under the production auspices of the Guardian, in which some of the stories have already appeared.Secret systems used by Israel in mass killings of Gaza civilians revealed in new filmRead moreThere are flaws: interviews were conducted on the condition of anonymity, but if no-one can be persuaded to put their name and face to their words (and of course it is terribly dangerous) then the impact of this as testimony is lessened. But even so, the film is casting a chilling light on what is happening now inGaza.Their faces in shadow, appearances and voices digitally altered, disillusioned Israeli intelligence officers and personnel speak to the directors about the war in Gaza. They do this semi-furtively on the dark night-time rooftops of Tel Aviv, the home of Israeli intelligence, supposedly for journalistic secrecy purposes – but it also provides a dramatic backdrop, as well as ambient footage of the city in all its eerie heedlessness and heartlessness. Periodically, the camera’s eye will drift across the gleaming apartment buildings, zooming in on glimpses of prosperous lives just 60km from Gaza.The interviewees reject the whole concept of “human shields”. They allege that it is not a question of Hamas operatives hiding behind civilians; rather, Israel’s intelligence services have subcontracted their attack recon to AI. A computer program reportedly analyses the call pattern on phones belonging to known Hamas terrorists and finds which of the other tens of thousands of phones they have under surveillance exhibit the same tendencies – and then attack the owner, invariably at night, in the apartments whose whereabouts are already minutely documented by the state. A 15% permitted “error” rate for this is mentioned at one stage, and another respondent talks about an expected “Naza” rate of 20 for each action – but clearly this is elastic to say the least. Gaza’s civilians are considered to be all tacitly complicit in the grotesque antisemitic pogrom of 7 October, and whole buildings and vast numbers of people can be wiped out in one computer-generated assault.Elsewhere, the officials talk about the logistics involved in “cleansing” northern Gaza and in sniper attacks on Gazan civilians who, desperate for food, don’t know they have crossed some invisible line into a militarised zone. Another part of the film talks about an intelligence unit unofficially loyal to prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu personally, engaging in dirty tricks undermining international human rights bodies who might be antipathetic to Israel’s political leadership.The ahistorical comparison to nazism is inevitably and glibly invoked by one speaker. But Gaza, however horrendous, is not the same as the Holocaust. This specious parallel is all too readily available; the bombing of Dresden is the more obvious comparison. At all events, the anguish of Gaza is brought into pin-sharp focus.NAZA screened at theVenice film festival.Explore more on these topicsVenice film festivalDocumentary filmsGazaIsraelPalestineFestivalsJonathan GlazerreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Tschabalala Self’s Lady in Blue review – this striding scupture fills the fourth plinth with humour and life | Fourth plinth | The Guardian
description: The swaggering statue’s luscious collision of brown and blue could stop traffic – and serves as a reminder of the big, beautiful, multicultural world we enjoy
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: The swaggering statue’s luscious collision of brown and blue could stop traffic – and serves as a reminder of the big, beautiful, multicultural world we enjoy
Content: ‘Not a vulnerable object of anyone’s gaze’ … Lady in Blue on the fourth plinth.Photograph: Kin Cheung/APView image in fullscreen‘Not a vulnerable object of anyone’s gaze’ … Lady in Blue on the fourth plinth.Photograph: Kin Cheung/APFourth plinthReviewTschabalala Self’s Lady in Blue review – this striding scupture fills the fourth plinth with humour and lifeTrafalgar Square, LondonThe swaggering statue’s luscious collision of brown and blue could stop traffic – and serves as a reminder of the big, beautiful, multicultural world we enjoyJonathan JonesThu 10 Sep 2026 11.09 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt hit me like a thunder clap. One moment I was bored and irritated by the official speeches before the unveiling of Tschabalala Self’s sculpture on the fourth plinth, which so insisted on its sociopolitical worth it sounded like Soviet propaganda. Then the covering slid off and I was in love with the Lady in Blue.Self has created one of the most beautiful sculptures put on Trafalgar Square’s empty plinth – and I don’t mean that in a cool, formalist way. There is a serious danger of traffic accidents as drivers passing the square stare a little too long at the Lady’s generous proportions, her long stride in platform shoes, her intensely physical, confident being.‘I’m not nervous, I’m ready’: Tschabalala Self on racist vandals and her bold striding woman for the Fourth PlinthRead moreLady in Blue brilliantly exploits the potential of the long rectangular plinth, built in 1841 for an equestrian statue that was never erected, to encompass a lolloping human gait. This is a homage to walking, and to Umberto Boccioni’s futurist striderUnique Forms of Continuity in Space, with Self’s figure extrapolated upward from her wide and fast walk, a massive curved leg thrusting forward out of her draping blue skirt, her head held high, but not absurdly high.This is no colossus but a statue that takes its scale and life from the surrounding city. There, I’ve said it: statue. The most memorable works on the fourth plinth, ever since it became a site for temporary art works back in 1999, have usually been human figures. ToMark Wallinger’s Ecce HomoandMarc Quinn’s Alison Lapper Pregnant, we can now add Self’s Lady as proof that what we really want and maybe need to see on a plinth is the human form, alive, profound and sexual.View image in fullscreenIt might melt withered hearts with its panache … onlookers admire Lady in Blue.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesWhat you first notice is the sheen of this polychrome woman: sunlight glints on her polished, plasticky surface as if she were covered from head to toe in nail varnish. Then your eyes adjust to the glare and you feel the luscious collision of brown flesh and heavenly blue. The blue is that of lapis lazuli, the rare mineral mined in Afghanistan that for millennia was coveted for jewellery and, then, for the most ethereal and expensive painter’s blue: ultramarine.It connects Lady in Blue with the paintings in the National Gallery behind it, many of which use ultramarine, maybe most of all with Bronzino’s brazenly eroticAllegory With Venus and Cupid, which sets hard flesh against silky blue. Self’s statue has the same provocatively fetishistic power.But this Lady is not a vulnerable object of anyone’s gaze. She swaggers in space with commanding girth, her bottom facing the National Gallery with flamboyant magnificence. This is the opposite of smooth classicism or catwalk perfection. In fact, it may be the opposite of traditional western sculpture. For all its apparent simplicity, Self’s figure seems rooted in African wood carvings, with their free transformations of the human body. On top of that is a head whose beauty and grace recall the bronze faces of the medieval queens of Ife.View image in fullscreen‘Her achievement goes beyond good intentions’ … Tschabalala Self with her sculpture.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesLady in Blue appears at the heart of a London where we’ve seen Tommy Robinson supporters march for a mono-racial, white nationalist UK. For all my impatience, it’s hard to disagree with the speeches at the unveiling – that we urgently need to uphold diversity and equality and reject intolerance.The question is how a work of art can help. Just putting up a positive image of a Black woman won’t silence racists, and might even offer them another horrible talking point in the culture wars. But Self’s achievement goes beyond good intentions. You can view it as a seductive and funny comment on our big, beautiful, multicultural world.Or you can just enjoy Lady in Blue aesthetically as a stonking sculpture that manages to meld multiple art histories to fill the fourth plinth with humour, fun and life. This is a carnivalesque masterpiece. But in a frightening world it also throws us a lifeline, something human to hold on to.Explore more on these topicsFourth plinthSculptureArtreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I was on the loo when I got the news!’ Strictly Come Dancing’s new hosts spill their scandalous secrets | Television | The Guardian
description: After a year of frenzied conjecture, the new hosts putting the razzle back into Strictly are Johannes Radebe, Emma Willis and Josh Widdicombe. They talk night sweats, sparkly pants – and the hilarious fake show cooked up to fool the press
Author: Michael Hogan
Headline: After a year of frenzied conjecture, the new hosts putting the razzle back into Strictly are Johannes Radebe, Emma Willis and Josh Widdicombe. They talk night sweats, sparkly pants – and the hilarious fake show cooked up to fool the press
Content: Three to tango … Josh Widdicombe, Johannes Radebe and Emma Willis, the new Strictly hosts.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThree to tango … Josh Widdicombe, Johannes Radebe and Emma Willis, the new Strictly hosts.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianTelevision‘I was on the loo when I got the news!’ Strictly Come Dancing’s new hosts spill their scandalous secretsAfter a year of frenzied conjecture, the new hosts putting the razzle back into Strictly are Johannes Radebe, Emma Willis and Josh Widdicombe. They talk night sweats, sparkly pants – and the hilarious fake show cooked up to fool the pressMichael HoganThu 10 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 08.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohannes Radebe, one of the three new presenters ofStrictly Come Dancing, can barely contain his glee. Asked where they were when they heard they’d got the job, Radebe is quick to wind up his co-hosts. “We’ll never forget that call,” he grins. “It was a weekday afternoon and I was at home, preparing for that night’s performance of [West End musical] Kinky Boots. But go on, tell the Guardian where you two were.”“We all got the same message, asking us to jump on a Zoom,” says Emma Willis. “We didn’t know if it was good news or bad news.” Josh Widdicombe picks up the story: “I thought, ‘Surely they wouldn’t tell me to my face if I hadn’t got it? They’d just text my agent or something.’”Radebe prompts him: “So where did you take the Zoom call, Joshy?” “In a graveyard in Birmingham,” confesses Widdicombe. “I was on tour, killing time walking around, and needed to go somewhere quiet. There’s nowhere quieter than a cemetery. Just to be clear, I sat against a tree, not on a grave.”Willis’s whereabouts were equally awkward. “I was at the hairdressers with my head in the sink. The BBC said: ‘Is there anywhere private you can go?’ I said: ‘Well, either out on the street or in the toilet.’ And they were like, ‘Probably the toilet.’ So I was sat on the loo with wet hair when I got the news. Not using it, I hasten to add. Seat down.” A Birmingham graveyard and a salon toilet. Who says showbiz is all glitz, glamour and glitterballs?View image in fullscreen‘It’s a baptism of fire’… Radebe, Willis and Widdicombe in all new Strictly Come Dancing.Photograph: Guy Levy/BBC/PAWhen long-serving duo Tess Daly and Claudia Winklemanhung up their ballroom shoeslast Christmas, it sparked frenzied conjecture about who would be next to helm the BBC blockbuster. You would’ve got long odds on the combo of reality TV stalwart Willis, standup comic Widdicombe and South Africa-born professional dancer Radebe.“We were all in shock but had to keep it secret for another fortnight,” says Willis. “The only people we could talk to about it were each other, so we immediately set up a WhatsApp group.” It’s called “OMG”, named that fateful afternoon and unchanged since. “You should never change group chat names,” says Widdicombe. “They’re historic monuments.”The big decision came after cloak-and-dagger auditions and secret screen tests. “It was a long old process,” says Willis. “I felt like a kid waiting for Christmas. It went on forever.” “We all had separate meetings, then a week of chemistry tests,” says Widdicombe. “You had no idea where you were going or who you’d be auditioning with. You just had to get in a car, then be smuggled in to avoid any lurking paparazzi.”From a Gavin and Stacey star to Dani Dyer’s return: every Strictly Come Dancing 2026 contestant ratedRead moreThe BBC even concocted a fake show to throw people off the scent. “It was called The Great Garden Glow Up,” says Widdicombe. “A producer told me ‘We wanted a show that feasibly all the auditionees would host.’ I was like, ‘I wouldn’t fucking host that, mate!’ There’s no way me and Jojo are fronting The Great Garden Glow Up! Although I could imagine Emma being good. With Tom Allen, maybe.” Willis laughs: “You wouldn’t say that if you saw the state of my garden.”Auditions were set up as a rough approximation of Elstree Studios. “It was like a homemade Blue Peter version of Strictly,” says Willis. “There was a wallpapering table with judges behind it. On my day, it was Anton, Motsi and a couple of stand-ins.” “Shout-out to producer Joe” says Widdicombe. “He did the best Craig impression I’ve ever seen.” “My first chemistry test was actually with Jojo,” says Willis. “We must’ve done something right.”The pair once nearly graced the ballroom in a whole different capacity. “I’d wanted to be a contestant for years and almost was,” says Willis. “A few years ago, I did a dance trial which happened to be with Jojo. We boogied together. It didn’t come to fruition but we kept in touch. When he walked into the screen test that day, I was like, ‘Yes!’” “They saw Emma with Jojo and thought, ‘That’s two-thirds of the chemistry we need!’” jokes Widdicombe.View image in fullscreenThree is the magic number … Radebe, Willis and Widdicombe.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianTalking of which, why three hosts instead of the traditional two? As Willis recalls: “When we were called back in, the producers said, ‘This is a bit of a curveball but having watched all the screen tests, we want to try a trio.’ They’d never considered it before. The first time we tested together, they only had scripts for duos.”By this stage, all three badly wanted the job. As Radebe puts it: “When we left that last chemistry test, I went home, summoned all my ancestors, got down on my knees and prayed. I desperately wanted to do it with these two. But all was not lost because if it was a no, I could come back as a dancer. It’s tough walking away from that but don’t worry, I’ll definitely find ways of dancing. I still need to be in my Cuban heels. I negotiated that in my contract!” They extol the virtues of being a trio, rather than the widely expected duo. “It feels like we’re a gang,” says Widdicombe. “There’s no ego. We’re all in this together. It also means we’re not like-for-like replacements for Claudia and Tess. It’s a new way of presenting the show and easier to make it our own.”Press reports say the trio blew bosses away with their chemistry. Willis bats this off: “I keep hearing that and I’m like, ‘Settle down, we have to do this on telly as well.’ Our chemistry might be off the charts now but we’ll be shitting our pants for that first live show. I hear the theme music in my sleep and wake up sweating.”Pundits assumed that Willis would be anchoring proceedings on the ballroom floor, like Daly did, with Widdicombe occupying Winkleman’s berth on the balcony and Radebe in a roving reporter role. “I understand that speculation but it’s wide of the mark,” says Willis. “There’s no roving reporter, no fixed positions. A three rather than a two is a nice point of difference but the core of the show is the same as ever. It’s about the contestants, the dancing and fantastic multi-generational fun.”“I’m actually replacing Dave Arch as the leader of the band,” says Widdicombe. “That’s an exclusive. No, people just need to wait and see.”As the first Black presenter of the main show, it’s another milestone for serial trailblazer Radebe. “All my life, I’ve been first in everything that I did,” he says. “It’s the perfect way to celebrate becoming a British citizen this year.” Widdicombe is proud to be part of such a progressive programme. “Strictly is a force for good,” he says. “Whether it’s disability or same-sex couples, it’s brilliant to have such an inclusive show at the centre of Britain’s entertainment industry.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenDance floor it … Radebe, Willis and Widdicombe.Photograph: Guy Levy/BBC/PAThe trio know all eyes will be on them and are braced for the scrutiny. “We’re all coming to this as Strictly fans ourselves,” says Willis. “We’re there to enjoy it alongside the viewers, rather than change anything. There’s no new set. It will still look and feel like Strictly. If any TV show is an institution, it’s this one. We just want to keep the ball in the air and not let down something so beloved by the nation.” “I squeal every time you say that,” giggles Radebe.Willis and Widdicombe truly are superfans. Asking about their all-time favourite contestants provokes an in-depth debate. “I loved Abbey Clancy in 2013,” says Willis. “And Rose Ayling-Ellis was sensational five years ago.” Widdicombe chips in: “Although Johannes and John Whaite were terrific that year as well.” “Thank you, darling,” beams Radebe.Widdicombe’s love of the show was prompted by parenthood. “I used to be out gigging every weekend but since we had our first daughter in 2017, it’s been our family ritual on a Saturday night. I adored Bill Bailey, Chris McCausland and Hamza Yassin. On the flipside of the coin, I found Tony Adams incredibly inspiring.” “You just liked his sparkly pants,” teases Willis.Widdicombe may be a Strictly aficionado, but work commitments prevented him from watching last year’s series. “I was on tour, so I followed it via your Guardian liveblogs,” he says. “I’ve got to ask, will you still be doing Frockwatch? Comparing what the three of us are wearing each week? Please say yes. Jojo’s suddenly got something to play for.”When we meet, they’re fresh from pre-recording a supersize group dance to open the series – with the new hosts front and centre. “You’re in for a treat,” says Radebe. “Josh has already been on the dancefloor [he performed a Charleston in the 2024 Christmas special while dressed as a penguin] but Emma had her first taste of what the celebs go through, especially the nerves.”“It was a baptism of fire,” says Willis. “We were terrified but, within 10 minutes, we were having the time of our lives. It looked like the end of Grease, where everyone comes together for a dance routine. I’m living my childhood dreams.” “I loved how seriously you took it,” says Radebe. “Emma sent me a video last week of her practising in her backyard.”Did Widdicombe’s penguin pedigree stand him in good stead? “Jojo seems to find that question amusing, for some strange reason,” deadpans Widdicombe. “They’re very different dance disciplines. I had to turn off my Charleston brain and turn on … whichever dance we were doing.” All three dissolve into laughter.Following that razzle-dazzle group number, this year’s pairing-up process will take a new form. “Celebs and pros are coupling up live on the floor with more dance than ever,” says Widdicombe. “It’ll make a thrilling start to the series.” “It’s roulette meets the Instant Dance Challenge,” says Radebe. “I’m jealous I won’t be part of it.” In another departure from the previous era, expect these hosts to don fancy dress for theme weeks. “Try and stop us!” chorus Willis and Widdicombe. “I’ll be in heaven,” says Radebe.They’re due back in the ballroom, so it’s time for one last question. How will the new-look line-up gauge their success? “I suppose if we’re asked back next year,” says Willis. “Getting a second series is always a good measure.” “I won’t consider this a success until I win Frockwatch,” says Widdicombe. “It’ll be the biggest upset in TV history!”Strictly Come Dancing returns to BBC One and BBC iPlayer on Saturday 19 September.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionStrictly Come DancingJosh WiddicombefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘That was all secret’: the ‘gay mole’ who fought the BBC to show the first queer kiss on kids’ TV | Television | The Guardian
description: Everyone thinks Byker Grove broke the taboo in 1994, but another teen drama got there first. Here’s the astonishing story of Two of Us, which put a gay relationship on UK screens – and was the original Heartstopper
Author: Scott Bryan
Headline: Everyone thinks Byker Grove broke the taboo in 1994, but another teen drama got there first. Here’s the astonishing story of Two of Us, which put a gay relationship on UK screens – and was the original Heartstopper
Content: ‘The most unusual programme in the history of TV’ … Jason Rush as Matthew and Lee Whitlock as Phil in Two of Us.Photograph: Scene/BBCView image in fullscreen‘The most unusual programme in the history of TV’ … Jason Rush as Matthew and Lee Whitlock as Phil in Two of Us.Photograph: Scene/BBCTelevision‘That was all secret’: the ‘gay mole’ who fought the BBC to show the first queer kiss on kids’ TVEveryone thinks Byker Grove broke the taboo in 1994, but another teen drama got there first. Here’s the astonishing story of Two of Us, which put a gay relationship on UK screens – and was the original HeartstopperScott BryanThu 10 Sep 2026 05.53 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 06.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I started looking for anything queer aimed at kids on TV from around the time I was born in 1989, I came across a children’s drama called Two of Us. Directed by Roger Tonge and written by Leslie Stewart, it was surprisingly akin to the2020s series Heartstopper, both in its plot and in the way it makes you feel. But the reaction at the time couldn’t have been more different.Both feature one character who realises he likes both boys and girls, who falls in love with another guy. Both are set at a comprehensive school. Both have characters who face homophobia and stigma but manage to find a way through because of their love and support for each other.Yet while Heartstopper resulted in near-universal critical acclaim and received a string of awards, Two of Us was pulled from its planned BBC transmission and was not shown until the following year, 1988. It ended up being shown late at night, with the happy ending changed and a single kiss between the boys removed. The Sun ran an editorial saying that the film should be “returned where it belongs: the closet.”View image in fullscreenHeartstopper.Photograph: Samuel Dore/Netflix“The real shock for me was that we were quite mild, really,” Stewart tells me now. “It was just a love story. I spoke to Roger. I said, the note we must keep, and that I’m keeping, is that it’s a love story, but it’s just two boys.”He’s right. It is mild. It is just a love story. I’ve seen it. It could be filmed and shown today, albeit without some playground humour between Phil (Lee Whitlock) and his girlfriend Sharon (Jenny Jay). Only 60 minutes long, the film starts with Phil smitten with Sharon but pulling away whenever he is near his close friend Matthew (Jason Rush). At a disco, Phil shares a slow dance with her but locks eyes with Matthew. I knew what was happening here; any queer viewer would. Phil is clearly developing feelings for Matthew and doesn’t know what to do with them.Later, he looks at Matthew’s physique for just a little too long while they shower together at a local pool. With just the two of them in the showers, Matthew faces Phil and places his hand first on his cheek, then on his shoulder. He tells him, reassuringly, that everything is going to be OK. This hits me right in the stomach. The first time I saw same-sex attraction depicted on television was deep into my teenage years, after I knew I was gay, the day before I came out. It was a confirmation rather than a realisation, long after a swirl of anxiety had started to play out in my head.Deep down, I could sense why the film had been pulled, but I wanted to find out more. So I went to Seaford in Sussex, where the two boys eventually run off together in the film. I bought some fish and chips and ate them on the seafront before going to see Roger Tonge. In his hallway, when I enter his house, there’s a framed front page of the tabloid Daily Express: “BBC ACCUSED OVER GAY TV FOR SCHOOLS” it says in a large font. It’s his film.View image in fullscreenThe stars of Two of Us.Photograph: Scene/BBCOriginally made to be shown in schools as part of the BBC’s Scene strand, aimed at teenagers, Two of Us was commissioned for the rare treat in class when the television came out on wheels. The standalone programmes were recorded by teachers for use in the classroom and also repeated in the early evening on the BBC, attracting millions of casual viewers. Tonge’s hope was that the film would reduce stigma, change attitudes and provide hope for any tormented viewers. The creators knew it would receive some heat. Matthew and Phil at that time were legally underage: until 1994 the age of consent was 21, before it was lowered to 18 (apart from Northern Ireland). Between two heterosexuals? It was 16. “That was one of the driving facts of writing,” says Stewart. “Twenty-one? Come on!”Yet the events of 1986 and 1987 set a course that would change a generation of young queer people, myself included. The LGBTQ+ community was already in significant hardship from the hostility of the tabloid press and the suffering and associated stigma from the HIV/Aids crisis. Now there was a new law on the horizon: Section 28. The commission and filming of Two of Us in 1986 coincided with that moral panic resulting in the law’s introduction.Taking place the same time as the rise of the Moral Right, a belief in traditional family values and anti-homosexual sentiment, prime minister Margaret Thatcher capitalised on this panic and demonisation ahead of the 1987 general election. It was a vote winner. A British Social Attitude Survey at the time said that 64% of adults found sexual relations between two people of the same sex “always wrong”, up from 50% four years earlier.The people who made Two of Us took precautions while filming. The crew were advised not to tell anyone what it was about. Nervous bosses quizzed Tonge about how far the intimacy of certain scenes was going to go. “Where would the hands go when Matthew touches Phil?” Tonge was asked. He wanted to give a physical re-creation. “The only thing to touch was a filing cabinet,” he tells me. “So the filing cabinet became Phil, and I was Matthew, and I approached the filing cabinet and made sure that my hand stayed with the top drawer and didn’t go down.”Two of Us was due to air in March 1987 but was pulled by the BBC before broadcast. In a statement, the BBC cited the heated political debate at the time meant “it would now be difficult for many teachers to use these programmes in the manner intended”. Tonge and Stewart hoped that after the election the heat would subside and they could show the film, but Thatcher doubled down: “Children who need to be taught to respect traditional moral values are being taught that they have an inalienable right to be gay.” Inalienable right, as if we get to choose.View image in fullscreen‘Heated political debate’ … Phil and Matthew share a tent in Two of Us.Photograph: Scene/BBCThat September, stark new guidelines about what could and could not be taught about sex education were sent to all schools, paving the way for Section 28. There was a chance Two of Us could have been buried altogether, yet the new BBC Schools head, Alan Rogers, championed the film. He believed that in order to get it screened, changes would need to be made. BBC bosses demanded dialogue cuts. Tonge and Stewart accepted a more ambiguous ending. A kiss between Matthew and Phil in a tent together was also cut.Two of Us was eventually shown on Friday 25 March 1988 at 11.30pm. The timing was suggested by lawyers so it wouldn’t be seen as a direct challenge to Section 28 and so teachers could record it and decide whether to show it to their pupils. The BBC continuity announcer warned that it contained “themes of a sensitive nature.”In subsequent years, Tonge heard from then teenage viewers who had gone up to their rooms to secretly watch it without their parents knowing. I’m shown some letters forwarded to the Radio Times following its airing. I cannot begin to tell you how they moved me. There’s one from a teacher counselling a 17-year-old who was gay and had attempted suicide. Another from a viewer who declared themselves as being previously antagonistic and then wrote: “You have made one viewer a little less bigoted.” Nearly all of the calls received by the BBC that day were positive.One letter stands out to me, deep in a numbered file: “Look, men of 45 don’t cry, especially about TV plays. So, I’m not crying, honestly. I’ve just got a bit of grit in my eye [...] There are pains that won’t go away, even if you push them to the very back of your memory. You think your scars are healed, and then pow! – along comes something which re-opens the old wound, and it hurts like hell again. [...]I watched Two of Us, and it was very painful. The fear, the hatred, the rejection, the uncomprehending ignorance it depicted rang true. But equally true was the evidence of fear and rejection in the real-life BBC. A simple love story was delayed for many months while worthy men in suits debated whether it could be allowed to sully our screens. Finally, it was given the go-ahead, around midnight, after a gentle kiss had been suppressed. Even at midnight, a kiss between two men is too dangerous for today’s prissy, repressive BBC.This hurts me deeply. And it hurts me to realise that gay kids in our schools must still suffer as I did 30 years ago. Oh, in due course they will become hardened, as I did. They will push the pain to the back of their memories, until they believe that it no longer hurts. But the pain won’t go away.”After reading this, I learned something staggering. Two of Us was sold to different markets around the world, but it had to feature the version the BBC aired – the ambiguous ending with the kiss removed. Yet Tonge actually slipped them the original version with the happy ending and the kiss intact. The film also aired in full at LGBTQ+ festivals. “That was all secret,” he tells me. “[The BBC] don’t check what is going on.” For a while, the only place you could not watch the original version was where it was made, in the UK. “That must make it the most unusual programme in the history of TV,” Tonge adds.View image in fullscreen‘The BBC don’t check what is going on’ … Phil and Matthew finally kiss.Photograph: Scene / BBCTwo of Us was eventually shown in the daytime in 1990. Another press storm ensued, including the Daily Express front page that now hangs in Tonge’s hall. Yet again, without telling his bosses, Tonge managed to find a way to keep the ending ambiguous, but it featured the kiss in the tent. Two of Us had been stored in a special cage in the BBC’s film library for controversial programmes, but Tonge says it was taken out for a short while by what he refers to as a “gay mole” to restore the kiss.The casual nature with which Tonge talked about this took me by complete surprise. The BBC sent me a copy of the 1990 transmission featuring the kiss and confirmed that senior executives at the time did not know about it being reinserted. No school complained. Byker Grove has been widely lauded as the first gay kiss on children’s television, but Two of Us was four years earlier. It was a kiss, inserted in secret, and broadcast on television as an act of defiance.In my early teenage years I was grappling with my identity, with a lack of television that made me feel like I was being seen. That absence most definitely left a hole. Thankfully, there were people like Tonge and Stewart trying to rectify it. All I know is that it is clear these shows and storylines were not missing: they were taken.This is an edited extract from Out Now: A Queer Journey Through ModernTelevisionby Scott Bryan, out now with Blink.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionLGBTQ+ rightsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sacha Baron Cohen lined up for Quentin Tarantino’s West End playwriting debut | Theatre | The Guardian
description: The Ali G and Borat creator is reported to be taking the lead in The Popinjay Cavalier, a swashbuckling comedy Tarantino is developing for early 2027
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: The Ali G and Borat creator is reported to be taking the lead in The Popinjay Cavalier, a swashbuckling comedy Tarantino is developing for early 2027
Content: ‘Armed with techniques that still get me into trouble’ … Sacha Baron Cohen.Photograph: Christopher Polk/Variety/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Armed with techniques that still get me into trouble’ … Sacha Baron Cohen.Photograph: Christopher Polk/Variety/Getty ImagesTheatreSacha Baron Cohen lined up for Quentin Tarantino’s West End playwriting debutThe Ali G and Borat creator is reported to be taking the lead in The Popinjay Cavalier, a swashbuckling comedy Tarantino is developing for early 2027Chris WiegandStage editorThu 10 Sep 2026 13.04 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 13.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHe will soon be seen resuming his old Staines rudeboy persona in the filmAli G: Who Iz I?, but Sacha Baron Cohen may also be eyeing a new departure – on stage.The actor will reportedly star inQuentin Tarantino’s first play, The Popinjay Cavalier, which is billed as a“rambunctious comedy of deception and disguise” and a “sweeping celebration of theatre and its heightened romance”, set in 1830s Europe.According to Deadline, Baron Cohen will play the swashbuckling title character in the play, which Tarantino will also direct.The Popinjay Cavalier, presented by Sonia Friedman Productions and Sony Pictures Entertainment, was announced in March and has a planned opening date of early 2027, in a West End theatre yet to be confirmed. Tarantino, who now lives in Tel Aviv, said last year that he would move to England with his family to work on the play and that it would take up between 18 and 24 months of his life.View image in fullscreenQuentin Tarantino in 2023.Photograph: Jacopo M Raule/Getty Images for Belles Rives GroupIn July, Friedman told the Sunday Times that Tarantino was “very theatre literate”, and that “the most refreshing thing about him, which not all writers and directors have, is his interest in the audience experience. He wants the audience to have the best freaking night out in the theatre they’ve had all year.”Baron Cohen, who took his successful TV characters such as Ali G and Borat from the small to the big screen with huge success, has not yet had a leading role in a major stage production. He trained with the French clown guru Philippe Gaulier. When Gaulier died earlier this year,the actor told the Guardian: “If I hadn’t crossed paths with him, I’d probably be doing something terribly sensible. Instead, I chose comedy – entirely because he believed in me, pushed me, and armed me with techniques that still get me into trouble.”Tarantino cast Baron Cohen in a small role in his 2012 western Django Unchained but the actorlater saidthat he withdrew from the production in order to star in Tom Hooper’s film version ofLes Misérables, based on the long-running West End musical.Ali G: Who Iz I? is released next month. Publicists for Baron Cohen and The Popinjay Cavalier did not confirm the casting when contacted.Explore more on these topicsTheatreWest EndSacha Baron CohenQuentin TarantinoComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)newsShareReuse this content

title: Elon Musk attacks film-maker behind documentary about him | Elon Musk | The Guardian
description: Tech mogul calls director Alex Gibney a ‘bitter old man’ who has ‘zero integrity’ in series of posts on X
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Tech mogul calls director Alex Gibney a ‘bitter old man’ who has ‘zero integrity’ in series of posts on X
Content: Elon Musk described the film as a ‘hit piece that misses’.Photograph: Gonzalo Fuentes/ReutersView image in fullscreenElon Musk described the film as a ‘hit piece that misses’.Photograph: Gonzalo Fuentes/ReutersElon MuskElon Musk attacks film-maker behind documentary about himTech mogul calls director Alex Gibney a ‘bitter old man’ who has ‘zero integrity’ in series of posts on XMichael SavageMedia editorThu 10 Sep 2026 08.29 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElon Muskhas issued an angry tirade at the film-maker behind a four-hour documentary about his life and influence, labelling the director, Alex Gibney, a “bitter old man” who has “zero integrity”.Gibney, who has previously made films about the collapse of Enron,WikiLeaksand Vladimir Putin, premiered his Musk documentary at theVenice film festivalthis week. He said he believed the world’s richest man was“extremely dangerous”.Musk review – epic study of the world’s richest and most banal manRead moreIn a series of posts on X, whichMusk bought for $44bn in 2022, the tech mogul railed against the film as a “hit piece that misses”, adding its four-hour length also made the documentary, which is highly critical of Musk, “as boring af”.Musk also appeared to push at conspiracy theory,reposting an imagedepicting the Democratic party as a puppet, controlling another puppet labelled “Team Soros” – a reference to the billionaire George Soros, who has supported progressive causes.That puppet in turn controls another one labelled “Alex Gibney”, while the Gibney puppet controls another labelled “Hollywood”. In response to the picture, Musk stated: “Accurate.”In response to a supporter who said he had never heard of Gibney until his Musk film, Musk replied: “It’s a psy op” – a reference to a planned “psychological operation” designed to influence the public’s thoughts.“Gibney has zero integrity. Zero,” said Musk. “Fortunately, his movies are boring af … It’s a hit piece that misses, and makes the fatal sin of being boring for 4 hours.“Gibney just assembled a hit list of people who either have an axe to grind or don’t even know me (but still have an axe to grind) … He’s a bitter old man who lost the plot long ago.“Dogshit is worth more respect than Gibney.”Musk’s lawyer has alsothreatened to sue Gibneyfor defamation, NPR reported on Thursday.State handouts, 10,000 lasers – and Trump’s election: six things we learned from the Elon Musk filmRead moreThe documentary has caused a stir since its premier, as have the claims made by some of those involved in the film.Musk specifically denied a claim made by his ex-partner, the former Maga influencer Ashley St Clair, that his team offered her $40m to sign a non-disclosure agreement about their time together. “She was never offered that and has a history of making false claims,” he wrote.Musk also amplified a post by the podcaster Katie Miller, the wife of Donald Trump’s powerful adviser Stephen Miller and former communications director for Musk’s “department of government efficiency” (Doge). Miller complained about the alleged absence of Musk acquaintances and allies in the film.“It simply can’t be ‘definitive’ if the people who were present didn’t participate,” she said. “This fictional movie is a hit job by a self-obsessed Hollywood director.”Musk’s influence on public discourse through X, and the content it prioritises, is making international waves. While he has repeatedly intervened in the immigration debate in the UK, he also celebrated the strong result for Germany’s far-right Alternative für Deutschland party in this week’sstate elections in Saxony-Anhalt.Speaking at a press conference in Venice, Gibney said he had encountered a “sense of fear” among people he approached over his film. He surmised that Musk’s childhood in South Africa may account for how he behaves now.“He had a childhood that was very difficult and traumatic,” Gibney said. “To some extent he’s now playing out that trauma on the rest of us, if I were to psychoanalyse the situation.”Explore more on these topicsElon MuskAlex GibneyDocumentary filmsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nick Mohammed takes Claudia Winkleman’s role in stage version of The Traitors | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Finalist in 2025’s inaugural celebrity iteration will be the host of several variants, which will see different characters banished, murdered and victorious
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Finalist in 2025’s inaugural celebrity iteration will be the host of several variants, which will see different characters banished, murdered and victorious
Content: She’s behind you … Nick Mohammed and Claudia Winkleman.Photograph: Euan CherryView image in fullscreenShe’s behind you … Nick Mohammed and Claudia Winkleman.Photograph: Euan CherryTheatreNick Mohammed takes Claudia Winkleman’s role in stage version of The TraitorsFinalist in 2025’s inaugural celebrity iteration will be the host of several variants, which will see different characters banished, murdered and victoriousChris WiegandStage editorThu 10 Sep 2026 08.46 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 12.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn another twist for the intrigue-cloaked world ofThe Traitors, Nick Mohammed is to star in the new West End play based on the ridiculously gripping TV series.Mohammed, a finalist in the BBC’s first series of The Celebrity Traitors last year, will now play the host of the show, effectively taking over the role of Claudia Winkleman for the stage version. There are several different variants of the play, written by John Finnemore and directed by Robert Hastie, so audiences over the course of its run will see different outcomes as characters are banished, “murdered” and exposed as faithful or treacherous in the fierce competition to win a cash prize.The Traitors – Acts of Betrayalbegins performances at the Gillian Lynne theatre in London in May.Mohammed, also known for playing his comic alter egoMr Swallowon stage, said it was a “wildly ambitious” project. “John Finnemore has crafted an absolute masterpiece: a cycle of five plays that are each as funny as they are moving, and of course, deeply, deeply unpredictable … To take on Claudia’s role, as it were, is not just a privilege but a real challenge as an actor – I simply don’t have enough hair! But I will do my utmost not to disappoint.”A video filmed at the 19th-century Ardross Castle in the Scottish Highlands, where theBBCversion of the international franchise takes place, shows Winkleman with Mohammed as he takes The Traitors’ “Host oath”.Stephen Lambert, CEO of Studio Lambert which is co-producing the play, said: “The actor who portrays the host in these plays has to hold a live audience through an entire game each evening, five different ways. It needs charm, mischief, acting talent and complete control of the stage. Nick has all four, and the fact that he played the game and knows its intricacies, is a wonderful bonus.”The play is billed as being akin to a full series of The Traitors that unfolds over the course of one night. At weekday performances, “the story begins identically but takes five different paths. Characters banished or murdered early in one version emerge victorious in another.” On Saturdays, the audience plays a part in determining the outcome.The set, no doubt featuring the series’ famous round table for heated discussions, will be designed by Ben Stones. The other creatives ratcheting up the tension include sound designer Alexandra Faye Braithwaite, lighting designer Mark Henderson, choreographer Kate Prince and composer Martin Lowe.‘Everyone’s gonna hate me!’ Nick Mohammed need not fear – Celebrity Traitors fans will love his fabulous comedyRead moreEarlier this year, Mohammed was the presenter for the50th anniversaryof the Olivier awards, which recognise achievements in theatre, dance and opera. As host of the ceremony at the Royal Albert Hall in London, he followed in the footsteps of his Ted Lasso co-star Hannah Waddingham, who presented the Oliviers in 2023 and 2024.In the finale of The Celebrity Traitors, which hit a peak of 15.4 million viewers according to the BBC, an emotional Alan Carr emerged victorious after successfully deceiving his housemates – and was promptly congratulated and comforted by “faithful” Mohammed. Several actors, including Richard E Grant, Bella Ramsey and Myha’la, are among the celebrities taking partin the second series.Explore more on these topicsTheatreWest EndThe TraitorsReality TVBBCTelevisionClaudia WinklemannewsShareReuse this content

title: The Odyssey and Spider-Man propel record-breaking summer box office worldwide | Film industry | The Guardian
description: The biggest May to September of all time was recorded in US cinemas, with the UK enjoying a 56% rise in audiences, outstripped by an 88% lift in the Middle East and Africa
Author: Catherine Shoard
Headline: The biggest May to September of all time was recorded in US cinemas, with the UK enjoying a 56% rise in audiences, outstripped by an 88% lift in the Middle East and Africa
Content: Hollywood’s Chinese theatre during opening weekend  of The Odyssey in July.Photograph: AaronP/Bauer-Griffin/GC ImagesView image in fullscreenHollywood’s Chinese theatre during opening weekend  of The Odyssey in July.Photograph: AaronP/Bauer-Griffin/GC ImagesFilm industryThe Odyssey and Spider-Man propel record-breaking summer box office worldwideThe biggest May to September of all time was recorded in US cinemas, with the UK enjoying a 56% rise in audiences, outstripped by an 88% lift in the Middle East and AfricaCatherine ShoardThu 10 Sep 2026 09.57 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs well as celebrating their wedding, the actors Tom Holland and Zendaya have something else to toast: their two summer blockbusters –The Odysseyand Spider-Man: Brand New Day – have officially made box office history.The films were credited as the driving force behind the US’s biggest summer season of all time, taking $4.761bn (£3.51bn) from 1 May-7 September, beating 2013’s $4.756bn.Spider-Man is currently on $2.4bn worldwide and likely to climb higher, while The Odyssey has made $1.6bn. Other key titles driving sales include Toy Story 5, Michael and The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, all of which have grossed over $1bn.The breadth of the success of Destin Daniel Cretton’s Spider-Man: Brand New Day was a particular surprise. The film is the best-performing of the year so far and the third highest-grossing film of all time. Its opening weekend was the second-best of all time behind Avengers: Endgame (2019) and it is also the second-fastest film to gross $1bn, doing so in six days.Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, meanwhile, is the highest-grossing “original” movie of the year, despite its adaptation from Homer’s epic poem. Low-budget original horror movies Backrooms ($394m) and Obsession ($513m) have also helped re-energise the box office.Sequels and spinoffs accounted for many of the underperformers, including Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu ($345.4m) , Supergirl ($126.4m) and Minions & Monsters ($518.1m – around half of 2022’s Minions: The Rise of Gru).Meanwhile, August cinema admissions in the UK rose 56% year-on-year to over 17m, according to the UK Cinema Association, signalling the biggest August since 2018 and the second-best performing month since July 2023, when Barbie and Oppenheimer opened together.Such an uptick is dwarfed by the picture in Europe, the Middle East and Africa, which saw an 88% year-on-year lift, according to Gower Street and the International Union of Cinemas. France’s 19.9m August admissions was the best number recorded during that month since records began 46 years ago, and marked a 50% increase from 2025.Italian cinemas recorded their best-ever June-August period, with 20.8m admissions and a take of €162.3m, as well as their best ever August. Spain saw a 71% year-on-year increase, while the Netherlands recorded a 77% lift.Explore more on these topicsFilm industryThe OdysseySpider-Man: Brand New ⁠DaynewsShareReuse this content

title: Secret systems used by Israel in mass killings of Gaza civilians revealed in new film | Israel | The Guardian
description: Testimony from Israeli military insiders involved in surveillance and remote killings features in documentary produced by the Guardian
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Testimony from Israeli military insiders involved in surveillance and remote killings features in documentary produced by the Guardian
Content: A scene from NAZA, a documentary produced by the Guardian and directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.Photograph: The GuardianView image in fullscreenA scene from NAZA, a documentary produced by the Guardian and directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.Photograph: The GuardianIsraelSecret systems used by Israel in mass killings of Gaza civilians revealed in new filmTestimony from Israeli military insiders involved in surveillance and remote killings features in documentary produced by the GuardianEmma Graham-Harrisonin Jerusalem andXan Brooksin VeniceThu 10 Sep 2026 09.42 EDTFirst published on Thu 10 Sep 2026 07.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTestimony from 24 Israeli military insiders ​on the secret ​systems used in ​the war on Gaza​ has been revealed in a new documentary film about the mass killing of Palestinian civilians.NAZA, a film from the Oscar-winning Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, was shown at theVenice international film festivalon Thursday as the only documentary competing for its prestigious Golden Lion award.The film’s title comes from an Israeli military acronym used euphemistically to refer to civilians expected to be killed in a military attack.Produced by the Guardian, it features extensive testimony from Israeli intelligence officers and soldiers involved in the surveillance and remote killing of Palestinian civilians.Interviews were filmed at night on rooftops in Tel Aviv, on the condition of anonymity because of the risks involved in speaking publicly about Israel’s war activities. The appearance and voices of participants in the film were digitally altered to disguise their identities.The interviewees detail the secret methods used by the Israeli military inGaza, including AI-based systems built to identify large numbers of potential low-ranking Hamas targets, who were then bombed in their homes at night, in the knowledge attacks would also kill their families.View image in fullscreenIsraeli soldiers at a military position overlooking the so-called yellow line in Gaza in May.Photograph: Ariel Schalit/APThe Israeli military hacked into phones to identify the location of such targets, and covertly listened into conversations with their wives and children moments before they were all killed.The film also features first-person accounts about the destruction of neighbourhoods where the Israeli military estimated that up to 25% of residents were still sheltering in their homes, the systematic burning of civilian homes, and the killing of civilians at a food distribution site.Abraham said at a press conference in Venice on Thursday: “We just told these officers: ‘Please describe to us what you did. How do these systems work? Sketch it out for us.’ Sometimes, in just asking the questions, you get the answers.“Some of them did not express remorse and some did. Some spoke out of indifference, some out of pride.”View image in fullscreenThe film’s directors, Rachel Szor and Yuval Abhram (centre), with producers and crew members at the Venice film festival on Thursday.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersSeveral interviewees worked in a secret intelligence unit that reports directly to the office of Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu; one said their mission was to “thwart peace”.“We made this film out of a sense of obligation to use our position as Israeli film-makers and journalists to examine the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians for which our country is responsible,” Abraham and Szor said in their directors’ statement.The directors stressed the film’s focus was not on “sporadic war crimes committed by rogue soldiers”. “It is on the orders themselves, the policies, the accepted practices, the language and logic that make those practices possible, and the people who operate within them,” they said. “The system and its cogs.”View image in fullscreenAn explosion after an Israeli airstrike in Gaza City on Wednesday.Photograph: Jehad Alshrafi/APThe documentary was co-produced by James Wilson and executive produced by Jonathan Glazer, the same team behind the Oscar-winning film The Zone of Interest.The film received a nearly 25-minute standing ovation after its screening, according to Variety, which called it a record for length of applause not just at Venice but at any major film festival and reported that Glazer embraced Abraham and Szor as it went on, while some members of the audience held up Palestinian flags.NAZA builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and the Guardian between 2023 and 2025. It was filmed and produced under tight security because of the risk to confidential journalistic sources, and its contents have remained a closely guarded secret before Thursday’s premiere.Paul Lewis, the Guardian’s head of investigations and an executive producer on the film, described NAZA as the culmination of “years of painstaking work to uncover and verify the systems used by Israeli military intelligence in Gaza”.Abraham said making the documentary had provided space to explore the collective impact of that work. “In this film we’re talking to 24 people. We are looking at systems of mass killing. There is something about cinema that allows you to explore structures and systems and how you put things together.”Before the premiere, Alberto Barbera, the Venice film festival’s artistic director, told journalists NAZA would be “truly groundbreaking”, calling it “a politically disruptive and cinematically extremely interesting work”.“It’s not just any collection of interviews,” Italy’s Cinecittà News quoted Barbera as saying. “It took them three years to convince these Israeli intelligence and military officials to share the work they did when the invasion of Gaza began, and I assure you, their testimonies are shocking.”NAZA review – Israeli intelligence officers cast chilling light on civilian deathsRead moreIsraeli attacks in Gaza since 2023 have killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, the majority of them civilians, and injured more than 174,000 others, together representing more than 10% of Gaza’s prewar population.Israeli restrictions on food shipments created a man-made famine last summer, and the Israeli military razed or damaged more than three-quarters of homes, so surviving Palestinians are now crowded into tent camps with little access to clean water or sanitation.Israel launched its war after the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, when more than 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken to Gaza by militants. The majority of the dead and hostages were civilians.Abraham and Szor were two of the four co-directors of No Other Land, whichwon the Oscar for best documentary in 2025.Drawing a connection between the two films, the directors said: “In the film No Other Land, we spent five years, together with [Palestinian co-directors] Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal, documenting the army destroying Palestinian homes in order to paint a larger picture of a system of occupation and ethnic supremacy aimed at the removal of Palestinians from the West Bank.“In NAZA, we are similarly connecting the dots of a system, gathering the testimonies of two dozen intelligence officers and soldiers and depicting the military systems used to perpetrate what a UN commission and the world’s leading human rights groups have described as a genocide.”Explore more on these topicsIsraelGazaVenice film festivalDocumentary filmsIsrael-Gaza warPalestineMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: The 2026 Proms: tell us about your favourite concerts | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: Ahead of Saturday’s Last Night, we want to hear what you’ve enjoyed this year. Has any of the new music made it on to your playlists? Which soloists wowed you? Did you sing along to Hey Jude with the Jupiter Ensemble? Share your listening experiences in the comments
Author: Imogen Tilden
Headline: Ahead of Saturday’s Last Night, we want to hear what you’ve enjoyed this year. Has any of the new music made it on to your playlists? Which soloists wowed you? Did you sing along to Hey Jude with the Jupiter Ensemble? Share your listening experiences in the comments
Content: Mirga Gražinytė-Tyla conducts violinist Patricia Kopatchinskaja and the Oslo Philharmonic at the Royal Albert Hall on 29 August.Photograph: BBC/Chris ChristodoulouView image in fullscreenMirga Gražinytė-Tyla conducts violinist Patricia Kopatchinskaja and the Oslo Philharmonic at the Royal Albert Hall on 29 August.Photograph: BBC/Chris ChristodoulouProms 2026The 2026 Proms: tell us about your favourite concertsAhead of Saturday’s Last Night, we want to hear what you’ve enjoyed this year. Has any of the new music made it on to your playlists? Which soloists wowed you? Did you sing along to Hey Jude with theJupiter Ensemble? Share your listening experiences in the commentsImogen TildenThu 10 Sep 2026 06.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith 86 concerts over eight weeks, the BBC Proms’ claim to be the world’s greatest and biggest classical music festival is hard to dispute. As the 2026 season draws to a close, we want to hear from you. Which proms have you enjoyed in the Royal Albert Hall, on the radio or online? Did you attend a concert inBristol, Sunderland, Gateshead or Mold?Our critics loved theBerlin Phil,John Wilson and his Sinfonia of London, theOslo Philharmonic with Mirga Gražinytė-Tyla, and Aurora Orchestra’s exploration and performance ofMahler’s 1stamong many others; while of the new music premiered this year, Turnage’sFesten Suitewas a riot of colour, Thea Musgrave’s Bassoon Concertowas a beguiling treatandJessie Montgomery’s Cello Concertoa mesmerising highlight.There were rarities –Poulenc’s Concerto for Two Pianoswas fun and brilliantly played by the Jussen brothers,Weber’s Oberonmade its Proms debut 200 years after its Covent Garden premiere, and there was a 250-strong choir bringing force and thrill to Berlioz’s Requiem, and then, on at the other extreme, the extraordinary intimacy of the six voices of theGesualdo Six holding the entire hall rapt with a programme of early musicin a late-night prom.View image in fullscreenDancing and beaming: Ladysmith Black Mambazo’s Under African Skies - The Songs of Graceland Prom.Photograph: Andy ParadiseSouth Africa’s Ladysmith Black Mambazo delighted a completely sold-out hall in a late night Prom in early August – I have never been to a concert where teenagers and pensioners alike were dancing and beaming. Listening on the radio, I lovedBritten’s Les Illuminationswith soprano Julie Roset (part of the Sinfonia of London’s second prom), and was stopped in my tracks by the extraordinary vocal acrobatics on display inStrauss’s Ariadne auf Naxos, brought to the Proms in a semi-staging by Glyndebourne.What did you think? Was there too much Beethoven and Berlioz and not enoughBax? What pieces did you hear for the first time and fall in love with? (For me, I didn’t know Bartók’s Music for Strings, Percussion and Celesta and was captivated by theBBC Scottish’s performance).All our proms reviewsare here, every Proms concert can be listened to on BBC Sounds until 11 October andthere’s a wide selection to watch on iPlayer,includingMartha Argerich’s Beethoven, theNational Youth Orchestra conducted by Thomas Adèsand theJames Bond celebration.Meanwhile next year is the centenary of the BBC’s funding and running the concerts. What would you like to see in 2027’s festival?Over to you …Explore more on these topicsProms 2026Classical musiccalloutShareReuse this content
