title: No food, no water, and a lone Abba record: my day out at Channel 4’s hellish new reality show | Television | The Guardian
description: Apocalypse dumps contestants in an abandoned town without essential supplies. Is it a serious test of endurance or just titillation? Our writer is parachuted in to find out
Author: Michael Segalov
Headline: Apocalypse dumps contestants in an abandoned town without essential supplies. Is it a serious test of endurance or just titillation? Our writer is parachuted in to find out
Content: ‘I found no water, no source of heat, no tin of pilchards’ … our writer on the set of Apocalypse.Photograph: Matthew Salacuse/C4View image in fullscreen‘I found no water, no source of heat, no tin of pilchards’ … our writer on the set of Apocalypse.Photograph: Matthew Salacuse/C4TelevisionNo food, no water, and a lone Abba record: my day out at Channel 4’s hellish new reality showApocalypse dumps contestants in an abandoned town without essential supplies. Is it a serious test of endurance or just titillation? Our writer is parachuted in to find outMichael SegalovThu 10 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 03.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIhave no shame confessing that I’d be a crap companion during the apocalypse. My practical skills are limited, I’d be a right Debbie Downer and I don’t respond well to sharing food. Still, last November, two survival experts spent a morning making a valiant effort to prepare me for Armageddon deep in the rural Indiana countryside.I had ventured to the US midwest to see the making of Apocalypse, an ambitious new Channel 4 reality series: an eight-parter following 16 people attempting to sustain themselves after an unexplained catastrophe from which only they appear to have survived.I was to experience the abridged version: my training only lasted a couple of hours, whereas the real participants will get three days of prep. They’ll then have to endure a month in the doomsday simulation. I only had to muddle on until dinnertime.After an hour spent in a gravel-pit junkyard, I could (theoretically) build a shower and make a torch with scavenged items. I’d learned how to open a tin of pilchards sans can opener (thwack it on concrete) and to start a fire without a lighter or matches (twigs, maybe?). Induction over, I was blindfolded and bundled into a minivan. We stopped, and I was shoved out, just as the show’s participants would be. As I peeled off my mask, I saw for the first time the extraordinary location in which Apocalypseis set: a thousand-acre abandoned town comprising hundreds of individual buildings.double quotation markIn a state of mild peril … I walked for miles … like I’d been dropped inside a video game, only without instructionsThe fictional town of Riverside wasn’t built from scratch for the show. The production took over Muscatatuck Urban Training Center, about 70 miles west of Cincinnati, a site usually used by police and military groups to train in urban warfare.There were no Big Brother-style CCTV cameras on set; kitting out the vast site would be impossible. Instead, a small team of producer-directors would live among Riverside’s residents, documenting every moment.Out there in Riverside on my own, in a state of mild peril, I started to explore. I walked past burnt-out vehicles and the remnants of a tanning salon; a multistorey car park and a smashed-up cop car. The Riverside Memorial High School building looked as if it had been ransacked. In every corner of every room in the hospital, I found meticulous attention to detail: IV drips, dusty bedpans, even a game of Twister left on its otherwise looted gift-shop shelves.Series producer Jake Smith was tasked with turning the training centre into a live-in stage. “I had to imagine what people might actually do in there,” he said, “start plotting out imaginary storylines: if they found this, what could they do?” He watched “grim” survival shows on YouTube and took inspiration from prepper content. Yes, scarcity of life’s essentials would see contestants struggle for our titillation, “but I also want there to be comedy and joy with the dark”.View image in fullscreenApocalypse contestant Scott looks around Riverside.Photograph:  /Channel 4Alongside functional necessities, Smith’s team included some surprises. A battery-powered candy floss machine was squirrelled away. “It’s so unexpected in an apocalypse context,” he said, “that I can envisage a funny sceneifthey find it.” There was also a disco ball, a dozen Christmas crackers, a record player and one record (Dancing Queen by Abba). Inside the bus station was a broken ATM, next to which Smith sprinkled $200 in cash. “They may talk about what it’s like to be in a world where money means nothing,” he said, “or how society could function differently.” They might just use the bills as toilet paper.Whether or not these potential plot points are discovered – and what happens if they are – is beyond Smith’s control. “That’s what I love about this,” he said. “It’s not formatted, like so much TV now. No elimination votes or must-win, set-up challenge.” There’s no prize money either. So much TV today feels “rinse and repeat”, he explained. “The Traitors comes out, then suddenly every network’s trying to do their version.” Granted, survival shows have been on our screens for more than a quarter of a century, “but a derelict city is a new environment. We’ve built it; now it’s over to them. We will see what they come up with in this ‘choose your own adventure’ world.”As for my own adventure? Let loose around the town, I walked for miles past a railway station (train included), a church, a prison, a motel and a lake with cars semi-submerged in water. It was like I’d been dropped inside a video game, only without instructions.Even the edges of its seemingly limitless playable area only became visible when I rubbed up against them: doors that didn’t open, walls that curved away from me, a row of stacked shipping containers blocking off the horizon.Darkness was approaching when the producers rescued me. I’d found no water, no source of heat, no tin of pilchards. There’d been talk of me spending the night on site – I’m not convinced I would have made it through. If I’d been caught on camera, my ineptitude might well have made for compelling watching, but it would have felt somewhat sadistic, too.View image in fullscreenContestants Steven and Kyra find their way around Riverside.Photograph: Channel 4Later I watched in production HQ as the participants entered. A wall of screens beamed back a series of live feeds, which a team monitored day and night. On one wall was a large white sheet split into 28 daily sections and titled “Architects of the apocalypse”. It’s here that storylines and character arcs would be produced in real time.Executive producers Jo Harcourt-Smith and Tim Whitwell spent years trying to get access to the site. With about 85% of the UK’s population living in urban areas, Harcourt-Smith felt that “if shit does hit the fan, it’s going to be in towns and cities that we all end up having to survive. We wanted to find out what that would be like.”“We’re interested in some of the practicalities and processes,” says Whitwell, “but it’s all about how youfeelwhen you’re in this situation. We’ve created a playground in which ordinary people will experience something extraordinary.”Months later I found myself mulling over this noble cause as I watched early episodes in which TV archetypes – blokey chef, heroic Paralympian, Welsh farmer, clueless posh man – muddle through with the content creators. The participants fail and succeed, fight and bond, cry and laugh. They go to the loo in buckets.double quotation markIn an era when reality TV ethics are being scrutinised, how can viewer pleasure be squared with participant discomfort?The series is firmly in the “factual-entertainment” reality television genre, in which human stories and emotions are evoked for the viewer’s enjoyment. It’s in the canon alongsideThe Island with Bear Grylls(Whitwell was an executive producer), ITV’sSurvivorfrom 2001-2 and early iterations ofShipwrecked.But in an era when the ethics of reality television are being increasingly scrutinised, how can viewer pleasure be squared with participant discomfort? What differentiates a worthwhile endeavour from a circus of manipulation?Su Holmes, a University of East Anglia professor and TV historian, tells me this tension has always been present, even in the earliest days of “fact-ent”. She points to prank show Candid Camera, which aired in the US in 1948, and the Americanquiz showscandals of the 1950sin which rigged outcomes and scripted performances caused national outrage. “Questions always arise when ‘ordinary’ people are put in a constructed reality,” she says. “How much is manufactured – real emotion versus performance? Where is the tipping point into exploitation?”View image in fullscreenContestants Kyra, Louise and Steven in ‘Riverside’ AKA Muscatatuck Urban Training Center.Photograph: Channel 4In the early days of reality TV, cast members had little concept of what it meant to be televised. Now contributors enter these environments eyes open. Few believe they’ll become overnight celebrities, and most understand the basic concept of an edit. A genuine interest in a money-can’t-buy experience remains a pull, as does the prospect of leveraging the exposure. Every Apocalypse participant I speak to after filming gushes about their time in Riverside.“It totally changed my perspective,” TikToker Steven Mckell tells me. “There, finding a bag of rice was the greatest feeling – it makes you appreciate the small things. I learned to be more in the moment, to let my guard down.” Cabbie Brooke McCreaner shares a similar sentiment. “I’ve been through the trenches. I’ve had some struggles. To be stripped of everything? It was the opportunity of a lifetime. I would go back in a heartbeat,” she says.Promotional material for Apocalypse bills it as “a bold and ambitious social experiment”. Broadcasters such as Channel 4 and the BBC have always framed fact-ent in lofty terms, Holmes believes, to justify the shows in their public service remit. “Look at the early 2000s adverts for Big Brother,” she says. “It’s not ‘Come gawp at these people’ – it was framed as a social experiment.”‘Men and boys need to see this’: Jo and Kush and the joy of Race Across the WorldRead moreThat’s not a criticism, she is quick to add. Holmes is a reality TV super-fan. She argues that “these shows can be exploitative and commercialisedandraise important questions, explore complex themes and expose ideas about society like nothing else can”.Back in Muscatatuck, as soon as the show’s participants-slash-human guinea pigs were let loose, I couldn’t tear my eyes away from the action. I wanted to see them succeed but also to witness their strains and blunders, how they coped with exhaustion and hunger; that first moment when they clocked that across the endless acres there wasn’t a single flushing loo.Prying on pressured human emotions may for ever be ethically dubious. That doesn’t make it any less engrossing. Fact-ent shows get greenlit because we keep watching them. And while that’s the case, I’d prefer to tune into shows that at least attempt to make my voyeurism feel vaguely worthwhile.Apocalypsestarts onChannel 4, 13 September, 9pm.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionReality TVfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: The Paper is back – with more hilarity from the US Office writers | Television | The Guardian
description: Domhnall Gleeson and scene-stealing Sabrina Impacciatore lead the shenanigans in the newsroom mockumentary. Plus: Ludwig returns. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Domhnall Gleeson and scene-stealing Sabrina Impacciatore lead the shenanigans in the newsroom mockumentary. Plus: Ludwig returns. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Domhnall Gleeson (left) as Ned with Chelsea Frei as Mare and Eric Rahill as Travis.Photograph: Peacock/SkyView image in fullscreenDomhnall Gleeson (left) as Ned with Chelsea Frei as Mare and Eric Rahill as Travis.Photograph: Peacock/SkyTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: The Paper is back – with more hilarity from the US Office writersDomhnall Gleeson and scene-stealing Sabrina Impacciatore lead the shenanigans in the newsroom mockumentary. Plus: Ludwig returns. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Hannah J Davies,Priya Elan,Phil HarrisonandSimon WardellThu 10 Sep 2026 01.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Paper9pm, Sky OneThe mockumentary about a local newspaper from the writers of The Office US is back – which, crucially, means the return of show-stealing Sabrina Impacciatore as clueless managing editor Esmeralda. New editor Ned (Domhnall Gleeson) may now have an award-winning team, but it has only made them hungry for more wild stories. Then there’s the added HR drama of a workplace romance …Hollie RichardsonRenovation Rescue8pm, Channel 4In between co-hosting this show, ex-Love Islander/DIY enthusiast Luke Mabbott has been doing up a 19th-century chapel in Cornwall. This episode follows his ambitious journey, involving a vaulted ceiling and bespoke gothic window – and he’s doing all this while also planning his lavish wedding.HRLudwig9pm, BBC OneView image in fullscreenBack on the case … David Mitchell in Ludwig.Photograph: BBC/Big TalkFamed for playing awkward eccentrics, Stephen Merchant is the perfect guest star for series two of the quirky crime drama, as a haughty snooker player accused of bumping off his rival. Meanwhile, Lucy (Anna Maxwell Martin) confronts shady MP Joanne (Sian Clifford), and unlikely hero John (David Mitchell) receives a warning.Hannah J DaviesLong Lost Family9pm, ITV1One of this week’s two subjects is Melissa, whose mother told her about another daughter she had to put up for adoption as a baby. What makes Melissa’s search for her older sister even more heartbreaking – and a race against time – is that their mum has been diagnosed with early onset dementia.HRTaskmaster9pm, Channel 4The comedians travel to a strange water feature to undertake tasks. But have Chloe Petts and Matt Lucas unintentionally missed a key part of the exercise (the camera operator certainly thinks so)? And what will impress Greg Davies less: Chloe’s one-eyed doll or a pair of moth-eaten pants procured by Isy Suttie?Priya ElanThe Great Plague: The Village That Saved Britain9pm, Channel 5This exploration of heroism in the 17th century has modern resonance given the events of 2020-21. In 1665, the Peak District village of Eyam quarantined itself after an outbreak of bubonic plague and, in doing so, prevented a wider spread. Ruth Goodman tells the story via individual tales of courage.Phil HarrisonFilm choicesCall My Agent! The Movie (Emilie Noblet, 2026), NetflixView image in fullscreenAction-packed … Camille Cottin in Call My Agent! The Movie.Photograph: Christophe Brachet/NetflixIt is five years since French talent agency ASK closed and the staff have scattered. Andréa (Camille Cottin) is about to direct her first film but is in need of a malleable producer, so she calls on Noémie (Laure Calamy), who now works on reality TV shows. From there, it’s a short step to getting the band back together – though everything that can go wrong does go wrong. With its starry cameos (Eva Longoria, George Clooney) and industry in-jokes, this spin-off from the TV show is a familiar pleasure.Simon WardellDune: Part Two (Denis Villeneuve, 2024), NetflixPart Three won’t land in cinemas until December, but such is the complexity of Frank Herbert’s fantasy saga that it’s best to get up to speed with the first two in the trilogy now. In this spectacular instalment, director Denis Villeneuve concentrates on the changing nature of Timothée Chalamet’s desert-planet messiahPaul Atreides and his relationship with Zendaya’s native warrior Chani. Prophecies and politics clash as an air of foreboding infiltrates events, while Austin Butler makes a memorable first impression as the smirking heir to Stellan Skarsgård’s evil Baron Harkonnen.SWSupergirl (Craig Gillespie,2026), 8.10am, 8pm, Sky Cinema PremiereFollowing her riotous introduction as Clark Kent’s cousin in last year’s Superman, Milly Alcock’s Kara Zor-El gets her own world(s) to play in. Director Craig Gillespie leans heavily into the scuzzy, Guardians of the Galaxy end of the comic-book spectrum, as the hard-partying Kara has to sober up after galactic pirates poison her dog, Krypto, and she has three days to find them and the antidote. Chuck in a plucky orphan girl (Eve Ridley) who is bent on killing the lead criminal and you’ve got yourself a 12A John Wick in space.SWExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightTV comedyReality TVDocumentaryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Eleventh Hour by Salman Rushdie audiobook review – stories with levity and laughter  | Salman Rushdie | The Guardian
description: The author explores themes of legacy, mortality and loneliness in the first work of fiction since his near-fatal attack
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: The author explores themes of legacy, mortality and loneliness in the first work of fiction since his near-fatal attack
Content: Salman Rushdie.Photograph: David Levenson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSalman Rushdie.Photograph: David Levenson/Getty ImagesAudiobook of the weekSalman RushdieReviewThe Eleventh Hour by Salman Rushdie audiobook review – stories with levity and laughterThe author explores themes of legacy, mortality and loneliness in the first work of fiction since his near-fatal attackFiona SturgesThu 10 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 10.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFive short stories and five readers make up Salman Rushdie’s collection, The Eleventh Hour, his first work of fiction since the near-fatal attack in 2022 where he sustained life-changing injuries. These tales find the author exploring legacy, mortality, loneliness and the ageing process. In these potentially bleak themes, Rushdie finds levity and laughter, as well as profundity.Late, read by the actor Naveen Andrews, is a ghost story set in King’s College, Cambridge, where an honorary fellow, SM Arthur, wakes up dead in his college room and wonders if he will be trapped there for eternity. He meets a lonely but very much alive Indian student, Rosa, who is stuck at college for the holidays. Sid Sagar reads The Old Man in the Piazza, an allegory about free speech and how “we have become bar room moralists. Does the thumb point upward. Does it turn down? … We are all now gladiators in the Colosseum of the Thumb.”The best of the stories,In the South, is narrated by Neil Shah who gives characterful voice to two elderly neighbours in Chennai, India, who spend their days bickering with each other on their porches. They are known as Senior and Junior because one is 17 days older than the other. Despite their cantankerousness, the two draw comfort from one another’s presence. When Junior dies on the street after being toppled by a passing Vespa – on the same day that a tsunami hits the south of the country – Senior comes to understand how “death and life [are] just adjacent verandas”.Available via Vintage Digital, 8hr 12minFurther listeningKinTayari Jones,Oneworld Audio,13hr,10minAngel Pean and Ashley J Hobbs narrate this sweeping tale of two best friends, born a few days apart in Louisiana, who grow up without mothers. As they get older, fate pulls them apart and they pursue different futures.LandMaggie O’Farrell,Tinder Press,16hr47minsNot long after the Irish famine, a cartographer’s son must finish a map of Ireland begun by his father away from the prying eyes of the British. This historical novel by the Hamnet author is read by Dane Whyte O’Hara.Explore more on these topicsSalman RushdieAudiobook of the weekreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Tony Gatlif obituary | Movies | The Guardian
description: Algerian-born French director of more than 20 films that celebrated Roma culture
Author: Garth Cartwright
Headline: Algerian-born French director of more than 20 films that celebrated Roma culture
Content: Tony Gatlif, right, with James Thierrée, on location for Korkoro, 2009.Photograph: Everett/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenTony Gatlif, right, with James Thierrée, on location for Korkoro, 2009.Photograph: Everett/ShutterstockMoviesObituaryTony Gatlif obituaryAlgerian-born French director of more than 20 films that celebrated Roma cultureGarth CartwrightThu 10 Sep 2026 11.28 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 11.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe French film director Tony Gatlif, who has died aged 77, was regularly described as “cinema’s Gypsy auteur”, so often did his films focus on Roma communities and their music. Between 1975 and 2025, Gatlif directed more than 20 films, beginning with La Tête en Ruine (The Ruined Head). That film was never released, and he struggled throughout the 1970s and 80s to get funding for his films, and then to find a distributor, before finally breaking through with Latcho Drom (1993, the title being Romany for “good journey”). An international arthouse hit,Latcho Dromis a meditative travelogue that blends footage of staged musical performances in contemporary Roma communities in Istanbul, Romania, Hungary, Slovakia, France and Spain, with historic recreations of such communities in Rajasthan and an Egyptian oasis.Latcho Drom conveys the centuries-long migration from Asia to western Europe of a nomadic people we now call Gypsies or Roma, as a fable told entirely in images and music. There is no voiceover, talking heads or text; instead Gatlif lets the striking settings and musical performances enchant viewers. It is an idealised portrait of the Roma, not a documentary (as some labelled it), and while Gatlif portrays the discrimination and persecution Roma communities experience, his emphasis was on celebrating Roma beauty and artistry.After the success of Latcho Drom, Gatlif went on to write and direct a feature film every couple of years, his most recent being Ange (2025). These films were all dramas and tended to focus either on a Roma community – Mondo (1995), Gadjo Dilo (1997), Vengo (2000), Swing (2001), Korkoro (2009) – or were road movies in which the protagonists drift across France, then head into eastern Europe or North Africa, seeking meaning and origins. His 2004 filmExilswon Gatlif the best director award at the Cannes film festival.View image in fullscreenA still from Latcho Drom, 1993.Photograph: Tom Specht/BarbicanHe was born Boualem Dahmani in Algiers, when Algeria was a part of France, to a Kabyle (Berber) father and a mother of Spanish and Roma heritage. His impoverished family lived in a shantytown on the outskirts of the city, he said, until 1960 when, with the Algerian war of independence raging, they joined a huge exodus of French Algerians in relocating to the south of France. A troubled adolescent, he regularly got into fights and engaged in antisocial behaviour, which led to him being sent to a reform school.He began using the name Tony Gatlif – choosing the surname from a local park in Algiers – so as to avoid the police in the Camargue region, who knew Dahmani too well. A meeting with the actorMichel Simonin 1966 led to Gatlif enrolling in a dramatic arts course in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, outside Paris, after Simon wrote a letter of recommendation.Gatlif worked as a jobbing actor while writing scripts for his prospective features. His second film, La Terre au Ventre (The Belly of the Earth, 1978), focused on a young mother and her four daughters, all dispossessed from Algeria. His third, Corre, Gitano (Run, Gypsy, 1981), was filmed in Spain and focused on a young Roma man accused of a crime he did not commit.Gatlif had now found his subject matter and rarely swayed from it thereafter. Les Princes (1983), about a petty, patriarchal Roma criminal living in a French housing estate, won him some attention, but it was Latcho Drom that established him as a film-maker of note. The film won the Un Certain Regard award at Cannes in 1993, and a growing interest in Gypsy music created a sizable international audience for Gatlif’s films.View image in fullscreenGatlif on the set of Transylvania, 2006.Photograph: Princes/Everett/ShutterstockGadjo Dilo (Crazy Foreigner, 1997) focuses on a young French man who drifts into a Romanian Roma community, begins a relationship with a Roma woman, then witnesses an anti-Roma pogrom. Providing career-defining roles forRomain Durisand Rona Hartner, Gadjo Dilo did so well that Gatlif cast its two young stars in his next film, Je Suis Né d’Une Cigogne (1998, Children of the Stork), a road movie heavily indebted toJean-Luc Godard’s 60s films, which received negative reviews and poor box office.He returned to the Roma with Vengo and Swing, set in Spain and France respectively, films that focus on flamenco and Manouche jazz musicians, with threadbare plots tacked on. Gatlif’s skills as a scriptwriter were marginal and the narratives of these two films, and two later road movies, Exils (again with Duris, this time heading to Algeria) andTransylvania(2006), are often clunky, no matter how striking the setting and music. Korkoro (2009), a period drama about the Nazi persecution of Roma in occupied France, laboured to convey the Porajmos (the Romani Holocaust) convincingly.Gatlif remained indifferent to such criticisms and continued making films his way, even if audiences diminished in recent years. In 2015 he was made a chevalier de la Légion d’honneur. He was taken ill and died in Arles, southern France, while working on a film.He is survived by his wife, Delphine, and three children, Elsa, Valentin and Lucia.Tony Gatlif (Boualem Dahmani), film-maker, born 10 September 1948; died 2 September 2026Explore more on these topicsFilmRoma, Gypsies and TravellersFolk musicobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Pressure review – stormy weather in tense D-day forecast retelling | Movies | The Guardian
description: Andrew Scott finds levels of complexity in a stoic character based on meteorologist James Stagg, the man who persuaded Eisenhower to delay Operation Overlord, for this slick wartime drama
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Andrew Scott finds levels of complexity in a stoic character based on meteorologist James Stagg, the man who persuaded Eisenhower to delay Operation Overlord, for this slick wartime drama
Content: Weather or not … Andrew Scott as James Stagg and Kerry Condon as Kay Summersby in Pressure.Photograph: Focus Features/PAView image in fullscreenWeather or not … Andrew Scott as James Stagg and Kerry Condon as Kay Summersby in Pressure.Photograph: Focus Features/PAMoviesReviewPressure review – stormy weather in tense D-day forecast retellingAndrew Scott finds levels of complexity in a stoic character based on  meteorologist James Stagg, the man who persuaded Eisenhower to delay Operation Overlord, for this slick wartime dramaPeter BradshawThu 10 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 11.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe historic gamble of D-day 1944 gets a new perspective in this slick and watchable, if slightly cheesy and unreflective, period drama, whose staginess reflects its origins in theatre; David Haig adapts his play with the director Anthony Maras. Andrew Scott – in RAF uniform, short-back-and-sides and ’tache – plays James Stagg, a brilliant Scottish meteorologist attached to the military during the war. Stagg arrives at the top-secret allied base of Southwick House in Hampshire stubbornly intent on telling allied Cmdr Dwight “Ike” Eisenhower, bullishly played byBrendan Fraser, that he has an outlier forecast of bad weather, which means D-day should be delayed from Eisenhower’s planned date of 5 June.This is to the rage of Col Irving P Krick (Chris Messina), the swaggeringly gung-ho American meteorologist who has always had Ike’s confidence until now. And if we were unsure about this character’s brash-Yank status, in his opening scene he literally shimmies and bops to theAndrews Sisters’ Boogie-Woogie Bugle Boyin the operations room to the uptight, thin-lipped astonishment of Stagg who, as overall commanding officer, tells the Americans to get that piano out of there.Krick figures they’re good to go on the 5 June, and Stagg’s obduracy also enrages the drawlingly contemptuous General Montgomery (Damien Lewis), who is mustard keen to get boots on the beach pronto. Everyone thinks they need to move right now. Stagg thinks they need to wait. But if he’s wrong, tens of thousands of personnel will die. And to top it off, his wife back in London is nine months pregnant. Pressure fronts of all sorts are closing in.Clearly, Stagg is someone who deserves to be as well-known in the annals of maverick wartime boffindom as code-breaker Alan Turing. But I think the movie is unsure if or how much to Turing-ify the character, which perhaps explains the casting of Scott, whose very presence seems to gesture at registers of complexity and even darkness that may not actually be there. His Stagg is cold, abrupt, arrogant; he has no interest or aptitude in reading the room. He arguably has Turing’s genius – despite insisting that meteorology is not a matter of certainty but assessment of probability or even simply educated guesswork.But Stagg clearly doesn’t have Turing’s inner pain, despite the pregnant-wife backstory; occasionally you can feel Scott as an actor straining for something in this material that will allow him to let rip. That something would appear to be his anguished fear that his wife and unborn child have been killed in a Nazi bombing raid – fears that Stagg just has to suppress. Scott cleverly has Stagg finger his wedding ring while making one of his shrill presentations to the frowning top brass. Kerry Condon plays Ike’s (real-life) private secretary Kay Summersby, whose job here is to show some female intuition and sympathy to Stagg on this point. But the movie mimics Stagg’s stoicism and it’s possible sometimes to forget what he’s silently going through.Of course, we know that, in the end, and to quote Eisenhower in the film, “the sun’s gonna have his hat on”. It’s a slick presentation and earnestly performed, with an important story to tell.Pressure is in UK and Irish cinemas from 9 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsPeriod and historical filmsSecond world warAndrew ScottBrendan FraserMeteorologyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: for colored girls who have considered suicide / when the rainbow is enuf review – ‘choreopoem’ of sisterhood | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Starkly staged panorama of Black female experience rushes through its scenes but is delivered with feeling by its terrific cast
Author: Anya Ryan
Headline: Starkly staged panorama of Black female experience rushes through its scenes but is delivered with feeling by its terrific cast
Content: A relief and a release … (from left) Ibilola Rossi, Tatenda Matsvai, Cherrelle Skeete, Alex Thomas-Smith and Nadine Higgin in for colored girls who have considered suicide / when the rainbow is enuf at the Yard Theatre, London.Photograph: Camilla GreenwellView image in fullscreenA relief and a release … (from left) Ibilola Rossi, Tatenda Matsvai, Cherrelle Skeete, Alex Thomas-Smith and Nadine Higgin in for colored girls who have considered suicide / when the rainbow is enuf at the Yard Theatre, London.Photograph: Camilla GreenwellTheatreReviewfor colored girls who have considered suicide / when the rainbow is enuf review – ‘choreopoem’ of sisterhoodYard theatre, LondonStarkly staged panorama of Black female experience rushes through its scenes but is delivered with feeling by terrific castAnya RyanThu 10 Sep 2026 07.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt has been 50 years since this “choreopoem” by Ntozake Shange premiered on Broadway and brought the emotions and experiences of Black women to the stage. And yet, until now – in this production directed by Diane Page for the Yard theatre’s reopening – it has never received a major London run.Collectively, the poems form a rich panorama: tales of domestic abuse bound up in a threatening marriage proposal; infidelity that brings a devastating HIV diagnosis; and an eight-year-old girl who is inspired by the Haitian revolutionary Toussaint Louverture. In so many ways, they could have been written yesterday. Journeying between US cities including Chicago, St Louis, New York and San Francisco, seven brightly coloured “Ladies” – played by five actors here – cry out their stories, ready to be heard. Shange’s lyrical writing mixes their pain with surges of joy, as each woman takes her turn in the spotlight while the others watch on in witness and support.View image in fullscreenNadine Higgin in for colored girls who have considered suicide / when the rainbow is enuf.Photograph: Camilla GreenwellWith repeated refrains and sections that feel like a chorus, the play becomes both a relief and a release. In Britain, we’re perhaps more familiar withRyan Calais Cameron’s stunning modern response,For Black Boys Who Have Considered Suicide When the Hue Gets Too Heavy. And here, you can see the blend of poetry, rage, music and movement that inspired it. Page’s production is stark, with the Ladies’ voices left to drive its emotional highs and lows. It could hang a little longer in each section; before we have time to fully absorb its effects, we’re already whizzing on to the next. We need a breath to catch up.for colored girls: the 40-year-old masterwork that’s still captivating audiencesRead moreSupported by a mesmeric new soundtrack by Jammz and choreography by Ingrid Mackinnon, the piece beats with raw feeling. The Ladies break into soulful, almost spiritual moments of dance, as Ali Hunter’s lighting design sends rainbows pulsing across the stage floor. The cast – Nadine Higgin, Tatenda Matsvai, Ibilola Rossi, Cherrelle Skeete and Alex Thomas-Smith – perform as though Shange’s words are being drawn from somewhere deep within them. In their moments of togetherness, the production reaches its most arresting force. Leading us through the many colours and shades of life, their sisterhood makes a case for hope.At theYard theatre, London, until 17 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Kimberly Akimbo review – hilarious musical about a sexagenarian teen is one for the ages | Stage | The Guardian
description: Maria Friedman plays a 15-year-old with a rare ageing condition in a heartfelt and funny show that manages to sustain its sweetness
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: Maria Friedman plays a 15-year-old with a rare ageing condition in a heartfelt and funny show that manages to sustain its sweetness
Content: Brighter than life … Maria Friedman with Gilli Jones in Kimberly Akimbo.Photograph: Marc BrennerView image in fullscreenBrighter than life … Maria Friedman with Gilli Jones in Kimberly Akimbo.Photograph: Marc BrennerStageReviewKimberly Akimbo review – hilarious musical about a sexagenarian teen is one for the agesHampstead theatre, LondonMaria Friedman plays a 15-year-old with a rare ageing condition in a heartfelt and funny show that manages to sustain its sweetnessLyndsey WinshipThu 10 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 11.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s a bizarre concept for a musical: a girl with a rare condition that causes her to age four times faster than her peers, in a family so dysfunctional that she’s the normal one. Meanwhile, the musical highlights are songs about cheque fraud and scurvy. And yet, somehow, through all this artifice and elaborate setup comes a show so sincerely heartfelt, one that is genuine, hilarious and utterly endearing.Kimberly Akimbo started out as a play, in 2001, by Pulitzer prize-winner David Lindsay-Abaire, adapted into a musical with composer Jeanine Tesori (Shrek, Fun Home, Caroline, or Change) in 2021. It was lauded on Broadway, where audiences fell for its feels and kooky charm and itwon five Tony awards.View image in fullscreenSunny … Maria Friedman as Kimberly Levaco.Photograph: Marc BrennerFor this London premiere, 66-year-old Maria Friedman plays the 15-year-old Kimberly Levaco, living with her pregnant mother Pattie (Niamh Perry) and alcoholic father Buddy (Peter Hannah). They have fled to a New Jersey neighbourhood after something unpleasant went down in their old town. Kimberly’s new-girl shyness soon gives way to a sunny, sweet character that Friedman plays wide-eyed and guileless, moving in the orbit of a quartet of misfit pals and the absolutely adorable Elvish-speaking, tuba-playing Seth (Gilli Jones). Their youthfulness is portrayed with an amped-up cutesiness, which works in a show where everything’s a little brighter than real life.Designer Soutra Gilmour puts the Levaco family in a three-storey house with a well-worn sofa and a well-used swear jar. It’s a brilliant set that rotates and turns into a skating rink, a school library, a corridor full of lockers decorated with stickers of Daria and Buffy the Vampire Slayer, in case there was any doubt we’re in the 1990s (see also: Seth’s Velcro wallet). Like everything else in this show it’s agile, slotting into place without heavy effort.This is a story, after all, that takes in criminality, alcoholism, neglect, thwarted dreams and life-limiting illness. It’s dealt with lightly – not dismissively – but with a deft handling of tone by Tesori and director Michael Longhurst. It is frequently laugh-out-loud funny (in an opening number about the joys of New Jersey and not fitting in: “I think Springsteen’s just OK,” sings Seth). Alice Fearn has great timing as Pattie’s felonious sister Debra who arrives with a get-rich-quick scheme.‘We all have an expiry date’: Kimberly Akimbo, the achingly funny musical about a teen with a 64-year-old bodyRead moreRather than anthemic choruses a la Springsteen, Tesori’s songs are conversational and colloquial (“Oh my God, I’m such a tool”), skating across musical styles from ukulele strums, to pop-soul and jazzy harmonies. But she can also suddenly pull the rug to land in more emotional territory, as in Kimberly’s desire just to sit at the table for dinner as a family for once.It’s a show about wanting things we can’t have and making the best of what we’ve got, and the privilege of having ordinary problems. Perhaps when the emotional climax comes, finally addressing the reality of Kimberly’s condition, the incredulity in the family dynamic is stretched a step too far, but there’s enough goodwill by that point for it not to matter.Kimberly Akimbo deals breezily with serious subjects and is all the more bittersweet for it. The average life expectancy of someone with her condition is 16, Kimberly tells Seth, as her birthday approaches. “It’s just an average!” she says brightly, and your heart melts at this winningly hopeful show.AtHampstead theatre, London, until 7 NovemberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatreMusicalsHampstead theatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Tubs: Hard Life review – indie’s Larry David spins self-loathing into glorious jangle-rock | Music | The Guardian
description: Britain’s best indie-rockers hold fast to their defiantly old-school sound, slipping wry sideways looks at despair in among hooky melodies that always sound like a good time
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Britain’s best indie-rockers hold fast to their defiantly old-school sound, slipping wry sideways looks at despair in among hooky melodies that always sound like a good time
Content: Punky heft … Dan Lucas, Owen Williams, Taylor Stewart and Max Warren of the Tubs.Photograph: Robin ChristianView image in fullscreenPunky heft … Dan Lucas, Owen Williams, Taylor Stewart and Max Warren of the Tubs.Photograph: Robin ChristianAlexis Petridis's album of the weekMusicReviewThe Tubs: Hard Life review – indie’s Larry David spins self-loathing into glorious jangle-rock(Merge)Britain’s best indie-rockers hold fast to their defiantly old-school sound, slipping wry sideways looks at despair in among hooky melodies that always sound like a good timeAlexis PetridisThu 10 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 10.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a track called Heaven or London from the Tubs’ third album, the quartet’s frontman, Owen Williams, offers a blunt self-assessment. He is, he suggests, “the singer of a rip-off band”, engaged in “wanking himself into an early grave”. It’s a strange thing to say given that the Tubs have recently become a critical cause célèbre. Their last album,Cotton Crown, was a regular fixture in best of 2025 lists. They have been unexpectedly clasped to the bosom of the heritage rock press and had a profile in the New Yorker, which called them a “British jangle-rock band, with a cheeky dirtbag edge”.View image in fullscreenThe artwork for Hard Life.That they’ve achieved this not by pandering to the dictates of musical fashion but by ploughing their own furrow makes it even more impressive. Much has been made of Williams’s vocal resemblance to folk-rock legend Richard Thompson, and you can understand why. But what the Tubs really sound like is old-school, pre-Madchester indie rock. Distorted guitars do battle with trebly acoustic or 12-string guitar, the punky heft and wistful melodies evocative of Hüsker Dü or the Replacements in their poppier, post-hardcore years. You could also throw pre-stadium REM into the mix: the most plangent of the lead guitar lines on Hard Life have a ring of Peter Buck about them, such as the lovely figures that spin around If You Don’t Love Me, and the arpeggio that drives In Your Place along for five and half minutes. The album comes liberally decorated with violin, which recalls Amanda Brown’s contributions to the Go-Betweens’ late-80s albums.None of these are particularly hip names to drop in 2026, an era in which what gets called “indie” largely cleaves to post-punk revivalism, misty shoegazing or the sound of the first Arctic Monkeys album – or the glossy 80s pop-rock that indie was once supposed to be an alternative to. O that might be part of the Tubs’ appeal: this is audibly not a band that’s been focus-grouped into existence or subject to the ministrations of an A&R department with a keen interest in Spotify playlists.The Tubs’ mounting success is a cheering thing, but it doesn’t seem to have cheered Williams much. Three tracks into Hard Life, he’s threatening to quit the band entirely. “I don’t wanna sell out this tour, don’t wanna play with the Tubs any more,” he complains when a relationship hits the rocks in If You Don’t Love Me. On The Way It Goes, meanwhile, he casts a gloomy eye Stateside, New Yorker correspondents and all. “If we go back to America, then it’s over,” he opines as guitars rage and sparkle around his pained voice, “because I can’t stand another fucking Yank telling me they’re sober”.The Tubs: Stoop to Me – videoBut as anyone familiar with the Tubs’ oeuvre to date would doubtless point out, this is very much par for the course with Williams’s writing. His songs exist in a peculiar space. On the one hand, they seem diaristic, alarmingly frank about a lot of heavy stuff, includinghis precarious mental health and his mother’s suicide. On the other, he freely admits to amping up their tone of self-loathing and painting himself as “more unlikable than I actually am” for blackly comic value, like a kind of alt-rock Larry David. On Hard Life, he takes this approach a stage further. Some of the songs seem to be entirely heartfelt; others are written from the viewpoint of a character whose primary concern seems to be underlining what an arsehole Owen Williams is: “The day never comes when you finally know exactly what you’re going to be,” he snaps on the title track, “apart from a fat bloke in a sad pub telling me ‘It’s a hard life’.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘There is an alternative to capitalism’: after addiction and losing a home to LA wildfires, indie rockers Diiv start againRead moreIt’s a curious, meta slant, but the results are grippingly entertaining and frequently hilarious, their impact intensified by the bright, hooky, major-key quality of the melodies and the blazing, live-in-the-studio energy of the Tubs’ playing: they sound like a good time, even when the lyrics are depicting the worst time imaginable. For a band with a resolutely traditional musical approach, they’re also not above throwing the listener a curveball. Do Yourself a Favour excavatesa lengthy 1982 Prince outtake from the Super Deluxe Edition of 1999, chops its running time in half and re-decorates it with layer upon layer of chiming guitars to stunning effect. You can perhaps also detect the influence of Prince in their odd predilection for backing vocals sped up to a cartoonish squeak.Perhaps some of the acclaim heaped on the Tubs is down to nostalgia – listeners of a certain age mistily recalling the music they heard on night-time Radio 1 in their teens. There’s doubtless some truth in that, but Hard Life, a moving, funny, immensely powerful album, suggests another, more prosaic reason: they’re very, very good at what they do.This week Alexis listened toMoses Boyd – Criticise (ft Amber-Simone)Not an Alexander O’Neal cover but a potent slice of 21st-century soul, complete with immense guitar solo and an emotive vocal from Amber-Simone.Explore more on these topicsMusicAlexis Petridis's album of the weekIndiePop and rockreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Todd Rundgren review – try-anything veteran doesn’t let his freak flag fully fly | Todd Rundgren | The Guardian
description: The 78-year-old has astonishing range but gets bogged down in middling rock, though later delivers some gorgeous acoustic songs – and a slinky Marvin Gaye cover
Author: Dorian Lynskey
Headline: The 78-year-old has astonishing range but gets bogged down in middling rock, though later delivers some gorgeous acoustic songs – and a slinky Marvin Gaye cover
Content: In resilient and versatile voice … Todd Rundgren.Photograph: Per Ole Hagen/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIn resilient and versatile voice … Todd Rundgren.Photograph: Per Ole Hagen/Getty ImagesTodd RundgrenReviewTodd Rundgren review – try-anything veteran doesn’t let his freak flag fully flyCadogan Hall, LondonThe 78-year-old has astonishing range but gets bogged down in middling rock, though later delivers some gorgeous acoustic songs – and a slinky Marvin Gaye coverDorian LynskeyThu 10 Sep 2026 05.38 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 05.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTodd Rundgren is a confusing man. After his tune-packed 1972 album Something/Anything? drew comparisons to Carole King and Brian Wilson, he took a pharmacopoeia of psychedelics and made a vexing masterpiece, A Wizard, a True Star, with no singles at all. He’s produced classic albums by Meat Loaf and the New York Dolls but he’s also released a record of nothing but vocals (A Cappella) and the world’s first interactive album (No World Order). Counting only the artists who appeared on his last two albums, his fans include Trent Reznor, Robyn and the Lemon Twigs. He called his memoir The Individualist.Rundgren certainly looks the part. With his Addams Family hair, tinted goggles and limber dance moves, he could be a goth raver. Everything he says sounds teasingly sarcastic, even when he’s thanking the audience for spending their “discretionary income” on a ticket. He says the curfew means he can’t tell stories about the songs but it would have been worth sacrificing a couple of his two-hour show’s stodgier numbers to hear them.Rundgren’s two sets represent more than half of his 26 solo albums as well as his bands, the Nazz and Utopia, but there’s scant evidence of the try-anything polymath who inspired generations of studio auteurs. While I Saw the Light is giddy power-pop perfection, there’s an awful lot of middling rock in part one. Due in part to the stuffiness of the all-seater venue and the advanced age of his fanbase, it never takes off.After the interval Rundgren travels to more rewarding destinations. A slinky cover of Marvin Gaye’s I Want You and an extraordinary a cappella folk song, Honest Work, showcase a voice far more resilient and versatile than most artists of 78. The acoustic section is simply gorgeous, with shades of Joni Mitchell’s capricious melodies on Cliche. When Rundgren grabs a baton to conduct his five-man band through the symphonic Kindness, he seems like the man who can do anything. What he chose to do this time is not the most interesting take on his unclassifiable career but as one man tells his friend on the way out, “You take what you’re given with Todd.”Todd Rundgren playsBristol Beacon, 10 September; then touring the UKuntil 13 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsTodd RundgrenPop and rocklive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Lise Davidsen: Verdi album review – star soprano gives opera’s leading ladies radiant power and vulnerability  | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Focusing on five Verdian heroines (and anti-heroines), the soprano has chosen roles that fit her formidable vocal talents perfectly. Edward Gardner and the London Philharmonic Orchestra provide detailed accompaniment for these striking portraits
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Focusing on five Verdian heroines (and anti-heroines), the soprano has chosen roles that fit her formidable vocal talents perfectly. Edward Gardner and the London Philharmonic Orchestra provide detailed accompaniment for these striking portraits
Content: ‘Her breath control alone deserves a Grammy’ … Lise Davidsen.Photograph: James HoleView image in fullscreen‘Her breath control alone deserves a Grammy’ … Lise Davidsen.Photograph: James HoleClassical musicReviewLise Davidsen: Verdi album review – star soprano gives opera’s leading ladies radiant power and vulnerability(Decca)Focusing on five Verdian heroines (and anti-heroines), the soprano has chosen roles that fit her formidable vocal talents perfectly. Edward Gardner and the London Philharmonic Orchestra  provide detailed accompaniment for these striking portraitsClive PagetThu 10 Sep 2026 09.45 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 10.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt some point, any star soprano worth her salt will try her hand at a Verdi album.Lise Davidsenavoids the fate of those who attempt to encompass the composer’s entire cast of leading ladies, focusing instead on five who fit her vocal talents like a glove.View image in fullscreenThe artwork for Lise Davidsen: Verdi.Photograph: DeccaShe opens with a commanding Lady Macbeth, her coloratura clean as a whistle and with gleaming, seemingly effortless top notes. Edward Gardner’s buoyant yet spacious way with the orchestral accompaniment affords Davidsen sufficient elbow room to create a more thoughtful schemer than is sometimes the case, culminating in a seamless sleepwalking scene where her breath control alone deserves a Grammy.For every kilowatt of power, she seeks out – and on the whole finds – moments of contrasting vulnerability (though none of Davidsen’s women are exactly shrinking violets). It’s most evident in the aria from Un Ballo in Maschera where Amelia pleads to see her child one last time. It’s there, too, in Elisabeth’s fatalistic Tu Che le Vanità from Don Carlo, but it can also be found in the darker recesses of Lady Macbeth’s La Luce Langue. Throughout, theLondon Philharmonic Orchestraprepares the detailed canvases for Davidsen’s striking portraits.There’s vocal beauty as Elisabeth comforts her dismissed lady-in-waiting and radiant stillness as Leonora raises her voice in prayer in La Forza del Destino. She’s at her most involving, though, in Amelia’s “gallows field” monologue from Ballo, and grappling with public versus private emotions in Aida’s Ritorna Vincitor!Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com. title: Make tracks: 8 of the UK’s best walking and cycling trails on former railway lines | Travel | The Guardian
description: Repurposed railway lines make accessible and family-friendly walking and cycling routes. Here are some of the best, from Somerset to the Highlands of Scotland
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Repurposed railway lines make accessible and family-friendly walking and cycling routes. Here are some of the best, from Somerset to the Highlands of Scotland
Content: The Headstone Viaduct on the Monsal Trail in the Peak District.Photograph: Lankowsky/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Headstone Viaduct on the Monsal Trail in the Peak District.Photograph: Lankowsky/AlamyGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.TravelMake tracks: 8 of the UK’s best walking and cycling trails on former railway linesRepurposed railway lines make accessible and family-friendly walking and cycling routes. Here are some of the best, from Somerset to the Highlands of ScotlandAnnabelle ThorpeThu 10 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheMonsal Trail,Peak District,DerbyshireStart/finishCoombs Road in Bakewellto Blackwell Mill inChee Dale, but there are lots of access points along the wayDistance8.5 milesCycle, hike or ride a horse along the Monsal Trail to explore a swathe of Derbyshire’s industrial history. This former stretch of the Midland Railway line winds past the imposing structures of two 18th-century cotton mills, through illuminated railway tunnels and over the Headstone Viaduct, which gives glorious views of the River Wye and Monsal Dale below. Interpretation and listening panels along the route explain the area’s history, geology and wildlife, while a short detour on to Monsal Head offers a panoramic view of the viaduct itself. Pause here for lunch or a pint atthe Monsal, or stop in atHassop Station Cafe, which offers bike rental alongside hefty sandwiches, homemade cakes and wood-fired pizza at weekends.monsaltrail.org.ukThe Strawberry Line,SomersetView image in fullscreenCycling on the Strawberry Line at Shute Shelve railway tunnel.Photograph: Joe Dunckley/AlamyStart/finishYattonrailwaystationto the old (unused)CheddarrailwaystationDistance10.7 milesNamed for the fruity cargo that trains once carried from the strawberry fields up to London, this flat, accessible route – shared by walkers, cyclists and wheelchair users – knits together former railway stations, cider orchards and small, historic towns. Direct trains run from Bristol to Yatton, where the not-for-profit, community-runStrawberry Line Cafeserves hearty breakfasts and homemade cakes, while next door theStrawberry Line Cycle Projectoffers bike hire and accessories such as child seats. The route runs through wildlife-rich wetlands, open grazing land and lush valleys, while the medieval square at Axbridge gives an insight into the region’s rich history, dating back to the 10th century, when it was a busy commercial centre. Settle in at theAlmshouse Teashop, in a building almost 600 years old, for freshly made soup and sweet treats, before setting off again.thestrawberryline.org.ukThe Mawddach Trail,Gwynedd,WalesView image in fullscreenThe toll bridge at Penmaenpool, over the Mawddach.Photograph: Henry Ciechanowicz/AlamyStart/finishMarian Mawr car parkinDolgellautoBarmouthviaductDistance9.5 milesMostly running alongside the Mawddach estuary, this tranquil trail is a great choice for birders, with peregrine falcons and buzzards whirling above, and curlews and oystercatchers in the salt marshes. The wide, even surface also makes it ideal for wheelchairs and mobility scooters, and there are several joining points along the trail, meaning you can walk or bike as little or as far as you like. Just next to the 150-year-old Penmaenpool wooden toll bridge, theGeorge III hotel and puboffers sweeping estuary views and classic pub food (including particularly fine pies), or pick up picnic supplies fromFork, Cork and Feathersin Dolgellau, which has a cold counter crammed with cured meats, cheeses and other local produce. There are seats and picnic tables dotted all the way along the trail.mawddachtrail.co.ukThe Cuckoo Trail,East SussexView image in fullscreenThe Cuckoo Trail.Photograph: Johan Siebke/AlamyStart/finishStation Road in HeathfieldtoHampden Park in EastbourneDistance14 milesA great choice for a family adventure, this mostly flat trail has five augmented reality “story stops” along the way – where, with just a quick scan of the QR code, children can interact with animated wildlife characters, solve puzzles and take a selfie with a grumpy badger. There are sculptures too, including carved wooden seats made from oak trees that fell during the great storm of 1987 and steel sculptures that act as mileposts.Cuckoo Shack Cafe, part of Priory Court Farm in Polegate, is set right on the trail and offers homemade-cakes, sandwiches and excellent coffee, but it is only open at weekends and during school holidays. Otherwise, a quick diversion into Hailsham offers a clutch of places to eat, including Neapolitan street food and wood-fired pizza atRustico.wealden.gov.ukThe Flitch Way, EssexView image in fullscreenThe former Rayne railway station, near Braintree.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyStart/finishBraintree station to Start Hill,near Bishop’s StortfordDistance15 milesDiscover a tranquil side of Essex by following this rural trail along the edge of the former royal hunting ground ofHatfield Forest– where fallow deer roam between the ancient oak trees – andGreat Notley Country Park, where families can take advantage of the 1.2km play trail, with slides, forts and swings. The main refreshment stop is 2 miles along the trail from Braintree at the Rayne Station centre, which combines theBooking Hall Cafewith the free-to-enterRailway Carriage Museum, a visitor centre and toilets. For something more sustaining (and a pint or two), theLion and Lambpub is just a short detour off the trail, in the pretty village of Little Canfield. Keep an eye out for kestrels and buzzards, plus brown hares dashing out of the hedgerows.explore-essex.comThe Wirral Way, Merseysideand CheshireView image in fullscreenThurstaston beach.Photograph: David Chapman/AlamyStart/finishWest Kirbyrailway station to Hootonrailway stationDistance12.2 milesOne of the first converted railway lines in England, the Wirral Way is now a dramatically beautiful coastal path running along the Wirral Peninsula. It takes in theWirral Country Park, whereWirral Way Bikesoffers cycle hire for adults and kids (including ebikes), and clifftop picnic spots have gorgeous views over the Dee estuary. Take a detour down the cliffs to Thurstaston beach for a spot of fossil hunting or a quick paddle, and pause at Hadlow Road station, which has been preserved in all its 1950s glory (when the passenger service stopped) as an open museum; it also operates as an information point for the trail. Time your walk or ride for sunset, when the mudflats glow rose-pink and gold as the sun drops below the Clwydian Hills, and take the short connecting path down to theHarp Inn, Little Neston, set directly on the estuary, for a sundowner to go with the view.visitcheshire.comThe Crab and Winkle Way, KentView image in fullscreenRewilded bison on the Blean.Photograph: Donovan Wright/PAStart/finishCanterbury West station to Whitstable HarbourDistance7.5 milesFollowing the route of one of the earliest railway lines, built in 1830, this hiking and cycling trail passes throughthe Blean, a large swathe of ancient woodland, home to the 13th-century church of St Cosmus and St Damian, and an RSPB reserve. It’s also home to Europe’s first free-roaming bison, introduced as part of arewilding initiativein 2022 by the Kent Wildlife Trust and Wildwood Trust. There’s not really anywhere en route to stop and eat, so either pick up treats for a picnic at theGoods Shedin Canterbury (an indoor farmers market, closed mondays) or save yourself for oysters and a glass of fizz at theWhitstable Oyster Company, right on the beach.explorekent.orgThe Dava Way,Moray and Highland, ScotlandView image in fullscreenThe collie dog memorial on the Dava Way.Photograph: John Bracegirdle/AlamyStart/finishMannachie Avenue in Forres to Dulicht Bridge in Grantown-on-SpeyDistance24 milesUnusually for a rail trail, the Dava Way includes a stiff climb from the Moray Firth up overDava Moorto the Dava Summit, at 320 metres (1,050ft), before heading back down to Grantown-on-Spey, following the Highland Railway line that operated for over a century, from 1863 to 1965. The ascent is well worth it for the spectacular views across the Moray Firth to Sutherland in the north, and south to the Cromdale Hills and the Cairngorms, while the ride back down is a breeze. TheDivie Viaduct, built in 1863, is the most famous landmark along the way, while the Halfway Hut is a restored shelter that makes a perfect spot for a picnic, with old photographs and route info on the walls (not for overnight stays).davaway.org.ukExplore more on these topicsTravelUnited Kingdom holidaysWalkingWalking holidaysCycling holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to choose the perfect wine for aperitivo hour | Wine | The Guardian
description: Whether you go for traditional champagne or sherry, or branch out with muscadet and picpoul, an appetite-whetting glass of wine will set you up for the evening ahead
Author: Mina Holland
Headline: Whether you go for traditional champagne or sherry, or branch out with muscadet and picpoul, an appetite-whetting glass of wine will set you up for the evening ahead
Content: Typically, an aperitif is light and crisp, which explains why sparkling wines are common choices.Photograph: AzmanL/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTypically, an aperitif is light and crisp, which explains why sparkling wines are common choices.Photograph: AzmanL/Getty ImagesWineHow to choose the perfect wine for aperitivo hourWhether you go for traditional champagne or sherry, or branch out with muscadet and picpoul, an appetite-whetting glass of wine will set you up for the evening aheadMina HollandThu 10 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBeginnings are important. As a writer, I’m all too aware of this: from the right introduction, the rest tends to flow. The same logic applies to drinks: a good beginning eases proceedings. For this reason, I am unbendingly particular about how I take my morning coffee and, if I’m drinking, what form an evening’s aperitif should take. Life’s too short for bad beverages, after all.An aperitif is arguably less a specific drink than an appetite-whetting moment with a glass of something. But what? Typically, when it comes to wine, an aperitif will be light and crisp, with any fruit character at the more green or citrussy end of the spectrum. Brioche-y sparkling wine, be that champagne, crémant or something English, and dry sherry such as fino and manzanilla, with their savoury notes, are traditional choices to ready your palate for food.One of my favourite wine discoveries of the past year or so has beenBodegas Alvearin the Montilla-Moriles region of Andalusia, which produces wines made exclusively with pedro ximénez (PX), a grape famous for producing the darkest, stickiest sherries out there. Its Tres Miradas cuvée in today’s pick is a unique dry white wine made with old vine PX grown in chalky soils; it has a light sherry note thanks to being aged under a layer of natural yeast (flor), but it is both fresh and structured, making for the sort of high-impact aperitif I’m after.Wines from maritime climates, particularly cooler ones, tend to be a safe bet, too, bringing the salinity and minerality I’m looking for to stimulate appetite. A txakoli from Spain’s Basque region, say, with punchy, citrus-apple notes and a touch of spritz to surprise the palate. Muscadet, made from the melon de bourgogne grape in the westernmost Loire, is another great, unsung white: crisp, affordable and a fine aperitif. Take a road trip along the northern French coast, and you’ll be spoiled for pre-dinner deals on a plate of oysters and a glass of this stuff. It’s often bottledsur lie– that is, with dead yeast cells that give the wine a rounder, almost bready flavour that works particularly well as an aperitif.Ocado has several available, with some for less than a tenner.There is also a breed of aperitif wine that both readies you for a meal and sees you all the way through it. Muscadet and its southern French cousin picpoul de pinet do this, as do albariño and zesty bourgogne aligoté, which usually has that Burgundian butteriness that can be hard to leave behind. Pale rosé is also a classic aperitif choice, as happy on its own as with a plate of crudites or a bowl of peanuts. The Pink Flamingo rosé in my pick, made in Europe’s largest organic vineyard in the Camargue wetlands west of Marseille, has a coastal freshness that I’d happily enjoy before, during and after a meal. After all, endings are as important as beginnings.Six wines that work brilliantly as aperitifsOliver Dubois Muscadet 2023/4£10.50 (with “mix six”) Majestic, 12%. A straightforwardly crowd-pleasing muscadet: lean, green and a great price.Pink Flamingo Organic Camargue Rosé£12.50 Waitrose, 12%. You’ll never want aperitif hour to end, nor does it have to. This peachy-pink, daisy-fresh number is food friendly, too.Rezabal Txakoli 2025£13.50 The Wine Society, 11%. Make your aperitif a Basque one with this energetic and petillant txakoli.Alvear Tres Miradas2022£17.50 The Whisky Exchange, ?13%. Green orchard fruit meets almonds and sourdough.Fortnum’s Muscadet Sur Lie Domaine de la Morinière £12.95, 11.5%. A lovely example of a muscadet aged on the lees. Lemony, saline and richly textured.Crémant de Loire, Domaine Catherine et Pierre Breton NV£23.40 Sip Wines, 13%. Possibly the perfect crémant, combining 40% red grapes with chenin blanc for a fizz that’s as generous as it’s refreshing.Explore more on these topicsWineFoodFrench food and drinkSpanish food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for a not-sachertorte | Cake | The Guardian
description: A chocolate cake inspired by the Sacher hotel in Vienna’s trademark creation and emulated by a local Roman pasticceria
Author: Rachel Roddy
Headline: A chocolate cake inspired by the Sacher hotel in Vienna’s trademark creation and emulated by a local Roman pasticceria
Content: Rachel Roddy’s not-sachertorte.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The Guardian.View image in fullscreenRachel Roddy’s not-sachertorte.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The Guardian.A kitchen in RomeCakeRachel Roddy’s recipe for a not-sachertorteA chocolate cake inspired by the Sacher hotel in Vienna’s trademark creation and emulated by a local Roman pasticceriaRachel RoddyThu 10 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis column began two years ago, almost to the day, when I made a birthday cake for a friend. “I don’t mind,” was her reply when I first asked what sort of cake she would like. But then, a few minutes later, she said: “Hang on, I mean chocolate with glossy icing. Like the mini ones they make atBarberini.”Barberini is a local bar and cake shop, and the mini cakes she was referring to are their sacher (inspired bysachertorte, of course) – chocolate sponge cakes with a heart of apricot jam and a glossy, chocolate glaze. At Barberini, each one is the size of a single draughts piece, but deep, so not quite two bites but slightly too big for one, unless you open your mouth very wide. “You mean sachertorte?” I said. “That would be great,” was her reply, before changing the subject to I can’t remember what. Walking home, I regretted asking.According to the Sacher hotelwebsite, its sachertorte (perhaps the world’s most famous cake) is still handmade using Franz Sacher’s original recipe. It also provides a recipe – a wonderful, quite complicated, anxiety-inducing recipe. It is also an approximate one, with a note in capital letters and highlighted red explaining that the original recipe must remain a tightly kept secret. I have never felt so relieved at not being given a recipe.It also meant Barberini must be approximating, so I would, too. I would approximate by using my own faithful chocolate sponge recipe, which is inspired byNigella Lawson’s faithful and tender sponge cake, filling it with my homemade peach jam and topping it with an enthusiastic attempt at the hotel’s approximate glaze recipe. I would make a not-sachertorte.“Make sure he doesn’t disgrace me tonight,” is, according to legend, what Prince Metternich said on discovering it was apprentice pastry chef Franz Sacher who was charged with making the impressive cake. I certainly worried that my glaze would be a disgrace as I poured it over the surface of the cake, both two years ago and again twice this week. My anxiety was unfounded: while not nearly as smooth as Barbarini’s (let alone the Sacher hotel’s), the results were smooth enough.The last bit of advice is from the Sacher hotel’s website, which notes that slices of sachertorte are best enjoyed with a dollop of unsweetened whipped cream. Slices of not-sachertorte are, too.Chocolate cake with peach jam and chocolate glaze – a not sachertorte recipeServes8-12200g plain flour200g caster sugar1 tsp baking powder½ tsp bicarbonate of soda40g cocoa powder175g soft unsalted butter,plus extra for greasing2 large eggs2 tsp vanilla extract150ml soured or single cream150g-200g peach or apricot jam200g caster sugar150gdark chocolate(at least 70% cocoa), choppedUnsweetened whipped cream, to serveHeat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4 and grease and line two 20cm cake tins, ideally with removable bases.Working in a large bowl, mix the flour, sugar, baking powder, bicarb and cocoa. In another bowl, beat the butter, eggs, vanilla and cream, until combined and creamy, then add to the flour bowl, beating well until smooth. (This can also be done in reverse – that is, wet first, then dry – in a food processor.)Divide the batter between the lined tins and bake for 25-35 minutes, or until a stand of spaghetti inserted into the centre comes out clean. Once out of the oven, wait 15 minutes, then invert the cakes on to a cooling rack – don’t worry about any cracks; the icing will cover that. Once the cakes are cool, sandwich them together using the jam.Next, make the glaze. Working in a small pan, heat the sugar and 125ml water, boiling hard and stirring constantly, for four minutes, until the sugar has dissolved. Take off the heat and leave cool for five minutes – this is really important – then gradually adding the chopped chocolate, stirring until it forms a thick, shiny glaze.Once the glaze is lukewarm and thick but not stiff, pour it over the cake (still on the wire rack so the glaze can drip through) and use a flat knife dipped in warm water to smooth it. Leave the glaze to set completely, then carefully transfer the cake to a plate, cut and serve with whipped cream.Explore more on these topicsCakeA kitchen in RomeFoodChocolateDessertBakingItalian food and drinkrecipesShareReuse this content

title: The start of autumn is the perfect time to turn to retro comfort food | Food | The Guardian
description: As the autumn nights draw in, I’m craving elevated classics that remind me of childhood. It’s all about fish fingers, pies, sausages and eggs – and chips with everything
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: As the autumn nights draw in, I’m craving elevated classics that remind me of childhood. It’s all about fish fingers, pies, sausages and eggs – and chips with everything
Content: Stanley Tucci’s Calabrian eggs poached in tomato sauce.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The GuardianView image in fullscreenStanley Tucci’s Calabrian eggs poached in tomato sauce.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.FeastFoodThe start of autumn is the perfect time to turn to retro comfort foodAs the colder nights draw in, I’m craving elevated classics that remind me of childhood. It’s all about fish fingers, pies, sausages and eggs – and chips with everythingSign up here for our weekly food newsletter, FeastFelicity CloakeThu 10 Sep 2026 09.17 EDTLast modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 09.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLast weekend, my family congregated at a restaurant in Edinburgh to celebrate my parents’ diamond wedding anniversary. Good though the meal was, the farewell lunch my mum prepared the next day sparked more in the way of fond reminiscence. With her retro feast of chicken kiev, oven chips and peas, we could almost have been back around our kitchen table 30 years ago (in those days, though, my mum wouldneverhave allowed the younger generation to add ketchup).It’s also the kind of meal that feels apt for the change of season, for the first weeks back at school or work, when everyone’s finding their feet and wants something easy and familiar. Thomasina Miers’fish fingers and mushy peasfit the bill, too, as does Rowley Leigh’sfish pieand Tim Hayward’s nan’scorned beef, with yet more chips and peas. If all that’s too much of a good thing,my own corned beef hashmight appeal instead? For a more specifically Scottish take on that combination, I love Colman Andrews’ idea of adding black pudding toclassic mince and tatties(Rachel Roddy’shearty cheese and chip omelette, meanwhile, would have been brilliant if we’d actually had any chips left over – time may move on, but teenagers don’t change).View image in fullscreenThomasina Miers’ fish fingers and mushy peas.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The GuardianIn the same vein, Angela Hartnett’s take onsausage and beanshas a bit more of an Italian feel than the kind we used to eat from a tin, and Rachel’s richsausage ragulooks a cut above our own 1990s spag bol; also on the Italian theme, Stanley Tucci’s father’seggs in tomato sauce(pictured top). But he and Rachel may wish to look away at the mention of Chris Russell’s1960s-style spaghetti with fried eggs; perhaps a little less authentic, but no less delicious.Although Chinese restaurants were an occasional treat, I’m not sure we ever ate fried rice at home, but Allegra McEvedy’sversatile recipefeels cut from the same simple, satisfying cloth. As does Kay Plunkett-Hogge’spad krapow mooand Meera Sodha’sbuttery mustard greens with corn roti. Likewise, though it didn’t feature in my childhood, Jacob Kenedy’s grandmother’s recipe forsauerkraut and pork bakesounds intriguing enough to become part of my adult repertoire.We had rhubarb crumble for pudding on that Sunday, but on a weekday, you might prefer a quick and easy bowl of sliced bananas and cold custard. That said, if you have more time on your hands, Ruby Tandoh has a rather fancybaked version, or you could even – whisper it – opt for a dish of butterscotch Angel Delight. Sadly, it seems we don’t have a recipe for a homemade version of the latter (though Claire Ptak’sbutterscotch creamlooks like a rather decadent substitute) – once I’ve unpacked from my trip, it might well prove a new project for a new term. Watch this space.My week in foodView image in fullscreenIce shortbread sandwiches are the cousins of the linzer cookie.Photograph: Ekaterina Smirnova/AlamyTakes the biscuit|Iced shortbread sandwiches, or empire biscuits, are rarely seen outside Scotland, despite the fact thatthese cousins of the linzer cookiewere known throughout the UK as German biscuits until the outbreak of the first world war (and continue to carry that name in Northern Ireland, or so I’m told). If they’ve been renamed once, it seems reasonable to suggest that they might be so again … In any case, I had such an enjoyable example from theBoardwalk Beach Clubat Silverknowes, in Edinburgh, that I’m determined tohave a go myself.Plum job|My icebox is full of plums, and one of the benefits of living alone is that I am quite sure no one has eaten them; in fact, I love them so much that I am miserly about their consumption. The čačanska najbolja and golden transparent gages I bought fromthe National Fruit Collection at Brogdalein Kent are too good not to eat from the hand, but the Welsh denbigh cooking variety proved delicious in an oat and plum knickerbocker recipe from Jeremy Lee’s new book,Kitchening. I’m also so tempted by the pork and plum meatballs in Ed Smith’s latestRocket & Squash newsletterthat I might seek out more punnets before they disappear for another year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFeastRecipes from all our star cooks, seasonal eating ideas and restaurant reviews. Get our best food writing every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSlop for dinner|I’m not alone in finding the uncanny imagesproliferating in food advertisingless than appetising. But I was, perhaps naively, startled to discover that AI has made its way on to our plates, too. According toa piece in the New Yorker(£), some pretty high-end restaurants are using it for inspiration, to generate “images and ideas foreign to classically trained chefs by pulling ingredient pairings and plating ideas from across the world”. Given that posters and flyers are already starting to look the same, I find this a bleak prospect for our palates.More retro delights|I was recently given 15 issues of theFanny and Johnnie Cradock Cookery Programme, “from concept to the last sprig of garnish”. Originally published in weekly parts during the early 1970s, it was found by a friend in a Suffolk charity shop. As anyone familiar with Fanny’s work might guess, the food styling is what caught her eye (sauteed pigeon breasts accessorised by wings in full feather, anyone?), but a cursory glance reveals greater treasure within, from W Somerset Maugham’s cook’s recipe for avocado ice-cream to a striking egg dish entitled L’oeuf monstrueux, or How to Show Off Very Easily. I’m looking forward to cooking my way through it, albeit selectively. In the meantime, I’m reminded of Cradock’s book Coping With Christmas, recently reissued and for which I wrote a foreword.
